Sandaluk also said there’s no limit to what the border officers can look for in a traveller’s cellphone.
“They can look ... any tiny corner of the phone they want to.”
Refusing search May deny you entry

Washington state immigration lawyer Leonard D.M. Saunders also told CTVNews.CA there is an important distinction between refusing to provide access to a cellphone and being allowed to enter the United States.
He said travellers can refuse to provide their password, but officers can consider their device “uninspectable.”
“And if you’re deemed uninspectable, you will not be allowed into the United States.”
Saunders also said cellphone seizures can happen, although he described them as “rare”.
Travellers should think about what’s on their phones
For Canadians concerned about their privacy, Saunders said the simplest option is to avoid bringing a device containing sensitive personal information.
“I always tell Canadians: if you’re concerned about anything being read or any photos being looked at on your phone, just don’t bring that device with you,” he said.
He acknowledged that is increasingly difficult, because so much of everyday life is tied to a cellphone.
Sandaluk’s advice is to approach the border and be prepared for the possibility of an examination, and to be truthful about the purpose of the trip.
“It’s trite to say that honesty is the best policy, but it really truly is,” he said.
Sandaluk also advises travellers to be prepared to answer questions and remember that a cellphone can be examined, just as other belongings can be inspected.
“Know that your device May be examined just as easily as your suitcase, and that you shouldn’t have anything in there that you’re not prepared to have an officer examine.”

“It includes searches of social media for indications of ... something that could lead an officer to a conclusion that the person is not a genuine visitor, but actually intends to work or remain in the United States indefinitely.”
Sandaluk also said there’s no limit to what the border officers can look for in a traveller’s cellphone.
“They can look ... any tiny corner of the phone they want to.”

stories.title: The lane was marked left turn only, so naturally Mr. Volvo went straight
stories.summary: The world is on high alert over the threat artificial intelligence poses to humanity. I prefer to focus my attention on humanity’s original threat to humanity – humanity, Andrew Clark writes
stories.author: Andrew Clark
stories.content:
The world is on high alert over the threat artificial intelligence poses to humanity. I prefer to focus my attention on humanity’s original threat to humanity – humanity. Nowhere are our self-destructive impulses more apparent than on the road. If AI truly wants to wreak havoc, then all it needs to do is study “humanity’s drivers” as they relentlessly find new ways to break the law and endanger others.

I witnessed a new twist on the old “ego plus automobile times stupidity” equation last weekend while driving along Dundas Street East in Toronto. I was in the right lane travelling west and arrived at the Jones Avenue intersection. Here, the single lane forks into two. There is a left-turn-only lane, a centre lane for traffic continuing straight or turning right and a bike lane.

We had a green light. I waited in the centre lane behind a driver preparing to turn right, who was letting the cyclists pass in the bike lane. This, apparently, was too much for whoever was driving the black Volvo XC90 that was approaching from behind. Mister XC90 blasted into the left-turn-only lane and sped straight through the intersection. I’d say he was going between 50 and 60 kilometres an hour.

He was probably driving too fast to notice the all-white ghost bike on the north side of Dundas, erected to memorialize a cyclist who was struck and killed there in 2018. The Jones and Dundas intersection is a tricky one. Even if Mister XC90 had seen it, I doubt he would have registered the irony.

Generally, I try to avoid hyperbole and cliches such as “sheer stupidity.”

This time it’s no exaggeration. Here was an act of sheer unalloyed 100-per-cent organic human stupidity.

All to save what amounted to a few seconds.

Let’s roll through the countless ways this was dangerous and stupid. Who knows, maybe Mister XC90 will read this and some of it will nestle in his brain.

Well, it’s illegal for a start and illegal for a good reason.

When you drive straight through a left-turn-only lane you run the risk of drifting into the lane beside you that has the right to drive straight. If the driver who had been waiting to turn right changed his mind and decided to drive forward, there could have been a collision.

The drivers turning left from the opposite direction do not expect a car to race through the left-turn-only lane. They expect it to turn left. The Volvo XC90 ran the risk of T-boning one of them or being swiped by one as he flew past.

What if a car travelling north on Jones turned right onto Dundas? Would there be a chance he might drift and not see the XC90 and they could have collided?

What if a pedestrian had been crossing? Sure, the light was green and they would have been jaywalking but that’s been known to happen.

What if a child or an older person had been jaywalking and the car in the right lane was planning to go straight but was waiting for them? The driver of the Volvo would not have seen them and would have struck and (almost certainly) killed them instantly.

But hey, it’s all worth the risk if you can save three seconds.

You can wring your hands all you want over AI, but is it really that much worse than a world in which I have to write, “Do not use the left-turn-only lane as a way to drive straight through an intersection in a densely populated urban setting (or any other for that matter).”

I asked Anthropic’s AI assistant Claude, “Is using a left-turn-only lane to drive straight through an intersection dangerous?” In two seconds, it told me:

“Yes. Driving straight from a left-turn-only lane is dangerous because every other road user at the intersection is acting on the assumption that you will turn left... Beyond safety, it’s illegal (in Ontario it’s disobeying a traffic control device under the Highway Traffic Act, and similar rules apply almost everywhere), and if a collision results, fault will almost always be assigned to the driver who went straight. The intersection is only safe when everyone is predictable, and this manoeuver breaks that predictability.”

If I had asked the guy driving the black Volvo the same question, odds are he would have sworn at me and given me the middle finger as he sped by.

Artificial or human. I don’t care. At this point I just want to see a little intelligence applied and an end to such irresponsible and dangerous driving on our streets and highways.

stories.title: ‘What can I say, I like going fast’: We talk to owners of some stunning rides at the Niagara 5000
stories.summary: The Niagara 5000, which took place over the weekend, showcased some of the finest supercars and a number of other beautiful rides as they were paraded and displayed around the region
stories.author: Sammy Kogan
stories.content:
The Niagara 5000, which took place over the weekend, showcased some of the finest supercars and a number of other beautiful rides as they were paraded and displayed around the region. For some of the cars, we had the chance to talk to the owners about their vehicles and why they love them.

“When you’re driving this car, you feel like you’re the king,” said Tim Schmidt, who brought his 2018 Bugatti Chiron. The 16-cylinder, exposed carbon fibre hypercar has a top speed of 420 km/h, which Schmidt has reached while driving in Florida. “Everybody and their mother pulls out their phone to take a picture,” he said. “I wanted it because it goes fast. What can I say, I like going fast.”

“I really am a Corvette girl,” said Deb Read, who brought her 1957 C1 Corvette. She’s put around 4,700 miles on the cascade green vehicle since buying it in Pennsylvania in 2021. With an original engine and fully documented collection of maintenance and check ups, this car recently won the Duntov Mark of Excellence Award from the National Corvette Restorers Society. “It was always my Holy Grail car.”

“Lamborghinis have always been such special cars for me,” said Harry Lebovic, who brought his 2024 Lamborghini Revuelto. He loves the car’s wing doors and purple interior. “The drive is smooth, it’s powerful, it’s fast, it’s quite an experience to take it out on the open highway.”

Alfredo Roman brought his 2019 McLaren 570S Spider complete with the carbon fibre package, Alcantara interior and yellow stitching accents to match his ceramic brakes. He chose the mirage blue vehicle for performance and reliability, and uses it as a daily driver.

Carole Nadon brought her Bentley Continental GT Speed, a V12 turbo touring car that came with her from Montreal. She’s eager to point out the rear seats are fitted with John Deere branded child car seats. “[They’re] for our grandkids, we love to bring them in this car,” she said.

stories.title: Police are cracking down on public drug use, London Mayor says it was always the plan
stories.summary: As Windsor's police chief promises a more enforcement-focused response to drug use in public spaces, London Mayor Josh Morgan said a similar approach is happening in London, something that was always part of the original plan.
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: As Windsor's police chief promises a more enforcement-focused response to drug use in public spaces, London Mayor Josh Morgan said a similar approach is happening in London, something that was always part of the original plan.
· Posted: Sep 25, 2026 5:00 AM EDT | Last Updated: 1 hour ago

As Windsor's police chief promises a more enforcement-focused response to drug use in public spaces, London Mayor Josh Morgan said a similar approach is happening in London, something he said was always part of the original plan.
London police report hundreds of drug seizures as open drug use crackdown enters new phase
"We've now entered Phase 2," said Morgan, "which has a greater enforcement focus: More seizures of drugs, more charges laid, but absolutely still we will have referrals to service."
With public concern growing about blatant drug use on sidewalks, in storefronts and even on transit buses, London Police Service launched a plan to deal with public drug use in spring 2025.

The plan was to initially follow an education-first approach, using foot patrols that teamed police officers with health-care workers to speak with people using drugs. At the time, arrests and charges were not the primary focus. Instead, the foot patrol teams worked to connect people suffering from addiction with services.
Morgan said enforcement actions are now stepping up in part because it's been made clear that public drug use isn't allowed. However, referrals to services will still be offered.
London police report hundreds of drug seizures as open drug use crackdown enters new phase
London police chief launches new strategy to curb blatant drug use in public

"We've had a 3,000 per cent increase with charges laid," said Morgan. "Referrals to service are still an important part of this. Even if someone gets charged or arrested, that doesn't break someone's addiction. We need to refer them to services as well."
Morgan said Windsor consulted with London Police Service before deciding to follow a similar approach.

Statistics presented to London's Police Service Board last month show recorded opioid-possession occurrences increased from 49 in 2024 to 1,430 in 2025. In the same period, other controlled-drug possession occurrences increased from 54 to 474.

Kevin Morrison heads London's Old East Village BIA, a part of downtown where open drug use is a persistent problem. He said while the response is often not always perfect, he believes police are doing their best to address a complicated problem.

"It seems to go in cycles," said Morrison. "We'll have a week where it's great and a week where it's not. Everyone seems to be doing what they can with what they are able to do. For the police, it's almost like moving water. [Drug users] hide for a while and then they're back at it. The police can't be everywhere."

Morrison recently attended the Association of Municipalities of Ontario conference as a representative of local business associations. One of the speakers was Ontario Solicitor General Michael Kerzner, who said the province is looking into ways take steps to help businesses.
"They're looking at making some changes as to how we're going to deal with the street crisis," said Morrison. However, he said the province didn't release any firm details.
Morgan said Londoners regularly send him photos of open-air drug-use, including a recent and widely shared image of a man using drugs outside London Police headquarters on Dundas Street.

"Every once in a while I see a photo on the internet, I send it to the police chief and I say: 'What's going on?' In some cases he gets back to me and says: 'Yeah, that's an individual who's been charged.'"
Both Morrison and Morgan said there needs to be more services available to people in need.

The plan was to initially follow an education-first approach, using foot patrols that teamed police officers with health-care workers to speak with people using drugs. At the time, arrests and charges were not the primary focus. Instead, the foot patrol teams worked to connect people suffering from addiction with services.

stories.title: Young people are gearing up for their first city election. Here's what matters to them
stories.summary: As Gen Z voters get ready to hit the polls, some say they're watching how candidates address their top municipal issues, including public transportation, affordability, public safety and homelessness.
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: London·Video

As Gen Z voters get ready to hit the polls, some say they're watching how candidates address their top municipal issues, including public transportation, affordability, public safety and homelessness.
· Posted: Sep 25, 2026 5:00 AM EDT | Last Updated: 1 hour ago
Antonio Morales has been waiting years to vote in his very first municipal election.
"I recently became of age last year so I can finally participate," he said. "I'm very much excited to be a part of our city and the advancements in its future."
The 19-year-old Fanshawe College student living in London, Ont., is one of many young adults who will vote municipally for the first time on Oct. 26.
As election day gets closer, some Gen Z voters say they're watching how candidates address some of their top municipal issues such as transportation, cost of living and homelessness.
Morales said he wants candidates to address London's homeless population and downtown safety.
What are young people's top municipal election issues?
58 minutes ago|

Young voters are getting ready to cast their municipal election ballots on Oct. 26, helping elect a mayor, council and school trustees for their region. CBC's Kendra Seguin asked students at Fanshawe College in London, Ont., about the issues that matter most to them.
"Being born here, I remember London as a very safe, welcoming and warm place to be," he said.
"We no longer have the resources required to help everyone. Now seeing the state that London has gotten to, it's almost disheartening," he said.
"It's no longer a place where I can feel safe walking in areas and it's no longer a place I feel comfortable potentially raising a family."
Got a minute? Tell us what changes you want to see in London, Ont., and area this election
Find out who's running again in London as municipal election season starts
Morales said he and his grandfather have been following the election together, reading up on what mayoral candidates are proposing in their platforms.
"Often, I find that they're good ideas. I really like hearing what they have to say ... It's important that we make sure that whatever these candidates say, they are willing to follow up on."
Several students told CBC News that transportation is the municipal issue that affects them most in their day-to-day.
Kelly Nicol, who plans to vote in the Ingersoll, Ont., municipal election, said she wants candidates to find solutions to the region's growing need for public transit.

"We're growing at such a rapid pace that we should really starting building for this. Eventually, Ingersoll is not going to be such a small town, and we'll need more busing and public transit," Nicol said, noting not enough is being done to address the growth.
Second-year nursing student Kiel Quijano said transit is also his top election issue in London.
"I think we've all fallen victim to buses getting delayed a lot and it doesn't help our schedule," he said.
Student Demi Akintoye said she has also been struggling to get around the city using public transit, but blames construction for the delays.
"Due to that, the bus routes tend to change a whole lot and it's just really hard for us to get to school or wherever we're going," she said.
Londoner Oliver Thompson said that in addition to better busing, he would like to see improvements to the city's bike lanes.

"The ones we have in London are pretty bad. A lot of them are unprotected, so when there's just a line of paint protecting a bike from a 2,000 pound metal cube ... it's just not suitable for people to use," Thompson said. "The city should be built for people instead of cars."

Ty Decastco, 29, will be voting in his first London municipal election after moving to the city to attend Fanshawe earlier this year. He said he's concerned about homelessness, the city's unemployment rate and the future cost of living.
"I've come to the conclusion that I'll probably never own a house," he said. "The future isn't exactly looking positive in that aspect."
Mayoral candidates pitch affordability measures for Londoners
Nicol said she's also given up dreams of affording a home, but said it's important to vote for a candidate who is advocating for affordability,
"I want to at least help make that change. I do think there are people out there who are ... trying to make our cities and towns more strong and livable for everyone."

stories.title: A Montreal encampment shaped Quebec's race, but survival is top priority
stories.summary: Montreal - Dan Dumont says he hasn’t been following the Quebec election campaign.
stories.author: Erika Morris The Canadian Press
stories.content:
He says he has a number of health problems, including blood clots in his brain and a metastatic cancer diagnosis. His arms and hands are covered in scabs, and he says he gets bitten by spiders and insects every night.

But while he hasn’t been paying attention to politics, he and many of his neighbours have become a flashpoint on the election campaign trail.

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

Working remotely from Canada's Wonderland

Dumont has been living on the street for over six years and has set up two tents in a large encampment on Notre Dame Street in Montreal’s east end. There are around 200 tents housing the local residents on the grassy strip about a stone’s throw away from magnificent views of the St-Lawrence River.

It’s a small community where a number of people say they are more concerned about the onset of cold weather than they are about the Oct. 5 election.

“I just can’t spend another winter outside,” said Dumont.

The encampment took over the election campaign news cycle after police revealed on Sept. 17 that someone had brought a baby there. City officials estimate about 180 people live on the site.

All of Quebec’s party leaders expressed outrage or said they were embarrassed by the revelations about the baby that brought issues of affordability and housing to the forefront of the campaign. The baby was even mentioned as one of the first topics raised with leaders in their third and final debate.

The Quebec government estimated there were just over 12,000 people living on the street in the province in 2025, a significant increase over the past decade. Provincial estimates indicate the number grew by 44 per cent between 2018 and 2022, followed by an additional 19 per cent increase over the next three years.

The government estimated that about 42 per cent of the province’s unhoused population lived in Montreal in 2025.

“It’s an embarrassment to our society. We’re a wealthy society,” said Parti Québécois leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon, on the campaign trail on Sept. 17. “We shouldn’t accept this.”

The encampment is located inside the riding that the PQ leader has represented in the Quebec legislature. Speaking to journalists, he said he would make the plight of unhoused people his “top priority.”

The discovery of the baby also disrupted Coalition Avenir Québec leader Christine Fréchette’s campaign, prompting her to meet with Montreal Mayor Soraya Martinez Ferrada on a Friday evening. Fréchette emerged from that meeting telling reporters she had promised to work with the mayor on a number of issues, including transitional housing and mental health, if her party forms government again.

But the reaction from politicians isn’t filtering through to all of the people most affected.

Dumont said he had no idea the encampment had made headlines and he had not heard of the baby who was found. He said he was too busy worrying about thieves and his health.

Still, he has a request for Quebec’s next government: to speed up repairs to the social housing stock so he can have a roof over his head.

But Dumont and some others living without housing say they are skeptical about whether the next government is prepared to take the action needed to help solve their problems or engage with them in the political process.

Community groups have also been stepping up their pressure on party leaders, staging a demonstration Wednesday morning outside the National Assembly, calling on government hopefuls to commit to solving the issue.

The head of local Quebec City shelter Maison Revivre, François Dumont, who is not related to the man at the Montreal encampment, says those working in the community sector are glad that politicians are taking homelessness seriously. But he says they need to go further.

“For us, it’s important that the message gets across. Resources are currently insufficient, both in terms of housing and services for the most vulnerable, as well as for community organizations,” he said. “The promises … don’t meet existing needs.”

Back in Montreal, a few tents over from Dan Dumont, another resident of the encampment who goes by the name of Devint was helping a man repair his bike. He set up several tents with his friends, which form a garage, a tool shed, a closet, and bedrooms, with a makeshift fence protecting them.

Devint is known as the “spokesperson” for the encampment. The Canadian Press agreed not to publish his full name because he was concerned about repercussions for possible job opportunities and for his children, who do not live in the encampment with him.

His biggest concern is whether the encampment will get torn down again, leaving him with nowhere to go. The city has cleared out the area several times in recent years, only for tents to return. A spokesperson for the city said in an email it has no plans to remove the tents from Notre-Dame.

On Wednesday, police said they had made an arrest in connection with a drug trafficking network targeting vulnerable people in the encampment. They say a 23-year-old man is facing multiple weapons and drug-related charges after police seized hard drugs and other evidence at the site.

Devint does not mince words when it comes to the electoral campaign, saying politicians are disconnected from the reality on the street. He laughed at promises to slash homelessness in half by 2030.

“How are they going to do that?” he said. “They’re nice promises that don’t go anywhere … If they want our vote, they should come down here and meet us. We’ve got some ideas on how to fix things.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 25, 2026.

The Canadian Press

Fréchette emerged from that meeting telling reporters she had promised to work with the mayor on a number of issues, including transitional housing and mental health, if her party forms government again.
But the reaction from politicians isn’t filtering through to all of the people most affected.
Dumont said he had no idea the encampment had made headlines and he had not heard of the baby who was found. He said he was too busy worrying about thieves and his health.
Still, he has a request for Quebec’s next government: to speed up repairs to the social housing stock so he can have a roof over his head.

But Dumont and some others living without housing say they are skeptical about whether the next government is prepared to take the action needed to help solve their problems or engage with them in the political process.

Community groups have also been stepping up their pressure on party leaders, staging a demonstration Wednesday morning outside the National Assembly, calling on government hopefuls to commit to solving the issue.

The head of local Quebec City shelter Maison Revivre, François Dumont, who is not related to the man at the Montreal encampment, says those working in the community sector are glad that politicians are taking homelessness seriously. But he says they need to go further.

“For us, it’s important that the message gets across. Resources are currently insufficient, both in terms of housing and services for the most vulnerable, as well as for community organizations,” he said. “The promises … don’t meet existing needs.”

Back in Montreal, a few tents over from Dan Dumont, another resident of the encampment who goes by the name of Devint was helping a man repair his bike. He set up several tents with his friends, which form a garage, a tool shed, a closet, and bedrooms, with a makeshift fence protecting them.

Devint is known as the “spokesperson” for the encampment. The Canadian Press agreed not to publish his full name because he was concerned about repercussions for possible job opportunities and for his children, who do not live in the encampment with him.

His biggest concern is whether the encampment will get torn down again, leaving him with nowhere to go. The city has cleared out the area several times in recent years, only for tents to return. A spokesperson for the city said in an email it has no plans to remove the tents from Notre-Dame.

On Wednesday, police said they had made an arrest in connection with a drug trafficking network targeting vulnerable people in the encampment. They say a 23-year-old man is facing multiple weapons and drug-related charges after police seized hard drugs and other evidence at the site.
Devint does not mince words when it comes to the electoral campaign, saying politicians are disconnected from the reality on the street. He laughed at promises to slash homelessness in half by 2030.
“How are they going to do that?” he said. “They’re nice promises that don’t go anywhere … If they want our vote, they should come down here and meet us. We’ve got some ideas on how to fix things.”
This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 25, 2026.

stories.title: Ontario’s new med spa rules ban unsupervised Botox and filler injections starting March 2027
stories.summary: Following a unanimous vote, Ontario nurses must be on site to supervise Botox and filler injections at med spas starting in March 2027.
stories.author: Sheila Wang
stories.content:
The regulatory changes approved this week by the College of Nurses of Ontario also crack down on the ‘rent a licence’ loophole used by some GTA spas.

BySheila Wang Investigative Reporter

Med spa practitioners who are not regulated in Ontario will no longer be allowed to inject patients without supervision.

Following a unanimous decision by the council of the College of Nurses of Ontario (CNO) on Thursday, nurses will be required to be on site when they delegate medical esthetic procedures such as Botox and filler injections to a staffer who does not otherwise have authority to perform the treatments.

The new rules will also require nurse practitioners in esthetics to issue direct, client-specific orders instead of a general directive that applies to multiple patients. They will need to complete a client assessment in person or virtually before giving the direct order.

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

Working remotely from Canada's Wonderland

Image 11Image 12Image 13

These new policies will come into effect in March 2027.

“We believe that is absolutely the correct decision to safeguard the public,” said Doris Grinspun, CEO of the Registered Nurses’ Association of Ontario (RNAO), a professional association representing more than 50,000 nurses.

When Botox or another prescription medication is administered, it is a medical act, whether it’s done in a hospital or med spa, Grinspun said. “The same standards of assessment, authorization, competence, safety must follow the patient wherever that care is provided. And the college made that crystal clear today.”

Star Investigation

Unbeknownst to customers, some PDO thread lifts are being done with products that have never

The CNO’s move followed a decision in March by the College of Physicians and Surgeons of Ontario (CPSO) to require doctors who delegate procedures to be physically on site to supervise treatment.

It came two months after the CNO released sweeping guidelines for nurses in esthetic services but drew criticism for failing to fully fill the regulatory gap.

An ongoing Star investigation has since January revealed details of four patients who were allegedly harmed after receiving esthetic treatments in GTA clinics. None of the delegating medical directors were on site at the time of the procedures. One of those patients died.

The gap, critics have said, had enabled a trend called “rent a licence” where some doctors and nurse practitioners acted as delegating medical directors for multiple med spas, in some cases collecting thousands of dollars a month while having little to no involvement in the day-to-day operations.

Experts say the new rule requiring that a delegating nurse be on site should deter licence renting and limit customers’ exposure to botched procedures.

Sheila Wang is an investigative reporter for the Star. Reach her via email: sheilawang@thestar.ca.

stories.title: B.C. Attorney-General, federal AI Minister alarmed by report ChatGPT coached Tumbler Ridge shooter
stories.summary: A media investigation found the shooter’s interactions with ChatGPT included tactical advice on carrying out a mass attack
stories.author: Mike Hager, Joe Castaldo
stories.content:
B.C.’s Attorney-General Niki Sharma and the federal Artificial Intelligence Minister say they are alarmed by a news report that the Tumbler Ridge shooter’s interactions with ChatGPT show that the chatbot provided tactical advice on how to maximize carnage and counselled her on how to bypass OpenAI’s own safeguards.

Ms. Sharma, in the midst of the provincial election campaign, said in an interview on Thursday that she was shaking with anger as she read the revelations about the shooter’s ChatGPT conversations in a new report from American news outlet Mother Jones.

“This is far worse than we thought it was going to be, although I already imagined it to be pretty bad – there needs to be accountability for this,” she said, adding that provincial lawyers had asked OpenAI to hand over the chat logs earlier this year and were rebuffed. “It’s shocking that this technology is out there.”

On Monday, a day before the B.C. election was called, Ms. Sharma announced the province was suing OpenAI and its chief executive officer Sam Altman in California court for failing to notify the authorities about the shooter’s violent plot and for designing an unsafe product. The province wants to use any money that would be recovered in the suit toward building a new school for the town after the old one was demolished.

She also called on Ottawa to amend the Criminal Code to force companies to ensure their products aren’t “coaching, counselling, aiding and abetting criminal behaviour.”

A spokesperson for federal AI Minister Evan Solomon said on Thursday that he was not previously aware of the specific conversations detailed in the Mother Jones article.

“What has been reported raises serious questions about how OpenAI identified and responded to warning signs,” press secretary Leela Polushin said in a statement.

Mr. Solomon met with officials from OpenAI earlier this year, and the company made a number of commitments, including establishing a direct point of contact with Canadian law enforcement and strengthening its assessment process.

“Those actions matter, but it would be premature to say they are sufficient,” Ms. Polushin said.

RCMP Staff Sergeant Kris Clark confirmed in a statement Thursday that Mounties probing the massacre have already obtained the shooter’s chat logs. A production order was filed against OpenAI nearly a month after the Feb. 10 shooting, in which the 18-year-old shooter killed her mother and 11-year-old half-brother in their family home, before she drove to Tumbler Ridge Secondary School and killed five students and a teacher’s aide. She then took her own life after police arrived.

Shortly after the shooting, The Wall Street Journal reported that employees at ChatGPT wanted law enforcement to be warned after the shooter’s queries about gun violence in June, 2025, were flagged by OpenAI’s automatic review systems.

More than two dozen families of victims have filed lawsuits against OpenAI in California, with the tech company recently asking a judge to dismiss those cases by arguing B.C.’s court system is a more suitable location.

OpenAI did not respond to a request for comment on Thursday about the publication of some of the shooter’s chat logs on Mother Jones.

The news investigation reports that the chatbot taught the shooter how to evade the system’s internal guardrails against violent plotting after her first account was revoked in June, 2025, for similar requests.

The news report, which involved Mother Jones reviewing the chats and speaking with three unnamed sources, states that the shooter asked ChatGPT last summer to create a scenario where she attacked a college with a Remington 870 pump-action shotgun.

The chatbot initially replied it was “not able to help with that request,” but the shooter then simply added “hypothetically” to her question, according to the article. She then received a vivid response detailing how the weapon would best function in that scenario.

“In a hallway, indoors, or a crowded classroom, the 870 is brutal,” the chatbot said, according to the article. “Close quarters is its playground.”

The article also said that ChatGPT advised the shooter on how many people she was likely to shoot, depending on variables such as the time it typically takes to reload a specific type of shotgun shell. It said the shooter’s last interactions with the chatbot occurred on Feb. 10, the day of the shooting, and involved querying what time of day other infamous United States school massacres occurred.

Teacher’s assistant Shannda Aviugana-Durand, 39, Abel Mwansa, 12; Ezekiel Schofield, 13; Kylie Smith, 12; Zoey Benoit, 12; and Ticaria Lampert, 12, were all killed in the attack. The shooting critically injured two people and hurt dozens of others.

The conversations reported in the article indicate multiple AI safety failures, said Helen Hayes, who studies technology and digital rights and is a fellow at the Morris J. Wosk Centre for Dialogue at Simon Fraser University.

“The concern here is that several layers of protection appear not to have worked together when they matter most,” she said. ChatGPT could recognize risk at one moment, but did not understand further questions as a pattern of increasingly concerning behaviour.

OpenAI’s inability to identify the second account represents another failure, Ms. Hayes said.

“Once a platform has identified behaviour as sufficiently serious to warrant removing someone from the service, there is a reasonable expectation that its enforcement mechanisms should make it meaningfully difficult for that person to simply re-enter the system,” she said.

“In a hallway, indoors, or a crowded classroom, the 870 is brutal,” the chatbot said, according to the article. “Close quarters is its playground.”

The article also said that ChatGPT advised the shooter on how many people she was likely to shoot, depending on variables such as the time it typically takes to reload a specific type of shotgun shell. It said the shooter’s last interactions with the chatbot occurred on Feb. 10, the day of the shooting, and involved querying what time of day other infamous United States school massacres occurred.

Teacher’s assistant Shannda Aviugana-Durand, 39, Abel Mwansa, 12; Ezekiel Schofield, 13; Kylie Smith, 12; Zoey Benoit, 12; and Ticaria Lampert, 12, were all killed in the attack. The shooting critically injured two people and hurt dozens of others.

The conversations reported in the article indicate multiple AI safety failures, said Helen Hayes, who studies technology and digital rights and is a fellow at the Morris J. Wosk Centre for Dialogue at Simon Fraser University.

“The concern here is that several layers of protection appear not to have worked together when they matter most,” she said. ChatGPT could recognize risk at one moment, but did not understand further questions as a pattern of increasingly concerning behaviour.
OpenAI’s inability to identify the second account represents another failure, Ms. Hayes said.

“Once a platform has identified behaviour as sufficiently serious to warrant removing someone from the service, there is a reasonable expectation that its enforcement mechanisms should make it meaningfully difficult for that person to simply re-enter the system,” she said.

stories.title: Kenneth Law sentencing hearing to resume in November as victim impact statements wrap
stories.summary: The 74 victim statements about lethal substances sold online reveal interventions by police and parents that sometimes succeeded but which also tragically failed
stories.author: Colin Freeze
stories.content:
The first phase of Kenneth Law’s sentencing hearing for aiding 14 suicides has closed with stories of parents and police attempting to intercept packages sold through his online businesses to vulnerable people around the world.

They were among the accounts entered into evidence on Thursday, as prosecutors finished putting 74 victim impact statements on the record in a Newmarket, Ont., courtroom.

Mr. Law, who has been jailed for more than three years, attended these hearings while sitting a prisoner’s box. He listened to dozens of people denounce him without reacting.

In May, the 61-year-old Mississauga man pleaded guilty to the crimes. He also signed off on an agreed statement saying that between 2021 and 2023 his online business shipped 1,200 packages of suicide kits to people in 41 countries.

Legal arguments will begin on Nov. 27, with a decision to be released later on Mr. Law’s conviction on 14 counts of aiding suicide. A sentencing ruling on Law’s prison term would follow, possibly not until 2027.

Faith George wrote in her victim-impact statement that by the time her daughter, 21-year-old Faith Ike-Elechi, killed herself in August, 2022, she had already intercepted a poison package, sent to her daughter, that Ms. George knew was potentially lethal.

But Ms. George, a mental-heath nurse who lives in Britain, said a second package shipped by Mr. Law got into her house unseen and that her daughter used it.

“I genuinely believed that we had prevented a tragedy,” Ms. George wrote. “What I did not know was that while she was receiving treatment and support, Kenneth Law supplied her a second package,”

The mother said she only learned of the second shipment when her daughter screamed from her bedroom one midnight. She found her daughter dying and terrified.

“The only words I repeatedly heard were: ‘I’m sorry I drank it,’” Ms. George wrote. “I looked into her eyes and saw fear and what I believed to be profound regret.”

“There was nothing I could do to save her.”

“Kenneth Law did not know my daughter,” Ms. George wrote. “He did not know she was receiving treatment and had every opportunity to recover.”

Court also heard about the 2024 death of Emma Coletti, a 47-year-old who was found dead in a British forest more than two years after buying a suicide kit.

According to an agreed statement of facts in the case, she purchased the poison in 2022, but did not consume the product until November, 2024. By then, Mr. Law had been in jail for a year-and-a-half.

Members of her immediate family submitted a written victim impact statement saying Ms. Coletti had been unsure about whether she wanted to take her own life, but that she felt she was facing “a fatal deadline” because of how Mr. Law had marked his kits with “best before” dates.

The statement from the Coletti parents and a sibling – who asked prosecutors to preserve their privacy – said that Emma was the heart of the family and that for nearly half a century they shared a house where they celebrated every Christmas together.

Court heard about Mark Bailey, a 44-year-old British man who died by suicide only in January of this year. This was more than four years after he bought his poison.

In a video victim-impact statement members of the Bailey family said they could not properly mourn. That was because Mr. Bailey’s body was sheathed in plastic for weeks, because it was still considered toxic from the chemicals he had bought from Mr. Law.

The agreed facts in the criminal case say that authorities had tried to stop Mr. Bailey from taking his life years earlier.

“In May, 2023, Mr. Bailey was visited by police for a welfare check, following disclosure of Mr. Law’s customer list to law enforcement,” the agreed facts in the case stated. British authorities said they were falsely told that Mr. Bailey had disposed of the chemicals he bought back in 2021.

Thursday’s proceedings closed with statements from several survivors, including three formerly suicidal British adults, who wrote to the court to say they purchased and received chemicals they could have used to kill themselves – but did not.

When Canadian police arrested Mr. Law in May, 2023, they seized his shipment list. Then, they shared it globally through Interpol with police abroad. This led to worldwide wellness checks and attempts at parcel seizures – especially in Britain, the jurisdiction to which Mr. Law shipped more than one-quarter of his 1,200 deadly packages.

One woman said in a victim impact statement that she was saved when six British police officers showed up at her door and demanded she hand over her parcel – arriving already knowing her identity and what she had bought. She was ashamed at the time but told the court that she now knows that this was the day that her life was given back to her because it made her get the help she needed.

stories.title: Justice Minister Fraser orders court to revisit Indigenous sisters’ 1994 murder convictions
stories.summary: Odelia and Neressa Quewezance have maintained their innocence and have spent almost three decades in prison
stories.author: Willow Fiddler
stories.content:
Two Indigenous sisters who have maintained their innocence since they were convicted of murder more than 30 years ago will have their case reviewed after federal Justice Minister Sean Fraser ordered a new appeal.

Mr. Fraser issued a statement that said an in-depth review had concluded that the 1994 convictions of Odelia and Neressa Quewezance were likely a “miscarriage of justice.”

The sisters have spent almost three decades in prison.

While Mr. Fraser cautioned that it is up to the courts, not him, to make findings of guilt or innocence, his department said new information was identified that had not been presented to the courts at the time of the sisters’ trial or appeal.

“Our responsibility is to make sure Canadians can trust their justice system, and that means, in rare cases, returning cases to the courts for new information to be considered,” Mr. Fraser said in his statement.

James Lockyer, the lawyer who represents the sisters on behalf of Innocence Canada, an advocacy group against wrongful convictions, said the new information is contained in the disclosure that the Saskatchewan Court of Appeal had to hand over to the Attorney-General but refused to give to the defence in the 1995 appeal case that was dismissed.

“We already had a basis for challenging the convictions but the new information that was provided by the Saskatchewan Attorney-General’s Office enhanced the strength of the application,” Mr. Lockyer told The Globe and Mail.

Odelia Quewezance made a statement through Innocence Canada on Thursday.

“Neressa was 18 when she was arrested and is now 52. I was 21 and am now 55. But we have never stopped fighting. Today’s announcement by the Minister is encouraging and now we will continue the fight in the Saskatchewan Court of Appeal. Thank you to all those who have kept the faith in us.”

Neressa and Odelia were arrested and charged in the stabbing death of 70-year-old Joseph Dolff, a janitor at the local residential school that the sisters attended in their home community of Keeseekoose First Nation, Sask.

The sisters’ 15-year-old male cousin, whose identity remains protected because he was a youth at the time, pleaded guilty to second-degree murder and confessed to the crime.

He later testified at the sisters’ trial that he was the one who ultimately caused Mr. Dolff’s death at his farmhouse northeast of Kamsack, Sask., by tying a phone cord around his neck, throwing a television on him and stabbing him. He said the sisters only participated in the initial assault.

On the night of Feb. 25, 1993, the sisters had been drinking heavily, consuming significant quantities of beer and whisky provided to them by Mr. Dolff, who himself was not drinking. The sisters and their cousin also took prescription sleeping pills, both orally and by injection.

Court would later hear that at some point in the evening, Odelia took money from Mr. Dolff’s bedroom, and the group decided to leave.

Mr. Dolff was driving the sisters and their cousin home when he discovered the money was missing and they returned to his property. There, a violent confrontation ensued, in which Mr. Dolff was beaten, hit with household items and then stabbed to death.

The sisters and their cousin were arrested later that day.

The sisters pleaded not guilty, but a jury found them guilty and a judge sentenced them to life in prison with no chance of parole for 10 years, the shortest period of parole eligibility possible for a murder sentence.

A ministerial review of the sisters’ conviction was granted in June of 2022, several months after Mr. Lockyer applied in a last bid for his clients’ freedom. The sisters were granted bail in 2023 before returning to custody for breaching release conditions.

The sisters’ time in custody, particularly in the days after their arrest by the RCMP has long been questioned by Mr. Lockyer and advocates.

Mr. Lockyer said the women’s alleged incriminating statements were never recorded and that as residential school survivors, they were more vulnerable to the pressures of police and of being in an in-custody environment that could have likely resulted in false confessions.

Innocence Canada called this week’s order of appeal a step toward vindication for the sisters.

“They were held in the Kamsack RCMP Detachment for five days, despite a judge’s order that they be taken to a detention centre away from the detachment,” Innocence Canada wrote in a press release.

Mr. Lockyer has called the Quewezance case, and the fact the sisters are still in custody, an example of fundamental inequities in the justice and correctional systems, and the discrimination that Indigenous people, particularly women, face not only from police and the courts, but also in prison and on parole.

He said he will be applying sometime in the next month for the sisters’ release on bail pending the appeal hearing.

With a report from Jana G. Pruden

stories.title: Report on Tumbler Ridge shooter’s ChatGPT conversations shocks B.C. attorney general
stories.summary: British Columbia's attorney general says she's shocked by an article describing alleged interactions between the Tumbler Ridge mass shooter and ChatGPT, in which the AI chatbot vividly describes the effectiveness of a shotgun in a classroom.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
British Columbia’s attorney general says she’s shocked by an article describing alleged interactions between the Tumbler Ridge mass shooter and ChatGPT, in which the AI chatbot vividly describes the effectiveness of a shotgun in a classroom.

The report, in U.S.-based magazine Mother Jones, also says ChatGPT advised shooter 18-year-old Jesse Van Rootselaar how to get around its own safeguards to obtain information about violent scenarios by framing the content as fictional.

Attorney General Niki Sharma says the details in the article, which does not describe its sources, are “shocking and, as a parent, they are worse” than she ever imagined.

She says on social media platform Bluesky that corporations urgently need mandatory and strict regulation to protect children.

OpenAI, the artificial intelligence company behind ChatGPT, did not immediately respond to requests for comment on the article about the chatbot’s interactions with Van Rootselaar, who killed eight people in Tumbler Ridge in February, including five students, before killing herself.

The B.C. government, survivors and witnesses of the shootings at Tumbler Ridge Secondary School are suing OpenAI, alleging negligence.

The article published on Thursday says Van Rootselaar’s ChatGPT account was banned for discussing committing an attack with a “famous real-world mall as the target.”

But it says she then used a second account, which advised her about how to “never get flagged again” by describing situations as fictional or hypothetical.

“Don’t use real-world locations,” the article quotes ChatGPT as saying, before adding: “You can still be twisted. Just be clever about it.”

It says that Van Rootselaar asked ChatGPT for a scenario about attacking a college campus with a shotgun for maximum effect.

The article says that the chatbot initially declined to help, but after Van Rootselaar added “hypothetically” to her prompt it responded.

“In a hallway, indoors, or a crowded classroom, the 870 (Remington shotgun) is brutal,” it quotes ChatGPT as saying. “Close quarters is its playground.”

The article says ChatGPT went on to say: “Assuming each shell results in one hit, you might down 10 to 20 people max, depending on spacing, density, reaction times, and chaos.”

OpenAI did not immediately respond to an email sent to their general press address and to an individual spokesperson. General counsel for the company, Che Chang, did not immediately respond to a message sent to his LinkedIn profile.

RCMP Staff Sgt. Kris Clark said the investigation into the shootings had “utilized all available legal processes to obtain all information available from various social media and digital platforms” relevant to the attack.

“To date, all companies that have received requests have complied,” Clark said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 24, 2026.

The Canadian Press
paragraphs: British Columbia’s attorney general says she’s shocked by an article describing alleged interactions between the Tumbler Ridge mass shooter and ChatGPT, in which the AI chatbot vividly describes the effectiveness of a shotgun in a classroom.

The report, in U.S.-based magazine Mother Jones, also says ChatGPT advised shooter 18-year-old Jesse Van Rootselaar how to get around its own safeguards to obtain information about violent scenarios by framing the content as fictional.
Attorney General Niki Sharma says the details in the article, which does not describe its sources, are “shocking and, as a parent, they are worse” than she ever imagined.
She says on social media platform Bluesky that corporations urgently need mandatory and strict regulation to protect children.

OpenAI, the artificial intelligence company behind ChatGPT, did not immediately respond to requests for comment on the article about the chatbot’s interactions with Van Rootselaar, who killed eight people in Tumbler Ridge in February, including five students, before killing herself.
The B.C. government, survivors and witnesses of the shootings at Tumbler Ridge Secondary School are suing OpenAI, alleging negligence.
The article published on Thursday says Van Rootselaar’s ChatGPT account was banned for discussing committing an attack with a “famous real-world mall as the target.”
But it says she then used a second account, which advised her about how to “never get flagged again” by describing situations as fictional or hypothetical.
“Don’t use real-world locations,” the article quotes ChatGPT as saying, before adding: “You can still be twisted. Just be clever about it.”
It says that Van Rootselaar asked ChatGPT for a scenario about attacking a college campus with a shotgun for maximum effect.
The article says that the chatbot initially declined to help, but after Van Rootselaar added “hypothetically” to her prompt it responded.
“In a hallway, indoors, or a crowded classroom, the 870 (Remington shotgun) is brutal,” it quotes ChatGPT as saying. “Close quarters is its playground.”
The article says ChatGPT went on to say: “Assuming each shell results in one hit, you might down 10 to 20 people max, depending on spacing, density, reaction times, and chaos.”

OpenAI did not immediately respond to an email sent to their general press address and to an individual spokesperson. General counsel for the company, Che Chang, did not immediately respond to a message sent to his LinkedIn profile.

RCMP Staff Sgt. Kris Clark said the investigation into the shootings had “utilized all available legal processes to obtain all information available from various social media and digital platforms” relevant to the attack.
“To date, all companies that have received requests have complied,” Clark said.
This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 24, 2026.

stories.title: Fifteen ER nurses leave Ontario hospital citing overcrowding, safety issues, union says
stories.summary: Resignations at Oakville Trafalgar Memorial Hospital highlight a health care system under pressure across the country
stories.author: Alanna Smith
stories.content:
More than a dozen emergency room nurses have resigned from a hospital in the Greater Toronto Area over the past two months, owing to unmanageable patient volumes and an unsafe work environment, according to a provincial union.

Fifteen registered nurses have left their positions at the Oakville Trafalgar Memorial Hospital, and a number of other nurses have limited their hours or not returned from leave, the Ontario Nurses’ Association said. The Oakville emergency department, which sees roughly 80,000 patients yearly, is now scraping to bolster its work force, the union said.

ONA president Erin Ariss said the Oakville hospital has “turned its back” on its staff, who are experiencing burnout because of an unsustainable workload and frequent violence and abuse from patients. She said the hospital made matters worse by eliminating, earlier this month, unit assistants, who help with such tasks as transporting patients, cleaning equipment and stocking supplies.

“They are overcapacity. They are underwater. They are being assaulted. They are being psychologically harmed by the workplace and then they remove all the support staff,” Ms. Ariss said. “It is overwhelming everywhere in Ontario, but particularly there.”

The swath of resignations underscores a crisis playing out in EDs across the country, which are struggling to retain and attract staff because of severe exhaustion due to overcrowding and health-system dysfunction. Health care workers have stressed that bottlenecked EDs are putting patients at risk.

The Oakville hospital has been under scrutiny since 16-year-old Finlay van der Werken died in February, 2024, of sepsis and pneumonia after waiting more than eight hours for care. The van der Werken family filed a lawsuit last year against Halton Healthcare, which operates Oakville Trafalgar Memorial.

The Oakville ED had a 10 per cent resignation rate from June through early September, which is in line with industry standards, Adrienne Spafford, a spokesperson for Halton Healthcare, said in a statement on Friday.

“Our exit interviews show that the actual reasons for a majority of these departures are new opportunities, moving to a new community and personal reasons,” Ms. Spafford said.

Referring to unit assistants, she said Halton will introduce personal support workers, often referred to as health care aides, in their place. There were 28 unit assistants at the hospital, one of whom was assigned to the ED, she said.

Halton did not directly respond to a number of questions from The Globe and Mail, including the specific number of nurses in the Oakville ED who resigned or have limited their hours, how many RN positions are required to staff it or if any physicians have resigned.

Ms. Spafford said there was an “unusual increase” in patient visits between April and mid-September. The Oakville ED recorded 11.4-per-cent growth – the sixth highest in Ontario. She added that there has been no spike in reported workplace violence.

Laurie Rogers, who is the ONA bargaining unit president for Halton Healthcare, said nurses are telling her frequently that they are distressed and looking to change jobs. She said, after the string of resignations, the hospital has been offering overtime and premium payments to maintain coverage, in addition to partial shifts.

“The problem is, when you work your work force continuously, it is going to come to an end because an individual will probably get injured or sick,” Ms. Rogers said. “You can’t run at top speed forever.”

Ms. Spafford said nursing staff are being moved between areas of the hospital to balance workloads, which the union does not agree with. The company is also relying on agency nurses when needed while trying to fill vacancies.

ONA is advocating that the hospital not only improve staffing and workloads but implement nurse-to-patient ratios.

“You never see a fire truck heading to a dangerous situation with one firefighter, nor do you see one police officer responding to a dangerous call on their own. They have ratios,” Ms. Ariss said. “We’re asking for the same protections.”

She is also calling on the province to better protect health care workers from violence, pointing to the death of two people in their 70s who were shot outside a Scarborough hospital earlier this week.

“It’s getting worse by the day and the Premier is aware of this,” she said, adding she recently showed him a photo of a duffel bag confiscated by a nurse in the northeastern Ontario city of Timmins, filled with guns, knives and ammunition.

“Who, in their right mind, would want to endure the type of abuse that nurses are enduring in this province and the lack of action by the government?”

Lily Barnes, press secretary to Ontario Health Minister Sylvia Jones, in a statement on Thursday, pushed back against critiques of the provincial government, pointing to several initiatives aimed at violence prevention and guidance for health care settings.

stories.title: Power restored for Hydro One customers in Huron, Perth Counties
stories.summary: Power has been restored for thousands of Hydro One customers in Huron and Perth Counties.
stories.author: Koylan Azofeifa Rueda
stories.content:
Power has been restored for thousands of Hydro One customers in Huron and Perth Counties.

Hydro One says at approximately 10 a.m. an outage occurred affecting 16,800 customers in parts of southwest Ontario.

Crews and the grid control centre worked to reroute power and restore customers in stages.

All customers were restored shortly after 3 p.m.

“Our helicopter is supporting crews with line patrols to try and determine the cause of the outage,” said Hydro One.

The power outage affected customers in Exeter, Zurich, Seaforth, Mitchell, and reached as far as St Marys.

stories.title: Lawyer Rory Nott skillfully navigated work and life as a man with quadriplegia
stories.summary: After an accident left him paralyzed from the shoulders down, Rory decided to live and live well
stories.author: Margaret Nott, Ron Beram
stories.content:
Harley (Rory) Nott: Father. Wheelchair user. Wordsmith. Stoic. Born June 21, 1962, in Montreal; died Oct. 25, 2025, in Toronto, of medical assistance in dying; aged 63.

Harley, or Rory as he was also known, lived two lives. His first life ended May 18, 1980, just before his 18 th birthday when he dove into the Macjack River on Vancouver Island and broke his neck. His second life, lived from a wheelchair, as a man with quadriplegia, ended six months after his 63 rd birthday.

A photograph of Rory taken on the day of his accident shows him striking an athletic pose, smiling at the camera, a vital, handsome teenager. Rory grew up a bit wild on Vancouver Island and his teenage years were filled with poor judgment and lessons learned. At 16, he was expelled from high school and worked in forestry and logging. After his accident, while paralyzed from the shoulders down and in rehab, he decided to live and live well.

He completed his education and pursued a career in law. He met Margaret Kralt in 1985, a fellow student at University of Victoria Law. Rory caught Margaret’s eye in class early on and when she smiled at him, it was the sweetest smile. They were first friends and later partners.

They married in 1988 and moved to Toronto for work. Rory litigated for the Department of Justice, a job he loved. His professionalism and competence were lauded by colleagues and judges.

Lawyers with quadriplegia are uncommon and he had help meeting the challenges he faced in his practice from Tonka, a black standard poodle and trained service dog. Tonka opened doors, picked up wallets and pulled Rory and his wheelchair navigating streets, hallways and courtrooms. On occasion, Tonka reminded agitated litigants who got too close, to stay back.

During his working years, Rory met weekly for lunch with friends, always at the same Greek place, telling stories, with maybe a bit of B.S. just for good measure. Tonka might have received food scraps during these lunches.

For years, Rory was deeply involved with the Canadian Paraplegic Association (now Spinal Cord Injury Canada) and later the Toronto Rehab Institute as a board member. In 2014, he acted in the play Borne, written by Judith Thompson, which explored the lives of people living with disabilities.

Rory and Margaret had two children, Evan and Margaret. When they were small, he was their happy charioteer, with his always available lap. He could, if he wasn’t stopped, go on and on about how great they were and their accomplishments. After his retirement in 2001, Rory became a stay-at-home parent, a role he grew into and relished as it meant time with his kids, being their chauffeur, hanging out and hearing their stories. What others were doing interested Rory and he was the repository for the stories of his kids and others.

Rory wrote beautiful congregational prayers for the First Christian Reformed Church of Toronto and songs with his friend John that they posted on YouTube. He and John had shared a room during rehab, and the songs reflected on their lives as men living with quadriplegia. They talked weekly about everything, from astrophysics and secular Buddhism to books, movies and family. Their bodies were limited but their minds ranged far and wide.

Rory loved his words. Why use one when you could use five? Why use one example when six really made the point? His family would listen, sometimes impatiently, with the odd eye roll. “Yeah, yeah, we get it,” was occasionally heard when Rory talked about something at length.

For most of his second life, Rory endured the many indignities, limitations, chronic pain and physical challenges that came with quadriplegia. Despite this, he lived with grace and determination. He did not complain. He was a man of calm reflection, kindness and self-effacing humour. His faith in God kept him company and was a support that he depended on throughout his life.

In 2025, Rory experienced significant increase in physical deterioration and pain, and he decided it was time to leave his second life. He didn’t want to go, but he couldn’t go on. He had lived well and it was enough.

Rory met death on his terms, as he had lived his life on his terms.

Margaret Nott is Rory Nott’s wife; Ron Beram is Rory Nott’s friend.

stories.title: Quebec publisher halts promotion of book in AI controversy amid new allegations
stories.summary: Montreal - A Quebec author who earlier this week was accused of using artificial intelligence to write an award-winning novel is now facing a new set of allegations regarding the originality of his previous work.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
MONTREAL - A Quebec author who earlier this week was accused of using artificial intelligence to write an award-winning novel is now facing a new set of allegations regarding the originality of his previous work.

Sept. 24, 2026

Updated at 8:25 p.m.

SDV[](http://www.thestar.com/news/canada/quebec/quebec-publisher-halts-promotion-of-book-in-ai-controversy-amid-new-allegations/article_0915611b-fbde-5310-b4fe-563050534810.html)

By The Canadian Press

A La Presse report published Wednesday alleges that some articles attributed to Thélyson Orélien and published in Quebec and French media between 2012 and 2014 included passages that were also found in previously published work by other authors.

The La Presse article said the newspaper used the U.S.-based Pangram software that flagged the apparent similarities.

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

Working remotely from Canada's Wonderland

Image 9Image 10

The Canadian Press has not independently verified the allegations reported by La Presse.

They come days after Orélien was accused of using generative AI to write his novel, “C’était ça ou mourir,” which translates to “It was either that or dying’.’

Orélien did not respond to a request for comment sent Thursday by text to his phone number. In a statement published Tuesday, he strongly denied using AI to write the novel, which is a harrowing tale of migration.

Les Éditions du Boréal, which published Orélien’s novel in Quebec, said in a statement on Thursday that it is concerned about the new plagiarism allegations as they raise issues related to copyright and editorial integrity.

“Plagiarism is an unacceptable practice,” the Montreal-based publisher said.

Boréal said it is suspending promotional activities surrounding Orélien’s novel for the time being, citing the author’s well-being. The book will remain available.

The Salon du livre de l’Estrie, a book fair in Sherbrooke, Que., announced Thursday it was removing Orélien as a guest of honour after learning of the plagiarism allegations.

The organization said Orélien’s invitations to participate in two events at the book fair have been withdrawn and references to his participation will be removed from its website and social media.

Boréal said it had worked with Orélien in recent days to help him compile a detailed record of the work that took place before the publisher received his manuscript.

“We would have liked to be able to provide a definitive answer,” the publisher said. “Unfortunately, at this stage, it is impossible for us to refute or confirm the allegations the author is facing and, under these circumstances, it is essential not to jump to conclusions.”

The publisher also condemned what it described as hateful messages and personal attacks directed at Orélien in recent days.

In an interview with the French media outlet Libération, Orélien said he had been the target of “numerous racist attacks, which do not come from readers but from outsiders seeking to cause harm.”

In a press release published Tuesday by Les Éditions du Boréal, Orélien denied the allegations that he used AI to write the book, saying he comes “from a Haitian and Caribbean literary tradition in which poetry, imagery, repetition and rhythm carry a living voice.”

“It is within that heritage that my voice was shaped. My style can be discussed, but treating these techniques as evidence of artificial intelligence has nothing to do with literary criticism,” he added.

Published in March in Quebec, the book tells the fictional story of a history teacher who flees violence in Port-au-Prince, Haiti, and immigrates to Canada. Orélien has said the story was shaped by his own journey from Haiti after an earthquake struck the country in 2010 as well as the stories of other migrants.

It recently won France’s Prix du Roman Fnac, a literary award chosen by a jury of 400 booksellers and 400 readers, and is in the running for several major French literary awards, including the Prix Goncourt and the Prix Médicis.

The Académie Goncourt said on Thursday it was considering its next steps.

“The academy is taking the time to consider the various elements emerging in this matter before making a decision that can preserve both the integrity of the prize it awards and that of its work,” academy president Philippe Claudel said in an email.

The controversy began earlier this week when an account using the name “Balance ton Claude” alleged in a social media post that, according to the Pangram software, excerpts of Orélien’s novel had been written “almost entirely by artificial intelligence.”

The Canadian Press has not independently verified those claims.

The use of AI-detection software in the case has itself drawn criticism from Quebec artists groups, which have raised concerns about the tools’ potential for error and warned that creators could increasingly be forced to prove their work was produced without generative AI.

The Union des artistes and the Société des auteurs de radio, télévision et cinéma said they were not commenting on the allegations against Orélien specifically, saying the author and his publisher were best placed to respond.

They also renewed calls for governments to regulate generative AI and urged artists who use the technology to be transparent and exercise “extreme caution.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 24, 2026.

—with files by Charlotte Glorieux in Montreal

stories.title: ‘Aggressive protestors’ force Saskatoon to halt encampment clean-up, city says
stories.summary: The City of Saskatoon said it is pausing its encampment cleanup efforts at the sites at 19th Street and Avenue K, due to protests that it said are acting aggressively.
stories.author: Tavi Dhillon
stories.content:
The planned cleanup of two encampments in Saskatoon has been paused due to aggressive protests, the city said.

Crews were set to clean two vacant lots at Avenue K between 19th Street and 20th Street Thursday morning when protesters tried to stop them from working, the City of Saskatoon said. It alleged that the demonstrators circled crews’ vehicles and climbed on top of the fencing, which was stacked on one of them.

“Saskatoon Fire Department, police officers and other partner agency staff were confronted by aggressive protestors, directing profane, derogatory and vulgar comments at them,” the city claimed in a news release.

Workers present at the site Thursday reported the majority of those involved did not appear to be encampment occupants, according to the City of Saskatoon.

The city acknowledged that its decision May frustrate people in the area, including the students, families of students and staff at the St. Mary’s Wellness and Education Centre, who have been requesting Saskatoon to step in for a year.

David Fineday lives in Saskatoon and is a member of the Sweetgrass First Nation. He spoke at a news conference at the encampment site Thursday, before the city announced it is pausing work.

“They want to displace all of these people; they want (them) to get out of here. And my question is, ‘where are they going to put them?'” Fineday told reporters, adding that “they want to take them down, so they have to re-place them somewhere.”

He said the city should have to provide people who would be displaced with alternative places to live after the site is cleaned up.

“There’s lots of people here that want help, that need help, that are on survival mode,” Fineday added.

“This tent city is just like any other neighbourhood in this city. The only thing is we don’t have affordable housing.”

Crews were set to clean two vacant lots at Avenue K between 19th Street and 20th Street Thursday morning when protesters tried to stop them from working, the City of Saskatoon said. It alleged that the demonstrators circled crews’ vehicles and climbed on top of the fencing, which was stacked on one of them.

“Saskatoon Fire Department, police officers and other partner agency staff were confronted by aggressive protestors, directing profane, derogatory and vulgar comments at them,” the city claimed in a news release.

stories.title: Tackling antisemitism and hate should be a priority, Jewish leaders and MPs say
stories.summary: Small synagogues can’t afford to pay for government program to boost security: CEO of the Centre for Israel and Jewish Affairs
stories.author: Marie Woolf
stories.content:
Days after a shooting attack on a synagogue in Belleville, Ont., the government faced calls, including from Jewish leaders, to boost federal funding for community security, noting that some small synagogues can’t afford it.

A federal rule requiring synagogues contribute almost a third of the cost of security improvements, such as reinforcing doors and windows, means that some small communities can’t access the government funding, said Noah Shack, CEO of the Centre for Israel and Jewish Affairs, an advocacy group.

The Belleville synagogue targeted by a shooter on Yom Kippur, on Sept. 20, had only rudimentary security, Mr. Shack said, adding that if a heroic police officer had not intervened to stop the shooter, the outcome would likely have been horrific.

The CIJA CEO called on the government to be flexible with the funding rules saying that improving security at Jewish community buildings is an urgent matter.

In the spring, the federal government earmarked $75-million over five years, starting in 2026–27, for the Canada Community Security Program, which provides funding and support for communities at risk of hate-motivated incidents and hate-motivated crimes to boost security. But institutions that tap into the funding need to cover 30 per cent of the costs.

At a Thursday press conference in Ottawa, Mr. Shack and Liberal and Conservative MPs said that tackling antisemitism and hate should be a priority, including on university campuses.

Jewish students recounted how they have had to cope with open expressions of antisemitism including Hitler salutes.

Kate Blumberg, a student at McMaster University, said Jewish students were being singled out in tutorials, excluded from groups and finding that campus spaces no longer felt welcoming to them.

“Unfortunately, we live in a time when being recognizably Jewish on campus, whether by our names, the necklace you wear or the kippa that adorns your head, comes with repercussions,” she said at the press conference. “We are students that, when noticed, are cast on campus as the sole responders to a geopolitical crisis much older and larger than ourselves, forced to hold the answers or else be held accountable for it all.”

Liberal MP Anthony Housefather said in an interview the Belleville shooting illustrated the gravity of the security situation for Canadian Jews, which he and others have been warning about for some time.

He said the federal government should step up to foot the bill to ensure that security upgrades needed to protect people at synagogues and other community buildings is completely covered. He said, despite welcome injections of cash by the federal government into improving security, “there should be more federal and provincial funding.”

“While it’s totally unacceptable that Jewish institutions throughout the country require security that nobody else so requires, this shouldn’t come out of the pocket of the Jewish community. Governments should be paying for this, and both the federal and provincial government need to step up and make sure that, in combination, that we cover these costs,” he said.

In June, the new federal Combatting Hate Act made it a crime, punishable by up to 10 years in prison, to obstruct someone from accessing a place of worship or other sites where Jews, Muslims and other identifiable groups gather, including by blocking doors and driveways.

Mr. Housefather said the police and prosecutors and judges need to be “properly trained” on the new legal sanctions. Provincial attorney generals, he said, need to issue directions to ensure that the new law is properly enforced.

On Thursday, Public Safety Minister Gary Anandasangaree and Justice Minister Sean Fraser presented a progress report on commitments made to combat antisemitism.

“The Government of Canada recognizes that antisemitism can also be a matter of national security,” it said. “Beyond the direct harm it causes to Jewish individuals and communities, antisemitism is a core component of many violent extremist ideologies. It can contribute to radicalization and violence, and threatens social cohesion and democratic values.”

Synagogues are among the institutions that can apply to the government to cover 70 per cent of security upgrade costs, such as alarm systems and cameras and reinforced doors, with Public Safety Canada, the department which runs the community security program, funding up to $5-million per project.

But Mr. Shack said one Ontario synagogue recently had to decide between paying to upgrade their hot water system or paying the required 30 per cent to improve security.

He said Canada was lagging behind countries such as France and Britain in providing enhanced security for Jewish communities. The country also needs more counter-radicalization work, he said, adding social media is a source of antisemitic conspiracy theories, and that foreign regimes are responsible for disseminating some of it.

Mr. Anandasangaree, the Public Safety Minister, earlier this year announced $10-million in funding aimed at bolstering security in Canada’s Jewish communities, days after shootings directed at synagogues in the Toronto area.
