stories.title: Nova Scotia government spent nearly $2-billion outside of budget
stories.summary: Province closed 2025-26 fiscal year with record-high deficit of $1.4-billion, Finance Minister says
stories.author: Lyndsay Armstrong
stories.content:
The Nova Scotia government says it spent a record $1.9-billion more than what the provincial legislature had approved for the 2025-26 fiscal year.

Finance Minister John Lohr said there are plenty of reasons why the Progressive Conservative government spent so much money on what the government describes as additional appropriations.

“We need to be flexible as a government, and we will continue to do that,” he said during a news conference Thursday.

Additional appropriations refer to extra spending that is not included in the budget, but is approved by cabinet without a vote in the legislature.

The province’s auditor general has repeatedly called for stronger oversight on how the government spends money not included in the budget.

Lohr said much of the additional spending in the most recent fiscal year went to health care services and seniors.

The government also used some of that additional funding to cover the $40.4-million cost of public works projects and another $13.8-million on emergency management for the 2025 wildfire season.

The Department of Finance also said the increased spending includes $420-million in funds that were set aside for some anticipated commitments which have not yet been finalized and, as a result, cannot be made public.

Lohr would not say if this was related to a previous government’s wage restriction bill that was deemed unconstitutional.

Bill 148 was passed by former Liberal premier Stephen McNeil to limit pay increases in 2015, and a Supreme Court judge decided it was unconstitutional in February.

“In terms of Bill 148, I can say that we have until February of this coming year to reach a settlement, we are working on that,” Lohr said.

Officials declined to comment on how much this settlement may cost, because the matter is before the courts.

The province closed the 2025-26 fiscal year with a record-high deficit of $1.4-billion. While revenue was slightly higher than expected, at just under $18-billion, it was outpaced by $19.4-billion in spending.

Net debt hit $24.1-billion.

For the 2026-27 fiscal year, the province is anticipating a $1.44-billion deficit.

Opposition parties slammed the Progressive Conservative government for its growing deficit and reliance on out-of-budget spending.

Interim Liberal leader Iain Rankin said Thursday’s update highlights the government’s inability to manage spending.

“We see a dozen departments, again, overspending and not going to the legislature to get approval. This is a government that loves to spend and there’s no accountability on the spending,” Rankin told reporters.

“It’s unprecedented,” he added.

NDP finance critic, Lisa Lachance, said the province needs to look critically at its spending.

“This government has dug a generational hole for Nova Scotians in terms of deficit spending, debt, debt servicing costs. And yet people still aren’t getting what they need,” Lachance said.

The NDP member said the province continues to deal with crises in health care and affordable housing, despite significant government spending.

Lohr said Nova Scotians remain concerned about affordability, housing, health and seniors’ care, and the government has focused on spending in these areas.

“There are still so many things we want to do for Nova Scotians, and to do that we need to grow our economy. I believe we have the fundamentals required for growth in defence, in clean energy, in housing, and in natural resources,” the finance minister said.

Bill 148 was passed by former Liberal premier Stephen McNeil to limit pay increases in 2015, and a Supreme Court judge decided it was unconstitutional in February.
“In terms of Bill 148, I can say that we have until February of this coming year to reach a settlement, we are working on that,” Lohr said.
Officials declined to comment on how much this settlement may cost, because the matter is before the courts.

The province closed the 2025-26 fiscal year with a record-high deficit of $1.4-billion. While revenue was slightly higher than expected, at just under $18-billion, it was outpaced by $19.4-billion in spending.
Net debt hit $24.1-billion.
For the 2026-27 fiscal year, the province is anticipating a $1.44-billion deficit.
Opposition parties slammed the Progressive Conservative government for its growing deficit and reliance on out-of-budget spending.
Interim Liberal leader Iain Rankin said Thursday’s update highlights the government’s inability to manage spending.

“We see a dozen departments, again, overspending and not going to the legislature to get approval. This is a government that loves to spend and there’s no accountability on the spending,” Rankin told reporters.
“It’s unprecedented,” he added.
NDP finance critic, Lisa Lachance, said the province needs to look critically at its spending.
“This government has dug a generational hole for Nova Scotians in terms of deficit spending, debt, debt servicing costs. And yet people still aren’t getting what they need,” Lachance said.
The NDP member said the province continues to deal with crises in health care and affordable housing, despite significant government spending.
Lohr said Nova Scotians remain concerned about affordability, housing, health and seniors’ care, and the government has focused on spending in these areas.

“There are still so many things we want to do for Nova Scotians, and to do that we need to grow our economy. I believe we have the fundamentals required for growth in defence, in clean energy, in housing, and in natural resources,” the finance minister said.

By Anja Karadeglija The Canadian Press

OTTAWA - A new report on child murders says institutional failures — and warnings from mothers that officials dismissed — played a role in the deaths of eight children in Canada.

“In each case, warning signs were present. Concerns about violence, coercion, abuse, or danger were raised. Yet those warnings did not lead to adequate protection,” Suzanne Zaccour, director of legal affairs at the National Association of Women and the Law, told a press conference on Parliament Hill Thursday.

“In all five cases, the person seeking protection for the children was a woman. She asked for help from the police, child protection, the courts, and was not heard.”

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

Working remotely from Canada's Wonderland

Institutions can prioritize a father-child relationship even in cases where there is a documented history of family violence, Zaccour said.

She urged Parliament to adopt a private members’ bill, introduced by Liberal MP Lisa Hepfner, which would curb parental alienation claims, among other measures.

Zaccour said parental alienation accusations are “systematically used as a litigation strategy to deflect attention from abuse, undermine a child’s disclosure of fear, and portray a protective mother as hostile, irrational, or manipulative.”

The report, published Thursday, analyzes the deaths of eight children in five different cases between 2011 and 2020. They include the case of four-year-old Keira Kagan, who was found dead alongside her biological father in a case that a review committee said was consistent with murder-suicide.

Philip Viater, a family lawyer and Keira’s stepfather, was also at the press conference.

“We brought an emergency motion asking that his parenting time be suspended or supervised because the risk was escalating,” he said.

Viater said the judge concluded that while the evidence was persuasive, the issue wasn’t urgent and child protection authorities could intervene in the meantime.

Two days before Keira died, a child protection worker said Keira’s father was “displaying behavior consistent with fathers who harm or kill their own children.”

“Yet they did not act. We were forced and directed to permit Keira to be in her biological father’s care unsupervised,” Viater said.

In another case outlined in the report, a seven-year-old girl was found unconscious in her room in Granby, Que., and later died in hospital. She had been placed in her father’s custody after being raised by her paternal grandparents.

Her grandmother had warned authorities there was a serious risk of sexual abuse, but she “lost custody after being perceived as hostile for reporting the dangers the girl was exposed to while in her son’s care,” the report says.

The child’s stepmother was found guilty of manslaughter and false imprisonment and the father pleaded guilty to false imprisonment.

At the press conference on Thursday, Hepfner urged her colleagues to support her proposed legislation, “because children’s lives are at stake.”

Bill C-223 says a court, with some exceptions, “shall not take into consideration any allegation that a spouse has, or is likely to, through deliberate manipulation, persuade or encourage a child to become estranged from or resist contact with the other spouse.”

The report says the concept of parental alienation is frequently invoked in Canada’s courts. It says it’s used by parties in child custody cases to explain why a child resists seeing a parent, and to cast doubt on allegations of domestic violence.

“By interpreting a child’s resistance or a protective parent’s warning signs as manipulation rather than as an indicator of danger, institutions may contribute to maintaining or imposing contact with an abusive parent, thereby increasing the child’s vulnerability,” the report says.

Viater said experts, including a UN special rapporteur, have said the concept of parental alienation does not have a scientific basis.

Hepfner’s bill also would make other changes to the Divorce Act. It would impose new requirements on lawyers to screen for signs of family violence during divorce cases.

It also would give judges new tools to identify the existence and impact of coercive control on children and to ensure that, in some circumstances, children can express their preferences to a judge in a custody dispute.

With files from Alessia Passafiume

The Canadian Press

stories.title: Bombardier CEO Éric Martel Report on Business Speaker Series
stories.summary: Watch live as ROB magazine editor speaks with Martel on the company’s reinvention and the future of Canada’s aerospace and technology sector
stories.author: Globe Staff
stories.content:
Welcome to the inaugural CEO Speaker Series, a series of Report on Business magazine events bringing together some of Canada’s largest corporate leaders for a monthly in-depth conversation with ROB magazine editor Dawn Calleja in Toronto.

On Friday, Calleja will have a fire-side chat with Éric Martel, President and CEO, Bombardier, as they explore lessons from the company’s reinvention, how renewed ambitions are reshaping the future of Canadian aerospace industry and what it will take for the country to compete in the world’s most high-value technology sectors.

For those who can’t attend in person, we’re livestreaming the event starting at 8:00 A.M. EST .

You can view the full schedule for the talk here .

stories.title: Ottawa orders Appeal Court to review Saskatchewan sisters’ murder convictions
stories.summary: Canada's federal justice minister ordered the courts to reopen the sisters' case, after they spent almost three decades in prison for what May be wrongful murder convictions.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Federal Justice Minister Sean Fraser has ordered the courts to reopen the case of two Saskatchewan sisters who spent almost three decades in prison for what may be wrongful murder convictions.

Fraser says he is sending the case of Odelia and Neressa Quewezance back to an Appeal Court for a review.

Fraser, in a statement Thursday, cited reasonable grounds to conclude that a miscarriage of justice occurred in the 1994 convictions.

“My decision does not decide guilt or innocence, as that will rest with the courts,” Fraser said.

“Our responsibility is to make sure Canadians can trust their justice system, and that means, in rare cases, returning cases to the courts.”

Fraser noted there is new information that was not before the courts during the trial or during the appeal.

James Lockyer, the sisters’ lawyer, said the information that led to their new appeal pertains to their time in custody after their arrest.

Lockyer said the women were held in an RCMP detachment in Kamsack, Sask., about 270 kilometres northeast of Saskatoon. They were questioned by white male police officers for days, he said, which was in violation of a court order to send them to the local jail.

“We’ve discovered some more information in that regard that I don’t feel free to talk about at the moment, but will certainly be presented to the Court of Appeal,” he said in a phone interview Thursday.

He said the women were more vulnerable to pressures from police because of their time spent in residential schools. He said their alleged incriminating statements were never recorded and their in-custody environment increases the likelihood their confessions were false.

Lockyer applied for a ministerial review in December 2021, which was granted in June 2022. The two Saulteaux sisters were granted bail in 2023, but have since been returned to custody for breaching bail conditions.

“It’s very difficult for them, when they’ve spent all this time in prison, to be able to readjust in the community,” said Lockyer.

He added they both struggle with substance abuse.

Court documents show both sisters attended St. Philips Indian Residential School and Qu’Appelle Indian Residential School. Their mother and stepmother both died from drug overdoses.

Lockyer said he will be bringing further bail applications for them in the Saskatchewan Court of Appeal.

The sisters said in a statement Thursday that they’re encouraged by the decision, but added that the battle continues.

“We have never stopped fighting,” Odelia said in the statement on behalf of her and her sibling.

“Thank you to all those who have kept the faith in us.”

The statement was issued through Innocence Canada, an organization that fights for those it believes were wrongfully convicted. It assisted the sisters in this case.

Lockyer, also a lawyer with Innocence Canada, said the Quewezance sisters’ case was flagged to the organization by David Milgaard, who spent 23 years in prison for the 1969 murder of a Saskatoon nursing student before his conviction was overturned. He died in 2022.

The two sisters were found guilty of second-degree murder in the 1993 stabbing death of 70-year-old farmer Anthony Joseph Dolff near Kamsack, Sask., about 270 kilometres northeast of Regina.

The women from the Keeseekoose First Nation have always maintained their innocence. Another person, who was a youth at the time, confessed to the killing and was sentenced to five years in prison.

Court has heard the sisters and the youth were drinking with Dolff at his farmhouse that fateful night when he was killed.

Court documents show Dolff was found dead in the bedroom of his home located near Keeseekoose First Nation. It says he had been stabbed 17 times and had a phone cord wrapped around his neck.

The sisters’ bid for an appeal was dismissed by the Supreme Court of Canada in 1996.

The federal Justice Department said after launching its review in June 2022 that there may be a reasonable basis to conclude there was a miscarriage of justice.

stories.title: Feds’ tariff response requires a ‘Team Canada’ approach, expert says
stories.summary: Municipalities are on the ground connecting with businesses and residents, which one economist said gives them valuable intel integral to Canada’s economic response.
stories.author: Rachel Morgan
stories.content:
Canada’s tariff response must ensure that no community is left behind, a new report says.

The report, released by the Federation of Canadian Municipalities , in partnership with the City of London and Ivey Business School found that the consequences of the U.S.-Canada trade war are felt all across Canada, but the severity of those impacts are unevenly distributed.

The industrial composition of a community is more closely tied to how it feels the pressure of tariffs than its size alone, the report said.

“There is an opportunity … to strengthen the Team Canada approach in terms of responding and creating resilience in the economy. I think we should take that seriously,” Romel Mostafa, an economist and assistant professor of international business at the Ivey Business School, told Global News.

Municipal governments are on the ground connecting with businesses and residents, which Mostafa said gives them valuable intel that is integral to the federal government’s economic response.

Whether it is Mackenzie, B.C., a town of 3,700 residents that relies on forestry and mining; Windsor, Ont., with deep roots in the auto industry; or a larger city that has multiple tariff-impacted industries, all of these communities have had to respond to the consequences of the trade war.

“Understanding these nuances means that there are different policy implications for it,” Mostafa said.

One of the biggest challenges for municipalities has been working through the uncertainty brought forth by a constantly evolving economic relationship with the U.S., London, Ont., Mayor Josh Morgan told Global News.

“The uncertainty has created a real pause in investment and job creation. In some cases there are job losses, in some cases, there are job gains,” he said. “For the most part, many businesses have just paused their decision-making, waiting to see a more stabilized environment because the unpredictability of the state we’re in is really not conducive to business investment.”

London recorded the highest unemployment rate among Canada’s 20 largest municipalities, sitting at 9.1 per cent in March, compared to six per cent a year earlier. But Morgan said the statistics don’t tell the whole story.

“We have seen actual net job creation. But we’ve seen a migration of the labour force from smaller communities that May be more impacted by the trade situation, migrating to larger cities like London for job opportunities,” he said. “And so the labour force has actually expanded at a pace faster than job creation we’ve had in the city.”

This context behind the statistics is the intel that Morgan said municipalities can bring to the table in discussions with upper levels of government as well as with cities on the other side of the border.

“Municipalities in Canada and municipalities in the U.S. are facing the same sort of impacts. We have that common ground and we are actively talking to each other,” he said. “We’re not against them, we’re on their side, we’re on the same team here.”

Mostafa said it is important to bring all of these voices into the conversation.

“I think there’s a real opportunity to think about, given the lanes that we have, how can we make the process of getting municipal intelligence to reach the policymakers at the higher order of the government?” he said.

stories.title: Lions eager for crucial clash with Roughriders
stories.summary: Mathieu Betts knows exactly what will be on the line when his B.C. Lions line up against the Saskatchewan Roughriders on Friday.
stories.author: Gemma Karstens-Smith
stories.content:
VANCOUVER – Mathieu Betts knows exactly what will be on the line when his B.C. Lions line up against the Saskatchewan Roughriders on Friday.

If everything goes Saskatchewan’s way, the Riders could punch their playoff ticket this week — and the Lions are looking to stop that from happening.

“It feels like the most important game of the year, and I’m pretty sure it’s not the last time I would tell you that this year,” Betts said.

“At the end of the day, to get where we want to go, we need to play good football. So no matter what’s at stake, we need to play good football.”

The Lions (7-6) come in with wins in six of their last seven contests, including a 48-29 victory over the Montreal Alouettes on Sept. 12 before the team headed into a bye week.

The Roughriders (8-5), meanwhile, sit second in the West Division and are coming off a 19-6 loss to the Winnipeg Blue Bombers on Sept. 12.

Saskatchewan could clinch a post-season berth this week, but will need help on the out-of-town scoreboard. The Riders need the Toronto Argonauts to beat the Bombers and the winless Ottawa Redblacks to upset the Calgary Stampeders.

Most importantly, the Riders need a victory over the Lions.

A Lions win would give B.C. a tiebreaker between the two sides in an ultracompetitive West Division where the second- and fifth-place teams are currently separated by just four points.

“We all understand where the standings are right now,” said Lions head coach Buck Pierce. “And both teams have put themselves in position to have everything they want in front of them, right? So, two competitive teams that are playing good football … getting healthy, hopefully at the right time. So it should be a good game.”

Friday will mark the final regular-season matchup between the two sides, and each team comes in with a win.

The Riders took first blood with a 31-27 home victory on June 13 before the Lions earned a 30-16 decision in Vancouver on Aug 23.

B.C.’s defence has grown stronger over the course of the season, said Saskatchewan head coach Corey Mace.

“I think just having a little bit more understanding of what they want to accomplish,” he said. “I think they play very well to the pieces that they have. They do a really good job, they can get after the passer, they do a bunch of stuff on the back end that makes it tough on quarterbacks, their linebackers run and hit.

“They’ve been doing a really good job making it tough on offences across the league.”

The Riders have been stingy all year, giving up a league-low 340 points.

Getting the right combination of players on defence has been an evolution, Mace said.

“We’re doing a good job,” he said. “We’ve just got to continue pushing the envelope and creating some turnovers. We’ve been a little bit more consistent with that. And giving ourselves an opportunity to, obviously, not only stay in the game but take it over.”

The Lions will see changes to their secondary this week after defensive backs Josh Hagerty and Ronald Kent Jr. were each suspended for following a melee in B.C.’s win over Montreal. Hagerty received a two-game ban while Kent was suspended one game. Alouettes defensive back Don Callis was also banned for one game and three other Alouettes players received fines.

Video of the dust up shows Hagerty punching Montreal running back Liam Talbot in the groin.

Asked whether there was an extra focus on discipline in practice this week, Betts noted that discipline is how football games are won and lost.

“When we talk about discipline, it’s in your assignment,” he said. “Also, taking penalties, you don’t want to give away free yards … If we want to go where we want to go at the end of the year, that’s something that’s going to be really, really important on all matters, in all phases for sure.”

The Lions signed American defensive backs Jordan Oladokun and Thomas Graham to the practice roster on Monday, then re-signed Robert Carter Jr. on Tuesday.

The American defensive back returns to B.C. after attending NFL training camp with the Indianapolis Colts.

Having new bodies in the lineup doesn’t change how the defence prepares or plays, said Betts, a veteran defensive lineman.

“To us, it’s whoever’s asked to be playing different roles, we have to take it,” he said. “So for us, it’s just everybody knows their assignment, know what’s going on defence, and to be ready when your name is called. But for us to be playing good football, it’s all about assignment, detail, communication, and playing with high energy.”

stories.title: Stevenson promises review of BRT spending, road construction if elected mayor
stories.summary: Mayoral candidate Susan Stevenson says she would push for a public accounting of London’s Bus Rapid Transit project and proposed North Link if elected.
stories.author: Reta Ismail
stories.content:
Mayoral candidate Susan Stevenson says she would push for a public accounting of London’s Bus Rapid Transit project and proposed North Link if elected.

Stevenson made the announcement Thursday morning in front of the BRT shelters at King and Burwell streets.

She outlined three commitments: A full public accounting of BRT and the proposed North Link, an annual road construction plan approved by council, and practical improvements to everyday travel.

Stevenson said she would take a closer look at how the city is spending money on major transportation projects, including BRT and the proposed North Link.

“People have a lot of questions. We spent almost half a billion dollars on this investment, and they would like to see it laid out in plain English in one spot where they can really see and get the answers as to what was spent,” Stevenson said.

“What was the reason for the $174 million overruns? Were there construction delays? Like, how well did we do in managing this project, and what is it that we’ve committed to going forward?”

Stevenson is also proposing an annual road construction plan aimed at better coordinating roadwork, utility projects and development, while keeping businesses and emergency routes accessible.

She said residents and businesses should receive more advance notice when construction is expected to affect them.

Her platform also calls for a review of traffic signals, turning restrictions and cycling lanes, along with a greater focus on road and sidewalk maintenance.

Stevenson said she would work with London Transit and local employers to explore transit options for industrial areas, including service timed around shift work.

“Getting around London should be something we can count on,” Stevenson said.

The current Ward 4 councillor said she would begin the BRT review and construction-coordination work within her first 100 days in office.

stories.title: Canada’s first F-35 takes flight in Texas
stories.summary: Canada’s first F-35 has taken to the skies. It’s the first new model of fighter jet with Canadian markings in 44 years.
stories.author: John Vennavally-Rao
stories.content:
Toronto - Canada’s first F-35 has taken to the skies. It’s the first new model of fighter jet with Canadian markings in 44 years.

The historic first flight took place Wednesday in Fort Worth, Texas, home to Lockheed Martin’s final assembly plant.

The F-35 will replace at least some of the Royal Canadian Air Force’s (Rcaf) aging CF-18 Hornets, which Canada first took delivery of in 1982.

Canada signed on in 2023 to buy 88 of the jets, but Prime Minister Mark Carney ordered a review in March 2025 amid tensions with the United States. The first 16 aircraft are committed, while the government weighs whether to buy the remaining 72 or turn to alternatives such as Sweden’s Saab Gripen.

The CF-35A Lightning II with “Canada” painted behind the cockpit and a maple leaf on the tail, took off just before noon for what witnesses say was a roughly 90-minute flight.

View this post on Instagram

“There were quite a few people!” Victoria Fontana told CTV News in a message when asked if there was a crowd. She said the Dallas-Fort Worth area has a sizable plane-spotting community that are interested in both military and commercial aircraft.

The only apparent official acknowledgement came from Lockheed Martin Canada’s X account, which posted: “The first CF-35A took to the skies for the first time today.”

The first CF-35A took to the skies for the first time today. pic.twitter.com/SAHsXdKwas — Lockheed Martin Canada (@LMCanadaNews) September 23, 2026

Asked for more details, a spokesperson for Lockheed Martin said, “questions would be best addressed by the Department of National Defence (DND).” CTV News has reached out to the DND for comment but has not yet received a response.

“I think the silence is ordered,” says Scott Clancy, a retired Rcaf major-general, an adviser at Henley Strategies and a fellow at the Canadian Global Affairs Institute.

“So, this is now just a political decision and that’s why the Canadian Armed Forces has been specifically told you will not comment on that,” said Clancy.

Clancy said pilots in the Canadian Armed Forces including future F-35 pilots are excited for the new plane.

“They’re very excited about this generational advancement that they’re going to make in terms of technology and they are preparing hard for that.”

Despite the controversy around the purchase of the jet, Clancy said Canadians should take notice of the first flight.

“I think we should be proud because a significant portion of that jet, although we call it an American jet, is Canadian,” he said.

Lockheed Martin says each F-35 contains more than $3 million in Canadian-made components from suppliers in six provinces, including the F-35A’s horizontal tail assemblies built by Magellan Aerospace in Winnipeg.

stories.title: Canada's population growth continues to slow, consistent with lowered immigration targets
stories.summary: The largest decreases in 2025/2026 were among study permit holders, down 140,827 and work and study permit holders, down 81,163.
stories.author: Stewart Lewis
stories.content:
Canada has just marked its lowest year-over year population growth since the Second World War, according to a new report from Statistics Canada.

The population reached an estimated 41,798,407 people on July 1, 2026, an increase of 189,425 people from July 1, 2025, however this is the lowest annual growth since 1944/1945, says StatCan, when it grew by 126,000.

“The rapid changes in the population growth rate since 2020 are almost entirely attributable to changes in international migration,” states StatCan.

Immigration targets under the Trudeau government were increased in 2016 from an annual average of 617,800 between 2000 to 2015 to approximately 1.4 million for 2016 to 2024. However, public concern about the impact on the affordability of housing resulted in substantial reductions, noted a Fraser Institute report. In the 2025 federal budget , the Carney government unveiled a new plan for 2026-28 immigration levels , outlining a more moderate approach, while focusing on steady economic immigration growth.

“ In 2018, 3.3 per cent of Canada’s population were temporary residents. By 2024, that number had more than doubled to 7.5 per cent, an unprecedented rate of growth that put pressure on housing supply, the healthcare system, and schools,” according to the 2025 Annual Report to Parliament on Immigration , which states that “ Canada’s new government recognizes that this system is no longer sustainable, and we are determined to make it so, for everyone who lives in and comes to this country.”

The number of new immigrants to Canada fell for the fourth consecutive year, down to 368,224 in 2025/2026, says this week’s StatCan report. That is “consistent” with lower targets set by Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada, notes StatCan. It’s the first time since 2021/2022 that the annual number of immigrants has fallen below 400,000.

Permanent immigration dropped in all provinces and Yukon, though it increased in the Northwest Territories and Nunavut.

Consistent with that drop, the number of non-permanent residents in Canada fell by 154,614 people on a July 2025 to July 2026 basis, settling at 2,779,774 as of July 1, 2026, or 6.7 per cent of the total population. StatCan says that is down from a high of 2,984,285 non-permanent residents on October 1, 2024, or 7.2 per cent of the total population. This year’s drop was the largest decrease in non-permanent residents since comparable records began in 1971/1972.

The largest decreases in 2025/2026 were among study permit holders, down 140,827 and work and study permit holders, down 81,163. (Statistics Canada says it applied adjustments to the estimates of non-permanent residents for this report. In an explanatory note, the agency said the increase in the number of permit extensions and the time required to process them has made it increasingly important to better account for individuals who remain in Canada while their extension application is being processed.)

This year’s growth was lower than the growth during the first year of the pandemic, when it grew by 211,226, despite border restrictions put in place to slow the spread of COVID-19. In 2021-2022 says StatCan it grew by 1.8 per cent, then 2.7 per cent in 2022/2023, reaching a high of 2.8 per cent growth in 2023/2024. However, the July-to-July population growth rate has since slowed. It fell to a 0.5 per cent increase in 2025/2026.

Despite these nationwide declines, Alberta continues to have the fastest growing population of all the provinces. From July 1, 2025 to July 1, 2026, Alberta’s population jumped by 1.5 per cent, says StatCan.

Growth was slower in all provinces over the same period, with the three largest provinces in Canada growing more slowly than the country overall: Ontario (+0.3 per cent), Quebec (+0.2 per cent) and British Columbia (+0.1 per cent). Those provinces tended, says StatCan, “to welcome the largest share of international migrants and are thus more affected by changes in international migration levels.”

High numbers of international migration from 2021/2022 to 2024/2025 resulted in decreases or stabilization of the average age. But now Canada’s population is aging again, with the average age on July 1, 2026 at 42.1 years.

The two five-year age groups with the largest decreases in 2025/2026 were 20 to 24 years (down 63,838 or 2.4 per cent) and 25 to 29 years (down 91,135 or 3.1 per cent). In total, says StatCan, there was a drop of 154,973 people in their 20s, which “is (again) consistent with the fall in the number of study permit holders in the country, since international students tend to be young adults.”

Meanwhile, the number of people in the 60-to-64 age group (2,658,594) has fallen for the past two years. Before 2024/2025, says StatCan, this age group had not decreased since 1996/1997. However, the smaller Generation X is entering this age group and the larger baby boomer generation is coming to the end of their lives.

This year’s drop was the largest decrease in non-permanent residents since comparable records began in 1971/1972.

The largest decreases in 2025/2026 were among study permit holders, down 140,827 and work and study permit holders, down 81,163. (Statistics Canada says it applied adjustments to the estimates of non-permanent residents for this report. In an explanatory note, the agency said the increase in the number of permit extensions and the time required to process them has made it increasingly important to better account for individuals who remain in Canada while their extension application is being processed.)

This year’s growth was lower than the growth during the first year of the pandemic, when it grew by 211,226, despite border restrictions put in place to slow the spread of COVID-19. In 2021-2022 says StatCan it grew by 1.8 per cent, then 2.7 per cent in 2022/2023, reaching a high of 2.8 per cent growth in 2023/2024. However, the July-to-July population growth rate has since slowed. It fell to a 0.5 per cent increase in 2025/2026.

Despite these nationwide declines, Alberta continues to have the fastest growing population of all the provinces. From July 1, 2025 to July 1, 2026, Alberta’s population jumped by 1.5 per cent, says StatCan.

Growth was slower in all provinces over the same period, with the three largest provinces in Canada growing more slowly than the country overall: Ontario (+0.3 per cent), Quebec (+0.2 per cent) and British Columbia (+0.1 per cent). Those provinces tended, says StatCan, “to welcome the largest share of international migrants and are thus more affected by changes in international migration levels.”

High numbers of international migration from 2021/2022 to 2024/2025 resulted in decreases or stabilization of the average age. But now Canada’s population is aging again, with the average age on July 1, 2026 at 42.1 years.

The two five-year age groups with the largest decreases in 2025/2026 were 20 to 24 years (down 63,838 or 2.4 per cent) and 25 to 29 years (down 91,135 or 3.1 per cent). In total, says StatCan, there was a drop of 154,973 people in their 20s, which “is (again) consistent with the fall in the number of study permit holders in the country, since international students tend to be young adults.”

Meanwhile, the number of people in the 60-to-64 age group (2,658,594) has fallen for the past two years. Before 2024/2025, says StatCan, this age group had not decreased since 1996/1997. However, the smaller Generation X is entering this age group and the larger baby boomer generation is coming to the end of their lives.

stories.title: Maple Leafs place Steven Lorentz on waivers
stories.summary: Lorentz first joined the Leafs on a training camp invite ahead of the 2024-25 season before signing with the team.
stories.author: Lucas Casaletto
stories.content:
The Toronto Maple Leafs have placed Steven Lorentz on waivers, the team announced on Thursday.

The Leafs are currently $2.8 million over the salary cap ahead of next Tuesday’s regular season opener against Montreal.

Lorentz, 30, has one year on his contract with an average annual salary of $1.35 million. The Kitchener, Ont., native appeared in 71 games with the Leafs last season, registering seven goals and 18 points.

Lorentz first joined the Leafs on a training camp invite ahead of the 2024-25 season before signing with the team. He agreed to a three-year contract extension in June 2025.

The Leafs announced on Wednesday that defencemen Dakota Mermis and Cole McWard were also placed on waivers. Should all three players clear, they will report to the Toronto Marlies.

Head coach Jim Hiller said this week that winger Dakota Joshua is likely to miss the start of the regular season as he deals with a core muscle injury. Nick Paul’s availability for next week’s season opener is also in doubt, Hiller said on Thursday.

Paul was acquired from the Tampa Bay Lightning over the summer for goalie Dennis Hildeby and two draft picks.

stories.title: Crombie proposes subway extension into Mississauga in election bid
stories.summary: Unveiling her transit proposals on Thursday, Crombie said she wanted to see Line 2 extended eastward from Kipling Station into downtown Mississauga.
stories.author: Isaac Callan
stories.content:
Mississauga mayoral hopeful Bonnie Crombie is pitching the idea of extending Toronto’s subway network into her city, hoping that, if she wins, she can convince Premier Doug Ford to fund the plan.

Unveiling her transit proposals on Thursday, Crombie said she wanted to see Line 2 extended westward from Kipling Station into downtown Mississauga , with a stop at Square One via Sherway Gardens.

“For the first time, residents should ultimately be able to board the subway in Mississauga and ride directly into Toronto,” Crombie wrote.

“Toronto has already directed planning work on a possible Line 2 extension from Kipling to Sherway Gardens. The Toronto Transit Commission (TTC) is also planning for a new western maintenance and storage facility needed to accommodate future Line 2 growth and expansion.”

Crombie served as Mississauga mayor from 2014 to 2024, leaving the post to become leader of the Ontario Liberal Party.

She is running against incumbent Carolyn Parrish, as well as councillors Alvin Tedjo and Dipika Damerla and several other candidates to take control of city council.

Tedjo’s campaign said a subway extension may be a “dream worth pursuing” but stressed a better relationship “with the province to secure the support and funding needed to make it happen” must be the first step.

Damela said the key was delivering “realistic” transit.

“I support a surface subway along Lakeshore,” she wrote in a statement. “This is where some of our biggest growth is happening, including Brightwater and Lakeview Village, and it’s where transit capacity will be needed most.”

Premier Ford, who campaigned in the 2025 snap election against Crombie’s Liberals, has made it clear he does not want her to win the Mississauga election and called for Parrish to be re-elected.

Global News also contacted Parrish’s campaign for comment.

stories.title: Canadian dollar hits two-month low as retail sales post monthly decline
stories.summary: U.S. dollar increases to a two-month high against a basket of major currencies
stories.author: Fergal Smith
stories.content:
The Canadian dollar weakened against its U.S. ​counterpart on Thursday as the ‌greenback notched broad-based gains and after domestic retail sales data failed to lift investor concern about Canada’s economic outlook.

The loonie was trading 0.2 per cent lower ⁠at ​1.4125 per US dollar, or 70.80 US cents, after touching its weakest intraday level since July 14 at 1.4149.

“The loonie’s slide looks more like a rates-and-USD story than a sudden Canada-specific ​shock,” said Tony Valente, a senior FX ‌dealer at AscendantFX.

The U.S. dollar rose to a two-month high against a basket of major currencies as investors bet on additional Federal Reserve interest rate hikes following recent strong economic data.

“The lack of a ‌trade and ​tariffs agreement with ‌the US isn’t helping the cause either,” Valente said. “That uncertainty is ​weighing on the Canadian growth outlook and ⁠limiting the Bank of Canada’s room to move, with ⁠this morning’s disappointing domestic retail sales data adding to the evidence of ​softer domestic demand.”

Canadian retail sales fell by 0.7 per cent in July, led by declines at general merchandise retailers. A preliminary estimate showed sales rebounding by 1.3 per cent in August but analysts don’t expect to see sustained strength.

“We doubt the momentum ⁠can last given renewed trade tensions that are set to cause the unemployment rate to rise, while elevated gasoline prices will also eat into discretionary spending power in the near term,” Katherine Judge, a senior economist at CIBC Capital Markets, said ⁠in a note.

U.S. crude oil ​futures were trading 2.3 per cent higher at US$94.25 a barrel as the U.S. ⁠and Iran discussed a phased deal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and per cent end ‌a US blockade. Oil is one of Canada’s major exports.

Canadian bond ​yields were mixed across a steeper curve, tracking moves in U.S. Treasuries.

The 2-year eased 1.6 basis points to 3.384 per cent, while the 10-year was barely changed at 3.956 per cent ​after earlier touching its highest level since November 2023 at 3.990 per cent.

stories.title: Grifols says plasma donor safety was not compromised as it works to regain licence
stories.summary: Winnipeg - A for-profit company that oversees plasma collection says it is working with Health Canada on a reopening plan after the federal health agency suspended one its operating licences for a clinic in Winnipeg.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
WINNIPEG - A for-profit company that oversees plasma collection says it is working with Health Canada on a reopening plan after the federal health agency suspended one its operating licences for a clinic in Winnipeg.

Sept. 24, 2026

Updated at 1:45 p.m.

New subscriber benefit!

Copied to clipboard

A gifted article has been claimed.

Out of gifts for the month

Unfortunately you've used all of your gifts this month. Your counter will reset on the first day of next month.

JK[](http://www.thestar.com/news/canada/manitoba/grifols-says-plasma-donor-safety-was-not-compromised-as-it-works-to-regain-licence/article_2a1d6654-9e65-5288-b765-53bfc1528b4e.html)

By The Canadian Press

Health Canada halted all collections at Grifols’ Taylor Avenue location on Wednesday after it found compliance problems at the privately run clinic that pays for plasma donations.

Grifols already suspended donation collections at all of its sites last month following reports of two people dying after donating at two separate Winnipeg locations.

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

Working remotely from Canada's Wonderland

Image 9Image 10

A Health Canada investigation found no link between the deaths of the plasma donors and the collection process, and Grifols says at no point was the safety of donors and patients compromised.

Grifols says despite being the majority owner of the Taylor Avenue location, the company was limited on its ability to direct operations at the centre.

It did not elaborate on what limitations it faced, instead citing that the governance structure and contractual arrangements impacted Grifols’ ability to control the operations.

The company acquired full ownership of the Taylor Avenue centre at the beginning of this month, Grifols said in a followup statement.

The company said it’s been conducting a review since it voluntarily suspended operations, including retraining staff and strengthening its procedures and quality systems.

“We have already implemented corrective and preventive measures and will continue working closely with Health Canada to demonstrate their effectiveness and support ongoing compliance at the Taylor Avenue location and across all our centres,” the company said in a statement on Thursday.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 24, 2026.

paragraphs: The Volkswagen subsidiary set to open an electric vehicle battery "gigafactory" in St. Thomas, Ont., announced the plant's opening is delayed by two years.

stories.title: Ontario deficit comes in better than projected at $13-billion
stories.summary: Province says revenue was higher than expected from government enterprises such as the Lcbo
stories.author: Liam Casey
stories.content:
Ontario says its deficit is slightly better than initially projected.

The province released the public accounts report for 2025-26 that shows the deficit at $13 billion, compared to the $14.6 billion projected in the 2025 budget.

The province ran a $1.1-billion deficit in 2024-25.

The government has said the shortfall was largely due to a $10-billion increase in program expenses in health and education.

Health-care spending increased by $6.2-billion to $97.5- billion total for 2025-26 while education spending increased by $2.3-billion to $40.1-billion.

The province says it had greater-than-projected revenue from government business enterprises, such as the LCBO and Ontario Lottery and Gaming Corp.

stories.title: Canadian astronaut ready for Nasa mission to International Space Station
stories.summary: Houston - Canadian astronaut Joshua Kutryk says he's been dreaming of going to space for a long time — and assuming everything goes to plan, he could fulfil that goal next week.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
HOUSTON - Canadian astronaut Joshua Kutryk said he’s been dreaming of going to space for a long time — and assuming everything goes to plan, he could fulfil that goal next week.

Sept. 24, 2026

Updated at 3:15 p.m.

New subscriber benefit!

Copied to clipboard

Out of gifts for the month

Unfortunately you've used all of your gifts this month. Your counter will reset on the first day of next month.

KGM[](http://www.thestar.com/news/canada/canadian-astronaut-ready-for-nasa-mission-to-international-space-station/article_4a660fff-ae71-55ff-bcf6-3d1a526c2225.html)

By The Canadian Press

“I always dreamt of it and thought it would be the most wonderful experience,” Kutryk said on Thursday.

The 44-year-old is one of four people assigned to NASA’s SpaceX Crew 13 mission heading to the International Space Station.

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

Working remotely from Canada's Wonderland

The crew will spend six months at the station conducting experiments, doing research and taking part in critical maintenance work.

Kutryk is currently quarantining in Houston but will travel to Florida for the launch, which is set to take place next Thursday at NASA’s Kennedy Space Center.

It will finally fulfil a lifelong goal for the astronaut, who has seen a previous flight aboard the Boeing Starliner-1 cancelled in 2024. Next week’s launch was supposed to take place earlier this month but it was delayed to fix a leak on the spacecraft.

Kutryk said one of the most important skills for an astronaut is the ability to deal with constant change.

“Through it all, the priority has been being ready when called to go fly this mission for Canada,” he said. “And I think that we are.”

The space station is a long way from the cattle farm where Kutryk grew up in eastern Alberta. But he has sent a small piece of his family’s history with him in a cargo shipment already at the station — a pocket watch his relatives brought from Ukraine to Canada four generations ago.

“I think it would have been completely impossible for them to have any inkling of an imagination of where that watch could be 100 years later … going into space,” Kutryk said. “I think it’s just this really important personal memento, but also a really neat metaphor for how much the world can change because of technology, because of how we explore.”

Kutryk will be joined on the mission by NASA’s Jessica Watkins and Luke Delaney, and Roscosmos cosmonaut Sergey Teteryatnikov. Kutryk said building trust among the team is critical to the success of the mission, which will confine the astronauts together in a small space for many months.

“We spend a lot of time together in situations that are designed deliberately to be stressful in that they will strain that relationship,” Kutryk said, adding that includes flying in high-performance jets and other expeditions.

It’s very important to demonstrate international collaboration at a time of geopolitical upheaval, Kutryk said. While the world may feel chaotic now, he said, space exploration can show people there is still a bright future ahead.

“One where countries are working together, not fighting. One where we’re looking after the world, not ruining it,” he said. “That’s the path and space helps us to do that.”

It’s been a high-profile few months for Canadian space exploration. Canadian astronaut Jeremy Hansen was part of the Artemis II mission that saw humanity return to the moon for the first time in more than 50 years.

Kutryk will be the fourth Canadian to take part in a long-duration mission to the International Space Station. Kutryk said he is proud to represent Canada and will be bringing Canadian flags with him on the journey.

The mission includes Canadian-led studies on how space travel and microgravity can affect human health. Kutryk said he feels lucky and grateful to be able to take part in that research.

Kutryk served as a CF-18 fighter pilot in Bagotville, Que., from 2007 to 2011, and was deployed to Libya and Afghanistan. He then worked as a test pilot in Cold Lake, Alta.

Kutryk’s experiences on the ground have prepared him for operational tasks in space, such as operating the Canadarm, the celebrated robotic system that was designed and built in Canada. And of course, he hopes to do some space walking.

“At the core of it, you’re operating really valuable, complicated technology in high-risk, high-consequence environments,” Kutryk said. “That’s what I’ve always enjoyed doing most in my career on Earth, and I think that’s what I look forward to the most in space.”

But like all the astronauts who came before him, Kutryk knows the first thing he’ll do when he gets to space is drift to the largest window he can find and take in the view.

“There is nothing that compares for how you change when you view the Earth from not being on the Earth,” he said.

“When you view it as this little blue perishable place where all of humanity has ever existed.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 24, 2026.

— By Kelly Geraldine Malone in Washington with files from Erika Morris in Montreal

The Canadian Press

stories.title: CP NewsAlert: Ottawa orders Appeal Court to review 2 Saskatchewan murder convictions
stories.summary: Ottawa - Federal Justice Minister Sean Fraser has ordered the courts to reopen the case of two Saskatchewan sisters who spent almost three decades in prison for what May be wrongful murder convictions.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Federal Justice Minister Sean Fraser has ordered the courts to reopen the case of two Saskatchewan sisters who spent almost three decades in prison for what may be wrongful murder convictions.

Sept. 24, 2026

Updated at 5:05 p.m.

New subscriber benefit!

Copied to clipboard

A gifted article has been claimed.

Out of gifts for the month

Unfortunately you've used all of your gifts this month. Your counter will reset on the first day of next month.

MLB[](http://www.thestar.com/news/canada/saskatchewan/cp-newsalert-ottawa-orders-appeal-court-to-review-2-saskatchewan-murder-convictions/article_5a7ddbef-6018-5008-8564-f57627154085.html)

By Dayne Patterson The Canadian Press

Fraser says he is sending the case of Odelia and Neressa Quewezance back to an Appeal Court for a review.

Fraser, in a statement Thursday, cited reasonable grounds to conclude that a miscarriage of justice occurred in the 1994 convictions.

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

Working remotely from Canada's Wonderland

“My decision does not decide guilt or innocence, as that will rest with the courts,” Fraser said.

“Our responsibility is to make sure Canadians can trust their justice system, and that means, in rare cases, returning cases to the courts.”

Fraser noted there is new information that was not before the courts during the trial or during the appeal.

James Lockyer, the sisters’ lawyer, said the information that led to their new appeal pertains to their time in custody after their arrest.

Lockyer said the women were held in an RCMP detachment in Kamsack, Sask., about 270 kilometres northeast of Saskatoon. They were questioned by white male police officers for days, he said, which was in violation of a court order to send them to the local jail.

“We’ve discovered some more information in that regard that I don’t feel free to talk about at the moment, but will certainly be presented to the Court of Appeal,” he said in a phone interview Thursday.

He said the women were more vulnerable to pressures from police because of their time spent in residential schools. He said their alleged incriminating statements were never recorded and their in-custody environment increases the likelihood their confessions were false.

Lockyer applied for a ministerial review in December 2021, which was granted in June 2022. The two Saulteaux sisters were granted bail in 2023, but have since been returned to custody for breaching bail conditions.

“It’s very difficult for them, when they’ve spent all this time in prison, to be able to readjust in the community,” said Lockyer.

He added they both struggle with substance abuse.

Court documents show both sisters attended St. Philips Indian Residential School and Qu’Appelle Indian Residential School. Their mother and stepmother both died from drug overdoses.

Lockyer said he will be bringing further bail applications for them in the Saskatchewan Court of Appeal.

The sisters said in a statement Thursday that they’re encouraged by the decision, but added that the battle continues.

“We have never stopped fighting,” Odelia said in the statement on behalf of her and her sibling.

“Thank you to all those who have kept the faith in us.”

The statement was issued through Innocence Canada, an organization that fights for those it believes were wrongfully convicted. It assisted the sisters in this case.

Lockyer, also a lawyer with Innocence Canada, said the Quewezance sisters’ case was flagged to the organization by David Milgaard, who spent 23 years in prison for the 1969 murder of a Saskatoon nursing student before his conviction was overturned. He died in 2022.

The two sisters were found guilty of second-degree murder in the 1993 stabbing death of 70-year-old farmer Anthony Joseph Dolff near Kamsack, Sask., about 270 kilometres northeast of Regina.

The women from the Keeseekoose First Nation have always maintained their innocence. Another person, who was a youth at the time, confessed to the killing and was sentenced to five years in prison.

Court has heard the sisters and the youth were drinking with Dolff at his farmhouse that fateful night when he was killed.

Court documents show Dolff was found dead in the bedroom of his home located near Keeseekoose First Nation. It says he had been stabbed 17 times and had a phone cord wrapped around his neck.

The sisters’ bid for an appeal was dismissed by the Supreme Court of Canada in 1996.

The federal Justice Department said after launching its review in June 2022 that there may be a reasonable basis to conclude there was a miscarriage of justice.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 24, 2026.

Note to readers:This is a corrected story; a previous version misspelled Neressa Quewezance’s first name.

By Dayne Patterson The Canadian Press
Fraser says he is sending the case of Odelia and Neressa Quewezance back to an Appeal Court for a review.
Fraser, in a statement Thursday, cited reasonable grounds to conclude that a miscarriage of justice occurred in the 1994 convictions.
ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW
Working remotely from Canada's Wonderland
“My decision does not decide guilt or innocence, as that will rest with the courts,” Fraser said.
“Our responsibility is to make sure Canadians can trust their justice system, and that means, in rare cases, returning cases to the courts.”
Fraser noted there is new information that was not before the courts during the trial or during the appeal.
James Lockyer, the sisters’ lawyer, said the information that led to their new appeal pertains to their time in custody after their arrest.

Lockyer said the women were held in an RCMP detachment in Kamsack, Sask., about 270 kilometres northeast of Saskatoon. They were questioned by white male police officers for days, he said, which was in violation of a court order to send them to the local jail.

“We’ve discovered some more information in that regard that I don’t feel free to talk about at the moment, but will certainly be presented to the Court of Appeal,” he said in a phone interview Thursday.

He said the women were more vulnerable to pressures from police because of their time spent in residential schools. He said their alleged incriminating statements were never recorded and their in-custody environment increases the likelihood their confessions were false.

Lockyer applied for a ministerial review in December 2021, which was granted in June 2022. The two Saulteaux sisters were granted bail in 2023, but have since been returned to custody for breaching bail conditions.
“It’s very difficult for them, when they’ve spent all this time in prison, to be able to readjust in the community,” said Lockyer.
He added they both struggle with substance abuse.
Court documents show both sisters attended St. Philips Indian Residential School and Qu’Appelle Indian Residential School. Their mother and stepmother both died from drug overdoses.
Lockyer said he will be bringing further bail applications for them in the Saskatchewan Court of Appeal.
The sisters said in a statement Thursday that they’re encouraged by the decision, but added that the battle continues.
“We have never stopped fighting,” Odelia said in the statement on behalf of her and her sibling.
“Thank you to all those who have kept the faith in us.”
The statement was issued through Innocence Canada, an organization that fights for those it believes were wrongfully convicted. It assisted the sisters in this case.

Lockyer, also a lawyer with Innocence Canada, said the Quewezance sisters’ case was flagged to the organization by David Milgaard, who spent 23 years in prison for the 1969 murder of a Saskatoon nursing student before his conviction was overturned. He died in 2022.
The two sisters were found guilty of second-degree murder in the 1993 stabbing death of 70-year-old farmer Anthony Joseph Dolff near Kamsack, Sask., about 270 kilometres northeast of Regina.
The women from the Keeseekoose First Nation have always maintained their innocence. Another person, who was a youth at the time, confessed to the killing and was sentenced to five years in prison.
Court has heard the sisters and the youth were drinking with Dolff at his farmhouse that fateful night when he was killed.
Court documents show Dolff was found dead in the bedroom of his home located near Keeseekoose First Nation. It says he had been stabbed 17 times and had a phone cord wrapped around his neck.
The sisters’ bid for an appeal was dismissed by the Supreme Court of Canada in 1996.
The federal Justice Department said after launching its review in June 2022 that there may be a reasonable basis to conclude there was a miscarriage of justice.

stories.title: London Cares launches initiative to combat homelessness misinformation
stories.summary: London Cares has unveiled a new campaign intending to help people spread awareness of homelessness, as well as...
stories.author: Ben Andrews
stories.content:
London Cares has unveiled a new campaign intending to help people spread awareness of homelessness, as well as ensuring that they are not spreading misinformation.

In an official media release, London Cares states that the purpose of this campaign, called Housing First, Hope Always , is to “… strengthen understanding of London Cares’ role, expertise and Housing First approach.”

“I t’s hard to find housing these days, especially at an affordable rate,” said Chris Moss, the executive director of London Cares homeless response services. “E very single month, my team finds between 30 and 50 people who are new to homelessness,”

Homelessness has been rising all across Ontario, with the number of homeless people in the province being estimated to have risen to 80,000 people.

Moss hopes that this campaign will help combat the common myths about homelessness, as well as bringing to attention just how serious the issue has gotten, and what London Cares is trying to do. “I t was really noticing the narrative getting off track, and feeling like when we’re out in the community, that people are misunderstanding who we are,” said Moss. “W e needed to really get out in front of that message and share as much as we could.”

“S ome of the misinformation comes where we hear rumours, like we give out drugs to people, we enable homelessness, we keep them in homelessness, so that we can make a lot of money,” clarified Moss. “As a housing first agency, we actually really want to move people from street to home as fast as possible.”

Moss says that due to budget cuts and lack of spending for the homeless, this campaign is also to remind the public and themselves that they have not lost hope. “T he province has not made enough housing, not enough affordable housing, not enough supportive housing, not enough housing that includes treatment beds or other types of things,” said Moss. We really need to call on the province to invest heavily in that.”

“W e recently had our funding reduced, eliminated with House of Hope,” Moss added. “W e had 45 people housed, and that program was defunded. … T his is sort of a little bit of a spinoff from that to saying we’re not losing track of h ope.”

“ But as a community, I’m pretty sure we could come together and get creative.”

stories.title: Judge removes University of New Brunswick from U.S. state senator’s defamation suit
stories.summary: An Oklahoma judge has removed UNB as a defendant in a defamation lawsuit filed by a Pennsylvania state senator with ties to U.S. President Donald Trump.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
An Oklahoma judge has removed the University of New Brunswick as a defendant in a defamation lawsuit filed by a Pennsylvania state senator with ties to U.S. President Donald Trump.

Sen. Doug Mastriano alleged defamation, racketeering, antitrust and other claims against UNB and almost two dozen academics in 2024 over criticism of his academic research into First World War hero Sgt. Alvin York.

The university granted Mastriano a doctorate for his research in 2013.

Mastriano attracted headlines in 2022 when Trump backed him for Pennsylvania governor during the senator’s unsuccessful campaign in 2022.

In the 2024 lawsuit, Mastriano was seeking millions of dollars in damages, claiming criticism of his research at the university cost him income from tourism-related events, as well as book, media, television and movie deals.

The university successfully argued that it was immune from the jurisdiction of the U.S. district court for the Western district of Oklahoma because the school is an “organ of a foreign state.”

Mastriano argued there were numerous exemptions to Unb’s immunity, but the judge disagreed and dismissed the case against the school.

Mastriano and UNB did not immediately responded to requests for comment.

— With files from The Associated Press.

stories.title: Quebec City man intended to build chemical weapon in attack for Islamic State, authorities say
stories.summary: A 24-year-old man from Quebec City is accused of intending to carry out an attack on behalf of the Islamic State. Authorities allege the man communicated online with members of the terrorist group and gathered information to build a chemical weapon that “could be used to poison Canadians.” The RCMP-led Integrated National Security Enforcement Team […]
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
A 24-year-old man from Quebec City is accused of intending to carry out a terrorist attack on Canadian soil on behalf of the Islamic State.

Authorities allege the man communicated online with members of the terrorist group and gathered information to build a poison or chemical weapon that “could be used to poison Canadians.”

Louay Angoud was arrested Wednesday by the RCMP-led Integrated National Security Enforcement Team (INSET), which probes threats to national security, following an investigation that began in April. He was charged with multiple terrorism-related offences, including participating in the activities of a terrorist group.

Mounties say at the time of Angoud’s arrest, he did not possess the materials needed to carry out the alleged plan.

“He did not have any products or anything else he could have used, so there was no imminent danger,” said RCMP Cpl. Martina Pillarova.

Police say Angoud is not a Canadian citizen and is currently in the country without legal status. He was scheduled to appear Thursday at the Montreal courthouse. The allegations against him have not been tested in court.

The charges he faces carry prison sentences ranging from 10 years to life imprisonment.

“Countering radicalization to violence is a top priority for the Government of Canada. The RCMP remains committed to countering religiously motivated violent extremism,” the RCMP’s Federal Policing Eastern Region said in a news release.

–With files from La Presse Canadienne

stories.title: Power restored for Hydro One customers in Huron, Perth Counties
stories.summary: Power has been restored for thousands of Hydro One customers in Huron and Perth Counties.
stories.author: Koylan Azofeifa Rueda
stories.content:
Power has been restored for thousands of Hydro One customers in Huron and Perth Counties.

Hydro One says at approximately 10 a.m. an outage occurred affecting 16,800 customers in parts of southwest Ontario.

Crews and the grid control centre worked to reroute power and restore customers in stages.

All customers were restored shortly after 3 p.m.

“Our helicopter is supporting crews with line patrols to try and determine the cause of the outage,” said Hydro One.

The power outage affected customers in Exeter, Zurich, Seaforth, Mitchell, and reached as far as St Marys.

stories.title: Western to build Bioconvergence Centre for transformative health research, impact
stories.summary: Western is constructing Canada's first purpose-built Bioconvergence Centre, accelerating health discoveries from lab to patient.
stories.author: Keri Ferguson
stories.content:
Western is constructing a new building in the heart of campus to deliver faster, more cohesive solutions to health challenges across Canada and the world.

The Bioconvergence Centre, an eight-storey, 383-000-square-foot facility, will be purpose-built to explore an emerging frontier that integrates biology with medicine, engineering, computational sciences and advanced technologies, such as AI, to accelerate commercialization of real-world interventions and treatments.

Researchers across disciplines will work side by side with industry partners in integrated labs to better understand what drives disease. Together, they will be able to move faster to develop advanced biotherapeutics – tailored therapies harnessing the body’s natural ability to fight disease.

The centre will also provide a vibrant training ground for the next generation of innovators.

Plans for the building, approved by Western’s Board of Governors Sept. 24, come at a turning point for health innovation in Canada. Western President Alan Shepard said Western has the strength and momentum to help lead a national bioconvergence strategy.

“We’ve entered a new era of health care, where life-changing breakthroughs are within our grasp,” Shepard said. “Western has a long record of global impact in health research, from early contributions to insulin to advances in cancer treatment, transplant medicine and medical imaging. The Bioconvergence Centre will build on that legacy, leveraging our expertise in biotherapeutics, medical devices, biomaterials, neuroscience and regenerative medicine.”

Shepard also spoke to the value of Western’s long-standing ties to hospitals and clinicians within London’s “world-leading hub for health innovation.”

“Our connections across Southwestern Ontario give us access to diverse health systems for clinical trials and partnerships with life sciences and manufacturing companies,” he said.

Artist rendering of exterior of Western’s Bioconvergence Centre. (HOK/aTRR)

The Bioconvergence Centre will be located between the Schulich School of Medicine & Dentistry and the Faculty of Science, on the site currently occupied by the Molecular Biology Laboratory, Health Sciences Addition, Kresge and Natural Sciences Centre buildings.

Construction is expected to start in 2027, with the building set to open in 2031.

Upon completion, Western will join a handful of globally recognized institutes in the bioconvergence field – Harvard, MIT, Stanford and UC Berkeley. Western’s will be the first centre in Canada built specifically for bioconvergence.

Its focus will be turning research into real-world patient care through biotherapeutics, precision medicine, medical devices and wearable devices, using tools and systems including data science and AI, molecular technologies and clinical trials.

The building’s design – with interdisciplinarity embedded in its very structure, bringing researchers from diverse fields together to solve challenges – was created to drive creative answers and advancements to critical health questions.

The centre’s model will help remove barriers standing in the way of innovative ideas.

“Canadians are facing increasingly complex challenges, including higher rates of cancer, neurodegenerative disease and chronic illness, compounded by an aging population. At the same time, scientific breakthroughs are accelerating,” said Florentine Strzelczyk, Western’s provost and vice-president (academic). “The problem is not a lack of talent, but the gap between discoveries and reaching the market and patients. Western’s Bioconvergence Centre is designed to close that gap.”

Artist rendering of interior of Western’s Bioconvergence Centre. (HOK/aTRR)

Key features of Western’s Bioconvergence Centre include:

Advanced labs: Adjacent wet (biological sciences) and dry labs (computational analysis, AI and simulations) to foster discoveries that help researchers better understand disease pathology and drive new treatments.

“Super core” facilities: Offering a full spectrum of advanced equipment, managed by on-site technicians and shared across faculties and with hospital and industry partners, increasing effectiveness and efficiency.

Researchers driving discoveries: The centre will be home to 74 leading principal investigators and more than 570 researchers – including postdoctoral scholars and graduate trainees. It will also serve hundreds of visiting scholars and industry partners, strengthening Western’s competitiveness nationally and globally.

Artist rendering of Western’s Bioconvergence Centre. (HOK/aTRR)

The new space will enhance and deepen Western’s existing interdisciplinary strengths by intentionally bringing principal investigators together with industry partners to accelerate commercialization.

That collaboration is key to the vision of the Bioconvergence Centre, said Penny Pexman, Western’s vice-president (research).

“By bringing people together to identify problems earlier, we can test assumptions faster,” Pexman said. “Validating ideas and evaluating their readiness for wider use will be built into daily research, with industry partners engaged right from the start to share insights on market needs and regulatory pathways. That translates into strong economic development for our region and better health for Canadians.”

Western’s Bioconvergence Centre will also transform the future of biomedical education.

Students from Schulich Medicine & Dentistry, engineering, science and health sciences will benefit from a rich learning environment, using the same tools as researchers and clinicians and gaining experience working in a collaborative environment.

Clinical skills and simulation spaces will help prepare graduates to innovate, collaborate and lead in modern health systems. The building also features updated chemistry teaching and instructional facilities.

The building is designed by HOK, a global leader in interdisciplinary design, and architects Tillmann Ruth Robinson, a local firm with extensive knowledge of Western.

In addition to wet and dry lab spaces, the design features flexible, bookable space for external partners and plenty of spaces for researchers to collaborate and innovate with industry colleagues.

“Opportunities for imagination and new discoveries are embedded right in the architecture,” said Lynn Logan, vice-president (operations and finance).

The centre will be constructed with Canadian steel and timber, retaining and incorporating portals from the former historic buildings it replaces.

As it’s built, the Bioconvergence Centre project is expected to generate an estimated 400 to 550 jobs annually across construction, engineering, manufacturing, transportation, material supply and related sectors. Aligned with Western’s Climate and Sustainability Strategy, the building will be heated and cooled by geothermal energy systems, targeting LEED Gold certification.

“This centre will be a jewel at the core of Western’s campus – from its iconic presence and expanded core facilities to its potential to become a dynamic research hub that accelerates discovery and interdisciplinary collaboration,” Logan said.
