paragraphs: Western is constructing a new building in the heart of campus to deliver faster, more cohesive solutions to health challenges across Canada and the world.

The Bioconvergence Centre, an eight-storey, 383-000-square-foot facility, will be purpose-built to explore an emerging frontier that integrates biology with medicine, engineering, computational sciences and advanced technologies, such as AI, to accelerate commercialization of real-world interventions and treatments.

Researchers across disciplines will work side by side with industry partners in integrated labs to better understand what drives disease. Together, they will be able to move faster to develop advanced biotherapeutics – tailored therapies harnessing the body’s natural ability to fight disease.
The centre will also provide a vibrant training ground for the next generation of innovators.

Plans for the building, approved by Western’s Board of Governors Sept. 24, come at a turning point for health innovation in Canada. Western President Alan Shepard said Western has the strength and momentum to help lead a national bioconvergence strategy.

“We’ve entered a new era of health care, where life-changing breakthroughs are within our grasp,” Shepard said. “Western has a long record of global impact in health research, from early contributions to insulin to advances in cancer treatment, transplant medicine and medical imaging. The Bioconvergence Centre will build on that legacy, leveraging our expertise in biotherapeutics, medical devices, biomaterials, neuroscience and regenerative medicine.”
Shepard also spoke to the value of Western’s long-standing ties to hospitals and clinicians within London’s “world-leading hub for health innovation.”
“Our connections across Southwestern Ontario give us access to diverse health systems for clinical trials and partnerships with life sciences and manufacturing companies,” he said.
Artist rendering of exterior of Western’s Bioconvergence Centre. (HOK/aTRR)

The Bioconvergence Centre will be located between the Schulich School of Medicine & Dentistry and the Faculty of Science, on the site currently occupied by the Molecular Biology Laboratory, Health Sciences Addition, Kresge and Natural Sciences Centre buildings.
Construction is expected to start in 2027, with the building set to open in 2031.

Upon completion, Western will join a handful of globally recognized institutes in the bioconvergence field – Harvard, MIT, Stanford and UC Berkeley. Western’s will be the first centre in Canada built specifically for bioconvergence.

Its focus will be turning research into real-world patient care through biotherapeutics, precision medicine, medical devices and wearable devices, using tools and systems including data science and AI, molecular technologies and clinical trials.

The building’s design – with interdisciplinarity embedded in its very structure, bringing researchers from diverse fields together to solve challenges – was created to drive creative answers and advancements to critical health questions.
The centre’s model will help remove barriers standing in the way of innovative ideas.

“Canadians are facing increasingly complex challenges, including higher rates of cancer, neurodegenerative disease and chronic illness, compounded by an aging population. At the same time, scientific breakthroughs are accelerating,” said Florentine Strzelczyk, Western’s provost and vice-president (academic). “The problem is not a lack of talent, but the gap between discoveries and reaching the market and patients. Western’s Bioconvergence Centre is designed to close that gap.”
Artist rendering of interior of Western’s Bioconvergence Centre. (HOK/aTRR)
Key features of Western’s Bioconvergence Centre include:

Advanced labs: Adjacent wet (biological sciences) and dry labs (computational analysis, AI and simulations) to foster discoveries that help researchers better understand disease pathology and drive new treatments.

“Super core” facilities: Offering a full spectrum of advanced equipment, managed by on-site technicians and shared across faculties and with hospital and industry partners, increasing effectiveness and efficiency.

Researchers driving discoveries: The centre will be home to 74 leading principal investigators and more than 570 researchers – including postdoctoral scholars and graduate trainees. It will also serve hundreds of visiting scholars and industry partners, strengthening Western’s competitiveness nationally and globally.
Artist rendering of Western’s Bioconvergence Centre. (HOK/aTRR)
The new space will enhance and deepen Western’s existing interdisciplinary strengths by intentionally bringing principal investigators together with industry partners to accelerate commercialization.
That collaboration is key to the vision of the Bioconvergence Centre, said Penny Pexman, Western’s vice-president (research).

“By bringing people together to identify problems earlier, we can test assumptions faster,” Pexman said. “Validating ideas and evaluating their readiness for wider use will be built into daily research, with industry partners engaged right from the start to share insights on market needs and regulatory pathways. That translates into strong economic development for our region and better health for Canadians.”
Western’s Bioconvergence Centre will also transform the future of biomedical education.

Students from Schulich Medicine & Dentistry, engineering, science and health sciences will benefit from a rich learning environment, using the same tools as researchers and clinicians and gaining experience working in a collaborative environment.

Clinical skills and simulation spaces will help prepare graduates to innovate, collaborate and lead in modern health systems. The building also features updated chemistry teaching and instructional facilities.
The building is designed by HOK, a global leader in interdisciplinary design, and architects Tillmann Ruth Robinson, a local firm with extensive knowledge of Western.
In addition to wet and dry lab spaces, the design features flexible, bookable space for external partners and plenty of spaces for researchers to collaborate and innovate with industry colleagues.
“Opportunities for imagination and new discoveries are embedded right in the architecture,” said Lynn Logan, vice-president (operations and finance).
The centre will be constructed with Canadian steel and timber, retaining and incorporating portals from the former historic buildings it replaces.

As it’s built, the Bioconvergence Centre project is expected to generate an estimated 400 to 550 jobs annually across construction, engineering, manufacturing, transportation, material supply and related sectors. Aligned with Western’s Climate and Sustainability Strategy, the building will be heated and cooled by geothermal energy systems, targeting LEED Gold certification.

“This centre will be a jewel at the core of Western’s campus – from its iconic presence and expanded core facilities to its potential to become a dynamic research hub that accelerates discovery and interdisciplinary collaboration,” Logan said.

stories.title: OpenAI’s agent hacked an Australian government website. What we know so far
stories.summary: The hack relates to the website for Medicare, Australia’s publicly funded universal health insurance plan, which was hacked in June.
stories.author: Uday Rana
stories.content:
Concerns around the dangers of artificial intelligence are escalating sharply after Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese revealed on Wednesday that a government website has been hacked by an OpenAI agent.

The June hack targeted the website for Medicare, Australia’s publicly funded universal health insurance plan, he said.

“I want to update Australians on an incident in which an artificial intelligence agent has infiltrated an Australian government website. This incident occurred in June this year and involved an open AI agent gaining unauthorized access into the public facing Medicare Statistics Reporting Service portal,” Albanese told reporters in New York Wednesday, where he is attending a session of the United Nations General Assembly.

The AI agent accessed “both public and non-public files,” Albanese said.

OpenAI said in a statement it had reviewed activity involving several Australian government departments and discovered “our models took actions we did not intend.”

The company notified Australia of the breach in an email to a government department’s generic address on Sept. 10, Albanese said.

“I spoke with the CEO of OpenAI, Sam Altman, to express Australia’s extreme concern about this incident,” he said, adding that he was forming a task force to “to provide an urgent and immediate review into this incident to determine whether existing processes are appropriate to respond to AI-related cyber incidents.”

Global News has reached out to AI Minister Evan Solomon’s office asking whether Canada also plans to review its safety regulations in light of the Australian hack.

Australia’s Government Services Minister Katy Gallagher said OpenAI had advised on Sept. 10 that an “AI agent had accessed infrastructure behind the public-facing” portal. OpenAI shared with the government the vulnerability the agent had found.

The Australian government had not been confident that it knew what the agent had been doing until officials held a technical briefing with OpenAI on Tuesday, Gallagher said.

Australian Deputy Prime Minister Richard Marles said the incident is the first time that an AI agent is known to have gained unauthorized access to the Australian government’s information technology systems.

2:08 AI could ‘kill all humans’ within next decade, top researcher warns

Altman was among heads of major AI firms who in speeches Wednesday to the United Nations called for regulating the fast-expanding technology that companies like his have been designing, despite the companies themselves taking few, if any, steps to scale back developments or wait for regulations.

“We could lose control of the future to AI. The risk is that it moves so fast that people can no longer follow what’s happening or intervene when needed,” Altman told the United Nations.

“This would obviously be terrible,” he added.

2:34 Trump downplays AI warnings as concerns grow

While this is the first time a government website has been hacked by a rogue AI agent, it is not the first such incident overall.

In July, OpenAI revealed that its artificial intelligence system escaped from a testing ground and used stolen credentials to break into the servers of Hugging Face, an AI development hub and marketplace, to obtain information it needed to carry out a task.

Since then, OpenAI’s rival company Anthropic said its AI models hacked into three other organizations during testing, triggering a company review into whether the models were able to access the internet from within testing environments that should have been sealed off.

Meta has said a “misconfiguration” during testing resulted in an AI model accessing the internet on its own and hacking another company. Google recently made a similar disclosure.

Generally, when AI companies are testing the capabilities of their agents, they are placed within a secure environment known as a “sandbox.”

“Normally when we use an AI agent, it has a very well-tested sandbox and it’s very difficult to break out of that box as a user and also the AI itself breaking out of its constraints,” said Randy Fortier, computer science professor at Ontario Tech University.

Last month, OpenAI published a sweeping report of its rogue AI agents hacking Hugging Face.

Not only did the agents break out of their “isolated environment,” the company said they were communicating with each other to coordinate the attack on Hugging Face.

“This incident demonstrated that autonomous agents can work together, circumvent production security controls, and successfully attack hardened production environments, and underscores the need for organizations to update their security strategies, controls, and response capabilities to address this changing threat landscape,” OpenAI said in the report.

The attack on Hugging Face was “extraordinarily complex,” an investigation by nonprofit research group Model Evaluation and Threat Research (METR) found.

During OpenAI’s experiments in July, 1,200 AI agents sent 70,000 messages to each other on unsanctioned message boards and 700 of them attacked Hugging Face, the investigation found.

“These agents were meant to be fully isolated from one another,” the report said, adding however that the agents “started trying to find a way to cheat.”

These incidents have become more frequent with AI companies “trying to push it into the cybersecurity industry,” Fortier said.

The priority of any regulations on AI should be “security first and capabilities next,” he added.

“I do think that more guardrails and more attention to the guardrails is something that we should be doing, which will, of course, slow it (AI development) down” he said.

While Altman told the UN that there was a need for “accurate and speedy incident reporting,” Fortier said it is not clear how swiftly OpenAI informed the Australian government of the breach.

“I do think that’s a little bit irresponsible because if there’s a vulnerability, at the very least, they (Australia) should have been notified (immediately) so that they could close up the vulnerability for threat actors,” he said.

Altman on Wednesday called on world leaders to ensure the “safeguards are sufficient” when it comes to AI.

“We do not have all the answers and we are very open to any better ideas. We are ready to work with you all and try our hardest to figure out the path forward,” Altman said.

“We are at a crossroads.”

–with files from Associated Press

stories.title: Definitions in Ottawa's budget framework are inconsistent: fiscal watchdog
stories.summary: Ottawa’s fiscal watchdog says the way the Liberal government defines certain types of spending in its new budget framework can be inconsistent.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa — Ottawa’s fiscal watchdog says the way the Liberal government defines certain types of spending in its new budget framework can be inconsistent and contradictory.

The Liberals under Prime Minister Mark Carney introduced a new budget framework that divides spending between day-to-day operating expenses and measures to stimulate capital investment.

A report released Thursday by the office of parliamentary budget officer Annette Ryan attempts to track Ottawa’s path to balancing the operating side of the budget — a key fiscal anchor set by the Carney government.

Latest economic news on BNNBloomberg.CA

The budget office says the government is improving fiscal transparency in some ways by offering explanations of how certain tax incentives, loan guarantees and other measures — the kind that normally would fall outside traditional accounting definitions of capital spending — are helping to meet its fiscal anchor.

But the PBO also argues the way Ottawa defines its operating and capital categories isn’t as stringent as the definition used in other jurisdictions that use a similar framework, such as the United Kingdom and Singapore.

For example, two programs under Agriculture and Agri-Food Canada appear contradictory in their accounting. The Agricultural Clean Technology and Agricultural Climate Solutions programs both encourage farms to invest in technology to reduce greenhouse gas emissions — but only the former program is considered capital spending under the framework.

The PBO says it found a broad pattern of spending programs like these that could arguably be classified as either operating or capital. The lack of “consistent, published rationale” on how to classify spending makes it hard to judge how future spending decisions will be sorted, the office says.

“Classification-based fiscal rules like the operating budget fiscal anchor do not limit overall government borrowing, and there is a risk that the classification definition can be arbitrary or change over time,” the report says.

Carney said last week the federal government is on track to balance its operating budget in fiscal 2027-28 — a year earlier than first promised.

The PBO projections anticipate Ottawa will instead hit that marker a year late, in fiscal 2029-30. Those estimates are based on federal figures as of the spring economic update in April, and do not include spending announcements or revenue changes over the summer.

John Fragos, spokesperson for Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne, said Thursday the government is sticking by its pledge to balance the operating budget a year early.

“A persistent commitment to fiscal prudence, discipline, and spending efficiency — underpinned by the government’s $60 billion in savings — has moved up balancing the operating budget agenda by a whole year despite today’s report purporting otherwise,” he said in a statement.

He said a focus on reducing operating expenditures is a “stricter guardrail” for federal finances than ratios like debt-to-GDP. The federal government’s other fiscal anchor is maintaining a declining deficit-to-GDP ratio.

The PBO notes that in its projection stating the government will miss balancing the operating budget in 2028-29, the deficit posted in that fiscal year is relatively small.

But that only shows how the Liberals’ subjective definitions of capital and operating spending can influence the government’s ability to meet its fiscal targets, the PBO argues.

“Classifying even a modest amount of spending as capital rather than operating, without any actual change in fiscal policy, May have been relevant to balance the initial operating budget fiscal track,” the report says.

Craig Lord, The Canadian Press

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 24, 2026.

stories.title: Pwhl to host all-star event for first time in Toronto
stories.summary: The Professional Women's Hockey League (Pwhl) will host an all-star event for the first time on March 7, 2027 in Toronto.
stories.author: Meredith Bond
stories.content:
The Professional Women’s Hockey League will return to a city it knows well for another league first later this season.

After holding the first-ever PWHL draft and first-ever PWHL game in Toronto, the league plans to host its first PWHL All-Star event in the Ontario capital on March 7.

The four-team three-on-three tournament will be played at Scotiabank Arena, the league announced Thursday.

“We wanted to find a place that made a lot of sense for the league and for the history of the sport and obviously found that here,” PWHL executive vice-president of hockey operations Jayna Hefford said after a news conference at the Hockey Hall of Fame.

Team names will include PWHL Canada, PWHL International, PWHL USA and PWHL Rookies. Each team will consist of a 10-player roster with six forwards, three defenders and one goaltender.

At the completion of round-robin play, the second- and third-ranked teams will play in a semifinal game. The winner will meet the first-ranked team in the final.

“Trying to find a way to make it really fun for our fans, to make something our players want to be a part of, make it competitive, but also be a great showcase for the women’s game is really important,” Hefford said.

Toronto and New York played in the first PWHL game on Jan. 1, 2024 at the Mattamy Athletic Centre, just over three months after the inaugural league draft.

PWHL players participated in a three-on-three showcase in February 2024 as part of the NHL’s all-star weekend at Scotiabank Arena.

Full PWHL all-star event details, including voting, roster construction, ticketing, and full gameplay rules will be announced closer to the event, the league said.

“It’s a big moment for our league,” said Amy Scheer, the PWHL’s executive vice-president of business operations. “It’s an event that is just about the PWHL. While we love our big brothers in the NHL, it’s a weekend where we can showcase our players and our personalities and really have an event for our fans and for our league.

“So a big moment for us and it’s an important one to be separate.”

The 12-team PWHL — which includes four expansion teams this season — is expected to kick off its 2026-27 campaign in late November or early December.

TSN will provide English-language coverage of the all-star event and Radio-Canada will provide French-language coverage, the league said.

The PWHL has yet to announce its Canadian broadcast coverage plans for the 2026-27 season. Scheer said the previous Canadian rights-holders would be returning and an announcement on specifics was expected next week.

All-star starters will be selected through a combination of fan, player, and media voting. Reserve players will be selected by league hockey operations.

“I think it is an awesome way to incorporate such a great mix of the players and a good representation of everybody, and I think its very exciting,” said Montreal Victoire alternate captain Laura Stacey, who is also PWHL Players’ Association president. “It just instils some of that competitiveness that we all have in us.”

Last month, PWHL advisory board member Stan Kasten confirmed the governance of the league would remain stable even as co-founder Mark Walter appears to be selling off pieces of his sports empire amid U.S. federal investigations into loans between his insurance companies and businesses with ties to Walter.

Hefford said “nothing has changed from our perspective.”

“We are fortunate to have the ownership we have,” she said. “We continue to grow and have the support we need to help this league grow and the sport grow. So nothing but excitement as we look forward.”

Training camps for the upcoming season will open Nov. 18 after the completion of the Nov. 6-16 IIHF Women’s World Championship in Herning and Esbjerg, Denmark.

“We’ve had a lot on our plate the first few years and each year we try to build out something else that’s new,” Hefford said. “Now that we’re at 12 teams and 180 games, it felt like this was a great time to introduce an all-star event for the first time.”

stories.title: Institutional failures, dismissed warning signs factors in deaths of eight children, report says
stories.summary: Report Thursday analyzed the deaths of eight children in five different cases
stories.author: Anja Karadeglija
stories.content:
A new report on child murders says institutional failures – and warnings from mothers that officials dismissed – played a role in the deaths of eight children in Canada.

“Our analysis reveals that significant warning signs were present before each death but did not result in adequate protective action,” says the report, drafted by the National Association of Women and the Law and law professors at the University of Sherbrooke.

“Mothers (and, in one case, a grandmother) who had previously identified safety risks were disbelieved or penalized, while the children were left in contact with fathers whose abusive conduct was already known to institutions,” the report says.

The report, published Thursday, analyzes the deaths of eight children in five different cases. It says in all of the cases, family members expressed concerns about the safety of the children and “repeatedly reached out” to police and family courts.

In one 2019 case, a seven-year-old girl was found unconscious in her room in Granby, Que., and later died in hospital. She had been placed in her father’s custody after being raised by her paternal grandparents.

Her grandmother had warned authorities there was a serious risk of sexual abuse, the report says.

But she “lost custody after being perceived as hostile for reporting the dangers the girl was exposed to while in her son’s care,” the report says.

The report cites several institutional failures in the case. It says the director of youth protection did not push for home visits and no action was taken after the girl was removed from school for a month.

The report says the child’s stepmother was found guilty of manslaughter and false imprisonment and the father pleaded guilty to false imprisonment.

The report authors are scheduled to present their work at a press conference on Parliament Hill Thursday morning.

They will be joined by Liberal MP Lisa Hepfner, who has introduced a private member’s bill that looks to curb parental alienation claims.

Her proposed legislation says a court, with some exceptions, “shall not take into consideration any allegation that a spouse has, or is likely to, through deliberate manipulation, persuade or encourage a child to become estranged from or resist contact with the other spouse.”

The report says the concept of parental alienation is frequently invoked in Canada’s courts. It says it’s used by parties in child custody cases to explain why a child resists seeing a parent, and to cast doubt on allegations of domestic violence.

“By interpreting a child’s resistance or a protective parent’s warning signs as manipulation rather than as an indicator of danger, institutions may contribute to maintaining or imposing contact with an abusive parent, thereby increasing the child’s vulnerability,” the report says.

Hepfner’s bill would also make other changes to the Divorce Act. It would impose new requirements on lawyers to screen for signs of family violence during divorce cases.

It also would give judges new tools to identify the existence and impact of coercive control on children and to ensure that, in some circumstances, children can express their preferences to a judge in a custody dispute.
paragraphs: A new report on child murders says institutional failures – and warnings from mothers that officials dismissed – played a role in the deaths of eight children in Canada.

“Our analysis reveals that significant warning signs were present before each death but did not result in adequate protective action,” says the report, drafted by the National Association of Women and the Law and law professors at the University of Sherbrooke.

“Mothers (and, in one case, a grandmother) who had previously identified safety risks were disbelieved or penalized, while the children were left in contact with fathers whose abusive conduct was already known to institutions,” the report says.

The report, published Thursday, analyzes the deaths of eight children in five different cases. It says in all of the cases, family members expressed concerns about the safety of the children and “repeatedly reached out” to police and family courts.

In one 2019 case, a seven-year-old girl was found unconscious in her room in Granby, Que., and later died in hospital. She had been placed in her father’s custody after being raised by her paternal grandparents.
Her grandmother had warned authorities there was a serious risk of sexual abuse, the report says.
But she “lost custody after being perceived as hostile for reporting the dangers the girl was exposed to while in her son’s care,” the report says.

The report cites several institutional failures in the case. It says the director of youth protection did not push for home visits and no action was taken after the girl was removed from school for a month.
The report says the child’s stepmother was found guilty of manslaughter and false imprisonment and the father pleaded guilty to false imprisonment.

stories.title: Man arrested in Ontario for promoting anti-Muslim violence online: police
stories.summary: "Acts that target, intimidate, threaten, or instill fear" are unacceptable and "will be thoroughly investigated," police said.
stories.author: Courtney Greenberg
stories.content:
Canada

'Acts that target, intimidate, threaten, or instill fear' are unacceptable and 'will be thoroughly investigated,' police said.

A new Durham Regional Police helicopter at Oshawa Airport.Photo by Jack Boland /Jack Boland/Toronto Sun

A 57-year-old man has been arrested for promoting anti-Muslim violence online, according to Durham Regional Police.

The Whitby resident identified as Sean Farro was charged on Wednesday with uttering threats and inciting hatred in a public place.

“The suspect willfully incited violence and harm against the Muslim community on social media platforms under the name ‘Sean Strife,'” police said in a news release.

“Acts that target, intimidate, threaten, or instill fear in any individual or group are unacceptable and will be thoroughly investigated.”

This arrest comes days after the Sept. 19 arrest of another Whitby man, 19-year-old Alexander Parfitt, who police said made threats online about shooting a synagogue.

In an unrelated incident, a suspect identified by police as Sean Ward shot a police officer stationed outside of a synagogue in Belleville, Ont. on Sept. 20. The officer, Const. Jeff Smith, was critically injured but is in stable condition.

The shooting occurred on Yom Kippur, the holiest day for the Jewish community.

None of the roughly 25 congregants inside the synagogue were injured.

Ward was injured in a shootout with police and was taken to hospital in life-threatening condition. He died on Tuesday.

stories.title: This dairy-free dessert is being recalled. Here’s why.
stories.summary: The Canadian Food Inspection Agency has published a recall for a brand of dairy-free frozen desserts due to “plastic-like” and “gravel-like fragments.”
stories.author: Devika Desai
stories.content:
The Canadian Food Inspection Agency (Cfia) has published a recall for a brand of dairy-free frozen desserts due to “plastic-like” and “gravel-like fragments.”

The notice from Sept. 22 affects 500-ml products of So Delicious Dairy Free salted caramel with a cashew base.

The products have a best-before date of Sept. 8 2027, Oct. 15 and 16 in 2027, Feb. 3 and 25 in 2028, and March 30 and 31 in 2028.

Consumers are advised to not use, sell, serve or distribute the affected product.

Caitlin Gray, external communications adviser for Sobeys, confirmed on Thursday that the recalled products have been removed from all banner stores in all regions.

The banner stores include FreshCo, Safeway, IGA and Foodland. The products have also been removed from Voilà by Sobeys, an online grocery delivery service owned by Sobeys’ parent company, Empire Company Ltd.

Danone Inc., the company that produces the products, issued its own recall notice in the U.S. on Sept. 15.

The notice affects all pints with best-by dates on and before April 3, 2028, due to the presence of “foreign materials,” such as small stones and other hard objects within the cashew inclusions.

The U.S. notice stated that the issue had been identified via consumer complaints and that the U.S. Food and Drug Administration has been informed of the recall. It added that unaffected product is still on shelves in retail stores and product shipped going forward is not affected by the recall.

A similar food recall notice was posted by the Cfia on Jan. 2, 2026, which applied to all pints with best-before dates from Feb. 13 of this year to July 10, 2027.

stories.title: 5 reasons to be optimistic about Raptors entering 2026-27 season
stories.summary: It was pretty easy to be optimistic about the Toronto Raptors back in May, when they were coming off a dramatic seven-game first-round loss to the Cleveland Cavaliers, which was the exclamation point on a 46-win regular season that represented a 16-win jump from the year before. Scottie Barnes opened eyes around the NBA with […]
stories.author: Lucas Casaletto
stories.content:
By Michael Grange, Sportsnet

Posted September 24, 2026 10:20 am.

It was pretty easy to be optimistic about the Toronto Raptors back in May, when they were coming off a dramatic seven-game first-round loss to the Cleveland Cavaliers, which was the exclamation point on a 46-win regular season that represented a 16-win jump from the year before.

Scottie Barnes opened eyes around the NBA with his dominant two-way showing against the Cavs, where he was the best player on either team and perhaps for the first time showed his potential to be the kind of player that teams can load with their wildest dreams.

The team’s youngsters grew up fast, with Jamal Shead, Ja’Kobe Walter and (then) rookie Collin Murray-Boyles building on strong regular seasons, collectively, by showing some real spark in the playoffs. RJ Barrett also proved himself a playoff riser, with his determination to crack the paint giving the Raptors’ offence just the gas required at key moments.

But as configured, was anyone looking at the Raptors as a team that could challenge the Eastern Conference elite? Were dreams of a run to the conference finals or beyond shared anywhere other than the most fervent, fanciful corners of the Raptors multiverse?

Not really. This was a team that was 0-5 in the season series against the eventual NBA champion New York Knicks and finished the regular season 1-11 against the top three teams in the East and 1-12 against the top six teams in the West.

But things were about to change. Perhaps buoyed by pushing the eventual conference finalist Cavaliers to seven games, or maybe flush with the confidence of the new five-year contract he signed back in June, Raptors general manager Bobby Webster cashed in some chips and pulled off one of the most stunning moves of the off-season: acquiring Kawhi Leonard from the Los Angeles Clippers for Brandon Ingram, Gradey Dick, two unprotected first-round picks (2031 and 2033), a first-round pick swap in 2027 and two second-round picks (2030 and 2033).

In an instant — well, a very long instant, given an NBA investigation into the Clippers for salary-cap circumvention as it relates to Leonard that dragged on until early September and delayed the deal being finalized for 10 weeks — expectations for the Raptors took a massive leap.

So, yeah, to the extent it was easy to be optimistic about the Raptors in May, it’s really easy to be excited now, with training camp opening in Quebec City next Tuesday.

Let’s get right to it: Five reasons to be optimistic about the Raptors heading into the 2026-27 season.

No need to dance around it. When you add a seven-time all-NBA selection to your roster, your team is better. A lot better. A cynic might note that the Los Angeles Clippers had Kawhi Leonard on their roster for seven years and won just three playoff series, their high point a run to the Western Conference Finals in 2021. Twice Leonard was injured and couldn’t complete a first-round series.

But we’re trying to be optimistic here.

In the 35 playoff games he did play for Los Angeles, Leonard averaged 27.7 points, 8.2 rebounds, 4.8 assists and two steals with a true shooting percentage (which reflects the value of free throws, two-pointers and three-pointers) of 62.8. No one in NBA history has ever done all of that. And while a lot has been made of Leonard coming off one of the best seasons of his career last year as he averaged 27.9 (a career best) with a TS% of 62.9 (a career best), while adding 2.0 steals per game and grabbing 6.4 rebounds, it’s worth pointing out that it might have been the best age-34 season in NBA history — no one has ever hit or surpassed all of those thresholds after age 32 — and one of the best seasons ever by any NBA player in their 30s.

He’s coming in hot, and relatively healthy, having suited up for 81 per cent of the Clippers games dating back to Jan. 23, 2025.

As an added bonus, Leonard’s specific strengths suit the Raptors perfectly: he’s one of the best ball hawks in NBA history and one of just five players in league history to average more steals (1.7) than fouls (1.6) for his career, meaning he should fit in just fine on one of the most aggressive defensive lineups in the league. He’s also an elite three-point shooter (39.1 per cent for his career) and especially effective pulling up from three, as his 37.9 per cent on deep pulls ranked second to only Jamal Murray among players with at least 60 games played and at least 3.5 pull-up attempts per game, which should help a Raptors team that ranked in the bottom third of the NBA in three-point attempts and percentage.

Obviously, the Raptors will be a different team with Leonard on the roster and Ingram with the Clippers, but they will most likely be a better version of the team they already were. Even when the Raptors were struggling under head coach Darko Rajakovic, they created a defensive identity that translated even as they became competitive last season. Recall that from Jan. 1, 2025, through the remainder of the 2024-25 season, the Raptors posted the seventh-best defensive rating in the NBA and were very nearly a .500 team — a stunning achievement for a club that was 7-26 on Dec. 31, 2024.

Last season, the Raptors won 46 games in large part because they finished tied for fifth in defensive rating, and fourth in percentage of loose balls recovered. All of that activity helped the Raptors to finish fifth in the NBA in percentage of their offence from opponent’s turnovers, a key boost for a team that struggled to score in the halfcourt.

Encouraging too is that all of those traits translated perfectly to the Raptors’ first-round series against the Cavaliers as the Raptors finished first among post-season teams in percentage of points off turnovers. Adding Leonard — a historically elite defensive player — should only enhance what the Raptors already do exceptionally well.

Leonard hasn’t spoken publicly since he rejoined the team, but in the most recent “Open Gym” episode — the Raptors’ typically excellent in-house documentary program — featuring footage from his visit to Toronto in early July, Leonard told Rajakovic: “If it’s Scottie’s team, it’s his team. I want to do whatever it takes to help you guys.”

The last time Leonard wasn’t the best player on his team, he was winning a championship alongside Hall of Famer Tim Duncan with the 2014 San Antonio Spurs. Presuming Barnes is the Raptors’ best player with Leonard on the roster is quite an assumption, given Leonard was second-team all-NBA last year — a level Barnes has yet to reach in five seasons.

But as Barnes enters his prime at age 25, it’s not crazy — especially after the Cleveland series where the Raptors’ two-time all-star scored more points than Cavs’ seven-time all-star Donovan Mitchell, more assists than (future) hall-of-fame point guard James Harden and more blocks than former defensive player of the year Evan Mobley.

It’s unfair to expect Barnes to match the line he put up against the Cavs (24.1 points, 8.6 assists, 6.1 rebounds with 1.1 steals and 1.7 blocks) for an entire season, but his performance was the most definitive proof yet that Barnes is capable of beating good teams with his offensive force — a prerequisite to being a top 10 player.

Even if Barnes goes for 22/7/7 this season and delivers the type of defence that earned him all-defence recognition for the first time last year, it might be enough to at least vie with Leonard as the Raptors’ best player. That would make the Raptors a very dangerous team.

This time a year ago, one of the Raptors’ biggest question marks was if the likes of Dick, Walter, Shead and rookie Murray-Boyles were ready for NBA prime time. That’s not really a question anymore, for better or worse.

After a promising second season, Dick fell off in his third year, never finding his shooting stroke and eventually falling out of Rajakovic’s rotation, which is why the Raptors were willing to include him in the trade for Leonard. Dick could end up the rare draft miss for the Raptors, but the progress of Walter and Shead in their second seasons counterbalances that, and the emergence of Murray-Boyles as an all-NBA level defender as a rookie is the kind of draft win that can change the direction of a team.

First, Walter: the second-year wing shot an eye-popping 47.6 per cent from three after the all-star break last season and also averaged 1.2 steals per game in just 24 minutes of floor time. A low-usage, offensively efficient wing who can guard at age 22 and is still on his rookie contract? Hard to do better than that when picking 19th, as the Raptors were in 2024 when they chose Walter there (and for what it’s worth, Allen Graves, who the Raptors picked 19th overall in 2026, was outstanding in NBA Summer League).

Meanwhile, Shead emerged as a quality back-up point guard who can play effectively alongside starter Immanuel Quickley. Shead was one of just nine players in the league to average at least five assists and make 1.5 turnovers or less and was the only one to do it while playing all 82 games.

Murray-Boyles struggled through multiple thumb injuries as a rookie that limited him to just 57 games, but he still earned all-rookie honours. He averaged 2.3 offensive rebounds per game (second among rookies), blocked 0.9 shots (second) and shot 57.9 per cent from the floor (second). His 0.9 steals per game was seventh among rookies, but everyone ahead of him on the list played significantly more minutes than the 21.9 minutes per game Murray-Boyles did.

But it was in the eye test where Murray-Boyles excelled the most, as his combination of size, strength, quickness and feel on both ends of the floor made him a game changer defensively and almost always a positive addition offensively. And then he averaged 14.4 points, 6.4 rebounds, 1.3 steals and 1.1 blocks while shooting 65.6 per cent from the floor against Cleveland’s big-man duo of Mobley and Jarrett Allen.

Did we mention the Raptors’ best shooter is likely third-year wing Jamison Battle? If the youngsters pick up where they left off, collectively, the Raptors rotation will be deeper and better than could possibly have been predicted a year ago.

If we’re being honest, it’s going to be really, really hard for the Raptors to emerge as the ‘winners’ of the 2023 trade that sent Anunoby to the New York Knicks in exchange for Barrett and Quickley. Anunoby has proven himself as the best defence-first wing in the league and delivered at the highest level possible as the Knicks won the NBA championship this past June.

All of that said, Barrett followed up an impressive regular season by averaging 24.1 points, 7.0 rebounds and 4.0 assists on strong shooting splits against Cleveland in the playoffs. He showed a strong ability to pound the paint, finishing third in points in the paint in the playoffs with 12.6 and was in the top 25 during the regular season among players with at least 50 games played.

Meanwhile, Quickley’s absence in the playoffs due to a hamstring pull could well have been the difference in the Raptors advancing to the second round or not. He was only one of six players to average at least 16 points (16.4), 5.5 assists (5.9), 1.2 steals (1.3) and 2.5 made threes last season — joining the likes of Donovan Mitchell, LaMelo Ball, Luka Doncic and Tyrese Maxey. And while Quickley hasn’t always shown that ‘sixth sense’ that the most elite point guards seem to have, he takes care of the ball (just 1.5 turnovers per game) and was a competitive all-around defender last season.

The Knicks got the best player, but Barrett and Quickley have shown they can be helpful starters on a playoff team, and there is reason to believe that at age 26 and 27, respectively, there is still another level each of them can reach.

So, yeah, to the extent it was easy to be optimistic about the Raptors in May, it’s really easy to be excited now, with training camp opening in Quebec City next Tuesday.
Let’s get right to it: Five reasons to be optimistic about the Raptors heading into the 2026-27 season.

No need to dance around it. When you add a seven-time all-NBA selection to your roster, your team is better. A lot better. A cynic might note that the Los Angeles Clippers had Kawhi Leonard on their roster for seven years and won just three playoff series, their high point a run to the Western Conference Finals in 2021. Twice Leonard was injured and couldn’t complete a first-round series.
But we’re trying to be optimistic here.

In the 35 playoff games he did play for Los Angeles, Leonard averaged 27.7 points, 8.2 rebounds, 4.8 assists and two steals with a true shooting percentage (which reflects the value of free throws, two-pointers and three-pointers) of 62.8. No one in NBA history has ever done all of that. And while a lot has been made of Leonard coming off one of the best seasons of his career last year as he averaged 27.9 (a career best) with a TS% of 62.9 (a career best), while adding 2.0 steals per game and grabbing 6.4 rebounds, it’s worth pointing out that it might have been the best age-34 season in NBA history — no one has ever hit or surpassed all of those thresholds after age 32 — and one of the best seasons ever by any NBA player in their 30s.
He’s coming in hot, and relatively healthy, having suited up for 81 per cent of the Clippers games dating back to Jan. 23, 2025.

As an added bonus, Leonard’s specific strengths suit the Raptors perfectly: he’s one of the best ball hawks in NBA history and one of just five players in league history to average more steals (1.7) than fouls (1.6) for his career, meaning he should fit in just fine on one of the most aggressive defensive lineups in the league. He’s also an elite three-point shooter (39.1 per cent for his career) and especially effective pulling up from three, as his 37.9 per cent on deep pulls ranked second to only Jamal Murray among players with at least 60 games played and at least 3.5 pull-up attempts per game, which should help a Raptors team that ranked in the bottom third of the NBA in three-point attempts and percentage.

Obviously, the Raptors will be a different team with Leonard on the roster and Ingram with the Clippers, but they will most likely be a better version of the team they already were. Even when the Raptors were struggling under head coach Darko Rajakovic, they created a defensive identity that translated even as they became competitive last season. Recall that from Jan. 1, 2025, through the remainder of the 2024-25 season, the Raptors posted the seventh-best defensive rating in the NBA and were very nearly a .500 team — a stunning achievement for a club that was 7-26 on Dec. 31, 2024.

Last season, the Raptors won 46 games in large part because they finished tied for fifth in defensive rating, and fourth in percentage of loose balls recovered. All of that activity helped the Raptors to finish fifth in the NBA in percentage of their offence from opponent’s turnovers, a key boost for a team that struggled to score in the halfcourt.

Encouraging too is that all of those traits translated perfectly to the Raptors’ first-round series against the Cavaliers as the Raptors finished first among post-season teams in percentage of points off turnovers. Adding Leonard — a historically elite defensive player — should only enhance what the Raptors already do exceptionally well.

Leonard hasn’t spoken publicly since he rejoined the team, but in the most recent “Open Gym” episode — the Raptors’ typically excellent in-house documentary program — featuring footage from his visit to Toronto in early July, Leonard told Rajakovic: “If it’s Scottie’s team, it’s his team. I want to do whatever it takes to help you guys.”

The last time Leonard wasn’t the best player on his team, he was winning a championship alongside Hall of Famer Tim Duncan with the 2014 San Antonio Spurs. Presuming Barnes is the Raptors’ best player with Leonard on the roster is quite an assumption, given Leonard was second-team all-NBA last year — a level Barnes has yet to reach in five seasons.

But as Barnes enters his prime at age 25, it’s not crazy — especially after the Cleveland series where the Raptors’ two-time all-star scored more points than Cavs’ seven-time all-star Donovan Mitchell, more assists than (future) hall-of-fame point guard James Harden and more blocks than former defensive player of the year Evan Mobley.

It’s unfair to expect Barnes to match the line he put up against the Cavs (24.1 points, 8.6 assists, 6.1 rebounds with 1.1 steals and 1.7 blocks) for an entire season, but his performance was the most definitive proof yet that Barnes is capable of beating good teams with his offensive force — a prerequisite to being a top 10 player.

Even if Barnes goes for 22/7/7 this season and delivers the type of defence that earned him all-defence recognition for the first time last year, it might be enough to at least vie with Leonard as the Raptors’ best player. That would make the Raptors a very dangerous team.

This time a year ago, one of the Raptors’ biggest question marks was if the likes of Dick, Walter, Shead and rookie Murray-Boyles were ready for NBA prime time. That’s not really a question anymore, for better or worse.

After a promising second season, Dick fell off in his third year, never finding his shooting stroke and eventually falling out of Rajakovic’s rotation, which is why the Raptors were willing to include him in the trade for Leonard. Dick could end up the rare draft miss for the Raptors, but the progress of Walter and Shead in their second seasons counterbalances that, and the emergence of Murray-Boyles as an all-NBA level defender as a rookie is the kind of draft win that can change the direction of a team.

First, Walter: the second-year wing shot an eye-popping 47.6 per cent from three after the all-star break last season and also averaged 1.2 steals per game in just 24 minutes of floor time. A low-usage, offensively efficient wing who can guard at age 22 and is still on his rookie contract? Hard to do better than that when picking 19th, as the Raptors were in 2024 when they chose Walter there (and for what it’s worth, Allen Graves, who the Raptors picked 19th overall in 2026, was outstanding in NBA Summer League).

Meanwhile, Shead emerged as a quality back-up point guard who can play effectively alongside starter Immanuel Quickley. Shead was one of just nine players in the league to average at least five assists and make 1.5 turnovers or less and was the only one to do it while playing all 82 games.

Murray-Boyles struggled through multiple thumb injuries as a rookie that limited him to just 57 games, but he still earned all-rookie honours. He averaged 2.3 offensive rebounds per game (second among rookies), blocked 0.9 shots (second) and shot 57.9 per cent from the floor (second). His 0.9 steals per game was seventh among rookies, but everyone ahead of him on the list played significantly more minutes than the 21.9 minutes per game Murray-Boyles did.

But it was in the eye test where Murray-Boyles excelled the most, as his combination of size, strength, quickness and feel on both ends of the floor made him a game changer defensively and almost always a positive addition offensively. And then he averaged 14.4 points, 6.4 rebounds, 1.3 steals and 1.1 blocks while shooting 65.6 per cent from the floor against Cleveland’s big-man duo of Mobley and Jarrett Allen.

Did we mention the Raptors’ best shooter is likely third-year wing Jamison Battle? If the youngsters pick up where they left off, collectively, the Raptors rotation will be deeper and better than could possibly have been predicted a year ago.

If we’re being honest, it’s going to be really, really hard for the Raptors to emerge as the ‘winners’ of the 2023 trade that sent Anunoby to the New York Knicks in exchange for Barrett and Quickley. Anunoby has proven himself as the best defence-first wing in the league and delivered at the highest level possible as the Knicks won the NBA championship this past June.

All of that said, Barrett followed up an impressive regular season by averaging 24.1 points, 7.0 rebounds and 4.0 assists on strong shooting splits against Cleveland in the playoffs. He showed a strong ability to pound the paint, finishing third in points in the paint in the playoffs with 12.6 and was in the top 25 during the regular season among players with at least 50 games played.

Meanwhile, Quickley’s absence in the playoffs due to a hamstring pull could well have been the difference in the Raptors advancing to the second round or not. He was only one of six players to average at least 16 points (16.4), 5.5 assists (5.9), 1.2 steals (1.3) and 2.5 made threes last season — joining the likes of Donovan Mitchell, LaMelo Ball, Luka Doncic and Tyrese Maxey. And while Quickley hasn’t always shown that ‘sixth sense’ that the most elite point guards seem to have, he takes care of the ball (just 1.5 turnovers per game) and was a competitive all-around defender last season.

The Knicks got the best player, but Barrett and Quickley have shown they can be helpful starters on a playoff team, and there is reason to believe that at age 26 and 27, respectively, there is still another level each of them can reach.

stories.title: Police chief to address Belleville, Ont., synagogue shooting
stories.summary: The police chief in Belleville, Ont., is set to hold a news conference today in the aftermath of the shooting outside a local synagogue.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
BELLEVILLE - The shooter who targeted a Belleville, Ont., synagogue shouted “you’re going to die for the Jews” before he opened fire on a police officer outside, the police chief said, describing Sunday’s attack as a thwarted mass killing of Jewish worshippers.

Sept. 24, 2026

Updated at 7:00 p.m.

New subscriber benefit!

Copied to clipboard

A gifted article has been claimed.

Out of gifts for the month

Unfortunately you've used all of your gifts this month. Your counter will reset on the first day of next month.

DPI[](http://www.thestar.com/news/ontario/police-chief-to-address-belleville-ont-synagogue-shooting/article_99b28eca-69a7-5109-b572-bab1126146e1.html)

By Maan Alhmidi The Canadian Press

Chief Murray Rodd said the shooter had multiple guns, significant amounts of ammunition, gasoline and the motive to carry out an extended attack at the Sons of Jacob synagogue as people gathered inside to observe Yom Kippur.

“This was a deliberate attack directed at members of the Jewish community during one of the holiest observances of the year,” Rodd said at a Thursday news conference, the first comments made by police about the shooter’s motive.

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

Working remotely from Canada's Wonderland

Image 9Image 10Image 11

“The only thing that stopped entry into the synagogue to execute the intent were the two officers,” Rodd said. “The loss of life and irreversible damage that could have ... rippled through our community for generations cannot be overstated.”

The shooter ambushed Const. Jeff Smith, who was stationed outside the synagogue, and the officer was shot before he had the chance to leave his vehicle, Rodd said. Police also played a video that captured what the shooter yelled before he opened fire.

Smith suffered multiple gunshot wounds to the head and body but “stayed engaged” with the attacker, the police chief said. About three minutes later, a second police officer, Const. Michael McCurdy, arrived and joined what Rodd described as an “active gunfight.”

The pair “prevented what would have become an unimaginable tragedy,” Rodd said.

No one inside the synagogue was injured. Smith is expected to undergo multiple surgeries to treat his gunshot wounds, police said.

The shooter, 29-year-old Sean Ward, was fatally injured and died in hospital the next day.

The Canadian Armed Forces have said that Ward was a former soldier who served for about five years before he was released from the military at the rank of corporal in 2022.

Norm Weddum, president of the Sons of Jacob synagogue, said he was glad police have publicly deemed the shooting a hate crime targeting the Jewish congregation.

“Obviously that’s what we were calling it from Day 1 anyway,” he told reporters on Thursday. “There’s no question (the shooter) had the means to eliminate all of us in the synagogue and then probably to destroy the synagogue as well.”

Rodd suggested more details about the shooter’s motive could soon be released as investigators continue to search Ward’s electronic devices and computers.

“There is evidence that has been discovered that will corroborate the intent in more detail and it’s too early for us to provide that,” Rodd said.

Police mostly deflected questions about Ward and how he may have been radicalized.

Citing anonymous military and national defence sources, the Globe and Mail and Global News both reported that Ward was released from the army after refusing to be vaccinated against COVID-19. One of the sources told Global News that Ward also voiced antisemitic conspiracies.

Documents obtained by The Canadian Press suggest he had joined a lawsuit against the Canadian Armed Forces’ vaccination mandate, claiming $140,000 in financial losses after he refused the vaccine “on religious grounds” and was released from service. In its statement of defence, the government argued that the lawsuit should be thrown out and that vaccinating against COVID-19 was a safe and appropriate response to the pandemic.

Sunday’s attack has underscored fears among Canada’s Jewish community about the rise in antisemitism and a string of violent incidents. Jewish groups have called for immediate government action to boost armed security and police presence at synagogues and Jewish institutions.

Ontario’s solicitor general, Michael Kerzner, denounced the shooting as a “hateful and antisemitic attack” and said it was lucky that no lives were lost at the synagogue.

Simon Wolle, CEO of B’nai Brith Canada, said the Jewish organization has been raising alarm about growing threats for a long time.

“We’ve talked about how we can’t ignore words. We talked about how we can’t ignore threats. We talked about how we can’t ignore vandalism,” he said Thursday. “We warned that each of those things will lead to bullets.”

Weddum said the Sons of Jacob synagogue plans to reopen “very soon, and we’ll be stronger and better,” even as he expects returning to the building will be difficult for some.

“This person is not going to deter us or stop us from doing what we do,” he said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 24, 2026.

—With files from Jordan Omstead

content_blocks.text: BELLEVILLE - The shooter who targeted a Belleville, Ont., synagogue shouted “you’re going to die for the Jews” before he opened fire on a police officer outside, the police chief said, describing Sunday’s attack as a thwarted mass killing of Jewish worshippers.
Updated at 7:00 p.m.

DPI[](http://www.thestar.com/news/ontario/police-chief-to-address-belleville-ont-synagogue-shooting/article_99b28eca-69a7-5109-b572-bab1126146e1.html)
By Maan Alhmidi The Canadian Press

Chief Murray Rodd said the shooter had multiple guns, significant amounts of ammunition, gasoline and the motive to carry out an extended attack at the Sons of Jacob synagogue as people gathered inside to observe Yom Kippur.

“This was a deliberate attack directed at members of the Jewish community during one of the holiest observances of the year,” Rodd said at a Thursday news conference, the first comments made by police about the shooter’s motive.
ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW
Working remotely from Canada's Wonderland
Image 9Image 10Image 11

“The only thing that stopped entry into the synagogue to execute the intent were the two officers,” Rodd said. “The loss of life and irreversible damage that could have ... rippled through our community for generations cannot be overstated.”

The shooter ambushed Const. Jeff Smith, who was stationed outside the synagogue, and the officer was shot before he had the chance to leave his vehicle, Rodd said. Police also played a video that captured what the shooter yelled before he opened fire.

Smith suffered multiple gunshot wounds to the head and body but “stayed engaged” with the attacker, the police chief said. About three minutes later, a second police officer, Const. Michael McCurdy, arrived and joined what Rodd described as an “active gunfight.”
The pair “prevented what would have become an unimaginable tragedy,” Rodd said.
No one inside the synagogue was injured. Smith is expected to undergo multiple surgeries to treat his gunshot wounds, police said.
The shooter, 29-year-old Sean Ward, was fatally injured and died in hospital the next day.
The Canadian Armed Forces have said that Ward was a former soldier who served for about five years before he was released from the military at the rank of corporal in 2022.
Norm Weddum, president of the Sons of Jacob synagogue, said he was glad police have publicly deemed the shooting a hate crime targeting the Jewish congregation.

“Obviously that’s what we were calling it from Day 1 anyway,” he told reporters on Thursday. “There’s no question (the shooter) had the means to eliminate all of us in the synagogue and then probably to destroy the synagogue as well.”
Rodd suggested more details about the shooter’s motive could soon be released as investigators continue to search Ward’s electronic devices and computers.
“There is evidence that has been discovered that will corroborate the intent in more detail and it’s too early for us to provide that,” Rodd said.
Police mostly deflected questions about Ward and how he may have been radicalized.

Citing anonymous military and national defence sources, the Globe and Mail and Global News both reported that Ward was released from the army after refusing to be vaccinated against COVID-19. One of the sources told Global News that Ward also voiced antisemitic conspiracies.

Documents obtained by The Canadian Press suggest he had joined a lawsuit against the Canadian Armed Forces’ vaccination mandate, claiming $140,000 in financial losses after he refused the vaccine “on religious grounds” and was released from service. In its statement of defence, the government argued that the lawsuit should be thrown out and that vaccinating against COVID-19 was a safe and appropriate response to the pandemic.

Sunday’s attack has underscored fears among Canada’s Jewish community about the rise in antisemitism and a string of violent incidents. Jewish groups have called for immediate government action to boost armed security and police presence at synagogues and Jewish institutions.
Ontario’s solicitor general, Michael Kerzner, denounced the shooting as a “hateful and antisemitic attack” and said it was lucky that no lives were lost at the synagogue.
Simon Wolle, CEO of B’nai Brith Canada, said the Jewish organization has been raising alarm about growing threats for a long time.

“We’ve talked about how we can’t ignore words. We talked about how we can’t ignore threats. We talked about how we can’t ignore vandalism,” he said Thursday. “We warned that each of those things will lead to bullets.”
Weddum said the Sons of Jacob synagogue plans to reopen “very soon, and we’ll be stronger and better,” even as he expects returning to the building will be difficult for some.
“This person is not going to deter us or stop us from doing what we do,” he said.
This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 24, 2026.

stories.title: Scientist Jim Bruce was a globally renowned voice on the dangers of climate change
stories.summary: A founding member of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, he was the only Canadian representative in the delegation that accepted the 2007 Nobel Peace Prize jointly with former U.S. vice-president Al Gore
stories.author: James Cullingham
stories.content:
Jim Bruce was one of Canada’s foremost scientists and international representatives concerning environmental and climate issues. He provided extraordinary leadership that helped to rehabilitate the Great Lakes and through proposing the UN’s Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) was among the first to show how the world could address the damaging climate change caused by the burning of fossil fuels. He became a globally renowned and trusted voice who raised awareness about the risks of climate change, especially flooding and drought.

“If climate change is a shark, water is its teeth,” Mr. Bruce said, according to MP Francis Scarpaleggia, who quoted the scientist when addressing the House of Commons in 2022. “Like a fish that doesn’t notice the shark until it feels its sharp bite, humans will first feel the effects of climate change through water.”

Mr. Bruce, a leading member of the IPCC, was the only Canadian representative in the delegation that accepted the 2007 Nobel Peace Prize jointly with former U.S. vice-president Al Gore, who was honoured for his work on climate change, including the Oscar-winning film An Inconvenient Truth .

Jim Bruce died at the age of 97 in Ottawa on Aug. 23. He had suffered for many years from inclusion body myositis (IBM).

“[Mr. Bruce] was one of the first to raise and develop to prominence so many issues like floodplain mapping, hydrometeorology, the imperative to control climate change. There’s both a scientific and organizational legacy,” said John Pomeroy, distinguished professor at the University of Saskatchewan. “He showed us that Canada could be leaders in such matters. He was a great Canadian.”

James Philip Bruce was born in Toronto on Sept. 29, 1928. His father, Peter Bruce, worked in the shoe department at Eaton’s department store. His mother, Winnifred Bruce, was an elementary school teacher who left her job when she had children. She later continued her vocation as an English as second language instructor. As a young person, Jim accompanied his father, a tenor vocalist, on piano and organ at church services.

Mr. Bruce received a bachelor’s degree from the University of Toronto in 1948. That year he began a career at the Meteorological Service of Canada working mostly at air force bases. In 1949 he married Ruth (née Richardson), to whom he was married for 77 years. In 1952, Mr. Bruce went back to the University of Toronto and earned a master’s degree in physics.

The devastation of Hurricane Hazel in 1954 was a pivotal moment in his understanding of climate. He did floodplain mapping which led to the mitigation of future risk in the immediate area of the Humber River in Toronto’s west end, where loss of life and extensive property damage had occurred, and elsewhere.

Mr. Bruce and others developed systems to prepare for and avoid risks of flooding in several parts of Canada. That work also led to the creation of park space around urban rivers. His son, Peter Bruce, a former senior civil servant and now a learning and leadership associate at the Institute on Governance, a think tank, posed the query: “Do you know why it’s green around the Don Valley Parkway [in Toronto]? It’s because of my father.”

He was head of hydrometeorology for the Meteorological Service of Canada, based in Toronto, from 1959 to 1967. Mr. Bruce then moved to Burlington, Ont., where he led the Centre for Inland Waters and became co-chair of the International Joint Commission (IJC), dedicated to protection of water quality of the Great Lakes. That was the beginning of a series of international roles that saw Mr. Bruce involved with IPCC and the World Meteorological Organization in Geneva.

In 1988, he helped organize a landmark conference in Toronto titled “The Changing Atmosphere: Implications for Global Security.” That gathering marked the first time a global conference called for a reduction – 20 per cent – in greenhouse gas emissions. Mr. Bruce helped write the conference statement, which began: “Humanity is conducting an unintended, uncontrolled, globally pervasive experiment whose ultimate consequences could be second only to a global nuclear war.”

Following that Toronto conference, Mr. Bruce was among an international team that formed the IPCC. This body provides scientific assessments that inform decision-makers at United Nations climate conferences, known as Conferences of the Parties (COPs), and has helped shape international agreements including the 2015 Paris Agreement.

Mr. Bruce reflected on his IPCC experience in his 2016 book A Canadian Environmental Chronicle (1954-2015) . “While many climate activists have rightly considered IPCC Reports to be cautious in tone, this characteristic is inevitable in reports that represent a consensus of a large, diverse, international group of scientists,” he wrote.

In a 2022 interview with John Woodside for Canada’s National Observer, Mr. Bruce signalled his growing dissatisfaction on the climate-change mitigation front: “Now it [the IPCC] hasn’t been very successful in getting real action, in my view, but that’s a political problem.”

Public awareness, however, has grown. Mr. Bruce wrote about the moment he and his colleagues returned to their hotel after the Nobel Peace Prize gala: “We were astonished to find a large crowd waiting for our return from the ceremony. They began shouting ‘I-P-C-C, I-P-C-C’ and continued for some time. In my experience, this only happened to winning sports teams.”

His daughter Cathy Bruce, president and vice-chancellor of Trent University, laughingly recalled chatting with her father before he headed to Oslo: “He asked, ‘Do you think I should rent a suit?’ I said, ‘Dad, maybe this is a time you should buy a new suit.’” Dr. Bruce said she tries to implement her father’s style in valuing mentoring and in striving to make complex ideas understandable both in speech and writing.

Dr. Pomeroy first met Mr. Bruce in 1981 at the University of Saskatchewan. “I was a 20-year-old undergraduate asked to drive to the airport to pick up this leading figure. I was terrified. It turns out he was a nice, humble person who immediately put me at ease.”

Earlier this month, Dr. Pomeroy was among the scientists who honoured Mr. Bruce at the World Climate Research Programme’s International Network for Alpine Research Catchment Hydrology meeting in Kananaskis, Alta.

Mr. Bruce’s scientific output alone is a significant legacy, Dr. Pomeroy said, pointing to a breakthrough 1965 text on hydrometeorology and the instrumentation embedded by Mr. Bruce’s team in the Canadian Rockies headwaters of the Bow River in the early 1960s that helped scientists later understand the causes of the massive floods of 2013 and how better to predict such events.

Elizabeth Dowdeswell, former lieutenant-governor of Ontario, met Mr. Bruce in the 1980s when they both worked for the federal government. She came from behavioural sciences rather than a meteorological or hydrological background.

“He was always there for you, teaching in the most gentle way. He was a mentor,” Ms. Dowdeswell said, adding that she felt welcomed by Mr. Bruce. She would assume senior roles at Canada’s Atmospheric Environmental Service and as head of the United Nations Environment Programme in Nairobi, Kenya. She fondly recalled an interaction early in her Ottawa stint when she was “flabbergasted” by the number of acronyms used in the governmental scientific reports. “I told Jim I was determined to write a report without acronyms. Jim said, ‘good luck with that!’”

Green Party Leader Elizabeth May, formerly an activist and environmental lawyer, first encountered Mr. Bruce after she became an adviser to Thomas McMillan, then federal minister of the environment, and through the intense period of the 1988 Toronto conference, after which Ms. May resigned from the minister’s office. Their relationship deepened from 1999 to 2005 when they both served on the board of the International Institute for Sustainable Development (IISD).

Ms. May admired Mr. Bruce’s ability to engage with diverse colleagues and to make complex scientific issues understandable. Mr. Bruce “was a kind of polymath,” she said. “He had moral courage, mental clarity and depth of scientific expertise. I relied on him and loved him enormously.”

Jim and Ruth Bruce led an active, engaged family life. As long as his health permitted, Mr. Bruce played both jazz and European classical on the piano. He particularly admired Oscar Peterson, Diana Krall and J.S. Bach. Both Cathy Bruce and her brother, Peter, remember music and travel as indelible parts of family life.

“My father took us on lots of adventures,” Peter recalled. “He was very interested in archaeology and history.” Skiing also figured at a family chalet at Mont Sainte-Marie in the Gatineau region and in the Alps when members of the extended family visited Jim and Ruth while they were stationed in Geneva.

Ms. May made a point of regularly dropping by Jim and Ruth Bruce’s condo overlooking the Ottawa River. Her most recent visit took place last winter. “Jim never lost hold of moral certainty based on clear evidence and science.” She recalled that even with his deteriorating medical condition, “I never heard a syllable that could amount to self-pity. He grabbed every moment to get all the joy from life that he could.”

Both Ms. May and Ms. Dowdeswell said their final conversations with Mr. Bruce included discussion of climate change. Mr. Bruce was particularly alarmed about Canadian backsliding, Ms. May said. “We were both angry to the point of tears.”

After leaving the federal civil service and WMO, Mr. Bruce remained engaged with writing, speaking at conferences and advising on domestic and international panels. He expressed mounting concern over what he saw as insufficient action on the environment.

“One of the long-standing requirements of government,” he wrote in his 2016 book, “is to ensure stewardship of our inherited land, air, water and wild creatures – to pass them largely unharmed to the next generation. This role has recently been abysmally short-changed.”

Before that book was published, Peter had expressed concern that the conclusion his father drafted might be too dire, so he advised his father to tone it down a bit, which he did. But more recently, upon reflection, Peter thought, “Well, Dad, I guess you were right again.”

Among his many honours, Jim Bruce was named an officer of the Order of Canada and Fellow of the Royal Society of Canada in 1997, was awarded honorary doctorates from McMaster and Waterloo universities as well as being a member of the IPCC delegation for the 2007 Nobel Peace Prize.

Mr. Bruce leaves his wife, Ruth; children, Peggy Marcoux, Peter Bruce, Connie Bruce and Cathy Bruce; eight grandchildren and seven great-grandchildren.

You can find more obituaries from The Globe and Mail here .

Elizabeth Dowdeswell, former lieutenant-governor of Ontario, met Mr. Bruce in the 1980s when they both worked for the federal government. She came from behavioural sciences rather than a meteorological or hydrological background.

“He was always there for you, teaching in the most gentle way. He was a mentor,” Ms. Dowdeswell said, adding that she felt welcomed by Mr. Bruce. She would assume senior roles at Canada’s Atmospheric Environmental Service and as head of the United Nations Environment Programme in Nairobi, Kenya. She fondly recalled an interaction early in her Ottawa stint when she was “flabbergasted” by the number of acronyms used in the governmental scientific reports. “I told Jim I was determined to write a report without acronyms. Jim said, ‘good luck with that!’”

content_blocks.caption: In 1988, Mr. Bruce helped organize a landmark conference in Toronto that called for a 20 per cent reduction in greenhouse gas emissions. John Evans/Supplied

content_blocks.text: Green Party Leader Elizabeth May, formerly an activist and environmental lawyer, first encountered Mr. Bruce after she became an adviser to Thomas McMillan, then federal minister of the environment, and through the intense period of the 1988 Toronto conference, after which Ms. May resigned from the minister’s office. Their relationship deepened from 1999 to 2005 when they both served on the board of the International Institute for Sustainable Development (IISD).

Ms. May admired Mr. Bruce’s ability to engage with diverse colleagues and to make complex scientific issues understandable. Mr. Bruce “was a kind of polymath,” she said. “He had moral courage, mental clarity and depth of scientific expertise. I relied on him and loved him enormously.”

Jim and Ruth Bruce led an active, engaged family life. As long as his health permitted, Mr. Bruce played both jazz and European classical on the piano. He particularly admired Oscar Peterson, Diana Krall and J.S. Bach. Both Cathy Bruce and her brother, Peter, remember music and travel as indelible parts of family life.

“My father took us on lots of adventures,” Peter recalled. “He was very interested in archaeology and history.” Skiing also figured at a family chalet at Mont Sainte-Marie in the Gatineau region and in the Alps when members of the extended family visited Jim and Ruth while they were stationed in Geneva.

Ms. May made a point of regularly dropping by Jim and Ruth Bruce’s condo overlooking the Ottawa River. Her most recent visit took place last winter. “Jim never lost hold of moral certainty based on clear evidence and science.” She recalled that even with his deteriorating medical condition, “I never heard a syllable that could amount to self-pity. He grabbed every moment to get all the joy from life that he could.”

Both Ms. May and Ms. Dowdeswell said their final conversations with Mr. Bruce included discussion of climate change. Mr. Bruce was particularly alarmed about Canadian backsliding, Ms. May said. “We were both angry to the point of tears.”

After leaving the federal civil service and WMO, Mr. Bruce remained engaged with writing, speaking at conferences and advising on domestic and international panels. He expressed mounting concern over what he saw as insufficient action on the environment.

“One of the long-standing requirements of government,” he wrote in his 2016 book, “is to ensure stewardship of our inherited land, air, water and wild creatures – to pass them largely unharmed to the next generation. This role has recently been abysmally short-changed.”

Before that book was published, Peter had expressed concern that the conclusion his father drafted might be too dire, so he advised his father to tone it down a bit, which he did. But more recently, upon reflection, Peter thought, “Well, Dad, I guess you were right again.”

Among his many honours, Jim Bruce was named an officer of the Order of Canada and Fellow of the Royal Society of Canada in 1997, was awarded honorary doctorates from McMaster and Waterloo universities as well as being a member of the IPCC delegation for the 2007 Nobel Peace Prize.
Mr. Bruce leaves his wife, Ruth; children, Peggy Marcoux, Peter Bruce, Connie Bruce and Cathy Bruce; eight grandchildren and seven great-grandchildren.
