stories.title: Two accused in sensational Toronto airport gold heist are now facing separate trials, pleading not guilty
stories.summary: Parmpal Sidhu and Archit Grover, both from Brampton, were to face a joint trial and had previously asked for it to be heard before a jury.
stories.author: Adrian Humphreys
stories.content:
Two men set to face a jury trial together for the astonishing Toronto Pearson airport gold heist have had their hearings separated, and will each now have only a judge decide their fate.

Parmpal Sidhu, 56, who worked at the Air Canada warehouse from where the $22-million shipment of gold bars and currency was stolen in 2023, and Archit Grover, 39, who allegedly owned the truck used to haul the shipment from the airport, will face separate trials a month apart, likely in front of different judges.

Ontario Superior Court Justice Nancy Dennison agreed to separate the prosecutions for the men, both from Brampton, Ont., ON Friday, at the request of Grover’s lawyer.

“Archit Grover stands in a different position than his co-accused who are going to trial or who are still on the run,” Grover’s lawyer, Andrew Furgiuele, told National Post. “The factual considerations relating to his co-accused have no relevance with respect to him.”

Grover was arrested May 6, 2024, at Pearson airport after he flew back to Canada from India. Peel Regional Police announced nine arrest warrants for the gold heist about three weeks before, ON the first anniversary of the heist. At the time, Grover was named as a fugitive.

“Mr. Grover is looking forward to his trial with the same confidence he had when he immediately came back to Canada to face his charges after the police announced the arrest warrants. He was not guilty then, is not guilty now, and will remain so after his trial,” Furgiuele said.

Sidhu, by contrast, had been quietly arrested in Canada on April 5, 2024, almost two weeks before the splashy police announcement.

Shale Wagman, Sidhu’s lawyer, professed his client’s innocence.

“He’s pleading not guilty for sure. He’s doing fine. He’s taking it well. He didn’t do anything wrong and he’s anxious to clear his name,” Wagman told National Post.

Neither Wagman nor the Crown prosecutor, Jelena Vlacic, opposed the severance motion, according to court records.

Both accused men then switched their trial choice from a jury trial to being heard by a judge only.

They were to face a joint trial and had previously asked for it to be heard before a jury. Jury selection was scheduled to begin Oct. 1. Instead, the trial for Sidhu is now scheduled to begin Oct. 5 and run for two or three weeks, and the trial for Grover is set for two weeks in late November. Both trials are to be in their hometown of Brampton.

Sidhu and Grover face the same two charges.

Each is accused of conspiring with others to commit theft over $5,000, and of stealing gold and bank notes worth more than $5,000 that were the property of the Toronto Dominion Centre, the global headquarters for the TD Bank. Both charges are tied to the date of the airport heist: April 17, 2023.

It is a quaintness in Canada’s laws that the largest gold heist in Canadian history, and the sixth largest in the world — valued at more than $22 million gold and cash — is prosecuted at the top criminal code threshold of just a $5,000 loss.

Investigators thought that other men might be facing trial for the heist as well.

Two men are considered fugitives-at-large.

Simran Preet Panesar, who was a 31-year-old Air Canada employee at the time of the theft resigned after the heist and left Canada before he was named as being wanted. He is believed to have travelled to India.

Prasath Paramalingam, 35 at the time of his arrest in 2024 and also from Brampton, was arrested in the original police sweep but later disappeared after his release on bail. He is now considered a fugitive after failing to appear in court on Aug. 19, 2024. Paramalingam is also wanted in the United States in a related gun-running case.

While technically a fugitive in Canada, the alleged driver of the truck is not on the run. Durante King-Mclean, 25, of Brampton is in custody in the United States after police stopped a car in Pennsylvania with 65 handguns in the trunk that were being smuggled into Canada. Authorities said a portion of the stolen gold was used to fund a cross-border gun-running plot. He recently pleaded guilty to firearms trafficking charges while he is still wanted in Canada for the gold heist.

Grover is wanted in the United States for alleged involvement in the same gun-running plot.

In April, the man named as the ringleader of the heist, Arsalan Chaudhary, a 43-year-old man formerly of Mississauga, Ont., was sentenced to four years. He too had fled Canada after the grab, settling in Dubai. After negotiations by his lawyer, Chaudhary returned to Canada in January and surrendered to Peel police waiting for him at Pearson airport. He pleaded guilty to theft over $5,000.

Three other men who had been arrested for the heist have since had their charges dropped.

In April, Ammad Chaudhary, 43, from Georgetown, who had been charged with theft over $5,000 and being accessory after the fact, had his charged dropped by the Crown.

Last week, charges against two more of the accused were dropped.

Ali Raza, 39, of Toronto, who was originally accused of melting stolen gold in his jewellery store workshop, and Amit Jalota, 42, of Oakville, originally accused of helping move the stolen gold to be melted, had all charges withdrawn and left court as free men.

Vlacic, the prosecutor, said evolving evidence meant there was no longer a reasonable prospect of conviction in either of those cases. The details of the evidentiary changes cannot be published under a court-ordered publication ban.

The shipping container at the heart of the case was filled with almost-pure gold bars, weighing 400.19 kilograms, and stolen from an Air Canada cargo facility shortly after arriving on an Air Canada flight from Zurich, Switzerland.

Police said a man walked into the warehouse alone and presented an Air Canada waybill for a shipment of seafood that had already been picked up; bizarrely a warehouse employee loaded the gold shipment onto the man’s truck with a forklift.

The theft was so smooth it wasn’t noticed until three hours later when Brink’s security arrived to collect the container and nobody could find it.

Only a small fraction of the gold has been recovered.

paragraphs: Two men set to face a jury trial together for the astonishing Toronto Pearson airport gold heist have had their hearings separated, and will each now have only a judge decide their fate.

Parmpal Sidhu, 56, who worked at the Air Canada warehouse from where the $22-million shipment of gold bars and currency was stolen in 2023, and Archit Grover, 39, who allegedly owned the truck used to haul the shipment from the airport, will face separate trials a month apart, likely in front of different judges.
Ontario Superior Court Justice Nancy Dennison agreed to separate the prosecutions for the men, both from Brampton, Ont., ON Friday, at the request of Grover’s lawyer.

“Archit Grover stands in a different position than his co-accused who are going to trial or who are still on the run,” Grover’s lawyer, Andrew Furgiuele, told National Post. “The factual considerations relating to his co-accused have no relevance with respect to him.”

Grover was arrested May 6, 2024, at Pearson airport after he flew back to Canada from India. Peel Regional Police announced nine arrest warrants for the gold heist about three weeks before, ON the first anniversary of the heist. At the time, Grover was named as a fugitive.

“Mr. Grover is looking forward to his trial with the same confidence he had when he immediately came back to Canada to face his charges after the police announced the arrest warrants. He was not guilty then, is not guilty now, and will remain so after his trial,” Furgiuele said.
Sidhu, by contrast, had been quietly arrested in Canada on April 5, 2024, almost two weeks before the splashy police announcement.
Shale Wagman, Sidhu’s lawyer, professed his client’s innocence.
“He’s pleading not guilty for sure. He’s doing fine. He’s taking it well. He didn’t do anything wrong and he’s anxious to clear his name,” Wagman told National Post.
Neither Wagman nor the Crown prosecutor, Jelena Vlacic, opposed the severance motion, according to court records.
Both accused men then switched their trial choice from a jury trial to being heard by a judge only.

They were to face a joint trial and had previously asked for it to be heard before a jury. Jury selection was scheduled to begin Oct. 1. Instead, the trial for Sidhu is now scheduled to begin Oct. 5 and run for two or three weeks, and the trial for Grover is set for two weeks in late November. Both trials are to be in their hometown of Brampton.
Sidhu and Grover face the same two charges.

Each is accused of conspiring with others to commit theft over $5,000, and of stealing gold and bank notes worth more than $5,000 that were the property of the Toronto Dominion Centre, the global headquarters for the TD Bank. Both charges are tied to the date of the airport heist: April 17, 2023.

It is a quaintness in Canada’s laws that the largest gold heist in Canadian history, and the sixth largest in the world — valued at more than $22 million gold and cash — is prosecuted at the top criminal code threshold of just a $5,000 loss.
Investigators thought that other men might be facing trial for the heist as well.
Two men are considered fugitives-at-large.

Simran Preet Panesar, who was a 31-year-old Air Canada employee at the time of the theft resigned after the heist and left Canada before he was named as being wanted. He is believed to have travelled to India.

Prasath Paramalingam, 35 at the time of his arrest in 2024 and also from Brampton, was arrested in the original police sweep but later disappeared after his release on bail. He is now considered a fugitive after failing to appear in court on Aug. 19, 2024. Paramalingam is also wanted in the United States in a related gun-running case.

While technically a fugitive in Canada, the alleged driver of the truck is not on the run. Durante King-Mclean, 25, of Brampton is in custody in the United States after police stopped a car in Pennsylvania with 65 handguns in the trunk that were being smuggled into Canada. Authorities said a portion of the stolen gold was used to fund a cross-border gun-running plot. He recently pleaded guilty to firearms trafficking charges while he is still wanted in Canada for the gold heist.
Grover is wanted in the United States for alleged involvement in the same gun-running plot.

In April, the man named as the ringleader of the heist, Arsalan Chaudhary, a 43-year-old man formerly of Mississauga, Ont., was sentenced to four years. He too had fled Canada after the grab, settling in Dubai. After negotiations by his lawyer, Chaudhary returned to Canada in January and surrendered to Peel police waiting for him at Pearson airport. He pleaded guilty to theft over $5,000.
Three other men who had been arrested for the heist have since had their charges dropped.
In April, Ammad Chaudhary, 43, from Georgetown, who had been charged with theft over $5,000 and being accessory after the fact, had his charged dropped by the Crown.
Last week, charges against two more of the accused were dropped.

Ali Raza, 39, of Toronto, who was originally accused of melting stolen gold in his jewellery store workshop, and Amit Jalota, 42, of Oakville, originally accused of helping move the stolen gold to be melted, had all charges withdrawn and left court as free men.

Vlacic, the prosecutor, said evolving evidence meant there was no longer a reasonable prospect of conviction in either of those cases. The details of the evidentiary changes cannot be published under a court-ordered publication ban.

The shipping container at the heart of the case was filled with almost-pure gold bars, weighing 400.19 kilograms, and stolen from an Air Canada cargo facility shortly after arriving on an Air Canada flight from Zurich, Switzerland.

Police said a man walked into the warehouse alone and presented an Air Canada waybill for a shipment of seafood that had already been picked up; bizarrely a warehouse employee loaded the gold shipment onto the man’s truck with a forklift.
The theft was so smooth it wasn’t noticed until three hours later when Brink’s security arrived to collect the container and nobody could find it.
Only a small fraction of the gold has been recovered.

stories.title: Ticket resellers fined for breaking Ontario’s price cap law take issue with charges
stories.summary: Some resale platforms say it’s hard to prove original pricing
stories.author: Mariya Postelnyak
stories.content:
Facing thousands of dollars in fines for violating Ontario’s new ticket price caps, resale platforms StubHub and SeatGeek say primary ticket issuers, such as Ticketmaster, are not sharing information needed to follow the law. Industry watchers, meanwhile, have cast doubt on their claims.

The Ontario government fined ticket reseller SeatGeek Canada $25,000 in August for allegedly flouting a price cap law while StubHub Canada Ltd. was fined $20,000 this week . The new rules, introduced in April, ban reselling tickets for more than the original total price paid to the primary seller.

StubHub spokesperson Jack Sterne said the company “strongly disagrees” with the fines being imposed and plans to appeal the decision.

“We are upholding our responsibility as best we can,” he said, despite the “law’s silence” on core issues, like how a vendor can actually verify the original price of a ticket.

SeatGeek’s vice-president of government affairs, Joe Freeman, said responsibility for sharing the face value of a ticket sits with the primary ticket issuer. “Ticketmaster has not been forthcoming with it,” he said.

Ministry of Public and Business Service Delivery and Procurement spokesperson Cristian Buzo Tingarov did not respond to questions on how the government is addressing gaps in the legislation shared by resellers. “The government continues to take action to ensure all ticket sellers comply with our legislation,” he said.

While some industry watchers say the resellers have a point, the success of face value resale platforms in other jurisdictions suggests when there’s a will there is a way for them to check original selling prices.

It does raise the question “how do you actually assess the price?” said Stephen Zolf, who co-leads the Competition, Antitrust and Foreign Investment Group and Sports and Entertainment at Aird & Berlis LLP. “They were not party to that original transaction.”

New York-based artist manager and live events technology consultant Randy Nichols, however, said if challenges exist in verifying the original price, they’re ones the platforms are eager to embrace. “It’s not difficult in the sense that it’s technologically hard.”

Resale platforms have the ability to monitor seller behaviour, such as the frequency of transactions, and use technology to identify large-scale operations whose activity on the platform can give off signals of abuse, Mr. Nichols said.

Smaller resale platforms such as CashorTrade and Tixel have long required customers to submit receipts or other documentation before listing tickets, and later developed partnerships with larger ticketing companies, including Ticketmaster, that provided their verified pricing information.

Ticketmaster Canada spokesperson Shabnum Durrani said “every ticket sale comes with a receipt that reflects the purchase price” and that the face price is also displayed directly on digital tickets.

“Any suggestion that this information cannot be made available to resale platforms is incorrect,” she said.

A StubHub spokesperson said a PDF of a receipt can be easily doctored with AI or software to change the price.

But Mr. Nichols said the small barriers such as requesting sellers to upload receipts – something that StubHub and Seatgeek generally don’t do – also have the simple benefit of adding friction that can help weed out at least some bad actors.

The concern is not a fan making “a couple of extra dollars” when they can’t attend a high-demand event, Mr. Nichols said. “What we want to disincentivize is $1-billion businesses investing in buying and selling tickets at scale.”

Brando Rich, the co-founder and CEO of CashorTrade , a face-value ticket resale platform based in Burlington, Vermont, said his company has been verifying ticket prices by examining receipts and metadata, using AI and by building out a crowd-monitored “member police” platform.

“Users actually have the ability to flag a post that violates the policy,” he said.

Most recently, his platform integrated with Ticketmaster along with five other primary ticketing platforms to get the original sale information by connecting their Application Programming Interfaces (APIs), a technical door between two services.

But while Mr. Rich supports ticket price caps, he said there needs to be more margin to support the resale market and competition. The company makes money by charging buyers a 10 per cent transaction fee on ticket purchases and through paid memberships for frequent users.

Ontario’s ticket price cap has zero wiggle room for margin, though an initiative proposed by the previous Liberal government in 2018 would have limited resale prices at 50 per cent above the tickets’ original face value. In the U.S., jurisdictions such as Washington, D.C., and California have proposed capping live event ticket resale prices at a maximum of 10 per cent above face value.

“Even 10 per cent makes it tough for a product or service to thrive,” Mr. Rich said. “There are a lot of technical pieces under the hood that require resources.”

Jake Farbman, an entertainment lawyer at Ferrara & Pisarek in Nashville and a former touring musician, said rules imposed only on the secondary market raise the risk of giving more market share to primary ticketing giants if they aren’t accompanied by mandatory price transparency or data-sharing requirements.

“A regulation intended to protect consumers could inadvertently make it more difficult for independent resale platforms to compete.”

stories.title: Novel ‘heart in a box’ technology gives London, Ont., patient ‘second life’
stories.summary: After a cardiac arrest and triple bypass, Raj Mittal learned he was a candidate for a transplant. His donor heart arrived warm and pumping
stories.author: Kristy Kirkup
stories.content:
Raj Mittal’s new heart came in an unusual package.

After a cardiac arrest and a triple bypass in June, 2025, he spent a month and a half sedated in intensive care at the London Health Sciences Centre in Ontario before he could return home to his wife and two children.

When his heart condition led to pneumonia in January and another hospital stay, he learned he was a candidate for a heart transplant.

Typically heart donors are patients who have been declared brain dead, but whose hearts are still beating. Once the organs are removed they are placed on ice, and can last in this state for only up to six hours, limiting how far they can travel.

But when Mr. Mittal’s heart arrived in February, two weeks after he was added to Ontario’s transplant list, it was still warm and pumping blood.

According to the London hospital, which performed the transplant, he was the first Canadian to receive what is colloquially called a “heart in a box.”

The box, which is actually a cart-sized medical device on wheels with a chamber where the organ can rest and receive blood through a system of tubes, doubles a donor heart’s potential lifespan to 12 hours. With the longer timeframe, a heart can travel much farther than was previously possible.

The box can also revive hearts after they stop beating, expanding the pool of donors to include patients who die after circulation stops. In ordinary circumstances, these organs wouldn’t be considered viable.

“It’s a second life for me,” said Mr. Mittal, a 50-year-old information technology professional.

Dave Nagpal, medical co-director of the multiorgan transplant program at the London Health Sciences Centre and its director of cardiac transplantation, called the technology “fascinating.”

The box, formally known as an Organ Care System, is made by TransMedics, a company headquartered in Massachusetts.

Once a donor heart is removed, Dr. Nagpal said, the device can be attached to the organ, which starts pumping again.

“You can hook the heart up to this device and actually watch it regain function and assess the function of the heart based on the visual appearance, but also based on the laboratory investigations that we can do on the device,” Dr. Nagpal said.

“This additional technology allows us to get more donor hearts into those recipients that really need them.”

He acknowledges it took a village for the technology to be made available in Ontario. Hearts from Canadian donors have previously been revived in the devices, but they were transplanted into American recipients.

Ontario Health, a provincial agency, financed the equipment. The acquisition took years of collaboration with the Trillium Gift of Life Network, an agency responsible for delivering and co-ordinating organ and tissue donation and transplantation services across the province. And the physicians who would use the device required special training.

Before Mr. Mittal’s transplant, the hospital’s cardiac surgeon, Rashmi Nedadur, had to retrieve the donor’s heart from another location that the hospital says it cannot disclose.

Dr. Nedadur assessed how the heart was functioning and deemed it viable for transplant. She brought it back to the London hospital, where a surgical team was prepped and ready to scrub in.

In the operating room, major vessels were trimmed to fit Mr. Mittal’s anatomy. The heart also needed to be protected through a process that involved special solutions and temperature control.

Once the heart was sewn into Mr. Mittal’s chest, Dr. Nedadur said, it “took off immediately.”

Just days after the transplant procedure Mr. Mittal started feeling more like himself.

He could get up and move in the intensive care unit, before he was transferred to the hospital’s transplant unit. He had to return briefly to the ICU to manage his blood pressure and fluid levels. But later that month he was able to go home.

These days, Mr. Mittal is recovering well. But he said he has to remind himself to go slow. He is doing cardiac rehabilitation and takes medication daily.

Although he remains on leave from his job, he is finding joy in simple things, such as being able to get outside for walks.

This is a marked improvement from life before the transplant, he said, when his energy levels were so low he couldn’t enjoy time with family.

He hopes that with more time, his new heart will eventually allow him to get back to doing more.

His main goals are to return to work, and, by next summer, get back on his bike. He enjoys riding alongside his children, now 11 and 17.

In the meantime, he is deeply grateful to the doctors, nurses and the technology that saved him.

“With God’s grace and friends’ and family wishes, I’m here today,” he said.

stories.title: Canadians are in the dark about their wildfire risk
stories.summary: Experts and politicians are endorsing a national strategy on wildfire hazard mapping, but the process would be far from simple
stories.author: Jesse Winter
stories.content:
Doug MacLeod could see the danger bearing down on him.

In early August, the forestry contractor was marking trails for heavy equipment to plow fire breaks on the mountainside above Faulder, a community near Summerland in British Columbia’s southern Okanagan valley.

He had tied only a single piece of flagging tape when he saw the Bald Range wildfire roaring through the forests toward him.

“This is death coming over the mountain,” Mr. MacLeod remembers thinking. He abandoned flagging and started pounding on residents’ doors, urging them to flee.

He watched as fire ripped across the valley and cut off Fish Lake Road, the only viable route out of the area. Knowing he and dozens of residents were now trapped, Mr. MacLeod leaned on his training and decades of wildfire experience to give those around him the best possible chance to survive.

He picked a grassy meadow as far from the tree line as he could get. If the fire went over them, he told people, they would lie face down, hands over their heads, pressing their lips into small air pockets scraped into the dirt. It would be a last-ditch effort to avoid death. They could survive, he thought, but there would be injuries.

Luckily, a wind shift in the nick of time allowed BC Wildfire Service helicopters to land and start what became a huge air-lift rescue effort.

It could have been much worse, Mr. MacLeod said. “This was so close to being a couple of hundred people [dead].”

The fire’s behaviour was unlike anything Mr. MacLeod had ever seen. After nearly 50 years of working in forests, he understood the growing hazard, driven by years-long drought and decades of unchecked forest ingrowth, before the Bald Range fire exploded.

But the scale of the danger is largely invisible to most Canadians until it’s too late. Though some wildfire hazard mapping is publicly available in B.C., there is a patchwork of incomplete data. And in the rest of the country, such information is virtually non-existent.

“I think people got to be aware of what’s around them, and communities have to be aware of what’s around them,” Mr. MacLeod said.

Experts warn that a failure by governments to make detailed hazard mapping publicly available has left towns and cities across the country more vulnerable to the threat of extreme wildfires. Without the information, communities continue to build new housing in high-hazard areas even as critical mitigation efforts are frequently delayed.

In light of these concerns, a Senate committee is calling for a new national hazard mapping strategy – and public data similar to what is already available in the United States.

But some critics worry governments May not be up to the complicated task. And even when there is an earnest effort to improve public data, officials can face significant backlash as property owners fear financial consequences. Fire officials in Oregon were forced to largely abandon detailed hazard mapping after trying to make better information publicly available.

There is no denying the trendline: Climate change is driving wildfires that are faster and hotter than ever before, and disasters like the Bald Range fire are becoming more common. Are Canadians ready to open their eyes to the risk?

Hoping to avoid such staggering losses in the future, state legislators also decided to tie each property’s hazard rating to legislated requirements for the property owners. New construction would have to meet a stricter, more fire-resistant building code. And landowners were handed retroactive requirements to do mitigation work like removing or pruning back trees on at-risk properties, efforts proven to help improve a home’s chances of surviving a wildfire.

Despite being backed up by sound science, the effort blew up in officials’ faces as livid homeowners accused the state of driving up insurance rates and driving down property values.

“We got death threats. We had to cancel meetings. Our state police said, ‘This [threat] is too credible. You can’t go to these particular communities,’” Mr. Dunn said.

Under pressure, the state quickly withdrew the new requirements for homeowners. The maps themselves were temporarily taken down and eventually replaced with simplified versions.

“What happened was a monumental public backlash, unlike anything we’ve seen in recent policy here,” Mr. Dunn said. “The public response was so entrenched in misinformation, misunderstandings that it was just not surmountable, and so the legislature pulled away.”

Most frustratingly for Mr. Dunn, the claim that the maps were driving up insurance rates or causing homeowners to lose coverage altogether was untrue.

Insurance companies in both the Canada and the U.S. have their own sophisticated risk modelling, Mr. Dunn said. They already know better than most homeowners what risks a particular home faces.

Liam McGuinty, vice-president of federal affairs for the Insurance Bureau of Canada, agreed the insurance industry has become sophisticated at gathering data to price wildfire risk.

“The quality of risk modelling and mapping has improved fairly significantly over the past several years, and so insurers know a lot.”

But as useful as that modelling is, insurance companies don’t make it public because it’s proprietary and expensive to produce. That’s another reason for better public hazard maps, experts say: They could help put homeowners on a more even footing with their insurance providers by giving them a neutral source of information about their properties.

Mr. McGuinty told the Senate committee his industry supports the call for better mapping. He said significant federal and provincial data exists that isn’t shared outside of government agencies.

There are two key questions, he said: whether provincial and municipal governments actually use the maps to guide development and hazard reduction work, and whether homeowners are empowered to understands the risks they face.

“In my view, the answer to both is no,” Mr. McGuinty said.

Nationally, he said, “we’re set to build 200,000 homes in high-risk wildfire areas in the next five years, unless policies change. We’re building right now in high-risk wildfire areas.”

Mr. McGuinty said he worries wildfire hazard mapping could suffer a fate similar to that of the federal government’s Flood Risk Finder tool, part of a $228-million effort by Ottawa to help Canadians understand the risks to their properties from floods.

That online map operates like a hypothetical fire hazard map could: Homeowners can punch in their addresses and, based on regional data, quickly get an estimated flood risk rating on a four-point scale from “low” to “extreme.”

The tool launched in April. The problem, Mr. McGuinty said, is that it’s currently useless because not a single province or territory has chosen to opt in. Visitors to the website are met only with a “coming soon” notice, and the search function greyed out.

The B.C. government said that, like with wildfire hazard mapping, it supports the flood risk finder tool in theory. “We have questions for the federal government about limitations of the tool and engagement with local governments and First Nations,” B.C.’s Ministry of Environment and Climate Readiness said in a statement to The Globe. Other provincial governments have given similar reasons for not signing on.

“The tools exist. The mapping exists. It’s ready to go. Consumers would benefit from it,” Mr. McGuinty said. “Are those maps perfect? No, but let’s not let perfect be the enemy of the good here.”

How you can make your home less vulnerable to wildfires

As the risk of impacts from wildland fire is increasing, FireSmart Canada has developed guidelines for home construction, maintenance, landscaping and evacuation planning to minimize risks when wildland fires occur.

Best practices for planning, design and construction

Non-combustible or ignition-resistant

Non-combustible gutters and downspouts

Deck/porch with non-combustible or fire-rated materials

Non-combustible materials such as gravel in the 1.5-metre area adjacent to the property

Multi-pane tempered glass windows

Fire-rated roofing materials

Metal vents with three-millimetre metal screening

Garage and exterior doors fitted with weather stripping to prevent ember entry

Deciduous plants instead of conifers

The home ignition zone

The HIZ is the area within 30 metres of your home, divided into three priority zones. By addressing fire risks from the Immediate zone outward, you can reduce your home's vulnerability to wildland fire.

Clear vegetation and combustible material down to mineral soil and cover with non-combustible materials like gravel, brick or concrete

Avoid planting woody shrubs or trees or dense vegetation.

Use fire-resistant, preferably deciduous, plants and non-combustible landscaping materials.

Keep the area free of woody debris, mulch and other combustible materials.

Space tree crowns at least three metres apart and prune branches up to two metres from the ground.

Regularly remove fallen branches, dry grass and needles to reduce surface fuels.

Before the Bald Range fire, local government knew about growing wildfire risks in the area – even though provincial data was incomplete and a federal map was not available.

The Regional District of Okanagan Similkameen, which is responsible for the rural areas around Summerland, including Faulder, said the district relied in part on data provided by private landowners who’d had their own hazard assessments completed.

The district worked to address the risks through the FireSmart B.C. program, which helps homeowners with tailored strategies like removing flammable plants, pruning or removing coniferous trees, and installing fire-resistant roofing and siding material.

It tends not to focus on the risks growing in forests beyond the immediate area around a house or structure, which is where public hazard mapping could play a bigger role. But when the wildfire reached the edges of Summerland itself, the efforts of the local community made a significant difference.

In Summerland, the neighbourhood of Deer Ridge used a FireSmart risk assessment to highlight areas that needed tree pruning and other vegetation clean up. After the fire, local fire chief Rob Robinson said that work helped prevent flying embers from landing farther into town, giving firefighters a critical advantage that helped save homes.

Funding ran out in February , and while the B.C. government added an extra $15-million to cover FireSmart projects in 2027, it has not yet said what the future of the program will be.

Given the history of wildfires in B.C.’s southern interior, many Summerland and Faulder residents are better informed about their wildfire risk than most Canadians. Even so, some didn’t fully comprehend the scale of the hazard the way Mr. MacLeod, the forestry contractor, had.

Brandon Bishop and his wife Alora lost their home to the wildfire last month. Their property was one of 73 that were levelled when the fire rolled into Faulder.

Mr. Bishop said the rural community was accustomed to life in the bush, and had a general sense that the forests were becoming very dense. Local officials had begun talking more about the need for FireSmart projects.

But he said he did not fully appreciate just how dense and loaded with fuel the forest and mountains around his home really were.

“To be honest, I knew it was hot and dry. But it didn’t seem any worse than usual. I mean, fire danger in our area is always high at that time of year,” Mr. Bishop said.

If public hazard maps were available, he thinks that could have motivated the community to press harder for protective measures, and get involved themselves.

“I think that people would probably get out in the forest a little bit more and be willing to help with that. Especially if it means saving their community in the long run,” he said.

“What happened was a monumental public backlash, unlike anything we’ve seen in recent policy here,” Mr. Dunn said. “The public response was so entrenched in misinformation, misunderstandings that it was just not surmountable, and so the legislature pulled away.”
Most frustratingly for Mr. Dunn, the claim that the maps were driving up insurance rates or causing homeowners to lose coverage altogether was untrue.
Insurance companies in both the Canada and the U.S. have their own sophisticated risk modelling, Mr. Dunn said. They already know better than most homeowners what risks a particular home faces.
Liam McGuinty, vice-president of federal affairs for the Insurance Bureau of Canada, agreed the insurance industry has become sophisticated at gathering data to price wildfire risk.
“The quality of risk modelling and mapping has improved fairly significantly over the past several years, and so insurers know a lot.”

But as useful as that modelling is, insurance companies don’t make it public because it’s proprietary and expensive to produce. That’s another reason for better public hazard maps, experts say: They could help put homeowners on a more even footing with their insurance providers by giving them a neutral source of information about their properties.
Mr. McGuinty told the Senate committee his industry supports the call for better mapping. He said significant federal and provincial data exists that isn’t shared outside of government agencies.

There are two key questions, he said: whether provincial and municipal governments actually use the maps to guide development and hazard reduction work, and whether homeowners are empowered to understands the risks they face.
“In my view, the answer to both is no,” Mr. McGuinty said.
Nationally, he said, “we’re set to build 200,000 homes in high-risk wildfire areas in the next five years, unless policies change. We’re building right now in high-risk wildfire areas.”

Mr. McGuinty said he worries wildfire hazard mapping could suffer a fate similar to that of the federal government’s Flood Risk Finder tool, part of a $228-million effort by Ottawa to help Canadians understand the risks to their properties from floods.

That online map operates like a hypothetical fire hazard map could: Homeowners can punch in their addresses and, based on regional data, quickly get an estimated flood risk rating on a four-point scale from “low” to “extreme.”

The tool launched in April. The problem, Mr. McGuinty said, is that it’s currently useless because not a single province or territory has chosen to opt in. Visitors to the website are met only with a “coming soon” notice, and the search function greyed out.

The B.C. government said that, like with wildfire hazard mapping, it supports the flood risk finder tool in theory. “We have questions for the federal government about limitations of the tool and engagement with local governments and First Nations,” B.C.’s Ministry of Environment and Climate Readiness said in a statement to The Globe. Other provincial governments have given similar reasons for not signing on.
“The tools exist. The mapping exists. It’s ready to go. Consumers would benefit from it,” Mr. McGuinty said. “Are those maps perfect? No, but let’s not let perfect be the enemy of the good here.”

Before the Bald Range fire, local government knew about growing wildfire risks in the area – even though provincial data was incomplete and a federal map was not available.

The Regional District of Okanagan Similkameen, which is responsible for the rural areas around Summerland, including Faulder, said the district relied in part on data provided by private landowners who’d had their own hazard assessments completed.

The district worked to address the risks through the FireSmart B.C. program, which helps homeowners with tailored strategies like removing flammable plants, pruning or removing coniferous trees, and installing fire-resistant roofing and siding material.

It tends not to focus on the risks growing in forests beyond the immediate area around a house or structure, which is where public hazard mapping could play a bigger role. But when the wildfire reached the edges of Summerland itself, the efforts of the local community made a significant difference.

In Summerland, the neighbourhood of Deer Ridge used a FireSmart risk assessment to highlight areas that needed tree pruning and other vegetation clean up. After the fire, local fire chief Rob Robinson said that work helped prevent flying embers from landing farther into town, giving firefighters a critical advantage that helped save homes.
Funding ran out in February , and while the B.C. government added an extra $15-million to cover FireSmart projects in 2027, it has not yet said what the future of the program will be.

Brandon Bishop and his wife Alora lost their home to the wildfire last month. Their property was one of 73 that were levelled when the fire rolled into Faulder.

In early August, the forestry contractor was marking trails for heavy equipment to plow fire breaks on the mountainside above Faulder, a community near Summerland in British Columbia’s southern Okanagan valley.
He had tied only a single piece of flagging tape when he saw the Bald Range wildfire roaring through the forests toward him.
“This is death coming over the mountain,” Mr. MacLeod remembers thinking. He abandoned flagging and started pounding on residents’ doors, urging them to flee.

He watched as fire ripped across the valley and cut off Fish Lake Road, the only viable route out of the area. Knowing he and dozens of residents were now trapped, Mr. MacLeod leaned on his training and decades of wildfire experience to give those around him the best possible chance to survive.

He picked a grassy meadow as far from the tree line as he could get. If the fire went over them, he told people, they would lie face down, hands over their heads, pressing their lips into small air pockets scraped into the dirt. It would be a last-ditch effort to avoid death. They could survive, he thought, but there would be injuries.
Luckily, a wind shift in the nick of time allowed BC Wildfire Service helicopters to land and start what became a huge air-lift rescue effort.
It could have been much worse, Mr. MacLeod said. “This was so close to being a couple of hundred people [dead].”

stories.title: London's Punk Rock Flea Market is turning 10. Here's how the underground event became a downtown tradition
stories.summary: celebrating its 10th anniversary with a three-day festival featuring live music, local vendors, art, skateboarding and other activities.
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: London·Video
London's Punk Rock Flea Market is celebrating its 10th anniversary with a three-day festival featuring live music, local vendors, art, skateboarding and other activities.
· Posted: Sep 24, 2026 5:00 AM EDT | Last Updated: 1 hour ago
Take a walk down London's Dundas Place during any Punk Rock Flea Market and you'll find an eclectic scene.

Vendors line the street, selling a mix of crochet sweaters and animal skulls. A skateboarder lands a trick, while a family of four smiles for a photo-op. Shoppers slow down to watch a local band play rock music that echoes through the downtown core.
It's a very different scene compared to 10 years ago, said co-organizer Shayna Patterson, when a handful of vendors crowded into music venue Call the Office for the first iteration of the event.
"[It was] a grungy, small bar with maybe 20 vendors and a very complicated layout," Patterson said. "Compared to three blocks of downtown London, they're very different worlds apart from each other."

This weekend marks a decade of London's Punk Rock Flea Market (PRFM), which organizers are celebrating with a free three-day festival filled with live music, vendors, art, skateboarding and other activities.
Looking back at 10 years of London's Punk Rock Flea Market
46 minutes ago|

The Punk Rock Flea Market in London, Ont., is celebrating 10 years, with a multi-day market, punk rock shows and an art exhibit at TAP Centre for Creativity. CBC's Kendra Seguin speaks with co-organizers Shayna Patterson and Alayna Hryclik about the exhibit and what has made the event stand out in the city for so long.

"We just have so many people coming out who have been part of Punk Rock Flea Market since the very beginning, in terms of musicians, artists, activators and people who have really grown in their practice over these 10 years," co-organizer Julie Kortekass said.
"Celebrating this milestone all together is so special."
Co-organizer Alayna Hryclik said the anniversary is also chance for new people to discover PRFM.

"It doesn't matter what walk of life you're from, who you are, your age, anything. There's something for everyone at Punk Rock Flea," Hryclik said. "It's a community who is enthusiastically going to welcome absolutely anyone.
Patterson said she started PRFM in 2016 as a solution to a problem she heard vendors were facing.
"We saw a gap in vendor markets for alternative vendors. There was not really any place that felt like the right fit or drew the crowds they were looking for," she explained.
Shoppers line up outside of Call the Office on York Street in July 2017 for Punk Rock Flea Market. (Submitted by Shayna Patterson)
More than 400 different vendors have participated in PRFM over the years, Patterson said, adding that some have come from as far as Winnipeg in Canada and San Francisco internationally.
In addition to regular markets, PRFM has also hosted winter holiday events and summer pop-ups, bringing it to a total of 34 markets in a decade.
Organizers spend weeks writing grant applications throughout the year, Kortekass said, so that all of the events can be free to attend. She said that helps both customers and vendors.

"We approach this market from a business standpoint," she said. "Making the events free, making the live music free, making the [activities] free just frees up some cash for people to spend on vendors"
Hryclik, who is also an artist and vendor who uses the name softflirt, said it's the positive community that keeps people coming back to PRFM.

"It's somewhere people can see themselves and feel heard in a slightly different, more alternative space," Hryclik said. "It also does bring out people who don't identify with the punk rock aesthetic or ideology, but they still get to see different makers."
"We love the idea that it's a space that bring people together who otherwise might not find each other."
To mark the anniversary, organizers are expanding the usual market into a three-day festival.
"This is how our three brains work together. We all know the look on each other's faces when we have a new, ridiculous idea that we're going to do no matter what," Patterson said.
Festivities start Thursday night at the TAP Centre for Creativity, where the walls will be filled with PRFM posters and memorabilia from the last 10 years.
Most of the artwork is by London artist Jeremy Bruneel, who's been doing posters for PRFM since 2017 and who's style has become synonymous with the event.

"It's surreal because it represents so many countless hours of organizing and also all the people who have been involved in every single one of these markets. It's overwhelming to think about and brings a tear to my eye," Kortekass said.
Opening night will also include a panel discussion, tattoo pop-up and live music performances.

Friday's festival will move to Dundas Place with a 35 vendors, a skateboarding demonstration and six-band music lineup, headlined by Toronto's Cancer Bats. London's Thunder Queens and Status/Non-Status are also on the bill.

PRFM's typical 80-vendor market takes over Dundas between Richmond and Wellington streets starting at 11 a.m. Saturday, with a lineup of music throughout the day. The event will also stretch down to King Street via Clarence Street for the first time for a full day of skateboarding.
Organizers are also hosting two after-parties, including live music at Supply and Demand on Friday night and Honey Dip on Saturday.

stories.title: Construction, public safety among key issues in race for London's Ward 12
stories.summary: Construction, public safety among key issues in race for London's Ward 12 CBC
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: For voters in London's Ward 12, public safety, taxes and roadwork have been top of mind going into the election season, according to candidates running for the council seat.
Sandwiched between Wards 9 and 14, Ward 12 serves as a gateway to the city from Hwy. 401, and is home to city's Cleardale, Highland, Longwoods and White Oaks neighbourhoods.
The ward was among those that had its boundaries redrawn, losing some rural ground to Ward 14, with its southern boundary now stopping at Hwy. 401 instead of Southminster Bourne.
In Ward 1, candidates debate city money for homeless response
Concerns over growth, traffic shaping the race in Ward 3

A fast-growing area of the city, the ward is home to a major development proposal for a new mixed-use subdivision, and several major infrastructure projects that have led to ongoing traffic troubles and frustration from residents.

Most of the city's Wellington Gateway bus rapid transit route sits along the ward's eastern boundary, and work has been underway for several years to extend Bradley Avenue from Wharncliffe Road to White Oak Road.
The slate of candidates running in the ward race include a two-time incumbent, an entrepreneurial engineering student, and a local business owner and former candidate.
Voters head to the polls on Oct. 26.
Ward 12 candidate and incumbent Elizabeth Peloza. (City of London)
The two-term councillor is seeking a third term representing Ward 12, telling CBC London that she has "more to give. I'm not done yet."

"(Being) the city's budget chair was an honour to help our community go through the process, as well as members of council, and have that leadership role," Peloza said, referring to the title she's held since 2021.

"But it does take time away from some things that were board-specific or issue-specific that I wanted to get to. I'm really looking forward to earning the trust of the public and being reelected to dig into some of those and bring forward policies and motions to change some things."
Video Stephen Orser floats homeowners homeless program as 'wide open' Ward 4 race kicks off
Video In London's fast-growing Ward 7, infrastructure lags top candidates' concerns

Two examples, she says, include working on more safe-city initiatives for women, girls and gender-diverse and trans people looking to flee abuse, and improving youth programming, especially into the evening, ensuring young people have a safety net in the community.

Peloza was first elected to council in 2018, receiving 52 per cent of the vote in the city's first, and so far only, ranked ballot election. She was elected to a second term in 2022, receiving 77 per cent of the vote against two other candidates, including current candidate Alexander Main.

She says issues she has heard from constituents while in office are the same ones she's been hearing canvassing, including public safety, street racing, loud vehicles, and construction. A stretch of the Wellington Gateway sits along the eastern edge of Ward 12.

"Can the city not work later into the evenings or on weekends and get it done faster?" is a question Peloza says she's been asked more than once, and adds she's interested in the idea of a pilot project that would look at the issue.
Traffic, transit and affordability top issues in London's Ward 8 election race
Similar concerns, but different approaches for London's Ward 14 election candidates

Peloza's run for reelection comes after months of chemotherapy and radiation following a breast cancer diagnosis last fall, something she first revealed publicly earlier this year. She admits she was concerned the diagnosis could be seen as a liability.

"Is it going to stop me from canvassing? How bad is it going to get?" she recalls asking herself. "Luckily, I can report surgery was fine, chemotherapy was a bit rough but that's done, and radiation has wrapped up. Energy levels, some days are lower than others, which is expected."
She says voters have been understanding, something which only reinforces her decision to go public.
"I could have stayed quiet and just went through it, but was hoping it would alleviate some fears of people and encourage them to look at their own health and seek treatment," she said.
Ward 12 Candidate Ribal Zebian (Ribal Zebian)

One of the youngest, if not the youngest, candidates running for council this election, the second-year Western University engineering student and entrepreneur says he's running, in part, to bring and implement "new, youthful ideas" that could help the city.
"Most of my work is engineering-related, designing and inventing things, things that could help the community and our country," Zebian, 19, told CBC London.

That includes building a fully electric, wooden replica of a Mercedes G-Class SUV in high school and donating it to the London Children's Museum, designing and building several modular homes, and developing AI-assisted software he believes could speed up some city procedures.
London Mayor Josh Morgan launches re-election campaign with 4-part platform
Susan Stevenson kicks off election campaign, promising safety and accountability
"When I saw that we could put some of this technology into our current system and support, I saw it was a great opportunity to get myself in and potentially start helping," he said.
Roadwork and taxes are among the main issues he's heard about while canvassing. Residents, he says, are frustrated by "never-ending road construction" that make them late for work.

"Heavy construction during the nighttime and emptying out the roadways during the daytime for cars to pass through is one thing we're looking at," he said. He pointed to Germany, where certain infrastructure is put under sidewalks instead of roads, as a possible source of inspiration.
As nominations open for city council, Josh Morgan already has a challenger for mayor
Education and the future of London's young people is another hot topic at people's doors.
"There's not much emphasis (being) put on the students and the younger people," he said.
"They're going to be leading (the world), and if they're not trained and mentored adequately enough from a young age, everything we build and work for right now won't exist in the future."

He's proposed putting the 35 per cent council pay increase toward the creation of scholarships, and creating a "micro contract bidding page" where youth could bid on jobs like cutting grass and cleaning up graffiti and garbage to earn money and fill their time.
Ward 12 Candidate Alexander Main (Alexander Main)
Main did not respond to interview requests from CBC News before publication
A local small business owner, Main previously ran for the Ward 12 seat back in 2022, placing third in a race of three candidates with just over 10 per cent of the vote.
Main's campaign website describes him as someone who rebuilt his life after experiencing homelessness, and launched his own business after managing teams and operations for a national retailer.
Voters in London, Ont., zero in on homelessness, drugs, roads as top election issues: survey
The role of school board trustees remains unclear. Here's why some Londoners want the job anyway
Main's time in office would be guided by something he has dubbed "The Safe Plan," built around safety, affordability, fiscal responsibility and enforcement.
"These principles will guide my decisions and provide a practical framework for addressing the issues that matter most to Ward 12 residents," the website states.

"London is at a crossroads. Ward 12 deserves leadership grounded in real-world experience, someone who understands the challenges residents face every day and is committed to ensuring this community has the voice it deserves."

stories.title: Some of our favourite cars from the Cobble Beach Concours d’Elegance – and what their owners say
stories.summary: Mark Richardson speaks to owners of a number of beauties including a 1903 Columbus electric and a 1898 Beeston Quadricycle
stories.author: Mark Richardson
stories.content:
Peter Fawcett, Oshawa, Ont.

It was made in Columbus, Ohio, and it’s serial number 78, and as far as I know, it’s the only one to exist. My father found it in Kingston, Ont. in 1957. I think he paid $400 for it in 1957 and it was pretty complete.

As a little kid, I remember him driving it around the yard, just on the lawn. It worked right away and it still works. The upholstery’s been redone, of course, and paint over the years, but it’s the original electric motor and wiring in this car and it’s still in good shape.

I’m guessing the range is about 30 miles, and I’ll guess it will do 30 miles an hour. I don’t know for how long, though. I never do that. We just drive it around slow and carefully. Today, we had a group of children who came to judge the car and I let them all sit in it, and let them all ring the bell. You’ve got to be able to touch it a little bit, right? You can’t be rough with it, but I showed them where to step and they didn’t hurt it. I think they’ll remember it today. To me, that’s important.

Michael Hoegl, Nobel, Ont.

The vehicle was built in 1898. They built two of them, in Coventry, England. This one here, the customer never picked up. It was kept in storage for 70 years. I bought it in 1995, because I liked it. None of the parts have been replaced. They’re all original parts except for the tires – they took me 17 years to find.

It has a Dion engine, which is a French engine, and with the single cylinder it’s about 350 ccs. It has a hot tube ignition, which is almost the equivalent to a diesel engine, with no spark plug, and no carburettor – it just takes the fumes out of the fuel tank. And the engine’s always engaged and that’s the hard part, because if you want to stop, you have to kill the engine. Then you’ve got to be pedalling until the engine takes over again. So it’s an exercise bike.

Ryan and Barrett Flemons, Burlington and North York, Ont.

Ryan: We’ve both had health issues over the last few years. I have Parkinson’s and (my son) Barrett had cancer, so we wanted to buy something together we could both enjoy.

Barrett: I had Stage 4 Hodgkins’ Lymphoma. It was a rough go, but it’s technically in remission and I’m still standing so I can’t complain too much.

stories.title: Where age is no limit, an immaculate 1932 Rohr Streamliner wins at Cobble Beach
stories.summary: The one-of-a-kind built in Germany with a 3.3-litre eight-cylinder engine under its extended hood and designed by Ferdinand Porsche
stories.author: Mark Richardson
stories.content:
There were 116 cars and one quadricycle parked on the links at Cobble Beach Golf Club last weekend for the annual Cobble Beach Concours d’Elegance.

This was the 12th year for the show near Owen Sound, Ont. that has become Canada’s premier automotive concours. Its entrants were considered by judges from all 10 provinces and 14 American states.

The coveted Best In Show award was presented to an immaculate 1932 Rohr 8 Type F Streamliner owned by Ted and Mary Stahl of Chesterfield, Mich. The unique car was built in Germany with a 3.3-litre eight-cylinder engine under its extended hood, designed by Ferdinand Porsche; it was first shown at the 1932 Paris Motor Show, then the Geneva Salon and then at the international auto show in Berlin the following year. It was brought to the United States after the war by an American military officer and eventually acquired by the Stahls in 2024, after extensive renovation.

The Stahl family owns 262 classic cars and more than 100 of them are displayed on rotation at their Motors and Music Experience museum near Detroit.

“Mr. Stahl has business operations around the world and he’s known for being a great caretaker for these automobiles, so it found its way to him,” said Al Rogers, publicist for the Stahl family who drove the car onto the victory stage. “We’re here for the Triple E’s – to entertain, engage and educate. This is their legacy. We can cross borders and people can be happy and support each other. This is very humbling.”

Not all the vehicles were vintage, but all were relatively rare, if not unique. General Motors brought along three historic Corvettes from its heritage collection and there were plenty of exotic sports cars and supercars. A privately owned 2026 Mercedes-AMG GT 63 APXGP even came with its own security guard to warn off sticky fingers from its matte black paint, but most owners were happy to let people get close to their cars.

“I enjoy allowing people to get in the car and have their picture taken,” said Stephen Burke, of Ypsilanti, Mich., standing beside his 1936 Packard Junior. “Then when they leave here, especially kids, they’ve got something to remember. It’s when you see the smiles on the people’s faces when they lean out the window to have their picture taken. It’s worth everything.”

The oldest vehicle at the show was the 1898 Beeston Quadricycle, owned by Michael Hoegl. He said he rides it once in a while around the local roads of his home north of Parry Sound, Ont. It’s so old he could not easily register its ownership with the Ministry of Transportation – the provincial computer system doesn’t recognize dates before 1900. Not to mention that it’s neither a motorcycle nor a car.

“I found out the system in Ontario runs on DOS,” he said. “So I have an ownership printed on a typewriter, giving me the correct information, and I have an ownership printed for 1900 that the computer recognizes. I had to involve my MPP – there was no other way.”

The Concours is an opportunity to recognize the development of today’s vehicles, said Rob McLeese, the event’s founder and chair, as well as just appreciate the design and engineering of some rare and exquisite examples of automotive history.

“I think it’s important for us to retain our heritage,” said McLeese. “I think it’s important for us to look back, as well as looking forward, because the past often defines the future. And you look at how things have developed and it will help guide you. It doesn’t always happen exactly that way, but I think that is important.

“Also, another aspect that I didn’t realize when we started, is that we’re actually able to raise significant sums here through this, because of these vehicles, for charity.”

The Concours has raised more than $1.5-million for charitable causes over its dozen years, he said, with most of that donated to the Sunnybrook Health Sciences Centre in Toronto, and also to the Brightshores Health System that manages the Brightshores Owen Sound Hospital.

And you look at how things have developed and it will help guide you. It doesn’t always happen exactly that way, but I think that is important.
“Also, another aspect that I didn’t realize when we started, is that we’re actually able to raise significant sums here through this, because of these vehicles, for charity.”

The Concours has raised more than $1.5-million for charitable causes over its dozen years, he said, with most of that donated to the Sunnybrook Health Sciences Centre in Toronto, and also to the Brightshores Health System that manages the Brightshores Owen Sound Hospital.

stories.title: Trump and Xi May extend their truce, but Canada still faces a rare earth squeeze
stories.summary: A U.S.-China deal could ensure Chinese rare-earth supply for Canadian manufacturers, but that comes at a cost.
stories.author: Tracy Moran
stories.content:
Washington, D.C. — Trade tensions are becoming a familiar problem for Washington and this week President Donald Trump is putting his deal-making skills to the test as he hosts China’s president at the White House.

Xi Jinping arrived in Washington, D.C., ON Wednesday, and he and Trump will hold talks on Thursday. They are expected to discuss Iran, Taiwan, and AI safety standards , but the main focus will be on trade — and particularly U.S. access to Chinese rare-earth magnets and processed materials that also feed Canadian supply chains.

The summit comes nearly a year after Xi and Trump forged a trade truce in Busan, South Korea, suspending selected retaliatory measures — including some Chinese export controls on rare-earth magnets and critical materials — and reducing some U.S. tariffs.

Now, that truce is set to expire on Nov. 10, and Trump is seeking an economic victory ahead of November’s midterms. He also must ensure the continued flow of Chinese rare-earth exports to U.S. manufacturers.

Canadian leaders will be watching for any sign of a deal, but trade analysts say Ottawa is likely to lose either way, whether Xi and Trump fail or succeed in coming to an agreement. A collapsed truce could disrupt Canadian manufacturers that rely on Chinese magnets and processed rare earths, while an extension could bring short-term stability but leave Canada dependent on Chinese supply. An extended truce would also leave Canada exposed to a wider U.S.-China trade deal that diverts sales and investment to the U.S.

“No matter what happens, the Canadians are going to be in a position [where] they’re worried about how much of the piece of the pie they’re going to lose,” said Stephen Nagy, senior fellow at the Macdonald-Laurier Institute.

China, pushing for greater stability, wants to extend the truce until the end of the Trump presidency, while the White House is pushing for just a six-month extension.

U.S. and China extend trade truce by two months as Xi met by Trump for start of visit

How China leveraged its critical minerals dominance over the U.S.

The rationale for the shorter extension, explained Dominic Chiu, a senior China and Northeast Asia analyst at Eurasia Group, is that the U.S. believes “it gives them more leverage to extract concessions and to continue the momentum to negotiate with the Chinese … in exchange for additional extensions along the way.”

The report on Washington’s Section 301 structural excess capacity investigation against China has reportedly been punted until after the summit, but that probe May be factoring into Trump’s timeline demands.

“Giving more than six months would effectively be indicating that the 301 investigation is null,” said China scholar Anna Ashton, of Ashton Intelligence.

“The U.S. side will want to have those 301 investigation findings as future leverage for the next round of talks,” she added, noting she expects a six-month extension of the truce to result.

Few expect major breakthroughs this week, but most of the trade watchers said a six-month to year-long truce extension is likely. Chiu said he’s mostly anticipating pomp and circumstance rather than tangible deliverables on Thursday. He expects a truce agreement to come closer to the November deadline. Neither Ashton nor Chiu, however, anticipate any concrete Chinese commitments on rare-earth licensing volumes, turnaround times, minimum supply levels, or enforcement.

If the truce lapses, Canadian manufacturers could face more costly and less reliable access to Chinese magnets and processed rare-earth materials. That could increase pressure for Ottawa to de-risk more quickly by building the infrastructure and industry Canada needs to mine and process rare earths domestically.

But there will be no quick Canadian replacement. Building rare-earth capacity takes years of sustained financing, permitting, infrastructure, and technical expertise. The Carney government has already signalled support for expanding the sector, but it will take several years.

“You don’t just open up supply chains in these rare earths quickly,” said Mark A. Smith, CEO of Colorado-based critical-minerals developer NioCorp Developments.

But Reza Hasmath, a politics professor at the University of Alberta, argues that a longer period of stability could be more useful to Canada’s industrial strategy than a supply crisis. A longer truce, he said, would give Canada more time to build the processing capacity and infrastructure it needs.

“From a strictly rare earth perspective, though, I would suggest that the greater the extension, the better it is for (Canada) because it gives manufacturers much more stability, but it also buys us time to develop that industry a bit more,” he said.

More broadly, however, he sees better U.S.-China relations as bad news for Ottawa.

“When Chinese-U.S. relations are terrible, that gives (Canada) the most leverage, and when they are less tense and when there is a greater truce, generally speaking, it’s not to (Canada’s) advantage,” he said.

Hasmath said a truce is still preferable for Canadian manufacturers, but he explained that Washington has more incentive to seek Canadian alternatives when its relationship with Beijing deteriorates.

According to Ashton, no truce or a shorter truce extension could give Beijing more incentive to preserve commercial options with Canada. That could boost Ottawa’s bargaining leverage as it seeks to extend Chinese tariff relief on Canadian canola meal, lobster, and crab, which is set to expire in December.

Nagy cautions, however, that if the U.S. administration takes a harder line on Beijing, Trump May demand Ottawa’s alignment under threat of more tariffs.

But the same stability that protects manufacturers could weaken the political case for building Canadian alternatives, some warned. More predictable Chinese supply could ease the political urgency — and public-financing momentum — to build Canadian processing capacity.

“On the whole, it’s beneficial to industry at large, but it could slow down the momentum for the critical minerals industry in Canada specifically,” said Chiu.

Smith said the underlying case for diversification should survive either way.

“We cannot sit here and be dependent on any single country for any single item. We have to have alternatives,” he said.

But Hasmath and Nagy agree an extended truce could pose another downside: a wider U.S.-China trade deal could undercut Canadian exporters.

The more the Chinese buy from the Americans, that’s less of our exports going to the Chinese

Most trade watchers believe Beijing will agree — whether it’s this week or in the weeks to come — to buy more U.S. agricultural goods and Boeing aircraft and that the two sides will announce an intention to begin AI-related security talks. Washington May offer China limited relief on access to lower-grade semiconductors, and it May reduce tariffs on some Chinese imports.

Those possible U.S. commercial wins could hurt Canada, because if Beijing buys more U.S. products, Canadian exporters May lose share in those markets.

“The more the Chinese buy from the Americans, that’s less of our exports going to the Chinese,” Hasmath said, pointing to three sectors that could be hit hard: agriculture, aircraft, and LNG.

The tradeoff is a catch-22, he said. Canada benefits when a truce keeps Chinese rare-earth materials flowing to manufacturers, but it has more geopolitical leverage when Washington needs non-Chinese alternatives.

So this week’s summit will not provide Canada with a win or a simple choice. An extended truce would help manufacturers with rare-earth supplies, but it would also prolong their reliance on China — and possibly weaken Ottawa’s push to build domestic processing capacity.

The test will be how Canada uses any period of stability a truce might bring. Will it use the time to build the infrastructure and domestic processing capability it needs to supply rare-earth materials itself? How it responds will determine whether the next U.S.-China trade spat leaves Canada with more leverage — or bigger supply problems.

stories.title: Five takeaways from final debate of Quebec election campaign
stories.summary: Montreal - After being greeted by a raucous crowd of supporters and protesters, the leaders of Quebec's five major political parties dove into their third and final debate of the election campaign, hosted by Radio-Canada on Wednesday evening.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
MONTREAL - After being greeted by a raucous crowd of supporters and protesters, the leaders of Quebec’s five major political parties dove into their third and final debate of the election campaign, hosted by Radio-Canada on Wednesday evening.

Here are five takeaways from a debate featuring Coalition Avenir Québec Leader Christine Fréchette, Quebec Liberal Leader Charles Milliard, Québec solidaire co-spokesperson Ruba Ghazal, Parti Québécois Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon and Quebec Conservative Leader Éric Duhaime.

1. There was a one-hour wait for sparring on sovereignty and a referendum.

The leaders discussed five major themes during Wednesday’s debate. But voters watching at home had to wait until the second hour to hear one of the evening’s most animated exchanges — during a segment about the future of Quebec.

The PQ leader and Québec solidaire’s co-spokesperson are both in favour of sovereignty, with slightly different approaches. Ruba Ghazal promoted her plan to get Indigenous people and English-speaking Quebecers to buy into a campaign to make the province a country. This was the only mention of Quebec’s English-speaking population in the entire debate.

St-Pierre Plamondon quickly found himself on the defensive over his recent pledge to wait until after U.S. President Donald Trump leaves the White House before triggering a referendum.

Milliard pressed St-Pierre Plamondon on whether this delay was an admission a referendum would weaken Quebec — a theory, the PQ leader dismissed.

“It’s proof that we are living a very unusual moment with the Americans that is unacceptable on the part of the Trump administration,” St-Pierre Plamondon said in French. “It’s not a serene climate (while Trump is president) to reflect on our future.”

The PQ leader has pledged to spend $130 million in government to organize a referendum. This would include money for a roving commission to hold consultations on the issue in the years leading up to a vote after January 2029.

Milliard said his rivals all support sovereignty or would have supported it in the past and argued his party was the only federalist option.

Fréchette and Duhaime have said Quebecers are not interested in a referendum.

2. Waiting times in hospitals are still a problem.

Fréchette found herself on the defensive early in the debate after being challenged by her rivals from the Liberals and Parti Québécois about broken health-care promises and long wait times in hospitals after her party’s eight years in government.

Milliard said Quebecers had been betrayed by the Coalition Avenir Québec’s promises to reduce emergency room wait times and ensure every Quebecer had a doctor. St-Pierre Plamondon agreed, saying the latter promise was “disrespectful of people’s intelligence.”

Fréchette acknowledged there was still work to do, but said her party had made improvements, including in increasing the number of surgeries performed and signing up hundreds of thousands of Quebecers for groups of family doctors.

3. St-Pierre Plamondon talked a lot.

Radio-Canada tracked how long each leader spoke during the debate.

By the end of the evening, the moderator, Radio-Canada journalist Patrice Roy, allowed the PQ leader to speak for nearly 24 minutes, while the Liberal and Conservative leaders got less than 18 minutes of airtime to talk about their policies and ideas.

Québec solidaire’s Ghazal spoke for a little more than 20 minutes, while Fréchette spoke for close to 21 minutes.

4. The baby that shook the campaign landed in debate.

A baby found at a homeless encampment in east Montreal in mid-September became the topic of one of the opening segments of the debate. Police say the discovery triggered an investigation and the intervention of social services and youth protection workers.

The story has brought the plight of unhoused people and affordability issues to the forefront of the Quebec campaign, with the leaders expressing shock and pledging to address them.

Each leader was asked about the incident and had a few seconds to respond before moving on to the next topic.

5. There were five leaders on stage.

Political analysts have said Quebec voters are fragmented in a tight race that could lead to a minority government when ballots are cast Oct. 5.

That dynamic was evident on stage as each leader tried to make their points, with multiple voices in the background.
