paragraphs: MONTREAL - After being greeted by a raucous crowd of supporters and protesters, the leaders of Quebec’s five major political parties dove into their third and final debate of the election campaign, hosted by Radio-Canada on Wednesday evening.

Here are five takeaways from a debate featuring Coalition Avenir Québec Leader Christine Fréchette, Quebec Liberal Leader Charles Milliard, Québec solidaire co-spokesperson Ruba Ghazal, Parti Québécois Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon and Quebec Conservative Leader Éric Duhaime.
1. There was a one-hour wait for sparring on sovereignty and a referendum.

The leaders discussed five major themes during Wednesday’s debate. But voters watching at home had to wait until the second hour to hear one of the evening’s most animated exchanges — during a segment about the future of Quebec.

The PQ leader and Québec solidaire’s co-spokesperson are both in favour of sovereignty, with slightly different approaches. Ruba Ghazal promoted her plan to get Indigenous people and English-speaking Quebecers to buy into a campaign to make the province a country. This was the only mention of Quebec’s English-speaking population in the entire debate.
St-Pierre Plamondon quickly found himself on the defensive over his recent pledge to wait until after U.S. President Donald Trump leaves the White House before triggering a referendum.
Milliard pressed St-Pierre Plamondon on whether this delay was an admission a referendum would weaken Quebec — a theory, the PQ leader dismissed.

“It’s proof that we are living a very unusual moment with the Americans that is unacceptable on the part of the Trump administration,” St-Pierre Plamondon said in French. “It’s not a serene climate (while Trump is president) to reflect on our future.”

The PQ leader has pledged to spend $130 million in government to organize a referendum. This would include money for a roving commission to hold consultations on the issue in the years leading up to a vote after January 2029.
Milliard said his rivals all support sovereignty or would have supported it in the past and argued his party was the only federalist option.
Fréchette and Duhaime have said Quebecers are not interested in a referendum.
2. Waiting times in hospitals are still a problem.

Fréchette found herself on the defensive early in the debate after being challenged by her rivals from the Liberals and Parti Québécois about broken health-care promises and long wait times in hospitals after her party’s eight years in government.

Milliard said Quebecers had been betrayed by the Coalition Avenir Québec’s promises to reduce emergency room wait times and ensure every Quebecer had a doctor. St-Pierre Plamondon agreed, saying the latter promise was “disrespectful of people’s intelligence.”

Fréchette acknowledged there was still work to do, but said her party had made improvements, including in increasing the number of surgeries performed and signing up hundreds of thousands of Quebecers for groups of family doctors.
3. St-Pierre Plamondon talked a lot.
Radio-Canada tracked how long each leader spoke during the debate.

By the end of the evening, the moderator, Radio-Canada journalist Patrice Roy, allowed the PQ leader to speak for nearly 24 minutes, while the Liberal and Conservative leaders got less than 18 minutes of airtime to talk about their policies and ideas.
Québec solidaire’s Ghazal spoke for a little more than 20 minutes, while Fréchette spoke for close to 21 minutes.
4. The baby that shook the campaign landed in debate.

A baby found at a homeless encampment in east Montreal in mid-September became the topic of one of the opening segments of the debate. Police say the discovery triggered an investigation and the intervention of social services and youth protection workers.
The story has brought the plight of unhoused people and affordability issues to the forefront of the Quebec campaign, with the leaders expressing shock and pledging to address them.
Each leader was asked about the incident and had a few seconds to respond before moving on to the next topic.
5. There were five leaders on stage.
Political analysts have said Quebec voters are fragmented in a tight race that could lead to a minority government when ballots are cast Oct. 5.
That dynamic was evident on stage as each leader tried to make their points, with multiple voices in the background.
There was limited opportunity for anyone to take specific aim at a rival before others interrupted or tried to change the topic.
This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 24, 2026

stories.title: Former candidate asks Conservatives to 'plug' noses for any concerns about leader
stories.summary: Victoria - A former British Columbia Conservative candidate has urged members of the party to "plug" their noses and accept Lorne Doerkson as their permanent leader if he's successful in the province's snap election on Oct. 24 and build from there.
stories.author: Wolfgang Depner The Canadian Press
stories.content:
New Democrat Leader David Eby says some members of the British Columbia Conservative Opposition have a vision of B.C. as a protectorate of the United States, and the party’s leader isn’t doing enough to rein them in.

Sept. 24, 2026

Updated at 5:55 p.m.

New subscriber benefit!

Copied to clipboard

A gifted article has been claimed.

Out of gifts for the month

Unfortunately you've used all of your gifts this month. Your counter will reset on the first day of next month.

DD[](http://www.thestar.com/news/canada/british-columbia/former-candidate-asks-conservatives-to-plug-noses-for-any-concerns-about-leader/article_97a98501-f9e6-50d7-aedd-bbecf5b70c9b.html)

By Marissa Birnie The Canadian Press

Eby said Thursday that interim Conservative leader Lorne Doerkson cold not stand up to U.S. President Donald Trump because he could not stand up to members of his own party whose ideologies aligned with MAGA-style politics to the south.

“Lorne Doerkson seems like a nice guy. But I never heard him say the word ‘Trump’ before this election,” Eby said.

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

Working remotely from Canada's Wonderland

Eby referred to a social media image reposted by Conservative MLA David Williams last year, showing parts of B.C. within the “Republic of Western Canada,” which was described as “a protectorate of the United States.”

He also criticized the decision by some Conservative caucus members to meet U.S. Ambassador to Canada Pete Hoekstra and said they suggested they would drop the province’s ban on U.S. alcohol, something Doerkson has denied.

Eby said the Opposition party promoted rolling over to Trump, and that the “chaos” would hurt B.C.

Doerkson has repeatedly described Trump as a “bully” since Eby called the snap Oct. 24 election on Tuesday, in a sharp change of tone from the Conservative leadership under Kerry-Lynne Findlay, who quit on Sunday.

He did so again on Thursday.

“Standing up to Donald Trump comes from taking real action, not press releases,” Doerkson said in a statement.

“You don’t stop a bully with tough talk three weeks before an election. You stop a bully by being strong enough that you don’t need him. The NDP had nine years to make B.C. that strong, and B.C. families are still waiting.”

The Conservatives meanwhile boasted of a surge in their poll numbers, according to figures released by the Angus Reid Institute.

The pollsters said the Conservatives have the support of 43 per cent of voters, with the NDP having 35 per cent. The institute also said it found 62 per cent of voters believed the election had been called too soon, based on a randomized online survey of a randomized sample of 801 B.C. adults conducted from Tuesday to Thursday.

The Canadian Research Insights Council, an industry organization that promotes polling standards, says online surveys cannot be assigned a margin of error because they do not randomly sample the population.

Eby spoke at a campaign event in Maple Ridge where he pledged new procurement rules for public infrastructure projects.

He said the province needed to be its own best customer and his government would bring in new rules requiring ministries, Crown agencies and health authorities to use products from B.C. and Canada when building projects.

The new approach would also immediately apply to the construction of the North Coast Transmission Line, he said, ensuring that Canadian steel is used in 70 per cent of Phase 1 of the project and 100 per cent in Phase 2.

Firefighting analogies from Eby’s speech outside Government House on Tuesday were notably absent Thursday.

He had previously spoken of building a “firebreak” against Trump’s economic attacks on Canada, a choice of words some critics characterized as insensitive. Hundreds of homes were destroyed by wildfires in B.C. this year.

“We can add fuel to the fire by following the chaotic direction of the conservative parties in this province ... we can’t afford to spread the fire,” he said Tuesday.

A resurfaced video from Global News shows Doerkson helping fight a wildfire near 100 Mile House with a hose in 2021, with critics now contrasting Doerkson’s literal firefighting with Eby’s metaphoric efforts.

“Lorne fights fires. Eby uses them for campaign metaphors,” the Conservatives said on social media.

Eby did not directly answer questions from reporters about whether he regretted his turn of phrase.

He said that if Doerkson won the election, the ultimate decision on whether he would remain premier would be in the hands of party members who would need to confirm him as their leader on a permanent basis.

The Conservatives’ directors have previously said they would “pursue the appropriate means” to keep Doerkson in power by amending their constitution.

“They want a blank check,” Eby said. “And the signatory on that check will be the same party members that sent Kerry-Lynne Findlay in as leader.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 24, 2026.

The Canadian Press

stories.title: AFN regional chiefs to represent First Nations at meeting with Carney, premiers
stories.summary: Ottawa — Assembly of First Nations regional chiefs will join premiers and Prime Minister Mark Carney for a rare meeting in late October — the first such meeting between chiefs and first ministers in decades.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
By Alessia Passafiume, The Canadian Press

Posted September 24, 2026 4:00 am.

Last Updated September 24, 2026 5:19 am.

Ottawa — Assembly of First Nations regional chiefs will join premiers and Prime Minister Mark Carney for a rare meeting in late October — the first such meeting between chiefs and first ministers in decades.

A source shared details of a Wednesday planning meeting held by the Assembly of First Nations on the condition they not be named because they were not authorized to discuss it.

The premiers, Carney and First Nations representatives are set to meet in Ottawa on Oct. 26, just as tensions are rising over the federal and provincial governments’ major projects agenda.

National Chief Cindy Woodhouse Nepinak has invited premiers and Carney to a daylong ceremony ahead of the October meeting. She told The Canadian Press last week that First Nations leaders want to bring their own cultural practices to that meeting and she hopes all premiers accept the invitation.

The meeting was promised by Carney earlier this year.

Woodhouse Nepinak and her predecessors have for years been calling for First Nations representation at meetings between the prime minister and the premiers. Those calls got louder last year when the federal and provincial governments started discussing among themselves ways to fast-track major infrastructure projects.

Woodhouse Nepinak has said the meeting will be a “big test” of Canada’s ability to reconcile economic growth with First Nations rights.

Topics up for discussion at the meeting include long-term political governance — including rights and treaties, jurisdiction, health care, policing and land — economic partnerships and prosperity, the source told The Canadian Press.

There will be 28 seats in the main meeting room — one for the prime minister, one for the national chief, 13 for provincial and territorial leaders and 13 for First Nations representatives. The First Nations representatives in the main meeting room will mostly be regional chiefs from the Assembly of First Nations.

An additional 44 First Nations leaders are invited to attend, including one youth representative and representatives from Treaties 6, 7 and 8. The Assembly of First Nations is calling for those 44 entry passes to be interchangeable so they can accommodate a larger number of leaders.

While the meeting will be livestreamed, it’s not clear if that livestream will be available for public viewing, as the AFN has requested.

BySheila Wang Investigative Reporter

Ontario’s nursing regulator is moving to ban unsupervised esthetic injections by unlicensed staff, amid growing concerns about oversight of the med spa industry.

The move comes after the College of Nurses of Ontario (CNO) had released sweeping guidelines for nurses in esthetic services but drew criticism for failing to fully fill a regulatory gap: Without being on site, nurses can delegate the injecting of customers to unsupervised staffers who are not overseen by a college.

The CNO is set to vote on the proposed change to its practice standards today, as the college continues to tighten its grip on esthetic services.

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

Working remotely from Canada's Wonderland

Since January, an ongoing Star investigation has revealed details of four patients who were allegedly harmed after receiving esthetic treatments in GTA clinics. None of the delegating medical directors were on site at the time of the procedures. One of those patients died.

After an esthetician allegedly applied lidocaine cream — a prescription numbing drug — over the 38-year-old woman’s face and body in preparation for microneedling, the woman started seizing and vomiting, and was pronounced dead at a nearby hospital. A coroner later found she died of lidocaine toxicity. The clinic’s medical director and delegating nurse, neither of whom were on site during the procedure, have denied they breached any duty of care.

Star Investigation

Loose policies have led to a flood of unsupervised medical procedures performed by unqualified

Under the CNO’s proposal, nurses must be on site when they delegate medical esthetic procedures such as Botox and filler injections, as well as microneedling, to a staffer who does not otherwise have authority to perform the treatments.

“It will very, very significantly improve the safety of the public,” nurse practitioner Negin Nikfar said.

Nikfar and other experts told the Star that the amendment is taking direct aim at a trend called “rent a licence,” where doctors and nurse practitioners have acted as delegating medical directors for multiple med spas, in some cases collecting thousands of dollars a month while having little to no involvement in the day-to-day operations. Experts have said the practice opened the floodgate for unsupervised medical procedures performed by unqualified people.

In March, the College of Physicians and Surgeons of Ontario (CPSO) began requiring doctors who delegate procedures to be physically on site to supervise treatment.

If the new rules are approved by the CNO council, nurse practitioners in esthetics will also be required to issue direct, client-specific orders instead of a general directive that applies to multiple patients. They would be required to complete a client assessment in person or virtually before giving the direct order.

“I think it’s a great step forward,” said Dr. Ashwani Singh, an Alberta-based veteran in the esthetic medicine industry. “It is going to return us to the roots of medicine, which was having you in front of your patient, examining your patient, having a conversation with your patient, getting a treatment protocol for that patient, and then treating that patient.”

Singh founded a forum of esthetics physicians from across the world advocating for stricter regulations around injectables. The CNO’s council agenda noted that the forum expressed its support for these proposals.

The proposed changes followed a public consultation, questions from media outlets, and a CNO analysis of recent professional conduct case files, according to the council agenda.

Singh, who said the CNO has been “slow” to address these concerns because of pushback from the esthetic industry, expects the new rules, if passed, will limit customers’ exposure to botched procedures.

“There is a lot of money to be lost,” if the proposed rules are approved and enforced, he said, noting that the on-site requirements for delegating nurses could have a significant impact on the business interest of medical directors paid by multiple clinics.

“At the end of the day it should only be one interest, the patient,” Singh said.

The majority of nursing regulators in Canada have established guidelines for safe client care in esthetic practice.

An online petition with more than 3,000 signatures has raised concerns about how the proposed requirement for a direct order for each patient would impact nursing autonomy and reduce access to regulated health care professionals, and wants the CNO to make regulations based on evidence.

“The concerns are legitimate,” said Nikfar, who is medical director of YMG Aesthetic Clinic and did not participate in the petition. “It will create additional documentation, administrative work, and some existing business models will need to change.”

The Star, simplified

She also called on the CNO for more clarity on how a nurse is expected to use a direct order for each patient to avoid what she worries will be “unnecessary documentations and unclear implementation.”

CNO spokesperson Elizabeth Almeida said that if a proper client-specific order is in place and the client’s condition and circumstances, as well as the treatment goals, remain unchanged, then a new assessment or order is not required for every visit.

Nikfar told the Star that though the proposed new rules have already prompted her to make a few adjustments at her clinic, she is very happy with the direction the CNO is taking to ensure patient safety.

“Business efficiency is important,” she added. “But it should not replace clinical accountability.”

Sheila Wang is an investigative reporter for the Star. Reach her via email: sheilawang@thestar.ca.

ByJacques Gallant Courts and Justice Reporter

An independent oversight body has delivered a clear message to Ontario’s only maximum-security psychiatric hospital when it comes to keeping patients in long-term isolation: It’s time you started following your own policies.

In a unanimous 33-page decision released last week, a five-member panel of the Ontario Review Board (ORB) provided its detailed reasons for why it ordered Waypoint Centre for Mental Health Care in Penetanguishene to implement measures to reduce the time that patient Andrew Azevedo spends in seclusion.

Azevedo, a 39-year-old man with treatment-resistant schizophrenia, has spent much of the last five years locked in his room alone due to what the hospital describes as aggressive behaviour caused by his hallucinations — a “troubling duration,” the board said.

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

Working remotely from Canada's Wonderland

The ORB had issued its orders earlier this month in a document called a disposition, in which it officially recognized that seclusion is harmful. It mandated that Waypoint improve its staff training, ensure that Azevedo gets a minimum amount of time out of his room on seclusion relief, that he be assessed in person daily before the hospital decides if his seclusion should be maintained, and that there be weekly communication between his treatment team and family.

“Essentially, for Mr. Azevedo’s disposition to maximize his potential for personal liberty while subject to detention at Waypoint, the panel is directing Waypoint’s treatment of him to be in compliance with its own policies,” says last week’s reasons written by panel member Eric Siebenmorgen, a retired Crown counsel.

Siebenmorgen returned to the need for Waypoint to follow its own policies repeatedly in the decision. He said the panel was “indebted” to corrections expert Andrea Monteiro, who prepared an independent assessment of Azevedo’s case; without her thorough work, it would have been “extremely difficult” for the board to provide proper oversight of Azevedo’s seclusion experience due to what Siebenmorgen described as incomplete and inaccurate information compiled by Waypoint.

Seclusion means locking a psychiatric patient up alone in a room.

Waypoint policies say it's a last resort, to be used for as brief a time as possible, with a patient who poses an imminent risk.

Waypoint has been keeping some patients in seclusion for years on end; for Camelott Hamblett, it's been 20 years.

Leading experts have described Waypoint's practices as “abusive” and unlike anything seen in other North American facilities.

Waypoint has refused to divulge how many patients are in long-term seclusion.

Waypoint says it is following a set of best practices called the Six Core Strategies to reduce seclusion.[](https://www.thestar.com/news/ontario/ontario-hospital-ceo-says-shes-adopted-the-best-strategies-to-end-years-long-patient-isolation-thats-clearly-not-true-the-strategies-creators-say/article_b5aabff7-c847-4b09-8985-09cfd3a5fbdf.html "https://www.thestar.com/news/ontario/ontario-hospital-ceo-says-shes-adopted-the-best-strategies-to-end-years-long-patient-isolation-thats-clearly-not-true-the-strategies-creators-say/article_b5aabff7-c847-4b09-8985-09cfd3a5fbdf.html")

The first of the six says the hospital CEO must be directly involved in the day-to-day use of seclusion.

Waypoint CEO Dr. Nadiya Sunderji has told the Star she will not do that, saying it would be inappropriate.

Warnings about “unethical” long-term seclusion at Waypoint and its predecessor, Oak Ridge, go back to at least 1984.

In 2019, a former Waypoint psychiatrist warned the Ford government the hospital's practices are "horrific" — but the Ministry of Health took no further action.

An independent report in the case of Andrew Azevedo found patients are being kept in conditions akin to the UN definition of torture.

That assessment also found the hospital routinely does not meet its own standards, including failing to give secluded patients two hours outside their rooms each day.

It’s important that the board gets accurate information about Azevedo’s experience, given “the significant deprivation of liberty, and associated potential negative impacts” on him,Siebenmorgen wrote.

Azevedowas profiled in the Star in April as part of its investigation into the use of long-term seclusion at Waypoint, a practice described by experts as “excessive,” akin to torture, and unlike anything seen in other North American hospitals.

Waypoint’s own policy stipulates that seclusion be only used as a last resort— and for as brief a time as possible— when dealing with a patient who poses an imminent risk of bodily harm to themselves or others, but the Star’s investigation has revealed that Waypoint is keeping patients secluded for years, including Camelott Hamblett, who has been locked in his room for 20 years and counting.

Monteiro concluded that Waypoint is using seclusion to pre-emptively manage a patient who might become violent later, a practice she said is now prohibited in many prisons. The ORB panel said it couldn’t make a finding about that because Azevedo’s psychiatrist, Dr. Achal Mishra, wasn’t asked about it during Azevedo’s hearing before the board last month.

But the panel said they hope their orders ensure that seclusion at Waypoint remains an exceptional measure “and does not become a long-term or ‘default’ risk management strategy.”

Azevedo remains detained after being found unfit to stand trial for allegedly assaulting a psychiatrist. The ORB, made up of retired judges, lawyers, doctors, and laypersons, is responsible for deciding annually whether a person found unfit to stand trial or not criminally responsible should remain detained in hospital or be released, and under what conditions.

The Star’s investigation hasalso focused on whether the board should have done more to help get patients out of long-term seclusion, given that it’s also supposed to supervise the treatment and living conditions of patients under its jurisdiction. For years, panels of the board maintained the detention of accused persons— including Azevedo— while making but a passing reference to their seclusion status, with no recommendations to get them out.

Azevedo’s lawyer, Anita Szigeti, described last week’s comprehensive ORB decision as a “watershed” moment that could have a positive ripple effect on other patients in long-term seclusion at Waypoint.

“You can feel the winds of change,” she said.

While other panels won’t be bound by the Azevedo panel’s decision, Szigeti said the decision is nevertheless persuasive.

“The next panel can take some comfort in the fact that this hearing panel has expressly recognized that the board plays an oversight role with respect to the conditions, the length, and the experience of seclusion,” she said.

Indeed, as Siebenmorgen wrote, just because the board was ordering that Azevedo remain detained at Waypoint — as agreed to by all parties— that “does not absolve the board of its responsibility to order conditions of his detention that seek to maximize his liberty while still protecting the public, including staff and other patients in the hospital.”

The panel also included lawyer and chairperson Janette Mills, psychiatrist Padraig Darby, psychologist Gjylena Nexhipi, and community member Cathy Plyley, a social service worker.

Ultimately, the ORB can only make orders with respect to the patient before them.And it has no jurisdiction over Waypoint patients who have not been accused of any crimes, such as 31-year-old Jake Gordon, a man with schizophrenia involuntarily admitted under the Mental Health Act.

Gordon, who was profiled in the Star this month, also spent five years in seclusion. Six hours of video footage from last year shows him living in a small, sparse room with little to do. He can be seen napping, eating and pacing, only occasionally interacting with staff at his doorway.

Szigeti reiterated her call for an independent and public review of the use of seclusion at Waypoint. “People really need to care about what’s going on,” she said.

Waypoint, which had urged the board not to issue any orders, has the option of appealing the Azevedo decision to the Ontario Court of Appeal; the hospital says it is reviewing the board’s reasons.

“Waypoint remains committed to our shared priorities with the ORB to deliver quality patient care while protecting public safety,” said CEO Dr. Nadiya Sunderji.

Azevedo is already on the cusp of being released from seclusion due to a significant improvement in his behaviour over the last few months that his psychiatrist attributes entirely to medication adjustments, while his family and Szigeti point to the heightened level of care and supports provided to him by the hospital in the wake of the Star’s coverage.

Azevedo’s sister-in-law, Susan, said he is “forever changed” by being in seclusion for so long, and the family can’t help but wonder what his life would have looked like had he received the kind of care he’s getting now.

“It didn’t have to be this way,” she said.

She said the family is grateful for the board’s decision. Azevedo is doing well and is currently allowed out of his room for six hours a day with staff, as the hospital gradually releases him from seclusion, Susan said.

“We know Andrew has a lifelong illness, and we will spend our lives advocating for him,” she said. “Being sick, having this severe level of schizophrenia, shouldn’t be a sentence to seclusion for the rest of your life with no treatment.”

The ORB panel said it felt it was “necessary and appropriate” to issue orders to “safeguard Mr. Azevedo’s liberty interests” should his condition deteriorate and should he be once again placed in seclusion. A number of those orders mirror recommendations Monteiro made in her independent assessment.

The hospital had argued that portions of Monteiro’s report dealing with staffing levels should be shielded from the public, arguing it could facilitate physical assaults in Azevedo’s unit, escapes, and the bringing of contraband.

The board disagreed, finding the arguments were speculative and stating that any restrictions on Monteiro’s report would “negatively impact the public’s ability to scrutinize in an informed manner” the board’s oversight of Azevedo’s detention.

The board ordered that Waypoint develop a staff training program specific to Azevedo’s needs to maximize his time out of seclusion. “This means ensuring that all staff are well-versed in Waypoint’s own policies concerning restraints and seclusion,” Siebenmorgen wrote, as some staff seemed unaware in their interviews with Monteiro about the threshold for placing someone in seclusion.

While Waypoint’s policy is that secluded patients should be offered a minimum of two hours of seclusion relief a day— when they are escorted out of their rooms and can engage in activities like going to the gym or listening to music— Monteiro learned that due to staff shortages, patients are generally offered one hour a day, and sometimes no time at all.

The panel ordered that Azevedo be offered at least two hours a day: “In light of Waypoint’s own policies, this is a minimum standard that should be non-controversial, and not merely an aspirational hope.”

And the panel specified that this does not include family visits and showers, after learning that Waypoint had been including those things in how it counts seclusion relief.

Finally, the panel ordered that Azevedo be assessed in person daily to determine whether his seclusion should be continued. Monteiro found that doctors were renewing a patient’s seclusion status every 24 hours by reviewing their charts and talking to their care team. She also found that the reasons for maintaining seclusion weren’t always noted.

Mishra, Azevedo’s psychiatrist, resisted this proposal, telling the panel last month that there aren’t enough doctors to conduct daily in-person assessments; in making its order, the board said the professional doing the assessment doesn’t have to be a physician, but should have appropriate skills and training with respect to the patient’s presentation and risk.

“It is difficult to understand how this scheme for reviewing, assessing and, if necessary, renewing orders to seclude a patient can properly operate in the absence of an in-person assessment of the patient,”Siebenmorgen wrote.

The panel ordered that Azevedo’s case return before it early— in six months—“to obtain an update on progress made by Waypoint regarding the above directions and the accused’s seclusion status.”

Leading experts have described Waypoint's practices as “abusive” and unlike anything seen in other North American facilities.
Waypoint has refused to divulge how many patients are in long-term seclusion.

Waypoint says it is following a set of best practices called the Six Core Strategies to reduce seclusion.[](https://www.thestar.com/news/ontario/ontario-hospital-ceo-says-shes-adopted-the-best-strategies-to-end-years-long-patient-isolation-thats-clearly-not-true-the-strategies-creators-say/article_b5aabff7-c847-4b09-8985-09cfd3a5fbdf.html "https://www.thestar.com/news/ontario/ontario-hospital-ceo-says-shes-adopted-the-best-strategies-to-end-years-long-patient-isolation-thats-clearly-not-true-the-strategies-creators-say/article_b5aabff7-c847-4b09-8985-09cfd3a5fbdf.html")
The first of the six says the hospital CEO must be directly involved in the day-to-day use of seclusion.
Waypoint CEO Dr. Nadiya Sunderji has told the Star she will not do that, saying it would be inappropriate.
Warnings about “unethical” long-term seclusion at Waypoint and its predecessor, Oak Ridge, go back to at least 1984.
In 2019, a former Waypoint psychiatrist warned the Ford government the hospital's practices are "horrific" — but the Ministry of Health took no further action.
An independent report in the case of Andrew Azevedo found patients are being kept in conditions akin to the UN definition of torture.
That assessment also found the hospital routinely does not meet its own standards, including failing to give secluded patients two hours outside their rooms each day.

content_blocks.text: It’s important that the board gets accurate information about Azevedo’s experience, given “the significant deprivation of liberty, and associated potential negative impacts” on him,Siebenmorgen wrote.

Azevedowas profiled in the Star in April as part of its investigation into the use of long-term seclusion at Waypoint, a practice described by experts as “excessive,” akin to torture, and unlike anything seen in other North American hospitals.

Waypoint’s own policy stipulates that seclusion be only used as a last resort— and for as brief a time as possible— when dealing with a patient who poses an imminent risk of bodily harm to themselves or others, but the Star’s investigation has revealed that Waypoint is keeping patients secluded for years, including Camelott Hamblett, who has been locked in his room for 20 years and counting.

Monteiro concluded that Waypoint is using seclusion to pre-emptively manage a patient who might become violent later, a practice she said is now prohibited in many prisons. The ORB panel said it couldn’t make a finding about that because Azevedo’s psychiatrist, Dr. Achal Mishra, wasn’t asked about it during Azevedo’s hearing before the board last month.
But the panel said they hope their orders ensure that seclusion at Waypoint remains an exceptional measure “and does not become a long-term or ‘default’ risk management strategy.”

Azevedo remains detained after being found unfit to stand trial for allegedly assaulting a psychiatrist. The ORB, made up of retired judges, lawyers, doctors, and laypersons, is responsible for deciding annually whether a person found unfit to stand trial or not criminally responsible should remain detained in hospital or be released, and under what conditions.

The Star’s investigation hasalso focused on whether the board should have done more to help get patients out of long-term seclusion, given that it’s also supposed to supervise the treatment and living conditions of patients under its jurisdiction. For years, panels of the board maintained the detention of accused persons— including Azevedo— while making but a passing reference to their seclusion status, with no recommendations to get them out.

Azevedo’s lawyer, Anita Szigeti, described last week’s comprehensive ORB decision as a “watershed” moment that could have a positive ripple effect on other patients in long-term seclusion at Waypoint.
“You can feel the winds of change,” she said.
While other panels won’t be bound by the Azevedo panel’s decision, Szigeti said the decision is nevertheless persuasive.

“The next panel can take some comfort in the fact that this hearing panel has expressly recognized that the board plays an oversight role with respect to the conditions, the length, and the experience of seclusion,” she said.

Indeed, as Siebenmorgen wrote, just because the board was ordering that Azevedo remain detained at Waypoint — as agreed to by all parties— that “does not absolve the board of its responsibility to order conditions of his detention that seek to maximize his liberty while still protecting the public, including staff and other patients in the hospital.”
The panel also included lawyer and chairperson Janette Mills, psychiatrist Padraig Darby, psychologist Gjylena Nexhipi, and community member Cathy Plyley, a social service worker.
‘It didn’t have to be this way,’ family says

Ultimately, the ORB can only make orders with respect to the patient before them.And it has no jurisdiction over Waypoint patients who have not been accused of any crimes, such as 31-year-old Jake Gordon, a man with schizophrenia involuntarily admitted under the Mental Health Act.

Gordon, who was profiled in the Star this month, also spent five years in seclusion. Six hours of video footage from last year shows him living in a small, sparse room with little to do. He can be seen napping, eating and pacing, only occasionally interacting with staff at his doorway.
Szigeti reiterated her call for an independent and public review of the use of seclusion at Waypoint. “People really need to care about what’s going on,” she said.
Waypoint, which had urged the board not to issue any orders, has the option of appealing the Azevedo decision to the Ontario Court of Appeal; the hospital says it is reviewing the board’s reasons.
“Waypoint remains committed to our shared priorities with the ORB to deliver quality patient care while protecting public safety,” said CEO Dr. Nadiya Sunderji.

Azevedo is already on the cusp of being released from seclusion due to a significant improvement in his behaviour over the last few months that his psychiatrist attributes entirely to medication adjustments, while his family and Szigeti point to the heightened level of care and supports provided to him by the hospital in the wake of the Star’s coverage.

Azevedo’s sister-in-law, Susan, said he is “forever changed” by being in seclusion for so long, and the family can’t help but wonder what his life would have looked like had he received the kind of care he’s getting now.
“It didn’t have to be this way,” she said.

She said the family is grateful for the board’s decision. Azevedo is doing well and is currently allowed out of his room for six hours a day with staff, as the hospital gradually releases him from seclusion, Susan said.

“We know Andrew has a lifelong illness, and we will spend our lives advocating for him,” she said. “Being sick, having this severe level of schizophrenia, shouldn’t be a sentence to seclusion for the rest of your life with no treatment.”

The ORB panel said it felt it was “necessary and appropriate” to issue orders to “safeguard Mr. Azevedo’s liberty interests” should his condition deteriorate and should he be once again placed in seclusion. A number of those orders mirror recommendations Monteiro made in her independent assessment.

The hospital had argued that portions of Monteiro’s report dealing with staffing levels should be shielded from the public, arguing it could facilitate physical assaults in Azevedo’s unit, escapes, and the bringing of contraband.

The board disagreed, finding the arguments were speculative and stating that any restrictions on Monteiro’s report would “negatively impact the public’s ability to scrutinize in an informed manner” the board’s oversight of Azevedo’s detention.

Waypoint ordered to make sure staff know hospital policies

The board ordered that Waypoint develop a staff training program specific to Azevedo’s needs to maximize his time out of seclusion. “This means ensuring that all staff are well-versed in Waypoint’s own policies concerning restraints and seclusion,” Siebenmorgen wrote, as some staff seemed unaware in their interviews with Monteiro about the threshold for placing someone in seclusion.

While Waypoint’s policy is that secluded patients should be offered a minimum of two hours of seclusion relief a day— when they are escorted out of their rooms and can engage in activities like going to the gym or listening to music— Monteiro learned that due to staff shortages, patients are generally offered one hour a day, and sometimes no time at all.

The panel ordered that Azevedo be offered at least two hours a day: “In light of Waypoint’s own policies, this is a minimum standard that should be non-controversial, and not merely an aspirational hope.”
And the panel specified that this does not include family visits and showers, after learning that Waypoint had been including those things in how it counts seclusion relief.

Finally, the panel ordered that Azevedo be assessed in person daily to determine whether his seclusion should be continued. Monteiro found that doctors were renewing a patient’s seclusion status every 24 hours by reviewing their charts and talking to their care team. She also found that the reasons for maintaining seclusion weren’t always noted.

Mishra, Azevedo’s psychiatrist, resisted this proposal, telling the panel last month that there aren’t enough doctors to conduct daily in-person assessments; in making its order, the board said the professional doing the assessment doesn’t have to be a physician, but should have appropriate skills and training with respect to the patient’s presentation and risk.

“It is difficult to understand how this scheme for reviewing, assessing and, if necessary, renewing orders to seclude a patient can properly operate in the absence of an in-person assessment of the patient,”Siebenmorgen wrote.
The panel ordered that Azevedo’s case return before it early— in six months—“to obtain an update on progress made by Waypoint regarding the above directions and the accused’s seclusion status.”

ByJoshua Smith Staff Reporter

He had a shotgun, a stockpile of ammunition and gasoline — enough, police say, to kill dozens of worshippers at a Belleville synagogue. Instead, a wounded officer stopped him, refusing to back down even after being shot multiple times.

The ambush atthe Sons of Jacob Synagogue during Yom Kippur last weekendinjured Const. Jeff Smith, who was stationed outside, Belleville Police Chief Murray Rodd told reporters Thursday.

Police played a video of the shooting, during which several loud shots can be heard.

A gunman attacked the Sons of Jacob Synagogue in Belleville during Yom Kippur last weekend, injuring one officer who was shot multiple times.

“Based on the evidence we’ve reviewed … (investigators) can confirm this was a hate-motivated crime,” Rodd said.

Smith was shot multiple times but “stayed engaged” with the attacker, Rodd said. About three minutes later, a second police officer,Const. Mike McCurdy, arrived and joined what Rodd described as an “active gunfight.”

“They are both heroes,” Rodd said of McCurdy and Smith.

“We know that there was a reconnaissance in the presence of our officer, but nothing that would have alarmed him or would have triggered him to be on the defensive. (Smith) was then ambushed on a second pass. That’s when the shooting started,” Rodd said.

Ward, a former Canadian Armed Forces infantry soldier, died of his injuries Monday; Rodd said Thursday that evidence — including a recorded threat singling out the Jewish community — confirms the attack was hate-motivated and aimed at mass casualties. The shooting has renewed alarm over antisemitic violence in Canada, with Ontario’s solicitor general and the RCMP commissioner both condemning the attack this week.

Police have not revealed a suspected motive for the shooting, which has left a police officer

“The suspect had the means, the motive and the mechanisms to cause a mass casualty (event) and the destruction of the Jewish synagogue,” Rodd added. “The loss of life and the irreversible damage that could have rippled through our community for generations cannot be overstated.”

Belleville police said Tuesday Smith remains in the ICU but has progressed very well in the last 24 hours. His wife, Ashley Smith, said in a post on social media that her husband “has a very long, difficult road ahead” but is “fighting.”

“He will have multiple surgeries. He has a long road to recover. But he was shot multiple times, multiple places,” Rodd said at the news conference. “He has everything extending from fractures to wounds still bearing shrapnel. We are encouraged … with his recovery, but he has a long road to travel .”

The police chief said the SIU is still leading the investigation and police are in the process of reviewing the evidence.

”(Ward) used the shotgun that we all spoke about. He had other resources available to him. He had a significant amount of ammunition on his person and available,” said Rodd.

He also had supplies like gasoline in his vehicle to possibly commit more damage, Rodd added.

In the message posted on Facebook, Ashley Smith, the wife of Belleville police Const. Jeff Smith

“A line of decency has been crossed in our province,” Ontario’s solicitor general, Michael Kerzner, said at the news conference in Belleville on Thursday. “Having an individual act in such a hateful and antisemitic attack is unacceptable.”

The shooting prompted a community vigil and renewed alarm over hate-motivated violence in the province.

“This was an exclusive threat to our Jewish community,” Rodd said. “There’s no indication there’s a threat to any other population or segment of our community.”

In Ottawa, RCMP Commissioner Michael Duheme lamented the rise of antisemitic extremism and attacks against places of worship in Canada on Thursday.

“Quite frankly, any Canadian citizen should be concerned about the escalation that we’re seeing across Canada,” he told reporters. “It’s interesting because the fact that we weren’t exposed to that in the past, and you see these ideologies, you see what’s going on around the world and how this is impacting Canadians.”

Ward, who was from Quinte West, was a member of the Canadian Armed Forces for nearly five years. He joined the army in July 2017 and was released in June 2022 at the rank of corporal, according to Department of National Defence spokesperson Andrée-Anne Poulin.

Sean Ward, 29, from Quinte West, was shot by police during an exchange of gunfire as he

He served as an infantry soldier with Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry and did not deploy during his service, Poulin said.

Documents obtained by The Canadian Press suggest he had joined a lawsuit against the Canadian Armed Forces’ vaccination mandate, claiming $140,000 in financial losses after he was released from service. In its statement of defence, the government argued that the lawsuit should be thrown out and that vaccinating against COVID-19 was a safe and appropriate response to the pandemic.

After the Belleville police chief’s remarks calling the shooting a hate-motivated attack on the Jewish community, Toronto leaders spoke out.

“The antisemitic attack on a Belleville synagogue is an attack on Jewish communities everywhere. It is an attack on everyone’s right to live together in peace,” Toronto mayor Olivia Chow wrote on X.

“Fear and uncertainty in Jewish communities is real … While there is no known threat to Toronto at this time, hate and violent extremism are concerns across Canada,” Toronto police wrote on X.

Toronto police chief Myron Demkiw said the police service’s command team met with its Jewish Community Consultative Committee, Toronto Police Service Board and the Board’s Jewish Advisory Table on Thursday to discuss concerns in the community after the hate-motivated shooting incident.

“We understand the fear and uncertainty that incidents like these create within the Jewish community,” Demkiw wrote in a social media post. “We will continue to maintain an increased presence around places of worship, schools, and community centres to ensure that community members are safe and feel safe.”

Public Safety Minister Gary Anandasangaree said Thursday the federal government, through a security infrastructure program, will pay for any security supports the Sons of Jacob Synagogue needs.

With files from Raju Mudhar, Mark Ramzy and The Canadian Press

Joshua Smith is a staff reporter with the Toronto Star. He can be reached atjoshuasmith@thestar.ca.

Belleville police said Tuesday Smith remains in the ICU but has progressed very well in the last 24 hours. His wife, Ashley Smith, said in a post on social media that her husband “has a very long, difficult road ahead” but is “fighting.”

“He will have multiple surgeries. He has a long road to recover. But he was shot multiple times, multiple places,” Rodd said at the news conference. “He has everything extending from fractures to wounds still bearing shrapnel. We are encouraged … with his recovery, but he has a long road to travel .”
Police reveal more details about synagogue shooting
The police chief said the SIU is still leading the investigation and police are in the process of reviewing the evidence.
”(Ward) used the shotgun that we all spoke about. He had other resources available to him. He had a significant amount of ammunition on his person and available,” said Rodd.
He also had supplies like gasoline in his vehicle to possibly commit more damage, Rodd added.
Wife of injured Belleville officer shot outside synagogue says he is fighting as support pours in
In the message posted on Facebook, Ashley Smith, the wife of Belleville police Const. Jeff Smith

“A line of decency has been crossed in our province,” Ontario’s solicitor general, Michael Kerzner, said at the news conference in Belleville on Thursday. “Having an individual act in such a hateful and antisemitic attack is unacceptable.”
The shooting prompted a community vigil and renewed alarm over hate-motivated violence in the province.
“This was an exclusive threat to our Jewish community,” Rodd said. “There’s no indication there’s a threat to any other population or segment of our community.”
In Ottawa, RCMP Commissioner Michael Duheme lamented the rise of antisemitic extremism and attacks against places of worship in Canada on Thursday.

“Quite frankly, any Canadian citizen should be concerned about the escalation that we’re seeing across Canada,” he told reporters. “It’s interesting because the fact that we weren’t exposed to that in the past, and you see these ideologies, you see what’s going on around the world and how this is impacting Canadians.”
Ward was former Canadian Forces member

Ward, who was from Quinte West, was a member of the Canadian Armed Forces for nearly five years. He joined the army in July 2017 and was released in June 2022 at the rank of corporal, according to Department of National Defence spokesperson Andrée-Anne Poulin.
New details about Belleville synagogue shooting suspect emerge following his death in hospital
Sean Ward, 29, from Quinte West, was shot by police during an exchange of gunfire as he
He served as an infantry soldier with Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry and did not deploy during his service, Poulin said.

Documents obtained by The Canadian Press suggest he had joined a lawsuit against the Canadian Armed Forces’ vaccination mandate, claiming $140,000 in financial losses after he was released from service. In its statement of defence, the government argued that the lawsuit should be thrown out and that vaccinating against COVID-19 was a safe and appropriate response to the pandemic.
Reaction from Toronto mayor, police
After the Belleville police chief’s remarks calling the shooting a hate-motivated attack on the Jewish community, Toronto leaders spoke out.
“The antisemitic attack on a Belleville synagogue is an attack on Jewish communities everywhere. It is an attack on everyone’s right to live together in peace,” Toronto mayor Olivia Chow wrote on X.
“Fear and uncertainty in Jewish communities is real … While there is no known threat to Toronto at this time, hate and violent extremism are concerns across Canada,” Toronto police wrote on X.

Toronto police chief Myron Demkiw said the police service’s command team met with its Jewish Community Consultative Committee, Toronto Police Service Board and the Board’s Jewish Advisory Table on Thursday to discuss concerns in the community after the hate-motivated shooting incident.

“We understand the fear and uncertainty that incidents like these create within the Jewish community,” Demkiw wrote in a social media post. “We will continue to maintain an increased presence around places of worship, schools, and community centres to ensure that community members are safe and feel safe.”
Public Safety Minister Gary Anandasangaree said Thursday the federal government, through a security infrastructure program, will pay for any security supports the Sons of Jacob Synagogue needs.

ByNicholas Keung Senior Immigration Reporter

The Trump administration has been accused of widespread human rights violations stemming from its “militarized immigration enforcement” in a new report that critics say Ottawa — and all Canadians — should heed.

Based on field research, Amnesty International USA documented incidents where officials with the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), Customs and Border Protection and other federal agencies were alleged to have breached the rights of migrants, bystanders and protesters.

The accusations included unlawful killings, some of which Amnesty said may amount to extrajudicial executions; racial profiling; arbitrary and discriminatory arrest; “incommunicado detentions,” in some cases in conditions that it said may violate the prohibition on torture; unlawful surveillance; and violent repression of peaceful protests.

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

Working remotely from Canada's Wonderland

Image 15Image 16

“They were neither isolated nor exceptional, but characteristic of the manner in which the operations were conducted and reflective of broader national patterns,”said the 137-page report, “We Had Whistles. They Had Guns,” released on Thursday.

The Trump administration has defended its enforcement operations as lawful and necessary, claiming to target only criminal aliens, gang members and those who are national security threats.

Stories of Canadians arrested and detained in U.S. have made headlines since Trump returned to the White House last year doubling down on immigration enforcement effort. The fear of being detained at the American border has contributed to the dramatic drop in Canadian travel to the U.S.

Review of U.S. asylum system following attack on National Guard in D.C. leads Afghans to wonder if they’d be safer in Canada — and if they could

Critics say the Amnesty findings should prompt the Carney government to reconsider whether the U.S. still qualifies as a safe country for asylum seekers — a designation with implications for Canada’s refugee system.

The Canada-U.S. Safe Third Country Agreement requires claimants to seek protection in the first safe country they arrive in. Unless they qualify for exceptions, they are sent back to the other country. The bilateral pact is built on the principle that both countries are safe, and respect human rights and international protection obligations.

“This report makes abundantly clear what, frankly, everybody knows, which is the United States is not a safe country to seek and receive asylum,” said law professor Audrey Macklin, chair in international human rights at University of Toronto.

Amnesty said ICE and CBP arrested more than 597,000 people between January 2025 and July 2026, up 41 per cent from the preceding 19-month period under the Biden administration. The number of people in detention reached an all-time high of 71,937 in January. Data tools developed by the Deportation Data Project showed there were 327 arrests with book-ins to ICE detention involving a Canadian citizen from January 2025 to July 2026.

At least 50 people have died in ICE custody while more than 605,000 people have been removed from the U.S., Amnesty said. More than 21,000 people have been deported to third countries, often without due process, it added.

The report said federal agents used excessive force when arresting people, including breaking down doors of homes without warrants and with guns drawn, conducting military-style raids in the middle of the night accompanied by Black Hawk helicopters, driving recklessly and boxing in vehicles, smashing car windows without justification, throwing people who were not resisting onto the ground.

The Amnesty report calls for ICE to be abolished. Neither ICE nor CBP responded to the Star’s requests for comment.

Macklin said the report highlighted “a discernible pattern” of rights violations directed at an objective rather than just exceptional acts, errors or negligence by individuals in isolation.

“Canada is not just an innocent bystander in observing what’s going on in the United States,” she explained. “Even less so is it entitled to clutch its pearls and feel morally superior, because Canada actually is implicated in harm that is being done to people in the United States who are asylum seekers or even people who are refugees. It does that by continuing to enforce the Safe Third Country Agreement.”

Amnesty’s research is based on testimonies from 154 people, as well as analysis of 29 videos and three photographs. The interviewees included migrants, their families, civil liberties groups and observers, focusing on the immigration raids in Chicago, New Orleans, Minneapolis-St. Paul and Washington, D.C.

Julia Sande, a lawyer with Amnesty International Canada, said what struck her the most was how entire communities are being terrorized.

“This behaviour not only was allowed to exist but was celebrated in many ways and encouraged, including by President Trump himself,” she noted. “It really demonstrates that when it comes to the rights of people who are in need of safety, we can’t just delegate our human rights obligations to the United States. It puts people directly in harm’s way.”

The Star, simplified

Since its inception in 2004, the Canada-U.S. Safe Third Country Agreement has been contested in Canadian courts.

In 2023, the Supreme Court of Canadaruled the agreement does not violate the Charter’s guarantees of liberty and security of the person. However, it declined to rule on arguments that it violates gender equality rights because the U.S. does not recognize gender-based violence as a ground of persecution. The justices sent that issue back to the Federal Court.

Currently, there are two other pending court cases, challenging whether “safety valves” such as legal schemes and discretionary exemptions exist in practice to protect would-be refugees from being returned to the U.S., as well as the cabinet’s obligation to review the designation of the U.S. as a safe country.

“We all knew about the different human rights failures in terms of the intimidation, the harassment, the conditions of detention, but the fact remains that we have the Safe Third Country Agreement in place,” said Toronto immigration and refugee lawyer Maureen Silcoff, a co-counsel in these two cases.

“This Amnesty report should sound the alarm for cabinet to take a meaningful look at the U.S. as a designated safe country.”

Silcoff said the last review was in 2022, before Trump returned to the White House.

The Immigration Department said the federal government uses a strong framework to continuously monitor U.S. developments and the impact that changes in policies and practices may have on the refugee protection system. This monitoring, it said, ensures the conditions required of the U.S. safe third country designation continue to be met.

“Designation as a Safe Third Country is continually assessed,” the department said in an email. “Canada has a proud humanitarian tradition and takes its international obligations regarding asylum seekers seriously.”

Nicholas Keung is a Toronto-based reporter covering immigration for the Star. Follow him on Twitter: @nkeung.

stories.title: London Health Sciences Centre completes Canadian first using "heart in a box" technology for cardiac transplantation
stories.summary: September 24, 2026
stories.content:
September 24, 2026

In a transplant first for a Canadian recipient, the provincially shared Transmedics Organ Care System kept a donor heart beating outside of the body, helping to expand transplant possibilities for London Health Sciences Centre patient, Raj Mittal.

The heart transplant team from London Health Sciences Centre (LHSC) completed a cardiac transplant using the Transmedics Organ Care System (OCS) organ care system, often referred to as a "heart in a box", to implant a donor heart that May otherwise May not have been available for transplant.

Taking place in February 2026, the milestone procedure was made possible through access to the provincially acquired TransMedics Organ Care System Heart technology, specialized team training, and years of collaboration with Ontario Health and Trillium Gift of Life Network.

Unlike traditional cold storage that preserves an organ using ice in a standard cooler during transport from one hospital to another, heart in a box systems are used to revive a donor heart that has stopped beating after circulatory death. It keeps the heart warm, beating, and perfused with oxygenated blood, while also providing the transplant team with real-time insight into heart function and suitability for transplantation.

With better preservation of organ quality, the technology also extends potential transport time to 12 hours, making it possible for a donor heart to reach a recipient that is much farther away from where it was retrieved than previously possible.

"This is a great example of the profound impact advancements and investments in technology can have on patients and their families," says Dr. Dave Nagpal, Medical Co-Director, Multi-Organ Transplant Program and Director of Cardiac Transplantation at LHSC. "With this technology we can now transplant organs that might not have been medically suitable otherwise. This gives patients on the organ donor waiting list a greater chance of receiving a lifesaving transplant and better allows teams to honour the wishes of donors and their families to generously give the gift of life."

For first patient Raj Mittal, the transplant followed a year of serious illness and uncertainty. In June 2025, Mittal was working in his backyard when he began feeling chest pain. His wife called 911 and he was taken to LHSC, where he later went into cardiac arrest and underwent a triple bypass surgery. Complications followed including pneumonia and kidney issues, and Mittal spent weeks between the intensive care and inpatient units, before being well enough to be discharged in September. At that time, his care team presented the possibility that one day he May need a heart transplant.

After another hospital admission in January of this year, Mittal was presented with two options; a left ventricular assistive device (Lvad) or a heart transplant. Following research to better understand the options, conversation and careful consideration, Mittal and his wife made the decision to move forward with a transplant, and he was placed on the provincial organ donation wait list. The call that a donor heart was available followed two weeks later.

Once the donor offer was accepted, a recovery team, led by Dr. Rashmi Nedadur, Cardiac Surgeon at LHSC traveled to the donor site, where the heart had been recovered and placed on the OCS machine. While beating in the system, the heart was assessed and deemed viable for transplant before being transported back to LHSC.

"The quality and function of the heart looked great when we arrived," says Dr. Nedadur. "When we implanted the heart, it took off immediately."

Heart transplantation is a highly coordinated and time-sensitive procedure. While one team recovers and assesses the donor heart, the recipient team prepares the patient for surgery.

During implantation, the surgical team examines the donor heart, trims the major vessels so they fit the recipient’s anatomy and carefully sews the new heart into place. The heart is protected throughout the process using specialized solutions and temperature control. Once the heart is in place, the team warms the patient, restores normal blood chemistry, and gradually transfers the work of circulation from the heart-lung machine to the new heart.

For Mittal, the impact of his transplant has been life changing. The day after surgery he was up and moving in the ICU. Within days, he was transferred to the transplant unit. Although his recovery included additional monitoring and a brief return to intensive care to manage blood pressure and fluid levels, he was discharged later that month and continues to improve.

"I am improving every day," says Mittal. "Before, I could not move much. I was sitting or lying down, and I could not spend time with my family. Now my energy is much better. I can walk, spend time with my family, and after the heart transplant there is hope I can get my normal life back."

For Dr. Nagpal and the teams at LHSC, the case reflects the combination of surgical expertise, innovation, and teamwork required to advance both complex cardiac care and the future of transplantation.

"There are a lot of details and nuances with transplantation, but the goal is always to make sure the donor heart is protected and that the recipient has the best possible chance at a successful outcome," says Dr. Nagpal. "Having this technology available marks an important step forward in what is possible in the field of organ donation and transplantation."

This cardiac transplant first builds on the rich legacy of excellence in donation and transplantation within LHSC’s Multi-Organ Transplant Program, home to the longest continuously running heart transplant program in Canada, offering new hope to patients who May benefit from expanded donor heart options in the future.

Taking place in February 2026, the milestone procedure was made possible through access to the provincially acquired TransMedics Organ Care System Heart technology, specialized team training, and years of collaboration with Ontario Health and Trillium Gift of Life Network.

Unlike traditional cold storage that preserves an organ using ice in a standard cooler during transport from one hospital to another, heart in a box systems are used to revive a donor heart that has stopped beating after circulatory death. With better preservation of organ quality, the technology also extends potential transport time to 12 hours, making it possible for a donor heart to reach a recipient that is much farther away from where it was retrieved than previously possible.

stories.title: Quebec doctors call for inquest after five physician suicides in five months
stories.summary: The signatories write that doctors face death and suffering every day and take on a lot of responsibility, sometimes without adequate support.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
If you or someone you know is thinking about suicide, support is available 24-7 by calling or texting 988, Canada’s national suicide prevention helpline.

Over 1,500 Quebec doctors are calling for a coroner’s inquest after five doctors in the province reportedly died by suicide over a five-month period this year.

The doctors sent a letter to Quebec’s chief coroner Sept. 18 asking for an inquest into suicides in their profession.

The signatories write that doctors face death and suffering every day and take on a lot of responsibility, sometimes without adequate support.

They also say some doctors avoid getting help for mental health issues because they fear professional repercussions.

Every suicide in Quebec is investigated by a coroner, regardless of the deceased person’s profession, to establish the causes and circumstances of the death.

Quebec’s coroner’s office told The Canadian Press it has begun an in-depth analysis of the doctors’ request.

“For now, it is too early to comment on whether such a public inquiry will be held,” it says.

Jean-Paul Brutus, a plastic surgeon who signed the letter, says growing workloads and the public denigration of doctors — sometimes referred to in Quebec as “doctor-bashing” — contribute to psychological distress.

He says successive governments have pointed fingers at doctors for years and blamed them “for all the failings of the public system.”

“There is more and more medical-administrative pressure, more and more patients, fewer and fewer resources to help us do the work we have to do,” Brutus says.

Brutus says the well-being of health-care workers can also affect the quality of care patients receive.

“This isn’t a doctors’ problem. This isn’t a health-care workers’ problem. It’s a public health problem,” he says.

The signatories argue the available information is not detailed enough to determine whether doctor suicides are increasing.

— With files from Katrine Desautels

stories.title: Carney says he studied risk of U.S.-led military action in NYT interview
stories.summary: Carney declined to discuss in detail what that examination involved, but he suggested it would be irresponsible not to prepare for what he called "extreme tail risk."
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney says he studied the possibility of U.S.-led military action in Canada.

In a lengthy New York Times interview published Wednesday, Carney declined to discuss in detail what that examination involved, but he suggested it would be irresponsible not to prepare for what he called “extreme tail risk.”

“I think you have a responsibility in these roles to look at extreme tail risk,” Carney told the Times. “That’s just risk management. That’s not a base case, but it would be irresponsible not to (prepare).”

U.S. President Donald Trump has repeatedly mused about turning Canada into the 51st state and while he ruled out using military force to annex Canada in January 2025, he has said he would consider using “economic force” to get Canada to become part of the United States.

Carney also spoke in the interview about Canada’s plans to reduce its reliance on Elon Musk’s Starlink satellite internet service.

He also discussed Canada considering alternatives to buying American F-35 fighter jets.

1:58 Carney says he studied risk of U.S. military invasion

Canada’s plan to procure a full fleet of F-35 stealth fighters remains under a political review by Carney’s government. The review was launched more than a year ago in response to the trade war started by Trump.

The trade war between Canada and the United States has been escalating after efforts to reach a trade deal failed in mid-August.

The day after talks broke down, Trump imposed 50 per cent duties on $28 billion in Canadian goods, while Canada implemented retaliatory tariffs in early September.

The president also signed an order to identify and remove products of Canadian origin from U.S. government procurement systems.

The New York Times report said Carney disclosed that he and Trump speak “frequently” even after trade talks collapsed, something the prime minister has said multiple times in recent weeks.

At a news conference with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy earlier this month, Carney said he speaks to Trump regularly and that they can “compartmentalize.” He added that part of their responsibility is to work together to resolve global issues like the war in Ukraine.

Earlier Wednesday, the president claimed on social media that Canada is “destroying itself” by allowing millions of people into the country “essentially unchecked and unvetted.”

Trump provided no evidence for these claims but called it a “Liberal takeover that will end very badly.”

Carney and Trump did not meet when they both attended the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly this week. It was Carney’s first trip to the United States since trade negotiations fell apart last month.

stories.title: Veteran’s alleged role in Belleville synagogue attack could tarnish military, former top soldier fears
stories.summary: Suspect Sean Ward served in the Canadian Armed Forces for five years before being deemed unsuitable for further service
stories.author: Mercedes Stephenson, Jill Mahoney, Greg Mercer, Stephanie Levitz
stories.content:
Canada’s former top soldier said he is appalled by the attack on a synagogue in Belleville, Ont., saying the alleged involvement of a veteran could risk tarring the reputation of the military.

Retired general Wayne Eyre led the military when suspect Sean Ward was released in 2022 from the Canadian Armed Forces after serving five years.

“I was horrified to hear of the events,” he said in an interview. “I was disappointed to learn of the perpetrator’s military affiliation.”

Mr. Ward was deemed unsuitable for further military service and released under a category called 5F, an involuntary discharge, The Globe and Mail reported on Wednesday according to two Department of National Defence sources. One source said Mr. Ward was removed because he refused to take the COVID-19 vaccine. The Globe is not identifying the sources, who were not authorized to publicly discuss the matter.

Mr. Eyre said that regardless of the fact that Mr. Ward was out of the military for several years, the Forces can still be tarred with the same brush and the same dishonour.

As chief of the defence staff from 2021 to 2024, Mr. Eyre enacted a vaccine mandate in October, 2021. At the time, he said it was a lawful order necessary for force protection and to maintain operational readiness.

The DND website says a 5F release refers to people who are removed from the military because they are considered “unsuitable for further service,” for multiple reasons. The military has used this administrative mechanism to oust troops accused of racism and sexual misconduct, among other behavioural issues. Mr. Eyre approved the 5F designation being used during the COVID mandate for those who refused an order to get vaccinated.

General Jennie Carignan, the current Chief of the Defence Staff, did not immediately provide comment for this story.

The 29-year-old Mr. Ward, of Quinte West, Ont., died in hospital on Monday night. He was injured in a gunfight with police outside the Sons of Jacob synagogue in Belleville on Sunday.

Mr. Ward allegedly opened fire on an officer stationed outside the small synagogue as worshippers gathered to mark Yom Kippur, the holiest day on the Jewish calendar.

Officials have not commented on a specific motive for the attack.

Liberal MP Chris Malette, whose riding includes Belleville, said he met with police, the mayor and the province’s Solicitor-General in the eastern Ontario city on Tuesday. He also went to the site of the shooting.

“What we found out about him just from seeing the scene – this individual clearly came with some intent to do some serious harm to these people, and we saw that graphic detail yesterday,” he told The Globe. He declined to discuss what police told him or what he saw at the crime scene, citing the continuing investigation.

On Wednesday, outside the Belleville home where a neighbour said Mr. Ward lived with his mother, there were seven police vehicles, including a black forensic investigation van, parked around the property. Two officers stood in the driveway.

Neighbour Sheri Skanes said Mr. Ward had lived at the house for several years. She said the situation, and the constant police presence, has rattled the neighbourhood.

“It’s shocking,” she said. “They were quiet people. They kept to themselves and didn’t cause a lot of noise.”

Her son, Jordan Skanes, said police had been at the address since Sunday night. He said apart from occasionally playing host to some visitors from Alberta, who stood out in the neighbourhood with their cowboy hats and out-of-province licence plates, there was nothing remarkable about the people who lived there. Mr. Ward could occasionally be seen using the backyard pool or playing with his dog, he said.

Mr. Ward served in the military from July, 2017, until June, 2022, when he was released with the rank of corporal, according to the Armed Forces. He was a member of the Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry regiment and did not deploy overseas during his service.

The Canadian military has not said where precisely Mr. Ward was posted. However, a private named Sean Ward was previously listed as a member of the Edmonton-based 3rd Battalion of the PPCLI, according to the regiment’s annual publication.

Mr. Ward attended Quinte Secondary School in Belleville, which closed in 2018 as part of a consolidation. He was an athlete and played on the rugby team, said former principal Liane Woodley.

Ms. Woodley said she has been in touch with past colleagues and students this week about the “very tragic” shooting.

“People are surprised, they’re shocked that someone that we’ve known could be involved in something like that,” she said.

The Special Investigations Unit, which handles cases involving Ontario police that result in death or serious injury, has wrapped up its investigation at the scene of the shooting.

A postmortem examination on Mr. Ward’s body took place in Kingston on Wednesday, said Kristy Denette, an SIU spokesperson.

Constable Jeff Smith, the Belleville Police Service officer who was wounded in the shootout with the suspect, remains in hospital in Kingston.

His wife, Ashley, thanked paramedics, police, “an angel neurosurgeon,” doctors, nurses, friends, neighbours, the Jewish community and other well-wishers in a Facebook post on Tuesday evening.

“Jeff has a very long, difficult road ahead. But he is not walking it alone. He has an army of love behind him,” she wrote in the post, which was shared by Belleville Police.

Early on Sunday evening, about 25 worshippers were about to begin evening prayers inside the Sons of Jacob synagogue, while Constable Smith kept watch in the parking lot in an unmarked vehicle.

According to the SIU, around 7 p.m., the suspect fired on Constable Smith with a shotgun and a gunfight began. A second officer arrived and fired at the suspect, who was injured in the exchange.

Dozens of shots were discharged during the incident, with about 20 coming through the synagogue’s front stained-glass window. None of the worshippers were injured.
