stories.title: Canada ratifies landmark High Seas Treaty, commits $82-million to ocean protection
stories.summary: Funding will support Arctic Ocean monitoring, underwater research and expanded efforts to track effects of climate change
stories.author: Jenn Thornhill Verma
stories.content:
Canada ratified the landmark High Seas Treaty to protect marine biodiversity on Wednesday and pledged $82-million over five years to a global ocean-monitoring alliance, Prime Minister Mark Carney announced in New York on the margins of the United Nations General Assembly.

“Canada is an ocean nation. We have the world’s longest coastline as a consequence of that. That’s our inheritance, and we recognize the obligations, the responsibilities, that come with that to help lead efforts to understand those oceans, and of course, to protect them,” said Mr. Carney, speaking at the launch of the OceanEye International Alliance , co-hosted by Canada and the European Union.

Amid shifting political winds, Canada gets more of the spotlight on the UN’s stage

The money will pay for year-round moorings in the Arctic Ocean, which is warming four times faster than the global average, said Mr. Carney. It will support autonomous underwater gliders beneath the ice, expanded monitoring of the Labrador Sea and Davis Strait. It will also more than double Canada’s contribution to the global Argo ocean climate monitoring network, and help modernize the National Oceanographic Data Centre, among other investments.

The treaty, meanwhile, which became international law in January, is the first legal framework for protected areas in waters beyond national jurisdiction, which make up nearly half the planet. OceanEye, which Mr. Carney agreed in June to co-chair with European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, pays for the instruments that monitor the global ocean’s changing condition.

Both commitments, one to protect the high seas and the other to monitor the ocean as a whole, land on a tension in Canada’s ocean record. As Ottawa builds partnerships abroad, scientists say it is dismantling the monitoring and research that underpin them at home.

“As Canadian scientists, working internationally, we are watching the instruments go dark,” wrote Frédéric Cyr and Brad deYoung in a commentary published Sunday .

Dr. Cyr, a former Fisheries and Oceans Canada oceanographer now at Memorial University of Newfoundland’s Marine Institute, and Dr. deYoung, a professor emeritus at Memorial, point to significant cutbacks at the federal department, whose own plan projects spending reductions of up to $194-million by 2028-29 and about 551 fewer full-time positions. They say Ottawa has scaled back the Atlantic Zone Monitoring Program , which has tracked changing ocean conditions for more than two decades, and withdrawn support for the international program that monitors the North Atlantic currents that regulate the climate.

In their letter, they urged Mr. Carney to reverse those cutbacks and attach sustained funding to Canada’s OceanEye role. Of today’s announcement, Dr. Cyr said he was encouraged by the investments the Prime Minister had committed, but still had questions.

Most concerningly, he hopes the funds will maintain Canada’s role in monitoring the North Atlantic currents that scientists worry could be headed for collapse.

“Our oceans form one interconnected system. Canada’s leadership on protecting the high seas is much needed. At the same time, any country that is going to lead on the high seas also needs to lead at home,” said Susanna Fuller, vice-president of conservation at Oceans North, a member of the High Seas Alliance, a coalition of more than 80 conservation groups that pushed for the treaty for over a decade.

Canada signed the High Seas Treaty in March, 2024. Becoming a party now gives Ottawa a seat when countries meet for the first time in January next year. Only 1.5 per cent of the high seas is currently protected. The treaty also requires environmental assessments for high-seas activities and sets rules for sharing the benefits of marine genetic resources found there. As of this week, nearly 100 parties have joined, with Germany, Papua New Guinea and Zimbabwe among the latest to ratify .

Analysis: Trump uses UN address to threaten and deride foes and allies alike, as usual

At Wednesday’s OceanEye Alliance event , countries were invited to pledge money or in-kind support to the UN-backed Global Ocean Observing System , the network behind the ocean data used in weather forecasts and climate models. The system draws on 8,000 instruments, from floats to moored buoys, that collect some 120,000 observations a day, according to the EU, noting it remains “vulnerable to financial and geopolitical disruptions,” given just nine countries pay for 90 per cent of that monitoring effort.

The event is the latest sign of Ottawa’s push to deepen ties with the EU, weeks before a Canada-EU summit in Canada on Oct. 29-30 .

The federal nature strategy, which Mr. Carney announced in March , set aside $24.4-million over five years, plus $1.8-million in continuing funding, to ratify the treaty and carry out its commitments.

Canada will also act as host of the Our Ocean Conference in Halifax May 10-11, 2027.

Mr. Carney took a moment to acknowledge Canada’s recently named Ocean Envoy and Chair , Diana Fox Carney, his wife. “We intend to be at every table, where the future of the ocean is decided and to continue to raise our ambitions,” he said.

This story is produced in partnership with the Pulitzer Center’s Ocean Reporting Network.

Most concerningly, he hopes the funds will maintain Canada’s role in monitoring the North Atlantic currents that scientists worry could be headed for collapse.

“Our oceans form one interconnected system. Canada’s leadership on protecting the high seas is much needed. At the same time, any country that is going to lead on the high seas also needs to lead at home,” said Susanna Fuller, vice-president of conservation at Oceans North, a member of the High Seas Alliance, a coalition of more than 80 conservation groups that pushed for the treaty for over a decade.

Canada signed the High Seas Treaty in March, 2024. Becoming a party now gives Ottawa a seat when countries meet for the first time in January next year. Only 1.5 per cent of the high seas is currently protected. The treaty also requires environmental assessments for high-seas activities and sets rules for sharing the benefits of marine genetic resources found there. As of this week, nearly 100 parties have joined, with Germany, Papua New Guinea and Zimbabwe among the latest to ratify .
Analysis: Trump uses UN address to threaten and deride foes and allies alike, as usual

At Wednesday’s OceanEye Alliance event , countries were invited to pledge money or in-kind support to the UN-backed Global Ocean Observing System , the network behind the ocean data used in weather forecasts and climate models. The system draws on 8,000 instruments, from floats to moored buoys, that collect some 120,000 observations a day, according to the EU, noting it remains “vulnerable to financial and geopolitical disruptions,” given just nine countries pay for 90 per cent of that monitoring effort.
The event is the latest sign of Ottawa’s push to deepen ties with the EU, weeks before a Canada-EU summit in Canada on Oct. 29-30 .

The federal nature strategy, which Mr. Carney announced in March , set aside $24.4-million over five years, plus $1.8-million in continuing funding, to ratify the treaty and carry out its commitments.
Canada will also act as host of the Our Ocean Conference in Halifax May 10-11, 2027.

Mr. Carney took a moment to acknowledge Canada’s recently named Ocean Envoy and Chair , Diana Fox Carney, his wife. “We intend to be at every table, where the future of the ocean is decided and to continue to raise our ambitions,” he said.

stories.title: Canadians want more alternative home ownership options, survey shows
stories.summary: A new survey suggests many Canadians are open to alternative home options if it means getting easier access to the real estate market.
stories.author: Ariel Rabinovitch
stories.content:
As housing affordability remains a challenge for millions of Canadians amid the heightened cost of living, a new survey suggests many are open to alternative options like modular homes if it means getting easier access to the real estate market.

The survey report was released Tuesday from Meridian Credit Union, which asked 1,500 Canadian consumers as well as a national panel of 250 construction industry owners, operators and executives between May 13 and June 8, 2026, about their outlook on the housing market.

More than three-quarters (77 per cent) of consumers said housing attainability is a critical issue for Canada’s future, and nearly two-thirds (62 per cent) said they would consider non-traditional housing options such as modular, prefabricated or tiny homes for getting into home ownership.

Modular or prefabricated homes are houses or other permanent shelters that get built in factories either as individual sections or components. Those homes and are shipped to customers to be assembled relatively quickly and at a lower cost than building a home on site from scratch.

Purchasing a home that is prefabricated or modular can mean a lower purchase price for consumers, and more affordable mortgage options compared to traditional homes that may have cost more to build.

Younger survey participants may be more inclined to consider these options, with 87 per cent of Millennials and 81 per cent of Gen Z reporting ongoing stress relating to housing costs.

“Canadians are showing us that homeownership is no longer one-size-fits-all,” said Jay-Ann Gilfoy, president and CEO of Meridian Credit Union in the report.

“From co-ownership arrangements to modular housing and rent-to-own models, people are adapting to today’s realities and looking for new ways to achieve their housing goals. The challenge is ensuring those options are supported by the financing, supply and partnerships needed to make them viable.”

This comes after the federal government announced last year that it was providing funding and federal land to add 540 modular homes in Downsview Park in Toronto . The government said at the time that at least 40 per cent of those homes would be affordable and the development would provide studios and one- to three-bedroom homes.

Even though the survey suggests there is heightened demand for these alternative housing options, businesses say they are struggling to meet that demand.

Among the group of construction industry participants in the survey, nearly two-thirds (63 per cent) said they are struggling to secure financing for projects because of rising costs for materials combined with general economic uncertainty.

Even if ideal financing was available and materials were relatively cheap, 78 per cent of construction firms and 94 per cent of enterprise level employers said a shortage of skilled trades people will still delay these projects from starting.

Forty-one per cent of builders also said that because there is a dwindling pool of skilled trades talent, the cost of available labour has skyrocketed.

Among the multiple types of construction related jobs businesses said they were having a tough time filling, 28 per cent said construction labourers were the hardest roles to fill, while 18 per cent said it was carpenters or framers.

“While builders want to build, many are facing a market where rising costs, financing pressures and reduced buyer confidence make it difficult to advance new projects,” said Jason Teal, vice president of business banking at Meridian in the report.

“To create more attainable housing, we need an environment where development is economically viable and where aspiring homeowners have the confidence and means to enter the market.”

– with a file from Global News’ Isaac Callan

stories.title: Canadians are flying back to the U.S. after three years of declining travel
stories.summary: Canadian resident return trips to the U.S. by air have increased for the first time in 34 months, according to the latest StatCan data.
stories.author: Ellie Hutchings
stories.content:
Canadian resident return trips to the U.S. by air have increased for the first time in 34 months, according to the latest data from Statistics Canada .

The figures, which reveal travel trends between Canada and other countries in July 2026, show that return trips to the U.S. by air edged up 0.6 per cent year over year to 567,000, marking the first increase since August 2023.

Combined with 2.2 million trips by automobile (a year-over-year increase of 12.6 per cent) and 26,400 by cruise ship, total return trips to the U.S. by Canadian residents reached 2.8 million in July, up 10.1 per cent year-over-year. This marked a fourth consecutive month of year-over-year growth, following 15 consecutive months of decline.

April 2026 marked the first year-over-year increase in overall return trips from the United States since December 2024, when return trips by automobile rose by 5.8 per cent compared to a year earlier. Although return trips by air had fallen 8.1 per cent, the figures meant overall Canadian-resident return trips from the U.S. rose by 1.4 per cent that month compared to April 2025.

But despite this recent shift in travel trends, Canadian resident return trips from the U.S. remained 25.6 per cent below their July 2024 level.

Political tensions between Canada and the U.S. contributed to the drop in travel in early 2025, following tariffs imposed by President Donald Trump and his repeated suggestions that Canada could become the 51st state . Meanwhile, heightened security at the border also discouraged many from travelling south.

While the July figures suggest the decline in travel to the U.S. May be easing, the data covers a period before the latest escalation in the Canada-U.S. trade war.

In August this year, Trump threatened to impose new 50 per cent tariffs and, after talks between the two countries broke down, the levies on $28 billion worth of Canadian goods came into effect on Aug. 22.

Canada retaliated, introducing counter-tariffs on U.S. imports earlier this month. Since then, Trump and other members of his administration have aimed insults and threats at Canada , including comparing Ontario Premier Doug Ford unfavourably to his late brother and sharing a photo of a bald eagle standing on the neck of a Canada Goose from the White House’s official X account.

On Aug. 27, Trump signed an executive order to rename Lake Ontario to “Lake America,” ordering the Department of the Interior to update maps and databases with the new name.

These events have fuelled a renewed ‘Buy Canadian’ movement, with one Made in Canada Facebook group seeing views increase roughly 300 per cent in August compared to June this year, according to administrator Jayne Little.

That sentiment May extend to travel to the U.S., and it remains to be seen whether the recent increase in Canadians heading south will continue.

Meanwhile, travel to Canada by U.S. residents also increased in July. There were 3.5 million trips made that month, up 9.1 per cent from the same month in 2025 and marking the sixth consecutive month of year-over-year growth. Arrivals by automobile rose 7.5 per cent to 2.1 million, while arrivals by air increased 5.3 per cent to 832,100.

StatCan also highlighted the number of trips made via the Gordie Howe International Bridge , which opened on July 27 and connects Windsor, Ont., and Detroit, Michigan.

From July 27 to 31, 23,500 returning Canadian residents and 19,600 U.S. residents entered Canada via the Gordie Howe International Bridge by automobile, bus, motorcycle and other land vehicles.

stories.title: 'Liquidity challenges' at Sireg Management leave Ontario condo investors scrambling
stories.summary: | CBC News | Posted: September 23, 2026 8:00 AM | Last Updated: September 23
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: | CBC News | Posted: September 23, 2026 8:00 AM | Last Updated: September 23
Up to 1,800 investors affected as company says rental payments can no longer be guaranteed

Investors in hundreds of rental condos across Ontario are scrambling after SIREG Management, a company that manages 1,800 condo units, announced that rent payments to its owners are no longer guaranteed.

In a statement sent to individual investor-owners last week, the Burlington, Ont.-based company said they are "currently experiencing market and liquidity challenges that are affecting our ability to make timely rental payments."
The company said it could not say when payments would resume, but assured owners that their ownership of the condos “remains secure.”
Several owners who spoke to CBC News said they were expecting rental payments last Friday that never arrived.
"We recognize how serious this is, particularly for investors who rely on these payments to meet financial obligations," SIREG said in its statement.

The situation affects investors, and potentially their tenants, in 21 condo buildings SIREG manages across Ontario. The buildings are in small and mid-sized towns and cities including Sarnia, Kitchener, Welland, North Bay and a notoriously troubled group of buildings on Kipps Lane in London.
“Without the rents, the bank is going to end up with my properties," said investor-owner Tanya Petryshen. "I don’t have a lot of room before I’m in trouble.”

The 55-year-old Mississauga resident owns six condo units operated by SIREG. She began investing with SIREG, an acronym for Simple Investor Real Estate Group, after attending a seminar the company held for potential investors back in 2013.

Petryshen started by purchasing two condo units in Kitchener for $110,000 each. She said she was attracted to a model that offered a way to become a landlord and real estate investor without having to deal directly with tenants.
"It was supposed to be totally hands off," said Petryshen, who condos through SIREG in Hamilton, Listowel and Waterloo.
Under the model, investors buy individual condominium units in buildings managed by SIREG. Many of the units are former apartments in older buildings.

Petryshen said the company charged her $600 a month per unit to collect rents, deal with any tenant issues and to cover the condo management fees. Owners were responsible for insurance and municipal taxes.

Petryshen said she netted about $400 a month for each of her six rental units, just enough to cover the mortgage payments. She hoped that once the loans were paid off, she'd have an appreciating asset and a source of passive income.
The rental payments were lower than she would have liked, she said, but they had never been missed.
“We were never in the red, but we were barely in the black," she said of the performance of the investment.
About a year ago, Petryshen saw signs SIREG might be in trouble and became worried about the financial position of the condo board managing the Listowel building.

Condo corporations are required to keep enough funds in reserve to cover maintenance of common areas, including elevators, roofs and parking garages. Even condo buildings filled with owner occupants can run into trouble in cases where repair costs escalate.

Last fall, Petryshen received notice that the rental payment date would shift to mid-month. She later received a $41,000 water bill for her units in Listowel (SIREG, or the tenants, generally covered utilities). A neighbour of one of her tenants who did not rent from a SIREG investor also warned her about potential problems with the building’s reserve fund.

Petryshen said she raised the issue with Todd C. Slater, president of SIREG, who until recently had a wide social media reach as a real estate investment advisor and real estate investing commentator.
“He assured us everything was fine," said Petryshen.
Then last week, the notice arrived informing investors that their rent payments could not be guaranteed. The statement said the company will provide a written update by Wednesday, Sept. 23.

Petryshen called Slater right away and said she couldn't get a hold of him or other SIREG managers. Then later received an automatic email reply to an email to Slater, which said he was away on medical leave.
CBC News reached out to SIREG for comment but did not receive a reply.
Around the same time the notice about rent payments went out, Slater's social media accounts across multiple platforms, including YouTube and Instagram, were taken down. The sections of the
SIREG website with information for potential investors became dead links.

A number of investors with concerns, but who did not want to be identified by name, reached out to CBC News. Many are trying to figure out how to proceed based on their comments posted to a handful of Reddit and Facebook groups for SIREG investors.

One immediate concern is how owners will collect rent if SIREG stops operating. Because the investment was marketed as a hands-off arrangement, some owners said they do not have contact information for their tenants.

Some condo owners said they visited their units last week, in some cases for the first time, to tell tenants that they may need to pay rent directly to them. Comments posted online suggest those visits have had mixed results.
One investor-owner trying to take action is Marcin Migdal of Oakville.

Migdal owns a unit in North Bay, Ont., and also bought into SIREG's joint investor group, which offers investors a chance to buy a share in the buildings' conversion projects. Migdal said the joint investor offerings started at $250,000.
He feels those investments could be particularly vulnerable because joint investors don't hold title to units they can sell or use for rental income.

"I've talked to investors that cashed out their savings with family and friends to invest," he said. "We're not talking about people who are massive millionaires. We're talking about people who are just gathering family assets and believe in this concept."

set up a website to gather information from other SIREG investors. He sees it as a first step of potentially launching a legal action if investors money can't be recovered any other way. More than 120 investors have already shared their information with him.
Migdal, who holds other real estate investments, said he's realistic about what might be recovered, particularly if SIREG can't find a way to continue operating.
"If I got 50 per cent back and did not have to wait years, I would be happy," he said.

stories.title: Why everyone wins with Kawhi Leonard-Raptors extension
stories.summary: The Raptors gave Kawhi Leonard a fully guaranteed deal that includes that player option on the second year.
stories.author: Lucas Casaletto
stories.content:
By Michael Grange, Sportsnet

Posted September 23, 2026 11:11 am.

It’s good to be in the NBA, and it’s especially good to be Kawhi Leonard.

Even if the contract extension the Toronto Raptors made official on Wednesday with their new/old star forward will be the last deal the 35-year-old signs, Leonard would retire after the 2028-29 season having earned nearly $500 million playing basketball. Plus, quite literally, who knows how much more via, ahem, his ‘endorsements.’

But context matters. And in the context of the Raptors signing Leonard , it matters that he signed for two years and $115 million — and not for the maximum $126-million extension he was eligible to sign on a deal that covers 2027-28 and 2028-29.

In the apron era, ever dollar saved matters.

Extended stay in the North. ???????? pic.twitter.com/6Q4khQQool — Toronto Raptors (@Raptors) September 23, 2026

The $11-million discount the Raptors got on Leonard’s contract represents $5.5 million per year of wiggle room general manager Bobby Webster will have heading into the next two off-seasons. It could be the difference in signing a veteran free agent to shore up a roster weakness or build on a strength.

The deal and the way it’s structured is also roughly comparable to a couple other contracts some older, yet highly productive, NBA stars have signed recently.

Kevin Durant, for example, signed a two-year, $90-million extension with the Houston Rockets last year that kicks in for this season. And while that’s less than Leonard got with the Raptors, Durant’s deal covers his age 38 and 39 seasons. It’s a lot of money, but like Leonard, Durant in his late 30s remains one of the NBA’s best players.

And then there’s the three-year, $96.5-million deal that James Harden signed with Cleveland this summer that will cover his age 37, 38 and 39 seasons. That matters in a different way, but we’ll get to that in a minute.

The deal is also indicative of Leonard’s determination to make things work with the Raptors.

How robust the market was for his services leaguewide is something we can’t quite know, but coming off an all-NBA season, it’s not hard to imagine a number of contenders and near-contenders believing Leonard could be the difference in winning a championship because it’s obvious to anyone who has ever seen him play at full gas that he is just that.

But Leonard put out the bat signal that he wanted to play in Toronto, that the only franchise he wanted to sign an extension with was the Raptors, and here we are. The framework of the contract remained consistent from when the Raptors first entertained the idea of acquiring Leonard back in June.

Leonard then waived his $7.5 million trade kicker to make the deal work under the Raptors’ current cap situation based on the $50.3 million he’ll earn this season — another act of faith, by NBA standards.

That all needs to be considered when evaluating the other element of the deal that raised some eyebrows around the NBA: Leonard’s deal includes a player option for its final season in 2028-29.

When I was talking with one long-time NBA executive about what the final deal might look like, he speculated that the Raptors would push to have only a partial guarantee for the second season of the deal or that the second year would only fully guarantee if Leonard — forever an injury risk — met certain thresholds for games played.

Instead, the Raptors gave Leonard a fully guaranteed deal that includes that player option on the second year, which is generally considered a concession by the team to the player.

That’s because, typically, a player option is nothing but a headache for the team. If the player underperforms or is injured or both, he picks up the last year of his deal and the team is stuck. Conversely, if the player is over-performing or has an eye on another market, the threat of him declining the option can force a team’s hand.

“I don’t understand why they would do that; there was no leverage here,” one prominent player agent said when asked about the deal. “It’s a great deal for Kawhi. Any time you get the player option it’s a win for the player.”

But again, context matters.

If we take Leonard at his word, he very much wants Toronto to be his final NBA destination.

“I’m not really championship chasing. … I didn’t want to put on a thousand jerseys,” Leonard said during the most recent episode of Open Gym , the Raptors’ in-house documentary program. “This city took a liking to my family, and I took a liking to this city … my son was born here, and he’s been asking me forever when he’s going to come back. Now he’s back, and he’s able to see it rather than me tell him the great stories that happened.”

With that in mind and given that it’s pretty unlikely that Leonard will go ring shopping heading into his age-37 season, the player option can be looked at a little differently.

Let’s presume that the Raptors, with Leonard continuing to defy the aging curve (his 27.9 points, 6.4 rebounds, two steals and 62.9 true-shooting marks with the Clippers last season represented not only one of Leonard’s best but one of the best seasons ever by a player in their mid-30s), head into the 2028-29 season with championship aspirations, but in need of one more piece.

That’s where the player option could be a win for everyone concerned.

In that scenario, Leonard would opt out of his deal and sign one more for, just to pick a number, two years and $80 million. Leonard gets another $23 million in his jeans and the Raptors would head into that third off-season with an extra $17.5 million to spend, which could very well be enough to sign that missing piece.

The rough analogy here is Harden, who opted out of the final year his deal on which he was slated to earn $42.3 million with Cleveland this year and signed for three at $96.5 million, giving the Cavaliers an additional $11 million of cap space which enabled them to sign Peyton Watson, the rangy free-agent wing Cleveland hopes will vault it into Finals contention.

So sure, Leonard gains some theoretical leverage by having a player option on the final year of his new deal, but given everyone’s goal that his return to Toronto is a homecoming rather than a way station, it’s more about the potential for making the final years of his career as competitive as possible.

There are still plenty of ifs and risks, as with any NBA contract that runs into nine figures and especially so for a player in his mid-to-late 30s.

But at least with Leonard, the Raptors know exactly the player they are getting, and precisely what it costs.

stories.title: Simcoe woman dies after Norfolk County house fire
stories.summary: Provincial police in Norfolk County say a woman has died after being found inside a burning residence in Simcoe on Monday afternoon.
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: Provincial police in Norfolk County say a woman has died after being found inside a burning residence in Simcoe on Monday afternoon.
CBC News · Posted: Sep 23, 2026 10:13 AM EDT | Last Updated: 2 hours ago
Ontario Provincial Police (OPP) in Norfolk County say they're working with the offices of the fire marshal and the chief coroner to investigate the cause of Monday's fire.(Ontario Provincial Police)
X 0

Ontario Provincial Police (OPP) in Norfolk County say a woman has died after being found inside a burning residence in Simcoe, east of London, on Monday afternoon.

At around 1 p.m. emergency crews were called to the fire at an Orchard Avenue address, police said. Firefighters were able to enter the residence and locate a 50-year-old individual. Despite life-saving efforts, she was later pronounced dead in hospital.
The Norfolk County OPP crime unit is investigating the cause of the fire along with the office of the fire marshal and the office of the chief coroner.
Anyone with information about the incident is asked to contact OPP or Crime Stoppers.

stories.title: Neil Peart documentary explores both the human and virtuoso sides of the Rush drummer
stories.summary: Neil Peart: No One’s Disciple is a celebration of the lyricist and musician, who died of brain cancer in 2020
stories.author: Brad Wheeler
stories.content:
For their new documentary on the late Rush drummer Neil Peart, directors Scot McFadyen and Sam Dunn recruited four top-flight drummers to play songs from the band’s catalogue with surviving band members Geddy Lee and Alex Lifeson in a studio. The idea was to have the performances, not talking heads, speak to Peart’s virtuosity.

Neil Peart: No One’s Disciple premiered last week at the Toronto International Film Festival and makes its debut on CBC and CBC Gem this week. It succeeds as a celebration of the lyricist and musician, who died of brain cancer in 2020 , not because of the tasty jams but in the way the guest drummers were humbled by the task at hand.

Rush’s Neil Peart was revered as one of the world’s best drummers

“That beginning was tricky, man,” Tool’s Danny Carey said after a problematic run at the overture to 2112 . King Crimson’s Gavin Harrison wrote out detailed charts before even attempting Dreamline from the 1991 album Roll the Bones . “When you get into the details of it, you realize how much thought went into every drum part,” he said. “There’s no extra fat lying around. It’s all very lean.”

Stewart Copeland of the Police wrestled with the compositional complexities of 1982’s New World Man : “The drums fill aren’t challenging to play. They’re challenging to remember!” And while Red Hot Chili Peppers’ Chad Smith pounded out Working Man with no issues, he was breathing heavily after it was over.

Lee refers to the four guest timekeepers as Peart’s “drum brothers,” and compares drummers in general to baseball catchers and hockey goalies. “They see a kinship to each other,” he explains.

In a way, the film is not only a tribute to Peart but a requiem for kick-drum people overall.

“There’s a sense that people don’t really know what it means to be a great drummer,” McFadyen said during a recent video call alongside co-director Dunn. “There’s a lot of talking in documentaries. We wanted something more experiential.”

McFadyen and Dunn co-own Toronto-based Banger Films, the production company behind such rock docs as Metal: A Headbanger’s Journey , Iron Maiden: Flight 666 , Super Duper Alice Cooper and a pair of Rush films, 2010’s Rush: Beyond the Lighted Stage and Time Machine 2011: Live in Cleveland .

The documentary was conceived and the performance scenes were filmed in Los Angeles before there was any talk of the Rush reunion tour Lee and Lifeson are currently undertaking with drummer Anika Nilles and keyboardist Loren Gold. The co-directors suspected something was up, though.

Rush makes long-awaited Toronto return, with a little help from Geddy Lee’s vocal coach

“From the moment we stepped into the jam room on day one with Gavin Harrison, it was clear that Alex and Geddy had been playing a lot longer and a lot more than they’d let on,” Dunn said. “I was struck by how good the songs sounded.”

While the studio sessions are bound to be catnip for Rush fans, the soul of the film rests in the thoughtful portrait of Peart. The drummer, nicknamed the Professor, was known to be private, even standoffish. He was leery of fans and wrote about it in the song Limelight : “Cast in this unlikely role, ill-equipped to act with insufficient tact / One must put up barriers to keep oneself intact.”

In the film, Lee comments on Peart’s unapproachability. He says he spoke to the drummer about it, telling him he couldn’t have it both ways − the applause without the contact. “You live on the stage and you pay the price,” Lee said.

Lee even calls it a character flaw in Peart, which is a surprising admission in a film that very easily could have slipped into hagiography.

“The film is mostly a celebration, but it’s not all adulation,” McFadyen said.

On the other hand, through interviews with those who knew him well (such as Jethro Tull drummer Doane Perry and childhood chum Brad French), the Peart that ultimately emerges is a loyal friend and a generous colleague. Other than drummer Nilles, only people close to Peart were interviewed.

“That was intentional,” Dunn explained. “The idea was a tighter sketch of what Neil was like as a person. We felt we were giving as intimate a portrait as we could.”

content_blocks.text: For their new documentary on the late Rush drummer Neil Peart, directors Scot McFadyen and Sam Dunn recruited four top-flight drummers to play songs from the band’s catalogue with surviving band members Geddy Lee and Alex Lifeson in a studio. The idea was to have the performances, not talking heads, speak to Peart’s virtuosity.

Neil Peart: No One’s Disciple premiered last week at the Toronto International Film Festival and makes its debut on CBC and CBC Gem this week. It succeeds as a celebration of the lyricist and musician, who died of brain cancer in 2020 , not because of the tasty jams but in the way the guest drummers were humbled by the task at hand.
Rush’s Neil Peart was revered as one of the world’s best drummers

“That beginning was tricky, man,” Tool’s Danny Carey said after a problematic run at the overture to 2112 . King Crimson’s Gavin Harrison wrote out detailed charts before even attempting Dreamline from the 1991 album Roll the Bones . “When you get into the details of it, you realize how much thought went into every drum part,” he said. “There’s no extra fat lying around. It’s all very lean.”

Stewart Copeland of the Police wrestled with the compositional complexities of 1982’s New World Man : “The drums fill aren’t challenging to play. They’re challenging to remember!” And while Red Hot Chili Peppers’ Chad Smith pounded out Working Man with no issues, he was breathing heavily after it was over.

content_blocks.text: Lee refers to the four guest timekeepers as Peart’s “drum brothers,” and compares drummers in general to baseball catchers and hockey goalies. “They see a kinship to each other,” he explains.
In a way, the film is not only a tribute to Peart but a requiem for kick-drum people overall.

“There’s a sense that people don’t really know what it means to be a great drummer,” McFadyen said during a recent video call alongside co-director Dunn. “There’s a lot of talking in documentaries. We wanted something more experiential.”

McFadyen and Dunn co-own Toronto-based Banger Films, the production company behind such rock docs as Metal: A Headbanger’s Journey , Iron Maiden: Flight 666 , Super Duper Alice Cooper and a pair of Rush films, 2010’s Rush: Beyond the Lighted Stage and Time Machine 2011: Live in Cleveland .

The documentary was conceived and the performance scenes were filmed in Los Angeles before there was any talk of the Rush reunion tour Lee and Lifeson are currently undertaking with drummer Anika Nilles and keyboardist Loren Gold. The co-directors suspected something was up, though.
Rush makes long-awaited Toronto return, with a little help from Geddy Lee’s vocal coach

“From the moment we stepped into the jam room on day one with Gavin Harrison, it was clear that Alex and Geddy had been playing a lot longer and a lot more than they’d let on,” Dunn said. “I was struck by how good the songs sounded.”

content_blocks.caption: Lifeson and Lee are on a Rush reunion tour with drummer Anika Nilles and keyboardist Loren Gold. Mark Blinch/Reuters

content_blocks.text: While the studio sessions are bound to be catnip for Rush fans, the soul of the film rests in the thoughtful portrait of Peart. The drummer, nicknamed the Professor, was known to be private, even standoffish. He was leery of fans and wrote about it in the song Limelight : “Cast in this unlikely role, ill-equipped to act with insufficient tact / One must put up barriers to keep oneself intact.”

In the film, Lee comments on Peart’s unapproachability. He says he spoke to the drummer about it, telling him he couldn’t have it both ways − the applause without the contact. “You live on the stage and you pay the price,” Lee said.
Lee even calls it a character flaw in Peart, which is a surprising admission in a film that very easily could have slipped into hagiography.
“The film is mostly a celebration, but it’s not all adulation,” McFadyen said.

On the other hand, through interviews with those who knew him well (such as Jethro Tull drummer Doane Perry and childhood chum Brad French), the Peart that ultimately emerges is a loyal friend and a generous colleague. Other than drummer Nilles, only people close to Peart were interviewed.
“That was intentional,” Dunn explained. “The idea was a tighter sketch of what Neil was like as a person. We felt we were giving as intimate a portrait as we could.”

stories.title: Introducing Fracette, a new sparkling wine from Niagara made using icewine
stories.summary: Fracette combines two of Niagara’s strong suits, bubbly and icewine
stories.author: Christopher Waters
stories.content:
Niagara winemakers have joined forces to create a new category of sparkling wine made using icewine as the catalyst for creating the fizz. The idea behind Fracette is to produce a fruity and frothy wine, with some of the distinctive flavours of the world-famous dessert wine but without the sweetness.

Fracette, which rhymes with cassette, was initiated by industry groups looking to give sparkling wine a regional identity by combining two of Niagara’s strong suits, bubbly and icewine. “When do you get to build a brand-new category of wine in the 21 st century?” wondered Paul Speck, president of Henry of Pelham Family Estate, one of the six wineries that helped launch Fracette this month.

“It creates a brand-new product that you can only get in Niagara, but we’re hoping to have it right across Canada. Hopefully others will join,” he added.

Provincial winemaking regulations were amended by the Ontario Wine Appellation Authority, formerly Vintners Quality Alliance, in November, 2025, to establish Fracette as a protected sparkling wine category using icewine as the sugar source for the secondary fermentation that creates the bubbles in the bottle or stainless-steel tank. The base wines must be made from vinifera grape varieties, such as riesling, chardonnay or pinot noir, and the finished wine cannot contain more than 15 grams a litre of residual sweetness, equivalent to the sugar content of champagne or prosecco made in an “extra dry” style.

Good Taste: Fostering a taste for icewine in Niagara-on-the-Lake

Speck said his winemaking team and other producers spent months conducting bench trials to determine the right amount of icewine required to create bubbles without leaving any trace of its sweetness behind. “We were after the texture and density of the icewine on the palate, but wanted to keep things really fresh,” he explains.

Sparkling wines typically feature lemon and apple flavours from grapes that are picked early to give winemakers a refreshing balance of sweetness and acidity. Icewine features richer flavours, such as apricot, pineapple and honey. Those bold flavours contribute more layers to Fracette wines.

There are other logistical considerations, which might hinder adoption of the Fracette by more wineries in Ontario and other Canadian winemaking regions. Production requires investing in specialized equipment, such as the high-pressure stainless-steel tanks that safely trap carbon dioxide while withstanding more than six-plus bars of pressure during the secondary fermentation process. There’s also the need for bottling equipment that prevents bubbles from escaping while the wine is transferred, filtered and bottled.

Fracette can also be made as a bottle-fermented sparkling wine, a more time-intensive production method that requires traditional method bubblies made in Ontario to age for at least nine months before release. (All six of the initial Fracette labels were tank fermented.)

Emma Garner, senior winemaker at Andrew Peller Limited and member of the Ontario Wine Appellation Authority’s standards development committee, explains that participating wineries worked for two years on research and development trials before making commercial volumes of the unique sparkler.

“I had never fermented two wines together like that,” she says. “It took some time to wrap my head around it, but I’m really happy with where it landed.”

When it came to establishing the winemaking rules behind the new category, Garner explains that the standards committee looked at ways to maintain an element of luxury and ensure a quality product while allowing individual wineries room to experiment with different grape varieties and approaches. Peller has introduced Fracettes from its Thirty Bench Estate, made from a base blend of riesling and chardonnay, and Peller Estates label, an aromatic rosé that blends chardonnay, gewurztraminer and gamay noir (for colour).

Peller Estates has an established traditional-method sparkling wine brand called Ice Cuvée, which adds a portion of Vidal Icewine to each bottle prior to final corking and release. The white and rosé versions of Ice Cuvée are noticeably sweet, each containing more than 20 g/litre residual sugar. The perceived sweetness of a wine is relative to the other components, most importantly acidity, in that wine as well as the taster’s sensitivity.

Fracette wines are made to balance sweetness and acidity so that the overall impression is refreshing. Garner says the expressions made at Peller are a work in progress. “We have one rendition and have learned what we might want to do differently.”

Good Taste: Three fortified wines to savour this fall

The winemaking and marketing teams at Peller, Henry of Pelham and Arterra, which owns Inniskillin, Jackson-Triggs and other wineries and brands in Ontario, worked together behind the scenes to invent Fracette.

“It has been a unique experience because not only are we launching a new category, we’re coming together as an industry to do it,” says Sandra Smith, senior marketing contractor at Arterra Wines Canada. Arterra properties, Kew, Saintly and Inniskillin, are making Fracette along with the company’s Saintly brand.

When it came time to introducing the new wines to buyers at the Lcbo, the Fracette wineries went as a group rather than individual wineries. “We showed up together, which I think was key in helping the Lcbo understand how serious we were,” she explains. “We all see the potential in bringing to light what Ontario is doing so well.”

The six labels, which range in price from $18.95 (Peller Estates Private Reserve Fracette Brut Rosé) to $34.95 (Inniskillin Fracette Rosé Sparkling 2025), are available in Ontario at the Lcbo, individual estates, the Wine Shops and the Wine Rack, and other participating retailers.

stories.title: Foreign influence watchdog ‘aware of concerns’ about Alberta referendum
stories.summary: Canadians acting on behalf of foreign nations to influence Alberta referendum question must register with new foreign influence commissioner or face penalties.
stories.author: Alex Boutilier
stories.content:
Canada’s foreign influence commissioner’s office says they’re “aware of concerns” about other states targeting the Alberta upcoming independence referendum.

In a statement Tuesday evening, Foreign Influence Commissioner Anton Boegman said his office has “proactively communicated” with both individuals and organizations that may be working with foreign governments to influence Albertans’ votes ahead of the Oct. 19 referendum.

Boegman’s office pushed any Canadian working with foreign governments to influence Canadian politics or government policy to review their website to decide whether they have to register under the Foreign Influence Transparency and Accountability Act.

So far, the registry lists just two names publicly. Anyone actively working with foreign governments must register before Oct. 3, in the case of longstanding relationships that began before Aug. 2026.

In the case of arrangements that began after Aug. 4, 2026, people working with foreign governments must register within two weeks of starting that work.

The Oct. 19 referendum will ask Albertans if, among other things, they want to begin the constitutionally required process to hold a binding vote on separating from Canada — essentially a referendum on if they want an official independence referendum.

Alberta separatist leaders have claimed to have already met with U.S. State Department officials in attempts to secure financing for a newly independent province. U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has previously publicly winked at the separatist cause, suggesting an independent Alberta would have allies within U.S. President Donald Trump’s administration.

The appeals to the Trump administration have raised concerns about U.S. foreign influence, or at least money, targeting the referendum.

Despite the concerns, public polling suggests that a strong majority of Albertans want their province to remain part of a united Canada. Poll aggregator 338Canada.com — using data from a number of different polling firms — suggests that 71 per cent of Albertans support remaining in Canada, to just 27 per cent who wish to leave the federation.

stories.title: Bestselling American author joins Western as writer-in-residence
stories.summary: Author Lisa Ko is joining Western University as 2026-27 writer-in-residence. It's one of the longest-running programs of its kind in Canada.
stories.author: Lauren daSilva
stories.content:
For award-winning author Lisa Ko, writing has always been rooted in everyday life, everyday people and the belief that stories – and the writing process – belong to everyone.

“Anyone can be a writer,” said Ko.

Hailing from New York, NY, Ko joins Western University this year as its new writer-in-residence, bringing her experiences and expertise from multiple critically acclaimed books to students and other writers on campus.

Ko’s impressive body of work includes novels Memory Piece– named one of Barack Obama’s favourite books of summer 2024 – and 2017 PEN/Bellwether Prize winner and National Book Award finalist The Leavers. She describes herself as a “long journey writer,” primarily writing long-form fiction.

Beyond writing knowledge, Ko also brings extensive higher-education experience. She holds a master of fine arts in creative writing and a master of library and information science. She has also served as a creative writing educator at schools such as the City University of New York and the University of Toronto School of Continuing Studies.

“I really love working with emerging writers; I’m particularly interested in getting to know the students and other writers on campus to talk about writing in all its forms,” Ko said.

Ko’s approach is intentionally non-prescriptive. Rather than imposing rules, she focuses on creative process – how each writer’s life stage, experiences and curiosities shape the way a story emerges. She is also interested in the ways community and collaboration can inform stories.

“We don’t write in a vacuum; we write about other people and experiences,” she said.

A unique background in archival research and information science also informs her work, making the writer-in-residence program a perfect fit.

Western has employed a writer-in-residence since 1972, one of the longest-running programs of its kind across Canada. The program runs in collaboration with the London Public Libraryto support the writer and provide both students and the London, Ont. community with the opportunity to engage.

“A n integral part of my own writing practice is about being in creative community with others, so I’m happy to be able to do that in London and at Western,” said Ko.

It’s central to Ko’s own practice. Her work is deeply inspired by her relationships and home. She said stories “are a way in which we see and make sense of the world.”

### “People in my family and community were some of my earliest lessons on storytelling and craft. It wasn’t because they were writing in the traditional sense; they were just great at telling stories. Those lessons were just as important as the ones I learned in the classroom.” – Lisa Ko, Western’s 2026-27 writer-in-residence

For Ko, the writer‑in‑residence role is about widening the circle. She hopes to challenge the idea that only certain people –_or achievements –_make someone a “real” writer.

“We receive a lot of messaging about whose stories are valuable,” she said. “But the material of stories is in our everyday lives and everyday people.”

Ko will be arranging public workshops throughout the year at Western and London’s Central Library branch. Appointments with the writer-in-residence are available to members of the Western University and London communities on Tuesdays throughout the fall and winter terms.

She encourages emerging writers to work with her, find other writers to work alongside, read widely and “pay close attention to the world around them.”

Attend an inaugural reading featuring Lisa Koand student writer-in-residence Cadence McGillicuddy on Oct. 28 to hear their work and listen as they discuss the craft.

Learn more about how Western is navigating new realities.

stories.title: This year, with shifting political winds, Canada gets more of the spotlight on UN’s stage
stories.summary: Canada and other countries launched a new group meant to stand up for economic cooperation and U.N.-style international collaboration.
stories.author: Lucas Casaletto
stories.content:
By Jennifer Peltz, The Associated Press

Posted September 23, 2026 10:26 am.

For years, Canada was a trouper in the drama of international affairs. An adept and experienced contributor, it didn’t often draw the spotlight when world leaders gathered at the U.N. each September.

This year, the nation of 41 million has a new posture on the planet’s biggest diplomatic stage.

Since a watershed speech to the World Economic Forum in January, Prime Minister Mark Carney has become a leading voice of what he and some others call “middle powers.” He has urged them to band together to update and preserve the international order, and protect their own interests, in an era of flexes by the United States and other global giants.

And he has shown himself willing to walk the walk when faced with U.S. President Donald Trump’s tariff’s. insults and cavalier talk of annexation . Carney rejected what he said were unacceptable U.S. trade demands and walked away from talks last month. Bluntly hedging his country’s decades-long bet on U.S. trade and partnership, he has been courting other prospects — Canada might even become the European Union’s first associate member .

“Partners are working with Canada because Canada’s predictable, reliable and principled in a world that’s anything but,” Carney told Canadian media at a news conference at the U.N. Tuesday as the General Assembly’s big meeting got into full swing.

It’s the international community’s premier gathering of the year. And to Carney, it’s an opportunity to demonstrate Canada’s vision of “values-based realism” that’s “both principled and pragmatic” — part commitment to such values as freedom, human rights and sustainability, part clear-eyed, “calibrated alliances” with partners that won’t sign onto the whole list.

That’s frankly practical talk for a forum that’s prone to either diplomatic caution or soaring rhetoric, be it doomsaying, idealistic or, often, both. And Carney is finding an ear.

Canada and a half-dozen other countries launched a new group Monday meant to stand up for economic cooperation and U.N.-style international collaboration. An air traffic control mess at New York airports kept Carney from making it to the “partners for multilateralism” kickoff event at the U.N. Monday night, but his schedule Tuesday included personal meetings with Jordan’s king, the presidents of Chile and Angola, and an Emirati cabinet minister.

He also co-hosted a meeting on the long-elusive two-state solution to the Israeli-Palestinian conflict and pledged 100 million Canadian dollars ($71 million) in humanitarian and security funding for Palestinians. Canada last year joined more than 150 countries that have recognized a Palestinian state, over the objections of Israel and its key ally, the U.S.

Asked whether he interacted Tuesday with Trump or members of his administration, Carney replied that he saw the huge meeting of world leaders as a chance to “meet those whom you don’t normally see.” He did attend Trump’s speech at the assembly, where the president made no mention of Canada — the country on the other side of the world’s longest international border, and now on the other end of a deepening trade war.

After speaking Wednesday at a U.N. meeting about oceans, Carney heads back to Canada for other commitments. Foreign Minister Anita Anand is set to deliver the country’s U.N. speech Saturday.

She said in an interview Tuesday that the address “will be very much about implementing the middle power strategy” that Carney has articulated — memorably when he told the World Economic Forum that as great power rivalries increasingly shake the international system, “middle powers must act together, because if we’re not at the table, we’re on the menu.” (There’s no official list of “middle powers,” but the term is often understood to mean countries that aren’t superpowers or their proxies but have some sway in global politics due to diplomatic or other strengths.)

Carney’s “message resonates with many audiences, particularly those in the global North,” says University of Ottawa international affairs professor Srdjan Vucetic.

He noted that the prime minister’s leadership is resonating at home, too. Carney, who took office in March 2025 , enjoys high approval ratings from Canadians. Many are galled by Trump’s remarks about making their country the U.S.’s “51st state,” his insistence on referring to Lake Ontario as “Lake America” and his trade policies . In Toronto, Canada’s most populous city, some neighborhoods are dotted with lawn signs encouraging eligible U.S. expatriates to vote absentee, and at least one coffee shop has crossed the Americano drink off its menu, substituting “Canadiano” instead.

Carney, 61, a former central bank chief with a doctorate in economics, aims to double Canada’s non-U.S. trade within a decade. He convened hundreds of international investment firm executives for a Canadian investment summit last week and is hoping for a trade deal with India, among others, by year’s end.

His government has touted security, defense and economic agreements with a roster of countries over the past year, and he has envisioned Canada as potentially forging an economic bridge of sorts between the EU and Pacific Rim countries.

His international efforts have drawn some questions , as when he became the first Canadian prime minister in over a quarter-century to visit Saudi Arabia . Predecessor Justin Trudeau’s government had assailed Saudi Arabia’s human rights record, spurring a five-year diplomatic split. The two countries restored full diplomatic relations in 2023.

Carney said at the time of the July visit that he cares deeply about human rights, that there’s no point in “lecturing countries from afar,” and that engaging with them doesn’t convey approval of their every move.

At his U.N. news conference Tuesday, he said his approach “means actively, actively taking on the world as it is, not passively waiting for a world we wish to be.”

“We have a strategy that, I believe, has already made our country stronger,” he added, “but we’ve only just begun.”

stories.title: Simcoe resident dead in Norfolk County house fire
stories.summary: Provincial police in Norfolk County say a woman has died after being found inside a burning residence in Simcoe on Monday afternoon.
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: Provincial police in Norfolk County say a woman has died after being found inside a burning residence in Simcoe on Monday afternoon.
CBC News · Posted: Sep 23, 2026 10:13 AM EDT | Last Updated: 18 minutes ago
Ontario Provincial Police (OPP) in Norfolk County say they're working with the offices of the fire marshal and the chief coroner to investigate the cause of Monday's fire.(Ontario Provincial Police)
X 0
Reddit 0
LinkedIn 0
Email 0
Ontario Provincial Police (OPP) in Norfolk County say a woman has died after being found inside a burning residence in Simcoe, east of London, on Monday afternoon.

At around 1 p.m. emergency crews were called to the fire at an Orchard Avenue address, police said. Firefighters were able to enter the residence and locate a 50-year-old individual. Despite life-saving efforts, she was later pronounced dead in hospital.
The Norfolk County OPP crime unit is investigating the cause of the fire along with the office of the fire marshal and the office of the chief coroner.
Anyone with information about the incident is asked to contact OPP or Crime Stoppers.

stories.title: Vancouver police say $5.8M of cocaine found in t-shirt order is record bust
stories.summary: Vancouver police say the largest cocaine seizure in the force's history was discovered by employees at a legitimate company sorting through an order.
stories.author: Aaron D'Andrea
stories.content:
Vancouver police say the largest cocaine seizure in the force’s history was discovered by employees at a legitimate company sorting through a t-shirt order.

The 328.55-kilogram seizure, worth an estimated $5.8 million, was found hidden among boxes of t-shirts that were ordered by a Vancouver-based business, police said Tuesday. The company’s staff found the drugs, and police were called to the business on July 21.

“Obviously, the business was shocked by what it found. They called police right away and are in no way associated with the seized cocaine,” said Sgt. Travis Fraser in a statement.

“This amount of drugs, as well as the stamps and packaging, clearly indicates organized crime is behind the shipment.”

Police said the seizure is traced back to a shipping container that left Honduras on May 18. It was loaded onto a vessel, then stopped in Jamaica on June 6, before arriving in Montreal on July 5.

“We believe the cocaine was supposed to be removed prior to its arrival at the company.,” Fraser said.

“For some reason, it was not unloaded.”

Police said it’s cooperating with authorities in Canada, Honduras, Jamaica and the U.S. as the investigation continues.

No suspect information was provided.

Anyone with information is asked to contact police.

stories.title: ‘Olivia’ was just dethroned as Canada’s most popular baby girl name
stories.summary: Noah continued its reign as the most popular name for baby boys in Canada for the fifth consecutive year, Statistics Canada said in a report Wednesday.
stories.author: Uday Rana
stories.content:
It had a good run, but Olivia is no longer the most popular among baby names for girls in Canada. There is a new queen of names in town.

After nine years at the top, Olivia was dethroned as the most popular baby girl name in the country, Statistics Canada said on Wednesday. In 2025, the top spot went to the name Charlotte, which ended the reign Olivia has enjoyed since 2015.

However, both names have remained in the top three: Charlotte since 2015 and Olivia since 2007. The name Emma rounds out the top three, retaining the third spot from 2024.

Sophia climbed to the fourth spot on the rankings, pushing Amelia to number five, while Sofia retained the number six spot. The name Chloe jumped to number seven, pushing Mia to number eight and Lily retained its popularity at number nine.

A new name entered the top 10 for girls, with Nora displacing Ava for the 10 th spot. Aside from 2023, Ava had been among the 10 most popular girl names since 2005.

Noah continued its reign as the most popular name for baby boys in Canada for the fifth consecutive year. It entered the list of top 10 boy names in 2005 and has remained there ever since, Statistics Canada said.

The name Theodore rose in popularity to the second spot, pushing Liam to the third spot while William and Oliver retained the fifth and sixth positions respectively.

In 2024, Jack dropped out of the top 10 list, only to return in 2025 and jump to the seventh spot.

Benjamin went up on position from ninth in 2024 to eight in 2025, while Lucas dropped from seventh spot to 10 th .

The name James also became less popular last year, with the name dropping from eighth position in 2024 to falling out of the top 10 list in 2025.

stories.title: Federal organizations to spend more than $18 million on return-to-office
stories.summary: Ottawa — Federal government departments and agencies are set to spend more than $18 million to get their employees to work in the office more often.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
OTTAWA — Federal government departments and agencies are set to spend more than $18 million to get their employees to work in the office more often.

Thousands of federal public servants started a new work schedule in July requiring them to be on-site in the office four days a week. Executive public servants returned to the office full-time in May.

In response to an order paper question from NDP MP Heather McPherson, 13 federal organizations said they plan to spend a combined $18,720,150 to reconfigure or acquire office space to accommodate the increased frequency of in-person work.

Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada said it will spend almost $5.7 million, while Fisheries and Oceans Canada said it will spend $4.2 million.

The Canada Border Services Agency estimated its costs at $3.9 million, while the Correctional Service of Canada said it plans to spend $1.37 million.

Some federal organizations said they have no costs associated with return-to-office, or that they were still being assessed. Several referred questions to Public Services and Procurement Canada, which said it was still evaluating the cost.

McPherson told The Canadian Press Wednesday the government clearly has not done the research to back up its claim that it’s cost-effective for workers to be back in the office.

She said it’s likely the total cost will be much larger once responses from other departments and agencies become available.

“They don’t have the information that they would need to make a good, informed decision that protects the rights of workers in this country,” she said. “And yet they’re moving ahead with decisions that are hurting people, that are hurting families, that hurting individual workers in the country.”

Treasury Board Secretary Bill Matthews told a House of Commons committee in May that the government’s decision on public servants’ return to the office was a “philosophical choice.”

“If you look outside the federal government — industry, municipalities, provinces — you will see the trend,” he said. “If you’re looking for a study that says this is a better way to do things, I don’t have one. I would describe this as a philosophical choice of the employer and a belief that teamwork is better.”

The responses to another order paper question asked by McPherson revealed that dozens of federal buildings have reported the presence of pests such as mice, rats, bats and bedbugs since 2020.

McPherson said the government is not respecting the rights of workers by sending them back into “unsafe or unproductive” working conditions.

A lack of office space is delaying public servants’ return in some departments.

Michèle LaRose, a spokesperson for Public Services and Procurement Canada, said last week that about 10 per cent of public servants aren’t able to return to the office under the new rules.

“At present, existing office space capacity can accommodate approximately 90 per cent of public servants on-site four days a week (five days for executives), through a combination of assigned and unassigned workstations,” she said. “Based on current information, this proportion is expected to increase to approximately 95 per cent by March 31, 2027.”

LaRose said organizations are implementing the rules based on available space and, in some cases, departments have phased in implementation for certain groups of employees.

LaRose also said that 266 federal co-working sites are being assigned to federal organizations to meet their space requirements and support increased on-site presence.

She said sites are being assigned to the Canada Revenue Agency, National Defence, Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada, Employment and Social Development Canada, Environment and Climate Change Canada, Fisheries and Oceans Canada and Public Services and Procurement Canada.

“As a common service provider, Public Services and Procurement Canada (PSPC) will continue to work with organizations to optimize existing office space and provide additional accommodations where needed, as quickly as possible,” LaRose said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 23, 2026.

Catherine Morrison, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Nicotine pouch regulation changes not being considered: health minister
stories.summary: Federal Health Minister Marjorie Michel says she's not considering changes to regulations that restrict the sale of nicotine pouches.
stories.author: Sarah Ritchie
stories.content:
Federal Health Minister Marjorie Michel says she’s not considering changes to regulations that restrict the sale of nicotine pouches , while tobacco control groups say the government needs to do more to tamp out the illicit market.

Health Canada regulates nicotine pouches as an aid to quit smoking and restricts their sales to adults. They are not allowed to be sold for recreational use and must be kept behind the counter at pharmacies.

Only one brand has been approved for sale since 2024. Zonnic, which is made by Imperial Tobacco, is sold in four milligram pouches and flavours are restricted to reduce their appeal to children.

“That’s not something I’m considering,” Michel said on Tuesday.

The minister said she agrees the illicit market is an issue. Pouches from brands like Zyn, from Philip Morris, are entering Canada and studies show they’re making their way into the hands of Canadian youth despite the rules.

Receive the latest medical news and health information delivered to you every Sunday.

Flory Doucas, co-director of the Quebec Coalition for Tobacco Control, said there’s not enough serious enforcement to control illicit sales, which are happening both online and in storefronts.

“The failure to enforce a regulation properly puts government in a very tricky situation and does open the door to weakening regulations,” she said.

“It shouldn’t be, but it sets a narrative that industry exploits.”

She said it’s worrying that lobbying efforts by the tobacco industry have reached the Prime Minister’s Office.

The National Post reported earlier this month that the Liberal government was open to the idea of loosening the regulations, after convenience store industry lobbyists met with Prime Minister Mark Carney’s chief of staff and other senior officials.

The pressure has also come from the government’s political opposition. Pierre Poilievre’s Conservatives pledged to “free the Zyn” during the 2025 election campaign.

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith wrote a letter to Carney last March arguing that the restrictions create barriers for adults who want to quit smoking and that the regulations have driven the growth of the black market.

Physicians for a Smoke-Free Canada, the Quebec Coalition for Tobacco Control and Action on Smoking and Health Canada said in a news release on Wednesday that research shows nicotine pouch use is rising among young Canadians and warned that allowing their sales more openly will make the product easier for youth to access.

Michel said stopping online sales is a particular challenge.

“I cannot say that as a health minister, I can track every single package in the illicit market. That would be completely not serious for me to say that,” she said, adding that her department favours a public health approach that involves educating people to help them make “the best decision for their health.”

Cynthia Callard, the executive director of Physicians for a Smoke-Free Canada, said it’s no surprise the major tobacco companies want to allow sales in retail stores.

“There was a day when people who smoked cigarettes smoked nothing but cigarettes. That was the way they got their nicotine. And now we have what the industry defines as a poly-market, where people use different products at different times of the day,” she said.

Callard called on the government to resist lobbying efforts and said the country needs a nicotine strategy that addresses the use of vapes and pouches and includes meaningful enforcement of illicit sales.

stories.title: Trump says Canada is destroying itself by allowing ‘millions into the country’
stories.summary: Donald Trump said on Wednesday “Canada is destroying itself by allowing millions and millions of people into the Country."
stories.author: Joseph Ryan
stories.content:
U.S. President Donald Trump took to Truth Social on Wednesday morning to once again criticize Canada, writing in part “Canada is destroying itself by allowing millions and millions of people into the Country, essentially unchecked and unvetted.”

Trump made the statement adding, “It is a Liberal takeover that will end very badly.” He says this is already resulting in high unemployment numbers.

However, Trump provided no evidence for these claims.

Canada’s unemployment rate in August was 6.4 per cent. The U.S. unemployment rate was 4.1 per cent last month.

Ottawa has reduced its immigration intake over the last two years after abandoning plans to work toward admitting 500,000 permanent residents annually. It also introduced targets for admissions of international students and temporary workers following sharp increases in both those populations.

Immigration Department data shows the number of temporary residents coming to Canada between January and July this year is 66 per cent lower than the number of arrivals over the same period in 2024, when reduction measures began.

Statistics Canada’s estimates show Canada’s population growth has been flat recently due to reduced immigration, and the parliamentary budget officer expects zero population growth this year.

The Immigration Department’s website says all visitors, temporary foreign workers, students, immigrants and refugees undergo comprehensive security screening protocols and can be deemed inadmissible on grounds of security, human or international rights violations, or organized criminality.

stories.title: What managing her mom’s estate at a young age taught Kimberly Wood about money
stories.summary: The wealth advisor at Johnstone Wealth Management Group at National Bank in Toronto discusses how a profound personal loss led her to a new career path.
stories.author: Unknown
stories.content:
What happens when you’re forced to navigate an estate before you’ve had much experience managing your own finances? For Kimberly Wood, becoming the executor of her mother’s estate at 23 was a life-changing education and the start of her career in wealth management. Today, Kim is a wealth advisor with Johnstone Wealth Management Group at National Bank in Toronto, where she focuses on investments, estate and financial planning.

She and Brenda discuss a financial choice that cost her a longtime friendship, why being the smartest person in the room can sometimes work against you, and the financial challenges of preparing to grow old alone.

stories.title: Live updates: Kenneth Law sentencing hearing for aiding suicides set to begin with victim impact statements
stories.summary: Ontario man who sold lethal substances online pleaded guilty to aiding 14 suicides in Canada and admitted to role in dozens more in U.K.
stories.author: Globe Staff
stories.content:
- Mike Hager, Colin Freeze

The sentencing hearing is scheduled to run for several days as the families of victims from Canada and the U.K. provide victim-impact statements. But many have shared that no words can capture the losses of their family members.

Kenneth Law’s victims in Ontario included two 16-year-olds, a 21-year-old found dead by his brother and a 19-year-old honour-roll student, as well as dozens more in the U.K. whose deaths he has admitted a role in.

Here are five of their stories .

Britain’s Crown Prosecution Service told the families of victims that they will not be seeking extradition and instead handed their evidence over to Canada for the judge to consider during Law’s sentencing.

“After careful assessment, we agreed that Mr. Law should be sentenced for the full extent of his offending within a single sentencing process in Canada. This approach is not unusual in cases involving serious offending that crosses international borders,” said a letter sent to the families in May. The CPS added that while “this May be painful to hear,” the decision was reached after a detailed consideration of all options.

In a press release that week, Britain’s National Crime Agency said Law’s actions in that country will be taken into account in his sentencing in Canada. This “is an outcome that guarantees all victims and families in the U.K. will see justice,” the press release said.

Read the full story here.

Some families are planning to use their victim impact statements to push for further scrutiny into how Kenneth Law’s operation continued for years.

Stephen Mitchell died in Toronto about a month before Kenneth Law was arrested. He was 21.

His father, Stephen Sr., said his son suffered from depression and stopped taking his medication. He paid US$87.17 via PayPal for a package of poison from Law and was found dead by his brother on March 25, 2023.

Mitchell said his son’s death was preventable and he plans to make that point when he gives his victim-impact statement.

“I do intend on calling for a formal inquiry,” he said in an interview with The Globe and Mail.

That anger is shared by the family of Imogen Nunn, who was 25 when she was found dead on New Year’s Day, 2023, after she purchased a poison packet from Law.

“I just think the government needs to just sit back and actually listen. Maybe they should be in their courtroom hearing about all our loved ones that we have lost,” her mother, Laurie Nunn, said in an interview from England. “The heartbreak, the pain that you know we’ve gone through and we’re still going through.

“It’s like .... it’s like we’ve just been left.”

Nunn said people need to pay attention the policy implications of the case, given how a Canadian online business escaped police scrutiny for years despite cultivating a global notoriety in selling suicide substances to young people who used them.

In May, Kenneth Law pleaded guilty in an Ontario court to aiding in the suicides of 14 people in Ontario, and also admitted to assisting in 79 other deaths in Britain by shipping toxic substances and suffocation equipment to people seeking to die.

Mr. Law operated an online business selling the products. He was charged in 2023 with the 14 deaths, including two minors. Each victim was named by the court.

Prior to pleading guilty to the 14 counts of aiding suicide, a grey-haired Mr. Law signed a lengthy agreed statement of facts, which was read aloud in court by prosecutors.

In the agreed facts, Mr. Law admits to shipping hundreds of packages of his products from a Canada Post office near his Mississauga home. Prosecutors named dozens of countries that received shipments but said most went to the United States (431 packages), Britain (330) and Canada (157).
