stories.title: A walk through Toronto’s Canary District reveals that architecture with charm is still possible
stories.summary: ‘It’s a by-the-book, best practice neighbourhood,’ says architect and Smart Density co-founder Naama Blonder
stories.author: Dave LeBlanc
stories.content:
“It’s a by-the-book, best practice neighbourhood,” says Smart Density co-founder Naama Blonder as she walks across Front Street East toward the Canadian National Railway Police Building (1923, James, Proctor and Redfern).

Bicycle lanes, exactly two automobile lanes and a streetcar right-of-way are all noted as we reach the wider-than-average sidewalk and continue east past the Cooper Koo Family Cherry Street Ymca and pause beside the colourful, slanted legs of the Lucie and Thornton Blackburn Conference Centre (a George Brown College building named for former slaves who came to Toronto via the Underground Railroad in 1834).

Here, and across Cooperage Street, the sidewalks are so wide they’ve been interrupted by street furniture, multiple planters and bicycle ring-and-post lockups.

“It’s everything City of Toronto planners ever wanted,” she continues, “and it’s beautiful.”

While Ms. Blonder and husband/co-founder Misha Bereznyak were not yet in the country in 2007, Google Streetview can show them what patrons of the old Canary Restaurant (which gave the new district its name) looked like before the planning party – and the accelerated development of the 2015 Pan Am Games – transformed this forgotten corner: narrow sidewalks, zero public transit infrastructure and a few lonely trees providing shade to squirrels rather than people.

The Architourist: A gentle paddle through Toronto’s new Don River mouth

Today, there are mid-rise residential buildings lining cobblestoned Front Street, from Cherry House at Canary Landing, with its rippling white façade with red brick below, to the interesting buff-and-beige brick ‘zipper’ patterning on Canary House (behind the old Canary Restaurant), retail such as coffee shops and greengrocers, and non-residential buildings to help animate the district, such as the new Indigenous Hub (the silver and red building with the ‘skirt’) with its dynamic sculpture, Equilibrium by Wendat First Nation sculptor Ludovic Boney.

But while Ms. Blonder, an architect, is praiseworthy of the new architecture, that’s not her focus. “It’s a question of scale,” she says.

Some neighbourhoods, and especially older ones such as Cabbagetown, can feel just fine with narrow sidewalks, because the human-scale of the Victorian houses and the slower pace of vehicular traffic allow the mind to be at ease. However, a narrow sidewalk beside six lanes of speeding traffic on Lawrence Avenue East lined with strip malls is a very different matter.

And, as with the case at the Distillery District just a stone’s throw away, tall towers don’t matter if what pedestrians interact with are the old red brick buildings of the Victorian age. The right scale is, well, scalable, but when planners get the formula correct, it creates charm. To that end, Ms. Blonder and Mr. Bereznyak have just released Building Charm: A hyper-practical guide to developing outstanding new neighborhoods [sic]. They write that “while details do play an important role in making a place charming, most new neighbourhoods fail to achieve charm because of their basic physical structure.”

The Architourist: New Toronto condo will feature porcelain tile handpicked in Italy

In other words, get the engine and the chassis right before throwing on that sexy sports car body.

The duo break down the “experiences that make up charm” into bite-sized thoughts, such as intimacy created by “a distinct break from the wider urban setting,” calmness achieved via “gentle transitions,” sensory engagement from “light and shadow,” and define lively places as “animated by the visible presence of people and everyday activity” and suggest that “even without direct interaction” there are benefits to the person walking through. As contrast, the authors discuss how designing for the automobile – something that occurred for most of the 20th century – can undermine charm.

To set the bar, five relatively new neighbourhoods are examined and assessed: Baldwin Park in Orlando (2002); Vauban in Freiburg, Germany (2001); Jakriborg near Malmo, Sweden (1999); Bo01 in Malmo (2001); and Seestadt Aspern in Vienna (2014). Some tick all of their boxes, and some do not.

In the chapter titled “Why Charm Is Still Possible Today,” the authors get down to brass tacks. They describe the kind of residential unit they’d find comfortable, and what kind of world they’d want to experience once outside their door. They write: “We want to step out into a charming little street or a lively plaza. We want to hear people chatting rather than the sounds of cars, and be in a place where our small children can run around safely …”

The Architourist: Women take the reins in family-friendly condo project

The “Scaling Down” system, they argue, can achieve this. Scale down vehicular impact by creating “people streets” for walkers and cyclists and “support streets” for cars and delivery vehicles. And scale down urban spaces by keeping human scale the focus, with “shorter blocks, and smaller, more numerous, and more diverse open spaces.” Low-rise buildings (or low-rise podiums) dominate, but tall buildings, when necessary, are “separated from the street” so as to be perceived as “a more distant view.”

And, to be clear, this is not a war on cars: “I’m not trying to convince people to ditch their cars,” Ms. Blonder says with a laugh.

The remainder of the book drills down to examine specific street configurations, how to manage traffic and parking, how to structure open space so it doesn’t become overwhelming, the question of simple versus elaborate buildings, and the ways in which buildings should (and shouldn’t) populate the street.

Ending our walk, we order espressos and enjoy them on Le Beau Croissanterie’s patio. As a TTC streetcar glides by, I note how close it is to our table, yet, because of the reassuring cobblestone underfoot, the sheltering aspect of the podium of Maple House (the rental apartment building above our heads) and the large round planter nearby, I feel perfectly safe … and feel that some developers might want to experience this as well.

“I want to believe that more developers will feel in their gut that what we’re talking about is needed,” finishes Ms. Blonder, “than the perception of them not caring about it.”

stories.title: Labour law changes are the ‘sunlight’ collective bargaining needs: minister
stories.summary: Jobs Minister Patty Hajdu says the Liberals' proposed changes to the Canada Labour Code would bring some much-needed "sunlight" to collective bargaining.
stories.author: Craig Lord
stories.content:
Jobs Minister Patty Hajdu says the Liberals’ proposed changes to the Canada Labour Code would bring some much-needed “sunlight” to collective bargaining in federally regulated sectors.

Hajdu tells The Canadian Press that one of the most consequential parts of the sweeping economic legislation tabled Monday looks to give the public a better sense of what’s happening when negotiations turn sour.

Jobs Minister Patty Hajdu says one of the most consequential proposed changes to the Canada Labour Code in the government’s new legislation is a special mediator role that will file a public report on sticking points in acrimonious negotiations.

That “sunlight” will help parties focus on getting a deal at the table, she says.

The Liberals are proposing to install a special mediator who would document both sides’ arguments and publish a report to identify where the sticking points are in a labour dispute before talks break down.

Hajdu says there are times in negotiations when employers or unions refuse to bargain in good faith and instead wait for the government to intervene.

She says making that report public would help put the responsibility for reaching a deal back on the parties and reduce the need for the government to get involved.

Labour leaders have come out strongly this week against other proposals in the bill that they believe would compromise workers’ rights to strike.

stories.title: Carney to co-host UN event with European Commission chief von der Leyen
stories.summary: The two leaders did not meet at the 81st Session of the United Nations General Assembly, Carney's first trip to the United States since trade negotiations fell apart last month.
stories.author: Kelly Geraldine Malone
stories.content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney is set to close out his time at the United Nations General Assembly by reuniting with European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen for an event to build collaboration around ocean observation.

The OceanEye International Alliance event will bring together other leaders, civil society partners and UN organizations to build a network to observe and share data around ocean changes and challenges.

It comes a week after von der Leyen opened the door to Canada becoming what she called the first “associate member.”

Carney’s emerging role as a key global champion of building alliances and defending multilateralism has brought repeated scorn from U.S. President Donald Trump.

The two leaders did not meet at the 81st Session of the United Nations General Assembly, Carney’s first trip to the United States since trade negotiations fell apart last month.

Carney on Tuesday said the United Nations was an opportunity to meet with other global leaders that he sees less often.

stories.title: Buyers picky, but good location and condition help spur a sale
stories.summary: Twenty-two bidders competed for a detached house in Toronto’s east end
stories.author: Carolyn Ireland
stories.content:
Last week in Toronto, 22 bidders entered a spirited competition for a detached house in the city’s east end. Most of those potential buyers likely didn’t realize that their most tenacious rivals were their neighbours vying for the same three-bedroom home.

“It was like an old-school 2017 offer night,” says real estate agent Shane Little of Sage Real Estate, who listed the property with his wife, Jenny Simon.

The enthusiasm stands out against a backdrop of trade tensions, jittery financial markets and an unpredictable economy, which have combined to make some buyers hesitant in many price ranges and parts of the city.

Buyers tend to be selective, cautions Mr. Little.

At 81 Woodfield Rd., the process turned into an “unofficial neighbourhood block party.”

The Next Move: Trade tensions likely to hold back aspiring home buyers this fall

Mr. Little sold the three-bedroom detached house for $1.7-million after listing the property with an asking price of $1.199-million.

Eighty per cent of the bidders currently live within four blocks of the house in the area near Queen Street East and Greenwood Avenue.

In an uneven market, the strategy of setting an eye-catching price and a date for reviewing offers can be risky, but Mr. Little reckoned the house with a detached garage and leafy backyard would be popular with move-up buyers in a neighbourhood where semi-detached homes far outnumber detached.

The circa 1910 house sits across the street from Duke of Connaught Public School, says Mr. Little, who knows that a cohort of families with children who attend the school are keen to trade up to a larger house in the same neighbourhood.

Six of the bidders – who all live nearby – participated in a second round of offers. The ultimate buyers live one street over.

The Next Move: Some home sellers recoil from a lethargic market as Canada-U.S. trade war adds uncertainty

That specific pocket attracts buyers because it sits where Leslieville and the Beaches meet, he says.

The house on Woodfield was also appealing because the sellers have lived there for more than 30 years and raised their own children there.

“It really felt like a family home,” he says. “It’s just the type of street people don’t leave.”

Mr. Little says activity has picked up in recent weeks, but the market is still patchy.

“There’s definitely this push-pull,” he says of the dynamic.

In many cases, buyers are not throwing caution to the wind, he says.

“I think that’s why it’s a tale of two markets.”

The Next Move: Toronto-area home buyers adjust to the new normal

Mr. Little believes homeowners who genuinely want to sell are setting realistic asking prices and finding a buyer before too long. Those who are testing the market are seeing “days on market” pile up.

“If you are speculating for a price, you’re going to sit – you will.”

Mr. Little adds that some buyers are still on the sidelines because the inventory of appealing homes remains limited in popular neighbourhoods such as the Beaches and Riverdale.

Many downsizers who have been in their houses a long time are not excited to move to a condo when they see the options available, he says.

The homeowners also realize prices are far below record levels, so they aren’t tempted by a cash windfall.

“The money becomes a sticking point when there’s no other motivation,” he says.

In Toronto’s midtown neighbourhoods surrounding Yonge Street and Lawrence Avenue, some homes have been selling briskly, says Cheri Dorsey McCann, broker with McCann Realty Group.

Realtors hoping for a rebound get side-swiped by trade war

Ms. McCann points to a four-bedroom house at 57 Snowdon Ave. which drew three offers after it was listed with an asking price of $2,599,880.

The house sold for $2.62-million after two days on market.

A dated two-bedroom bungalow at 172 Roslin Ave. near Mount Pleasant Road and Lawrence Avenue East recently sold for $1.28-million after it was listed with an asking price of $999,999.

At 27 Taunton Rd., near Mount Pleasant and Eglinton Avenue East, a four-bedroom semi was listed with an asking price of $1.995-million and sold for $2.1-million.

Ms. McCann also points to a three-bedroom detached house with many original elements at 77 St. Germain Ave., which was listed in July with an asking price of $1.75-million.

The property failed to find a buyer, so in September it was relisted with an asking price of $1.585-million. The house sold after four days for $1.6-million.

Ms. McCann says the house, which needs “tender loving care” will likely be rebuilt.

The Next Move: Toronto-area shows slow signs of real estate recovery, but risks abound

A few years ago, the same property would have likely sold for $2-million or more, she adds.

“It’s surprising the amount we’ve come down in all categories,” she says.

In some areas, homes are trading hands at 25 to 30 per below peak values.

She adds that some listings that landed on the market during the slower summer months were overlooked by buyers – even if the asking price was realistic.

“No one really was looking in the summer.”

Ms. McCann adds that buyers continue to pay a premium for a good location, and that the houses that spur competition tend to be move-in ready.

“The more challenging locations are harder to sell. The builders aren’t necessarily picking up the houses that needed to be renovated or torn down.”

The Next Move: In the Toronto-area real estate market, some buyers are bottom fishing

But she does believe that buyers are feeling more confident that prices do not have much farther to fall.

“It’s a tricky time for pricing because prices have adjusted so much,” she says.

Ms. McCann cautions that higher interest rates or an economic shock from the trade war with the United States could slow momentum.

Royal Bank of Canada economist Rachel Battaglia says the fragility of the housing market recovery in many cities was apparent in August, when national sales retreated to May levels.

“The pullback coincided with an escalation in trade tensions, which appears to have rattled buyer confidence while prompting more sellers to list,” Ms. Battaglia says in a note to clients.

Ms. Battaglia expects a gradual improvement in stability during the remaining months of 2026 and into 2027.

stories.title: Seller of Swansea penthouse sets baked-in price buffer
stories.summary: Two-bedroom suite with 525-square-foot terrace was something of a find
stories.author: Sydnia Yu
stories.content:
22 Southport St. No. 1033, Toronto

Asking price: $1,099,000 (July, 2026)

Selling price: $1,057,500 (August, 2026)

Taxes: $3,547 (2026)

Days on the market: 32

Listing agent: Christopher Bibby, Re/Max Hallmark Bibby Group Realty

Most of the units in this 37-year-old building, less than a kilometre from Sunnyside Beach on Lake Ontario, do not have private outdoor space. The exceptions are half a dozen penthouses, like this one, which have terraces. The last one sold more than 20 years ago, so this two-bedroom suite with a 525-square-foot terrace was something of a find. It had 16 visitors over four weeks this summer.

“In this building, there are only six units with terraces, and the last time a terrace unit had come out publicly was 23 years ago,” said agent Christopher Bibby.

“These are the only units with exterior space in the building. You’re either getting a terrace or nothing.”

The first offer to come in was significantly below the asking price, which, given the current condo market in Toronto, was no surprise to Mr. Bibby. His client shaved $41,500 off his ask, forging a deal at $1,057,500.

“The data shows, in this market, buyers want to negotiate and feel they pushed us off the price,” Mr. Bibby said.

“We baked in a negotiation buffer and achieved our goal. This ended up being a record sale in the complex in a period that’s supposed to be slow.”

This 1,709-square-foot unit has hardwood flooring and floor-to-ceiling windows in each room, including the eat-in kitchen and the bedrooms.

The terrace, facing east and south, is accessed from the living and dining area.

There are two full bathrooms, including an updated, primary ensuite bathroom.

The unit has one storage locker and one parking spot. Monthly fees of $1,895 cover utilities and cable, as well as concierge and use of amenities, such as a party room, a gym and an indoor pool.

“It’s a unique space,” Mr. Bibby said. “We hadn’t seen any unit in this range – over 1,700 square feet – go for sale within years.”

stories.title: Permanent resident who sexually interfered with girl, 15, aimed to dodge deportation
stories.summary: The judge sentenced the man to more than double the time he was seeking, giving him 15 months behind bars, plus three years of probation.
stories.author: Chris Lambie
stories.content:
A Hamilton, Ont., man who followed a 15-year-old down a dark trail just before midnight, grabbed her by the hair from behind, then showed her an explicit video and exposed himself has failed to convince a judge to tailor his sentence so he can avoid deportation.

Harpreet Singh, 30, was convicted in the Ontario Court of Justice for sexual interference, making sexually explicit material available to a child for the purpose of facilitating sexual interference, and exposure to a person under the age of 16 years for a sexual purpose. The permanent Canadian resident, who was born and raised in Punjab, India, argued unsuccessfully for 182 days in jail followed by two years of probation.

“Mr. Singh, a permanent resident of Canada, asks the court to impose a sentence that would preserve his right to appeal a deportation order arising from his convictions,” Justice Joe Patrick Paul Fiorucci said in his Sept. 15 decision.

“I find that such a sentence would be neither fit nor proportionate.”

Instead, the judge sentenced Singh to more than double that: 15 months behind bars, followed by three years of probation.

Reducing Singh’s “sentence to 182 days would materially understate both the gravity of the offence and the offender’s moral culpability,” said the judge.

“Such a sentence would fail to adequately reflect the seriousness of the offence, the significant harm suffered by the victim, and Parliament’s direction that denunciation and deterrence receive primary emphasis in cases involving the sexual abuse of children.”

Fiorucci accepted that Singh faces potentially significant immigration consequences. “However, those consequences do not justify reducing the sentence to a level that would otherwise be demonstrably unfit. While immigration consequences are entitled to serious consideration, they cannot be permitted to dominate the sentencing exercise or create a separate sentencing regime for offenders facing possible removal from Canada.”

The court heard that Singh sat across from the teenage girl on May 1, 2023, as they travelled on the same city bus.

“During the ride, Mr. Singh watched a sexually explicit video on his phone,” according to the decision.

The two — who were strangers to each other — both got off at the bus at the same location at 11:23 p.m.

“He followed her onto a dark trail, grabbed her by the collar (and hair) from behind, then moved in front of her holding his erect penis in one hand and his phone in the other while displaying the sexually explicit video to her,” said the decision.

The teen, whose identity is protected by a publication ban, elbowed and pushed Singh away, then fled.

stories.title: Toronto’s Elevate tech conference rebrands, plans to expand
stories.summary: Annual festival now named Nrth as organizers aim to reflect changes in the tech industry
stories.author: Tara Deschamps
stories.content:
Toronto tech conference Elevate is getting a new name.

Organizers say they’re rebranding the annual festival and the non-profit that hosts it as Nrth.

They decided to change the name because they say the tech industry has transformed since Elevate’s conception a year ago and they want the event to evolve as well.

In addition to rebranding the three-day conference, organizers say they also have plans to host more frequent events starting in 2027.

They announced their future plans and the new name Tuesday evening at the opening of the conference, where former Toronto Raptor Kyle Lowry and Dragon’s Den star Arlene Dickinson were scheduled to speak.

Over the next two days, executives from Canadian artificial intelligence firm Cohere, social media platform Reddit, cryptocurrency business Coinbase and geography tool MapQuest are expected to appear.

stories.title: The courage needed to face down hatred
stories.summary: Belleville police officers risked their lives to stop a gunman outside a synagogue. Surely, politicians can find a fraction of that bravery
stories.author: The Editorial Board
stories.content:
On the eve of Yom Kippur, the holiest time on the Jewish calendar, a man armed with a shotgun attacked the Sons of Jacob synagogue in Belleville, Ont., a dangerous escalation in a cycle of antisemitic violence in this country.

It looks likely that only through a police officer’s heroic actions were the two dozen congregants – and Canada as a whole – spared unfathomable bloodshed, a terrible equivalent to Australia’s Bondi Beach attack last December, where Islamic State-inspired terrorist attackers killed 15 people.

Constable Jeff Smith, who was shot and is still in critical condition in hospital, stopped the gunman in his tracks, wounding him and ultimately preventing the suspect from inflicting even greater carnage.

The motives of the gunman, who died from his wounds on Monday night, are not yet known. But all antisemitic attacks, whether from extremists on the left or the right, draw from the same well of Jew-hatred.

The Belleville synagogue is woven into the fabric of a small city, an unobtrusive bungalow-sized building in a leafy neighbourhood. Its membership is just 35 families. That a police officer had to be stationed outside during services is unutterably sad for what it says about Canada. That he proved to be desperately needed is beyond horrifying.

Suspect in shooting outside Belleville synagogue has died, police watchdog says

The environment for Jews in Canada has grown hostile since the Hamas terror attacks that killed 1,200 people in Israel on Oct. 7, 2023, and the war in Gaza that followed, with Israel’s military counteroffensive killing tens of thousands of Gazans.

There have been more than a dozen shootings targeting Jewish institutions, including synagogues. An elderly woman was stabbed in Ottawa. Jewish-owned businesses have burned. Extreme adherents of anti-Zionism have gone so far as to harass residents of some Jewish neighbourhoods. Some have organized to decertify Jewish summer camps, an example we have used before because it plainly shows the attempt to make Canada unliveable for Jews, including Jewish children. Others have made life miserable for Jewish postsecondary students – in one case, a professor asked them to identify themselves as Jews in class.

Belleville appears to be an escalation, the first synagogue shooting in Canada during services. A day earlier, police in Whitby, Ont., near Toronto, arrested a man and charged him with allegedly threatening to shoot a synagogue. And protesters taunted Jews on Sunday outside a Toronto building as they made their way to worship.

In this volatile moment, we seem a step closer to Bondi Beach – but our leaders, for the most part, have not faced up to the dangers.

Prime Minister Mark Carney has denounced antisemitism but declined to stand up for the principle behind Zionism – Jewish self-determination in a threatening world. Anti-Zionism has been the core of the antisemitism problem in Canada and elsewhere since Oct. 7. After the Belleville shooting, he tweeted a rote “thoughts are with you” that offered a disheartening contrast to his eloquent speech last week at the European Parliament. Mr. Carney set up a committee last February, with one of its tasks being to look at antisemitism. It took him four months to announce its members.

Toronto Metropolitan University has taken a similar slow-footed approach. It commissioned a retired judge, Mary Lou Benotto, to look at the campus climate. She found authorities turning a blind eye to antisemitism, and made recommendations for action. The university’s response: an “implementation committee” that won’t report till next March.

Robyn Urback: Avi Lewis’s foolish statement on ‘Jewish people’ should be disqualifying

And New Democratic Party Leader Avi Lewis issued a tweet imputing collective guilt to Jewish Canadians for Israeli actions in Gaza. His post came before news broke of the shooting in Belleville. “This year,” Mr. Lewis wrote of himself on Yom Kippur, a day where Jews atone, “I’m reflecting on the fact that we failed to do our part” – Mr. Lewis is Jewish – “to stop an ongoing genocide committed in our name.” He threw tinder on the fire.

It was a reckless act, and an alarming and dangerous misuse of leadership. Collective blame risks inciting collective harm, whether from the left or the right.

Let’s hope Constable Smith’s heroism is not in vain, and that he soon returns to duty. And let’s hope that political leaders can summon a fraction of the courage that he and other officers showed on Sunday.

stories.title: Number of Ontario LTC homes requiring ‘exceptional circumstance’ bail outs growing
stories.summary: Data shows how much money Ontario spends every year from its "homes in distress" fund, a pot set aside for long-term care operations on the brink of collapse.
stories.author: Isaac Callan, Colin D'Mello
stories.content:
The number of Ontario long-term care homes receiving emergency funding to bail them out in exceptional circumstances has grown in recent years, new internal data shows, as the sector worries about how it is going to care for an aging population.

Data obtained using freedom of information laws shows how much money Ontario spends every year from its “homes in distress” fund, a pot set aside for long-term care operations on the brink of collapse.

In the data and documents released to Global News, civil servants offered a broad overview of a funding stream that appears to be growing.

“In the event a home experiences acute or unforeseen financial challenges that affects its cashflow, it can liaise with Ontario Health to assess the immediate financial risks,” staff wrote.

“Ontario Health may seek support from the Ministry. In exceptional circumstances, the Ministry can approve a one-time payment to provide relief to a home to help the home achieve financial stability.”

The data suggests the number of exceptional circumstances where homes require an emergency bailout from the government is growing.

The data, obtained by Global News using freedom of information laws, shows Ontario approves millions of dollars in emergency funding every year.

In 2021-22, the Ford government spent just $2.4 million bailing out long-term care homes, with one non-profit and three for-profit homes receiving funds. That year, for-profit homes received an average of $350,000 each.

In 2022-23, the total spiked to $9.7 million, although only $1.2 million went to for-profit homes. In 2023-24, four non-profit homes split $9.7 million in bailouts, a figure that skyrocketed to $17.2 million across six homes in 2024-25.

In the 2025-26 year, four non-profit homes required $10.9 million in short-term bailouts.

Laura Tamblyn-Watts, the CEO of seniors advocacy group CanAge, said the growing bailouts were an insight into an industry in desperate need of more funding.

“These numbers are clearly a red flag for many people,” she said.

“When we’re looking at where the investments are — and the Ford government has made significant investments in long-term care — what we’re seeing is the tip of an iceberg. It is really an aging population and people living longer in long-term care homes with high, high degrees of frailty, the kinds of frailty we’ve never seen before.”

Over the past five years, Ontario sent millions to non-profit homes in emergency bailouts. For-profit long-term care companies received roughly $2.2 million in public money.

A spokesperson for the Ministry of Long-Term Care emphasized how much the Ford government has spent overall.

“Our government continues to make record investments into the long-term care sector, including over $9 billion allocated this year alone. This included increasing Level of Care funding by over year $139.4 this year on top of the over $2 billion we are investing each year to add and support healthcare workers in the sector,” they wrote in a statement.

“While individual long term care homes are responsible for their day-to-day operations including their financial accounting, the Ministry provides the sector with many tools and resources to support them as they provide care to residents.”

In some cases, the data shows, recent bailouts saw large sums sent to a single home.

According to the data sent to Global News, the largest single bailouts were:

2021-22: $1.3 million

2022-23: $6 million

2023-24: $6.6 million

2024-25: $7 million

2025-26: $6.3 million

Tramblyn-Watts said the Ford government had shown a preference for supporting non-profit long-term care homes financially because they’re bound by stricter rules in some areas than their for-profit rivals.

“There has been clear indicators that they’re looking to support the nonprofit sector more,” she said. “That’s perhaps not as much of a surprise. The for-profit homes often have the ability to charge for extra types of services.”

Lisa Levin, the CEO of AdvantAge Ontario, which says it represents 89 per cent of Ontario’s non-profit homes, said the numbers don’t tell the whole story.

“What we do know is that the vast majority of long-term care homes that have ceased operating entirely in recent years have been for-profit homes,” she wrote in a statement.

At a time when Ontario needs every available long-term care bed, the ability of homes to remain open and continue serving residents is an important part of the picture.”

stories.title: Hamed Shafia, who helped in 'honour killing' of sisters and stepmother, allowed to tour lower security prison
stories.summary: Hamed Shafia was 18 when he helped his parents push his sisters' car into the Rideau Canal. Now, 17 years later, he says his cultural views have changed
stories.author: Adrian Humphreys
stories.content:
Hamed Shafia, at the age 18, helped his father kill three of his sisters and his stepmother by drowning them in the Rideau Canal in a so-called “honour killing” because his “cultural upbringing outweighed any moral obligation,” but now, 17 years later, he says his views have softened.

Shafia’s account of his development since the four horrifying murders in 2009 and details of his prison life since his arrest in Kingston, Ont., are revealed in a written decision released Tuesday by the Parole Board of Canada on his request for a series of visits outside his prison.

Shafia, now 35, was given a life sentence for four counts of first-degree murder in January 2012.

He asked the parole board to approve two escorted temporary absences for personal development. One was to visit a minimum-security prison, the other to attend a mosque to speak with an imam. The prison visit was approved at Friday’s hearing, but the mosque visit was denied.

The board members said at the hearing their reasons would be released in writing. Their decision reveals much about a deeply shocking crime and the family behind it.

On the morning of June 30, 2009, a Nissan Sentra was spotted submerged in the water of a lock on the Rideau Canal near Kingston, Ont. The bodies of four females were found inside, identified as Hamed Shafia’s three sisters — Zainab Shafia, 19, Sahar Shafia, 17, and 13-year-old Geeti Shafia — and his stepmother, Rona Amir Mohammad, 52, who was his father’s first wife.

Police investigators found the car was registered to Hamed Shafia’s father, Montreal businessman Mohammad Shafia.

Three hours later, Hamed Shafia went with his father and mother, Tooba Mohammad Yahya, to the Kingston police station to report the Nissan missing. The father told police three of his daughters and his “cousin” were also missing. He said the family, who had immigrated to Canada from Afghanistan, was returning from a trip to Niagara Falls, travelling in two cars.

The police investigation, however, disclosed that neither the missing Nissan nor the missing women were really a mystery to the father. Nor was the oldest victim his cousin, but one of Mohammad Shafia’s two wives.

Both of the family’s cars were at the lock when the Nissan, with the four passengers inside, was pushed into the water. Police deemed the deaths planned and deliberate murders and all three of the Shafias were charged with four counts of first-degree murder.

The killings were deemed a so-called “honour killings” in the context of the family’s “strict Afghan culture.” The case caused shock and alarm and caused headlines around the world.

Hamed Shafia and his parents were found guilty at trial. Their parole eligibility was automatically set at 25 years.

“It is difficult to conceive of a more heinous, more despicable and more honourless crime,” the trial judge, Robert Maranger, said at the time. “The apparent reason behind these cold-blooded, shameful murders was that the four completely innocent victims offended your twisted notion of honour — a notion of honour that is founded upon the domination and control of women, a sick notion of honour that has absolutely no place in any civilized society.”

In the parole board’s 11-page decision on his leave requests, the panel addressed their comments directly to Hamed Shafia.

“Following the dismissal of your appeal, you eventually admitted the murders were planned and deliberate, that you and your parents tried to disguise the murders as an accident, and confirmed the victims were conscious when the vehicle entered the water. You admitted to being in the vehicle with your mother and father while your father drove the vehicle to push the other vehicle into the water,” the board wrote.

“You acknowledged that months prior to the murders, three of your sisters started to push back against following the extremely strict Afghan culture where women were subservient, that you and your father did not like the Western values your sisters were expressing, and you felt embarrassed and ashamed of their actions, believing it brought shame to your family.”

Hamed Shafia was born in Afghanistan but raised in Dubai from the age of five until he was 16, when the Shafia family moved to Canada. He never became a Canadian citizen and now has a deportation order issued against him and an arrest warrant from Canada Border Services Agency on file with the prison to be activated upon his release.

“You described your childhood as stable, denying any form of abuse. You acknowledged being raised with problematic beliefs that were cultural and not part of the Islamic culture,” the board said.

“At the time of offending, you were living with your mother, father, stepmother, and six siblings. You maintain regular contact with your mother and three living siblings and have little contact with your father. You have never been married and do not have children. You reported dating before and during your incarceration, but you are currently single.

“You did not complete your high school education prior to your arrest. You have no employment history, other than collecting the rent on your father’s commercial properties. You denied ever using alcohol or drugs,” the board said.

He was in involuntary protective custody until July 2012 because of the nature of his crimes. He was transferred to a medium-security prison in 2015.

He has several in-prison incidents in his prison record, the board heard. In 2013, he was involved in an altercation with another prisoner; in 2014, he refused to remove his window coverings on his cell, and he and other prisoners refused lock-up. In 2017, after a private family visit with his brother he was found with 10 items of unauthorized clothing; and he and other prisoners entered the school area when not permitted.

Since 2016 he has been living in the most sought-after living unit at the institution, where offenders have single cells and are responsible for ordering their own groceries, managing a budget and cooking for themselves.

While he has had family visits with a brother and sister and video visits with his mother, he has had little contact with his father.

“Your father has reached out to you through a letter, and you asked your sister to pass on a response to him that you are well, and this is the extent of your contact with him,” the board said.

Hamed Shafia was denied a request for a compassionate escorted absence to visit family in 2019 to honour his maternal grandmother.

He speaks regularly with the prison’s imam, was described by prison officials as treating all prison staff (male and female) with respect and has continuously taken in-prison employment.

While incarcerated, he completed his high school diploma and taken in-cell post-secondary courses. He has completed prison programs, including a violence prevention course.

His escorted absence request to visit a minimum-security prison is part of a plan to help his transfer to a lower security facility. The prison he wants to be transferred to didn’t support his transfer without him showing compliance with escorted absences. The visit would include a tour of the facility and a question period with staff.

His requested private visit to a mosque was to give him an opportunity to discuss “the beliefs you held at the time of the index offences, including honour, the role of women in a family, and your responsibility to restore honour to the family, with another authority from the Muslim faith, outside of just the Imam who you see at the institution.” The prison’s plan was to escort him to the mosque in a prison vehicle while he wore restraints.

Psychological risk assessments deemed him at low risk for general recidivism, and low to low-moderate range of risk for violent recidivism.

At his parole hearing, Sharif was questioned about his crimes.

“You were able to discuss what was going on in your life at the time of the index offences. You spoke about being young and to the influence that your parents had over you, which you did not question. You were new to Canada, and you had not had the chance to grow and mature,” the board summarized his answers.

“Your lifestyle was predominately focused on being with your family and you stated that you had not yet adjusted to Western culture. You spoke about the views and beliefs that were held by your culture regarding women and control, that were not questioned or challenged.

“The option of choosing murder as a consequence for your family member’s behaviour was questioned (by board members), which you explained was an accepted and common result of dishonourable behaviour.

“You noted that while you struggled with the actions that your family took towards the victims, you felt that your cultural upbringing outweighed any moral obligation you May have had and followed through with the plan. Your loyalty and closeness with your father also influenced your behaviour, in comparison to the relationship you had with the victims. You wanted to live up to expectations of your father and did not want to disappoint him.”

He said his views have since changed.

“You noted that your siblings are not religious. You also shared how your views have changed over time with respect to your culture and now align more with your siblings’ views. It was clarified that you are not religious, but you are/were influenced by culture. You do not think about religion much in your life,” the board said.

The board said the “horrific nature” of his crime could not be overlooked: “The fear and panic that the victims would have experienced at the time of their deaths has not been lost on the Board and the profound harm and trauma caused to other members of the family will be lifelong.”

The board said prison visits would help his rehabilitation but took a different view of a trip to the mosque.

“You currently attend mosque consistently within the institution and work with the Imam. Further exploring this work in the community is not assessed as offering a different form or benefit of rehabilitation from what you are currently doing now. You noted that getting a different perspective from a different Imam is one of your goals, however the Board was unable to determine how this would be of benefit in any significant way in your change process.”

content_blocks.text: Hamed Shafia, at the age 18, helped his father kill three of his sisters and his stepmother by drowning them in the Rideau Canal in a so-called “honour killing” because his “cultural upbringing outweighed any moral obligation,” but now, 17 years later, he says his views have softened.

Shafia’s account of his development since the four horrifying murders in 2009 and details of his prison life since his arrest in Kingston, Ont., are revealed in a written decision released Tuesday by the Parole Board of Canada on his request for a series of visits outside his prison.
Shafia, now 35, was given a life sentence for four counts of first-degree murder in January 2012.

He asked the parole board to approve two escorted temporary absences for personal development. One was to visit a minimum-security prison, the other to attend a mosque to speak with an imam. The prison visit was approved at Friday’s hearing, but the mosque visit was denied.
The board members said at the hearing their reasons would be released in writing. Their decision reveals much about a deeply shocking crime and the family behind it.

On the morning of June 30, 2009, a Nissan Sentra was spotted submerged in the water of a lock on the Rideau Canal near Kingston, Ont. The bodies of four females were found inside, identified as Hamed Shafia’s three sisters — Zainab Shafia, 19, Sahar Shafia, 17, and 13-year-old Geeti Shafia — and his stepmother, Rona Amir Mohammad, 52, who was his father’s first wife.
Police investigators found the car was registered to Hamed Shafia’s father, Montreal businessman Mohammad Shafia.

Three hours later, Hamed Shafia went with his father and mother, Tooba Mohammad Yahya, to the Kingston police station to report the Nissan missing. The father told police three of his daughters and his “cousin” were also missing. He said the family, who had immigrated to Canada from Afghanistan, was returning from a trip to Niagara Falls, travelling in two cars.

The police investigation, however, disclosed that neither the missing Nissan nor the missing women were really a mystery to the father. Nor was the oldest victim his cousin, but one of Mohammad Shafia’s two wives.

Both of the family’s cars were at the lock when the Nissan, with the four passengers inside, was pushed into the water. Police deemed the deaths planned and deliberate murders and all three of the Shafias were charged with four counts of first-degree murder.
The killings were deemed a so-called “honour killings” in the context of the family’s “strict Afghan culture.” The case caused shock and alarm and caused headlines around the world.
Hamed Shafia and his parents were found guilty at trial. Their parole eligibility was automatically set at 25 years.

“It is difficult to conceive of a more heinous, more despicable and more honourless crime,” the trial judge, Robert Maranger, said at the time. “The apparent reason behind these cold-blooded, shameful murders was that the four completely innocent victims offended your twisted notion of honour — a notion of honour that is founded upon the domination and control of women, a sick notion of honour that has absolutely no place in any civilized society.”
In the parole board’s 11-page decision on his leave requests, the panel addressed their comments directly to Hamed Shafia.

“Following the dismissal of your appeal, you eventually admitted the murders were planned and deliberate, that you and your parents tried to disguise the murders as an accident, and confirmed the victims were conscious when the vehicle entered the water. You admitted to being in the vehicle with your mother and father while your father drove the vehicle to push the other vehicle into the water,” the board wrote.

“You acknowledged that months prior to the murders, three of your sisters started to push back against following the extremely strict Afghan culture where women were subservient, that you and your father did not like the Western values your sisters were expressing, and you felt embarrassed and ashamed of their actions, believing it brought shame to your family.”

Hamed Shafia was born in Afghanistan but raised in Dubai from the age of five until he was 16, when the Shafia family moved to Canada. He never became a Canadian citizen and now has a deportation order issued against him and an arrest warrant from Canada Border Services Agency on file with the prison to be activated upon his release.
“You described your childhood as stable, denying any form of abuse. You acknowledged being raised with problematic beliefs that were cultural and not part of the Islamic culture,” the board said.

“At the time of offending, you were living with your mother, father, stepmother, and six siblings. You maintain regular contact with your mother and three living siblings and have little contact with your father. You have never been married and do not have children. You reported dating before and during your incarceration, but you are currently single.

“You did not complete your high school education prior to your arrest. You have no employment history, other than collecting the rent on your father’s commercial properties. You denied ever using alcohol or drugs,” the board said.
He was in involuntary protective custody until July 2012 because of the nature of his crimes. He was transferred to a medium-security prison in 2015.

stories.title: Southwestern Ontario poised for stretch of sunny fall weather
stories.summary: A stretch of sunshine and seasonable temperatures is expected across southwestern Ontario through the weekend as a strong ridge of high pressure settles over the region.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
A stretch of sunshine and seasonable temperatures is expected across southwestern Ontario through the weekend as a strong ridge of high pressure settles over the region.

According to Reta Ismail, the weather pattern will keep conditions largely dry and sunny for the next several days, with only some cloud cover lingering near the Lake Erie shoreline from a weak low-pressure system over the United States.

The clouds are expected to clear, allowing temperatures to cool overnight. Lows are forecast to fall to between 5 C and 8 C, making for crisp starts to both Thursday and Friday.

“It’s this ridge of high pressure that will dominate the forecast for the next few days into the weekend,” Ismail said.

Daytime temperatures, however, will rebound under sunny skies. Thursday is expected to reach a high of about 20 C, which is in line with seasonal averages for late September.

Ismail said there could be a brief period of cloud cover early Friday morning, but sunshine is expected to prevail heading into the weekend.

For those with outdoor plans, the forecast looks favourable, with mainly sunny skies and dry conditions expected through Sunday.

Temperatures are also forecast to trend upward early next week, climbing above seasonal values on Monday and Tuesday.

“The next chance for moisture doesn’t arrive until late Tuesday into Wednesday when we could see a few showers,” Ismail said.

Until then, southwestern Ontario residents can expect a prolonged stretch of clear skies and comfortable fall weather.

stories.title: Seeking to save the oyster industry, a PEI lab sees big potential in tiny seeds
stories.summary: Scientists are working to create a homegrown shellfish with better defences against MSX parasites
stories.author: Lindsay Jones, Photography by Vanessa Tignanelli
stories.content:
Inside an oyster hatchery on the Western shore of PEI, an array of plastic vessels pumps algae-rich water to millions of tiny black dots – some as small as poppy seeds. They’re teeny, tiny baby oysters, specifically bred from the few that have survived multinucleate sphere unknown, or MSX, a deadly oyster disease caused by microscopic parasites.

These babies’ genetics are considered the best way forward for an industry on the brink of destruction as a result of the disease, which has ravaged wild and cultured oyster farms in Eastern Canada. It’s one of several responses to help Pei’s $27-million industry recover from the disease, which was first detected on the island two years ago and can kill 95 per cent of infected oysters. The Canadian Food Inspection Agency says it poses zero threat to human health or food safety.

“It is a terrible epizootic,” said Guy Perry, a molecular geneticist and manager of the Bideford Shellfish Hatchery on Lennox Island First Nation. “I have not seen anything worse than this ever, but at the same time as it does all this damage, we have a lot of hope because of the tools we have.”

At the Bideford marine research facility on the edge of an estuary on Malpeque Bay, giant bags of algae in seawater ranging in colour from green pond scum to honey-brown lager bubble away like witches’ brew – the primary source of food for baby oysters.

The hatchery is working to create homegrown disease-resistant oyster seed to sell to the aquaculture industry, which relies on infected coastal waters as a growth environment for its oyster crop. To do so, they’re breeding and hybridizing survivors from local growers and from Bedeque Bay, ground zero for the disease on the island.

MSX was first detected in Canada in 2002 when the disease was found in Nova Scotia’s Bras d’Or Lake. It wiped out the wild oyster fishery there. Dr. Perry said it’s unfortunate more wasn’t done then to create an MSX resistant oyster in Canada. “The whole industry’s short on time. This should have been started 20 years ago.”

Earlier this year, the federal government approved importing oyster seed for breeding from the U.S. to develop disease-resistant oysters for aquaculture use in Atlantic Canada.

American hatcheries and universities have spent decades selectively breeding oysters for MSX resistance. Their oyster strains can achieve up to 89-per-cent survival rates against the lethal parasitic disease, which was first discovered in 1957 in Delaware Bay. Today, MSX has affected waters from the Damariscotta River in Maine to Biscayne Bay in Florida, according to the Virginia Institute of Marine Science.

Warming winter temperatures caused by climate change May be a factor in the proliferation of MSX in Canada, according to researchers. The prevalence of MSX is influenced by water temperature and salinity and is suppressed by low levels of both.

MSX was first confirmed in PEI in July 2024, and Dermo, another parasite that affects oyster growth rates and mortality, was first confirmed in PEI in July 2025. The federal government says Dermo also doesn’t pose a threat to human health.

The vast majority of Bideford’s oyster seed – 85 per cent – has survived the first year of exposure, said Adrian Desbarats, the hatchery’s aquaculture business development adviser, though he noted MSX kills 95 per cent of oysters within two to three years of infection.

“They are not dying so they are, in our opinion, the real deal,” he said. “We feel that we’re getting somewhere.”

The hatchery is also using genomic tools and hybrid breeding methods – which Dr. Perry says are fast, accurate and widely used in modern agriculture.

This involves analyzing the genes of oysters that have survived and those that have died of MSX, and running their genetic profiles through software that looks at millions of genes in rapid succession. This process has identified three genotypes in the survivors that distinguish them from those that died. Dr. Perry used the survivors’ genomic profiles for breeding oysters that are expected to be resistant to MSX.

“This could be the first genomically selected cohort for MSX resistance in Canada,” he said.

“I have high hopes for this and, frankly, the mathematics are on our side.”

The oyster seed supplier is funded by the federal Atlantic Integrated Commercial Fisheries Initiative and the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency. Lennox Island First Nation, a Mi’kmaq community and band, owns and operates it.

The hatchery currently produces 20 million oyster seeds annually. While it plans to double that number next year, it’s only a fraction of the 400 million required to sustain the island’s pre-MSX aquaculture industry. “We have a desperate situation in the industry,” Mr. Desbarats said. “We’re trying to provide a solution but we recognize that we can’t be the only solution. We don’t have the capacity to provide for everybody.”

A little east of the Bideford facility, Raspberry Point, a big player in the island’s oyster aquaculture industry, is also planning to build a hatchery to grow its own disease-resistant seed, the company’s general manager, James Power, has said.

In August, the federal government announced an oyster licence buyback program to support fishers who want to exit the industry and to ease pressures on the wild oyster population while scientists keep working on MSX and Dermo, and while the industry adapts and rebuilds. The wild oyster fishery accounted for between 25 and 30 per cent of Pei’s oyster sector, valued at an estimated at $6.8-million in 2024, the federal government says.

The PEI and New Brunswick governments have also responded to the crisis this year by providing financial relief to producers affected by the diseases.

Teaming up on salmon hunts, orcas and dolphins in B.C. have developed a strategy that really clicks

Teaming up on salmon hunts, orcas and dolphins in B.C. have developed a strategy that really clicks

content_blocks.text: Inside an oyster hatchery on the Western shore of PEI, an array of plastic vessels pumps algae-rich water to millions of tiny black dots – some as small as poppy seeds. They’re teeny, tiny baby oysters, specifically bred from the few that have survived multinucleate sphere unknown, or MSX, a deadly oyster disease caused by microscopic parasites.

These babies’ genetics are considered the best way forward for an industry on the brink of destruction as a result of the disease, which has ravaged wild and cultured oyster farms in Eastern Canada. It’s one of several responses to help Pei’s $27-million industry recover from the disease, which was first detected on the island two years ago and can kill 95 per cent of infected oysters. The Canadian Food Inspection Agency says it poses zero threat to human health or food safety.

“It is a terrible epizootic,” said Guy Perry, a molecular geneticist and manager of the Bideford Shellfish Hatchery on Lennox Island First Nation. “I have not seen anything worse than this ever, but at the same time as it does all this damage, we have a lot of hope because of the tools we have.”

content_blocks.caption: A larval oyster, enclosed in a tiny shell, is just a few millimetres wide. Much of the footprint of the hatchery is dedicated to growing algae in heavy-duty plastic bags. Algae is the main source of food to grow the millions of seeds the hatchery produces annually.

content_blocks.text: At the Bideford marine research facility on the edge of an estuary on Malpeque Bay, giant bags of algae in seawater ranging in colour from green pond scum to honey-brown lager bubble away like witches’ brew – the primary source of food for baby oysters.

The hatchery is working to create homegrown disease-resistant oyster seed to sell to the aquaculture industry, which relies on infected coastal waters as a growth environment for its oyster crop. To do so, they’re breeding and hybridizing survivors from local growers and from Bedeque Bay, ground zero for the disease on the island.

MSX was first detected in Canada in 2002 when the disease was found in Nova Scotia’s Bras d’Or Lake. It wiped out the wild oyster fishery there. Dr. Perry said it’s unfortunate more wasn’t done then to create an MSX resistant oyster in Canada. “The whole industry’s short on time. This should have been started 20 years ago.”

content_blocks.caption: MSX and another parasite, Dermo, have done a number on this specimen at Raspberry Point Oyster Co. in New London Bay. Soft and foul-smelling meat are telltale signs; workers say some infected oysters are empty shells.

content_blocks.text: Earlier this year, the federal government approved importing oyster seed for breeding from the U.S. to develop disease-resistant oysters for aquaculture use in Atlantic Canada.

American hatcheries and universities have spent decades selectively breeding oysters for MSX resistance. Their oyster strains can achieve up to 89-per-cent survival rates against the lethal parasitic disease, which was first discovered in 1957 in Delaware Bay. Today, MSX has affected waters from the Damariscotta River in Maine to Biscayne Bay in Florida, according to the Virginia Institute of Marine Science.

Warming winter temperatures caused by climate change May be a factor in the proliferation of MSX in Canada, according to researchers. The prevalence of MSX is influenced by water temperature and salinity and is suppressed by low levels of both.

MSX was first confirmed in PEI in July 2024, and Dermo, another parasite that affects oyster growth rates and mortality, was first confirmed in PEI in July 2025. The federal government says Dermo also doesn’t pose a threat to human health.

content_blocks.caption: The Bideford River, dotted with oyster cages, is a short drive from Bedeque Bay on the other side of the island. Bedeque is considered the epicentre of MSX in the province.

content_blocks.text: The vast majority of Bideford’s oyster seed – 85 per cent – has survived the first year of exposure, said Adrian Desbarats, the hatchery’s aquaculture business development adviser, though he noted MSX kills 95 per cent of oysters within two to three years of infection.
“They are not dying so they are, in our opinion, the real deal,” he said. “We feel that we’re getting somewhere.”
The hatchery is also using genomic tools and hybrid breeding methods – which Dr. Perry says are fast, accurate and widely used in modern agriculture.

This involves analyzing the genes of oysters that have survived and those that have died of MSX, and running their genetic profiles through software that looks at millions of genes in rapid succession. This process has identified three genotypes in the survivors that distinguish them from those that died. Dr. Perry used the survivors’ genomic profiles for breeding oysters that are expected to be resistant to MSX.
“This could be the first genomically selected cohort for MSX resistance in Canada,” he said.
“I have high hopes for this and, frankly, the mathematics are on our side.”

The oyster seed supplier is funded by the federal Atlantic Integrated Commercial Fisheries Initiative and the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency. Lennox Island First Nation, a Mi’kmaq community and band, owns and operates it.

The hatchery currently produces 20 million oyster seeds annually. While it plans to double that number next year, it’s only a fraction of the 400 million required to sustain the island’s pre-MSX aquaculture industry. “We have a desperate situation in the industry,” Mr. Desbarats said. “We’re trying to provide a solution but we recognize that we can’t be the only solution. We don’t have the capacity to provide for everybody.”

A little east of the Bideford facility, Raspberry Point, a big player in the island’s oyster aquaculture industry, is also planning to build a hatchery to grow its own disease-resistant seed, the company’s general manager, James Power, has said.

content_blocks.caption: Raspberry Point has piled up millions of dead oysters on the Hope River this year as MSX and Dermo take their tolls.

content_blocks.text: In August, the federal government announced an oyster licence buyback program to support fishers who want to exit the industry and to ease pressures on the wild oyster population while scientists keep working on MSX and Dermo, and while the industry adapts and rebuilds. The wild oyster fishery accounted for between 25 and 30 per cent of Pei’s oyster sector, valued at an estimated at $6.8-million in 2024, the federal government says.
The PEI and New Brunswick governments have also responded to the crisis this year by providing financial relief to producers affected by the diseases.

stories.title: A Canadian guide to the US Midterms
stories.summary: Aaron Parnas, a US-based journalist and commentator about what Canadians need to know about the upcoming U.S. midterm election, and whether or not a new congress could put a check on the President.
stories.author: Joseph Ryan
stories.content:
U.S. voters will soon head to the polls to determine who will control their Senate and House of Representatives.

Happening halfway through President Trump’s second term, the midterms are often considered a barometer of how Americans feel their leader is doing – and poll after poll show Trump’s approval rating continue to dip to historic lows.

Host Caryn Ceolin speaks to Aaron Parnas, a US-based independent journalist and commentator about what Canadians need to know about this upcoming midterm election, what Trump means when he tells Americans to “vote like my name is on the ballot”, and whether or not a new congress could finally put a check on the President.

You can subscribe to The Big Story podcast on Apple Podcasts and Spotify .

stories.title: Amid shifting political winds, Canada gets more of the spotlight on the UN’s stage
stories.summary: Since a watershed speech to the World Economic Forum in January, Carney has become a leading voice of what he and some others call ‘middle powers’
stories.author: Jennifer Peltz
stories.content:
For years, Canada was a trouper in the drama of international affairs. An adept and experienced contributor, it didn’t often draw the spotlight when world leaders gathered at the UN each September.

This year, the nation of 41 million has a new posture on the planet’s biggest diplomatic stage.

Since a watershed speech to the World Economic Forum in January, Prime Minister Mark Carney has become a leading voice of what he and some others call “middle powers.” He has urged them to band together to update and preserve the international order, and protect their own interests, in an era of flexes by the United States and other global giants.

And he has shown himself willing to walk the walk when faced with U.S. President Donald Trump’s tariffs, insults and cavalier talk of annexation. Carney rejected what he said were unacceptable U.S. trade demands and walked away from talks last month. Bluntly hedging his country’s decades-long bet on U.S. trade and partnership, he has been courting other prospects – Canada might even become the European Union’s first associate member.

Carney, other world leaders launch effort to spur middle power co-operation

“Partners are working with Canada because Canada’s predictable, reliable and principled in a world that’s anything but,” Carney told Canadian media at a news conference at the UN Tuesday as the General Assembly’s big meeting got into full swing.

It’s the international community’s premier gathering of the year. And to Carney, it’s an opportunity to demonstrate Canada’s vision of “values-based realism” that’s “both principled and pragmatic” – part commitment to such values as freedom, human rights and sustainability, part clear-eyed, “calibrated alliances” with partners that won’t sign onto the whole list.

That’s frankly practical talk for a forum that’s prone to either diplomatic caution or soaring rhetoric, be it doomsaying, idealistic or, often, both. And Carney is finding an ear.

Canada and a half-dozen other countries launched a new group Monday meant to stand up for economic co-operation and UN-style international collaboration. An air traffic control mess at New York airports kept Carney from making it to the “partners for multilateralism” kickoff event at the UN Monday night, but his schedule Tuesday included personal meetings with Jordan’s king, the presidents of Chile and Angola, and an Emirati cabinet minister.

He also co-hosted a meeting on the long-elusive two-state solution to the Israeli-Palestinian conflict and pledged $100-million in humanitarian and security funding for Palestinians. Canada last year joined more than 150 countries that have recognized a Palestinian state, over the objections of Israel and its key ally, the U.S.

Asked whether he interacted Tuesday with Trump or members of his administration, Carney replied that he saw the huge meeting of world leaders as a chance to “meet those whom you don’t normally see.” He did attend Trump’s speech at the assembly, where the president made no mention of Canada – the country on the other side of the world’s longest international border, and now on the other end of a deepening trade war.

Trump defends Iran war in address to UN General Assembly, claims agreement is close

After speaking Wednesday at a UN meeting about oceans, Carney heads back to Canada for other commitments. Foreign Minister Anita Anand is set to deliver the country’s UN speech Saturday.

She said in an interview Tuesday that the address “will be very much about implementing the middle power strategy” that Carney has articulated – memorably when he told the World Economic Forum that as great power rivalries increasingly shake the international system, “middle powers must act together, because if we’re not at the table, we’re on the menu.” (There’s no official list of “middle powers,” but the term is often understood to mean countries that aren’t superpowers or their proxies but have some sway in global politics due to diplomatic or other strengths.)

Carney’s “message resonates with many audiences, particularly those in the global North,” says University of Ottawa international affairs professor Srdjan Vucetic.

He noted that the prime minister’s leadership is resonating at home, too. Carney, who took office in March, 2025, enjoys high approval ratings from Canadians. Many are galled by Trump’s remarks about making their country the U.S.’s “51st state,” his insistence on referring to Lake Ontario as “Lake America” and his trade policies. In Toronto, Canada’s most populous city, some neighbourhoods are dotted with lawn signs encouraging eligible U.S. expatriates to vote absentee, and at least one coffee shop has crossed the Americano drink off its menu, substituting “Canadiano” instead.

Carney, 61, a former central bank chief with a doctorate in economics, aims to double Canada’s non-U.S. trade within a decade. He convened hundreds of international investment firm executives for a Canadian investment summit last week and is hoping for a trade deal with India, among others, by year’s end.

His government has touted security, defence and economic agreements with a roster of countries over the past year, and he has envisioned Canada as potentially forging an economic bridge of sorts between the EU and Pacific Rim countries.

His international efforts have drawn some questions, as when he became the first Canadian prime minister in over a quarter-century to visit Saudi Arabia. Predecessor Justin Trudeau’s government had assailed Saudi Arabia’s human rights record, spurring a five-year diplomatic split. The two countries restored full diplomatic relations in 2023.

Analysis: Trump uses UN address to threaten and deride foes and allies alike, as usual

Carney said at the time of the July visit that he cares deeply about human rights, that there’s no point in “lecturing countries from afar,” and that engaging with them doesn’t convey approval of their every move.

At his UN news conference Tuesday, he said his approach “means actively, actively taking on the world as it is, not passively waiting for a world we wish to be.”

“We have a strategy that, I believe, has already made our country stronger,” he added, “but we’ve only just begun.”

stories.title: London-area farmers say this season's yields are looking good, despite challenges
stories.summary: Farmers in southwestern Ontario have faced challenges this year, from dry spells and summer rain storms to the increasing price of diesel fuel and certain parts. But overall, they say yields are looking good as the fall harvest approaches.
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: Farmers in southwestern Ontario have faced challenges this year, from dry spells and summer rain storms to the increasing price of diesel fuel and certain parts. But overall, they say yields are looking good as the fall harvest approaches.
· Posted: Sep 23, 2026 5:00 AM EDT | Last Updated: 1 hour ago
Farmers in southwestern Ontario have faced challenges this year, from dry spells and summer rain storms to the increasing price of diesel fuel and certain parts.
But overall, they say yields are looking good as the fall harvest approaches.

At Phillips' Family Farms in west London, the fall pumpkins and squash have been growing as expected, setting the business up well for the Thanksgiving rush, when people look to buy decorative gourds and squash for soups—and then the Halloween season when families buy pumpkins for carving.
The farm also grows sweet corn, which did hit a rough patch of hot, dry weather in July and into early August.
"We noticed a big difference with that real dry spell," said Ian Phillips, a partner at the farm.
"Some of the cobs weren't getting as big as they could have been, and the yield was down. But then things that came on later in the summer... when they had lots of moisture, that helped."
A pumpkin crop at one of their other farms didn't grow as well they hoped, he said, with that location getting less moisture.
But the bigger concern for Phillips is the possibility of a wet fall, which could lead to pumpkins rotting in the field, he said.

Marcel Meyer, president of the Middlesex Federation of Agriculture, grows soybeans, wheat, corn and hay. It was a challenging summer for hay, with the forecast often calling for rain when he planned to cut it, he said.
Wheat, on the other hand, has produced "incredible yields" in the region, though his own crops' yields were slightly down, he said, potentially due to heavy spring rains after spreading fertilizer.
But other regions across the province faced much bigger challenges than Middlesex County with weather events and dryness, he added.

"Every year is different and every year we complain about the weather," he said. "But this year is one of those years where we shouldn't be, because we've been blessed compared to many other parts of Ontario."

A severe storm in early September leveled corn fields and toppled farm buildings in nearby Perth and Huron counties, he pointed out, adding that farmers in Middlesex have been fortunate not to face the same hardships.
Storm that hammered south, southwestern Ontario leaves 'significant' damage, outages as cleanup continues
Video High winds flatten farm shed, as family scrambles into basement in Huron East
"We did have some golf ball-sized hail come through in that same event, but minimal damage at best," he said.
The price of diesel fuel is "astronomical" right now, Meyer said, leaving many farmers with no choice but to eat the rising costs.
Diesel costs are soaring with Canadians in key industries preparing for pain

The increased costs of fuel are a direct result of the conflict between the United States, Israel and Iran, and the latter government's power to disrupt global oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz.

stories.title: Summer season ends with steep, and rising, hydro bills for some Londoners
stories.summary: | CBC News | Posted: September 23, 2026 9:00 AM | Last Updated: September 23
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: | CBC News | Posted: September 23, 2026 9:00 AM | Last Updated: September 23
For one resident, high summer bill follows a steep, gradual increase over 2 years
For Liona Turvey, opening up her mom’s London Hydro bill last month came with a shock.
The amount owed had risen by more than $100 from the month before, to $436, and followed a steep but gradual increase in the household’s average monthly bills for reasons Turvey can’t fully explain.

“Everything London Hydro suggests, you know, the LED lights, certain times of day, energy efficiency — my mom got a new washer to try to save on that — we’re doing absolutely everything … and it doesn’t change anything,” said Turvey, who has shared a home with her mother and children since 2023.

The family’s London Hydro bill, reviewed by CBC News, shows a slow climb in the average price, from $170 in 2024, to $298 in 2025, and $345 for the first seven months of this year. The bills indicate higher usage, but Turvey says they aren’t entirely sure what’s behind it.

“There’s nobody here even during the day. No lights are on. No usage … It makes no sense for that to have such an increase. I did notice rates have gone up, but it still shouldn’t be that high,” she said, noting assessments of their air conditioner, hot water tank and power meter found no issues.

Even in milder months, the bills show usage as significantly higher than a year earlier. “We're really conscious of the time and the usage and these things, but it just keeps going up no matter how much less we use and how much more energy efficient we get.”
recent post on a local neighbourhood Facebook group generated dozens of comments from users expressing shock and frustration at their rising bills.
While individual circumstances such as Turvey's vary, there may be several reasons why some customer bills are so much higher, according to London Hydro.
For one thing, bills due in August and September reflects usage from mid-July to mid-August, when multiple heat events kept power-hungry air conditioners and dehumidifiers humming.

“A portion of the bill for residential customers is actually a fixed charge. On the electricity side, it may very well be because of consumption back in those periods,” said Elizabeth Carswell, London Hydro’s vice-president of customer and employee experience.
It may also depend on how a customer is billed. Those on time-of-use pricing were shifted onto weekday summer rates on May 1, when power between 11 a.m. and 5 p.m.
costs slightly more , while tiered plans have a lower summer threshold of 600 kilowatt hours (kWh).
Electronics can also continue drawing power despite being off or on standby, something

Base electricity rates are set by the Ontario Energy Board (OEB), which also regulates returns allowed by the utilities that generate, transmit and distribute power and natural gas, said Adam Fremeth, an associate professor at Ivey Business School, and associate director of Ivey Energy Policy and Management Centre.
The OEB adjusts rates in November, and increased them late last year by around 29 per cent for time-of-use and tiered plans, and
38 per cent for the ultra-low overnight plan for weekday on-peak and overnight use.

At the time, it blamed larger than anticipated costs in the nuclear sector, and higher spending on electricity conservation programs. (Such rate increases are reflected in Turvey’s bill, but that alone wouldn’t be enough to cause the steep bills the family is seeing.)

Customer bills also include a delivery fee from the local utility that includes a network charge, connection charge, and a fixed monthly cost for things like line maintenance, upgrades and outage repairs.

“That’s only about a fifth of your bill,” Fremeth said. “The remaining 80 per cent comes down to generation and transmission costs, well beyond what the local distribution company is providing. London Hydro is responsible for billing and collecting those fees on behalf of all the entities in the value chain.”
While higher rates and higher summertime usage can lead to a higher hydro bill, an overlooked factor for some may be water and wastewater, Carswell said.

“In those summer months, folks might have been watering their lawns, even doing water play with their kids,” Carswell said. London Hydro bills for water on behalf of the city, which sets the rates. (For Turvey, her bills show similar water usage this year and last.)
Monthly water and wastewater charges vary based on factors including metre size and usage, and costs add up.

“When we speak with customers, sometimes we learn that it's the water portion that's causing the bill to increase … Maybe something got left on,” or there is a leak, she said. Customers with a serious plumbing issue can apply for a
The province does provide relief through several subsidy programs, including the
Ontario Electricity Support Program , and a
23.5 per cent monthly rebate , but opposition parties have called on Queen’s Park to do more.
Terence Kernaghan, the NDP MPP for London North Centre, said he has had several constituents reach out saying their bills had also risen significantly.

“I’m very happy for programs administered by the Salvation Army, such as the LEAP program, as well there’s the OESP, but they have certain limitations," Kernaghan said. "People are struggling to pay their bills, and the answer should not be to most folks to tighten your belt. The government could step up.”
