stories.title: Six ways to keep the momentum going in your practice
stories.summary: Panellists at the RIA conference discussed the importance of strategic plans, delegation and communicating your values
stories.author: Deanne Gage
stories.content:
Many advisors succeed in building a solid practice, but struggle to keep the momentum going.

Practice management experts shared strategies that distinguish advisors who consistently grow their practices at the Responsible Investment Association’s (RIA) annual conference in Toronto last week.

Robyn Reid-Riviere, founder of wealth management consulting firm Dimensions Advisory Group in Toronto, says advisors conduct work that clients never see and that needs to be articulated. She calls this “making the invisible visible.”

As fees become more transparent, “being able to show them all the work you do on a daily basis is important,” she says.

Ms. Reid-Riviere says advisors who learn to delegate tend to have the most successful practices. She suggests adopting the four Ps: philosophy, process, people and performance.

Philosophy means every team member shares the same business beliefs.

From there, Ms. Reid-Riviere says a detailed process for how things work is needed.

“It’s about documentation and everyone understanding your systems and how things work. Systemize the things you can so others can take responsibility.”

Once that’s in place, she says it will be easier for the advisor to put people into specific roles and understand individual and team responsibilities.

The next step is tracking performance using metrics.

“The goal is for [the advisor] to be the most involved where they matter the most – with clients,” she says.

Lack of long-term business planning is often the cause of team misalignment, says Mark Toren, president and chief executive officer of wealth management recruitment and advisory firm Toren & Associates in Markham, Ont.

Determining at least three measurable goals will help move the goalpost for your practice.

“Strategic discussions bind partners together,” he says. “If you don’t sit down and have those discussions, you’re not going to get where you want to go.”

Rony Malev, a financial advisor at Raymond James Ltd. in Toronto, says she uses a mix of passive and active prospecting to grow her practice.

On the passive front, she hosted a cottage succession planning seminar before the summer – a timely topic for cottage owners who worry about family disputes when passing down the property.

“The [seminars] are really about getting the information out there,” Ms. Malev says, with the conversations often leading attendees to realize they need professional help.

On the active side, Ms. Malev has centres of influence beyond the traditional lawyers and accountants. She thought about the services her clients May need and landed on interior decorating, as most of her clients own homes and often speak about wanting to redecorate.

“Building a successful practice really comes down to building that relationship with your client to make sure you are their go-to person for just about anything,” she says.

Building your practice starts with finding authentic connections with potential clients, Ms. Malev says. Many professionals use LinkedIn for networking, but few do their homework before offering a cold introductory note to a stranger online.

“It makes me cringe when someone reaches out to me that way,” she says. “Showing some curiosity and preparedness first will make a difference to get that response back from the person.”

Even spending five minutes looking at the prospect’s profile for details about their education and former employers can help.

For example, Ms. Malev found a client on LinkedIn after discovering they both went to the same university in Atlantic Canada.

Ms. Malev likes to connect with clients about their money values, which can change over time. Open-ended questions – such as, “What does money mean to you?” – can generate discussion.

Ms. Reid-Riviere likes “what if” questions that throw a curveball at plans.

“When you ask those questions, you really get to see people and how they manage those situations if they’re forced,” she says.

Ms. Reid-Riviere says advisors who learn to delegate tend to have the most successful practices. She suggests adopting the four Ps: philosophy, process, people and performance.
Philosophy means every team member shares the same business beliefs.
From there, Ms. Reid-Riviere says a detailed process for how things work is needed.
“It’s about documentation and everyone understanding your systems and how things work. Systemize the things you can so others can take responsibility.”
Once that’s in place, she says it will be easier for the advisor to put people into specific roles and understand individual and team responsibilities.
The next step is tracking performance using metrics.
“The goal is for [the advisor] to be the most involved where they matter the most – with clients,” she says.

Lack of long-term business planning is often the cause of team misalignment, says Mark Toren, president and chief executive officer of wealth management recruitment and advisory firm Toren & Associates in Markham, Ont.
Determining at least three measurable goals will help move the goalpost for your practice.
“Strategic discussions bind partners together,” he says. “If you don’t sit down and have those discussions, you’re not going to get where you want to go.”
Rony Malev, a financial advisor at Raymond James Ltd. in Toronto, says she uses a mix of passive and active prospecting to grow her practice.
On the passive front, she hosted a cottage succession planning seminar before the summer – a timely topic for cottage owners who worry about family disputes when passing down the property.
“The [seminars] are really about getting the information out there,” Ms. Malev says, with the conversations often leading attendees to realize they need professional help.

On the active side, Ms. Malev has centres of influence beyond the traditional lawyers and accountants. She thought about the services her clients May need and landed on interior decorating, as most of her clients own homes and often speak about wanting to redecorate.
“Building a successful practice really comes down to building that relationship with your client to make sure you are their go-to person for just about anything,” she says.

Building your practice starts with finding authentic connections with potential clients, Ms. Malev says. Many professionals use LinkedIn for networking, but few do their homework before offering a cold introductory note to a stranger online.
“It makes me cringe when someone reaches out to me that way,” she says. “Showing some curiosity and preparedness first will make a difference to get that response back from the person.”
Even spending five minutes looking at the prospect’s profile for details about their education and former employers can help.
For example, Ms. Malev found a client on LinkedIn after discovering they both went to the same university in Atlantic Canada.
Ms. Malev likes to connect with clients about their money values, which can change over time. Open-ended questions – such as, “What does money mean to you?” – can generate discussion.
Ms. Reid-Riviere likes “what if” questions that throw a curveball at plans.
“When you ask those questions, you really get to see people and how they manage those situations if they’re forced,” she says.

stories.title: Carney government's retaliation May weaken the legal case against Trump's tariffs, think tank argues
stories.summary: The Carney government’s latest round of counter-tariffs May weaken the legal case against the Trump tariffs.
stories.author: Simon Tuck
stories.content:
Ottawa — The Carney government’s latest round of counter-tariffs May weaken the legal case against the Trump tariffs, because they directly discriminate against American imports, a new think tank report says.

In a report to be released Wednesday, the Montreal Economic Institute (MEI), wrote that U.S. President Donald Trump’s recent tariffs against Canada May rest legally on 1930 legislation that is often blamed for almost immediately fuelling the Great Depression.

But that legislation, the Smoot-Hawley tariff, states that American tariffs are to be used to fight back against discriminatory tariffs from another country, perhaps such as those launched earlier this month by Canada.

Ilya Somin, a law professor at George Mason University in Arlington, Va. and one of the authors of the MEI report, said he understands the political pressure to fight back against the Trump tariffs against Canada, but that the counter-tariffs are not without risk.

Counter-tariffs are by definition discriminatory, he said, which could legally justify Trump’s tariffs and therefore threaten the legal argument against them.

“Ideally, they shouldn’t do this but i do recognize there are political advantages,” said Somin, who is also a senior fellow at the MEI.

U.S. opponents could certainly still win a legal argument against the Trump tariffs, Somin said, but it’s far from certain.

“It is hard to predict how a court would handle this particular point,” the report concludes.

In July, Trump imposed 50 per cent tariffs on a range of Canadian imports and then expanded the list a month later. Canada responded earlier this month with counter-tariffs at the same rate on a basket of American imports.

While Trump hasn’t directly invoked Smoot-Hawley to justify any of his various tariffs, that legislation from 96 years ago did establish a precedent of sorts in allowing a president to adjust tariff rates that had already been approved by Congress if discrimination were involved.

The MEI report acknowledges that these latest rounds of Trump tariffs could be struck down in court despite the Canadian counter-tariffs because the 1930 legislation has since been supplanted by more recent legislation. The document describes the Trump tariffs, which have caused harm to a number of Canadian businesses and sectors, as “harmful, illegal and indefensible.”

The MEI isn’t alone in questioning the Carney government’s counter-tariffs.

Economists have said that tariffs and counter-tariffs cost both sides because they raise prices and make both economies less efficient.

Industry Minister Mélanie Joly has said Ottawa’s counter-tariffs will help Canadian negotiators in future talks with the U.S.

stories.title: Leader of B.C. Conservatives says they are united, ready after snap election call
stories.summary: The interim leader of British Columbia's Conservatives says they are united and ready to fight an Oct. 24 election, putting the chaotic final weeks of Kerry-Lynne Findlay's leadership behind them.
stories.author: Wolfgang Depner The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The British Columbia Conservatives moved Wednesday to head off suggestions that interim leader Lorne Doerkson would not remain premier if he wins the Oct. 24 election, as it announced former leader John Rustad would not be among its candidates.

A statement from the party said Rustad, who brought the Conservative party to the brink of power in 2024, was not seeking re-election in his northern B.C. riding of Nechako Lakes. He was first elected to the legislature in 2005.

Rustad was forced out of the leadership post last December after a period of instability and defections that only intensified under the brief and tumultuous reign of Kerry-Lynne Findlay, who quit on Sunday and was replaced by Doerkson.

An interim leader cannot run for the position permanently under the party’s constitution. But the party said its board would “pursue the appropriate means” to keep Doerkson in power after the snap election called by NDP Leader David Eby on Tuesday.

“A premier chosen by British Columbians deserves the certainty of leading his party,” the directors said.

The constitution would be amended to keep Doerkson in charge, the party said.

But changing the constitution requires a two-thirds vote of members present at an annual general meeting or special general meeting.

The NDP said that represented a gamble.

“What the B.C. Conservatives are saying is that British Columbians should write a blank cheque to the same far-right party members that just picked Kerry-Lynne Findlay as their leader,” Mike Farnworth, a New Democrat candidate and longtime cabinet minister, said in a statement issued by the caucus.

“Why would people ever trust them after what we’ve seen?”

Doerkson returned from a holiday in Africa over the weekend to take over from Findlay, whose divisive leadership saw 13 legislators exit the Conservative caucus in the final weeks of a reign that tilted the party further right.

Doerkson moved swiftly to shore up the party’s ranks, bringing legislators back to the Conservative fold, while describing U.S. President Donald Trump as a bully and declaring that B.C. would never become the 51st state on his watch.

Lawyer Tim Thielmann, a former Conservative candidate and former research director for the party’s caucus, said if Doerkson won, it was “extremely unlikely” that enough discontented members would block amendments to keep him in charge.

“So, I think the wisest course for people who are angry about the process that led to Doerkson being appointed leader is to vote out the NDP now and … spend the next four years building the party that you want,” he said.

“Grassroots Conservatives can’t punish the politicos that put Doerkson into power without rewarding the politicos that put Eby into power,” he added.

Eby said Wednesday that his party was the clear choice to stand up to Trump while the Conservatives would turn the province into “America Junior,” complete with health-care privatization.

On the first full day of campaigning, Eby touted his government’s success in recruiting American health-care workers and said the NDP would triple the funding for the campaign to $15 million.

“When we put forward a $5-million campaign, just $5 million, to recruit these health-care workers, the Conservatives called it irresponsible,” Eby said at a stop in front of the Peace Arch border crossing in Surrey, B.C.

The campaign resulted in the hiring of 800 health-care workers from south of the border and ultimately saved the province money, Eby said.

Eby said the NDP has set a goal of recruiting 2,400 more health workers from across the border in a renewed campaign that would expand into Republican-controlled states, with laws that restrict the provision of reproductive health care.

“If we turn our province into America Junior, we put all of that at risk,” he said.

The Conservatives under Rustad had campaigned on a promise to expand private clinics to help fix what he called a system in crisis.

Eby also highlighted the prosperity agreement between B.C. and Ottawa, unveiled in July, saying it comes with federal funding to advance major projects, including liquefied natural gas facilities and the expansions of a mine and several ports.

Eby said Conservatives running under Doerkson had opposed the deal with Prime Minister Mark Carney’s Liberal government.

“Whether it’s any one of the last four leaders of the Conservatives in the last 10 months, the ideas are the same,” he said.

A Conservative news release from the time, quoting two of the legislators who flanked Doerkson as he addressed reporters in Vancouver on Tuesday, criticized the agreement for maintaining the tanker ban along B.C.‘s North Coast.

Rustad isn’t the only high-profile politician to step away from the snap campaign.

Former finance minister Brenda Bailey said Wednesday she wouldn’t run for re-election, the fourth cabinet member to make such an announcement.

Bailey left the finance portfolio to take on the Jobs Ministry in August as she underwent cancer treatment. In a statement, Bailey said she’d had surgery and she was happy to be cancer free.

But she said she wouldn’t run again in her riding of Vancouver-South Granville, calling the decision “incredibly difficult.”

Health Minister Ravi Kahlon, Emergency Management Minister Kelly Greene and Agriculture Minister Lana Popham have already said they wouldn’t seek re-election.

Asked about Kahlon’s decision on Wednesday, Eby said he was “heartbroken” but understood Kahlon’s need to prioritize his family.

Green Leader Emily Lowan, meanwhile, announced she plans to run in the Victoria-area seat of Saanich North and the Islands, held by the Greens’ Rob Botterell — who had been part of a caucus of two with Jeremy Valeriote since the 2024 election.

Lowan, who’s never had a seat in the legislature, said both major parties have lost the confidence of B.C. residents but the Greens offer a different vision.

“The Greens are ready to serve with conviction, not stoke fears or squabble in division,” she told reporters in Victoria on Wednesday.

Lowan said just two Greens have made a difference in the legislature.

“In this election, we have a path to grow and hold the balance of power,” she said. “We can hold the government to account and get real results to make our province safer, healthier and more democratic.”

Lowan said the Greens were gearing up to field a full slate of candidates, though the majority of their electoral resources would be focused on southern Vancouver Island.

B.C.‘s chief electoral officer, Shipra Verma, said Elections BC was also planning for the election and needs to hire 17,000 people if it’s to deliver the same services as it did in 2024.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 23, 2026.

— With files from Nono Shen and Brenna Owen

stories.title: Quebec party leaders to take the stage for final debate of election campaign
stories.summary: Montreal - Quebec party leaders are gearing up for their third and final debate of the provincial election campaign in the evening.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
MONTREAL - Parti Québecois Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon urged Quebecers not to be afraid of a referendum, as the five main party leaders clashed Wednesday on sovereignty, finances and the cost of living in the third and final leaders’ debate of the provincial election campaign.

The moderator, Radio-Canada journalist Patrice Roy, asked the Parti Québécois leader whether he would rethink a promise to hold a sovereignty vote in the next four years if public sentiment remains against it.

St-Pierre Plamondon reiterated his promise to hold the vote in a first PQ term, after U.S. President Donald Trump leaves office.

“It’s (former Quebec premier) Jacques Parizeau who said this, but don’t be afraid of your democracy, don’t be afraid of going to the polls, don’t be afraid to think about our future,” St-Paul Plamondon said. “I think these are fundamental messages, the liberty of a people and democracy.”

Conservative Leader Éric Duhaime, who has promised to try to block a sovereignty vote if he’s elected, said St-Pierre Plamondon should listen to the 70 per cent of Quebecers who don’t want a referendum.

“Why do you want to send Quebec into a wall?” he asked.

Liberal Leader Charles Milliard painted himself as the lone federalist on the stage, noting that Duhaime and Coalition Avenir Leader Christine Fréchette voted yes to leaving Canada in the 1995 referendum, and that Québec solidaire is also a sovereigntist party.

“I see you as four shades of yes,” he said.

Québec solidaire co-spokesperson Ruba Ghazal said she is in favour of Quebec independence, but promised to build a consensus that includes Indigenous people, immigrants and anglophones.

“For me, it’s a fundamentally democratic project, Quebec independence,” she said.

Fréchette fended off criticism about her party’s management of health care services in the opening minutes, as she was challenged by Milliard and St-Pierre Plamondon for what they described as her party’s broken promises over its last eight years in government.

Milliard said Quebecers had been betrayed by the Coalition Avenir Québec’s promises to reduce emergency room wait times and ensure every Quebecer had a doctor. St-Pierre Plamondon agreed, saying the latter promise was “disrespectful of people’s intelligence.”

Fréchette acknowledged there was a lot of work to do but said her party had made improvements, including increasing the number of surgeries performed and signing up hundreds of thousands of Quebecers for groups of family doctors.

In a segment on the province’s finances, St-Pierre Plamondon was challenged on his promise to cut spending on public sector salaries by 2.5 per cent over three years, or by $1.6 billion per year.

“Who are these people … who will lose their jobs on Oct. 6?” Milliard asked him.

St-Pierre Plamondon, in response, said his party would not cut any jobs that provide services, but would attack what he called the “explosion” of the size of bureaucracy under the Coalition Avenir Québec.

Ghazal said her party was the only one not promising austerity.

“When we look at the financial frameworks of all the other parties, what they want is to cut a little, a lot or very passionately,” she said.

The two-hour debate, hosted in French by Radio-Canada, opened with Roy asking the five leaders what distinguished them from their rivals.

Fréchette stumbled slightly as the first to answer, listing a few promises to make life more affordable for families, before Roy cut her off for going over her allotted time.

Ghazal said she knew voters who were concerned about the crisis provoked by escalating tariffs between the U.S. and Canada, pledging a long-term plan that would address problems beyond the next four years of a mandate.

Duhaime pledged to overhaul bureaucratic waste in government, turning savings into tax cuts.

He also said Quebec needed to make more room for the private sector in the province’s health care system.

As the leaders arrived for the debate at the CBC/Radio-Canada building, east of downtown Montreal, they were greeted by a raucous crowd of supporters and protesters.

The crowd included striking paramedics, pro-Palestinian activists and environmental groups.

The leaders have faced questions in recent days about potential alliances if no party succeeds in forming a majority.

Poll aggregator Qc125 suggests the Parti Québécois remains the front-runner but that a minority outcome remains the most likely scenario.

In the debate’s final question, the leaders said they would collaborate with the other parties after the vote, although Duhaime, Fréchette and Milliard all used their final seconds to speak out against a referendum.

St-Pierre Plamondon said he didn’t want to presume what voters’ choices would be and suggested Quebecers could still gather around a “stable” government.

Quebec voters go to the polls Oct. 5.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 23, 2026.

stories.content:
The number of older Ontarians living with opioid use disorder (OUD) has more than doubled over the past decade, according to new research that highlights how the country is not currently equipped to support this growing population.

The Ontario Drug Policy Research Network, in a report released on Wednesday, said there were 15,231 Ontarians aged 55 and older with OUD by the end of last year, up from 7,116 in 2017. This amounts to roughly one in every 350 older adults in the province.

Additionally, the study highlighted that the rate of older adults on opioid agonist therapy, which involves the use of medications to treat opioid addiction, has more than tripled since 2013. The proportion of deaths in this age group involving fentanyl also spiked, reflecting the growing reach of the illicit drug market.

For Hamiltonians battling addiction, peer support is a dose of empathy

Epidemiologist Tara Gomes, the principal investigator of the Odprn, said this population, which faces distinct risks compared with younger people, has not been studied enough. But it should be a focus in the drug toxicity crisis as Canada’s population ages, she added.

“We are likely going to see more and more people with complex needs around drug use and who need specific supports in our health care system that we May not be ready for if we don’t start paying attention now,” said Dr. Gomes.

Conversations on the opioid crisis have largely focused on younger age groups, specifically men between the age of 30 and 39 who are dying in the greatest numbers. But Dr. Gomes said the drug-using population is aging, specifically those who were first exposed to prescription opioids in the 1990s and 2000s and have transitioned to the illicit market.

Substance use is associated with accelerated aging and earlier onset of age-related disease and morbidity, according to the study, which can lead to increased clinical complexity and health care needs. There are also social factors to consider, such as loneliness, isolation and lacking supports.

The authors of the report concluded that there is a “pressing need” for Ontario’s health care and social service systems, including institutional settings such as long-term care, to improve their substance-use supports for older people.

The Odprn said there is “an urgent need to proactively adapt care delivery, resourcing, and training to ensure high-quality care for people who use substances as they age.”

Data used in the report came from Ices, a non-profit Ontario research institute, covering the period between January, 2013, and December, 2025.

The Odprn chose to look at adults aged 55 and older, instead of the seniors’ benchmark of 65, because people who use drugs in that age group often have chronic health conditions and medical complexities that mirror the profile of someone much older.

In depth: Could GLP-1s spell relief for opioid addiction?

Dr. Gomes said long-term care is a setting that needs significant attention, pointing to data included in the report that showed the rate of admissions for people with OUD has not changed since 2017 despite there being a growing population. She said some older people can find long-term care spaces that help manage their substance use but said “that’s the exception, not the norm.”

Many pharmacies and long-term care homes will not dispense opioid agonist treatments, such as methadone and buprenorphine, adding barriers for the older drug-using population.

These settings must “have the policies and skills and infrastructure in place to offer beds to people with opioid use disorder,” said Dr. Gomes. She added that new models for supportive housing that can serve this population are needed.

Improvements can also be made in the screening and diagnosis of OUD in the older population and improving access to harm-reduction services, such as drug checking, and existing treatments, according to the report.

Accessibility, too, is an obstacle to care, specifically for adults with disabilities, mobility issues, transportation limitations and those in congregate settings.

Dr. Gomes said the report is a “first step” to increase awareness and push the conversation forward on how to best serve this population and prevent deaths.

stories.title: Carney to co-host event with European Commission president at UN
stories.summary: United Nations - Prime Minister Mark Carney is set to close out his time at the United Nations General Assembly by reuniting with European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen for an event to build collaboration around ocean observation.
stories.author: Kelly Geraldine Malone The Canadian Press
stories.content:
UNITED NATIONS - Prime Minister Mark Carney pledged $82 million over five years to bolster ocean monitoring as he continued his support for international collaboration at the United Nations General Assembly on Wednesday.

“Canada is an ocean nation,” Carney said.

Carney’s emerging role as a key global champion of alliances and multilateralism has made him a frequent target of U.S. President Donald Trump.

Earlier Wednesday, the president claimed on social media that Canada is “destroying itself” by allowing millions of people into the country “essentially unchecked and unvetted.”

Trump provided no evidence for these claims but called it a “Liberal takeover that will end very badly.”

Carney and Trump did not meet when they both attended the 81st Session of the United Nations General Assembly this week. It was Carney’s first trip to the United States since trade negotiations with the U.S. fell apart last month.

In recent weeks, Trump has hit Canada with 50 per cent tariffs on an array of goods and is set to completely block imports of others later this month.

The president also signed an order to identify and remove products of Canadian origin from U.S. government procurement systems.

Carney appeared undeterred and continued to meet with other world leaders while at the UN event. He said Tuesday the General Assembly offers him an opportunity to meet with leaders he sees less often.

Wednesday’s event saw Carney reunite with European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen a week after she opened the door to Canada becoming what she called the first “associate member” of the European Union.

Wednesday’s OceanEye International Alliance event on the sidelines of the General Assembly brought together other leaders, civil society partners and UN organizations in an effort to build a network to collect and share data on the state of the world’s oceans.

Carney said the funding commitment will allow for year-round ocean monitoring and support the deployment of autonomous underwater gliders that can travel under the ice.

The European Commission president said 30 countries have promised to support OceanEye.

“We must listen to the ocean and we must protect it much more,” von der Leyen said.

Last week, Fisheries Minister Joanne Thompson announced that Carney’s wife, Diana Fox Carney, will serve as Canada’s “ocean envoy.”

A news release from Fisheries and Oceans Canada said Fox Carney is expected to “advance Canada’s leadership by connecting ocean conservation, climate action, Indigenous leadership, economic resilience and maritime security.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 23, 2026.

stories.title: Western literacy expert gives back through Dolly Parton’s Imagination Library of London
stories.summary: Western education instructor Betsy Reilly founded Dolly Parton's Imagination Library of London to help improve early literacy among children.
stories.author: Megan Stacey
stories.content:
Western education instructor Betsy Reilly runs Dolly Parton’s Imagination Library of London, a local affiliate of the global movement started by the late singer and philanthropist. Parton’s initiative, which provides a free book each month to children from birth until they turn five years old, has sent more than 300 million books to kids worldwide. In the wake of her death, hundreds of new families registered for the book program in London, Ont.

Reilly founded the local chapter after seeing a variety of reading abilities and needs as an elementary-school educator. Now an instructor in Western’s bachelor of education program – with a focus on language arts for teachers of primary and junior grades – she introduces teacher candidates to the importance of early literacy.

As the Imagination Library gears up for a day of fundraising on Sept. 25 – 9/25, in honour of Parton’s iconic song by the same name – Reilly explains the impact of the free-book program and reflects on Parton’s legacy.

Betsy Reilly (BR): Dolly Parton’s Imagination Library of London is one of over 400 affiliates of The Dollywood Foundation of Canada. We are a community book-gifting program, devoted to supporting early literacy, stimulating language comprehension and increasing parental engagement and bonding. Children in the program, from newborns up to five years old, receive a high quality, age-appropriate book in the mail every month – free of charge.

Among the 60 books children can receive over their five years in the program, 80 per cent are Canadian publications reflecting our culture and values. There are dual language Indigenous books for each year, with English alongside a traditional Indigenous language. The Imagination Library of London is embedded within the London Community Foundation, which covers local financial administration so that every cent donated goes to the local cost of books and mailing.

The Dollywood Foundation of Canada covers all administration, our database registration system and negotiates an extremely low book cost with Penguin Canada. Our local volunteer team is responsible for registering families and fundraising for costs of books, $3.85 each plus postage.

BR:After years of teaching in the primary grades for the Thames Valley District School Board, I could always tell which children were read to at home based on their oral language, early literacy skills and love of reading.

After the pandemic, I observed how young children were struggling and wanted to find a way to help us all recover. As a lecturer in Western’s Teacher Education program, in Primary Junior Language Arts, I tell teacher candidates if there is one thing families can do at home to support their child’s literacy development, it is read to them daily.

BR:Dolly’s father, much like mine, was illiterate. She saw how that limited his opportunities in life. She wanted to find a way to support children’s education in her own community of Pidgeon Forge, Tenn. I was impressed by her willingness to listen to experts who advised that she start with the youngest children, aged 0 to 5, as that’s when the greatest brain development occurs. Her belief in the power of literacy and education was evident in so many of her philanthropic projects.

BR:Her commitment expanded throughout the United States. Canada was her first international commitment 20 years ago, followed by the U.K., Ireland and Australia. While it was no surprise, it meant a great deal to see research published that affirmed the impact of the program. It documented how parent and caregiver behaviours changed when books were in the home. They were more likely to read four or more times a week and talk with their children about images and words. Kids in the program developed a larger vocabulary and were more eager to read. The Imagination Library works – and it is cost effective!

BR:We currently have 1,700 children in the program, with 266 who graduated from the program on their fifth birthday. In the three years since we began, we have mailed more than 27,000 books to London children.

BR:Soon after Dolly’s death, we received a very moving message from the international head of Imagination Library that “Dolly had planned for this moment” – she made sure the program would continue for generations of children.

We also saw a response locally. Within 36 hours after Dolly’s death, we received over 200 new registrations due to increased awareness of the program. We have had to temporarily pause registrations while we continue to fundraise.

BR:When a book arrives in the mail every month, one dad reported his little boy won’t leave the front steps of the porch until they read the whole book at least once. Another parent wrote to me about the day the “graduation book”, Welcome to Kindergarten, arrived on her daughter’s fifth birthday month. She cried and refused to open the book “because it means I won’t be getting any more books now that I’m 5.”

BR:We encourage members of the London and Western community, businesses, book clubs and student groups to donate and consider fundraising with us. Our current fundraiser is for 9-2-5 Give Like Dolly Day on Sept. 25, encouraging folks to donate $9.25 or $92.50 (which would cover two children for a year).

Get creative! One business is encouraging everyone to dress like Dolly (rhinestones, wigs and bling) and donate for the “privilege.” We are also happy to present to any interested groups who want to learn more about the Imagination Library. You can find more information or donate on our website.

Learn more about how Western is preparing future leaders and global citizens.

Now an instructor in Western’s bachelor of education program – with a focus on language arts for teachers of primary and junior grades – she introduces teacher candidates to the importance of early literacy.

As the Imagination Library gears up for a day of fundraising on Sept. 25 – 9/25, in honour of Parton’s iconic song by the same name – Reilly explains the impact of the free-book program and reflects on Parton’s legacy.
What is the Imagination Library of London? How does it work?

Betsy Reilly (BR): Dolly Parton’s Imagination Library of London is one of over 400 affiliates of The Dollywood Foundation of Canada. We are a community book-gifting program, devoted to supporting early literacy, stimulating language comprehension and increasing parental engagement and bonding. Children in the program, from newborns up to five years old, receive a high quality, age-appropriate book in the mail every month – free of charge.

Among the 60 books children can receive over their five years in the program, 80 per cent are Canadian publications reflecting our culture and values. There are dual language Indigenous books for each year, with English alongside a traditional Indigenous language. The Imagination Library of London is embedded within the London Community Foundation, which covers local financial administration so that every cent donated goes to the local cost of books and mailing.

The Dollywood Foundation of Canada covers all administration, our database registration system and negotiates an extremely low book cost with Penguin Canada. Our local volunteer team is responsible for registering families and fundraising for costs of books, $3.85 each plus postage.
What inspired you to bring the Imagination Library to London?

BR:After years of teaching in the primary grades for the Thames Valley District School Board, I could always tell which children were read to at home based on their oral language, early literacy skills and love of reading.

After the pandemic, I observed how young children were struggling and wanted to find a way to help us all recover. As a lecturer in Western’s Teacher Education program, in Primary Junior Language Arts, I tell teacher candidates if there is one thing families can do at home to support their child’s literacy development, it is read to them daily.
What stands out most to you about Dolly Parton’s life and legacy?

BR:Dolly’s father, much like mine, was illiterate. She saw how that limited his opportunities in life. She wanted to find a way to support children’s education in her own community of Pidgeon Forge, Tenn. I was impressed by her willingness to listen to experts who advised that she start with the youngest children, aged 0 to 5, as that’s when the greatest brain development occurs. Her belief in the power of literacy and education was evident in so many of her philanthropic projects.
What does her commitment to children’s literacy mean to you as an educator?

BR:Her commitment expanded throughout the United States. Canada was her first international commitment 20 years ago, followed by the U.K., Ireland and Australia. While it was no surprise, it meant a great deal to see research published that affirmed the impact of the program. It documented how parent and caregiver behaviours changed when books were in the home. They were more likely to read four or more times a week and talk with their children about images and words. Kids in the program developed a larger vocabulary and were more eager to read. The Imagination Library works – and it is cost effective!
How many children locally are receiving books? How many have been shared in total?

BR:We currently have 1,700 children in the program, with 266 who graduated from the program on their fifth birthday. In the three years since we began, we have mailed more than 27,000 books to London children.
Will there be any changes to the program after her death?

BR:Soon after Dolly’s death, we received a very moving message from the international head of Imagination Library that “Dolly had planned for this moment” – she made sure the program would continue for generations of children.

We also saw a response locally. Within 36 hours after Dolly’s death, we received over 200 new registrations due to increased awareness of the program. We have had to temporarily pause registrations while we continue to fundraise.
What do you hear from families about the importance of the program?

BR:When a book arrives in the mail every month, one dad reported his little boy won’t leave the front steps of the porch until they read the whole book at least once. Another parent wrote to me about the day the “graduation book”, Welcome to Kindergarten, arrived on her daughter’s fifth birthday month. She cried and refused to open the book “because it means I won’t be getting any more books now that I’m 5.”
How can people get involved?

BR:We encourage members of the London and Western community, businesses, book clubs and student groups to donate and consider fundraising with us. Our current fundraiser is for 9-2-5 Give Like Dolly Day on Sept. 25, encouraging folks to donate $9.25 or $92.50 (which would cover two children for a year).

Get creative! One business is encouraging everyone to dress like Dolly (rhinestones, wigs and bling) and donate for the “privilege.” We are also happy to present to any interested groups who want to learn more about the Imagination Library. You can find more information or donate on our website.
Learn more about how Western is preparing future leaders and global citizens.

stories.title: Four debut novelists among five authors shortlisted for the $70,000 Atwood Gibson Writers’ Trust Fiction Prize
stories.summary: Also on the list is is veteran author and Giller Prize-nominee Lisa Robertson for Riverwork
stories.author: Brad Wheeler
stories.content:
Cult-favourite author, poet and essayist Lisa Robertson is one of five shortlisted nominees for Canada’s Atwood Gibson Writers’ Trust Fiction Prize. The other finalists are all first-time novelists.

Ms. Robertson’s Riverwork , published by Coach House Books, is also one of 14 books longlisted for this year’s Giller Prize. The protagonist in the Paris-set novel is a domestic who inherits her great-aunt’s journal entries, written a century earlier.

“I’m often motivated by topics and details that seem to be left out of the official narratives,” the Toronto-born, France-based writer told The Globe and Mail recently. “One of those absences has been the labour of women, particularly working-class women. They are barely present in the big books of history and literature, although they hold up the world. I’m interested in what women keep, what we take, what we do in secret, what we pass on, and how we do that.”

Ms. Robertson once ran Proprioception Books, a Vancouver store that specialized in poetry, theory and criticism. Her first novel, The Baudelaire Fractal , was a finalist for the Governor-General’s Award for English-language fiction in 2020.

The Atwood Gibson jury cited Riverwork as a “stunning foray into a river of language” and an “insightful meditation on the nature of being.”

The jury, consisting of writers Conor Kerr of Edmonton, Kathleen Winter of Quebec’s Eastern Townships and past winner David Chariandy of Toronto, considered 118 titles representing 62 publishing imprints. The prize purse totals $100,000, with the winner receiving $70,000 and the other finalists getting $7,500 each.

The distinguished literary award was founded in 1997 as the Rogers Writers’ Trust Fiction Prize. It was renamed in 2021 to honour Canadian literary couple Margaret Atwood and Graeme Gibson (who died in 2019).

Five books shortlisted for the Hilary Weston Writers’ Trust Prize for Nonfiction

This year’s shortlisted authors include Zak Jones for Fancy Gap , published by Hamish Hamilton Canada. One of the characters in the story, about three estranged generations in Appalachia, is a soldier dishonourably discharged from the military. The Toronto-based author is a U.S. Army veteran and dual Canadian-American citizen who won the Writers’ Trust of Canada’s Bronwen Wallace Award for Emerging Writers in 2023.

The jury called Fancy Gap an “exceptional, uncanny read” that brings Appalachia alive and entails beauty, despair, longing and a search for community.

Toronto-based Congo-Canadian poet and fiction writer Téa Mutonji was shortlisted for My Person , published by Random House Canada. Her debut collection of short stories, Shut Up You’re Pretty , was a finalist for the Atwood Gibson prize in 2019.

The jury praised My Person as a “witty, moving and fiercely authentic” portrait of millennial life and the complex realities of interracial relationships.

Blair Palmer Yoxall, a member of the Métis Nation of Alberta, was nominated for Treat Them as Buffalo , published by Harper Avenue. The anti-Western, about resilient Métis women and missing teenaged Indigenous boys in the late 19th century, was described by the jury as a story that “moves with high energy and suspense in an ambitious way.”

The fifth finalist is Toronto’s Ashraf Zaghal, a Palestinian-Canadian poet and novelist born and raised in Jerusalem. His Seven Heavens Away , published by House of Anansi Press, follows a Palestinian teenager who comes of age amid escalating violence in Jerusalem.

“The writing exhibits a miracle of tenderness in a harsh and perilous surround, treasuring the protagonist’s young internal voice within its larger, older cultural context of tension, loyalty and violence,” the jury said.

Among the previous Atwood Gibson winners are Austin Clarke, Helen Humphreys, Alice Munro, Joseph Boyden, Lawrence Hill, Miriam Toews, Emma Donoghue, André Alexis and last year’s prize-taker Maria Reva, for her novel Endling .

This year’s winner will be revealed at the Writers’ Trust Awards in Toronto on Nov. 10.

stories.title: Court set to hear from victims’ families in case of international poison seller, Kenneth Law
stories.summary: "It doesn't change the depth of the grief or the sadness that I've experienced," said mom Kim Prosser.
stories.author: Omar Mosleh
stories.content:
A court is set to hear victim impact statements on Wednesday from loved ones about how their lives were torn apart due to the actions of Kenneth Law, the Mississauga man who sold poisons to hundreds of people and who pleaded guilty to helping 14 Ontarians die by suicide.

The hearing is set to be the start of what will likely be a long process, with Law’s ultimate sentence to be delivered at a later date. This hearing could last up to three days, if needed. It’s expected that the Crown will go over evidence for the deaths Law took responsibility for in Ontario, and that the court will hear several victim impact statements.

Kim Prosser, whose son Ashtyn died by suicide on March 30, 2023, at age 19 through materials purchased from Law, will be attending the hearing. She has told the Star she doesn’t hold hate or resentment toward Law, but was grateful for his guilty plea.

“It doesn’t change the depth of the grief or the sadness that I’ve experienced,” she said.

But she added she’s been frustrated with how the court hearings have played out, and the overall scope of the investigation. At his last plea hearing, the court heard the stories of 79 people in the United Kingdom that authorities connected to Law, for which he accepted responsibility.

“The thing that made me so angry the first time was like, (the courts) gave a voice for 79 people. What about everyone else? Because people still have that product. And they’re using it and ending their lives,” she said.

Law’s counsel, Matthew Gourlay, said arguments on sentencing will be submitted on Nov. 27, and his sentence May be imposed after that.

Law was initially charged with 14 counts of first-degree murder in a case with vast international implications; he remains accused of selling poisons used in dozens upon dozens of suicides outside Canada.

In May, Law pleaded guilty instead to 14 charges of aiding and abetting suicide connected to 14 Ontarians, ages 16 to 36. The Crown withdrew the murder charges, explaining there was no reasonable prospect of him being convicted of murder.

At his plea, Law also took responsibility for 79 deaths in the United Kingdom.

It is not yet clear how Law’s decision to accept responsibility for the U.K. deaths will impact his Canadian sentence.

The sprawling case of poison-seller Kenneth Law

The true number of people who died through Law’s assistance is likely staggering.

He sent 1,209 packages containing a food additive that can be lethal in certain doses, as well as other materials used for self-harm, to more than 40 countries, selling the materials via four websites that operated under the guise of selling cooking materials and industrial equipment.

Many of the people he sent packages to suffered from severe mental health conditions, and some were children.

“This was an opportunity for Canada to put its foot down,” said David Parfett, whose 22-year-old

Canadian investigators say Law sent 78 shipments to Ontario recipients, with 28 people who received them dying by suicide.

Law was busiest from 2021 to 2023, and most victims purchased the product for roughly $80 (U.S.); Law admitted to making nearly $300,000 through sales, using platforms such as Shopify and PayPal.

Had Law been tried and convicted of murder, a life sentence would be automatic.

The charge of counselling or aiding suicide instead carries a maximum sentence of 14 years in prison, to be decided at a later date.

Criminal defence lawyers who previously spoke to the Star have said that the magnitude of his crimes suggests his sentence could land in the range of 15-20 years if the judge rules his convictions should be served consecutively.

Law has been in custody for more than three years and will likely be credited for time served.

Family members of Law’s victims have called for a public inquiry in both Canada and the U.K. to probe how Law’s websites could have operated for years before his arrest.

If you are having thoughts of suicide or are worried about a loved one, call or text 988 for suicide-prevention support at any time of day or night, or call the Talk Suicide Canada helpline at 1-833-456-4566.

stories.title: Ontario raises tire recycling target after a year of industry chaos and stockpiles across the province
stories.summary: The province is also expanding collection sites to 6,500 after a target drop in 2025 left garages and yards unable to get used tires picked up.
stories.author: Patty Winsa
stories.content:
The Ontario government is raising the recycling target for tires after more than a year of chaos in the industry caused by an earlier provincial decision to reduce the level.

The new target requires tire producers to recycle, reuse or retread 80 per cent, by weight, of the tires they sell in the province, up from 65 per cent, one of a series of amendments to the Resource Recovery and Circular Economy Act of 2016 announced by the province on Monday.

The Ontario Tire Dealers Association, which has been advocating for the increase, said it is reviewing the amendments, but that the changes by the environment ministry look positive “at a high level.”

The new target should kick-start a once-robust tire recycling industry that was hit hard when the government lowered the recycling target at the beginning of 2025. The reduction meant hundreds of garages and tire dealers couldn't get their used tires picked up because the producer responsibility organizations (PROs) that handle recycling for tire companies didn't need them to meet the lowered target.

Tire haulers were put out of work, or had to lay off staff. And processing facilities that recycle used tires into crumb operated at reduced capacity despite the fact that consumers bankroll the industry through the eco-fees they pay on new tires.

Adam Moffatt, CEO of the tire dealers association, warned that the province’s recycling capacity cannot be restored overnight and that the PROs that manage recycling for tire companies also need time to assess the new requirements and implement their collection plans.

“The question now is how quickly those plans can be put into action and how quickly the collection and processing system can respond, particularly as we enter one of the busiest times of the year for Ontario’s tire dealers,” said Moffatt.

The province’s amendments also include a requirement that PROs collect from more sites, as in garages and tire dealers, from 4,300 to 6,500 beginning in 2027.

Both the increase in the recycling target and the number of collection sites weren’t in the original amendments put out by the government earlier this year for public consultation in response to the slowdown in the industry.

Instead, the province was looking at ways to implement timelines that would encourage PROs to pick up tires more quickly.

But the environment ministry determined that a higher recycling target, and an increase in collection sites, “would be the most direct way to address backlogs and improve the reliability of tire collection services in Ontario,” said the ministry in an email.

“Our expectation remains that producers and producer responsibility organizations collect and manage all end-of-life tires as they become available, regardless of targets,” said the ministry on Tuesday.
paragraphs: The Ontario government is raising the recycling target for tires after more than a year of chaos in the industry caused by an earlier provincial decision to reduce the level.

The new target requires tire producers to recycle, reuse or retread 80 per cent, by weight, of the tires they sell in the province, up from 65 per cent, one of a series of amendments to the Resource Recovery and Circular Economy Act of 2016 announced by the province on Monday.

The Ontario Tire Dealers Association, which has been advocating for the increase, said it is reviewing the amendments, but that the changes by the environment ministry look positive “at a high level.”

The new target should kick-start a once-robust tire recycling industry that was hit hard when the government lowered the recycling target at the beginning of 2025. The reduction meant hundreds of garages and tire dealers couldn't get their used tires picked up because the producer responsibility organizations (PROs) that handle recycling for tire companies didn't need them to meet the lowered target.

Tire haulers were put out of work, or had to lay off staff. And processing facilities that recycle used tires into crumb operated at reduced capacity despite the fact that consumers bankroll the industry through the eco-fees they pay on new tires.

Adam Moffatt, CEO of the tire dealers association, warned that the province’s recycling capacity cannot be restored overnight and that the PROs that manage recycling for tire companies also need time to assess the new requirements and implement their collection plans.

“The question now is how quickly those plans can be put into action and how quickly the collection and processing system can respond, particularly as we enter one of the busiest times of the year for Ontario’s tire dealers,” said Moffatt.
The province’s amendments also include a requirement that PROs collect from more sites, as in garages and tire dealers, from 4,300 to 6,500 beginning in 2027.

Both the increase in the recycling target and the number of collection sites weren’t in the original amendments put out by the government earlier this year for public consultation in response to the slowdown in the industry.

stories.title: Ontario must reconsider denying cancer patient access to new treatment in U.S., court rules
stories.summary: Ontario Divisional Court panel directs Ontario government to reconsider denial to fund Alex Shved’s treatment in the U.S.
stories.author: Megan Ogilvie
stories.content:
Doctors have told Alex Shved, a 37-year-old with metastatic melanoma, that a therapy exists that could extend his life.

On Tuesday, a panel of the Ontario Divisional Court agreed, directing the provincial government to reconsider its earlier denial to fund his treatment in the U.S.

The court ordered an expedited review of Shved’s case and gave the government until Oct. 2 — or earlier if possible — to make a new decision, noting Shved’s terminal diagnosis.

“The record discloses that he will likely be dead by Christmas if he does not receive the requested treatment within a few weeks,” the panel wrote in its ruling.

Shved is seeking a personalized cell treatment that was approved by Health Canada last year but is not yet covered by provincial drug plans.

Called tumour-infiltrating lymphocyte therapy, or TIL therapy, the treatment uses a patient’s own cells to train their immune system to find and attack cancer. The treatment is produced by a U.S. company and is marketed as lifileucel, also known by its brand name Amtagvi.

On the advice of his doctor, Shved earlier this year applied to the province for out-of-country coverage to go to a U.S. hospital for treatment. His application was denied, and Shved’s subsequent appeal to the Health Services Appeal and Review Board (Hsarb) was dismissed.

The tumour-infiltrating lymphocyte therapy uses a patient’s own cells to train their immune system to attack cancer.

Shved, who lives in Etobicoke with his wife and two young daughters, launched a judicial review of the province’s decision, representing himself at the Sept. 8 hearing.

He called Tuesday’s court decision “vindicating” and said he hopes the decision is a “wakeup call” to the province, adding that he knows of at least two Ontario patients with the same cancer who have died after being denied out-of-country access to TIL therapy.

“It makes me upset thinking about all of the people who have been wronged by this process and this system,” Shved said.

The Health Ministry did not respond to a request for comment Tuesday night but a spokesperson for Health Minister Sylvia Jones previously told the Star that provinces and territories do not provide out-of-country funding for treatments that have not yet gone through Canada’s drug funding system.

That funding process, which includes price negotiations between the manufacturer and the pan-Canadian Pharmaceutical Alliance, can take more than two years.

Shved launched a judicial review of Ontario’s funding denial for his TIL treatment in June. His central argument was that the out-of-country program is in place for treatments and health services that are unavailable to Ontario patients, and that the program is most needed for patients facing terminal diagnoses with no alternatives.

Shved also argued that denying him funding disregarded expert evidence from doctors who stated the treatment was not only safe but the best available choice, offering Shved a 30 per cent chance of a sustained response. A Florida hospital quoted Shved $1.3 million for TIL therapy, which requires chemotherapy and time in hospital, in addition to producing the personalized cell treatment.

In Tuesday’s ruling, the panel stated the province provided no evidence that funding Shved’s TIL therapy would undermine drug pricing negotiations while also underscoring both Shved’s immediate need and recommendations from medical experts.

“As we have noted more than once, this presents as a life-or-death decision for Mr. Shved,” the panel wrote. “His expert physicians have recommended the treatment, which is available in the United States and is under active consideration for use in Ontario.”

A majority of the three-justice panel ordered the expedited review of Shved’s funding application through the province’s established programs, while one justice recommended an immediate recommendation to fund the treatment.

Shved, who last week had surgery to rebuild his left arm after a tumour broke through the bone, said he is hopeful the province will fund his TIL treatment. In the meantime, he said, he is focusing on regaining enough arm strength to easily cradle his five-month-old daughter.

Wednesday, September 23, 2026

The City of London, local first responders and Western University are reminding the community to prioritize safety and well-being during this weekend’s celebrations. Those celebrating are encouraged to look out for one another and avoid large, unsanctioned street gatherings, which can create serious safety risks.

The Unsanctioned Street Party Task Force has been preparing for anticipated gatherings this weekend, bringing together agencies from across London with a shared focus on keeping students,residents and the community safe. The task force includes representatives from the City of London, the London Police Service, the London Fire Department, Middlesex-London Paramedic Service, Western University and Fanshawe College, with operational support from London Health Sciences Centre and St. Joseph’s Health Care London.

Getting there

On Saturday, September 26, access to Western’s campus from Richmond Street will be closed.Additional road closures may be implemented as needed to address large gatherings and support public safety.

Safety and enforcement

First responders and enforcement agencies will be visible and active throughout the weekend in key areas to ensure community safety. Unsanctioned gatherings pose safety risks and may result in fines and/or charges. Fines can be issued for multiple infractions, and the same person can be fined multiple times in one day. Examples of fines include:

Hosting a nuisance party: $1130

Attending a nuisance party: $930

Failing to leave premises: $65

Using of a closed road: $615

Make/cause/permit noise likely to disturb inhabitants: $305

Urinating in a public place: $305

Beyond financial consequences, the top priority remains the safety and well-being of students and the wider community.

Gender-based and sexual violence (GBSV)resources

Gender-based and sexual violence (GBSV)can occur anywhere in the community and disproportionately affects women, gender-diverse and trans people. There is zero tolerance for any form of GBSV,including unwanted comments(such as catcalling),inappropriate gestures and unwanted physical contact.

Community members are encouraged to speak up and safely intervene if they witness sexual violence.Learn how to safely intervene and prevent sexual violence by exploringbystander intervention actions.

Those who experience GBSV can report their experience anonymously through the London Police Service’sSpeak Outwebsite, contact ANOVA’s 24/7 crisis and support line at 519-642-3000 or call 2-1-1 for 24/7 crisis counselling and referrals.Western University students can access additional resources on theGetting Help After Experiencing GBSV webpage.

“We’re looking forward to welcoming new and returning students to London,” says Amanda Pfeffer,Director, Municipal Compliance, City of London.“While Homecoming is an exciting time for students, we encourage everyone to keep safety,kindness and respect top of mind. Celebrate responsibly, look out for one another, and remember to be respectful of your neighbours and the broader community.”

"Homecoming brings a unique energy and excitement to Western’s campus. As we welcome thousands of alumni for the weekend, we want everyone to celebrate safely and responsibly,”says John Doerksen, Vice-Provost (Students), Western University. “We’re encouraging students to participate in the many sanctioned events happening on campus and to take care of themselves, their friends, and our broader community."

“As Homecoming weekend approaches, we would like to remind everyone to celebrate responsibly,” said Superintendent Bill Berg, of the London Police Service. “There will be an increased police presence in key areas of the city, with a focus on addressing nuisance parties, open alcohol consumption, underage drinking, and public intoxication. As we have in previous years, we will also be supported by additional policing partners to help ensure a safe and coordinated response throughout the weekend. While we encourage everyone to have an enjoyable weekend, we also ask that those in attendance show respect for the city, community members, and one another. Education will continue throughout the weekend; however, enforcement action will be taken when necessary.”

Wednesday, September 23, 2026

The City of London, local first responders and Western University are reminding the community to prioritize safety and well-being during this weekend’s celebrations. Those celebrating are encouraged to look out for one another and avoid large, unsanctioned street gatherings, which can create serious safety risks.

The Unsanctioned Street Party Task Force has been preparing for anticipated gatherings this weekend, bringing together agencies from across London with a shared focus on keeping students,residents and the community safe. The task force includes representatives from the City of London, the London Police Service, the London Fire Department, Middlesex-London Paramedic Service, Western University and Fanshawe College, with operational support from London Health Sciences Centre and St. Joseph’s Health Care London.
Getting there
On Saturday, September 26, access to Western’s campus from Richmond Street will be closed.Additional road closures may be implemented as needed to address large gatherings and support public safety.
Safety and enforcement

First responders and enforcement agencies will be visible and active throughout the weekend in key areas to ensure community safety. Unsanctioned gatherings pose safety risks and may result in fines and/or charges. Fines can be issued for multiple infractions, and the same person can be fined multiple times in one day. Examples of fines include:
Hosting a nuisance party: $1130
Attending a nuisance party: $930
Failing to leave premises: $65
Using of a closed road: $615
Make/cause/permit noise likely to disturb inhabitants: $305
Urinating in a public place: $305
Beyond financial consequences, the top priority remains the safety and well-being of students and the wider community.
Gender-based and sexual violence (GBSV)resources

Gender-based and sexual violence (GBSV)can occur anywhere in the community and disproportionately affects women, gender-diverse and trans people. There is zero tolerance for any form of GBSV,including unwanted comments(such as catcalling),inappropriate gestures and unwanted physical contact.
Community members are encouraged to speak up and safely intervene if they witness sexual violence.Learn how to safely intervene and prevent sexual violence by exploringbystander intervention actions.

Those who experience GBSV can report their experience anonymously through the London Police Service’sSpeak Outwebsite, contact ANOVA’s 24/7 crisis and support line at 519-642-3000 or call 2-1-1 for 24/7 crisis counselling and referrals.Western University students can access additional resources on theGetting Help After Experiencing GBSV webpage.

“We’re looking forward to welcoming new and returning students to London,” says Amanda Pfeffer,Director, Municipal Compliance, City of London.“While Homecoming is an exciting time for students, we encourage everyone to keep safety,kindness and respect top of mind. Celebrate responsibly, look out for one another, and remember to be respectful of your neighbours and the broader community.”

"Homecoming brings a unique energy and excitement to Western’s campus. As we welcome thousands of alumni for the weekend, we want everyone to celebrate safely and responsibly,”says John Doerksen, Vice-Provost (Students), Western University. “We’re encouraging students to participate in the many sanctioned events happening on campus and to take care of themselves, their friends, and our broader community."

“As Homecoming weekend approaches, we would like to remind everyone to celebrate responsibly,” said Superintendent Bill Berg, of the London Police Service. “There will be an increased police presence in key areas of the city, with a focus on addressing nuisance parties, open alcohol consumption, underage drinking, and public intoxication. As we have in previous years, we will also be supported by additional policing partners to help ensure a safe and coordinated response throughout the weekend. While we encourage everyone to have an enjoyable weekend, we also ask that those in attendance show respect for the city, community members, and one another. Education will continue throughout the weekend; however, enforcement action will be taken when necessary.”

stories.title: The value of a college education - lifelong and flexible learning
stories.summary: As Fanshawe looks toward 2035, our leaders will share their perspectives on the issues that m
stories.content:
As Fanshawe looks toward 2035, our leaders will share their perspectives on the issues that matter. This series explores the opportunities, challenges and innovations shaping the future of education, workforce development and our community.

The fall semester is now underway, and we have welcomed over 8,300 level one students beginning their full-time post-secondary studies at Fanshawe College. After a quieter summer, it’s wonderful to see the halls full of students bravely embracing this next stage of their life. We take care to thoughtfully plan events, activities and ongoing supports that provide a sense of belonging for students who are embarking on this journey from many paths.

At a time when approximately 30 per cent of our incoming students have arrived directly from high school, we are increasingly welcoming mature students seeking flexible, accessible and targeted offerings that meet the needs of diverse learners throughout their lifelong learning journey.

For decades, the post-secondary path was relatively predictable: complete a program, earn a credential and begin a career. Today, that linear journey has given way to a more dynamic reality. Our graduates are navigating a labour market that increasingly rewards skills, adaptability and experience alongside credentials. Technological advancement, economic transformation and evolving workforce needs mean that individuals will likely reskill and upskill multiple times throughout their working lives. Post-secondary education can no longer be viewed as a one-time experience. It must become a lifelong journey.

Colleges are uniquely positioned to meet this challenge. Increasingly, our role extends beyond delivering traditional post-secondary learning models, to providing continuous opportunities for career development, professional growth and lifelong learning. Fanshawe College is addressing this priority with a focus on developing and supporting more part-time, online, modular and stackable offerings that empower students with choice and remove barriers, creating new possibilities for our prospective students’ personal and professional advancement. Prior Learning Assessment and Recognition (Plar) offers academic credit that recognizes previous post-secondary studies, workplace experience, volunteer activities and other forms of experiential learning. Micro-credentials, short-duration training and flexible delivery options allow learners to access education when and where they need it most.

One example of this approach to non-traditional models is our accelerated delivery of Early Childhood Education at the Simcoe/Norfolk Regional Campus. The continuous intake and modular delivery format welcomes new students every six weeks, providing eight entry points throughout the year. Students can complete the diploma in as little as twelve consecutive months, while a combination of virtual and in-person HyFlex classes are designed specifically to meet the needs of working ECEs seeking their diploma. Fanshawe is also focusing on the community and economic impact of the programming we offer for our students. By aligning students’ learning with local and regional workforce needs, the benefits extend well beyond the personal impact for our graduates. Employers gain access to the talent they need to grow and innovate their businesses, while communities become more resilient and regional economies become stronger and more competitive.

The skilled trades provide a powerful example of this impact. A highly skilled workforce has become central to Canada's economic future, as evidenced in Canada Strong and Protect Ontario priorities. Demand continues to grow for highly skilled trades professionals who can support infrastructure development, advanced manufacturing, housing construction and emerging technologies. Fanshawe’s programs are preparing graduates for these careers that offer meaningful work and long-term stability while addressing critical workforce shortages.

For example, Canada is experiencing a sustained shortage of Aircraft Maintenance Engineers, driven by an aging workforce, increased consumer commercial flight demand, and continued growth across the aviation sector. Fanshawe is committed to growing our enrolment to meet the ongoing need to expand Transport Canada-approved training capacity and develop a strong pipeline of qualified maintenance professionals to support Canada's aviation industry.

Success in preparing learners for these and other opportunities depend on strong employer partnerships. Close collaboration with industry through our various Program Advisory Committees help ensure curriculum remains current, practical and aligned with real-world expectations. Apprenticeships, co-operative education, applied learning and other work-integrated learning experiences prepare our graduates with both technical expertise and the professional skills employers value most.

As we support our students on their learning journey this fall, we are reminded that some are preparing for their first career, while many more are on other paths. By continuing to innovate how we deliver education and by strengthening partnerships with employers and communities, we are transforming individual and community potential into ongoing impact. Behind every enrolment is an individual taking a courageous step toward a brighter future, and we are privileged to be part of that journey.

stories.title: Rock duo Angine de Poitrine wins Polaris Prize
stories.summary: The Quebec group took home the $30,000 prize, and also won the $10,000 song prize for their song ‘Fabienk’
stories.author: Kaitlyn McGrath
stories.content:
Angine de Poitrine has won the Polaris Music Prize for their album “Vol II.”

About 200 music industry experts selected the second album by the costume-clad rock duo for the $30,000 prize, naming it the best Canadian record of the year based solely on artistic merit.

The Quebec group also took home the $10,000 song prize for the tune “Fabienk.”

How Angine de Poitrine’s global success benefits their friends at home in Quebec

The recognition continues a breakout year for the anonymous rockers, who dress in polka-dot outfits and describe themselves as 333-year-old aliens.

The Polaris is considered one of the country’s most prestigious music awards.

A change to the voting process saw this year’s winner selected by a voting pool rather than an 11-person jury, as in previous years.

stories.title: Bennett Bridge crash brings Central Okanagan traffic to a standstill
stories.summary: The latest closure has renewed calls from local politicians and residents for a second crossing of Okanagan Lake.
stories.author: Klaudia Van Emmerik
stories.content:
Tuesday morning’s commute in the Central Okanagan was brought to a standstill following a serious multi-vehicle collision on the Bennett Bridge.

“At this time, RCMP is unable to confirm what factors May have contributed to the collision, nor the extent of injuries which May have been sustained,” said Kelowna RCMP Cpl. Steven Lang. “Further details regarding the investigation will be released when it is appropriate to do so.”

The crash happened shortly after 4 a.m., shutting down all three southbound lanes into West Kelowna and temporarily impacting one of the two northbound lanes into Kelowna.

The nearly five-hour incident caused major traffic backups in both directions and forced Mt. Boucherie Secondary School to cancel classes for the day after staff were unable to get to work.

Motorists were advised that the best alternate southbound route was to travel north to Vernon before taking Westside Road — a roughly 130-kilometre detour.

The latest closure has renewed calls from local politicians and residents for a second crossing of Okanagan Lake.

Gavin Dew, Conservative MLA for Kelowna-Mission, said incidents such as Tuesday’s crash highlight the need for additional transportation infrastructure.

“Every time there is a closure on the bridge, it’s a reminder of the fact that we are still waiting for significant traffic improvements that are overdue,” Dew said.

The idea of a second crossing has been raised by community leaders and residents for years.

However, another bridge was not included in the 20-year transportation plan unveiled by the province in 2023.

Macklin McCall, Conservative MLA for West Kelowna-Peachland, said congestion and the need for another crossing have been ongoing concerns.

“This didn’t just spring up overnight. This was an issue with the second crossing and congestion for quite some time,” McCall said. “We still haven’t had meaningful conversations. The province hasn’t said, you know, this is one of the fastest-growing areas in British Columbia and there hasn’t even been discussions on it. But I’ll tell you this, people in the region are certainly discussing it.”

West Kelowna’s Stephen Johnston, who has been acclaimed as the city’s next mayor, told Global News that a second bridge remains a long-term solution but he wants to see action now.

“The bridge should be properly six-laned, with a new pedestrian and active transportation lane cantilevered off the side,” Johnston stated in an email to Global News. “It was originally designed to accommodate this, and we need to leverage that opportunity. This would add much-needed capacity while providing greater flexibility to keep traffic moving in both directions when an accident occurs.”

McCall said transportation infrastructure is a major issue for the Okanagan region.

“If it doesn’t get addressed, it’s only going to get worse,” McCall said.
