stories.title: No ‘blanket answer’ on when Ottawa would end strikes under proposed changes: Hajdu
stories.summary: Ottawa — The federal jobs minister says she can't give a "blanket answer" on when the federal government would move to end a strike or lockout under the new labour legislation tabled Monday.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
OTTAWA — Labour leaders are denouncing what they call a direct attack on the right to strike in the sweeping economic bill the Liberal government tabled Monday.

The Canadian Labour Congress on Tuesday accused the federal government of enshrining in the proposed legislation new powers allowing the federal government to quash strikes on a minister’s whim.

The Liberals claim the bill would place “guardrails” around a minister’s power to end work stoppages in federally regulated industries. Jobs Minister Patty Hajdu argues the changes in Bill C-39 are aimed at improving labour relations and reducing the number of times negotiations hit a boiling point.

According to the proposed Building Canada Strong Act, a work stoppage must be affecting the “national interest” before the minister can trigger Section 107 of the Canada Labour Code to end a strike or lockout.

The government says it must balance threats to the national interest — which could include economic impacts or social disruptions — with the need to protect the right to free association and to strike.

Section 107 has been used repeatedly by the federal labour minister in recent years to refer deadlocked parties to the Canada Industrial Relations Board to declare an impasse, end a work stoppage and move talks into binding arbitration.

But those actions have been the subject of numerous court challenges which argue that Section 107 never gave the minister the power to end a strike.

Bea Bruske, president of the Canadian Labour Congress, told reporters in Ottawa on Tuesday that the proposed amendments would formalize the government’s power to break strikes.

“The government said it would protect the workers’ right to strike, but instead this bill explicitly gives government the power to end legal strikes when a minister decides that a strike is or could become contrary to the national interest,” she said.

Bruske said labour leaders are considering legal avenues to address the proposed changes but suggested those conversations are still in the early stages.

Unifor National president Lana Payne also accused the government of compromising workers’ right to strike in a media statement on Tuesday.

“At a time when we should be standing together as a country to fend off attacks from the Trump trade war, workers and their unions must now also defend the right to fair and free collective bargaining,” she said.

In an interview after the bill was tabled on Monday, Hajdu said the government is trying to make it harder to use Section 107 so that it becomes an “in-emergency-break-glass kind of tool.”

The minister said there’s no set timeline on when the federal government would move to end a strike or lockout under the new labour legislation.

“It is a high bar to establish a national interest,” Hajdu said. “What I would say is that each strike in each industry is different and so it’s very hard to answer that with a blanket answer.”

The federal government has leaned on Section 107 in recent years to end walkouts at Canada Post, the CN and CPKC railways, and at the B.C. and Montreal ports. Air Canada flight attendants defied an attempt to use the measure to end their strike in 2025.

Hajdu said strikes could still happen under the proposed legislation and acknowledged the point of a work stoppage is to inflict economic pressure in a labour dispute.

But she said that pressure can mount quickly when, for example, a work stoppage hits the transportation sector and puts perishable goods at risk. She said the government will be evaluating each strike individually.

A senior government official briefing reporters on Monday on Bill C-39 said the jobs minister would gain no additional powers through the legislation.

The Canadian Labour Congress and some legal experts disagree with that reading.

Brent Marks, a lawyer in the labour and employment division at Nelligan Law, said Tuesday that Bill C-39 would introduce language to the Canada Labour Code that implies “a new express power” is being given to the minister.

“One of the things the minister can direct the Canadian Industrial Relations Board to do is order the resumption of operations or services. So, in clearer words, end a strike,” he said.

The government may argue that it always had that power, Marks said.

But he said Ottawa has received a lot of pushback when it has attempted to use that section to end strikes in recent years, and this may be a way “to make that road easier for them.”

Bruske said the government already has an option available to it to end strikes in federally regulated sectors — tabling and passing back-to-work legislation in Parliament. That avenue would see debate and a recorded vote to show Canadians where their MPs stood on workers’ rights, she said.

“That is how these issues should be resolved, not by the stroke of the minister’s pen,” Bruske said.

Asked whether the government was trying to avoid the public scrutiny of back-to-work legislation, Hajdu said there may be situations where Section 107 is the only option available to a minister because Parliament isn’t sitting or can’t be easily recalled. The legislative route is also subject to parties playing politics, she said.

Other proposed changes to the labour code in the bill include the introduction of a special mediator to publish a report outlining both sides’ positions in an impasse. The minister must consider that report before using Section 107 to end a labour disruption.

Bruske said labour leaders can support many features of the proposed legislation. She welcomed additional resources for the Canada Industrial Relations Board and for workplace safety inspections, as well as efforts to crack down on wage theft and contract flipping.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 22, 2026.

Craig Lord, The Canadian Press

stories.title: New website helping shoppers buy Canadian
stories.summary: It's no secret Canadians have been trying to buy Canadian, given the rhetoric coming from our neighbours to the south. One website aims to help.
stories.author: Emma Crawford
stories.content:
It’s no secret Canadians have been trying to buy Canadian, given the rhetoric coming from our neighbours to the south.

So when Vancouver’s Tomáš Švec saw a need to help Canadians find Canadian, he got right to work.

That’s when he created trycanadian.ca , a website that tells you how Canadian a product is — or isn’t — and presents you with more Canadian alternatives.

“I saw there were only a few websites that covered this topic so I thought, I can do better,” Švec said.

“So I started working on it.”

He says that currently, there are 600 to 700 U.S. companies listed on the site, which he matches with Canadian counterparts. He is adding roughly 40 companies to the site every day, researching company ownership, founding and headquarters locations, and where products are made. The information is then presented in a simple format.

The site comes as many apps designed to help shoppers buy Canadian-made products face criticism. For example, some apps will consider a product based on where it is made, while others look at ownership, where ingredients come from, and where the money goes.

This can leave shoppers with a confusing range of options.

Švec says his site isn’t meant to tell you what to buy, but aims to lay out information and make choosing Canadian easier.

He shared the example of a specific product that claims to use 100 per cent Canadian mustard seeds, but if you look closely, the label tells a different story.

“You can type in the producer, and you can see it’s an American company, and you can see some Canadian alternatives.”

Švec says the site accepts donations, but he wants everyone to have access to the information it provides.

“The website is free and will stay free and be accessible to everyone,” he said.

stories.title: Fourth Marineland whale dies after relocation, third at Shedd Aquarium in Chicago
stories.summary: A fourth whale that was moved out of Marineland in July has died.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
A fourth whale that was moved out of Marineland in July has died after struggling with its health after arriving at her new home in Chicago, Shedd Aquarium said Monday.

The park said 26-year-old Osiris died Monday morning. The female beluga was one of 10 that came to Shedd from Marineland, the shuttered tourist attraction in Niagara Falls, Ont.

It was part of the world’s biggest collective move of captive whales. Marineland had said it was running out of money and could no longer care for its animals.

Over a series of moves beginning in July, Marineland moved 30 belugas and four dolphins to five aquariums abroad: Shedd in Chicago, SeaWorld locations in San Antonio and San Diego, Georgia Aquarium in Atlanta and Oceanografic Valencia in Spain.

Osiris was “not a consistent eater” but had improved recently after receiving fluids and medication, Shedd said.

The park will conduct a necropsy to try to better understand what happened.

Two other Marineland whales, Rain and Peekachu, died at Shedd within weeks of the move. One longtime Shedd resident beluga, Beethoven, also recently died.

All are being investigated, but the results have not yet returned, Shedd said.

Another Marineland beluga, Jelly Bean, died at Oceanografic last week.

The whales were cleared by veterinarians at Marineland and the other parks to move and Fisheries Minister Joanne Thompson also signed off on the relocation.

Last week, Shedd said it is concerned about the health of another recently moved whale, Secord.

Marineland originally sought to move the whales to China after securing a deal to sell all 30 of its belugas to Chimelong Ocean Kingdom, which has a Guinness Book of World Record for the largest aquarium in the world.

Thompson blocked that move, saying it was not in the best interest of the whales and inconsistent with a 2019 federal law. That law banned whale and dolphin captivity, but grandfathered in Marineland’s whales. It also banned breeding, which forced Marineland to separate its whales by sex. And the law banned performances.

Marineland turned to an American-led consortium to house the world’s biggest pod of captive belugas, but they needed five aquariums to house them all.

There are no breeding or performing restrictions at belugas’ new homes.

Marineland’s whales had struggled in recent years. Nineteen belugas and one killer whale died at the park between 2019 and 2025.

The park blames some of those deaths on the new federal laws.

Sources have said Marineland, which is about a kilometre from Horseshoe Falls, has been sold on the condition that all animals are gone.

Several hundred deer remain .

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 21, 2026.

Liam Casey, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Big banks exploring Canadian dollar-based digital money with tokenized deposits
stories.summary: Toronto — Canada's big banks are exploring the development of Canadian dollar-based digital money, starting with a tokenized deposits initiative.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
TORONTO — Canada’s big banks are exploring the development of Canadian dollar-based digital money, starting with a tokenized deposits initiative.

Tokenized deposits are traditional bank deposits recorded on a decentralized database or distributed ledger, such as a blockchain. The plan seeks to deliver faster, more efficient and programmable payments to Canadian customers while preserving safety, stability and effective regulatory oversight.

It means Canadian dollars could be converted into tokens on blockchain for easier transfers, said Claire Célérier, Canada Research Chair in household finance at the University of Toronto’s Rotman School of Management.

“My understanding is that the six banks will share the same blockchain, and so it implies that transactions can be made instantaneously across wallets with tokens,” she said.

Bank of Montreal, CIBC, National Bank, Royal Bank, Scotiabank and TD Bank are taking a collaborative approach to the project.

The tokens would be issued by commercial banks and from a legal perspective, depositors can treat them the same as traditional bank deposits.

The banks say the first phase aims to move tokenized deposits between Canadian financial institutions.

“It’s really exploratory now. I think what they’re saying is that they’re willing to work together to develop the technology,” Célérier said.

She said the potential capabilities would be of particular benefit to large companies or institutional investors, allowing them to complete “more sophisticated transactions.”

“What I expect is that these tokenized dollars will be mostly used by large companies and so on who have accounts across these Canadian banks, and it will be used to move large amounts of money,” she said.

Cristian Bravo, professor and Canada Research Chair in banking and insurance analytics at Western University, said the potential change could allow large producers to settle accounts far faster than their typical 30-day window.

“If you have an instant settlement, you’re closing that gap and closing that inefficiency in the market. And the fact that you have the money when you fulfil the contract, that can help reduce dependency on working capital and mobilize that capital faster,” he said.

But Bravo said that due to the lack of historical examples, it is not clear how much of an effect the move could have on the bottom lines of companies or institutional investors that use it.

Bravo said it is also notable that digital money is not the same as cryptocurrency, but rather a “digital ledger to move deposits in a very quick, instant way.”

In September, the Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions released a statement on tokenized and other digitally represented assets. It said that the tokenized deposits were not legally different from traditional deposits.

“The underlying technology of a financial product or service does not determine its legal nature. To be clear, we focus on what the product or service is, not how it is built or delivered,” the statement reads.

The Bank of Canada said on its website in June that it, along with other central banks, was studying tokenized systems to assess use cases.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 22, 2026.

stories.title: Traffic, transit and affordability top issues in London's Ward 8 election race
stories.summary: Traffic, transit and affordability top issues in London's Ward 8 election race CBC
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: Incumbent Coun. Steve Lehman is facing challengers Coralia Tudor and Osam Ali in the race to represent Ward 8.
· Posted: Sep 22, 2026 5:00 AM EDT | Last Updated: 31 minutes ago
Incumbent Coun. Steve Lehman, Coralia Tudor, and Osam Ali are running to represent London's Ward 8 in the upcoming municipal elections.((left to right) Steve Lehman/Coralia Tudor/Osam Ali)
Traffic, transit and the rising cost of living are among the issues shaping the race for London's Ward 8, where three candidates are vying for a seat on city council.
Incumbent Coun. Steve Lehman is seeking a third term, while Coralia Tudor and Osam Ali are challenging him in the Oct. 26 municipal election.

The candidates say residents have raised broader city issues, including property taxes, affordability, homelessness and addiction, while also pointing to concerns closer to home, from traffic and transit to residential development and road safety.
Here's what the candidates say they would focus on if elected.
Incumbent Coun. Steve Lehman is hoping to secure a third term representing Ward 8. (Steve Lehman)
Lehman was first elected to Council in 2018, and won a second term in 2022.
He said he's seeking another term because there is "still work to be done for Ward 8 and the city" and he is eager to continue it.
For Lehman, traffic is one of the most pressing issues facing the rapidly growing west end.
"We've seen a bottleneck in the north-south," he said. "We've seen Wonderland come to almost a standstill every day from Spring Bank up to Sarnia Road, and that's pushed traffic over to Hyde Park."
Lehman said he worked to have the widening of Wonderland Road included again in the city's Master Mobility Plan. He wants to continue pushing for the project if he is re-elected.

He has also been in contact with Ontario's Transportation Minister Rob Flack over bringing an extension of Highway 402 up to the north end of the city, to help people get down to the 401 without clogging inner-city roads.
"We have an opportunity right now on the west side of London before it is all developed," he said.
"Now is the time to act, and I'm not thinking about the next five years, I'm thinking about the next 20 years for London."
Coralia Tudor is running to represent Ward 8 in west London. (Submitted by Coralia Tudor)
Tudor is a former educator and paralegal who said she now works in philanthropy and volunteers with a number of community organizations.
She said she decided to run because she believes the city could be doing better on a number of issues.
"I'm seeing a lot of things that I don't like happening in our city, things that I think we could be doing better and I want to make that change," she said.
Transit is one of the issues she said she hears about most from Ward 8 residents.
Tudor said some routes don't work well for people trying to travel within the west end or get to Western University.
"The number one joke I get from residents is 'well, I suppose transit is so bad everyone's just had to buy their kids a car,'" she said. "But that's not a good answer, right?"
Tudor said she would redesign routes around where people actually need to travel. She also wants to see more bus stops designed so buses can pull out of traffic while passengers board and exit.
She said that could improve both transit service and traffic flow.
Residential infill is also an issue Tudor wants to address, she said, adding that residents are concerned about high-density developments.
"It's not that people are opposed to apartments per se, but heights are being changed, volumes are being exceeded for what the capacity is able to hold on those streets," she said.
Osam ALi is running to represent Ward 8 in west London. (Submitted by Osam Ali)

A 20-year resident of London, Ali has lived in Ward 8 for five years. With a PhD in software engineering, he has worked for London Health Sciences Centre for 18 years, and teaches at Fanshawe College.
Ali previously ran in the 2018 election for Ward 8, capturing around six per cent of the vote.
One of the big concerns he hears from voters is that City Hall is not responsive enough. He said it can take weeks for people to get a response to emails.

He also wants to see more support for small businesses in the area. There is a Business Improvement Area (BIA) for Hyde Park, but that only extends about one block into Ward 8, with the majority of the BIA situated in neighbouring Ward 7.
Ali also has concerns about road safety in the area, pointing to a lack of sidewalks in the Hunt Club neighbourhood, and to Hyde Park Road, where he said accidents have become frequent.
"When I talk to the residents over there, they complain that the city is not doing a good job," he said. "For example, with speeding on Hyde Park, or the same area getting hit three times with cars."
Londoners will head to the polls to elect a mayor and council on Oct. 26.

stories.title: Police find 2 bodies in burnt-out vehicles on opposite ends of Toronto
stories.summary: Toronto police are investigating after emergency crews found two bodies in two burnt-out vehicles on opposite ends of the city within hours of each other.
stories.author: Aaron D'Andrea
stories.content:
Toronto police are investigating after emergency crews found two bodies in two burnt-out vehicles on opposite ends of the city.

Police told Global News it received calls for both incidents within hours of each other late Monday night and early Tuesday morning.

The first incident was reported to police around 11:24 p.m. Officers were called to a hydro field on Reesor Road, near Steeles Avenue East.

It was reported that there was a vehicle on fire. When crews arrived on scene, they found a body inside the vehicle.

At 12:55 a.m., police were called to James Garden Park in Etobicoke for another vehicle on fire. Police said smoke was seen coming from the park, and there were reports of what sounded like an explosion.

After crews arrived, a body was found inside the car.

Police said it’s too early to determine if both incidents are related. The causes of death for both individuals is unknown.

The homicide squad has been notified, and the Office of the Fire Marshal is looking into the cause of the fires.

An investigation is ongoing.

Anyone with information is asked to call police.

stories.title: Ottawa approves FortisBC’s Tilbury LNG expansion
stories.summary: Saying potential adverse effects justified by project’s benefits
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The federal government has approved expansion of the Tilbury LNG facility in Delta, B.C., saying potential adverse effects are justified by the project’s benefits.

Monday’s approval under the “one project, one review” principle came immediately after the B.C. government issued an environmental assessment certificate to FortisBC for the project on Tilbury Island in the Fraser River.

The province says the project could generate 6,200 full-time-equivalent years of employment during construction and 100 permanent jobs, and contribute up to $1.7-billion to provincial GDP during construction.

Federal Environment Minister Julie Dabrusin says in a statement the project shows how to “create jobs and grow the economy while protecting the environment and advancing reconciliation.”

The project involves adding a large new storage tank and equipment to produce up to 7,700 tonnes of liquefied natural gas per day.

But it has faced opposition from within the B.C. government, with Kelly Greene, minister of emergency management and climate readiness, saying in July she was “disappointed” by FortisBC’s decision to move forward with the project, citing safety concerns.

“For months, I have listened to safety concerns from people in my community. I raised those issues with government at every opportunity. I am disappointed with FortisBC’s decision, as I know many of those I represent will be,” she said at the time.

Greene said her opposition had remained unchanged since before she was elected to the legislature, while NDP Premier David Eby said his government has a “big tent,” which allowed Greene to criticize the plan.

Federal Energy Minister Tim Hodgson called the approval “a step forward in our mission to get major nation-building projects built faster.”

“Today’s approval of the Tilbury Phase 2 LNG expansion project will power BC Ferries with cleaner fuel, strengthen Canada’s energy security and create economic opportunities for British Columbians,” he said on social media on Monday.

The B.C. government had touted the expansion as helping meet rising demand for LNG at the Port of Vancouver and improving access to fuel for vessels that travel the coast and across the Pacific.

The province said in a statement on Monday that the environmental assessment certificate included “18 legally binding conditions related to air quality, wildlife protection, greenhouse-gas reduction, health and emergency planning, and ongoing monitoring of impacts to First Nations.”

It said the Environmental Assessment Office sought consensus with 12 Indigenous nations, while 13 other Indigenous groups were informed of key milestones.

The assessment process was initiated in February 2020, but the province said it was delayed by the COVID-19 pandemic, and FortisBC submitted a revised application in February 2026.

Monday’s approval under the “one project, one review” principle came immediately after the B.C. government issued an environmental assessment certificate to FortisBC for the project on Tilbury Island in the Fraser River.

The province says the project could generate 6,200 full-time-equivalent years of employment during construction and 100 permanent jobs, and contribute up to $1.7-billion to provincial GDP during construction.
Federal Environment Minister Julie Dabrusin says in a statement the project shows how to “create jobs and grow the economy while protecting the environment and advancing reconciliation.”
The project involves adding a large new storage tank and equipment to produce up to 7,700 tonnes of liquefied natural gas per day.

But it has faced opposition from within the B.C. government, with Kelly Greene, minister of emergency management and climate readiness, saying in July she was “disappointed” by FortisBC’s decision to move forward with the project, citing safety concerns.

“For months, I have listened to safety concerns from people in my community. I raised those issues with government at every opportunity. I am disappointed with FortisBC’s decision, as I know many of those I represent will be,” she said at the time.

Greene said her opposition had remained unchanged since before she was elected to the legislature, while NDP Premier David Eby said his government has a “big tent,” which allowed Greene to criticize the plan.
Federal Energy Minister Tim Hodgson called the approval “a step forward in our mission to get major nation-building projects built faster.”

“Today’s approval of the Tilbury Phase 2 LNG expansion project will power BC Ferries with cleaner fuel, strengthen Canada’s energy security and create economic opportunities for British Columbians,” he said on social media on Monday.
The B.C. government had touted the expansion as helping meet rising demand for LNG at the Port of Vancouver and improving access to fuel for vessels that travel the coast and across the Pacific.

The province said in a statement on Monday that the environmental assessment certificate included “18 legally binding conditions related to air quality, wildlife protection, greenhouse-gas reduction, health and emergency planning, and ongoing monitoring of impacts to First Nations.”
It said the Environmental Assessment Office sought consensus with 12 Indigenous nations, while 13 other Indigenous groups were informed of key milestones.
The assessment process was initiated in February 2020, but the province said it was delayed by the COVID-19 pandemic, and FortisBC submitted a revised application in February 2026.

stories.title: Trump to speak at UN General Assembly amid trade war and tariff threats
stories.summary: U.S. President Donald Trump is set to address the 81st Session of the United Nations General Assembly on Tuesday.
stories.author: Kelly Geraldine Malone
stories.content:
U.S. President Donald Trump returned to the U.N. General Assembly on Tuesday at a tumultuous moment for the world — and for his presidency — and made the case that he’s shown fortitude while other leaders have equivocated.

The president started his address ticking off progress — including adding private sector jobs, stemming illegal migration and curbing crime before turning to a fulsome defence of his decision to start a war with Iran.

Trump accused Iran of stalling to make a deal to fully reopen the Strait of Hormuz and negotiate an endgame to the war until after the midterm elections in the United States.

“I gave absolutely no credence and will not give credence to the election when it comes to Iran,” Trump said. “It doesn’t even enter my mind.”

Iran’s delegation walked out as Trump railed against the Islamic Republic.

The global economy has been shaken by his decision to launch a war in the Middle East. Anxiety about the social impact being wrought by artificial intelligence is surging. And questions linger about the future of the United Nations itself with Trump’s scaling back U.S. financial support for the United Nations.

2:12 Trump says he wants potash from Belarus for “substantially less” than Canada

As he arrived at the U.N., Trump briefly spoke to reporters, telling them it was an honor to address the world body before his attention suddenly shifted to his resentments with the news media.

Trump over the weekend announced a White House ban on CNN, MS NOW and Politico, claiming that their coverage of his presidency was biased. The news outlets have filed a lawsuit to restore their access to White House grounds. Trump snapped at a CNN reporter in the U.N. scrum.

“I’m surprised that CNN is here covering me,” Trump said. “You shouldn’t be here.”

After his speech to the annual gathering of world leaders, Trump is expected to hold talks with new British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, and a more informal meeting with Venezuela’s acting President Delcy Rodríguez, according to the White House.

He’s also set to meet with leaders and senior officials from Gulf Cooperation Council nations — Bahrain, Kuwait, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and United Arab Emirates — to discuss the way ahead with the war in Iran and growing concern about recent Iran-backed rebel attacks on Saudi Arabia. Trump also plans to take part in an event on the Shield of Americas, an initiative Trump launched with Latin American countries earlier this year focused on combatting violent cartels.

6:10 Trump’s threat to annihilate Iran takes centre stage at UN General Assembly

The visit to the U.N. comes when Trump’s foreign policy approach — particularly his decision to start a war with Iran — has become a drag on his fellow Republicans’ hopes of retaining control of both chambers of Congress during the coming midterm elections. Nevertheless, Trump is making the case in his address that the world is better off for his leadership.

“As president of the most extraordinary nation in history,” Trump said. “I have no interest in leaving dangers to grow for another day. I do not believe in letting problems fester.”

1:54 Canada facing growing diesel crisis amid trade tensions with U.S.

In last year’s address at the U.N., Trump claimed the U.S. had “demolished” Iran’s nuclear capabilities after he ordered the June 2025 bombardment of three key facilities.

He returned to the General Assembly nearing the seven-month mark of a new war against Iran that he insists is necessary to address a nuclear threat posed by Iran.

The war has grown more complicated even though strikes by the United States and Israel have killed much of Iran’s top leadership and destroyed its air force and navy, while a U.S. blockade of Iranian oil has left Tehran in economic shambles.

The energy market continues to be spooked by the war and oil prices remain elevated. Saudi Arabia earlier this month shuttered a key pipeline that acted as a relief valve for oil blocked in the Gulf. The kingdom made the move after the pipeline came under attack by Iran-backed militants in Iraq.

At the same time, territorial grabs by the Yemen-based Houthi rebels, another Iranian-backed group, near the Bab al-Mandab Strait has now made it treacherous for oil carriers to use that Red Sea shipping lane.

Majed al-Ansari, chief spokesman for the Qatari Foreign Ministry, said Monday that Qatar and other mediators are trying to penetrate a “deep deficit of trust” between the U.S. and Iran and get the sides back to negotiations.

“Either we sign a deal now or sign a deal 10 months away,” said said al-Ansari, speaking at the Concordia Annual Summit, a global affairs forum taking place during the U.N.’s high-level week. “The only difference is the number of dead and destruction that we see.”

Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Tuesday that Trump is open to meeting with Iran’s president, Masoud Pezeshkian, while he’s in New York for the General Assembly.

“This is a president that will meet with anybody for the most part, because he believes that engaging with people is important if you’re going to solve problems,” Rubio said on NBC’s “Today” show. “It doesn’t mean you’re going to end up agreeing with them, but it’s important.”

The administration will sign a Greenland deal

At last year’s General Assembly, Trump touted his record as a peacemaker and claimed that “everyone says that I should get the Nobel Peace Prize” for his administration’s efforts mediating several conflicts around the globe.

This year, Trump is set to sign an agreement on the sidelines of the General Assembly with Danish and Greenlandic leaders that aims to set the pathway for the expansion of the U.S. military’s footprint on Greenland.

The deal, announced last week, came together after Trump repeatedly threatened to “take over” Greenland, a territory of NATO-ally Denmark, by military force if necessary.

Under the deal, Greenland remains Denmark’s territory.

0:33 Canada will address Arctic sovereignty at UNGA after U.S.-Denmark deal on Greenland security: Anand

Trump's frustration with Russia-Ukraine war mounts

The president could also touch on Russia’s continuing war against Ukraine during the address — a conflict that during his 2024 campaign he predicted would be resolved on Day One of his second term.

The president has routinely expressed frustration about the conflict. He hasn’t obscured that his patience is being tested by Ukraine’s targeting of Russia’s diesel refineries — an issue that’s added to oil markets’ volatility — and Russia’s targeting of Ukraine’s energy grid.

Trump last week asserted that he got the two sides to agree to not target each other’s energy infrastructure. Zelenskyy, who is scheduled to meet with Trump on Tuesday afternoon, said he was willing to go along with Trump’s plan if Russia abided by it. Russia said it could only go along with Trump’s energy truce proposal if Western energy sanctions on Moscow were lifted first.

The two sides have continued carrying out strikes on refineries and other energy infrastructure.

stories.title: Police allege sword used in London attack
stories.summary: A man has been charged in connection with an assault with a weapon investigation.
stories.author: Kate Otterbein
stories.content:
A man has been charged in connection with an assault with a weapon investigation.

On Saturday around 3:45 a.m., officers said a man was asleep in a structure in a wooded area near Clarke Road and Oxford Street, when a suspect woke him up. The suspect allegedly hit the man with a sword, causing serious but non-life-threatening injuries.

The victim ran and called 911.

A police drone was launched to help find the suspect. They were arrested without incident. The LPS confirmed both the victim and suspect were known to each other.

A 36-year-old man from London has been charged with assault with a weapon and assault causing bodily harm.

stories.title: Cat dies in St. Thomas house fire, investigators looking into cause
stories.summary: A house fire that broke out early Monday morning on First Avenue in St. Thomas, claimed the life of a cat and prompted a temporary road closure as emergency crews worked to contain the blaze.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
A house fire that broke out early Monday morning on First Avenue in St. Thomas, claimed the life of a cat and prompted a temporary road closure as emergency crews worked to contain the blaze.

Firefighters were called to the home at about 6 a.m. after one of the tenants dialed 911 to report the fire. A second tenant, who was not home when the fire started, later returned to assist.

When crews arrived, smoke was visible from the rear of the house. Firefighters were able to contain the fire to the basement, preventing it from spreading to the rest of the residence.

As crews battled the blaze, First Avenue was closed between Chestnut and Locust streets for safety reasons.

A cat inside the home died as a result of the fire. No injuries to residents or firefighters were reported.

The cause of the fire remains under investigation. Fire investigators and police remained on scene Monday as they worked to determine how the blaze started.

No damage estimate was immediately available.

With files from CTV News London’s Sean Irvine

stories.title: New B.C. Conservative leader Doerkson to appear with caucus amid election speculation
stories.summary: The new interim leader of the British Columbia Conservatives will face reporters Tuesday as he works to reconstruct the Opposition caucus after weeks of upheaval.
stories.author: Wolfgang Depner
stories.content:
The new interim leader of the British Columbia Conservatives will face reporters Tuesday as he works to reconstruct the Opposition caucus after weeks of upheaval ahead of a potential early election.

Lorne Doerkson, who was appointed after Sunday’s resignation of Kerry-Lynne Findlay, is scheduled to appear in Richmond, B.C., with members of his caucus.

The party’s parliamentary group grew to 29 members on Monday after the return of five MLAs, who either quit in recent weeks or were kicked out of caucus by Findlay in the dying days of her leadership.

The Conservatives have been trying to put up a united front after the recent turmoil, amid anticipation of a snap election.

The government has been making a series of campaign-style pledges, while the NDP caucus met on Sunday night to discuss election plans and Findlay’s exit.

Premier David Eby last week said his caucus needed to be “election ready,” while pledging to temporarily pause the expansion of the provincial sales tax and order that BC Ferries’ next round of vessels be built in British Columbia.

Infrastructure Minister Bowinn Ma on Monday announced that government had renewed plans for the expansion of Burnaby Hospital.

Agriculture Minister Lana Popham, meanwhile, said she would not be running for a sixth term after 17 years in elected office.

stories.title: Rise of the robots: How Aces Robotics sells gently used machines
stories.summary: A six-month backlog for some new machines and a dearth of skilled labourers has given robot resurrector Aces Robotics a boost
stories.author: Dawn Calleja, Photography by Sandy Nicholson
stories.content:
Ed Summers is a robot man. The owner of Aces Robotics in Toronto presides over a 64,000-square-foot showroom stocked with 300-odd used machines, most of them made by Japanese manufacturers Fanuc and Motoman.

A couple of factors are giving his nine-year-old business a boost: a six-month backlog for some new machines, (due in part to a chip shortage) and a dearth of skilled labourers like welders.

“A robot would be like having two or three welders, so if you purchased a robot for 50 grand” – versus upward of $150,000 new – “the return on investment would be paid within a year, and you’d have that labour savings for the next 10 years,” he says. And Aces can have one delivered within 30 days.

Some of the company’s stock has been saved from the literal scrap-heap. One auto maker, he says, “just goes in with a machine and pulls them right out of the concrete and puts them into the trash bin.”

Others come from manufacturers like Magna, which buys thousands of new machines each year, meaning they’re always getting rid of others. “Magna pricing is the best pricing – nobody buys robots cheaper than Magna,” he says.

Aces has six employees, including a pair of robotics technicians, and one who cleans, paints and restores each machine. Their shipping guy has sent eight robots to the U.S. so far this year, though tariffs have put a damper on that business. Eventually, Summers plans to open an outpost stateside.

“U.S. companies are a lot better to deal with – you tell them it’s 20 grand, and they say no problem and send the money,” he says, “whereas Canadian companies are a pain to deal with.”

Summers has a network of scouts who earn a finder’s fee for each robot. The older the machine, the better: “They’re using cheaper parts nowadays, with plastic gears, so they don’t have the same lifespan as ones that are 15, 20 years old,” he says. “A lot of robots from the ’80s are still working today.”

So if you come across any out-of-work robots, you know who to call.

stories.title: Ex-Quebec doctor convicted of killing his children to have parole board hearing
stories.summary: A Quebec man found guilty of second-degree murder in the stabbing deaths of his two children is expected to appear Tuesday before the Parole Board of Canada.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
A Quebec man found guilty of second-degree murder in the stabbing deaths of his two children is expected to appear Tuesday before the Parole Board of Canada.

Guy Turcotte is expected to make a request for temporary escorted absences from prison.

The former cardiologist was found guilty in December 2015 after stabbing his five-year-old son Olivier and his three-year-old daughter Anne-Sophie dozens of times in 2009.

The now 54-year-old was sentenced to life in prison with no possibility of parole for 17 years.

Turcotte was originally found not criminally responsible of the murders in 2011, but that verdict was overturned on appeal.

A spokesperson for the Parole Board of Canada says decisions on escorted temporary absence requests are not published, but May be delivered orally at the end of the hearing.

stories.title: This pharmacy technician had $425,000 to buy a condo in Scarborough, Ont. What did she buy?
stories.summary: Ms. Inciong was looking for an one-bedroom with some outdoor space, a gym or pool and accessible public transit
stories.author: Andrea Yu
stories.content:
In 2023, Patricia Inciong moved to Toronto from her hometown of Manila, Philippines, to complete a two-year pharmacy technician program at Centennial College. She rented a room in a shared apartment in Scarborough for $1,000. In her second year, Ms. Inciong rented a basement apartment with classmates and again paid $1,000 a month for her room.

While in her second rental, in 2024, Inciong, now 28, imagined buying a place for herself one day. “I was paying $1,000 every month,” she said. “I thought, is there a way for me to invest this towards myself instead?” She saved everything she could, hoping to purchase a home eventually. Ms. Inciong worked multiple part-time jobs as a pharmacy technician student at a hospital and a Shoppers Drug Mart location in Toronto’s east end, alongside her full-time schooling.

In April, 2025, after graduating, she landed a full-time job as a regulated pharmacy technician at the Shoppers location where she had worked part-time. Then, that September, she came across a realtor’s post on Instagram describing how the down payment for a condo around Toronto could be as low as $20,000.

The post piqued Ms. Inciong’s interest. She reached out to a real estate agent she knew, Jaleesa Bell, who told her that a condo purchase was possible with her budget. There were units in Scarborough selling for less than $400,000 at the time, which Ms. Inciong could just about afford. At the time, Ms. Bell was seeing an increase in first-time homebuyers entering the condo market. “I was noticing a lot more solo female buyers,” Ms. Bell said. “A lot of first-time homebuyers assume they can’t afford to buy, but there’s so much opportunity out there.”

Determined to get a Nova Scotia property near water, what did $150,000 get this buyer?

Ms. Inciong sought out a mortgage preapproval for $375,000. She also had some savings from working as a pharmacist back home in Manila, which pushed her top price up to $425,000. That included nearly $80,000 for a down payment – around 20 per cent of her total budget. She hoped to find a one-bedroom condo with a layout that would allow her to host family visiting from the Philippines. Ms. Inciong also wanted some outdoor space and a building with a gym or pool. She also needed to be close to public transit for her commute to work in Toronto’s east end, and she preferred to stay in Scarborough since she knew the area well and had friends nearby.

Here were her top three options:

While Ms. Inciong wasn’t initially considering a stacked townhouse, this one-bedroom unit caught her eye. “It was in the middle of everything,” she said. “There was a grocery store nearby, and it was very accessible to public transportation.” She’d only be a 30-minute transit ride from work. Ms. Inciong loved the modern-looking façade, but the lower-level unit had limited natural light. It was also small – just 512 square feet – and its layout didn’t leave much room for hosting overnight guests in the living area. The condo was priced at $374,900, but it had no shared amenities available, like a pool or gym. But the unit itself did have a decent patio space by its front entrance.

At 649 square feet, this was the largest unit Ms. Inciong viewed. While it had been recently renovated with marble countertops and stainless-steel appliances, the lobby of the building, which was completed in 1989, felt dated. There was, however, a shared gym and pool, and the unit itself had large windows that let in plenty of natural light, although there was no balcony. She also wasn’t sure where she would host overnight guests in the space. This condo would mean a longer commute to her workplace, around one hour by bus and subway. The unit was listed for $387,000.

While this unit was smaller than the previous one, at 598 square feet, it came with a den that had a window and a sliding door where visiting family members could stay overnight. As a ground-floor unit, she’d have a convenient outdoor patio, but wondered whether its location on a busy street would be noisy and prone to break-ins. She did like that the building was a mid-rise, with just 10 storeys, and that there were views of Scarborough Bluffs from the rooftop. There was also a shared gym in the building she could use, but there wasn’t a pool. Her commute to work from here would be 50 minutes by bus and subway. This unit was listed for $399,999.

As the only unit with a den, the midrise condo won out for having a separate place for hosting Ms. Inciong’s overnight guests. Ms. Bell, her realtor, suggested that they could get a lower price for the unit. After some back-and-forth negotiations, Ms. Inciong and the seller settled on a price of $389,000, about $11,000 off the listing price. She moved into her new home in October, 2025, just a few weeks after seeing the realtor’s Instagram post and starting her condo-buying journey.

In the summer of 2026, Ms. Inciong’s mom and aunt came from the Philippines to stay with her for an extended two-month visit. “I was really happy that I was able to house them instead of renting an Airbnb,” Ms. Inciong says. She’s made good use of her proximity to the lake with visits to the Scarborough Bluffs, although she’s more often enjoying the view of the water from her rooftop after a long day at work. There haven’t been any issues with noise or safety at her new place.

Above all, Ms. Inciong loves that she’s got a home to call her own. “It was so nice to finally have a place for myself,” she said. “My mornings are quiet, and at night I can just lie back and watch TV.” Ms. Inciong’s purchase has even inspired some of her fellow newcomer classmates and friends to explore the possibility of buying a condo. “I was so happy that I was able to accomplish this within a few years of moving here,” she said. “I’m happy that it all panned out.”

In April, 2025, after graduating, she landed a full-time job as a regulated pharmacy technician at the Shoppers location where she had worked part-time. Then, that September, she came across a realtor’s post on Instagram describing how the down payment for a condo around Toronto could be as low as $20,000.

The post piqued Ms. Inciong’s interest. She reached out to a real estate agent she knew, Jaleesa Bell, who told her that a condo purchase was possible with her budget. There were units in Scarborough selling for less than $400,000 at the time, which Ms. Inciong could just about afford. At the time, Ms. Bell was seeing an increase in first-time homebuyers entering the condo market. “I was noticing a lot more solo female buyers,” Ms. Bell said. “A lot of first-time homebuyers assume they can’t afford to buy, but there’s so much opportunity out there.”
Determined to get a Nova Scotia property near water, what did $150,000 get this buyer?

Ms. Inciong sought out a mortgage preapproval for $375,000. She also had some savings from working as a pharmacist back home in Manila, which pushed her top price up to $425,000. That included nearly $80,000 for a down payment – around 20 per cent of her total budget. She hoped to find a one-bedroom condo with a layout that would allow her to host family visiting from the Philippines. Ms. Inciong also wanted some outdoor space and a building with a gym or pool. She also needed to be close to public transit for her commute to work in Toronto’s east end, and she preferred to stay in Scarborough since she knew the area well and had friends nearby.
Here were her top three options:

While Ms. Inciong wasn’t initially considering a stacked townhouse, this one-bedroom unit caught her eye. “It was in the middle of everything,” she said. “There was a grocery store nearby, and it was very accessible to public transportation.” She’d only be a 30-minute transit ride from work. Ms. Inciong loved the modern-looking façade, but the lower-level unit had limited natural light. It was also small – just 512 square feet – and its layout didn’t leave much room for hosting overnight guests in the living area. The condo was priced at $374,900, but it had no shared amenities available, like a pool or gym. But the unit itself did have a decent patio space by its front entrance.

At 649 square feet, this was the largest unit Ms. Inciong viewed. While it had been recently renovated with marble countertops and stainless-steel appliances, the lobby of the building, which was completed in 1989, felt dated. There was, however, a shared gym and pool, and the unit itself had large windows that let in plenty of natural light, although there was no balcony. She also wasn’t sure where she would host overnight guests in the space. This condo would mean a longer commute to her workplace, around one hour by bus and subway. The unit was listed for $387,000.

While this unit was smaller than the previous one, at 598 square feet, it came with a den that had a window and a sliding door where visiting family members could stay overnight. As a ground-floor unit, she’d have a convenient outdoor patio, but wondered whether its location on a busy street would be noisy and prone to break-ins. She did like that the building was a mid-rise, with just 10 storeys, and that there were views of Scarborough Bluffs from the rooftop. There was also a shared gym in the building she could use, but there wasn’t a pool. Her commute to work from here would be 50 minutes by bus and subway. This unit was listed for $399,999.

As the only unit with a den, the midrise condo won out for having a separate place for hosting Ms. Inciong’s overnight guests. Ms. Bell, her realtor, suggested that they could get a lower price for the unit. After some back-and-forth negotiations, Ms. Inciong and the seller settled on a price of $389,000, about $11,000 off the listing price. She moved into her new home in October, 2025, just a few weeks after seeing the realtor’s Instagram post and starting her condo-buying journey.

In the summer of 2026, Ms. Inciong’s mom and aunt came from the Philippines to stay with her for an extended two-month visit. “I was really happy that I was able to house them instead of renting an Airbnb,” Ms. Inciong says. She’s made good use of her proximity to the lake with visits to the Scarborough Bluffs, although she’s more often enjoying the view of the water from her rooftop after a long day at work. There haven’t been any issues with noise or safety at her new place.

Above all, Ms. Inciong loves that she’s got a home to call her own. “It was so nice to finally have a place for myself,” she said. “My mornings are quiet, and at night I can just lie back and watch TV.” Ms. Inciong’s purchase has even inspired some of her fellow newcomer classmates and friends to explore the possibility of buying a condo. “I was so happy that I was able to accomplish this within a few years of moving here,” she said. “I’m happy that it all panned out.”

stories.title: Ottawa home’s high bedroom count factors into sale
stories.summary: Detached house has 1,969 square feet of living space, including separate living and dining areas
stories.author: Sydnia Yu
stories.content:
657 Dundonald Dr., Ottawa

Asking price: $738,888 (June, 2026)

Selling price: $728,888 (July, 2026)

Previous selling price: $356,771 (March, 2016)

Taxes: $5,507 (2025)

Days on the market: 28

Listing agent: Raymond Chin, Coldwell Banker First Ottawa Realty

This four-bedroom house was one of about a dozen properties listed for sale this June in a family-friendly subdivision near Highway 416, about 25 kilometres south of Parliament Hill. Agent Raymond Chin was concerned it might spend months on the market, as have many other local properties, but his fears subsided as a steady string of buyers turned up to tour the home.

“This year, things take a little bit longer to sell because of the amount of inventory and selection people have,” said Mr. Chin.

“There were quite a number of homes that went through price reductions, and we gave it a couple of weeks more before doing one because we did have decent traffic.”

About a week after Canada Day, the sellers of the 10-year-old home received an offer $10,000 below the asking price, which they accepted. Mr. Chin said it helped that the home was in excellent condition and that there were two additional bedrooms in the basement.

“It was staged, it was cleaned and small repairs were done to give it that turnkey look,” Mr. Chin said.

“The main selling feature, judging by what else was on the market at that time and didn’t sell, was the number of bedrooms we had.”

This detached house has 1,969 square feet of living space, including separate living and dining areas, and an eat-in kitchen with sliding doors to a south-facing patio on the 30-by-89-foot lot.

There are four bathrooms, including a four-piece ensuite in the primary bedroom, and a laundry room with a sink upstairs.

The main floor has interior entry to the garage. Two cars can park on the private driveway.

“It’s within a nice suburb,” Mr. Chin said. “It was steps to a park.”

stories.title: London man arrested for assault with a sword
stories.summary: A man was asleep inside a structure in wooded area near Clarke Road and Oxford Street early Saturday morning, police said. At around 3:45 a.m., the male suspect entered the structure, woke the man and struck him with a sword.
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: A man was asleep inside a structure in wooded area near Clarke Road and Oxford Street early Saturday morning, police said. At around 3:45 a.m., the male suspect entered the structure, woke the man and struck him with a sword.
· Posted: Sep 22, 2026 7:39 AM EDT | Last Updated: 1 hour ago
London police are investigating after a sword-wielding man struck another man in the city's east end early Saturday morning.

Police said a man was asleep inside a structure in a wooded area near Clarke Road and Oxford Street overnight. At around 3:45 a.m., the suspect entered the structure, woke the man and struck him with a sword.
The victim faced serious, but non-life-threatening injuries. He fled the scene and called 9-1-1. Police used a drone to help locate the suspect and officers arrested him.
A 36-year-old London man has been charged with assault with a weapon and assault causing bodily harm. He has been released from custody and is expected to reappear in court Oct. 28.
The victim and suspect were known to each other, police said.
Police are asking anyone with information about the incident to contact them at 519-661-5670 or Crime Stoppers at 1-800-222-8477.

stories.title: Huron Perth Children’s Aid Society gets $831,000 for roof repairs
stories.summary: The Huron Perth Children’s Aid Society is receiving $831,000 from the Ontario government for roof replacement and repairs.
stories.author: Koylan Azofeifa Rueda
stories.content:
The Huron Perth Children’s Aid Society is receiving $831,000 from the Ontario government for roof replacement and repairs.

The funding comes through the provincial government’s Partner Facility Renewal program, which is providing more than $25 million this year for critical infrastructure repairs at community service organizations.

“I appreciate the important work the Huron Perth Children’s Aid Society does every day to support children and families in our communities,” Perth-Wellington MPP Matthew Rae said in Monday’s announcement.

“This provincial investment will support the physical space they need to continue delivering that support and serving local families.”

Huron-Bruce MPP Lisa Thompson said the Huron-Perth Children’s Aid Society plays an important role across the community.

“This investment will help provide the organization with a safe, reliable and welcoming space to continue its important work,” Thompson said.

The provincial funding program also supports shelters, residences for people with developmental disabilities, facilities serving survivors of human trafficking and organizations supporting Indigenous communities, among others.

Children, Community and Social Services Minister Michael Parsa said community organizations play an important role in delivering services across Ontario.

“Through these investments, our government is supporting hundreds of agencies so they can continue providing children, youth and families with the tools and support they need,” Parsa said.

Kristian Wilson, executive director of the Huron Perth Children’s Aid Society, said the organization is grateful for the investment.

“We are deeply grateful for this investment in our building and in the children, youth, and families we serve. Spaces matter,” Wilson said.

The funding will help ensure the society’s facility remains a safe and welcoming place for members of the community accessing its services.

stories.title: Sunny skies, cool nights ahead for southern Ontario
stories.summary: Southern Ontario residents can expect a cool but sunny stretch of weather as high pressure settles over the region for the remainder of the week, according to meteorologist Julie Atchison.
stories.author: Koylan Azofeifa Rueda
stories.content:
Southern Ontario residents can expect a cool but sunny stretch of weather as high pressure settles over the region for the remainder of the week, according to meteorologist Julie Atchison.

Atchison said temperatures Tuesday afternoon have been on the cool side, with northeasterly winds and highs expected to range between 14 C and 17 C.

“There’s a low-pressure system to the south that’s still spinning up a bit of cloud cover toward parts of southern Ontario,” Atchison said. “But most of that high cloud cover is allowing sunshine to filter through as high pressure builds in from northern Ontario.”

She said the high-pressure system will take hold over the next several days, bringing plenty of sunshine to the region.

Temperatures are expected to cool significantly overnight, dropping into the single digits across much of southwestern Ontario. Areas including Mount Forest, Kitchener-Waterloo and London could see lows between 5 C and 8 C.

Atchison said the cooler nights May give residents a chance to turn off air conditioners and open their windows.

Daytime temperatures will gradually rebound through the week, reaching a high of 19 C on Wednesday and 21 C on Thursday under mainly sunny skies.

The sunny weather is expected to continue into Friday and through the weekend.

“The weekend is looking absolutely beautiful,” Atchison said, noting both Saturday and Sunday are expected to feature abundant sunshine as the region welcomes the arrival of fall.

The autumn season officially begins Tuesday evening at 8:05 p.m. EDT.

“The weekend is looking absolutely beautiful,” Atchison said, noting both Saturday and Sunday are expected to feature abundant sunshine as the region welcomes the arrival of fall.
The autumn season officially begins Tuesday evening at 8:05 p.m. EDT.

stories.title: Bateman the latest injury for Toronto as Blue Jays near elimination with loss in Baltimore
stories.summary: Blue Jays starting pitcher Trey Yesavage was limited to two innings in his first game back from knee inflammation.
stories.author: Lucas Casaletto
stories.content:
The defending American League champions are on the brink — and a little beat up as well.

Toronto’s last-ditch push for a playoff spot took another significant blow Monday night when the Blue Jays lost 4-3 to the Baltimore Orioles, who are also on the verge of elimination. Already dealing with health concerns for Dylan Cease and Vladimir Guerrero Jr., the Blue Jays lost rookie outfielder Brett Bateman when he hurt his hip making a sliding catch in the second inning.

“Jammed his right hip,” manager John Schneider said. “Kind of looked like his knee or his ankle, glad it wasn’t that. He got X-rays, which were negative, and just a little tender. … Take it day by day.”

The Blue Jays scored three quick runs in the first inning, but their offense went dormant after that, and they finally fell behind when Pete Alonso hit his second homer of the game, a two-run shot in the eighth.

Toronto is 3 1/2 games behind the Chicago White Sox for the final AL wild card. Baltimore is 4 1/2 games behind. Both the Blue Jays and Orioles can be eliminated as soon as Tuesday.

Bateman held onto the ball to retire Baltimore’s Rece Hinds in the second, but his slide left a divot in the ground — not a great sign — and he rolled over awkwardly after making the catch. Bateman was able to walk off the field, but very slowly, and he was replaced the next time Toronto was in the field.

Meanwhile, Guerrero was out of the lineup because of back trouble. Starting pitcher Trey Yesavage was limited to two innings in his first game back from knee inflammation. Cease is dealing with shoulder issues and it’s not clear when or if he’ll make another start this season.

It’s felt for a while that it simply isn’t Toronto’s year.

“It’s baseball,” Schneider said. “Baseball will be baseball. You dwell on it a little bit, but you’ve got to continue to move forward and just keep going.”

Toronto acquired Bateman in the August trade that sent Kevin Gausman to the Chicago Cubs. Bateman has hit .320 in 38 games since making his big league debut for the Blue Jays on Aug. 7.

Yesavage, who was so impressive during last year’s postseason run, was back on the mound for the first time since Aug. 4. The Blue Jays wanted to limit his pitch count, and he threw 40.

“I felt really good,” Yesavage said. “I felt like I could have gone more, but it’s smart to progressively go more and more.”

stories.title: Family of killed Toronto officer calls for Ottawa to make major changes to the parole system
stories.summary: Victims' families are calling for parole reforms, urging changes to Canada's justice system.
stories.author: Adrian Ghobrial
stories.content:
Toronto - “We’re talking about a guy who walked over, put the gun to my brother’s head, and pulled the goddamn trigger,” said Cory Baylis, as he gestures to his own head, his hand mimicking the gun that killed his brother.

It was June 1994. Baylis was in Florida when he learned that his big brother, Toronto Police Constable Todd Baylis had been shot and killed on the job. Todd was just 25 years old at the time and had been chasing after a suspected drug dealer who pulled out a gun and opened fire, shooting him in the head.

Clinton Gayle was found guilty of first-degree murder and attempted murder for shooting Baylis’ partner who survived. Gayle was sentenced to life in prison with no chance at parole for 25 years.

The Baylis family now must appear at a parole hearing every two years. They’ve already had to attend four separate parole reviews.

Speaking to CTV News from his home in Brampton, Ont., Baylis shared his mounting frustration after having to attend yet another hearing this past July, reliving the trauma of losing his brother.

“2019, 2021, 2024, 2026. We’ll have to go back in 2027 or 2028, it’s ridiculous,” said Baylis.

Gayle and others facing life sentences can request a parole hearing every two years, once the initial 25 years of their sentence has been served.

CTV News has obtained a copy of a letter written by the Toronto Police Association, requesting that the federal government increase the time between parole hearings from “five to seven years” and allow judges the power to impose “parole ineligibility periods for up to 35 years” for those convicted of first-degree murder.

This coming January, serial rapist and killer Paul Bernardo will have his fourth parole hearing.

“It’s just pure entertainment for him. He has no remorse,” said trial lawyer Tim Danson.

Danson represents the families of victims Leslie Mahaffy and Kristen French, who were both murdered by Bernardo. He attends each parole hearing pro bono, to support the Mahaffy and French families.

He still sees a “sadistic, sexual psychopath” in Paul Bernado.

“When he’s asked during a parole review why he would carry out these horrific attacks on these teenage girls he answers by saying ‘well, they weren’t doing what I told them,’” Danson said.

“He answers these questions like you and I would talk about the weather.”

Danson says the French, Mahaffy and Baylis families are all asking for parole reform, and they believe that Canada’s worst convicted killers shouldn’t be allowed to traumatize a family every two years.

Our justice system shouldn’t be one size fits all, we’re not talking about someone “stealing candy from a candy store” said Baylis.

“It’s horrific what the justice system does to victims’ families. They drag us through this process, and I find myself asking why. Well, I’ll tell you, it’s because a killer’s rights are more important that mine, my dead brother’s, yours, or anybody else’s.”

The Toronto Police Association’s letter, sent to multiple members of parliament, says in part that the federal government “committed to us earlier this year that this issue would be addressed in the fall. We are now two weeks into September, and with the latest news about Paul Bernardo, the issue could not be more urgent.”

The Department of Justice has not responded to a request for comment.

stories.title: The dangerous wait for battery regulations
stories.summary: Many lithium-ion battery fires could be avoided with proper regulation
stories.author: The Editorial Board
stories.content:
In a 72 hour-period last month, Toronto Fire Services rushed to put out five different fires caused by lithium-ion batteries. One spread from a garage into a home, and another occurred in a garbage truck. Another fire, inside a Toronto Community Housing building, resulted in three people going to the hospital.

Cities across the country are seeing a steep rise in fires caused by rechargeable lithium-ion batteries. At the start of September, Toronto alone had already seen 92 already this year, resulting in 13 injuries and one death. The problems are often the result of regulatory gaps, and many of these fires could be avoided with proper regulation and enforcement.

Lithium-ion batteries are used in electric vehicles and in many consumer devices, but most of the fires are caused by batteries for electric bikes and scooters. Fire chiefs warn these blazes can be more intense , and they produce more hazardous smoke, resulting in greater risk for firefighters and the public.

Fires can start when batteries are overcharged or when incompatible chargers are used. Batteries that are left in the sun , damaged or modified are also dangerous. Cheap batteries available online are often poorly designed and manufactured, and are more likely to cause fires. Fires can also occur when batteries aren’t disposed of at city drop-offs, and are instead thrown into garbage or recycling bins.

Currently, there are no specific regulations regarding lithium-ion batteries in Canada. Mayors and fire chiefs have been asking the federal and provincial governments to regulate them and enforce basic safety standards.

Health Canada is currently looking to introduce mandatory requirements for lithium-ion batteries and consumer products containing them under the Canada Consumer Product Safety Act. This could involve creating rules that would require all batteries that are imported, manufactured or sold meet third-party quality certifications. For example, organizations such as UL Solutions test the quality of lithium-ion batteries to ensure they are safe. Health Canada closed its consultation on the issue in February and the feedback is being analyzed.

Federal regulations would be a step in the right direction, but unfortunately, batteries used in e-bikes and e-scooters are excluded from the initiative. Health Canada says they are considered vehicles under the Motor Vehicle Safety Act, and so they fall under different regulations. The department says it is working closely with Transport Canada, and the initiative could have a future impact on motor vehicle regulations.

The situation is frustrating to alternative transportation advocates, such as Michael Longfield of Cycle Toronto. The initiative should be sped up and expanded so that the batteries that pose the greatest risk can be immediately included.

Opinion: What should be done about the scourge of e-scooters?

Better regulation at the provincial level can also help. Ontario is currently looking to modernize its e-bike rules, and the proposed changes would make it easier to draw a line between e-bikes mostly relying on pedal power, and faster and more powerful moped and motorcycle-style electric vehicles.

Under Ontario’s proposed rules, the more powerful electric vehicles would need to be registered, and their drivers would require a motorcycle licence and insurance. The vehicles would also need to meet federal motor vehicle safety standards, and riders who don’t follow the rules could lose their licenses. The provinces should go farther and spell out safety requirements for batteries for all e-bikes and e-scooters.

More public education would also help. Individual cities and fire departments are trying to spread the word about the batteries’ dangers, but a bigger, coordinated campaign should be implemented once national standards are in place.

Firefighters are also asking for the federal government to establish a national safety initiative around lithium-ion battery fires, something they called for at the Canadian conference of the International Association of Fire Fighters earlier this year. It would make sense to have a national body track incidents, research the impact on firefighter health and standardize training.

Government lapses are creating a dangerous situation, and the growing popularity of e-bikes and e-scooters will only make the problems worse. Policymakers need to move quickly to close the regulatory gaps before further tragedies take place.

stories.title: Over 288 bottles of alcohol seized, illegal distillery shut down in Sarnia
stories.summary: An illegal distillery has been shut down in Sarnia by police, operating under the name Triple Eh Brews.
stories.author: Lauren Kuivenhoven
stories.content:
An illegal distillery has been shut down in Sarnia by police, operating under the name Triple Eh Brews.

The business was run under a false Manufacturer’s Licence, selling their illegally manufactured alcohol at summer festivals, markets throughout Ontario and over online delivery services.

The Alcohol and Gaming Commission of Ontario notified police of the business in July 2025, and police conducted a search warrant on Sept. 18 at a Lanark Drive residence and Green Street commercial building.

Police seized a counterfeit Manufacturer’s Licence, 288 bottles of illegally manufactured alcohol, distillery equipment, point of sale machine and digital devices and printer.

The owner faces the following charges by police:

Uttering forged document (two counts)

Possession of a counterfeit mark

Keep for sale, offer for sale, or sell liquor, contrary to the Liquor License and Control Act, 2019

Unlawfully possessing liquor, contrary to the Liquor License and Control Act, 2019

Police say they continue to investigate and are seeking any additional information about the illegal operations.

The Agco CEO Dr. Karin Schnarr said they’ll continue to work closely with law enforcement, as the unlicensed production and sales of alcohol poses “significant risks to public safety.”

stories.title: Youngest Canadians more accepting of collective blame against religious, ethnic groups: poll
stories.summary: Most Canadians reject collective blame, while younger cohorts are more accepting of sweeping claims about religious and ethnic groups.
stories.author: Kenn Oliver
stories.content:
While most Canadians reject collective blame and sweeping claims about religious and ethnic groups, younger Canadians are substantially more likely to accept them, according to a new poll.

Data collected by the Association for Canadian Studies (ACS) found that more 57 per cent of Canadians find it unacceptable — not very or not at all — to suggest that a particular religion has harmful beliefs. The only outlier among the age groups was 18-24-year-olds, 56 per cent of whom felt it was somewhat or very acceptable to say that.

Nearly seven in ten respondents (69 per cent) think it’s either degree of unacceptable to say that members of a specific ethnic or religious group cannot be trusted. The youngest cohort was the only one with observable conflict, with 42 per cent of on the accepting side.

When it comes to holding members of a religious group collectively responsible for the actions of a foreign government, three quarters (75 per cent) deemed it unacceptable, but, again, nearly a third (32 per cent) under 25 were more accepting.

People in the 25-34 age group (30 per cent) and the 45-55 demographic (31 per cent) also registered above the overall net acceptable number (25 per cent).

“There needs to be some increasing thought and sensitivity about the extent to which people make those connections,” ACS president Jack Jedwab told National Post in an interview, noting that none of that should ever be acceptable “in democracies like ours.”

Without ascribing any symmetry to the subjects, the poll sought to understand which religious or ethnic groups Canadians feel should be apologizing for the one they are perceived to be affiliated with outside of Canada.

It found that 43 per cent of respondents are most likely to think that Muslims should be expected to publicly condemn terrorist acts carried out in the name of Islam. Meanwhile, 36 per cent suggested Russian Canadians should be expected to publicly condemn actions of the Russian government with which they disagree, and 32 per cent felt the same about Jewish Canadians and the Israeli government.

“I’m not comparing the acts of the Israeli government to the actions of terrorism in the name of Islam,” said Jedwab.

“But what is common about it is the accusation of responsibility for such actions, because I sometimes get the impression that some people feel that some of this is okay, but the other sort of expression of it isn’t.”

Acs’s data also showed that the people most likely to say that members of a specific ethnic or religious group are responsible for the actions of a foreign government are the ones who expected to publicly condemn acts “over which they have no individual control or responsibility.​”

A plurality of people who feel that’s very (73.2 per cent) or somewhat acceptable (54 per cent) who feel that way said Muslim Canadians should be expected to publicly condemn terrorist acts carried out in the name of Islam.

Asked if Jewish Canadians should be expected to publicly condemn actions of the Israeli government with which they disagree, the majority (52.7 per cent) from the very acceptable ranks agreed, as did 38.2% among those on the somewhat acceptable side.

“People who make that statement, who support those views, think that it’s okay for Muslim Canadians to publicly condemn terrorist acts carried out in the name of Islam — it’s not okay,” Jedwab said, noting the same holds for Jewish and Russian Canadians.

“These aren’t free expression issues. They’re a threat to free expression.”

The poll of 1,538 respondents, conducted by Leger on behalf of the Association for Canadian Studies, was conducted Sept. 4-6. A margin of error cannot be associated with a non-probability sample in a panel survey for comparison purposes. However, a probability sample of this size would have a margin of error of 2.5 per cent, 19 times out of 20.​

stories.title: Sunny skies, cool nights ahead for southern Ontario
stories.summary: Southern Ontario residents can expect a cool but sunny stretch of weather as high pressure settles over the region for the remainder of the week, according to meteorologist Julie Atchison.
stories.author: Koylan Azofeifa Rueda
stories.content:
Southern Ontario residents can expect a cool but sunny stretch of weather as high pressure settles over the region for the remainder of the week, according to meteorologist Julie Atchison.

Atchison said temperatures Tuesday afternoon have been on the cool side, with northeasterly winds and highs expected to range between 14 C and 17 C.

“There’s a low-pressure system to the south that’s still spinning up a bit of cloud cover toward parts of southern Ontario,” Atchison said. “But most of that high cloud cover is allowing sunshine to filter through as high pressure builds in from northern Ontario.”

She said the high-pressure system will take hold over the next several days, bringing plenty of sunshine to the region.

Temperatures are expected to cool significantly overnight, dropping into the single digits across much of southwestern Ontario. Areas including Mount Forest, Kitchener-Waterloo and London could see lows between 5 C and 8 C.

Atchison said the cooler nights May give residents a chance to turn off air conditioners and open their windows.

Daytime temperatures will gradually rebound through the week, reaching a high of 19 C on Wednesday and 21 C on Thursday under mainly sunny skies.

The sunny weather is expected to continue into Friday and through the weekend.

“The weekend is looking absolutely beautiful,” Atchison said, noting both Saturday and Sunday are expected to feature abundant sunshine as the region welcomes the arrival of fall.

The autumn season officially begins Tuesday evening at 8:05 p.m. EDT.
