stories.title: A snapshot of Canada’s climate vulnerabilities, from Grise Fiord to the place where you live
stories.summary: Ahead of a major climate-change conference, The Globe asked scientists to map out where Canada’s threats lie. First stop: Nunavut
stories.author: Ivan Semeniuk, Jenn Thornhill Verma
stories.content:
Canada’s northernmost community sits on a narrow shelf of land veined with streams that run down the slopes of Ellesmere Island into the waters of Jones Sound.

With a population of about 150, Grise Fiord depends on those streams for its drinking water, which it collects and stores in large silos. In late summer, when rainfall is sparse, the streams are fed by meltwater from the glacier above town.

The community’s Inuktitut name, Ausuittuq, means “the place that never thaws.” But now the glacier is retreating, taking a key component of the water supply with it.

“Glaciers everywhere have receded or disappeared. That one used to be so huge it would overhang along the edge,” says Larry Audlaluk, an elder who was a child when the Canadian government relocated his family in 1953 from northern Quebec to the hamlet, which is located 1,160 kilometres north of the Arctic Circle.

“Now you got to go somewhere high to look for it, or on the plane,” he says.

Unlike other Nunavut communities, Grise Fiord has no lake or other natural water source to fall back on when the streams run low. So, with support from Ottawa and the territorial government, the hamlet is building one. Construction is under way on a treatment plant and three storage tanks that will hold enough water to supply residents year round.

The work highlights an obvious fact: Climate change stopped being a hypothetical threat in Grise Fiord years ago. It is now a permanent reality – and Grise Fiord is hardly unique.

In a major new assessment released last month, federal scientists show how every part of Canada is already experiencing the effects of a warming climate, with Northern, coastal and Indigenous communities among the most vulnerable.

Grise Fiord is among the 13 case studies in the report of First Nations, Inuit or Métis communities that are on the front lines of climate change, already having to adapt.

“It just reinforces the fact that Canada is seeing, right now, the impacts of climate change in a very large way,” federal Environment Minister Julie Dabrusin told The Globe and Mail. And while the assessment focuses on the physical effects of climate change, rather than how to manage them, it underlines just how much work will be needed “to help communities to meet the challenges that we’re going to be facing,” she said.

Those challenge will be the focus this week of Adaptation Canada 2026 , a climate conference organized by Local Governments for Sustainability Canada . The organization includes more than 400 municipalities across the country and is part of a larger international network.

The gathering is an opportunity for participants representing government, science, industry and Indigenous groups to take stock of what lies ahead as the country continues to warm through this century – and how that will play out where it is most relevant to people: their local communities.

To that end, the newly issued federal report serves as both a warning and a guide. Much of it is related to shifts in the environment that are now considered inevitable.

In Grise Fiord, for example, glacier melt, permafrost thaw and sea level rise are certainties. These changes are unfolding already, slowly but surely, as a result of greenhouse gases emitted into the atmosphere.

The consequences, which include an eroding shoreline, will be felt for decades – or millennia, in the case of rising seas – and that won’t change even if temperatures are stabilized today.

Because of this, the town faces “multiple hazards converging at once,” said David Didier, an Arctic coastal scientist at the University of Quebec in Rimouski who has studied the situation at Grise Fiord.

Across Canada, communities can expect to be similarly challenged by a range of interacting effects all driven by a climate that is warmer than at any point on historical record.

To help address this, the federal report has a section on climate services whose purpose is “getting information in the hands of the people who need it, in a form that they can use,” said Chris Derksen, the report’s lead scientist who heads the government’s climate modelling research division.

Where the Meteorological Service of Canada issues forecasts and warnings, climate services handle the longer time scales, issuing climate data for a city planner or engineer. In addition to the national organization, the Canadian Centre for Climate Services , regional centres exist in British Columbia and Yukon , the Prairies , Ontario , Quebec and Atlantic Canada .

There is no such regional organization for the other Northern territories. Only one Arctic municipality, the hamlet of Ulukhaktok, received support from a countrywide $34.2-million climate-resilience fund announced last month. Other avenues exist for funding Northern infrastructure built for a changing climate – such as Grise Fiord’s new water plant – but Canada is still playing catch-up in the North as communities there try to prepare for what is coming.

None of this addresses the elephant in the room: While communities spend public resources to build resilience and manage the effects of climate change, it’s clear that Canada – along with the rest of the world – is not curbing greenhouse gas emissions to a level that will significantly reduce climate risks and their associated costs.

Ms. Dabrusin said the government remains committed to emissions reduction. Many of the conversations she was involved in at last week’s Canada Investment Summit in Toronto, she added, were about projects that would facilitate the switch to a low carbon future, including in the North. Still, she acknowledged the report paints a sobering portrait for decision-makers. “This sets a very stark piece about where we’re at and why we need to continue to take action.”

Because of Canada’s northern latitude and other factors, climate change is causing the country to warm faster than the planet as a whole. While Earth is now about 1.4 degrees C warmer than it was 150 years ago, Canada is already 2.2 degrees warmer.

Canada is on track for a warmer future, but how hot it gets depends on what emissions policies are put in place today

Climate Report 2026

what emissions policies are put in place today

As the latest federal report on climate change makes clear, if current emissions policies continue, climate models project Canada is on track to be five degrees warmer (and still rising) by the end of this century. If emissions are not controlled, that number increases to seven degrees warmer.

Alternatively, if the world achieves a net zero emissions scenario, the temperature will rise about only one degree more (because of the carbon already released) and then level off.

Whichever path Canada follows, all scenarios will bring new challenges to communities dealing with the effects of a warmer atmosphere and more extreme weather.

In the next 15 years, “it’s virtually certain that we’ll experience another degree of warming,” Dr. Derksen said.

Ahead of Adaptation Canada 2026, the national climate conference that opens on Sept. 21, The Globe and Mail asked climate scientists about the biggest environmental changes ahead and how certain they are about them.

The threats listed here are the most direct physical consequences of a warming atmosphere. These effects are not uniformly distributed, and their severity May vary depending on how rapidly the country warms, but all have been observed and are forcing communities to adapt.

The list is also not complete. Secondary effects – for example, the spread of insect-borne disease – are expected to worsen as temperatures rise.

“This is not a future problem,” Dr. Derksen said. “We’re living it now.”

Drought/water cycle

Changing Climate Report 2026

Prognosis: Hot extremes are more intense and frequent

Confidence level: High

Canada’s hottest day of the year is predicted to warm by 2.6 degrees in the near term, and 3.1 to 6.2 degrees by century’s end depending on emissions.

“We have high confidence that the frequency and intensity of hot extremes in Canada have increased since the mid-20th century, and that human influence on the climate is the dominant driver,” said Alex Cannon, one of the report’s authors. “With additional global warming, hot extremes will intensify in every region of Canada.”

They will also seem more frequent. At four degrees of global warming, a heat extreme that used to arrive once a decade happens 6.7 times as often, while a once-in-50-year extreme happens 16.2 times as often. Heat stress, which combines temperature and humidity and is closer to what people experience, is rising too.

Under current policies, winter in much of Nunavut has a better-than-even chance of warming more than 10 degrees above pre-industrial levels by century’s end.

Prognosis: Flash flooding becomes more frequent and intense

Confidence level: High for flash flooding, low for hurricanes reaching Eastern Canada

Heavier single-day and five-day downpours are projected for every region of Canada, along with the short-duration rainfall that overwhelms storm sewers – together driving more flash flooding. Atmospheric rivers – broad bands of airflow that carry vast quantities of water vapour – are expected to strengthen over the West Coast.

“Increases in the frequency and intensity of extreme rainfall will lead to more frequent and intense flash flooding,” report author Barrie Bonsal said. “These extremes will require adaptive measures and integrated water management approaches to ensure water security and resilience.”

River floods, however, show no consistent trend. North Atlantic storms have strengthened and carry more rain, but scientists have low confidence in how much has reached Eastern Canada, even after Hurricane Fiona in 2022. Compound effects are also likely on coastlines where sea level is already higher, with heavy rain arriving on top of storm surges.

Prognosis: Water arrives earlier, and there is less of it in summer

Confidence level: High

Snowmelt, spring freshet (from heavy rains and melted snow) and groundwater recharge have all shifted to earlier in the year. Streamflow has risen in winter and spring while falling in summer in some regions.

“These changes are projected to continue and will alter the expected timing of freshwater supplies, particularly in the many snowmelt-fed basins across Canada that rely on this water source during the summer season,” Dr. Bonsal said.

That’s a problem for basins that depend on stored snow and ice through the dry months and for Western watersheds where glaciers have already stopped contributing. Summer droughts are projected to grow longer, more frequent and more intense across central and southern Canada, though periodic drought has always occurred there and no long-term trend is detectable. Groundwater is expected to hold up better than surface water.

Prognosis: Fire seasons are longer and extreme fire weather is more frequent

Confidence level: High (medium for area burned)

Fire season has lengthened across most of the country and will continue with every increment of warming, though the observed trend in fire weather is clearest in Alberta and British Columbia.

“We have high confidence that, under more global warming, Canada will see further increases in the length of the fire season, the occurrence of extreme fire weather conditions and the total area burned,” said report author Megan Kirchmeier-Young.

The report assigns medium confidence to annual area burned having increased since the early 1980s. That’s because fire varies so much year to year that even an intense season such as 2023 cannot lift a short record above the noise. The projections are clearer: Area burned rises 46 per cent under net zero emissions by century’s end and 287 per cent if climate policies are rolled back.

Prognosis: Losing mass under every emissions scenario

Confidence level: Very high

Every glacier in Western Canada and the Canadian Arctic has thinned over the past 25 years, and reference glaciers have been losing mass since at least the 1960s, with the rate accelerating.

“Glaciers in both Western Canada and Arctic Canada are melting rapidly and will continue to thin and lose mass beyond the end of this century,” report author Lawrence Mudryk said.

In Western Canada, about 94 per cent of glacier mass is predicted to disappear under current policies. Even under a net zero scenario, three-quarters of the glaciers are gone.

Several Western watersheds have already recorded declines in what glaciers contribute to summer streamflow, marking an irreversible loss of a critical source of freshwater. Meltwater from the Canadian Arctic, meanwhile, will remain among the largest glacier contributors to global sea level rise well beyond 2100.

Prognosis: Warming and thawing, with the ground giving way

Confidence level: Very high for thawing, low on where and when

Permafrost at monitored sites across Northern Canada has warmed and thawed since the 1980s, causing land to settle and slump, ponds to form and lakes to drain, putting buildings, roads and runways at risk.

“Permafrost warming and thaw has been occurring in Northern Canada for decades and is expected to continue while global temperatures continue to increase,” Dr. Mudryk said.

The thaw will continue even if the climate stabilizes because deep ground responds slowly to what happens above. What scientists cannot say is precisely how fast or where this will occur. Farther south, the number of days with seasonally frozen ground is falling too.

Prognosis: Rising, and continuing to rise for millennia

Confidence level: Very high for the observed rise, high that Atlantic Canada and the Western Arctic exceed the global average

Global sea level has risen about 20 centimetres since 1900, and the rate has accelerated over the past three decades.

“Local sea level is projected to rise faster than the global average along parts of the Atlantic and Western Arctic coastlines,” report author Thomas James said.

The Canadian picture is not uniform because the land is still adjusting to the weight of ice that left after the last glaciation. Where the land is sinking, in southern Atlantic Canada and the Western Arctic, the sea level has climbed as much as 34 centimetres a century. Where the land is lifting faster than the ocean is rising, the waterline has dropped – the equivalent of 88 centimetres a century in Western Hudson Bay.

Where the sea is rising, extreme high-water events will come more often, worsened by storm surges and waves that reach farther as sea ice retreats. The sea level keeps climbing for thousands of years even after warming stops.

Prognosis: Warming, acidifying and losing oxygen

Confidence level: High for warming and marine heat waves, very high for acidification

Summer sea surface temperatures have risen everywhere around Canada, most sharply in Atlantic Canada and Hudson Bay, by as much as 2.5 degrees.

“More frequent and intense marine heat waves have been observed in the Pacific and Atlantic oceans around Canada since the 1980s, and such events are expected to continue to increase because of human influence on the climate system,” report author Blair Greenan said.

Warmer, fresher surface water also layers more sharply over what lies beneath, reducing the mixing that carries nutrients up to where marine life feeds. The ocean absorbs roughly a quarter of the carbon dioxide humans release, making it more acidic while oxygen declines beneath the surface off the northeast Pacific, in the Gulf of St. Lawrence and on the Scotian Shelf.

“Acidification projected for the latter half of this century will strongly depend on the level of future CO2 emissions,” report author Roberta Hamme said.

“Glaciers everywhere have receded or disappeared. That one used to be so huge it would overhang along the edge,” says Larry Audlaluk, an elder who was a child when the Canadian government relocated his family in 1953 from northern Quebec to the hamlet, which is located 1,160 kilometres north of the Arctic Circle.

Unlike other Nunavut communities, Grise Fiord has no lake or other natural water source to fall back on when the streams run low. Construction is under way on a treatment plant and three storage tanks that will hold enough water to supply residents year round.
The work highlights an obvious fact: Climate change stopped being a hypothetical threat in Grise Fiord years ago. It is now a permanent reality – and Grise Fiord is hardly unique.

In a major new assessment released last month, federal scientists show how every part of Canada is already experiencing the effects of a warming climate, with Northern, coastal and Indigenous communities among the most vulnerable.
Grise Fiord is among the 13 case studies in the report of First Nations, Inuit or Métis communities that are on the front lines of climate change, already having to adapt.

“It just reinforces the fact that Canada is seeing, right now, the impacts of climate change in a very large way,” federal Environment Minister Julie Dabrusin told The Globe and Mail. And while the assessment focuses on the physical effects of climate change, rather than how to manage them, it underlines just how much work will be needed “to help communities to meet the challenges that we’re going to be facing,” she said.

Those challenge will be the focus this week of Adaptation Canada 2026 , a climate conference organized by Local Governments for Sustainability Canada . The organization includes more than 400 municipalities across the country and is part of a larger international network.

The gathering is an opportunity for participants representing government, science, industry and Indigenous groups to take stock of what lies ahead as the country continues to warm through this century – and how that will play out where it is most relevant to people: their local communities.
To that end, the newly issued federal report serves as both a warning and a guide. Much of it is related to shifts in the environment that are now considered inevitable.

In Grise Fiord, for example, glacier melt, permafrost thaw and sea level rise are certainties. These changes are unfolding already, slowly but surely, as a result of greenhouse gases emitted into the atmosphere.
The consequences, which include an eroding shoreline, will be felt for decades – or millennia, in the case of rising seas – and that won’t change even if temperatures are stabilized today.

Because of this, the town faces “multiple hazards converging at once,” said David Didier, an Arctic coastal scientist at the University of Quebec in Rimouski who has studied the situation at Grise Fiord.
Across Canada, communities can expect to be similarly challenged by a range of interacting effects all driven by a climate that is warmer than at any point on historical record.

To help address this, the federal report has a section on climate services whose purpose is “getting information in the hands of the people who need it, in a form that they can use,” said Chris Derksen, the report’s lead scientist who heads the government’s climate modelling research division.

Where the Meteorological Service of Canada issues forecasts and warnings, climate services handle the longer time scales, issuing climate data for a city planner or engineer. In addition to the national organization, the Canadian Centre for Climate Services , regional centres exist in British Columbia and Yukon , the Prairies , Ontario , Quebec and Atlantic Canada .

There is no such regional organization for the other Northern territories. Only one Arctic municipality, the hamlet of Ulukhaktok, received support from a countrywide $34.2-million climate-resilience fund announced last month. Other avenues exist for funding Northern infrastructure built for a changing climate – such as Grise Fiord’s new water plant – but Canada is still playing catch-up in the North as communities there try to prepare for what is coming.

None of this addresses the elephant in the room: While communities spend public resources to build resilience and manage the effects of climate change, it’s clear that Canada – along with the rest of the world – is not curbing greenhouse gas emissions to a level that will significantly reduce climate risks and their associated costs.

Ms. Dabrusin said the government remains committed to emissions reduction. Many of the conversations she was involved in at last week’s Canada Investment Summit in Toronto, she added, were about projects that would facilitate the switch to a low carbon future, including in the North. Still, she acknowledged the report paints a sobering portrait for decision-makers. “This sets a very stark piece about where we’re at and why we need to continue to take action.”

“Permafrost warming and thaw has been occurring in Northern Canada for decades and is expected to continue while global temperatures continue to increase,” Dr. Mudryk said.

The thaw will continue even if the climate stabilizes because deep ground responds slowly to what happens above. What scientists cannot say is precisely how fast or where this will occur. Farther south, the number of days with seasonally frozen ground is falling too.

items: Prognosis: Rising, and continuing to rise for millennia
Confidence level: Very high for the observed rise, high that Atlantic Canada and the Western Arctic exceed the global average

content_blocks.caption: Îles-de-la-Madeleine, Que., is wary of rising sea levels as accelerating erosion eats away at the Quebec archipelago. Sebastien St-Jean/AFP via Getty Images

content_blocks.text: Global sea level has risen about 20 centimetres since 1900, and the rate has accelerated over the past three decades.
“Local sea level is projected to rise faster than the global average along parts of the Atlantic and Western Arctic coastlines,” report author Thomas James said.

The Canadian picture is not uniform because the land is still adjusting to the weight of ice that left after the last glaciation. Where the land is sinking, in southern Atlantic Canada and the Western Arctic, the sea level has climbed as much as 34 centimetres a century. Where the land is lifting faster than the ocean is rising, the waterline has dropped – the equivalent of 88 centimetres a century in Western Hudson Bay.

Where the sea is rising, extreme high-water events will come more often, worsened by storm surges and waves that reach farther as sea ice retreats. The sea level keeps climbing for thousands of years even after warming stops.

items: Prognosis: Warming, acidifying and losing oxygen
Confidence level: High for warming and marine heat waves, very high for acidification

content_blocks.caption: In warmer, more acidic oceans, clams are one of the species that suffer. Those conditions make it harder to collect and keep calcium for a sturdy shell. Jesse Winter/The Globe and Mail/The Globe and Mail

content_blocks.text: Summer sea surface temperatures have risen everywhere around Canada, most sharply in Atlantic Canada and Hudson Bay, by as much as 2.5 degrees.

“More frequent and intense marine heat waves have been observed in the Pacific and Atlantic oceans around Canada since the 1980s, and such events are expected to continue to increase because of human influence on the climate system,” report author Blair Greenan said.

Warmer, fresher surface water also layers more sharply over what lies beneath, reducing the mixing that carries nutrients up to where marine life feeds. The ocean absorbs roughly a quarter of the carbon dioxide humans release, making it more acidic while oxygen declines beneath the surface off the northeast Pacific, in the Gulf of St. Lawrence and on the Scotian Shelf.
“Acidification projected for the latter half of this century will strongly depend on the level of future CO2 emissions,” report author Roberta Hamme said.

stories.title: Should some doctors be forced to practise in underserviced areas?
stories.summary: In B.C., a judge rejected the two-tier system that affects where foreign-trained doctors can work
stories.author: André Picard
stories.content:
A B.C. Supreme Court justice has ruled that the province does not have the legal right to force international medical graduates (IMGs) to work in underserviced areas as a prerequisite for a spot in residency training.

Eliminating mandatory “return of service” agreements for IMGs has potentially far-reaching implications, not only in B.C. but across the country, because foreign-trained doctors provide a lot of the primary care services in rural and remote areas of Canada.

As a result, Judge Matthew Kirchner has suspended the ruling for six months to give Minister of Health Ravi Kahlon time to respond.

Mr. Kahlon said that the program is so essential that he will do “whatever is required” to ensure it continues.

It’s important to note here that Judge Kirchner’s ruling is fairly technical. It says that while the minister has the executive authority to sign contracts, in this case, the return of service contract is being used as a form of regulation.

That means the government needs to table legislation or amend current regulations to make the contractual process legal. Doing so would mean a return to the status quo.

Ontario launches medical school tuition grants worth $220-million for family doctors

The lawsuit at the heart of this case was filed by the Society for Canadians Studying Medicine Abroad, which argues that medical students trained outside Canada are unjustly shut out of access to medical residency training because priority is given to graduates of Canadian medical schools.

In B.C., for example, 294 residency spots are reserved for Canadian medical graduates, and only 58 for international medical graduates.

IMGs must undergo qualifying exams, and only the top 200 – or about 20 per cent – are even eligible to apply for residency. Almost all IMGs practise family medicine because the ability to choose another specialty is limited. Finally, before being offered a residency spot, IMGs must agree to practise in an underserviced area for two to three years after their training. Breaching those agreements can trigger heavy financial penalties of up to $900,000.

In his ruling Judge Kirchner rejected one of the petitioner’s principal arguments, saying there is nothing inherently wrong with a two-stream system. From a policy perspective, it makes sense to favour domestic graduates to ensure the province’s investment in medical education results in licensed physicians.

Similarly, the judge notes that a valid argument can be made for return of service agreements being a practical way to address persistent physician shortages in remote and rural areas.

But Judge Kirchner also notes that the “Minister has offered little to explain why IMGs are singled out for this obligation.”

That’s a really good point, and one that will no doubt be the object of a constitutional challenge.

(In the case, the petitioners claimed the current rules violate sections 6, 7, 12 and 15 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms. The judge addressed those claims briefly but the parties agreed to defer a more in-depth Charter challenge to a later date.)

André Picard: All Canadians should be eligible for a free shingles vaccine

If we’re going to coerce wannabe doctors to practise in rural and remote areas, why pick only on those trained outside the country? Are they inherently more suited to rural medicine? Or are they being treated as second-class citizens?

In fact, is coercion the way to resolve this issue, or should we be offering incentives for doctors to practise in underserviced areas? These could include better pay packages, tuition refunds, low-cost or no-cost housing and so on. Or perhaps ensuring the work is less onerous.

Residency is essentially on-the-job training, a prerequisite for licensing as a physician. Having strict rules during education and training is fine.

But Judge Kirchner underscores that the problem with the current return of service contracts is the requirement to practise in a specific location after residency. At that point, IMGs are the same as every other physician, and should not be deprived of choice on where to live and work.

Similar legal issues arise in Quebec, where the government is trying to compel doctors trained in the province to stay there by demanding that those who leave the province repay the costs of their training, ranging from $435,000 and $790,000.

Canada has persistent problems ensuring citizens have access to care, particularly primary care.

We are also highly dependent on international medical graduates . There are nuances and complexities ensuring IMGs are integrated smoothly into the health system.

But we owe it to them – and ourselves – to get our policy choices right.

And we should be doing so proactively, not waiting for the courts to force legislators to grudgingly act more smartly.

stories.title: Crowded political landscape leaves Quebec voters lukewarm as election nears
stories.summary: Five parties are likely to win seats, but none has attained a critical mass of support in lead-up to Oct. 5
stories.author: Maura Forrest
stories.content:
Voters in Quebec are facing an almost unprecedented array of choices in this fall’s election, but amid the noise and bluster of a crowded field, they have yet to fall in love with any of their options.

On Oct. 5, Quebeckers will select from five major political parties who are all likely to win at least a handful of seats in the province’s National Assembly. It should be an embarrassment of riches, but voters seem unable to muster much enthusiasm for anything on the menu.

The Parti Québécois is favoured to win the most seats, but is hamstrung by its promise to hold a referendum on Quebec sovereignty that most people don’t want. The Coalition Avenir Québec is weighed down by the baggage of eight years in power. The opposition Liberals are stubbornly unpopular among francophones.

When the CAQ formed its first government in 2018, promising a new brand of nationalism that didn’t include a referendum on separation, it blew up a political landscape that had been defined for decades by the debate over sovereignty. Eight years on, the electoral battlefield is littered with shrapnel from that explosion.

Konrad Yakabuski: The Quebec election could result in a ripple, not a wave

The result is five parties that all cater to subsets of the Quebec electorate. But none of those parties has so far proved capable of seducing a critical mass of voters in a campaign that feels strangely stagnant.

Each of the five contenders has a core of loyal support, often concentrated in certain regions. Sovereigntists mostly vote for the PQ. Anglophones (largely in and around Montreal) consistently support the Liberals. The CAQ is the party of choice for older francophones who don’t want a referendum. Urban progressives support Québec solidaire, a left-leaning sovereigntist party, while the Conservatives have a strong base among right-leaning voters around Quebec City.

But with all five parties polling below 30 per cent, two- and three-way races are playing out in ridings across the province. The three leading parties – the PQ, CAQ and Liberals – are all within a few points of each other, while roughly 40 per cent of voters still say their choice isn’t locked in.

On a doorstep in the Quebec City suburb of Charlesbourg, PQ candidate Gabriel Coulombe recently made his pitch to a couple who said they haven’t made up their minds about which way to vote.

“The goods were not delivered” under the CAQ government, Mr. Coulombe told the couple.

But Gilles Simard and Sylvie Dinel were unconvinced. They later told The Globe and Mail they have no interest in the sovereignty referendum promised by PQ Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon, which would be the province’s third vote on the question of whether Quebec should remain in Canada.

Ms. Dinel said she’s thinking about voting for the Quebec Conservatives, a relatively new party projected to win seats for the first time this year. She voted for the CAQ four years ago, but they made some “bad choices,” she said.

Mr. Simard seemed more inclined to give the CAQ another chance, though he didn’t offer the party a ringing endorsement. Leader Christine Fréchette “is already in place,” he said. “There won’t be a bunch of surprises.”

The riding of Charlesbourg voted solidly CAQ in the last two elections. But as voters seek change this time around, the campaign is a tight three-way race between the PQ, the CAQ and the Conservatives.

“It’s the kind of election that could be decided by a few hundred or a few dozen votes,” Mr. Coulombe said in an interview.

Quebeckers have once before elected members of five parties to the provincial legislature, back in 1976. That election was an inflection point for the province, said Youri Rivest, co-founder of polling firm Synopsis Recherche. That year, René Lévesque led the Parti Québécois to form its first government, while the once-powerful Union Nationale won seats for the last time. Two of the other parties were bit players that dissolved not long after.

This time, Mr. Rivest said, the five parties competing for votes are the result of a “fragmentation of the sociopolitical values of Quebeckers.” After decades of elections fought between the sovereigntist Parti Québécois and the federalist Liberals, the CAQ in 2018 suddenly made it possible to vote on other issues.

“There was a very strong tension between federalists and sovereigntists,” he said. “But once you remove that tension, it reveals another axis – one that’s left-right.”

Québec solidaire, the left-leaning party, won 10 seats for the first time in 2018. The Conservatives claimed nearly 13 per cent of the vote four years ago, but won no seats.

Evelyne Brie, an assistant professor of political science at Université de Montréal, said the regionalization of politics is not unique to Quebec, and is partly driven by the rise of alternative media.

“It’s possible to get information from media outlets that are very specialized,” she said. “This creates echo chambers.”

Two weeks ahead of election day, none of the leaders has managed to trigger one of the waves of popular sentiment for which Quebec is known, and the result on Oct. 5 will most likely be a minority government. With the electorate so fragmented, polls have shown little movement since the early days of the campaign.

In Charlesbourg, that suits some voters just fine. In a campaign that has lacked much sizzle, there is at least some genuine excitement here about the prospect of a Conservative caucus in the National Assembly. Leader Éric Duhaime has campaigned mostly in the Quebec City region, and is hoping to hold the balance of power.

His candidate in the suburban riding is 23-year-old Eloïse Coulombe – no relation of the PQ candidate. While door-knocking one evening this month, Ms. Coulombe was stopped on the sidewalk by Réjean Laliberté, an older voter who wanted to show his support.

“I’m fed up with having the same old people in government squandering our money,” he later told The Globe. If the Conservatives form an opposition party, he added, “I’ll be the happiest man in the world.”

Across the street, a woman opened her door to call out to Ms. Coulombe. “Bravo!” she shouted. “We’re voting for you!”

A poised and articulate university student, Ms. Coulombe embodies Mr. Duhaime’s reinvention of his party. Four years ago, the Conservative leader drummed up support by railing against pandemic public-health restrictions. Today, he has recast his party as a sober watchdog fighting to protect taxpayers from state profligacy. He has proposed major tax cuts and more private health care.

Prof. Brie said it’s a “nice problem” to have a proliferation of parties that resonate with certain segments of the population. “That’s actually healthy for a democracy,” she said.

But in a province where political movements ebb and flow, it remains to be seen whether such a congested playing field can last. Four years ago, the PQ was on the verge of extinction when it won just three seats in the legislature. Earlier this year, the CAQ was about to be wiped out. Both have made unlikely comebacks.

“Something is going to be reconfigured,” said Mr. Rivest. “The system isn’t designed to handle this.”

But with all five parties polling below 30 per cent, two- and three-way races are playing out in ridings across the province. The three leading parties – the PQ, CAQ and Liberals – are all within a few points of each other, while roughly 40 per cent of voters still say their choice isn’t locked in.
On a doorstep in the Quebec City suburb of Charlesbourg, PQ candidate Gabriel Coulombe recently made his pitch to a couple who said they haven’t made up their minds about which way to vote.
“The goods were not delivered” under the CAQ government, Mr. Coulombe told the couple.

content_blocks.caption: Mr. Coulombe campaigns in Charlesbourg. While favoured to win the most seats, the PQ is hamstrung by its promise to hold a sovereignty referendum. Renaud Philippe/The Globe and Mail

content_blocks.text: But Gilles Simard and Sylvie Dinel were unconvinced. They later told The Globe and Mail they have no interest in the sovereignty referendum promised by PQ Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon, which would be the province’s third vote on the question of whether Quebec should remain in Canada.

Ms. Dinel said she’s thinking about voting for the Quebec Conservatives, a relatively new party projected to win seats for the first time this year. She voted for the CAQ four years ago, but they made some “bad choices,” she said.

Mr. Simard seemed more inclined to give the CAQ another chance, though he didn’t offer the party a ringing endorsement. Leader Christine Fréchette “is already in place,” he said. “There won’t be a bunch of surprises.”

The riding of Charlesbourg voted solidly CAQ in the last two elections. But as voters seek change this time around, the campaign is a tight three-way race between the PQ, the CAQ and the Conservatives.
“It’s the kind of election that could be decided by a few hundred or a few dozen votes,” Mr. Coulombe said in an interview.

Quebeckers have once before elected members of five parties to the provincial legislature, back in 1976. That election was an inflection point for the province, said Youri Rivest, co-founder of polling firm Synopsis Recherche. That year, René Lévesque led the Parti Québécois to form its first government, while the once-powerful Union Nationale won seats for the last time. Two of the other parties were bit players that dissolved not long after.

content_blocks.caption: René Lévesque, shown in 1983, was the first premier from the Parti Québécois. The Globe and Mail

content_blocks.text: This time, Mr. Rivest said, the five parties competing for votes are the result of a “fragmentation of the sociopolitical values of Quebeckers.” After decades of elections fought between the sovereigntist Parti Québécois and the federalist Liberals, the CAQ in 2018 suddenly made it possible to vote on other issues.
“There was a very strong tension between federalists and sovereigntists,” he said. “But once you remove that tension, it reveals another axis – one that’s left-right.”
Québec solidaire, the left-leaning party, won 10 seats for the first time in 2018. The Conservatives claimed nearly 13 per cent of the vote four years ago, but won no seats.

Evelyne Brie, an assistant professor of political science at Université de Montréal, said the regionalization of politics is not unique to Quebec, and is partly driven by the rise of alternative media.
“It’s possible to get information from media outlets that are very specialized,” she said. “This creates echo chambers.”

Two weeks ahead of election day, none of the leaders has managed to trigger one of the waves of popular sentiment for which Quebec is known, and the result on Oct. 5 will most likely be a minority government. With the electorate so fragmented, polls have shown little movement since the early days of the campaign.

In Charlesbourg, that suits some voters just fine. In a campaign that has lacked much sizzle, there is at least some genuine excitement here about the prospect of a Conservative caucus in the National Assembly. Leader Éric Duhaime has campaigned mostly in the Quebec City region, and is hoping to hold the balance of power.

His candidate in the suburban riding is 23-year-old Eloïse Coulombe – no relation of the PQ candidate. While door-knocking one evening this month, Ms. Coulombe was stopped on the sidewalk by Réjean Laliberté, an older voter who wanted to show his support.

“I’m fed up with having the same old people in government squandering our money,” he later told The Globe. If the Conservatives form an opposition party, he added, “I’ll be the happiest man in the world.”

content_blocks.caption: University student Eloïse Coulombe is the Conservative candidate in Charlesbourg. Renaud Philippe/The Globe and Mail

content_blocks.text: Across the street, a woman opened her door to call out to Ms. Coulombe. “Bravo!” she shouted. “We’re voting for you!”

A poised and articulate university student, Ms. Coulombe embodies Mr. Duhaime’s reinvention of his party. Four years ago, the Conservative leader drummed up support by railing against pandemic public-health restrictions. Today, he has recast his party as a sober watchdog fighting to protect taxpayers from state profligacy. He has proposed major tax cuts and more private health care.
Prof. Brie said it’s a “nice problem” to have a proliferation of parties that resonate with certain segments of the population. “That’s actually healthy for a democracy,” she said.

But in a province where political movements ebb and flow, it remains to be seen whether such a congested playing field can last. Four years ago, the PQ was on the verge of extinction when it won just three seats in the legislature. Earlier this year, the CAQ was about to be wiped out. Both have made unlikely comebacks.
“Something is going to be reconfigured,” said Mr. Rivest. “The system isn’t designed to handle this.”

stories.title: Heritage Property tax relief approved by city committee, long road ahead to creation
stories.summary: London City Council's Planning and Environment Committee took a step toward the potential creation of a tax discount program to help property owners pay for the upkeep of historic buildings, Monday.
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: CBC News | Posted: September 22, 2026 9:14 AM | Last Updated: 6 hours ago
A program May not be realized until 2028 at the earliest, when the city's next budgeting process occurs
London City Council's Planning and Environment Committee took a step toward the potential creation of a tax discount program to help property owners pay for the upkeep of historic buildings, Monday.

The five-person committee voted unanimously to have a recommendation to implement such a program brought to the next council for consideration during the creation of the city's 2027-2031 strategic plan and next multi-year budgeting process.
While the committee voted in favour of moving closer to the creation of an eventual program, there's little information on what it might look like and what the impact would be on taxpayers.
A long-defunct pilot program to offer tax refunds to heritage property owners previously existed in the city from 2007 to 2010.
Under the previous program, owners of eligible properties entered agreements with the city that ensured the property was maintained.

In exchange, the city offered up to 40 per cent off the tax bill for the property up to $3,000 for multi-residential properties. For apartment, commercial and mixed-use buildings, the tax break was up to 20 per cent to a maximum of $5,000.
Annual funding for the program per year was capped at $50,000 and applications were first-come, first-served.
In a report to the planning committee, city staff noted that program was well-liked and used by landowners, despite ultimately not being renewed when it expired in 2010.
Deputy Mayor Shawn Lewis, who sits on the committee as deputy chair, expressed concern over the lack of a concrete vision for what the program might look like.
Lewis suggested a model similar to what Collingwood, Ont., uses, which is similar to London's previous program.

"What I'm really looking for is the preservation and maintenance agreement, and a recommendation on a budget allocation," said Lewis. "It might not be $50,000, but a recommendation based on the number of heritage designations we have."
Differing from London's previous program, the Collingwood model offers a flat 20 per cent reduction across all types of heritage properties.

Members of the committee agreed municipal staff should be required to include a recommendation for a model based on Collingwood's approach when the matter is brought before the next council during budgeting.
With the planning committee's approval, the prospect of creating a heritage property tax relief program in London must still be approved by the entirety of City Council before moving forward.
Council meets Wednesday.

stories.title: Family of killed Toronto officer calls for Ottawa to make major changes to the parole system
stories.summary: Victims' families are calling for parole reforms, urging changes to Canada's justice system.
stories.author: Adrian Ghobrial
stories.content:
Toronto - “We’re talking about a guy who walked over, put the gun to my brother’s head, and pulled the goddamn trigger,” said Cory Baylis, as he gestures to his own head, his hand mimicking the gun that killed his brother.

It was June 1994. Baylis was in Florida when he learned that his big brother, Toronto Police Constable Todd Baylis had been shot and killed on the job. Todd was just 25 years old at the time and had been chasing after a suspected drug dealer who pulled out a gun and opened fire, shooting him in the head.

Clinton Gayle was found guilty of first-degree murder and attempted murder for shooting Baylis’ partner who survived. Gayle was sentenced to life in prison with no chance at parole for 25 years.

The Baylis family now must appear at a parole hearing every two years. They’ve already had to attend four separate parole reviews.

Speaking to CTV News from his home in Brampton, Ont., Baylis shared his mounting frustration after having to attend yet another hearing this past July, reliving the trauma of losing his brother.

“2019, 2021, 2024, 2026. We’ll have to go back in 2027 or 2028, it’s ridiculous,” said Baylis.

Gayle and others facing life sentences can request a parole hearing every two years, once the initial 25 years of their sentence has been served.

CTV News has obtained a copy of a letter written by the Toronto Police Association, requesting that the federal government increase the time between parole hearings from “five to seven years” and allow judges the power to impose “parole ineligibility periods for up to 35 years” for those convicted of first-degree murder.

This coming January, serial rapist and killer Paul Bernardo will have his fourth parole hearing.

“It’s just pure entertainment for him. He has no remorse,” said trial lawyer Tim Danson.

Danson represents the families of victims Leslie Mahaffy and Kristen French, who were both murdered by Bernardo. He attends each parole hearing pro bono, to support the Mahaffy and French families.

He still sees a “sadistic, sexual psychopath” in Paul Bernado.

“When he’s asked during a parole review why he would carry out these horrific attacks on these teenage girls he answers by saying ‘well, they weren’t doing what I told them,’” Danson said.

“He answers these questions like you and I would talk about the weather.”

Danson says the French, Mahaffy and Baylis families are all asking for parole reform, and they believe that Canada’s worst convicted killers shouldn’t be allowed to traumatize a family every two years.

Our justice system shouldn’t be one size fits all, we’re not talking about someone “stealing candy from a candy store” said Baylis.

“It’s horrific what the justice system does to victims’ families. They drag us through this process, and I find myself asking why. Well, I’ll tell you, it’s because a killer’s rights are more important that mine, my dead brother’s, yours, or anybody else’s.”

The Toronto Police Association’s letter, sent to multiple members of parliament, says in part that the federal government “committed to us earlier this year that this issue would be addressed in the fall. We are now two weeks into September, and with the latest news about Paul Bernardo, the issue could not be more urgent.”

The Department of Justice has not responded to a request for comment.

stories.title: Canadian airports can anchor a global infrastructure champion
stories.summary: Ottawa decision to sell concessions in four major domestic hubs promises to be a win for passengers and taxpayers
stories.author: Andrew Willis
stories.content:
If you are reading this while killing time waiting for a flight in one of Canada’s major airports, you are sitting in what should be the country’s next global corporate champion.

The federal government’s long-overdue decision to sell concessions in four major domestic hubs – Vancouver, Calgary, Toronto and Montreal – promises to be a win for passengers and taxpayers. After years of analysis paralysis, Prime Minister Mark Carney has an opportunity to improve the passenger experience while raising billions of dollars.

The ultimate goal in this exercise, clearly visible to a Prime Minister who started his career as a Goldman Sachs banker advising governments on privatizations, should be creating a private-sector operator of Canadian airports that does business around the world.

At least one domestic pension fund, Montreal-based PSP Investments, is already well down this runway.

In June, months before Mr. Carney announced plans to sell airport concessions at last Tuesday’s Canada Investment Summit, Montreal-based consultant Fethi Chebil published a sector study that started with a metaphysical question for the government.

Carney details plans to open up Canada’s four largest airports to private investment

“What is an airport for? An asset to sell, or a tool to build a national operator?” Dr. Chebil said in his June report.

For governments, Dr. Chebil concluded that launching a business beats selling a few terminals. To support his argument, Dr. Chebil pointed to the success that Canada’s largest pension funds have enjoyed internationally as owners of airport operators, and the virtues of this model for frequent flyers.

The poster child for airport operators globally is PSP, which pays for the retirements of soldiers, Mounties and civil servants. The $321-billion fund manager has built a global business that should serve as a road map for Canadian airport ownership.

In 2013, PSP acquired a collection of European airports from a German infrastructure fund for €1.1-billion. The wholly owned subsidiary, branded as AviAlliance, now operates seven facilities in Scotland, Germany, England and Puerto Rico.

AviAlliance is the largest holding in a PSP infrastructure portfolio that handily beat performance benchmarks over the past decade.

What could airport privatization mean for travellers in Canada?

AviAlliance airports also charge travellers less for food, beverages and fees than Canadian airports, according to Dr. Chebil’s research. Domestic airports operate as non-profit, debt-funded Crown corporations, a cumbersome, only-in-Canada ownership approach devised in 1992. Dr. Chebil said in his report: “The 1992 structure is not delivering lower costs to users.”

Private airport owners would create more opportunities for travellers to drop stupid amounts of money on cucumber-lined Hendrick’s martinis or Rolex watches. That’s discretionary consumer spending. Want to curtail the cost of a trip? Avoid airport restaurants and retailers.

The experience in Europe and Australia, where governments sold airport concessions, is to keep costs down by regulating fees on monopoly services such as baggage handling or aeronautical services including navigation. Governments use the same approach to ensure pipeline operators and electrical utilities don’t gouge consumers.

In 2016, former federal finance minister Bill Morneau launched an economic review that said selling airports was among the best options for a government that needed to find money for infrastructure projects. A decade later, Mr. Carney is following through.

For insight into how the Prime Minister thinks about finance, recall Mr. Carney’s pointed criticism of the billions in “dead money” on corporate balance sheets back in 2012, when he was governor of the Bank of Canada.

Airline industry group opposes privatization of Canadian airports

In a Q&A after a speech to the Canadian Auto Workers union, the then-central banker took CEOs and boards to task for being excessively cautious by sitting on cash, rather than investing in growth or returning money to shareholders.

There is a straight line from what Governor Carney said about dead money years ago to what Prime Minister Carney announced on airports last week.

Last Tuesday, in his opening speech at the investment summit, Mr. Carney said by selling airport concessions, while retaining ownership of the assets, “we will unlock their true value, by bringing in new capital and expertise into their operations and growth.”

“We will reinvest the tens of billions of dollars of capital we raise into the infrastructure that Canada needs,” the Prime Minister said.

Airports represent dead money on the federal government’s balance sheet. Selling concessions to operate Vancouver, Calgary, Toronto and Montreal’s terminals can make flying more pleasant, without boosting the cost of travel.

And placing the country’s four major airports in the proven hands of a fund manager such as PSP could create a global champion in a critical infrastructure sector.

The federal government’s long-overdue decision to sell concessions in four major domestic hubs – Vancouver, Calgary, Toronto and Montreal – promises to be a win for passengers and taxpayers. After years of analysis paralysis, Prime Minister Mark Carney has an opportunity to improve the passenger experience while raising billions of dollars.

The ultimate goal in this exercise, clearly visible to a Prime Minister who started his career as a Goldman Sachs banker advising governments on privatizations, should be creating a private-sector operator of Canadian airports that does business around the world.
At least one domestic pension fund, Montreal-based PSP Investments, is already well down this runway.

In June, months before Mr. Carney announced plans to sell airport concessions at last Tuesday’s Canada Investment Summit, Montreal-based consultant Fethi Chebil published a sector study that started with a metaphysical question for the government.
Carney details plans to open up Canada’s four largest airports to private investment
“What is an airport for? An asset to sell, or a tool to build a national operator?” Dr. Chebil said in his June report.

For governments, Dr. Chebil concluded that launching a business beats selling a few terminals. To support his argument, Dr. Chebil pointed to the success that Canada’s largest pension funds have enjoyed internationally as owners of airport operators, and the virtues of this model for frequent flyers.

The poster child for airport operators globally is PSP, which pays for the retirements of soldiers, Mounties and civil servants. The $321-billion fund manager has built a global business that should serve as a road map for Canadian airport ownership.

In 2013, PSP acquired a collection of European airports from a German infrastructure fund for €1.1-billion. The wholly owned subsidiary, branded as AviAlliance, now operates seven facilities in Scotland, Germany, England and Puerto Rico.
AviAlliance is the largest holding in a PSP infrastructure portfolio that handily beat performance benchmarks over the past decade.
What could airport privatization mean for travellers in Canada?

AviAlliance airports also charge travellers less for food, beverages and fees than Canadian airports, according to Dr. Chebil’s research. Domestic airports operate as non-profit, debt-funded Crown corporations, a cumbersome, only-in-Canada ownership approach devised in 1992. Dr. Chebil said in his report: “The 1992 structure is not delivering lower costs to users.”

Private airport owners would create more opportunities for travellers to drop stupid amounts of money on cucumber-lined Hendrick’s martinis or Rolex watches. That’s discretionary consumer spending. Want to curtail the cost of a trip? Avoid airport restaurants and retailers.

The experience in Europe and Australia, where governments sold airport concessions, is to keep costs down by regulating fees on monopoly services such as baggage handling or aeronautical services including navigation. Governments use the same approach to ensure pipeline operators and electrical utilities don’t gouge consumers.

In 2016, former federal finance minister Bill Morneau launched an economic review that said selling airports was among the best options for a government that needed to find money for infrastructure projects. A decade later, Mr. Carney is following through.

For insight into how the Prime Minister thinks about finance, recall Mr. Carney’s pointed criticism of the billions in “dead money” on corporate balance sheets back in 2012, when he was governor of the Bank of Canada.
Airline industry group opposes privatization of Canadian airports

In a Q&A after a speech to the Canadian Auto Workers union, the then-central banker took CEOs and boards to task for being excessively cautious by sitting on cash, rather than investing in growth or returning money to shareholders.
There is a straight line from what Governor Carney said about dead money years ago to what Prime Minister Carney announced on airports last week.

Last Tuesday, in his opening speech at the investment summit, Mr. Carney said by selling airport concessions, while retaining ownership of the assets, “we will unlock their true value, by bringing in new capital and expertise into their operations and growth.”
“We will reinvest the tens of billions of dollars of capital we raise into the infrastructure that Canada needs,” the Prime Minister said.

Airports represent dead money on the federal government’s balance sheet. Selling concessions to operate Vancouver, Calgary, Toronto and Montreal’s terminals can make flying more pleasant, without boosting the cost of travel.
And placing the country’s four major airports in the proven hands of a fund manager such as PSP could create a global champion in a critical infrastructure sector.

stories.title: Ontario hospitals ordered to improve detection protocols for sepsis
stories.summary: Several sepsis-related deaths in the province in recent years, including that of a 16-year-old, have sparked public outcry
stories.author: Kristy Kirkup
stories.content:
Hospitals in Canada’s most populous province will be required by Ontario Health to establish protocols by early next year to identify and respond to sepsis, which can be fatal if patients do not receive timely medical intervention.

A copy of a clinical memorandum, sent in the spring and obtained by The Globe and Mail, details how Ontario Health, a government agency designed to modernize the health care system, is working to set consistent provincial expectations for how hospitals respond to potential cases of sepsis. The new protocols must be in place by March, 2027, according to the memorandum.

There have been several sepsis-related deaths in Ontario hospitals in recent years that have sparked public outcry, including that of 16-year-old Finlay van der Werken . In February, 2024, he waited more than eight hours in an Oakville, Ont., emergency department to be seen by a doctor before he died of sepsis and pneumonia.

Nova Scotia’s approach to sepsis treatment offers life-saving lessons, advocates say

Sepsis is when the body kicks into overdrive in response to an infection. If it is not recognized early, it can lead to shock, organ failure and death. As of 2020, it was estimated 75,000 cases of sepsis occur every year in Canada, leading to 18,000 deaths .

The clinical memorandum, dated April 20, pegs the cost of sepsis to Ontario’s health care system to be more than $1-billion a year. The document, sent to chief medical executives and hospitals in the province, said institutions must have sepsis screening or warning mechanisms in place for inpatient units by March 31, 2027.

“Hospitals can fulfill this requirement by using a health information system (HIS) with an integrated early warning system or by implementing a routine screening process – either on paper or electronically – for acutely ill, high-risk patients,” it said.

The document also cites strong evidence that early identification and timely sepsis treatment improves patient outcomes, but that benefits can only be achieved when protocols are embedded in workflows and consistent.

Lily Barnes, a spokesperson for Ontario’s Health Minister Sylvia Jones, said the provincial government is working to promote standardized practices and clinical awareness.

“As per the Minister’s direction, Ontario Health has convened an expert panel of leading clinicians to review currently established sepsis guidelines and opportunities for improvement,” she said in an e-mail.

Last October, the van der Werken family met with Ms. Jones to call for changes to how emergency care is delivered in Ontario, including standardized maximum ER wait times for vulnerable pediatric patients.

The circumstances of Finlay’s death will be the subject of a future discretionary coroner’s inquest , but a date has not been set.

Ontario resident, Gurinder Sidhu, has also called for reforms to ensure early intervention and treatment of sepsis. He says his wife, Ravinder, with whom he has three children, developed postpartum sepsis that caused organ failure and led to her death in June, 2025.

Kassandra Costabile is also pushing for accountability following her sister’s death, which she believes was preventable. Rheanna Laderoute died in February, 2022, after showing signs of septic shock following an abortion.

Last October, Nova Scotia rolled out a provincewide approach that authorized emergency room nurses to administer antibiotics and IV fluids to anyone suspected of having sepsis.

The measure was applauded by advocates who want the approach expanded to other provinces and territories.

Nova Scotia’s changes were implemented following several prominent sepsis cases that resulted in legal action.

For its action plan, the provincial health authority drew lessons from NHS Scotland, the publicly funded health care system in that country, and the B.C. Sepsis Network, a clinician initiative in that province.

In New York State, sepsis detection regulations in place for the past 13 years have been credited with saving tens of thousands of lives . They include strict timelines for interventions, including early delivery of antibiotics.

The measures, known as Rory’s Regulations, were put in place after the April 1, 2012, death of 12-year-old Rory Staunton, who had undiagnosed and untreated sepsis. His parents, Ciaran and Orlaith Staunton, founded the U.S. advocacy organization, End Sepsis , the year of his death.

In a recent interview, Ms. Staunton said she has spoken with the van der Werken family and that she was heartbroken to learn Finlay waited so long before being seen by a doctor.

Finlay and Rory’s deaths were preventable, she said.

“I think it’s about time Canada got their act together. What’s stopping them?”

stories.title: Quebec election campaign enters 27th day as final debate nears
stories.summary: Montreal - Quebec's party leaders are expected to be back out on the campaign trail today, with less than two weeks to go before the provincial election vote.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
MONTREAL - With less than two weeks to go in the Quebec election campaign, party leaders are gearing up for a third and final debate that could see Parti Québécois Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon at the centre of attention.

“Everyone is taking aim at the Parti Québécois,” said André Lamoureux, political scientist and professor at Université du Québec à Montréal.

The Radio-Canada debate on Wednesday will be the last opportunity for leaders to spar before the vote on Oct. 5. They met twice already on the debate stage last week.

But in the last few days, Lamoureux has noted how the PQ has become a frequent target of attacks by other parties, with public opinion polls suggesting it is leading in the campaign.

But the political analyst noted how some of the criticism can backfire.

For example, last week, when Liberal Leader Charles Milliard said that 70 per cent of Quebecers did not want a referendum, St-Pierre Plamondon responded by saying that 80 per cent of the province did not want the Quebec Liberals in government.

“That’s what I’m looking forward to seeing. Will it be effective against the Parti Québécois? Or will Paul St-Pierre Plamondon take those attacks and redirect them with even more efficiency?” he said.

Coalition Avenir Québec Leader Christine Fréchette is struggling to position her party as an alternative to the Parti Québecois, said Lamoureux. He noted how she is also trying to distance herself from the track record of her predecessor, François Legault who led the province as premier for close to eight years.

“Quebecers don’t trust this party,” he said.

Lamoureux expects Fréchette to try to regain momentum in this last debate.

“She is going to try to give it her all. That’s where we’ll see if her leadership … can give mass appeal to her message and turn the tide,” he said.

Anne-Marie Gingras, retired political science professor, still expects a close battle between the Coalition Avenir Québec and the Parti Québécois in many ridings, while also warning that some voters are tuning out.

“People don’t know where to turn to find a solution. And that is at the core of the Coalition Avenir Québec’s decline over the last few days, because (people feel like) everything is going wrong,” she said.

She also said the Coalition Avenir Québec has not managed to get voters to focus on any of its achievements while in government.

“With everything that has happened over the past eight years, there have been successes and there have been mistakes, but the successes aren’t really being highlighted,” she said.

The Quebec Liberal Party is currently the official Opposition, but its support is concentrated in urban ridings in Montreal and the English-speaking community, and Lamoureux said he does not expect them to make headway among French-speaking voters.

“For francophones, right now, the Quebec Liberal Party is going through the worst period in its history,” he said.

Lamoureux described the Conservative party as a “surprise” and may win seats in the election, he said, which would be a first in its history.

At the last general elections, the conservatives won close to 13 per cent of the popular vote but elected no candidates. Before the legislature dissolved, the Conservatives had one member who had crossed the floor from the Coalition Avenir Québec.

Lamoureux sees Québec solidaire as failing to convince voters of their message and losing support with francophone voters.

The party leaders have faced questions in recent days about potential alliances if no party succeeds in forming a majority.

Parti Québécois Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon said Monday that an alliance was out of the question, after his rivals suggested his ideas are similar to those of Conservative Leader Éric Duhaime.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 22, 2026.

stories.title: Trump to address UN General Assembly as Carney becomes voice of multilateralism
stories.summary: United Nations - U.S. President Donald Trump is set to address the 81st Session of the United Nations General Assembly on Tuesday, despite his administration's efforts to undermine multilateralism and to target allies with threats and tariffs.
stories.author: Kelly Geraldine Malone The Canadian Press
stories.content:
UNITED NATIONS - U.S. President Donald Trump told the United Nations General Assembly on Tuesday he has a choice to make on Iran: negotiate a deal or “annihilate the Islamic Republic.”

In a wide-ranging speech, Trump defended his war on Iran and boasted of American strength, claiming that “while others have talked, I have acted.”

He celebrated the U.S. military operation to oust Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro earlier this year and a new agreement to expand the American military presence in Greenland, which came after his threats of annexation.

But those actions have upended U.S. relationships with other nations, including traditional allies. Many of those allies have used the United Nations forum to call for a return to international law.

This 81st Session of the United Nations General Assembly is taking place as the world grapples with oil supply shocks and rising prices driven by the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, and under the shadow of Trump’s constant attacks on multilateralism.

Canada, like most countries, has not been able to escape the geopolitical effects of Trump’s erratic deployment of military force and tariffs.

Prime Minister Mark Carney said one of the shared challenges of the moment is a multilateral system that doesn’t reflect the times and cannot respond to them.

“But at the same time, the need for multilateral co-operation is very much alive,” Carney told reporters on Tuesday.

Carney — who has emerged in recent weeks as a key global champion of multilateralism and alliances in the face of Trump’s repeated attacks — said no one country, no matter how powerful, can manage the world’s challenges alone.

“Co-operation, therefore, is not an act of idealism. It is a practical necessity,” he said. “And the question is not whether multilateralism can survive but how it must evolve to meet the challenges of the moment.”

Trump has demanded massive reforms at the UN and has held back funding for the institution, putting it in turmoil. The Trump administration has withdrawn from multiple UN organizations, including the World Health Organization.

Carney, meanwhile, has been making the case for continued global collaboration to address crises like climate change, financial instability and war.

For nearly a year now, Carney has been travelling the globe calling on middle powers to band together in defence of what he has called “shared interests, and occasionally shared values, rather than shared institutions.”

Carney has sought to build a bridge between the European Union and a Pacific Rim trading bloc called CPTPP so middle powers can better resist economic coercion by the United States and China.

The prime minister’s efforts have caught the attention of the Trump administration, especially since trade negotiations between Canada and the United States ended acrimoniously last month.

After European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen last week opened the door to Canada becoming what she called the first “associate member” of the European Union, Trump said it could be a “hostile act.”

Carney did not hold any official meetings with Trump or members of the U.S. administration while in New York this week — his first return to the United States since trade negotiations fell apart last month.

The prime minister said during a gathering of global leaders “it’s most valuable to meet those who you don’t normally see.”

Carney held bilateral meetings with Chilean President Jose Antonio Kast and Angola President Joao Lourenco on the sidelines of the assembly. He also met with King of Jordan Abdullah II and a delegation from the United Arab Emirates.

Earlier Tuesday, Carney was quickly greeted by Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese when he arrived for the opening of the General Assembly. He also walked across the floor to speak with Crown Prince of the State of Kuwait Sabah Al-Khalid Al-Sabah before formal speeches began.

Carney co-hosted with France and the United Kingdom an event on the two-state solution — one year after the three countries recognized an independent Palestinian state at the General Assembly. More than 150 countries followed the move to recognize Palestinian statehood.

At the General Assembly last year, Trump said recognizing a Palestinian state would amount to rewarding Hamas for the “horrible atrocities” of the Oct. 7, 2023, attack on Israel. Trump also claimed the move could hinder Canada’s ability to make a trade deal with the United States.

Canada and the United States now seem further than ever from reaching that deal. Bilateral relations have continued to deteriorate as the trade war has escalated.

Trump, meanwhile, partially walked back remarks he’d made on social media about getting potash from Belarus instead of Canada. During a bilateral meeting on Tuesday with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Trump said “we’ll continue to go with Canada (for potash), but Belarus would like to sell it for a much lower price.”

Asked about Trump’s change of tone, Carney said “the Canadian potash industry is one of admiration.”

“I think that there is a real opportunity, if we so choose, and it’s one of many, many opportunities that Canada and the United States have to co-operate and to become fertilizer-independent,” Carney said.

“Not just potash, but across all ammonia and other fertilizers. That would be good for Canadian farmers, it would be great for American farmers.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 22, 2026.

— With files from The Associated Press

In a wide-ranging speech, Trump defended his war on Iran and boasted of American strength, claiming that “while others have talked, I have acted.”

He celebrated the U.S. military operation to oust Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro earlier this year and a new agreement to expand the American military presence in Greenland, which came after his threats of annexation.
But those actions have upended U.S. relationships with other nations, including traditional allies. Many of those allies have used the United Nations forum to call for a return to international law.

This 81st Session of the United Nations General Assembly is taking place as the world grapples with oil supply shocks and rising prices driven by the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, and under the shadow of Trump’s constant attacks on multilateralism.
Canada, like most countries, has not been able to escape the geopolitical effects of Trump’s erratic deployment of military force and tariffs.
Prime Minister Mark Carney said one of the shared challenges of the moment is a multilateral system that doesn’t reflect the times and cannot respond to them.
“But at the same time, the need for multilateral co-operation is very much alive,” Carney told reporters on Tuesday.

Carney — who has emerged in recent weeks as a key global champion of multilateralism and alliances in the face of Trump’s repeated attacks — said no one country, no matter how powerful, can manage the world’s challenges alone.

“Co-operation, therefore, is not an act of idealism. It is a practical necessity,” he said. “And the question is not whether multilateralism can survive but how it must evolve to meet the challenges of the moment.”

Trump has demanded massive reforms at the UN and has held back funding for the institution, putting it in turmoil. The Trump administration has withdrawn from multiple UN organizations, including the World Health Organization.
Carney, meanwhile, has been making the case for continued global collaboration to address crises like climate change, financial instability and war.

For nearly a year now, Carney has been travelling the globe calling on middle powers to band together in defence of what he has called “shared interests, and occasionally shared values, rather than shared institutions.”
Carney has sought to build a bridge between the European Union and a Pacific Rim trading bloc called CPTPP so middle powers can better resist economic coercion by the United States and China.
The prime minister’s efforts have caught the attention of the Trump administration, especially since trade negotiations between Canada and the United States ended acrimoniously last month.

After European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen last week opened the door to Canada becoming what she called the first “associate member” of the European Union, Trump said it could be a “hostile act.”

Carney did not hold any official meetings with Trump or members of the U.S. administration while in New York this week — his first return to the United States since trade negotiations fell apart last month.
The prime minister said during a gathering of global leaders “it’s most valuable to meet those who you don’t normally see.”

Carney held bilateral meetings with Chilean President Jose Antonio Kast and Angola President Joao Lourenco on the sidelines of the assembly. He also met with King of Jordan Abdullah II and a delegation from the United Arab Emirates.

Earlier Tuesday, Carney was quickly greeted by Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese when he arrived for the opening of the General Assembly. He also walked across the floor to speak with Crown Prince of the State of Kuwait Sabah Al-Khalid Al-Sabah before formal speeches began.

Carney co-hosted with France and the United Kingdom an event on the two-state solution — one year after the three countries recognized an independent Palestinian state at the General Assembly. More than 150 countries followed the move to recognize Palestinian statehood.

At the General Assembly last year, Trump said recognizing a Palestinian state would amount to rewarding Hamas for the “horrible atrocities” of the Oct. 7, 2023, attack on Israel. Trump also claimed the move could hinder Canada’s ability to make a trade deal with the United States.
Canada and the United States now seem further than ever from reaching that deal. Bilateral relations have continued to deteriorate as the trade war has escalated.

Trump, meanwhile, partially walked back remarks he’d made on social media about getting potash from Belarus instead of Canada. During a bilateral meeting on Tuesday with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Trump said “we’ll continue to go with Canada (for potash), but Belarus would like to sell it for a much lower price.”
Asked about Trump’s change of tone, Carney said “the Canadian potash industry is one of admiration.”

“I think that there is a real opportunity, if we so choose, and it’s one of many, many opportunities that Canada and the United States have to co-operate and to become fertilizer-independent,” Carney said.
“Not just potash, but across all ammonia and other fertilizers. That would be good for Canadian farmers, it would be great for American farmers.”
This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 22, 2026.
— With files from The Associated Press
Kelly Geraldine Malone, The Canadian Press
