stories.title: B.C. NDP caucus meets to discuss potential early election after Findlay resignation
stories.summary: Conservative board of directors appointed MLA Lorne Doerkson as interim leader
stories.author: Wolfgang Depner
stories.content:
The caucus of British Columbia’s governing NDP has met to discuss a potential early election after the resignation of Opposition B.C. Conservative leader Kerry-Lynne Findlay.

Findlay quit Sunday, saying it was the right move for the party and province, and the Conservative board of directors appointed MLA Lorne Doerkson as interim leader hours later.

But the Conservative constitution prohibits an interim head from seeking the party’s leadership in a subsequent ballot, so if an election is called soon, the official Opposition candidate for premier would not immediately be clear.

Findlay’s resignation follows weeks of upheaval in the Conservative caucus, with 13 defections or expulsions, including former leader John Rustad, who was ejected with two others on Friday.

Rustad is set to address reporters in Victoria today.

Gary Mason: The shocking implosion of B.C.’s Conservative Party

NDP MLAs met last night to discuss Findlay’s departure, according to an email from party staff that was inadvertently sent to all legislators on Sunday, instead of just those on the government benches.

“I’m sure you’ve seen by now, but KLF has resigned as leader of the BC Conservatives,” the email obtained by The Canadian Press says.

It goes on to say the meeting was to “to discuss and hear from Cheryl and her team,” an apparent reference to Cheryl Oates, Premier David Eby’s former chief of staff, who has been appointed to manage the NDP campaign for the next election, whenever it is held.

Eby said last week that he told his legislators they need to be “election ready.”

Doerkson was first elected in the riding of Cariboo—Chilcotin in 2020 as a member of the BC Liberal party, which rebranded as B.C. United, before crossing the floor to join the Conservatives and being reelected in 2024.

stories.title: ‘Blood potash’: Scott Moe reacts to Trump’s Belarus deal
stories.summary: U.S. President Donald Trump says he is working on a “massive deal” to purchase potash from Belarus.
stories.author: Kayla Thompson
stories.content:
U.S. President Donald Trump says he is working on a “massive deal” to purchase potash from Belarus.

“The pricing would be for substantially less than we are currently paying to Canada, very good news for our Farmers and Ranchers,” he posted to Truth Social on Monday .

Canada is the leading exporter of potash, shipping about 22.9 million tonnes in 2024, accounting for over 39 per cent of global exports according to the Government of Canada.

The leading destination of Canadian exports of potash is the United States. The U.S. imports nearly 85 per cent of its potash from Canada.

Belarus ranks third in potash production behind Russia and Canada.

According to Belarusian media reports Monday , President Alexander Lukashenko said even if there was a desire to enter Western markets, there is nothing left to supply.

Reuters reported that potash from Belarus remains under EU sanctions , and the landlocked country has been barred from exporting via the Lithuanian port of Klaipeda since February 2022.

Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe, whose province provides the U.S. with more than 86 per cent of its potash supply from Canada, said Trump’s tentative deal is “wrong and it doesn’t make sense.”

“More than 40 countries - Canada and its allies - have sanctions against Belarus for supporting war criminal Putin’s invasion of Ukraine. Buying blood potash from Belarus is supporting Russian aggression,” he posted to X Monday afternoon.

“Does anyone believe Belarusian blood potash shipped through Russia is going to be more affordable, more sustainable or more ethical than potash shipped from Saskatchewan - right here in North America?”

More than 40 countries - Canada and its allies - have sanctions against Belarus for supporting war criminal Putin’s invasion of Ukraine. Buying blood potash from Belarus is supporting Russian aggression. It’s wrong and it doesn’t make sense. All of that potash has to be… pic.twitter.com/Omat5YxNOq — Scott Moe (@PremierScottMoe) September 21, 2026

Potash leverage in U.S.-Canada trade war

In June, Trump told reporters that there is nothing the U.S. needs from Canada. However, U.S. Ambassador Pete Hoekstra said America needs a “tremendous amount of things” including Canadian potash, since there are “not lots of other places that you can get it.”

Canada’s premiers have been at odds about whether to leverage the critical mineral against the U.S. amid trade war tensions.

While Ontario Premier Doug Ford has previously pushed to retaliate against Trump’s tariffs by cutting U.S. access to electricity, oil and other minerals, Alberta Premier Danielle Smith and Moe said they were concerned about the long-term consequences for those industries.

Canada’s 10 active potash mines are located in Saskatchewan.

Moe has said the province would not support any kind of export taxes or withholding supply for the U.S., as losing its biggest customer would cause job losses, price hikes and a tremendous hit to the local economy.

“The United States of America, most assuredly, would switch to buying potash from other nations around the world. We would lose a long-term customer to some degree,” Moe said during trade talks.

Smith also echoed Moe in July, when she told reporters oil and potash being used as retaliatory measures is “not going to happen.”

Canadian potash has remained exempt from Trump’s tariffs amid the ongoing trade war. However, the U.S. looking to Belarus for potash supply signifies the latest escalation.

The move comes after Prime Minister Mark Carney welcomed the “ambition” to become the European Union’s first associate member, which Trump said he’ll retaliate against if he deems it to be a “hostile act.”

The U.S., Canada and EU have all imposed sanctions on Belarus for its crackdown on human rights and for allowing its territory to be used by Russia for its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

However, in December 2025, the U.S. agreed to lift sanctions on Belarusian potash, after Lukashenko freed 123 prisoners with the help of Trump’s envoy.

With files from The Canadian Press

stories.title: Tiff 2026 exposed festival’s stellar cinematic taste, and worst institutional instincts
stories.summary: This year’s festival felt as if it was using a handful of exhilarating moments to paper over many, larger structural fissures and fault lines
stories.author: Barry Hertz
stories.content:
Halfway into the new historical drama La Bola Negra , which follows three generations of gay Spanish men as they wrestle with devastation and desire, Penélope Cruz shows up for 10 minutes and brings the house down. Playing a 1930s showgirl who bewitches a troupe of soldiers during the Spanish Civil War, the actress delivers a quick but enduring jolt of energy to Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi’s feature – a movie that, while beautiful in its aesthetics and epic in its construction, mostly feels distended and reaching for a profundity just beyond its grasp.

It is that defining tension of La Bola Negra – a wannabe showstopper in which you can see its seams stretch and fray as it struggles to please its eager crowd – that was top of mind Sunday as the Toronto International Film Festival closed out its 51st edition by awarding Calvo and Ambrossi’s movie its coveted People’s Choice Award . Like the film that it was honouring, this year’s TIFF seemed, from a distance, to be a rather gorgeous, glamorous and highly ambitious affair. But upon closer inspection, TIFF 2026 also felt as if it was using a handful of exhilarating moments of Cruz-like potency to paper over many larger, structural fissures and fault lines .

We can start with La Bola Negra ’s own curious path from Cannes to the People’s Choice Award, a seeming moment of triumph that was offset by confusion when it was announced, just seconds before, that the British drama Elsinore had won the International People’s Choice Award.

Last year, TIFF organizers introduced a new “international” version of the PCA, in which audiences vote for the best festival film produced outside of Canada and the United States. Theoretically, this allows TIFF to spotlight foreign titles that might otherwise be overshadowed by the winner of the “real” PCA, which has long been considered an Oscars bellwether and has often gone to an English-language movie made in the Hollywood system.

But in practice, the new international award feels both confounding – unless you’ve read the fine print of the eligibility rules, you’d be rightly perplexed as to why the Spanish-language La Bola Negra won the “real” PCA, and the English-language Elsinore earned the international version – and nakedly opportunistic. TIFF is not spreading the wealth here for filmmakers, but for its own reputation as an Oscars kingmaker. Why settle for saying that your festival can cement the Academy Awards chances for one film when you can boast that you solidify the prospects for two?

Well, because almost everyone in the industry can see straight through the ploy. Just as all those players are taking an especially hard look at TIFF’s other big recent initiative, albeit one engineered and executed on a far grander scale: the launch of an official market .

The inaugural edition of TIFF: The Market, which ran parallel to the festival’s official screenings, gathered buyers, sellers and creators of film and TV under the roof of the Metro Toronto Convention Centre for seven days of meetings and potential deal-making. But if organizers hope that TIFF’s market will eventually match the reputation (and earned revenues) of Berlin’s European Film Market and the Marché du Film in Cannes, they’re going to need to embrace some sizable course corrections.

Not only did attendees highlight serious technical issues – hours-long waits to pick up badges, an app that felt designed in a hurry – but, to borrow the language of the industry’s coveted Gen Y demographic, the vibe was off.

Between a lack of foot traffic, a sizable portion of the convention floor being taken up by a sparsely populated food court, and too many stands occupied not by highly valued sales agencies, production companies or buyers but various countries’ national film bodies (Telefilm’s space was easily the busiest), the space often felt like a particularly sleepy version of a tourism conference. Sure, the high-profile Paris-based Goodfellas sales agency and production company had a large pavilion in the centre of the floor, but also a noticeable lack of on-site activity. Any producer hoping to score a connection from a walk-up there would likely need to keep on, well, walking.

Already, TIFF seems eager to crown the market an out-of-the-gate success – but in its rush to do so, organizers appear to have tripped over some key figures.

According to a press release sent Friday, market chief Charles Tremblay noted that 7,010 industry delegates were registered this year, a 40 per cent increase compared to TIFF’s “informal, previous offering, which typically drew 5,000 people to the city.” Yet according to TIFF’s own numbers from its 2025 edition, the festival attracted 6,000 industry delegates last year, making the actual jump in attendance just 16 per cent. At the same time, about 200 delegates, mostly international buyers who had either never attended TIFF or not been in several years, had their travel and accommodation subsidized. Will they return on their own dime?

Market organizers also boasted that the exhibition floor contained 238 exhibitors. But the official convention centre directory only listed about 100, depending on how you counted outfits that shared pavilion space and whether you included filmmakers participating in the “Innovation Hub” showcasing interactive media projects.

Meanwhile, higher-end companies, including AGC Studios, WME and StudioCanal, were holed up on floors inside the InterContinental and Ritz-Carlton hotels – spaces not quite as accessible and amenable to the kind of pop-in meetings that participation in the market intimated.

Then there were the market-only screenings, in which sellers paid TIFF to show films designed to spark buyer interest – presentations that represent a key revenue driver for the market and can act as a barometer of industry activity. Last year, TIFF said it would provide 650 market screening slots . But in the recently released figures, organizers said just 196 were booked, suggesting a lack of appetite compared to available inventory. (Even if that 650 figure included both private market-only screenings and the festival’s combined “press and market” screenings, for which every film in the official program receives at least one , then initial expectations were still not met.)

Finally, if the market was intended to spark a flurry of bidding wars that would prove Toronto to be an unmissable stop on the global industry calendar, then organizers can only so far point to the sale of a movie that was not technically up for sale at all: the horror movie River , which Universal paid US$10-million to acquire from IFC, which already had the film’s distribution rights coming into TIFF. (It is not unprecedented for a smaller distributor to give up a film to a larger company, but it is highly unusual; IFC must have figured that the deal was more than they’d be able to earn if they released the film on their own.)

The market was launched with significant support from the federal government, but Ottawa’s three-year $23-million commitment runs out this coming March . With or without Prime Minister Mark Carney’s help, TIFF will have to be flexible in vision if it hopes to keep the event going, let alone growing to a projected target of 12,000 delegates by 2030.

It is not even unreasonable to wonder, given where the industry winds appear to be blowing, whether TIFF should have accepted the federal cash in the first place and instead focused on sustaining its core asset, the festival. There is a pattern inside the organization, it feels, of introducing a new problem for itself instead of finding a solution to the challenges it already has.

Thankfully, one of TIFF’s longest continuing challenges – its programming – wasn’t as thorny this time around. Sure, Toronto missed out on a handful of titles that burnished the reputations of its festival-circuit rivals (Venice had the headline-making documentary NAZA ; Telluride had the buzzy Nathan Fielder/Elizabeth Holmes doc You Can See Everything ; New York will soon debut the OpenAI docudrama Artificial ). But for the most part, nearly every prestige fall title available made its way onto TIFF screens.

Watching Mahershala Ali’s Muslim hitman destroy legions of racist henchmen in Bassam Tariq’s audacious Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother was a surreal delight. Peeling back the layers of class and contempt nestled inside Lee Chang-dong’s Possible Love was a beguiling experience. Discovering an emerging Canadian director such as Toy Gun Bandit ’ s Rémi St-Michel was a real-time thrill. And seeing the 83-year-old Mike Leigh standing proud inside the Lightbox Cinema 1 after the premiere of his latest, and possibly final, drama Tender Loving Care was a singular privilege.

Of course, there was bloat – any festival with nearly 300 titles will do that – and there were a handful of selections that called into question the faculties of its programmers. Bring me the head of whoever approved Zack Snyder’s irredeemable The Last Photograph . And we’ve got to find out what is going on with the Gala slate, whose selections are instantly vaporized from memory.

But there were enough startling, pinch-me moments of cinematic joy to prove that TIFF is an institution worth fighting for. And that work needs to begin now – no matter how far La Bola Negra (or Elsinore) goes in the Oscar race.

paragraphs: Halfway into the new historical drama La Bola Negra , which follows three generations of gay Spanish men as they wrestle with devastation and desire, Penélope Cruz shows up for 10 minutes and brings the house down. Playing a 1930s showgirl who bewitches a troupe of soldiers during the Spanish Civil War, the actress delivers a quick but enduring jolt of energy to Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi’s feature – a movie that, while beautiful in its aesthetics and epic in its construction, mostly feels distended and reaching for a profundity just beyond its grasp.

It is that defining tension of La Bola Negra – a wannabe showstopper in which you can see its seams stretch and fray as it struggles to please its eager crowd – that was top of mind Sunday as the Toronto International Film Festival closed out its 51st edition by awarding Calvo and Ambrossi’s movie its coveted People’s Choice Award . Like the film that it was honouring, this year’s TIFF seemed, from a distance, to be a rather gorgeous, glamorous and highly ambitious affair. But upon closer inspection, TIFF 2026 also felt as if it was using a handful of exhilarating moments of Cruz-like potency to paper over many larger, structural fissures and fault lines .

We can start with La Bola Negra ’s own curious path from Cannes to the People’s Choice Award, a seeming moment of triumph that was offset by confusion when it was announced, just seconds before, that the British drama Elsinore had won the International People’s Choice Award.

Last year, TIFF organizers introduced a new “international” version of the PCA, in which audiences vote for the best festival film produced outside of Canada and the United States. Theoretically, this allows TIFF to spotlight foreign titles that might otherwise be overshadowed by the winner of the “real” PCA, which has long been considered an Oscars bellwether and has often gone to an English-language movie made in the Hollywood system.

But in practice, the new international award feels both confounding – unless you’ve read the fine print of the eligibility rules, you’d be rightly perplexed as to why the Spanish-language La Bola Negra won the “real” PCA, and the English-language Elsinore earned the international version – and nakedly opportunistic. TIFF is not spreading the wealth here for filmmakers, but for its own reputation as an Oscars kingmaker. Why settle for saying that your festival can cement the Academy Awards chances for one film when you can boast that you solidify the prospects for two?

Well, because almost everyone in the industry can see straight through the ploy. Just as all those players are taking an especially hard look at TIFF’s other big recent initiative, albeit one engineered and executed on a far grander scale: the launch of an official market .

The inaugural edition of TIFF: The Market, which ran parallel to the festival’s official screenings, gathered buyers, sellers and creators of film and TV under the roof of the Metro Toronto Convention Centre for seven days of meetings and potential deal-making. But if organizers hope that TIFF’s market will eventually match the reputation (and earned revenues) of Berlin’s European Film Market and the Marché du Film in Cannes, they’re going to need to embrace some sizable course corrections.

Not only did attendees highlight serious technical issues – hours-long waits to pick up badges, an app that felt designed in a hurry – but, to borrow the language of the industry’s coveted Gen Y demographic, the vibe was off.

Between a lack of foot traffic, a sizable portion of the convention floor being taken up by a sparsely populated food court, and too many stands occupied not by highly valued sales agencies, production companies or buyers but various countries’ national film bodies (Telefilm’s space was easily the busiest), the space often felt like a particularly sleepy version of a tourism conference. Sure, the high-profile Paris-based Goodfellas sales agency and production company had a large pavilion in the centre of the floor, but also a noticeable lack of on-site activity. Any producer hoping to score a connection from a walk-up there would likely need to keep on, well, walking.
Already, TIFF seems eager to crown the market an out-of-the-gate success – but in its rush to do so, organizers appear to have tripped over some key figures.

According to a press release sent Friday, market chief Charles Tremblay noted that 7,010 industry delegates were registered this year, a 40 per cent increase compared to TIFF’s “informal, previous offering, which typically drew 5,000 people to the city.” Yet according to TIFF’s own numbers from its 2025 edition, the festival attracted 6,000 industry delegates last year, making the actual jump in attendance just 16 per cent. At the same time, about 200 delegates, mostly international buyers who had either never attended TIFF or not been in several years, had their travel and accommodation subsidized. Will they return on their own dime?

Market organizers also boasted that the exhibition floor contained 238 exhibitors. But the official convention centre directory only listed about 100, depending on how you counted outfits that shared pavilion space and whether you included filmmakers participating in the “Innovation Hub” showcasing interactive media projects.

Meanwhile, higher-end companies, including AGC Studios, WME and StudioCanal, were holed up on floors inside the InterContinental and Ritz-Carlton hotels – spaces not quite as accessible and amenable to the kind of pop-in meetings that participation in the market intimated.

Then there were the market-only screenings, in which sellers paid TIFF to show films designed to spark buyer interest – presentations that represent a key revenue driver for the market and can act as a barometer of industry activity. Last year, TIFF said it would provide 650 market screening slots . But in the recently released figures, organizers said just 196 were booked, suggesting a lack of appetite compared to available inventory. (Even if that 650 figure included both private market-only screenings and the festival’s combined “press and market” screenings, for which every film in the official program receives at least one , then initial expectations were still not met.)

Finally, if the market was intended to spark a flurry of bidding wars that would prove Toronto to be an unmissable stop on the global industry calendar, then organizers can only so far point to the sale of a movie that was not technically up for sale at all: the horror movie River , which Universal paid US$10-million to acquire from IFC, which already had the film’s distribution rights coming into TIFF. (It is not unprecedented for a smaller distributor to give up a film to a larger company, but it is highly unusual; IFC must have figured that the deal was more than they’d be able to earn if they released the film on their own.)

The market was launched with significant support from the federal government, but Ottawa’s three-year $23-million commitment runs out this coming March . With or without Prime Minister Mark Carney’s help, TIFF will have to be flexible in vision if it hopes to keep the event going, let alone growing to a projected target of 12,000 delegates by 2030.

It is not even unreasonable to wonder, given where the industry winds appear to be blowing, whether TIFF should have accepted the federal cash in the first place and instead focused on sustaining its core asset, the festival. There is a pattern inside the organization, it feels, of introducing a new problem for itself instead of finding a solution to the challenges it already has.

Thankfully, one of TIFF’s longest continuing challenges – its programming – wasn’t as thorny this time around. Sure, Toronto missed out on a handful of titles that burnished the reputations of its festival-circuit rivals (Venice had the headline-making documentary NAZA ; Telluride had the buzzy Nathan Fielder/Elizabeth Holmes doc You Can See Everything ; New York will soon debut the OpenAI docudrama Artificial ). Peeling back the layers of class and contempt nestled inside Lee Chang-dong’s Possible Love was a beguiling experience. Discovering an emerging Canadian director such as Toy Gun Bandit ’ s Rémi St-Michel was a real-time thrill. And seeing the 83-year-old Mike Leigh standing proud inside the Lightbox Cinema 1 after the premiere of his latest, and possibly final, drama Tender Loving Care was a singular privilege.

Of course, there was bloat – any festival with nearly 300 titles will do that – and there were a handful of selections that called into question the faculties of its programmers. Bring me the head of whoever approved Zack Snyder’s irredeemable The Last Photograph . And we’ve got to find out what is going on with the Gala slate, whose selections are instantly vaporized from memory.

But there were enough startling, pinch-me moments of cinematic joy to prove that TIFF is an institution worth fighting for. And that work needs to begin now – no matter how far La Bola Negra (or Elsinore) goes in the Oscar race.

stories.title: 'Bang! Bang! Bang!': Witnesses recount confusion, gunshots during Belleville synagogue shooting
stories.summary: "I yelled for everyone to get on the floor, to crouch right down," said the synagogue's president.
stories.author: Courtney Greenberg
stories.content:
One resident told National Post he saw an officer on a stretcher being carried into the back of an ambulance

“Bang! Bang! Bang!”

Norman Weddum recalled the sound of bullets hitting the stained glass at the Sons of Jacob Synagogue in Belleville, Ont., ON Yom Kippur, the holiest day of the year for the Jewish community.

Weddum, who has been the synagogue’s president for the past eight years, attended the Sunday-night service with around 25 congregants.

When he first arrived, he said he spoke briefly to the police officer who was stationed in front of the building. He said he thanked him for being there. “We (request an officer) when we have a lot of people in the building, just for safety concerns,” he told National Post.

The choice to proactively have an officer at Sons of Jacob comes after several targeted shootings at synagogues across Canada. One person at the scene, a security guard, told Belleville publication The Intelligencer that he believed it was that officer who intercepted the suspect.

By the time Weddum walked into the building, it was 6:45 p.m.

Congregants were ushered into the inner sanctuary of the synagogue around 7 p.m. for the prayer service to start.

“At that point, that’s when the first, ‘Bang! Bang! Bang!’ started, and we all kind of stopped in our tracks,” he said.

And then another round of shots.

A handful of congregants, including Weddum, went out into the main lobby to see what had occurred. Again, they heard the same noise. “And this time it was so loud and deafening … that there was no question that was shot being fired.”

They ran back into the area where the service was being held and shut the doors.

“I yelled for everyone to get on the floor, to crouch right down,” said Weddum. The shots were still being fired and they could hear it hitting the stained glass windows that decorated the outer part of the synagogue.

The shooting stopped eventually, after what felt like hours. “We waited and waited,” said Weddum.

He could see a heavy police presence outside.

“There were two officers who were tending to an injured officer that was sitting on the ground,” he said.

While Weddum said he never expected such an incident to occur in Belleville, another congregant and Belleville resident Doug Lobel told National Post he “almost predicted this was going to happen.”

Lobel was also at the synagogue on Sunday night, with his wife, Eva.

He was walking into the service when he heard loud noises. He said it was confusing because they heard “a lot of shots” but had no idea what was going on outside.

“Sitting there, we hear, ‘Pop! Pop! Pop!’ We don’t know if there’s only one shooter. For me the biggest concern was … are they going to get into the building?”

He said when the shooting stopped, police entered to do a sweep of the building. Congregants were taken by bus to the police station and then dropped off at home.

“(The mayor’s) response was really tone deaf because he said if you don’t feel safe contact the Belleville police,” said Lobel.

In a statement to National Post, Ellis said that he could not comment on the details of an individual interaction, but the “concerns about safety and antisemitism are taken seriously.”

“The safety and security of everyone in our community is our highest priority,” the mayor’s statement continued. “The Belleville Police Service is responsible for public safety and for responding to incidents such as this, and I have the utmost confidence in their professionalism and their ability to keep our community safe.”

She texted him anxiously just after 7 p.m. He decided to go to the scene to see what was going on and arrived near the synagogue around 7:20 p.m. He saw officers with their guns drawn.

One yelled at him: “Get out of here! Get out of here! There’s an active shooter!”

Gannon said he could still see smoke in the air and smell gun powder. He saw an officer on a stretcher being carried into the back of an ambulance. The officer was awake but seemed like he was in pain, he said.

“We’ve never had anything like this. This is like a first for Belleville,” he said. “Small town. Everybody’s friendly here. We’ve had shootings before but nothing this major.”

On Monday, he said police continued to scour the area.

“It just seems like there’s so much hate out there right now in the world,” he said. “You can just sense it. If you go online, it’s everywhere.”

A woman identified by her first name, Jose, was at home nearby when she heard a total of 25 to 30 gunshots, she told The Intelligencer . She said it sounded like two different kinds of weapons, perhaps a shotgun and a handgun, exchanging fire.

“I stepped out on the porch to kind of see like where is it coming from … and I saw a truck driving off of the road onto the sidewalk,” she said.

She eventually called 911 after hearing more shots.

Another resident, identified by his first name, Sheldon, told the publication that he heard the shots at Meyers Pier. The pier is roughly 2.5 kilometres away from the synagogue. He went to the area where police lights were flashing to see what was happening. On two occasions, he said he saw people telling officers that their mothers were in the synagogue.

The synagogue remained closed Monday to the roughly 100 families who are members, Weddum said.

“We should have had all-day service and concluding tonight at sundown. But we can’t do that,” he said. “We’ll have services again. We will continue on. This is not going to stop us.”

On Monday, Belleville Police Service’s Deputy Chief Sheri Meeks identified the officer who was stationed outside the synagogue as Const. Jeff Smith. He is in critical but stable condition.

Because Smith and another officer discharged their weapons, the Special Investigations Unit (SIU), Ontario’s police watchdog, is leading the investigation.

SIU spokesperson Kristy Denette said it is believed that the 29-year-old suspect drove to the area in a truck and opened fire on Smith with a shotgun. A second officer arrived at the scene, followed shortly after by multiple other officers.

The suspect remains in hospital in life-threatening condition.

Belleville police said it could not comment further on the criminal side of the investigation at this time.

This comes nearly a year after a deadly terror attack at a synagogue in Manchester, England, ON Yom Kippur. On Oct. 2, 2025, two people were stabbed to death and a third was killed by police after being caught in the crossfire.

Later that year, in December, members of the Jewish community were celebrating Hannukah, known as the Festival of Lights, at Bondi Beach in Sydney, Australia, when more than a dozen were shot to death .

stories.title: Ontario to standardize entry-level truck driver training after auditor-general report
stories.summary: Scathing report showed the province was not effectively monitoring commercial truck driver training and licensing
stories.author: Liam Casey
stories.content:
The Ontario government says it will standardize commercial truck driver training in the wake of a scathing Auditor-General report that identified widespread issues with instruction and licensing in the province.

Ontario will work with industry stakeholders to develop a new curriculum aimed at strengthening road safety, Minister of Transportation Prabmeet Sarkaria said on Monday. But some representatives of the trucking industry say additional measures are required to address their concerns with training and oversight of commercial truck drivers.

The announcement follows a May report from provincial Auditor-General Shelley Spence, which found some private career colleges in Ontario were accrediting drivers without the minimum training requirements, and in some cases had altered student records to falsify their qualifications.

Currently, aspiring commercial truck drivers in Ontario must complete mandatory entry-level training, which consists of a minimum of 103.5 hours of instruction. Private career colleges must submit their curriculum details for approval to the Ministry of Colleges, Universities, Research Excellence and Security to ensure they meet provincial standards.

The Transport Ministry said that under the new approach schools will be required to follow a standardized curriculum that will include “more than 103 hours of clear, robust and consistent training.” The plan is expected to be implemented by early 2027, after consultation with industry stakeholders.

While large trucks represent about 3 per cent of all vehicles on provincial roads, they accounted for 12 per cent of all fatal collisions between 2019 and 2023, Ms. Spence’s report noted. Truck driver violations in Ontario have also spiked in recent years. For example, between 2020 and 2024, the percentage of truck drivers found in violation of rules requiring them to keep daily vehicle inspection logs increased by 135 per cent.

It is not clear how the new curriculum proposals will differ from the province’s existing practices, but the province said it is considering additional training subjects such as fatigue management and rural driving.

Rolf VanderZwaag, one of the architects of Ontario’s mandatory entry-level training standards, which were implemented in 2017, said the essential driving skills program he helped develop is “effectively a standardized curriculum.”

“Most Ontario schools already use it,” said Mr. VanderZwaag, who is the CEO of Techni-Com Inc., which produces compliance and training products for the trucking industry.

Mike Millian, president of the Private Motor Truck Council of Canada, a national association representing companies with in-house commercial trucking fleets, said any improvement in training standards are welcome.

However, additional reforms are urgently needed to address industry’s concerns around training and oversight, he said.

“Having a standardized curriculum is not what our key issue is. Our key issue is people aren’t following the curriculums that they’re submitting,” he said.

Around one quarter of the 216 private colleges offering truck driver training in the province had never been inspected by the provincial colleges ministry, the report found – noting the ministry employed just eight inspectors to audit all 595 private colleges in Ontario.

As part of the research conducted for the May report, Ms. Spence’s office sent students undercover to five unnamed private colleges and found that some students were not taught the required elements of truck driving, including reverse parking and emergency stopping.

As previously reported by The Globe, industry groups have called on the province to overhaul training and licensing procedures, and for the Transport Ministry to take full carriage of the file from the Ministry of Colleges and Universities.

The Private Motor Truck Council of Canada has called for more inspections at private career colleges and heftier fines for those who fail to meet provincial training standards for truck drivers.

Currently, private career colleges face fines of between $250 and $1,000 for first offences, according to the Auditor-General report.

In its statement Monday, the Transport Ministry said it was introducing a dedicated integrity manager for truck driver testing across the province and weekly reviews of commercial driver training schools.

The Professional Truck Training Alliance of Canada (Pttac), which advocates for progress in education and training in the transportation sector, has also called for numerous reforms, including stricter screening of aspiring drivers’ criminal record and driver abstracts. The organization has also advocated for testing instructors to be equipped with body cameras as a fraud prevention tactic, and has called for dual-facing cameras to be required in training vehicles.

“We want to continue to see improvement, but at the end of the day, regulation and compliance without any enforcement falls on deaf ears,” said Kim Richardson, a senior adviser to Pttac.

The Private Motor Truck Council’s Mr. Millian said any improvements to the provincial curriculum must include more one-on-one training time for drivers.

“The key area that we see as an issue in the industry is people’s ability to back up the vehicle and operate the truck safely up and down the highway,” he said.

After completing entry-level training, aspiring drivers must take road exams at DriveTest centres. These are run by a third-party provider, Serco, for the Transport Ministry.

As previously reported by The Globe, five employees of driver-licensing centres in Ontario were also charged earlier this year with allegedly accepting bribes to manipulate the results of commercial truck-driving tests.

Mr. Millian says Serco’s Brampton, Ont. testing campus already employs two integrity officers to prevent cheating on road tests.

“We have seen some increases in enforcement, which is welcome,” he said. “But we need to go further.”

stories.title: Police officer, suspect wounded in shooting near Belleville synagogue on Yom Kippur
stories.summary: Carney condemns incident as an alleged attack targeting the Jewish community
stories.author: Jill Mahoney
stories.content:
A shooting at a small synagogue on a residential street in Belleville, Ont., left a police officer in critical condition and bullet holes in the building’s stained-glass windows as worshippers gathered on Sunday night to mark Yom Kippur, the holiest day of the Jewish calendar.

A 29-year-old man armed with a shotgun opened fire on a policeman stationed outside the Sons of Jacob synagogue around 7:10 p.m., initiating a shootout, said Kristy Denette, spokeswoman for the Special Investigations Unit. The agency handles cases involving Ontario police that result in death or serious injury.

The suspect was also injured and is in hospital in life-threatening condition, according to the SIU. The officer, Constable Jeff Smith of the Belleville Police Service, is in critical but stable condition. A second officer also fired their weapon, Ms. Denette said.

“There are dozens of bullet holes in the street behind me, and some homes have been hit and there are some vehicles with shot-out windows, that sort of thing,” she told reporters. “So it would have been quite the scene.”

Prime Minister Mark Carney and other politicians condemned the shooting as an attack on the Jewish community. Canada has seen an increase in violence targeting Jewish institutions in recent months, including attacks at synagogues, schools and businesses. Many institutions have ramped up security for the high holidays. Police have so far not commented on a specific motive for the attack in Belleville.

Unlike most of the other attacks, which have targeted Jewish institutions in large urban areas, Sunday’s shooting occurred at a synagogue with a tiny congregation in a small city. The Sons of Jacob has a membership of roughly 35 families and doesn’t even have a part-time rabbi.

“Who would think it would happen here, of all places?” Norm Weddum, president of the congregation, said in an interview.

Less than half an hour before the attack, Mr. Weddum said hello to Constable Smith, who was stationed in the synagogue’s parking lot in an unmarked vehicle, and thanked him for his work.

Mr. Weddum said shooting erupted outside the synagogue as about 25 worshippers were milling around, about to begin evening prayers. He yelled at the crowd to take cover in the building’s sanctuary. Then, about 20 shots were fired through the synagogue’s front stained-glass windows, he said.

“All hell broke loose at that point,” he said. “We’re all crouched down. The glass is breaking.”

Among the crowd was Mary Cohen, the congregation’s treasurer, who dropped to the floor and then hid behind some curtains with her husband.

“It’s our most holy holiday of the year, and to experience something like that on this kind of a day, it’s a trauma to all the members,” she said.

Mr. Weddum credited Constable Smith with preventing a tragedy.

“If that officer had not been there, I probably wouldn’t be talking to you right now. Simple as that,” he said, adding, “That officer, he saved everyone’s lives in that building.”

Belleville Police Deputy Chief Sheri Meeks said Constable Smith is recovering in intensive care. He is part of the emergency response unit and a 12-year member of the police force.

“While he continues to face a significant road to recovery, his condition has stabilized, and we remain hopeful and encouraged by his progress,” she said.

Deputy Chief Meeks identified the suspect as Sean Ward, 29, of Quinte West, Ont.

Ms. Denette of the SIU said the suspect was critically injured in the shootout and had no vital signs, “but was sort of brought back to life, so to speak.”

The scene was cordoned off with yellow police tape Monday as police scoured the area for evidence. Ammunition casings and what appeared to be a long gun were still visible on the pavement, as were several vehicles with what looked like bullet scars and broken glass.

Scott Granville, who lives around the corner from the synagogue, was out for a walk Sunday evening when he heard an explosion of gunfire. He said he heard between 20 and 30 shots exchanged in a relatively short time.

“I knew right away that it was a shootout, not just shots, because there were different calibres. You could tell there were different guns going off,” Mr. Granville said.

Melissa Walker was working in her front yard on Victoria Street about a block away when she heard the gunfire and approached to see what was happening. She saw a gunman in a white T-shirt crouched low at the side of a vehicle, she said, as police fired at him from their location nearer to the synagogue.

“I saw him get shot,” Ms. Walker said.

“The closer I went, shots were still ringing out, and my body just told me not to go further.”

Then police pulled up and shouted at the suspect to get down, she said. At that point he was already down and looked to have been hit multiple times, she said. Then the officers kicked away what appeared to be a long gun, she added.

Darren Millar, who also lives nearby, said he was just around the corner sitting on his porch when he heard gunfire.

“I heard three loud explosions. I guess it was a shotgun, but it sounded like a bomb or a grenade or something. It was really loud. It was louder than any gun I’ve ever heard,” he said.

About 30 seconds after the shooting stopped, he jumped in his vehicle and drove down the street toward the synagogue. His dash cam captured the scene as three officers ran toward the suspect and two others stood over him as he lay on the ground.

Mr. Weddum said he sees the attack as targeting the Jewish community.

“We view it as a hate crime,” he said. “I mean, you know, a guy shows up on a Sunday, walking towards a synagogue that is packed due to the high holiday services, carrying a rifle. Now he is not out for a Sunday stroll.”

Deputy Chief Meeks said there was no threat to public safety but added that police have increased patrols in Belleville and are working closely with community leaders.

“Let me be very clear – antisemitism, hate and violence have no place in our community. Every person deserves to feel safe when attending a place of worship, gathering with loved ones or participating in community life,” she told reporters.

A national-security source told The Globe and Mail that the RCMP-led Integrated National Security Enforcement Team, which oversees terrorism investigations, was not involved in the Belleville investigation as of Monday. However, the source said the Ontario Provincial Police’s Provincial Anti-Terrorism Section is assisting. The Globe is not identifying the source because they were not authorized to discuss the matter publicly.

Mr. Carney condemned the shooting as an attack on the Jewish community.

“Jewish people must be able to worship safely. To live free, open, proud Jewish lives,” he said in a statement on Monday. “Canada’s government will do everything in our power to support law enforcement in ensuring that the perpetrator is held accountable to the fullest extent of the law.”

Ontario Premier Doug Ford paid tribute to the officer injured in the shooting, calling him a hero who “stopped a tragedy.”

“I find it disgusting, someone would go into a synagogue, or potentially go into a synagogue, ON Yom Kippur or any day, or any place of worship, it’s disgusting,” Mr. Ford told reporters at Queen’s Park on Monday.

He also said the suspect should face consequences: “Whoever the assailant was needs to be charged, and I don’t care if he’s in the hospital or not. Unacceptable.”

Probes into Toronto’s shooter-for-hire network thwarted by impenetrable phone, police source says

SIU investigators are canvassing for witnesses and plan to review footage from officers’ body-worn cameras and vehicles. Ms. Denette said the team expects to spend two days processing the scene.

“It’s quite a complex scene and there’s a lot of cartridge cases to collect,” she said. “There’s multiple firearms. There’s a number of vehicles that are involved.”

Meanwhile, police in Durham Region said Monday that they charged a 19-year-old man with making threats motivated by hate for alleged online posts about carrying out a shooting at an area synagogue.

“Let me be very clear – antisemitism, hate and violence have no place in our community. Every person deserves to feel safe when attending a place of worship, gathering with loved ones or participating in community life,” she told reporters.

content_blocks.caption: The SIU work the scene of the shooting on Monday. Sammy Kogan/The Globe and Mail

content_blocks.text: A national-security source told The Globe and Mail that the RCMP-led Integrated National Security Enforcement Team, which oversees terrorism investigations, was not involved in the Belleville investigation as of Monday. However, the source said the Ontario Provincial Police’s Provincial Anti-Terrorism Section is assisting. The Globe is not identifying the source because they were not authorized to discuss the matter publicly.
Mr. Carney condemned the shooting as an attack on the Jewish community.

“Jewish people must be able to worship safely. To live free, open, proud Jewish lives,” he said in a statement on Monday. “Canada’s government will do everything in our power to support law enforcement in ensuring that the perpetrator is held accountable to the fullest extent of the law.”
Ontario Premier Doug Ford paid tribute to the officer injured in the shooting, calling him a hero who “stopped a tragedy.”

“I find it disgusting, someone would go into a synagogue, or potentially go into a synagogue, ON Yom Kippur or any day, or any place of worship, it’s disgusting,” Mr. Ford told reporters at Queen’s Park on Monday.
He also said the suspect should face consequences: “Whoever the assailant was needs to be charged, and I don’t care if he’s in the hospital or not. Unacceptable.”
Probes into Toronto’s shooter-for-hire network thwarted by impenetrable phone, police source says
SIU investigators are canvassing for witnesses and plan to review footage from officers’ body-worn cameras and vehicles. Ms. Denette said the team expects to spend two days processing the scene.
“It’s quite a complex scene and there’s a lot of cartridge cases to collect,” she said. “There’s multiple firearms. There’s a number of vehicles that are involved.”
Meanwhile, police in Durham Region said Monday that they charged a 19-year-old man with making threats motivated by hate for alleged online posts about carrying out a shooting at an area synagogue.
With reports from Laura Stone, Mercedes Stephenson and Tu Thanh Ha

stories.title: Grain, oil exports fuel record cargo volumes at Port of Vancouver amid shift from U.S.
stories.summary: U.S. accounted for only a fifth of crude exports through Vancouver terminals versus one-third the year before
stories.author: Christopher Reynolds
stories.content:
The head of the Vancouver Fraser Port Authority says surging oil and grain exports drove a record amount of cargo through its gates in the first half of the year as part of a push away from U.S. markets, with Alberta crude fuelling the pivot.

Freight volumes at the Port of Vancouver rode a rising tide of crude oil and canola seed to a three per cent year-over-year increase for the six months ended June 30, the federal agency said Monday.

Port authority chief executive Peter Xotta described “a degree of focus and urgency” to hauling loads – fossil fuels included – to and from countries that lie beyond North American shores.

“The U.S. percentage of crude oil shipments is declining ... as those global destinations for Alberta crude increase,” he said in a phone interview from Canada Place, which overlooks Vancouver Harbour.

“China and other Asian destinations are playing a pretty significant role in that.”

As Asia’s oil intake swelled by 24 per cent – America’s shrank, a marked change from 2025. The share of U.S.-bound crude exports via Vancouver dropped to one-fifth versus a third the year before, Xotta said.

In the first half of 2026, crude oil exports from the port rose three per cent year-over-year to a record 12 million tonnes. The increase comes after the Trans Mountain expansion – the twinned pipeline runs between Edmonton and Burnaby, B.C. – opened the floodgate to fossil fuel shipments bound for China and South Korea in 2024.

“The Trans Mountain expansion is really continuing to be a much more dominant commodity in the gateway than we have experienced historically,” Xotta said.

Crude exports accounted for most of the port’s petroleum shipments, but aviation fuel imports also shot up by a quarter as airlines were forced to source their kerosene from regions other than the Middle East, where the Iran war has slowed exports to a trickle. Aviation fuel shipments from South Korea alone jumped 305 per cent to roughly 160,000 tonnes – approaching half of the total – according to the port authority.

Meanwhile, bulk grain exports leaped 14 per cent year-over-year to a record 17.4 million tonnes by the end of June.

“Canadian agriculture is really surging, partly on the back of good crop outcomes in the last year, and frankly the last two years,” Xotta said.

China, Japan and South Korea remained the traditional big consumers of Canadian bulk grain. But containerized shipments of lentils, peas and beans grew by nearly two-thirds as countries such as Bangladesh, India and other “emerging markets” ratcheted up their imports, the CEO said. Europe and Mexico also took in boatloads of canola seed, on top of China.

Beijing imposed 100 per cent tariffs on Canadian canola oil in March 2025 in retaliation for Ottawa’s levies on Chinese electric vehicles, and topped it off with a 76 per cent anti-dumping duty on canola seed in August of that year.

China has since lowered the duty on seeds to 15 per cent, but kept the 100 per cent tariff on canola oil – a barrier that helps explain the 14 per cent year-over-year dip in vegetable and animal oil volumes shipped through Vancouver.

Shipments of chemicals, basic metals and minerals slumped three per cent year-over-year, partly due to U.S. tariffs on steel and aluminum, Xotta said.

Auto volumes through the port rose 10 per cent year-over-year in the first half of 2026, as carmakers sought alternatives to the U.S. market and imports from Japan and South Korea spiked.

Container imports rose two per cent and exports four per cent, a sign of “resilience in the face of an uncertain and unpredictable geopolitical landscape,” Xotta said, noting that the port handles about half of the country’s two-way container trade.

Faced with a more protectionist United States, he said he wants to help Canada double its exports to non-U.S. markets within a decade.

The share of trade to America via the port “for sure” is not on the rise, he said. The United States accounted for less than 15 per cent of Port of Vancouver shipments, roughly on par with the first half of 2025, port figures show.

Americans themselves remain eager to come north. Cruise operations at the port were on course for the busiest season ever, with a record 141 ships depositing 560,000 passengers – at least 60 per cent of them U.S. residents, often en route to Alaska, Xotta said – from February through June.

stories.content:
OPP are advising of a road closure in Elgin County following a multi-vehicle crash.

According to police, Highway 3 is closed in both directions between Yarmouth Centre Road and Tower Road between St. Thomas and Aylmer.

OPP are asking motorists to plan alternate routes.

No details have been shared as it relates to how many vehicles are involved or possible injuries.

More information will be provided as it becomes available.

stories.title: Belleville synagogue shooting live: Exchange of gunfire between man armed with rifle and officer; SIU to provide update
stories.summary: The shooting near the Sons of Jacob Synagogue on Sunday night happened as many were gathering for Yom Kippur, one of the holiest days in the Jewish faith.
stories.author: Star staff
stories.content:
Authorities in Belleville are investigating after an exchange of gunfire between a man armed with a rifle and police officers near a synagogue Sunday evening, as many were gathering for Yom Kippur, one of the holiest days in the Jewish faith.

This file is no longer being updated.

A forensics officer points toward a police vehicle (out of frame) at the scene of a shooting on Monday in Belleville.

The Belleville tragedy was front and centre during Monday’s question period as the country’s top political leaders met for the first time in months in the House of Commons.

Opposition leader Pierre Poilievre expressed condolences and condemnation of the shooting, hailing the “courageous” actions of Const. Jeff Smith, saying “the Jewish people deserve to live in freedom and peace as they express their faith.” He called on Prime Minister Mark Carney to join him in expressing “prayers and love” for Smith, support for the Jewish community and condemnation of “all forms of violence.”

Carney echoed Poilievre, saying the government stands ”against all forms of hate, all forms of violence.” He added, “May this House continue to come together to support the Jewish community in Canada and all Canadians to live their full lives.”

A 19-year-old man was arrested over the weekend after an online threat was made to carry out a shooting at a Durham region synagogue, police said on Monday.

The announcement of the arrest comes less than a day after police in Belleville responded to a shooting outside a synagogue as many were gathering to observe Yom Kippur on Sunday evening.

On Saturday, officers were made aware of threats posted to an online message board, Durham police wrote in a news release . The man was arrested at his residence the following day on Saturday and was charged with threats motivated by hate.

He was held for a bail hearing, police said. Durham police said it has increased their presence outside places of worships in the region for the Jewish High Holidays.

Local residents speak about what they witnessed at a shooting in Belleville on Sunday evening.

It was a chaotic scene according to one witness who lives near the Belleville synagogue where shots rang out on Sunday evening.

Melissa Walker was outside doing yard work when the shots rang out at about 7 p.m.

“I heard gunshots and pops and I just kind of thought, is that fireworks? Like, what’s going on? And I kind of went out to the sidewalk and went a little closer and that’s when I saw people. I saw the suspect behind the car and gunshots were ringing out,” said Walker, who ran inside to get her phone and called police.

“I called and I ran a little bit further up, and I witnessed him get shot,” said Walker, who said the suspect was behind an older model Honda CRV. “He was actually just hiding, he was crouching behind that car, and I saw him get shot, he went down, I was going to run up and help, because I didn’t know what was going on,” said Walker.

She said then officers arrived, surrounded the man and started yelling.

“They kicked his gun away. To me, he was deceased. I don’t know why they’re saying that he’s alive. They didn’t give him any medical attention. He was on the ground, no movement, nothing, for about five minutes. And then the paramedics pulled up, loaded his body on, and that was it,” said Walker.

According to police at an afternoon press conference, the shooter was “vital signs absent,” but paramedics helped revive him and he is currently in critical condition.

A man at the scene showed the Star dashcam footage that shows a man lying on roadway near the entrance of the synagogue while two police officers with their firearms drawn stood over him. Several officers with their weapons drawn were also seen running towards where the man was on the ground.

The Sons of Jacob Synagogue is shown in Belleville, Ont., on Monday.

Norm Weddum, president of the congregation at Sons of Jacob synagogue, who was inside at the time of the shooting, said a “firefight started and all hell broke loose” outside the building in the east end of Belleville. He said there were some teenagers but no small children inside the building at the time.

“We’re traumatized,” he said.

He said the officer, who was shot, was stationed outside the synagogue in an unmarked police cruiser.

He said if the officer was not stationed there at the time, “it would’ve been a different outcome, that’s for sure and I probably wouldn’t be standing here talking to you.”

He said the officer was sitting inside a black pickup truck that was parked on the driveway of the synagogue. The Star observed that the right passenger side of the truck was riddled with bullets.

“He was on duty for us,” he said. “We had made arrangements with the police for them, which we normally would do for any type of event.”

He said he had a brief conversation with the officer stationed outside, shortly before 7 p.m., before heading inside to join the congregation.

“I went and said hello and thanked him for coming,” said of his conversation with the officer.

He said at about 7 p.m., “we were trying to get everybody in to start the service. At that point, the first shots were fired — bang, bang, bang.”

He said at first it was unclear what was causing the loud explosion coming from outside the building.

“Then it happened again: bang, bang, bang.”

He said a few of the members including himself went to the lobby of the building to see if they could observe what was happening. That’s when another round of gunshots was heard, he said.

“We rushed back into the auditorium,” he said of efforts to take cover. “I closed the doors behind me, because I didn’t want to be a visual target.”

“I yelled, ‘everyone hit the floor, get on the floor immediately, those are gunshots,’ which is what everyone did.”

He said several people were on their phones seeking help from police.

“There wasn’t panic or anything, and there wasn’t screaming,” he said of the congregation maintaining some degree of composure.

He said the members started taking cover.

“We’re all on the floor” he said. “At this point, gunfire is continuing.”

He said several of the bullets struck the building, piercing several windows.

“If you look through the stained-glass windows, there’s about 20 bullet holes in one of them,” he said.

He said after things had calmed down, “ I was able to look out the door, and I saw there was a huge police presence at that point in time, and I saw two officers attending to the one (officer) that got shot.”

“I did see them put him in an ambulance and they sent him off. And then a second ambulance came and took away the shooter,” he added.

Weddum said, “It shouldn’t be happening in Belleville. It shouldn’t be happening anywhere for that matter.”

Police and the Ontario Special Investigations Unit are shown at the scene of the Sons of Jacob Synagogue in Belleville, on Monday.

Chris Malette, the Liberal MP for the Bay of Quinte, which includes Belleville, told the Star, “I don’t think you can put into words just how shocking this is for our community.”

Malette who lives a few blocks from where the shooting happened said “anyone who’s lived in Belleville knows what a tolerant place it is.”

“We have had interactions between police in an armed situation, but nothing to this extent where I guess, you know, an individual with intent appeared to be preparing or maybe be preparing to do harm to a certain group of people,” he said. “It’s shocking.”

Malette said he and another local MP had met with members of the synagogue earlier this year to discuss their concerns about safety and efforts to bolster security outside the building.

“What we learned at that time is that they have had to have security whenever they have a gathering at the synagogue,” he said. “They’re worried for their safety.”

Malette said members of the synagogue had engaged Bellville police to have an officers stationed outside the property, for security, during major gatherings.

Arriving on Parliament Hill Monday morning, Prime Minister Mark Carney told a CBC News crew the shooting was “deeply disturbing,” and added that “our hearts go out to the community. It’s why we pass legislation ... combating hate. It’s why we’re reinforcing protections. Why we’re working with community police. And I appeal to those with knowledge of the incident and those who support law enforcement that we bring this to justice.”

Belleville police and the Special Investigations Unit provided an update on the shooting investigation outside the Sons of Jacob Synagogue on Monday afternoon.

The suspect has been identified as 29-year-old Sean Ward from Quinte West, and the officer struck is Const. Jeff Smith, Belleville police Deputy Chief Sheri Meeks said at a joint news conference with the SIU. Smith has been with the Belleville police since December 2013, Meeks said.

A man carrying a shotgun at about 7 p.m. Sunday night fired on a Belleville police officer who was stationed outside the synagogue, SIU spokesperson Kristy Denette said at the news conference. The officer returned fire and another officer then fired their weapon.

The officer who first returned fire and the suspect were taken to hospital, and the suspect is in life-threatening condition. The injured officer is in critical but stable condition in hospital, Denette said.

Denette estimated that “20 or 30 gunshots” were fired.

However, the provincial police watchdog spokesperson deflected most of the reporters’ questions Monday. Meanwhile, Meeks deferred to the SIU because it had invoked its mandate.

Bullet holes pierced the stain glass window at the Sons of Jacob synagogue in Belleville.

If the Yom Kippur service had started on time at the Sons of Jacob synagogue, the shooting might’ve been deadly inside, according to one witness.

Belleville teacher Kyle Moffat, 29, was inside the synagogue when the shots were fired right at 7:06 pm., he said. The service was supposed to get underway right at 6:45 p.m., but he said people were still arriving and getting settled when the gunfire erupted outside.

“People are starting to take their seats. I was standing up right by the window to put on my tallis and then there was a bang. I thought it was just a car backfiring or something and then bang, bang, like rhythmic every three or four seconds,” said Moffat.

He said that he also thought it might be some kid throwing rocks at the windows — a common occurrence, he says — but then the sounds continued.

“It got faster and there’s clearly it was a different type of banging and then everybody just dove to the deck. And then it started hitting the buildings and the windows near us. The glass started breaking. I could hear the bullets hitting like the wood accents (around the window) and breaking light bulbs inside the synagogue. Then it kind of tapered off after a couple minutes.”

Moffat believes that is it was a matter of timing that saved the rabbi from serious injury.

“If we started on time, like we were supposed too, the bullets came through the glass right where the rabbi would be standing. So, he would have been hit a 100 per cent. The fact that we were just trickling in when it started, probably saved some people,” he said.

It was a few minutes after the gunfire that police entered the synagogue and told them what was happening. More police in tactical gear arrived and did a sweep inside.

He said they were told that the officer who was shot was in good spirits and the shooter was known to police.

The congregates were there until about 8:30 p.m., when they were packed onto bus and taken to the police station for questioning. But before that, despite what happened, and surrounded by heavy police presence, he said the 25 people wanted to continue to observe Yom Kippur.

“Weirdly enough, we continued the service inside the synagogue with the police all around, sang, prayed, chanted, did all that stuff. We had to rent a rabbi, because we don’t have a local one, and he was from Israel, so, he was calmer than you’d expect through the whole thing and just said, ‘Hey, this is kind of what happens sometimes and we’ll keep going,’ ” said Moffat.

Belleville Mayor Neil Ellis is calling for “zero tolerance” for suspected hate-motivated attacks after a shooting outside the Sons of Jacob Synagogue on Sunday night sent shock waves through his city.

“There’s a lot of different information coming out because it’s an SIU case, we’re limited (in what we can say), but I’m saddened in what happened yesterday and with the violence of this nature, we don’t usually have this in our community and it has no place,” Ellis told the Star in an interview on Monday morning.

The shooting in the community of 55,000 people follows similar incidents outside and at synagogues in Toronto over the past year.

“This will affect everybody in the Jewish community across Canada. Everybody’s going to be impacted. It echoes through the whole community across the world. I had calls last night from Hawaii, bad news travels fast. I’m thinking today of the injured officer, families, the Jewish community, what they all went through last night,” said Ellis.

Ellis said there were about 25 community members at the synagogue observing Yom Kippur and confirmed that the police officer that was shot is in stable condition.

Ellis, who wasn’t at the synagogue on Sunday night, said from what he has learned about the shooting an individual “was approached by police and it was ended there.”

He says now the focus is on making everyone in the community feel safer.

“Everybody has a right to feel safe in our community, including when gathering and practicing our faith. Jeff Smith, saying “the Jewish people deserve to live in freedom and peace as they express their faith.” He called on Prime Minister Mark Carney to join him in expressing “prayers and love” for Smith, support for the Jewish community and condemnation of “all forms of violence.”

Carney echoed Poilievre, saying the government stands ”against all forms of hate, all forms of violence.” He added, “May this House continue to come together to support the Jewish community in Canada and all Canadians to live their full lives.”
A 19-year-old man was arrested over the weekend after an online threat was made to carry out a shooting at a Durham region synagogue, police said on Monday.
The announcement of the arrest comes less than a day after police in Belleville responded to a shooting outside a synagogue as many were gathering to observe Yom Kippur on Sunday evening.

On Saturday, officers were made aware of threats posted to an online message board, Durham police wrote in a news release . The man was arrested at his residence the following day on Saturday and was charged with threats motivated by hate.
He was held for a bail hearing, police said. Durham police said it has increased their presence outside places of worships in the region for the Jewish High Holidays.
Local residents speak about what they witnessed at a shooting in Belleville on Sunday evening.
It was a chaotic scene according to one witness who lives near the Belleville synagogue where shots rang out on Sunday evening.
Melissa Walker was outside doing yard work when the shots rang out at about 7 p.m.

“I heard gunshots and pops and I just kind of thought, is that fireworks? Like, what’s going on? And I kind of went out to the sidewalk and went a little closer and that’s when I saw people. I saw the suspect behind the car and gunshots were ringing out,” said Walker, who ran inside to get her phone and called police.

“I called and I ran a little bit further up, and I witnessed him get shot,” said Walker, who said the suspect was behind an older model Honda CRV. “He was actually just hiding, he was crouching behind that car, and I saw him get shot, he went down, I was going to run up and help, because I didn’t know what was going on,” said Walker.
She said then officers arrived, surrounded the man and started yelling.

“They kicked his gun away. To me, he was deceased. I don’t know why they’re saying that he’s alive. They didn’t give him any medical attention. He was on the ground, no movement, nothing, for about five minutes. And then the paramedics pulled up, loaded his body on, and that was it,” said Walker.
According to police at an afternoon press conference, the shooter was “vital signs absent,” but paramedics helped revive him and he is currently in critical condition.

A man at the scene showed the Star dashcam footage that shows a man lying on roadway near the entrance of the synagogue while two police officers with their firearms drawn stood over him. Several officers with their weapons drawn were also seen running towards where the man was on the ground.
The Sons of Jacob Synagogue is shown in Belleville, Ont., on Monday.

Norm Weddum, president of the congregation at Sons of Jacob synagogue, who was inside at the time of the shooting, said a “firefight started and all hell broke loose” outside the building in the east end of Belleville. He said there were some teenagers but no small children inside the building at the time.
“We’re traumatized,” he said.
He said the officer, who was shot, was stationed outside the synagogue in an unmarked police cruiser.
He said if the officer was not stationed there at the time, “it would’ve been a different outcome, that’s for sure and I probably wouldn’t be standing here talking to you.”
He said the officer was sitting inside a black pickup truck that was parked on the driveway of the synagogue. The Star observed that the right passenger side of the truck was riddled with bullets.
“He was on duty for us,” he said. “We had made arrangements with the police for them, which we normally would do for any type of event.”
He said he had a brief conversation with the officer stationed outside, shortly before 7 p.m., before heading inside to join the congregation.
“I went and said hello and thanked him for coming,” said of his conversation with the officer.
He said at about 7 p.m., “we were trying to get everybody in to start the service. At that point, the first shots were fired — bang, bang, bang.”
He said at first it was unclear what was causing the loud explosion coming from outside the building.
“Then it happened again: bang, bang, bang.”
He said a few of the members including himself went to the lobby of the building to see if they could observe what was happening. That’s when another round of gunshots was heard, he said.
“We rushed back into the auditorium,” he said of efforts to take cover. “I closed the doors behind me, because I didn’t want to be a visual target.”
“I yelled, ‘everyone hit the floor, get on the floor immediately, those are gunshots,’ which is what everyone did.”
He said several people were on their phones seeking help from police.
“There wasn’t panic or anything, and there wasn’t screaming,” he said of the congregation maintaining some degree of composure.
He said the members started taking cover.
“We’re all on the floor” he said. “At this point, gunfire is continuing.”
He said several of the bullets struck the building, piercing several windows.
“If you look through the stained-glass windows, there’s about 20 bullet holes in one of them,” he said.

He said after things had calmed down, “ I was able to look out the door, and I saw there was a huge police presence at that point in time, and I saw two officers attending to the one (officer) that got shot.”
“I did see them put him in an ambulance and they sent him off. And then a second ambulance came and took away the shooter,” he added.
Weddum said, “It shouldn’t be happening in Belleville. It shouldn’t be happening anywhere for that matter.”
Police and the Ontario Special Investigations Unit are shown at the scene of the Sons of Jacob Synagogue in Belleville, on Monday.
Chris Malette, the Liberal MP for the Bay of Quinte, which includes Belleville, told the Star, “I don’t think you can put into words just how shocking this is for our community.”
Malette who lives a few blocks from where the shooting happened said “anyone who’s lived in Belleville knows what a tolerant place it is.”

“We have had interactions between police in an armed situation, but nothing to this extent where I guess, you know, an individual with intent appeared to be preparing or maybe be preparing to do harm to a certain group of people,” he said. “It’s shocking.”
Malette said he and another local MP had met with members of the synagogue earlier this year to discuss their concerns about safety and efforts to bolster security outside the building.
“What we learned at that time is that they have had to have security whenever they have a gathering at the synagogue,” he said. “They’re worried for their safety.”
Malette said members of the synagogue had engaged Bellville police to have an officers stationed outside the property, for security, during major gatherings.

Arriving on Parliament Hill Monday morning, Prime Minister Mark Carney told a CBC News crew the shooting was “deeply disturbing,” and added that “our hearts go out to the community. It’s why we pass legislation ... combating hate. It’s why we’re reinforcing protections. Why we’re working with community police. And I appeal to those with knowledge of the incident and those who support law enforcement that we bring this to justice.”
Belleville police and the Special Investigations Unit provided an update on the shooting investigation outside the Sons of Jacob Synagogue on Monday afternoon.

The suspect has been identified as 29-year-old Sean Ward from Quinte West, and the officer struck is Const. Jeff Smith, Belleville police Deputy Chief Sheri Meeks said at a joint news conference with the SIU. Smith has been with the Belleville police since December 2013, Meeks said.

The officer who first returned fire and the suspect were taken to hospital, and the suspect is in life-threatening condition. The injured officer is in critical but stable condition in hospital, Denette said.
Denette estimated that “20 or 30 gunshots” were fired.
However, the provincial police watchdog spokesperson deflected most of the reporters’ questions Monday. Meanwhile, Meeks deferred to the SIU because it had invoked its mandate.

Belleville teacher Kyle Moffat, 29, was inside the synagogue when the shots were fired right at 7:06 pm., he said. The service was supposed to get underway right at 6:45 p.m., but he said people were still arriving and getting settled when the gunfire erupted outside.

“People are starting to take their seats. I was standing up right by the window to put on my tallis and then there was a bang. I thought it was just a car backfiring or something and then bang, bang, like rhythmic every three or four seconds,” said Moffat.
He said that he also thought it might be some kid throwing rocks at the windows — a common occurrence, he says — but then the sounds continued.

“It got faster and there’s clearly it was a different type of banging and then everybody just dove to the deck. And then it started hitting the buildings and the windows near us. The glass started breaking. I could hear the bullets hitting like the wood accents (around the window) and breaking light bulbs inside the synagogue. Then it kind of tapered off after a couple minutes.”
Moffat believes that is it was a matter of timing that saved the rabbi from serious injury.

“If we started on time, like we were supposed too, the bullets came through the glass right where the rabbi would be standing. So, he would have been hit a 100 per cent. The fact that we were just trickling in when it started, probably saved some people,” he said.
It was a few minutes after the gunfire that police entered the synagogue and told them what was happening. More police in tactical gear arrived and did a sweep inside.
He said they were told that the officer who was shot was in good spirits and the shooter was known to police.

The congregates were there until about 8:30 p.m., when they were packed onto bus and taken to the police station for questioning. But before that, despite what happened, and surrounded by heavy police presence, he said the 25 people wanted to continue to observe Yom Kippur.

“Weirdly enough, we continued the service inside the synagogue with the police all around, sang, prayed, chanted, did all that stuff. We had to rent a rabbi, because we don’t have a local one, and he was from Israel, so, he was calmer than you’d expect through the whole thing and just said, ‘Hey, this is kind of what happens sometimes and we’ll keep going,’ ” said Moffat.

content_blocks.text: “People are starting to take their seats. I was standing up right by the window to put on my tallis and then there was a bang. I thought it was just a car backfiring or something and then bang, bang, like rhythmic every three or four seconds,” said Moffat.
