stories.title: MPs, senators on intelligence committee review Canada’s foreign spying capabilities
stories.summary: The reviews comes as the Carney government prepares the first national security strategy in more than two decades
stories.author: Jim Bronskill
stories.content:
Parliamentarians are taking a hard look at Canada’s overseas intelligence gathering capabilities as debate simmers over the need for a new foreign spy agency.

The MPs and senators who make up the National Security and Intelligence Committee of Parliamentarians are examining the effectiveness of Canada’s foreign intelligence collection.

The secretariat of the highly secretive committee would not elaborate on the scope, timeframe or potential findings of the review, which was announced in a brief June statement. It also declined to make chair Darren Fisher, a Liberal MP, available for an interview.

A recent academic paper on the decades-long discussion about whether Canada should launch a foreign spy agency was to be included in the material presented to committee members as background for their investigation.

Records recently disclosed by Public Safety Canada under the Access to Information Act indicate cabinet ministers have been briefed on the idea of expanding Canada’s capacity to gather and act on foreign intelligence.

The Communications Security Establishment, Canada’s cyberspy agency, collects foreign intelligence through electronic means. Global Affairs Canada contributes diplomatic reporting, while the military gathers defence-specific intelligence.

CSIS is permitted to gather intelligence in Canada and abroad about security threats such as terrorism and espionage. It is allowed to gather foreign intelligence — information about the activities, capabilities and intentions of foreign people, organizations and states — only within Canada, not overseas.

A CSIS memo prepared last year said that in an uncertain geopolitical environment, Canada’s demand for such foreign intelligence might grow.

“Canada can only learn and act so much through its current collection and authorities, and has historically relied on allied partnerships for certain foreign intelligence reporting,” the memo said.

Various proposals for a Canadian foreign intelligence service have been debated since the end of the Second World War.

The committee review of Canada’s foreign intelligence capacity comes as the Carney government prepares the first national security strategy in more than two decades. Such a strategy could shed light on the government’s intelligence needs and whether current mechanisms can satisfy them.

Briefing materials prepared in February for Public Safety Minister Gary Anandasangaree said the national security strategy would focus on building autonomy and resilience to help Canada adapt to unexpected changes.

The strategy would also, for the first time, recognize the centrality of economic security to national security, the notes said. “Prosperity must be built on a secure foundation, and a strong economy increases our ability to act autonomously.”

During the 2006 election campaign, Stephen Harper’s Conservatives promised to create a foreign intelligence agency to gather intelligence overseas and independently counter threats before they reach Canada. Such an agency did not materialize.

Goran Samuel Pesic recalls working on the issue in 2007 as an adviser to Stockwell Day, the public safety minister at the time.

Pesic, a political strategist and lobbyist, said successive governments have shied away from creating a dedicated foreign spy service because public servants told them it wasn’t necessary and, ultimately, because of the cost.

A foreign intelligence agency can help foster sovereignty and the national interest, he said in an interview.

“To be an independent country, we must possess the tools of statecraft,” he said.

“Today’s environments are such that everything is now international, and what happens in other places will have massive ramifications in Canada.”

A foreign intelligence service could provide insights from around the world that help Canada anticipate events, he said.

“The political question is, do we make one or not? And if we’re prepared to make one, what does it going to look like? What mandate will it serve? How it will complement existing intelligence collection architecture, and ultimately what will be the long-term funding model to support this?” Pesic said.

“I don’t buy for one single moment that it’s too expensive. Life is expensive. Canadian interests are priceless.”

A foreign intelligence agency can help foster sovereignty and the national interest, he said in an interview.
“To be an independent country, we must possess the tools of statecraft,” he said.
“Today’s environments are such that everything is now international, and what happens in other places will have massive ramifications in Canada.”
A foreign intelligence service could provide insights from around the world that help Canada anticipate events, he said.

“The political question is, do we make one or not? And if we’re prepared to make one, what does it going to look like? What mandate will it serve? How it will complement existing intelligence collection architecture, and ultimately what will be the long-term funding model to support this?” Pesic said.
“I don’t buy for one single moment that it’s too expensive. Life is expensive. Canadian interests are priceless.”

stories.title: Private Canadian English language school shutters, files for bankruptcy
stories.summary: The school said in a notice it had done "everything possible" to ensure it had the resources it needed to operate, but it could no longer continue to operate.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
The International Language Academy of Canada says it has filed for bankruptcy protection and cancelled all classes and programming.

A notice posted on the private language school’s website, better known as Ilac, says it has faced growing financial challenges over the past three years due to what it calls significant regulatory challenges affecting the sector.

The notice says the school had done “everything possible” to ensure it had the resources it needed to operate, but it could no longer continue to operate.

It says the school, which had campuses in Vancouver and Toronto, was working to minimize impacts on students, employees and partners.

The notice says Kpmg Inc. has been appointed as the licensed insolvency trustee, and additional information about the process will be issued soon.

It says the bankruptcy filing was made Friday.

“We understand and deeply regret the challenges our community will face because of this news,” the statement says.

A separate statement on the school’s website says Ilac had operated for more than 30 years, helping international students build community and careers.

“Information regarding current programs, student services and next steps will be communicated directly to those affected and will be updated on this website as information becomes available,” it says.

stories.title: Canada’s ability to spy overseas under microscope by MPs, senators
stories.summary: A Csis memo prepared last year said that in an uncertain geopolitical environment, Canada's demand for such foreign intelligence might grow.
stories.author: Jim Bronskill
stories.content:
Parliamentarians are taking a hard look at Canada’s overseas intelligence gathering capabilities as debate simmers over the need for a new foreign spy agency.

The MPs and senators who make up the National Security and Intelligence Committee of Parliamentarians are examining the effectiveness of Canada’s foreign intelligence collection.

The secretariat of the highly secretive committee would not elaborate on the scope, timeframe or potential findings of the review, which was announced in a brief June statement. It also declined to make chair Darren Fisher, a Liberal MP, available for an interview.

A recent academic paper on the decades-long discussion about whether Canada should launch a foreign spy agency was to be included in the material presented to committee members as background for their investigation.

Records recently disclosed by Public Safety Canada under the Access to Information Act indicate cabinet ministers have been briefed on the idea of expanding Canada’s capacity to gather and act on foreign intelligence.

The Communications Security Establishment, Canada’s cyberspy agency, collects foreign intelligence through electronic means. Global Affairs Canada contributes diplomatic reporting, while the military gathers defence-specific intelligence.

Csis is permitted to gather intelligence in Canada and abroad about security threats such as terrorism and espionage. It is allowed to gather foreign intelligence — information about the activities, capabilities and intentions of foreign people, organizations and states — only within Canada, not overseas.

A Csis memo prepared last year said that in an uncertain geopolitical environment, Canada’s demand for such foreign intelligence might grow.

“Canada can only learn and act so much through its current collection and authorities, and has historically relied on allied partnerships for certain foreign intelligence reporting,” the memo said.

Various proposals for a Canadian foreign intelligence service have been debated since the end of the Second World War.

The committee review of Canada’s foreign intelligence capacity comes as the Carney government prepares the first national security strategy in more than two decades. Such a strategy could shed light on the government’s intelligence needs and whether current mechanisms can satisfy them.

Briefing materials prepared in February for Public Safety Minister Gary Anandasangaree said the national security strategy would focus on building autonomy and resilience to help Canada adapt to unexpected changes.

The strategy would also, for the first time, recognize the centrality of economic security to national security, the notes said. “Prosperity must be built on a secure foundation, and a strong economy increases our ability to act autonomously.”

During the 2006 election campaign, Stephen Harper’s Conservatives promised to create a foreign intelligence agency to gather intelligence overseas and independently counter threats before they reach Canada. Such an agency did not materialize.

Goran Samuel Pesic recalls working on the issue in 2007 as an adviser to Stockwell Day, the public safety minister at the time.

Pesic, a political strategist and lobbyist, said successive governments have shied away from creating a dedicated foreign spy service because public servants told them it wasn’t necessary and, ultimately, because of the cost.

A foreign intelligence agency can help foster sovereignty and the national interest, he said in an interview.

“To be an independent country, we must possess the tools of statecraft,” he said.

“Today’s environments are such that everything is now international, and what happens in other places will have massive ramifications in Canada.”

A foreign intelligence service could provide insights from around the world that help Canada anticipate events, he said.

“The political question is, do we make one or not? And if we’re prepared to make one, what does it going to look like? What mandate will it serve? How it will complement existing intelligence collection architecture, and ultimately what will be the long-term funding model to support this?” Pesic said.

“I don’t buy for one single moment that it’s too expensive. Life is expensive. Canadian interests are priceless.”

stories.title: Carney heading to Saint-Pierre-et-Miquelon for meeting with Macron
stories.summary: During the visit, the two leaders will discuss a number of partnerships including in aerospace, energy and critical minerals
stories.author: Catherine Morrison
stories.content:
Canada and France will start sharing space-launch systems and satellite data reception facilities, Prime Minister Mark Carney announced after a meeting with French President Emmanuel Macron on Saint-Pierre and Miquelon Sunday.

The two leaders − both headed to New York next week for United Nations General Assembly sessions − could have met in Manhattan. But Mr. Carney and Mr. Macron chose to hold a working lunch on the archipelago, a territory of France where nearly 6,000 French citizens live, located 25 kilometres off Newfoundland and Labrador’s Burin Peninsula.

The meeting was meant as a show of solidarity and confirmation of sovereignty in the face of U.S. President Donald Trump’s threats to annex America’s neighbours. It was also a demonstration of how Canada is deepening ties with other allies as Ottawa stares down an increasingly volatile and protectionist U.S. government.

It took place only a few days after Canada was offered “associate membership” in the EU and less than two weeks after Mr. Trump, who has made no secret of his desire to control Greenland and Canada, released a social-media post with the U.S. flag covering all of North America, including parts of the Caribbean and the area where Saint-Pierre and Miquelon lies.

“Only a few kilometres separate Canada and France at their closest point,” Mr. Carney said Sunday. “Our values ​​are even closer.“

Carney’s pivot to Europe takes him to French islands off Newfoundland

He laid wreaths with Mr. Macron at a monument to the Free French forces and local volunteers who peacefully seized control of the archipelago in 1941, rejecting the puppet Vichy regime that governed France under the Nazis.

“They acted on principle,” Mr. Carney said of those who rallied to France’s defence during the Second World War. “History remembers those who act. Those who stand up for their sovereignty.”

He said the Canada-France partnership lies at the heart of this country’s broader relationship with Europe.

“France is now Canada’s third-largest export market within the European Union. Strong cultural and linguistic ties unite us − and Canada is proud to host the 2028 Francophonie Summit,” he said, referring to the biennial gathering of countries and regions with linguistic and historical ties to France.

Mr. Carney said he and Mr. Macron intend to strengthen co-operation on space. “We’ve tasked our space agencies and defence ministries to develop and share common infrastructure, including space-launch systems and ground-based reception facilities.”

Editorial: Stronger ties with the European Union aren’t a lifeline for Canada

The Prime Minister’s Office explained that the reception facilities are for receiving data from satellites.

Mr. Carney said a regional co-operation commission between Atlantic Canada and Saint-Pierre and Miquelon will conduct joint work on fighting climate change, transitioning to clean energy and promoting economic growth.

He did not mention Mr. Trump by name but talked of how Canada and France are “being shaken by new storms − the upheaval caused by climate change and the erosion of democratic norms and new threats to our sovereignty."

He said sovereignty today goes beyond feeding, fuelling and defending a country’s population. “It requires secure access to AI, semiconductors, critical minerals, payment systems, clean energy technologies, vaccines and space-based communications.”

Later in the day Sunday, Mr. Carney announced a space co-operation agreement with Norway during an evening news conference on Parliament Hill with Jonas Gahr Store, the Norwegian Prime Minister.

The two leaders said they had finalized a memorandum of understanding announced in March under which the two nations have agreed to collaborate on space-based co-operation related to Arctic and northern needs.

During a news conference, Mr. Carney was asked to respond to Mr. Trump’s recent comment that he May consider Canada’s latest outreach to the European Union to be a hostile act.

“Deeper ties between Nato allies makes those Nato allies stronger, makes Nato stronger, and helps to achieve the common goals of all Nato members, very much the United States included,” Mr. Carney replied.

Mr. Carney’s trip to Saint-Pierre and Miquelon marks the first time a Canadian prime minister has made an official visit there. Former prime minister Pierre Trudeau made a personal visit in 1971.

Saint-Pierre and Miquelon survives on tourism and government subsidies these days − a remnant of the French empire that once sprawled across North America.

Visa-free travel to be part of Canada-EU talks, Carney says

Locals said they hope the Prime Minister’s visit opens a new chapter in relations between Canada and the self-governing French territory.

Franck Detcheverry, the mayor of Miquelon-Langlade, one of the eight islands that comprise the archipelago, said he supports closer ties between Canada and the EU.

“Europe, I think, needs allies like Canada to do business, to have trade agreements. Europe needs Canada’s riches, and Canada needs a big market like Europe to sell its products, to do business. And we’d rather see them turn toward us than toward Trump – we’re against Trump.”

Mr. Detcheverry said the territory has had a hard time adjusting to the collapse of its fishing industry and restrictions on its ability to harvest seafood.

“For years now, since the 1990s, we’ve had big difficulties with Canada and the fisheries issue. And we, the people of Saint-Pierre-et-Miquelon and the Canadians, we’ve been struggling economically, especially here with Newfoundland right next to us,” he said.

But he remains an optimist.

Ottawa seeks tighter ties with EU without sacrificing sovereignty

“It’s exceptional to see Macron and the Canadian Prime Minister here. And the fact that Canada wants to move closer to the European Union is, for us, maybe good news. We hope that Saint-Pierre-et-Miquelon will make itself heard more with Canadians and that certain issues that we would like to see move forward will move forward.”

Mr. Macron’s visit is only the third time a French president has visited the islands.

“There are people who don’t really like the President – it’s President Macron, and he’s not always popular – but in spite of everything, it’s very rare for a president to come to Saint-Pierre-et-Miquelon,” Mr. Detcheverry said.

The islands are a victim of climate change, and the French government said in a briefing Thursday that among the priorities of Mr. Macron’s visit are discussions about relocating the low-lying village of Miquelon, which is being swallowed gradually by rising seas and worsening storms, as well as the replacement for the sole naval patrol vessel based in the archipelago.

The village is just two metres above sea level. When President François Hollande came here in 2014, he said it was at risk because of rising sea levels. As a result, no more building was allowed, and the government began making plans to move it.

From the archives: What is Europe even for? Decline and tragedy at the heart of the West

Several storms, in particular Hurricane Fiona in 2022, got the project going.

After Fiona, “the government said, ‘Right, we’re going to move,’” Mr. Detcheverry said. “There’s a risk, there’s a risk of huge waves, of marine submersion. There’s a risk of waves going right into the village. So it’s not a good place for houses.”

The village has about 300 homes and 600 residents. So far, 10 houses have been moved.

The French government is buying the houses and paying for reconstruction roughly two kilometres away at a higher elevation − 10 to 50 metres above sea level.

The total cost of the project is about €200-million ($321-million).

With a report from Bill Curry

Editor’s note: A previous version of this article incorrectly stated that Emmanuel Macron is the second French president to have visited the islands of Saint-Pierre and Miquelon. He is the third.

The islands are a victim of climate change, and the French government said in a briefing Thursday that among the priorities of Mr. Macron’s visit are discussions about relocating the low-lying village of Miquelon, which is being swallowed gradually by rising seas and worsening storms, as well as the replacement for the sole naval patrol vessel based in the archipelago.

The village has about 300 homes and 600 residents. So far, 10 houses have been moved.

stories.title: The highly strategic city that the Canada Investment Summit forgot
stories.summary: Opinion: Cities like Sudbury are the engines of the prosperity touted by Mark Carney. So why does it feel so cash-strapped?
stories.author: Donna Kennedy-Glans
stories.content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney was in Toronto this week selling Canada as a place that still builds things. The prospectus for his inaugural investment summit runs to 167 projects: mines, ports, LNG, data centres, powered by the usual nation-building adjectives.

Nobody in that room had to plow the roads that get the ore to the smelter. Paul Lefebvre does.

Lefebvre, Greater Sudbury’s mayor, is asking Ottawa and Queen’s Park a rude little question: if this city is going to carry a national industrial load, why does the profit leave town before the potholes are filled?

Sudbury is not a pit stop with a gift shop. It is Ontario’s largest city by land area — more than 3,200 square kilometres of Canadian Shield, lakes and rural road. Mike Harris-era amalgamation in 2001 glued seven municipalities into one; people live from one edge to the other. “We have roads going everywhere,” Lefebvre says, “rural roads that are very costly to maintain.”

A few weeks ago Doug Ford was on site at Glencore’s Craig Mine for first access to ore at the Onaping Depth project. To get that ore to the smelter, Lefebvre says, the trucks run about 70 kilometres, all of it on municipal pavement. Nine operating mines, more coming, two smelters — the whole circuit lies inside city limits. “This does not exist anywhere else in the world,” he says, meaning both mining and processing inside a 50-kilometre radius.

Ontario’s mining tax is 10 per cent of profit on non-remote mines and five per cent on remote ones. Sudbury’s camp is not remote so companies pay the higher rate. That revenue does not land at Sudbury’s Tom Davies Square; it goes to Toronto’s Queen’s Park. Corporate income tax goes to Ottawa. The city is left with property tax on the assessable surface land and buildings — to support a road network built for a national supply chain.

Lefebvre will not join the bar-stool chorus that the mining companies should simply be shaken down. “Mines are paying their taxes and their royalties,” he says. The frustration is aimed at the split of revenues. “Help us help the province grow this,” he tells me. “We’re pro-mining here.” He even likes Carney’s new capital-cost break. He just cannot pave 3,600 lane-kilometres with applause.

This startles me; I still think of Sudbury as the poster child for Big Nickel. In the last world war, International Nickel and the Sudbury workforce supplied on the order of 95 per cent of Allied nickel. In February 1942, C.D. Howe told Sudbury nickel workers that if production there stopped, “the whole character of the war will be changed.” In the early 1960s, the same city put up a ring of civil-defence sirens and sent kids under their desks at school. We are happy to call the place strategic; we are less eager to pay for the roads that still move the metal.

Lefebvre is not a naïf about the partisan map. He was a two-term Liberal MP under Justin Trudeau. Progressive Conservative Premier Doug Ford heads the provincial government and two NDP MPPs hold the local ridings in Sudbury. Lefebvre is running for re-election as mayor on Oct. 26. “My job as mayor is to develop good relations with the province,” he says, “and I’ve done that.”

The ask on the table is to designate Greater Sudbury as a special economic zone (SEZ) and park some of the mining-tax stream where the trucks actually roll. There’s an important distinction: Ontario’s new SEZ law is a permitting tool; it does not, by itself, redirect royalties. That part is still a negotiation, the mayor explains.

Lefebvre encourages Indigenous participation in the mining sector, and has taken his pitch to the chiefs of the two First Nations whose communities sit in and around the city. “They were shocked when I told them, ‘No, no, no. We don’t get direct benefits,’” from the province or the companies.

Operating Sudbury mines and smelters did not turn up among the named Investment Summit files. Yet Lefebvre is not wounded: Vale is Brazilian, with a Saudi slice; Glencore is Swiss; Kghm, working the Victoria Mine, is Polish and state-tied. “Why would they be on the list when they can fund themselves?” he posits.

The local name he wants noticed — for investment — is Magna Mining, a Canadian outfit bringing old mines back with people who used to work them. Frontier Lithium, ON the Carney prospectus, is Sudbury-headquartered; the deposit is in the northwest of the province.

For a country that has spent a year talking about nickel as a weapon in an economic war with Washington, Lefebvre’s take on America is almost unfashionably calm. The only operating U.S. nickel mine, he says, is in Michigan. The ore is milled there; the concentrate still comes to Sudbury to be smelted. Sudbury metal has fed American armour and aerospace alloys since before the last world war. “It’s a strong partnership,” he muses. “I think sometimes we forget that.”

The summit will produce communiqués. Those ore trucks will still chew up the roads. Sudbury has to find money for that; for the homelessness and addiction that have hit the North, hard; and for everything else.

If Canada wants the minerals, it can decide whether the city that already has the mines, the smelters and the muscle memory is a partner — or just the struggling host city that keeps the roads open while the resource revenue leaves town.

stories.title: Ride along in a vintage plane from the Second World War as it loops around Parliament
stories.summary: The 1943 Douglas C-47 Skytrain transport plane was part of one of Canada’s biggest ever military missions, dropping troops into Normandy.
stories.author: National Post
stories.content:
Canada

The 1943 Douglas C-47 Skytrain transport plane was part of one of Canada’s biggest ever military missions

Last updated 29 minutes ago[](http://nationalpost.com/news/Canada/ride-along-in-a-vintage-plane-from-the-second-world-war-as-it-loops-around-parliament#comments-area)

Ottawa — The 1943 Douglas C-47 Skytrain, or Dakota, transport plane was part of one of Canada’s biggest ever military missions, dropping troops into Normandy on D-Day.

Media were invited on Sept. 16 to ride aboard as it flew past Parliament Hill.

The C-47’s pilot, Bill Craig, is a member of Canadian Warplane Heritage, an organization that takes the public on C-47 flights out of Hamilton to Niagara Falls and back. They also fly other vintage planes out of Hamilton, including a Lancaster Heavy Bomber that adds a little jaunt across Lake Ontario, around the CN Tower, and then back to Hamilton.

Asked whether that meant flying over “Lake America,” Craig laughed and said a firm “No.”

Craig has been flying since 1966 and is a former commercial airline pilot who joined Canadian Warplane Heritage upon his retirement.

The media flight was arranged to help promote the Aero Gatineau-Ottawa airshow running at the Gatineau airport from September 18-20.

The airshow boasts a huge collection of both performing and static planes, jets and helicopters, and an appearance by Canada’s Snowbird acrobatic team.

After this season, the Snowbirds will pause operations.

“We understand the reasons for this difficult decision, and remain committed to our partnership with the Royal Canadian Air Force (Rcaf) and to showcasing its evolving fleet and capabilities in the years ahead. We also remain dedicated to supporting the Canadian Forces’ objectives in recruiting and community engagement,” said John Bennett, Director General of Aero Gatineau-Ottawa.

“Aero Gatineau-Ottawa is privileged to host one of the Snowbirds’ final public Canadian airshow performances before they pause operations,” Bennett said. “Though bittersweet, we will mark the occasion with a celebration befitting this iconic team.”

stories.title: Showery conditions linger as fall weather settles into London
stories.summary: Expect a stretch of cool, unsettled weather this week, with cloudy skies dominating the forecast and periodic chances of showers through midweek.
stories.author: CTVNewsLondon.ca Staff
stories.content:
London-area residents can expect a stretch of cool, unsettled weather this week, with cloudy skies dominating the forecast and periodic chances of showers through midweek.

Environment Canada is calling for cloudy conditions Sunday, with a 40 per cent chance of showers in the morning. Northeasterly winds are expected to strengthen to 20 km/h, gusting up to 40 km/h, while temperatures reach a high of 21 C.

Skies are forecast to become partly cloudy overnight, with the gusty northeast wind continuing and temperatures dropping to about 10 C.

Monday is expected to remain mainly cloudy, with a high of 18 C and northeast winds of 20 km/h, gusting to 40 km/h. Cloudy conditions are expected to persist Monday night, along with a 30 per cent chance of showers and a low of 10 C.

The unsettled pattern is forecast to continue Tuesday, with cloudy skies and a 30 per cent chance of showers. Daytime temperatures are expected to reach 18 C before falling to 12 C overnight, when the chance of showers increases to 40 per cent.

Wednesday is expected to be similarly cool and cloudy, with a 40 per cent chance of showers and a high of 17 C. Overnight temperatures will dip to around 10 C.

The forecast improves slightly Thursday, when a mix of sun and cloud is expected, along with a high of 18 C.

stories.title: Van Gorp scores twice as Knights complete sweep of Spitfires
stories.summary: London broke open a close game with four unanswered goals in the middle frame and never looked back en route to its second consecutive victory over Windsor.
stories.author: CTVNewsLondon.ca Staff
stories.content:
The London Knights used a four-goal second period to defeat the Windsor Spitfires 6-2 on Sunday, completing a weekend sweep of their Western Conference rivals.

London broke open a close game with four unanswered goals in the middle frame and never looked back en route to its second consecutive victory over Windsor.

Evan Van Gorp led the Knights offensively with two goals and an assist for a three-point performance. Eloan Le Gallic, Cooper McAslan, Thomas Zocco and Jake Ritson each added a goal and an assist.

Brian Cooke turned aside 28 shots to earn his first Ontario Hockey League victory.

Bogdan Yakushevsky scored his second goal of the season for the Spitfires and added an assist in the loss.

The Knights had six different players finding the scoresheet and several contributing multiple points.

The win capped a successful opening weekend for the Knights, who outscored Windsor over back-to-back games.

stories.title: The crosswinds of Canadian conservatism
stories.summary: Right-leaning parties need to reject conspiracy-theory-tinged populism, and deliver on a credible governing alternative focused on the idea that Canadians, not Ottawa, know best
stories.author: The Editorial Board
stories.content:
Kerry-Lynne Findlay, elected in May to her fleeting tenure as leader of the Conservative Party of British Columbia, May or May not win the Sept. 26 by-election in Abbotsford-Mission, which would give her a seat in the legislature. Regardless of the outcome, both her future and that of the BC Conservatives look grim.

In recent weeks, nine Conservative members of the Legislative Assembly have left the caucus , complaining of ideological extremism and unethical behaviour by the leader and her advisers. On Friday, three more, including former leader John Rustad, were expelled. On Sunday, another MLA resigned. And then later that day, Ms. Findlay stepped down as leader.

One of the defectors, Scott McInnis, said that under Ms. Findlay’s leadership the party had become “an exclusive private club more concerned with ideological bona fides than building the broad coalition.” Ms. Findlay has placed people with reported links to the Alberta separatist movement on her staff, reportedly accused one of her MLAs of having ties to the Chinese Communist Party – the MLA in question, Teresa Wat, quit the caucus in protest – and allegedly encouraged MLAs to replace the term First Nations with other words, including Indian.

In the wake of these departures, David Eby’s troubled B.C. NDP government has gone from rivalling the Conservatives in popular support to establishing a clear lead, according to recent polls – clear enough that Mr. Eby was hinting, before Ms. Findlay’s resignation, that he May call a snap election.

When Stephen Harper led the federal Conservative Party, he emphasized conservative economic principles such as lowering taxes, eliminating regulations and preserving fiscal balance, but for the most part avoided socially conservative issues or right-wing populism. Voters rewarded him with three successive electoral victories.

Now, after four consecutive Liberal wins in the past 11 years at the federal level, conservatives are asking whether economic conservatism without a social component is adequate. Aggressive right-wing populism gave Donald Trump his second term and is growing in popularity across Europe.

Conservatism as practised by Ms. Findlay echoed that populism, with her promotion of “faith, family and freedom.” She narrowly defeated a more moderate conservative candidate, Caroline Elliott, to win her party’s leadership. Her approach would have seemingly replaced social engineering of a progressive bent with a conservative version.

There are echoes federally as well. Earlier in the year, Durham MP Jamil Jivani met in Washington with Vice-President JD Vance, who is his friend, and conversed, he said, with Mr. Trump. On a conservative media site, Mr. Jivani accused Canadians of getting into an “anti-America hissy fit” over the trade dispute between Canada and the United States.

By contrast, federal Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre has talked about how the idea of freedom is the keystone of his party’s electoral coalition, a libertarian-tinged approach that brushes aside the idea of social engineering.

The conservative movement in Canada is clearly at a crossroads. There is one path – chosen by Ms. Findlay among others – that focuses on divisive social issues and fringe conspiracy theories that excite some partisans, but is an electoral dead end.

And then there is the path to power: building a credible governing alternative focused on economic growth, putting an end to Ottawa’s incessant economic meddling and leaning into the belief that Canadians, not Ottawa, are best able to decide how to live their lives.

It’s an issue that should concern all Canadians, not just conservative partisans. Conservative parties focused on the fringe will be unelectable, allowing progressive parties to simply win by default. Policy and governance will suffer, as British Columbia is currently finding out. Even voters who would never contemplate casting a ballot for a conservative party should hope that they eschew extremism. It is a good thing, a very good thing, that the federal Conservative Party has maintained a moderate course even as counterparts in other countries have veered into demagoguery.

As Jason Kenney, the former premier of Alberta who served as a senior minister in Mr. Harper’s government, said on social media: “I have every right, and I believe responsibility, to advocate for a patriotic, principled, positive conservatism that is not characterized by submission to a foreign adversary, xenophobia, hostility to modern medical science, separatism, etc. …To my fellow Conservatives I would say: if we become identified with those and similar views, we will never win another election, because we won’t deserve to.”

That does not mean simply focusing on fiscal matters. A conservative family-friendly policy could aim at, for instance, increasing fertility rates – while being agnostic on the composition of those families. A conservative education policy could aim at flushing out progressive dogma from schools – and replacing that ideology not with a right-tinged equivalent, but with a focus on scholastic basics, and achievement.

In a recently published book called Anti-Civilization: The Collapse of Society & the Case for the Common Good , Étienne-Alexandre Beauregard called for a Canadian conservatism rooted in family, community and tradition, while fighting the atomizing agenda of unelected elites. “In line with Western tradition, from Aristotle to Christianity, let us think of a humanity that strengthens society, rather than setting itself against it,” the Gen Z writer concluded.

While Mr. Poilievre’s rhetoric is sometimes populist, he broadly echoes the economic-but-not-social conservatism practised by Mr. Harper, his former leader. The soundtrack May be louder, but the script remains essentially the same.

Mr. Poilievre appeared certain to defeat the Liberals in the 2025 election. But he not only lost the election to the new Liberal Leader, Mark Carney, he lost his own seat in Ottawa as well, though the national result appeared to be less a repudiation of conservatism and more a vote of confidence in Mr. Carney, a former central banker, as the leader best suited to take on Mr. Trump and his tariffs.

Conservative politicians should certainly support established values and institutions in opposition to secular progressives – that is the very essence of conservative philosophy. But emphasizing a form of social conservatism rooted in religion, supportive only of a traditional understanding of family and opposed to high levels of immigration May limit the party’s attraction to suburban voters, many of them immigrants or the children of immigrants, who make up two-thirds of the population and who elect governments at all levels.

And it goes without saying that any conservative party that embraces conspiracy theories or that would support a vote for independence from Canada is destined for the kind of electoral oblivion that Maxime Bernier endured when he founded the People’s Party of Canada. The PPC won only 0.7 per cent of the popular vote – and of course no seats – in the last election.

Most Canadians will not vote for a party that favours white, Christian conformity over our country’s multicultural and secular reality.

Regardless of the party or the province or the generation, conservatives win when they offer a practical, moderate approach emphasizing smaller government, balanced books and a market-focused economy.

Anything more extreme is certain to result in the failure that Mr. Kenney predicts – and that Ms. Findlay is currently experiencing.

As Jason Kenney, the former premier of Alberta who served as a senior minister in Mr. Harper’s government, said on social media: “I have every right, and I believe responsibility, to advocate for a patriotic, principled, positive conservatism that is not characterized by submission to a foreign adversary, xenophobia, hostility to modern medical science, separatism, etc. …To my fellow Conservatives I would say: if we become identified with those and similar views, we will never win another election, because we won’t deserve to.”

That does not mean simply focusing on fiscal matters. A conservative family-friendly policy could aim at, for instance, increasing fertility rates – while being agnostic on the composition of those families. A conservative education policy could aim at flushing out progressive dogma from schools – and replacing that ideology not with a right-tinged equivalent, but with a focus on scholastic basics, and achievement.

In a recently published book called Anti-Civilization: The Collapse of Society & the Case for the Common Good , Étienne-Alexandre Beauregard called for a Canadian conservatism rooted in family, community and tradition, while fighting the atomizing agenda of unelected elites. “In line with Western tradition, from Aristotle to Christianity, let us think of a humanity that strengthens society, rather than setting itself against it,” the Gen Z writer concluded.

content_blocks.text: While Mr. Poilievre’s rhetoric is sometimes populist, he broadly echoes the economic-but-not-social conservatism practised by Mr. Harper, his former leader. The soundtrack May be louder, but the script remains essentially the same.

Mr. Poilievre appeared certain to defeat the Liberals in the 2025 election. But he not only lost the election to the new Liberal Leader, Mark Carney, he lost his own seat in Ottawa as well, though the national result appeared to be less a repudiation of conservatism and more a vote of confidence in Mr. Carney, a former central banker, as the leader best suited to take on Mr. Trump and his tariffs.

Conservative politicians should certainly support established values and institutions in opposition to secular progressives – that is the very essence of conservative philosophy. But emphasizing a form of social conservatism rooted in religion, supportive only of a traditional understanding of family and opposed to high levels of immigration May limit the party’s attraction to suburban voters, many of them immigrants or the children of immigrants, who make up two-thirds of the population and who elect governments at all levels.

The PPC won only 0.7 per cent of the popular vote – and of course no seats – in the last election.
Most Canadians will not vote for a party that favours white, Christian conformity over our country’s multicultural and secular reality.

Regardless of the party or the province or the generation, conservatives win when they offer a practical, moderate approach emphasizing smaller government, balanced books and a market-focused economy.
Anything more extreme is certain to result in the failure that Mr. Kenney predicts – and that Ms. Findlay is currently experiencing.

stories.title: Parliament returns with a big agenda and a fight brewing between Carney and labour unions
stories.summary: Parliament is set to return after a summer break on Monday and the Liberal government's agenda will be jammed packed this fall.
stories.author: Jordan Gowling
stories.content:
Ottawa – Parliament is set to return after a three-month long summer break on Monday and the Liberal government’s agenda will be jammed packed this fall.

Prime Minister Mark Carney is running high in the polls, and his government maintains a majority of seats in the House of Commons, which gives the Liberal leader ample room to implement his policies.

Topping the legislative agenda for the fall session will be legislation designed to accelerate the federal approval processes around all major projects, changes to the Canada Labour Code and moves to strengthen supply chain certainty.

Government House Leader Steve MacKinnon would not elaborate further on Friday about what’s in the legislation, citing parliamentary privilege, but said the bill will help Canada “attract investment, create jobs, and trade with the world.”

Carlene Variyan, Liberal strategist and partner at Summa Strategies, said the bill is a follow-up to the investment summit last week in Toronto, where Carney pitched Canada as an attractive place to invest for global investors. The prime minister aims to attract $500 billion in private investment by the end of the decade. Carney also announced at the summit that Ottawa will seek private investment to operate the country’s four biggest airports.

“This supply chains bill will be a critical part of the prime minister’s ongoing efforts to ensure that Canada is viewed as a place that makes sense to invest in, that’s competitive to invest in, relative to other countries,” said Variyan.

Labour unions have already voiced their opposition to making changes to the Canada Labour Code, noting that the expedited consultations and review seem to be motivated by corporate interests.

Erin Morrison, NDP strategist and vice-president at Texture Communications, said Carney is walking into a fight with the country’s largest labour unions.

“(Jobs) Minister Patty Hajdu was doing a consultation, although I hesitate to call it a consultation because it was so short and surface level, that there is fear of the possibility of impacting the right to strike,” she said. “If that is the case, the NDP will be fighting tooth-and-nail this fall.”

Morrison said this could ultimately hurt Carney’s economic agenda, because he needs workers onside to build the infrastructure and projects his government is targeting.

“We’ve been out consulting all summer on this, we’ve listened, we’ve made some adjustments,” Carney told his caucus on Friday in Ottawa. “The bottom line, though, is this: for projects, federal projects, and supply chains, our standard will be simple: one project, one review, one year.”

Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre huddled with his caucus this past week in Penticton, B.C., to talk about strategy for the upcoming parliamentary session.

Poilievre faces an uphill battle with Canadian voters, a recent poll published by the Angus Reid Institute showed that 13 per cent of respondents who voted Conservative in the 2025 federal election, would now vote for Carney if given the chance.

Even the deputy leader of the party, Melissa Lantsman, acknowledged that her and her caucus colleagues are “not in the position that we want to be in.”

The Conservative leader remains focused on affordability concerns, which runs a close second to the U.S. trade war in terms of issues Canadian voters care about.

On Monday, Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne will table a bill that extends the holiday on the gas excise tax until the end of January, after the Conservatives called on the federal government make the pause on the tax permanent.

Yaroslav Baran, Conservative strategist and co-founder of Pendulum Group, said Champagne can expect the Conservatives to hammer the Liberals on their fiscal track record.

“One can argue that in broad strokes, Mr. Carney is this governing with a considerably more Conservative agenda than his predecessor,” he said. “But if you look at the public accounts, deficits and debt are skyrocketing, and that’s going to be a very obvious opening for the Conservatives.”

The federal budget will be tabled during the fall session, which will provide an update on the country’s finances.

Poilievre told his caucus members at his caucus retreat that he has found $150 billion in savings the Liberals can capitalize on, with proposed cuts to foreign aid, federal bureaucracy and government’s proposed high-speed rail project.

The federal government has made several new spending announcements over the summer months, including a national AI strategy, a food security strategy, a West Coast pipeline project and a cooperative prosperity agreement with the province of British Columbia.

Carney told his caucus on Friday that his government will “maintain its fiscal advantage” while also acknowledging the cost of borrowing for governments is increasing globally as bond yields rise.

Economists will be watching for how the government accounts for its new spending initiatives and how that impacts Canada’s deficit track going forward, though oil prices are expected to be an upside for government revenues.

Budget watchers will also be looking for the federal government’s Nato defence spending plan and how it plans to achieve a four per cent of GDP spending target by 2030, as outlined by Carney himself this past spring.

Champagne wrapped up his pre-budget consultations earlier this month. At the investment summit, the government announced a “Productivity Super-Deduction” which will lower Canada’s marginal corporate effective tax rate on new business investment from roughly 13 per cent to 6.4 per cent. Carney also announced his government intends to privatize the operations of Canada’s four largest airports.

“The big question mark to me, and what I think a lot of political watchers will be watching for this fall, is what the budget looks like,” said Variyan.

She noted that the government has already announced significant spending initiatives, including a $51-billion Build Communities Strong Fund for infrastructure and significant defence spending commitments.

“I don’t see very much left in terms of big-ticket spending items for this fall budget, which means they’ll need something else to put in the shop window to create that sense of momentum and of doing things,” she added.

If you look at the public accounts, deficits and debt are skyrocketing, and that’s going to be a very obvious opening for the Conservatives

The U.S. trade war will also continue to loom large on Canadian domestic politics. Carney decided pause negotiations on a deal on sectoral tariffs with the U.S. last month, citing several last-minute demands from American negotiators that made a deal untenable.

As a result, both countries have slapped each other with tariffs on nearly $28 billion worth of goods.

While polling suggests the majority of Canadians support Carney walking away from the deal, the economic fallout from tariffs on key sectors of the Canadian economy could persist and worsen.

Baran said the Conservatives will continue to pressure the government on achieving a good agreement with the U.S.

Mexico and the U.S. are currently in the process of negotiating a bilateral agreement, with Reuters reporting that the two parties are working towards a deal before the U.S. midterm elections on Nov. 3.

Variyan said Mexico reaching a deal before Canada will not sway the prime minister’s negotiation strategy with the U.S. administration.

“I think that the prime minister has shown this summer that he’s not afraid to walk away from the table when a deal is offered that isn’t in our best interests, and so the dynamic will play out in the news cycle as something that creates some pressure,” said Variyan. “But I don’t think that you’ll see this prime minister let himself be too swayed by that chatter, and he’s an eye on the prize kind of guy.”

In the meantime, the Liberal government will continue its trade diversification agenda.

Canada will host a summit with the European Union leadership in October in Montreal, which will be a forum to discuss the EU extending a potential “associate membership” to Canada. It remains unclear what this membership will consist of, but Carney has promised any arrangement will be subject to debate and a vote in Parliament.

Baran said the details will be very important, noting that Conservatives would be open to more trade with the bloc, more foreign direct investment deals and more opportunities for Canadian students to study in the EU.

However, the Conservatives would be opposed to the burdens of EU membership.

“The flags the Conservatives have already planted in the ground is no EU taxes, no EU regulations, and no EU immigration policy,” he said.

Canadians can also expect the government to finalize two free trade agreements by the end of 2026, one with Brazil and one with India, which could bring new opportunities and new markets in digital trade, agriculture and manufacturing.

The House of Commons returns on Monday with six vacant seats, three of which are in Quebec. Contests of interest will be the seats of former Liberal environment minister Steven Guilbeault and former NDP MP Alexandre Boulerice, both Montreal-area ridings.

“The Liberals’ advantage is, of course, that they have far more funds right now to run a by-election than the NDP does,” said Morrison. “It will be a challenge for the NDP to hold the seat if the Liberal juggernaut and financial giant really wants it.”

Still, Morrison said the NDP remains popular in that riding, and she said the NDP could still win.

Variyan said the Liberals are not under any illusions that Guilbeault’s seat will be an easy one to keep.

“My understanding is that it’s not a campaign that the Liberal party will be able to sleepwalk their way through in the byelection,” she said. “They will need to put effort and resources into (it) and have a candidate who is a strong campaigner in order to hold the seat.”

Conservative MP Larry Brock also officially resigned his Ontario seat on Friday, which means a seat in Brantford, Ont., is also up for grabs.

The big question mark to me, and what I think a lot of political watchers will be watching for this fall, is what the budget looks like

Historically, the seat has been a Conservative stronghold, but some pollsters have mused that the riding could become competitive under this political climate.

“I’ve seen speculation that this riding might be a fight,” said Baran. “I haven’t seen any polling myself, that says it will be a fight.”

Poilievre is expected in Brantford, Ont., ON Sunday, where he will hold a rally.

Ultimately, opposition parties will be faced with the challenge of staying relevant during this parliamentary session, given Carney’s popularity in the polls and his government’s majority in the House of Commons.

Baran said given that Carney is governing on a centre-right agenda, the Conservatives have really only two options; either going more far right than Carney, which Baran does not recommend, or taking on a role as an accountability watchdog.

“You have set these lofty goals, are you delivering on them,” said Baran. “Frankly, there is plenty of space to be critical of the government on those measures.”

Morrison said there is an opportunity for the NDP to take up space on the left, now that Carney has abandoned some of those more progressive voters.

“For the NDP, they now have a wide road on the left side, occupying not just all of the traditional NDP voters, but the progressive Liberals as well, who will be having some sense of voters’ remorse over Mark Carney’s choices, particularly if we see things like attacks on working people and the privatization of major airports,” said Morrison.

“That is a huge challenge when you have a small caucus, smaller party budget, so (NDP Leader Avis Lewis) and his team really have to throw their back into it to make sure that if if the values are there, if the opportunity is there, that they’re able to capitalize,” she added.

Budget watchers will also be looking for the federal government’s Nato defence spending plan and how it plans to achieve a four per cent of GDP spending target by 2030, as outlined by Carney himself this past spring.

Champagne wrapped up his pre-budget consultations earlier this month. At the investment summit, the government announced a “Productivity Super-Deduction” which will lower Canada’s marginal corporate effective tax rate on new business investment from roughly 13 per cent to 6.4 per cent. Carney also announced his government intends to privatize the operations of Canada’s four largest airports.
“The big question mark to me, and what I think a lot of political watchers will be watching for this fall, is what the budget looks like,” said Variyan.

She noted that the government has already announced significant spending initiatives, including a $51-billion Build Communities Strong Fund for infrastructure and significant defence spending commitments.

“I don’t see very much left in terms of big-ticket spending items for this fall budget, which means they’ll need something else to put in the shop window to create that sense of momentum and of doing things,” she added.
If you look at the public accounts, deficits and debt are skyrocketing, and that’s going to be a very obvious opening for the Conservatives

The U.S. trade war will also continue to loom large on Canadian domestic politics. Carney decided pause negotiations on a deal on sectoral tariffs with the U.S. last month, citing several last-minute demands from American negotiators that made a deal untenable.
As a result, both countries have slapped each other with tariffs on nearly $28 billion worth of goods.
While polling suggests the majority of Canadians support Carney walking away from the deal, the economic fallout from tariffs on key sectors of the Canadian economy could persist and worsen.
Baran said the Conservatives will continue to pressure the government on achieving a good agreement with the U.S.

Mexico and the U.S. are currently in the process of negotiating a bilateral agreement, with Reuters reporting that the two parties are working towards a deal before the U.S. midterm elections on Nov. 3.
Variyan said Mexico reaching a deal before Canada will not sway the prime minister’s negotiation strategy with the U.S. administration.

“I think that the prime minister has shown this summer that he’s not afraid to walk away from the table when a deal is offered that isn’t in our best interests, and so the dynamic will play out in the news cycle as something that creates some pressure,” said Variyan. “But I don’t think that you’ll see this prime minister let himself be too swayed by that chatter, and he’s an eye on the prize kind of guy.”
In the meantime, the Liberal government will continue its trade diversification agenda.

Canada will host a summit with the European Union leadership in October in Montreal, which will be a forum to discuss the EU extending a potential “associate membership” to Canada. It remains unclear what this membership will consist of, but Carney has promised any arrangement will be subject to debate and a vote in Parliament.

content_blocks.alt: Man vacuuming in House of Commons .
content_blocks.caption: A worker cleans the House of Commons ahead of next week’s opening of Parliament, in Ottawa on September 17, 2026. Photo by Blair Gable/Postmedia

content_blocks.text: Baran said the details will be very important, noting that Conservatives would be open to more trade with the bloc, more foreign direct investment deals and more opportunities for Canadian students to study in the EU.
However, the Conservatives would be opposed to the burdens of EU membership.
“The flags the Conservatives have already planted in the ground is no EU taxes, no EU regulations, and no EU immigration policy,” he said.

Canadians can also expect the government to finalize two free trade agreements by the end of 2026, one with Brazil and one with India, which could bring new opportunities and new markets in digital trade, agriculture and manufacturing.

The House of Commons returns on Monday with six vacant seats, three of which are in Quebec. Contests of interest will be the seats of former Liberal environment minister Steven Guilbeault and former NDP MP Alexandre Boulerice, both Montreal-area ridings.

“The Liberals’ advantage is, of course, that they have far more funds right now to run a by-election than the NDP does,” said Morrison. “It will be a challenge for the NDP to hold the seat if the Liberal juggernaut and financial giant really wants it.”
Still, Morrison said the NDP remains popular in that riding, and she said the NDP could still win.
Variyan said the Liberals are not under any illusions that Guilbeault’s seat will be an easy one to keep.

“My understanding is that it’s not a campaign that the Liberal party will be able to sleepwalk their way through in the byelection,” she said. “They will need to put effort and resources into (it) and have a candidate who is a strong campaigner in order to hold the seat.”
Conservative MP Larry Brock also officially resigned his Ontario seat on Friday, which means a seat in Brantford, Ont., is also up for grabs.
The big question mark to me, and what I think a lot of political watchers will be watching for this fall, is what the budget looks like
Historically, the seat has been a Conservative stronghold, but some pollsters have mused that the riding could become competitive under this political climate.
“I’ve seen speculation that this riding might be a fight,” said Baran. “I haven’t seen any polling myself, that says it will be a fight.”
Poilievre is expected in Brantford, Ont., ON Sunday, where he will hold a rally.

Ultimately, opposition parties will be faced with the challenge of staying relevant during this parliamentary session, given Carney’s popularity in the polls and his government’s majority in the House of Commons.

Baran said given that Carney is governing on a centre-right agenda, the Conservatives have really only two options; either going more far right than Carney, which Baran does not recommend, or taking on a role as an accountability watchdog.
“You have set these lofty goals, are you delivering on them,” said Baran. “Frankly, there is plenty of space to be critical of the government on those measures.”
Morrison said there is an opportunity for the NDP to take up space on the left, now that Carney has abandoned some of those more progressive voters.

“For the NDP, they now have a wide road on the left side, occupying not just all of the traditional NDP voters, but the progressive Liberals as well, who will be having some sense of voters’ remorse over Mark Carney’s choices, particularly if we see things like attacks on working people and the privatization of major airports,” said Morrison.

“That is a huge challenge when you have a small caucus, smaller party budget, so (NDP Leader Avis Lewis) and his team really have to throw their back into it to make sure that if if the values are there, if the opportunity is there, that they’re able to capitalize,” she added.

stories.title: MPs, senators on intelligence committee scrutinize Canada’s ability to spy overseas
stories.summary: Ottawa — Parliamentarians are taking a hard look at Canada's overseas intelligence gathering capabilities as debate simmers over the need for a new foreign spy agency.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
By Jim Bronskill, The Canadian Press

Posted September 20, 2026 6:00 am.

Last Updated September 20, 2026 7:05 am.

Ottawa — Parliamentarians are taking a hard look at Canada’s overseas intelligence gathering capabilities as debate simmers over the need for a new foreign spy agency.

The MPs and senators who make up the National Security and Intelligence Committee of Parliamentarians are examining the effectiveness of Canada’s foreign intelligence collection.

The secretariat of the highly secretive committee would not elaborate on the scope, timeframe or potential findings of the review, which was announced in a brief June statement. It also declined to make chair Darren Fisher, a Liberal MP, available for an interview.

A recent academic paper on the decades-long discussion about whether Canada should launch a foreign spy agency was to be included in the material presented to committee members as background for their investigation.

Records recently disclosed by Public Safety Canada under the Access to Information Act indicate cabinet ministers have been briefed on the idea of expanding Canada’s capacity to gather and act on foreign intelligence.

The Communications Security Establishment, Canada’s cyberspy agency, collects foreign intelligence through electronic means. Global Affairs Canada contributes diplomatic reporting, while the military gathers defence-specific intelligence.

Csis is permitted to gather intelligence in Canada and abroad about security threats such as terrorism and espionage. It is allowed to gather foreign intelligence — information about the activities, capabilities and intentions of foreign people, organizations and states — only within Canada, not overseas.

A Csis memo prepared last year said that in an uncertain geopolitical environment, Canada’s demand for such foreign intelligence might grow.

“Canada can only learn and act so much through its current collection and authorities, and has historically relied on allied partnerships for certain foreign intelligence reporting,” the memo said.

Various proposals for a Canadian foreign intelligence service have been debated since the end of the Second World War.

The committee review of Canada’s foreign intelligence capacity comes as the Carney government prepares the first national security strategy in more than two decades. Such a strategy could shed light on the government’s intelligence needs and whether current mechanisms can satisfy them.

Briefing materials prepared in February for Public Safety Minister Gary Anandasangaree said the national security strategy would focus on building autonomy and resilience to help Canada adapt to unexpected changes.

The strategy would also, for the first time, recognize the centrality of economic security to national security, the notes said. “Prosperity must be built on a secure foundation, and a strong economy increases our ability to act autonomously.”

During the 2006 election campaign, Stephen Harper’s Conservatives promised to create a foreign intelligence agency to gather intelligence overseas and independently counter threats before they reach Canada. Such an agency did not materialize.

Goran Samuel Pesic recalls working on the issue in 2007 as an adviser to Stockwell Day, the public safety minister at the time.

Pesic, a political strategist and lobbyist, said successive governments have shied away from creating a dedicated foreign spy service because public servants told them it wasn’t necessary and, ultimately, because of the cost.

A foreign intelligence agency can help foster sovereignty and the national interest, he said in an interview.

“To be an independent country, we must possess the tools of statecraft,” he said.

“Today’s environments are such that everything is now international, and what happens in other places will have massive ramifications in Canada.”

A foreign intelligence service could provide insights from around the world that help Canada anticipate events, he said.

“The political question is, do we make one or not? And if we’re prepared to make one, what does it going to look like? What mandate will it serve? How it will complement existing intelligence collection architecture, and ultimately what will be the long-term funding model to support this?” Pesic said.

“I don’t buy for one single moment that it’s too expensive. Life is expensive. Canadian interests are priceless.”

stories.title: Bills, byelections and bilats: what you need to know as MPs return to Parliament Hill
stories.summary: Ottawa — Members of Parliament are making their way back to Ottawa for the fall sitting of the House of Commons that gets underway on Monday.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
By Sarah Ritchie, The Canadian Press

Posted September 20, 2026 6:00 am.

Last Updated September 20, 2026 7:11 am.

OTTAWA — Members of Parliament are making their way back to Ottawa for the fall sitting of the House of Commons that gets underway on Monday.

It’s set to be a busy season with the release of the federal budget, debate on legislation and looming byelections.

Here are five things to watch for:

Prime Minister Mark Carney’s government decided last year to buck tradition and move the release of its annual spending plan to the fall, rather than the spring. It also split the document into an operating budget and a capital budget.

Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne has spent the summer consulting with a wide range of stakeholders about the budget but has not yet set a date to release the next fiscal plan.

The prime minister did offer a hint about what to expect from the coming budget. Carney told investors gathered for last week’s investment summit that his government plans to balance the operating budget next year, 12 months ahead of schedule.

The government projected a deficit of $65.3 billion for the current fiscal year in April’s spring economic update, though many economists expect high global oil prices will boost Ottawa’s bottom line in the fall budget.

Government House leader Steven MacKinnon said Friday that “very significant economic legislation” will be the centrepiece of the fall sitting.

Carney said Friday the government will introduce legislation, to be called the Building Canada Strong Act, that will help speed up approval of new federal projects.

“One project, one review, one year,” the prime minister told reporters.

There will also be legislation to enact the fuel excise tax extension that Carney announced on Sept. 2. That bill will formalize the decision to extend the tax break on gas and diesel, introduced in response to higher oil prices caused by the ongoing conflict in Iran.

The federal government consulted with employers and unions over the summer about the state of labour relations following contract disputes at railways, ports and airlines in recent years.

Jobs Minister Patty Hajdu would not say Friday whether the Liberals are planning to propose changes to the Labour Code this fall, though MacKinnon hinted “improvements” to the code are on the agenda.

Debate will also continue on some controversial government legislation. Bill C-22, the lawful access bill, is before the Senate. The digital safety bill, which seeks to regulate AI chatbots and restrict social media access for kids under 16, is before the House.

A First Nations water bill was reintroduced in the spring — though critics say it’s a weaker version of a previous bill that recognized First Nations’ right to clean water on their territories.

Tariffs and trade

Trade talks with the U.S. are off — at least for now — but that doesn’t mean the issue is going away. Conservatives have been calling on the government to release the deal that was hammered out with the Americans before the Canadian side walked away from the negotiating table.

Carney has said that Canada’s new alliance (or associate membership) with the European Union will come to Parliament for debate.

Conservatives have called for a Commons debate on the EU deal and are insisting that Canada should not import what they say are bad European policies on things like immigration and taxes.

Three new Liberal MPs will take their seats for the first time this fall after winning byelections in late August.

Six more byelections are set to be called in the coming months in Saskatchewan, Ontario and Quebec.

In Yorkton-Melville, voters will replace longtime Conservative MP Cathay Wagantall. Her caucus colleague Larry Brock resigned Friday as the representative for Brantford-Brant South.

Two Liberals also stepped down: Shaun Chen left his seat in Scarborough North and former minister Steven Guilbeault made a high-profile decision to walk away from Carney’s caucus, leaving an opening in Laurier-Sainte-Marie.

Voters in two other Quebec ridings are also set to replace MPs who left federal politics to run provincially.

In Rosemont-La Petite-Patrie, a vote will be held to replace New Democrat Alexandre Boulerice, and Saint-Hyacinthe-Bagot-Acton will choose a new representative after Simon-Pierre Savard-Tremblay left the Bloc Québécois.

Carney has six months after a seat becomes vacant to set a date for a byelection. It’s likely the races in Quebec won’t happen before the provincial election on Oct. 5.

Bilateral meetings with world leaders

Carney, who is fresh off a trip to France to speak to the European Parliament, is also expected to travel to the United Nations General Assembly this week in New York City.

Carney is set to host world leaders who are interested in his pledge to diversify trade beyond the U.S.

Vietnamese President To Lam will make a state visit to Ottawa next week, and Indian media reports that Prime Minister Narendra Modi is expected to visit in December.

The prime minister typically attends a couple of big international summits that are held in November: the Association of Southeast Asian Nations is being hosted by the Philippines this year, and the Asia-Pacific Economic Co-operation forum will be in China.

The summit of La Francophonie is being held in Cambodia, also in November, and the United States is playing host to the Group of 20 nations in December.

There will also be legislation to enact the fuel excise tax extension that Carney announced on Sept. 2. That bill will formalize the decision to extend the tax break on gas and diesel, introduced in response to higher oil prices caused by the ongoing conflict in Iran.
The federal government consulted with employers and unions over the summer about the state of labour relations following contract disputes at railways, ports and airlines in recent years.
Jobs Minister Patty Hajdu would not say Friday whether the Liberals are planning to propose changes to the Labour Code this fall, though MacKinnon hinted “improvements” to the code are on the agenda.

Debate will also continue on some controversial government legislation. Bill C-22, the lawful access bill, is before the Senate. The digital safety bill, which seeks to regulate AI chatbots and restrict social media access for kids under 16, is before the House.
A First Nations water bill was reintroduced in the spring — though critics say it’s a weaker version of a previous bill that recognized First Nations’ right to clean water on their territories.
Tariffs and trade

Trade talks with the U.S. are off — at least for now — but that doesn’t mean the issue is going away. Conservatives have been calling on the government to release the deal that was hammered out with the Americans before the Canadian side walked away from the negotiating table.
Carney has said that Canada’s new alliance (or associate membership) with the European Union will come to Parliament for debate.
Conservatives have called for a Commons debate on the EU deal and are insisting that Canada should not import what they say are bad European policies on things like immigration and taxes.
Three new Liberal MPs will take their seats for the first time this fall after winning byelections in late August.
Six more byelections are set to be called in the coming months in Saskatchewan, Ontario and Quebec.
In Yorkton-Melville, voters will replace longtime Conservative MP Cathay Wagantall. Her caucus colleague Larry Brock resigned Friday as the representative for Brantford-Brant South.

Two Liberals also stepped down: Shaun Chen left his seat in Scarborough North and former minister Steven Guilbeault made a high-profile decision to walk away from Carney’s caucus, leaving an opening in Laurier-Sainte-Marie.
Voters in two other Quebec ridings are also set to replace MPs who left federal politics to run provincially.

In Rosemont-La Petite-Patrie, a vote will be held to replace New Democrat Alexandre Boulerice, and Saint-Hyacinthe-Bagot-Acton will choose a new representative after Simon-Pierre Savard-Tremblay left the Bloc Québécois.
Carney has six months after a seat becomes vacant to set a date for a byelection. It’s likely the races in Quebec won’t happen before the provincial election on Oct. 5.
Bilateral meetings with world leaders
Carney, who is fresh off a trip to France to speak to the European Parliament, is also expected to travel to the United Nations General Assembly this week in New York City.
Carney is set to host world leaders who are interested in his pledge to diversify trade beyond the U.S.
Vietnamese President To Lam will make a state visit to Ottawa next week, and Indian media reports that Prime Minister Narendra Modi is expected to visit in December.

The prime minister typically attends a couple of big international summits that are held in November: the Association of Southeast Asian Nations is being hosted by the Philippines this year, and the Asia-Pacific Economic Co-operation forum will be in China.
The summit of La Francophonie is being held in Cambodia, also in November, and the United States is playing host to the Group of 20 nations in December.

stories.title: Film jobs are booming in Newfoundland. So where are they going to shoot?
stories.summary: Audiences in St. John’s got a sneak peek Wednesday at the latest big-budget production showcasing Newfoundland and Labrador to the world.
stories.author: Garrett Barry
stories.content:
ST. John’s - Audiences in St. John’s got a sneak peek Wednesday at the latest big-budget production showcasing Newfoundland and Labrador to the world.

Dozens were invited to a special screening of Below, a drama starring Josh Hartnett headed for a worldwide release next month on streaming giant Netflix.

Not only is the miniseries shot in Newfoundland, but it’s thoroughly set in Newfoundland — portraying the province’s nostalgia for a pre-resettlement-program world; the complicated feelings of young men and women moving “out west” for work; and jokes that land a little bit deeper with Newfoundlanders and Labradorians than they would for just about anyone else.

“I think it, for one, really sends a message to Hollywood and to Canada at large that we’re capable of telling stories that are big in scale and scope,” said Chris Hatcher, an executive producer on the project.

“We can really execute that.”

The production spent big during its shooting in 2025, helping boost the film industry to a milestone year.

Industry incubator PictureNL — a project by Newfoundland and Labrador’s provincial government — said spending in 2025 hit more than $150 million across multiple productions.

“We’re on track to go beyond that $150 million in production activity this year already,” added director Laura Churchill.

The next step for the growing industry, she says, is a way to tackle the province’s moody weather.

Although productions like Below have traded on the province’s natural beauty, Newfoundland and Labrador is infamously foggy, rainy and grey — especially when compared to other major filming hubs in Toronto and Montreal.

A dedicated, purpose-built indoor sound stage would help filming crews keep more work inside the province and be less dependent on the fog burning off.

“It would be a great next step,” Churchill said. “Again, it’s about bringing production that can be here year-round. We do great with ‘on-location’ now, but if we did have bespoke sound stage, I think we would be able to get (to) that next tier.”

Although PictureNL — a creature of the provincial government — does invest in TV and film production to incentivize it to come to the province, Churchill says a sound stage would be best kept as private infrastructure.

“There’s been interest on a regular basis. We have conversations about this fairly regularly,” she said.

Portions of hit movies Peter Pan & Wendy and Aquaman were shot in the province, as well as portions of the TV shows Frontier , Reacher and Severance .

“It’s the warmest reception I’ve ever had, in any place I’ve ever been in my life,” actor Josh Hartnett told the audience on Wednesday evening at the Majestic Theatre in St. John’s. “Open and hospitable in a way that felt completely natural, and not just for me.”

“I will tell you, the word is out,” Churchill added. “The buzz is really exciting. I think we’ve got a lot of longevity and more to come here in Newfoundland and Labrador.”

Churchill says the local industry currently supports about 800 jobs, but with a new local film campus graduating roughly 70 students every year, growth is important.

She believes a sound stage is a natural next step, if the industry can find an investor willing to foot the bill.

“We want it to be a full year round industry where people can be working, staying and living here in Newfoundland and Labrador,” she said.
