stories.title: ‘We lived at a lucky time’: Vancouver seniors relive childhood freedom on three wheels
stories.summary: Many Vancouver seniors are hitching a ride with Cycling Without Age, a volunteer-powered charity that gives older adults the opportunity to get outside on three-wheeled e-bicycles.
stories.author: Andrew Johnson
stories.content:
Vancouver – Lorraine McKendry remembers the freedom of childhood bike rides in Calgary, when she and her friends would set out during summer vacation: destination unknown.

“Your parents didn’t know where you were. You just got to go on your bike, with a lunch, and be home for supper,” McKendry recalled. “We lived at a lucky time.”

Decades later, she is getting a chance to feel some of that freedom again.

McKendry is among the many Vancouver seniors hitching rides with Cycling Without Age, a volunteer-powered charity that gives older adults the opportunity to get outside on three-wheeled e-bicycles – also known as trishaws – even when they can no longer pedal themselves.

The organization’s trained volunteers, known as pilots, pedal seniors and their loved ones around Vancouver’s parks, seawall and scenic neighbourhoods on specially designed trishaws.

The rides, as McKendry can attest, are about more than cycling.

Cycling Without Age says its goal is to help seniors reconnect with the outdoors, their communities and other people. The organization operates from May through October, with rides arranged through care homes, senior organizations or by seniors living independently.

The organization currently has about 80 volunteers in Vancouver, many seniors themselves who have recently retired. But not all of them.

“We have teachers, we have physicians, we have police officers. We have a lot of pilots and retired flight attendants,” said Jake Winn, executive director of Cycling Without Age Vancouver.

The program has become increasingly popular. In July, about 750 seniors took part in rides in Vancouver, with dozens of care homes already on the waitlist.

“Our bikes are booked Monday through Sunday, morning and afternoon, every single week.” Winn said. “We still can’t meet the demand for the rides.”

Winn said the rides can help combat the isolation that can accompany aging.

“There’s a huge joy in just being outside and seeing people,” he said. “Everyone feels like royalty.”

Lisa Wong is one of the volunteers helping make that happen. For her, the reward is bringing joy to people she feels society often forgets.

“Just that sense of feeling alive again,” Wong said. “It’s so heartwarming. Like, I come back from every ride just with this warmth in my heart.”

Cycling Without Age Vancouver relies on volunteers, fundraising and grants to keep the program running. It is also hoping to purchase more trishaws (at a cost of $25,000 each) and secure more storage space within the city.

For McKendry, all the work that goes into offering the program has helped her travel back in time. “I have these wonderful people who are letting me have that feeling again and I can’t thank them enough,” she said.

stories.title: Transport minister won’t guarantee prices won’t go up after airport privatization, promises fees will be ‘partially regulated’
stories.summary: Transport Minister Steven MacKinnon won’t guarantee the cost to fly won’t go up for travellers if the federal government follows through on its plan to privatize Canada’s four largest airports but does promise an improved experience and partial regulation.
stories.author: Spencer Van Dyk
stories.content:
Ottawa — Transport Minister Steven MacKinnon won’t guarantee the cost to fly won’t go up for travellers if the federal government follows through on its plan to privatize Canada’s four largest airports but does promise an improved experience and partial regulation.

On Tuesday, Prime Minister Mark Carney announced the federal government is seeking private investment to run Canada’s four major airports: Toronto-Pearson, Montreal-Trudeau, Calgary and Vancouver.

In an interview on CTV Question Period airing Sunday, host Vassy Kapelos pressed MacKinnon repeatedly on whether he could guarantee ticket prices will not go up for travellers, and the transport minister would only promise no ‘unjustified’ increases.

“We will have a program, as the prime minister announced, that will reward regional connectivity in Canada,” MacKinnon said. “Airfares are too expensive.”

“This program is designed to reinvest partly in our air travel in Canada and make the regions and our largest airports more connected,” he added, pointing to the number of communities that have a lack or absence of service, and that do not have proper infrastructure in place.

The transport minister also insisted there will be investment in the “passenger experience,” adding he doesn’t think travellers will notice a difference as the airports shift from public to private ownership.

Speaking about how it will work, MacKinnon said the operating model for the four airports will be regulated, “so fares and fees will be partially regulated.”

In announcing the plan this week, Carney said the federal government will retain ownership of the underlying land and assets, but can “unlock” the airports’ “true value” by privatizing their operations. He insisted the move will lead to a “better passenger experience.”

When pressed again by Kapelos to guarantee Canadians airfare won’t go up any further, considering the already high prices travellers pay, MacKinnon said: “We believe that we can put in place agreements, solid agreements, as we go through this process that will reassure Canadians that there will be no unjustified increases in those kinds of fees.”

Asked about a timeline to execute on the plan and whether legislation would be necessary, MacKinnon said the federal government will reveal more details in the coming weeks and months.

MacKinnon in his interview also discussed the Liberals’ legislative agenda for the fall sitting in the House of Commons, which starts Monday.

You can watch Transport Minister and Government House Leader Steven MacKinnon’s full interview on CTV Question Period Sunday at 11 a.m. ET.

With files from CTV News’ Stephanie Ha

paragraphs: TORONTO - Five things to watch for in the Canadian business world in the coming week:
Macklem speech

Bank of Canada governor Tiff Macklem will give a speech in Halifax on Monday. The central bank kept its key interest rate on hold at 2.25 per cent earlier this month, but said that risks for inflation have increased and new tariffs have made economic growth prospects more uncertain.
House returns

The MPs will return to the House of Commons on Monday as the fall sitting begins. Trade and the economy are expected to be top of mind they return to Ottawa and deal with new U.S. tariffs and Canada’s response.
Elevate conference

The Elevate tech conference starts in Toronto on Tuesday. AI will be a hot topic at the meeting with discussions on what is coming for the technology and how it is reshaping the world. The conference comes amid an ongoing debate over the speed of AI development and safety.
Retail sales

Statistics Canada will release its July figures for retail sales on Thursday. The agency’s advance estimate released last month suggested sales fell 0.8 per cent in July, following an increase of 0.6 per cent in June.
Banff conference
The annual Global Business Forum conference in Banff, Alta., starts on Thursday. The two-day meeting brings together business, academic and government leaders.
This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 20, 2026.

stories.title: Terry Fox documentary premieres at Toronto International Film Festival
stories.summary: As Canadians lace up for the annual Terry Fox Run, a new documentary offers unseen footage of the young man behind it all.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
TORONTO — As Canadians lace up for the annual Terry Fox Run, a new documentary offers unseen footage of the young man behind it all.

Run Terry Run, directed by Sean Menard, follows Fox’s journey as a 21-year-old with an amputated right leg from osteosarcoma who sets out to traverse the country to raise money for cancer research.

Fox’s brother, Darrell Fox, joined Canadian athletes gathered at the Toronto International Film Festival for a screening on Saturday.

He was part of his brother’s Marathon of Hope, which began in St. John’s, Nfld., in April 1980, and says he cherishes those memories.

Terry Fox ran a marathon every day for 140 days, spanning more than 5,000 kilometres.

He reached Thunder Bay, Ont., where he found out the cancer had spread to his lungs, forcing him to stop, and he died ten months later.

Darrell Fox is an executive producer of the film and said the 180-minute documentary offers an intimate view of his brother’s life and journey.

“I haven’t forgotten that run,” he said on the TIFF red carpet. “It’s impossible, you know, and I cherish those memories of spending 93 days in a row with him.”

Canadian Paralympic ice hockey player Billy Bridges attended the red carpet, along with more than a dozen other Olympians, to reflect on Fox’s legacy.

“As a disabled Canadian, growing up, our heroes were few and far between,” Bridges said. “There’s something special about what Terry accomplished and the passion that he lit within every single Canadian.”

Bridges said Terry Fox planted a seed he knew he wouldn’t get to see grow. “But without that we wouldn’t be where we are today with the support that we have for Canadians and cancer research.”

Others in attendance included Andre De Grasse, Alysha Newman, Paul Poirier and Piper Gilles.

paragraphs: TORONTO — As Canadians lace up for the annual Terry Fox Run, a new documentary offers unseen footage of the young man behind it all.
Run Terry Run, directed by Sean Menard, follows Fox’s journey as a 21-year-old with an amputated right leg from osteosarcoma who sets out to traverse the country to raise money for cancer research.
Fox’s brother, Darrell Fox, joined Canadian athletes gathered at the Toronto International Film Festival for a screening on Saturday.
He was part of his brother’s Marathon of Hope, which began in St. John’s, Nfld., in April 1980, and says he cherishes those memories.
Terry Fox ran a marathon every day for 140 days, spanning more than 5,000 kilometres.
He reached Thunder Bay, Ont., where he found out the cancer had spread to his lungs, forcing him to stop, and he died ten months later.
Darrell Fox is an executive producer of the film and said the 180-minute documentary offers an intimate view of his brother’s life and journey.
“I haven’t forgotten that run,” he said on the TIFF red carpet. “It’s impossible, you know, and I cherish those memories of spending 93 days in a row with him.”
Canadian Paralympic ice hockey player Billy Bridges attended the red carpet, along with more than a dozen other Olympians, to reflect on Fox’s legacy.

“As a disabled Canadian, growing up, our heroes were few and far between,” Bridges said. “There’s something special about what Terry accomplished and the passion that he lit within every single Canadian.”
Bridges said Terry Fox planted a seed he knew he wouldn’t get to see grow. “But without that we wouldn’t be where we are today with the support that we have for Canadians and cancer research.”
Others in attendance included Andre De Grasse, Alysha Newman, Paul Poirier and Piper Gilles.
The Terry Fox Run takes place on Sept. 20 across Canada.

stories.title: Closer ties with Europe could offer opportunities for Canada, but come with challenges
stories.summary: Canadians May welcome the prospect of closer ties with the European Union, but pollster Nik Nanos says the issue could become a political minefield for Prime Minister Mark Carney.
stories.author: Michael Serapio
stories.content:
Ottawa - Canadians May welcome the prospect of closer ties with the European Union, but pollster Nik Nanos says the issue could become a political minefield for Prime Minister Mark Carney.

On Wednesday, the EU made a historic overture to Canada , inviting the country to explore possible associate membership in the world’s largest trading bloc.

The proposal would not involve full membership. Instead, Canada could become the EU’s first associate member — a status that does not currently exist.

In extending the invitation, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen pointed to shared values between Canada and the EU.

“We see the world with the same eyes, from AI to climate change, from the Arctic to geopolitics,” she said. “And we have stood together on Ukraine, ON defence, ON raw materials and supply chains.”

Above all, she said, Europe and Canada share a commitment to democracy.

Carney welcomed the invitation on Thursday, but his earlier comments emphasized the possibility of a unique, collaborative partnership. He was also clear that Canada is not seeking full EU membership.

That May prove politically prudent, given that public support for closer European ties has limits.

In an interview with CTV News on Saturday, Nanos said polling conducted by his firm earlier this summer found broad support for greater economic co-operation with Europe.

“Support for strengthening economic ties with the European Union is exceptionally strong, at around eight out of every 10 Canadians,” Nanos said. “So right across the board, young, old, regardless of what part of the country that you’re from, you’re open to stronger economic ties.”

But that support falls to about five in 10 when EU membership itself is raised as a possibility, he said.

“Canadians are just not interested in exchanging dependence on the United States with dependence on another part of the world,” Nanos said.

That May help explain why the prime minister has been deliberate in his language around the EU.

“I think it explains why every time he talks about it, he uses the phrase ‘as long as it does not impact Canada’s sovereignty,’” Nanos said. “Because I think that’s the key question that Canadians would want to know: What are the details of what is potentially being discussed? How will it work, and what might it mean for Canadian sovereignty?”

There are also practical challenges Canada would have to consider, depending on how closely Ottawa pursued an associate relationship with the EU.

One of the biggest would be the adoption of European standards for Canadian exports, which could come at a significant cost.

“Truly aligning standards, codes and regulations with the EU, I think that’s further than most Canadian governments and most Canadians want to go,” said Brett House, a Canadian economist who teaches at Columbia University in New York.

Norway and Switzerland are not EU members but participate in the European free-trade area. To facilitate that relationship, both countries have had to harmonize legislation and regulations with EU rules in several markets.

That is why House said the debate over whether Canada should become an EU associate member May be less important than the policy discussions that could result from exploring the possibility.

Those discussions could also encourage countries to make better use of the Canada-European Union Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement, or Ceta, which is already in place.

“What really matters is that we take advantage of that existing trade agreement,” House said. “We enable Canadian companies to actually participate in it. We ensure that it covers all of the European Union, and we make it easy for Canadians to benefit from it.”

Still, the world is watching what happens next.

Australia, Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland are among the jurisdictions seeking greater co-operation with the European Union. What emerges from Canada’s discussions could therefore be instructive for others considering closer ties.

U.S. officials are watching, too.

The U.S. president has warned the EU against moving forward with its Canadian proposal, saying it could be viewed as a “hostile act” by the United States.

stories.title: As climate change pushes lobster north, some N.L. fishers want in on the harvest
stories.summary: Lobster is big business in Atlantic Provinces, but the lack of lobster licences in N.L. is making it hard to catch up
stories.author: Devin Stevens
stories.content:
Carl Hedderson has been fishing for 50 years, but never thought he’d see as many lobsters as he does now around Newfoundland ’s remote and rugged Great Northern Peninsula.

Based in Noddy Bay, 300 kilometres north of Deer Lake at the peninsula’s northern tip, Hedderson says he’s gone walking on the beach at night with a flashlight looking for squid all his life.

“I never ever saw a lobster, but now you do it and you see lobsters crawl around by the beach in the nighttime,” he said in a recent interview.

“The weather (has) changed. The temperature’s changed. I guess it got right for them, and with (lobster) moving north, I guess they got a better survival rate and are growing faster.”

Lobster is big business in the other Atlantic Provinces, but has traditionally been less valuable in Newfoundland and Labrador. Nova Scotia landed nearly $962-million worth of the crustacean in 2024 according to Fisheries and Oceans Canada. New Brunswick brought in about $323-million while Prince Edward Island clawed in almost $318-million.

Newfoundland and Labrador’s reported landings were about 3,300 tonnes in 2018, worth about $48-million. The lobster catch has more than doubled since, with 9,400 tonnes worth $137-million reported in 2024.

Darrell Mullowney, a fisheries department research scientist, says lobsters prefer a “Goldilocks zone” where the water isn’t too hot or too cold. Traditionally that zone has been around the northeast waters of the U.S. and around the Maritime provinces, with Quebec and Newfoundland at the extreme north of the range. He says in recent years climate change has pushed the centre of that Goldilocks zone north.

“It’s becoming very important to us in terms of rankings of economic returns from important fisheries in Newfoundland,” Mullowney said in an interview. “Snow crab dominates, but lobster is now creeping up to number two or number three in recent years, kind of rivalling northern shrimp. So it’s put itself on the radar.”

Hedderson says officials opened other areas of the province to fishing for species such snow crab or northern shrimp when the cod fishery collapsed in 1992, but that didn’t happen in his area where just a handful of people have lobster licenses. He says participation in the local fishery has dwindled over the decades and that’s had a big impact in a rural area with few other economic options.

“All our young people are gone,” he said. “We would have been booming if they could have (fished) lobster. The young people could have stayed. They could have made some money.”

Fisheries and Oceans Canada announced dozens of new exploratory lobster licenses for Quebec for the spring of 2025 in order to assess the area’s ability to support additional catches. Ottawa has not done the same for Newfoundland and Labrador where there are currently 2,175 licenses.

The department did not directly answer when asked if it was considering an increase, saying in an e-mail that the province’s lobster fishery is limited entry “which means the number of licences is restricted.”

Sherry Glynn, secretary treasurer of Newfoundland and Labrador’s Fish, Food and Allied Workers Union, said its members have been clear that the value of lobster licenses are increasing with some fetching between $350,000 and $500,000.

“So what kind of precedent does it set when new licenses just get issued to harvesters? Does it have the impact of devaluing the licences that already exist?’” she asked in an interview.

Glynn said there’s also a lack of infrastructure in the province, noting there was a shortage of lobster crates available when the caches started to increase a few years back. That’s since been resolved, but airport capacity for exports remains another bottleneck, as is the number of lobster pounds and live holding facilities, which are much more developed in the Maritimes.

“It takes time for all parts of the industry to catch up (to the increased catch) and for the infrastructure to develop around it,” said Glynn.

She said the provincial government, which regulates seafood processing, has begun in recent years to allow buyers to purchase seafood, including lobster, for processing in other provinces such as New Brunswick and Nova Scotia. In the spring, the government moved to streamline applications for new processing licenses, including a conditional license for companies committed to buying or building a fish processing plant.

Meanwhile, Hedderson says fishermen in rural areas are getting older and there’s less interest from the new generation, who have watched their parents struggle.

“When people are just sitting around twiddling their thumbs, when you’re sitting around a couple of months with no income and just piddling around your door waiting . . . to start fishing, it’s not helping anybody,” he said.

stories.title: Ottawa to introduce legislation to curb federal strike interventions
stories.summary: Jobs Minister Patty Hajdu says upcoming legislation will help reduce the number of times the federal government has to intervene in strikes
stories.author: Catherine Morrison
stories.content:
Jobs Minister Patty Hajdu says upcoming legislation will help reduce the number of times the federal government has to intervene in strikes.

Speaking to reporters on Parliament Hill Saturday, Hajdu did not provide many details about expected plans to amend the Canada Labour Code.

However, she said no government wants to intervene in a strike and that parties are better off if they can solve problems themselves at the negotiating table.

“The government already has the power to intervene,” she said. “The point is to reduce the times that the government is forced to solve the problem for employers and unions.”

Employers and unions have disagreed strongly on the use of Section 107 of the labour code, which has been used increasingly to curb work stoppages in key industries by referring disputes to the Canada Industrial Relations Board.

Fifteen months into his tenure as Prime Minister, Carney is drawing the ire of union heads

Employment and Social Development Canada said in a report earlier this month that employers and unions are divided over how much power Ottawa should have to intervene in labour disputes.

Transport Minister Steven MacKinnon told reporters Saturday that the legislation – which could be introduced in the House of Commons as early as next week – isn’t targeting the right to strike.

“What we want to do is make achieving collective agreements easier,” he said.

Bea Bruske, president of the Canadian Labour Congress, said in a statement that the right to strike is in the national interest.

“Canada’s economic security depends on workers having the power to bargain for better wages, working conditions and job security,” she said. “Any new power to prevent or shut down a legal strike, including before it begins, would weaken that power. Canada needs workers with our elbows up, not our hands tied.”

Derrick Hynes, CEO of Federally Regulated Employers–Transportation and Communications, said changes to the Canada Labour Code must include new tools to avoid “catastrophic” labour disruptions.

“The inclusion of a neutral, third-party special mediator who can provide a public report on bargaining and inform government actions would be a significant step forward,” he said.

Hynes added that in the rare circumstance where the impacts of a labour disruption on the Canadian economy are so extreme that they run counter to the national public interest, and an agreement is unlikely to be struck, cabinet must have the ability to impose binding arbitration “before the damage is done.”

Prime Minister Mark Carney met with his Liberal caucus in Ottawa on Friday and Saturday as MPs prepare to return to the House of Commons next week.

Looking ahead to the fall sitting of Parliament, several MPs said Saturday that they expect the pace to be fast.

Speaking to reporters Saturday, Liberal MP Robert Oliphant said, “It’s Prime Minister Carney, it’ll be fast.”

Carney promises sweeping economic legislation, fast pace this fall during caucus meeting

Carney said Friday his government is focused on bringing down costs for Canadians and defending the country’s sovereignty, though he acknowledged some of those efforts are in their early stages.

“This is a crucial session of the House of Commons,” he told the caucus. “We are going to introduce some of the most consequential legislation not just of this government, but in decades.”

Carney said the government will introduce legislation this fall to streamline project reviews, to be known as the Building Canada Strong Act.

“For projects and supply chains, our standard will be simple – one project, one review, one year,” he said.

“If we’re going to say no, say no quickly. If we are going to say yes, say yes on time. When Canada decides a project should go ahead, that project will go ahead.”

The Liberal government is also set to release a new budget in the fall sitting.

This all comes against a backdrop of continued threats from U.S. President Donald Trump ’s White House against Canada’s sovereignty and economy.

Carney and his negotiating team walked away from talks with the White House in August, saying that what was on the table was a bad deal for Canada. The trade conflict then escalated, with Trump imposing another volley of tariffs and threatening even more, while Canada imposed its own counter-tariffs.

Industry Minister Melanie Joly said Saturday she is meeting with several Democratic politicians.

Opinion: Carney to meet with leaders of France, Norway closer to home after whirlwind Euro trip

On Saturday, she discussed her recent trip to Chicago, where she met with Democratic Governor J.B. Pritzker. She said the goals of that trip were to work with him on how to eliminate tariffs and to speak with several companies.

Regardless of the outcome of the upcoming U.S. midterm elections, Joly believes – like Carney – that the trade relationship with the United States will never be the same as it was before.

“I think the prime minister is right when he says this represents a rupture,” she said in French. “I think we must always keep in mind that our Plan A is to build our country and ensure we attract investment here. And looking to Europe is important, but so is looking to Asia to reduce our dependence on the United States.”

Carney is set to attend the United Nations General Assembly next week. Canadian officials said earlier this week the General Assembly is large event and Carney and Trump could run into each other. They added that there are no meetings currently scheduled with members of the U.S. administration.

On Saturday, Carney did not give a clear answer when asked if he has any plans to meet with Trump in New York.

stories.title: Carney and Macron to meet in Saint-Pierre-et-Miquelon on Sunday
stories.summary: Prime Minister Mark Carney and French President Emmanuel Macron are holding a symbolic meeting on an archipelago 20 kilometres off the southern coast of Newfoundland on Sunday.
stories.author: Catherine Morrison
stories.content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney and French President Emmanuel Macron are holding a symbolic meeting on an archipelago 20 kilometres off the southern coast of Newfoundland on Sunday, in what both countries say is a show of unity and mutual respect.

The two leaders will hold a working lunch and attend a wreath-laying ceremony in Saint-Pierre-et-Miquelon, a French territory which just barely beats out Greenland as the geographically closest European territory to Canada.

The meeting comes as Canada and the European Union are in talks to create a tighter alliance amid ongoing animosity with the United States and President Donald Trump.

“In a world characterized by a return to power politics, geopolitical tensions and new dependencies, France and Canada share a common ambition: to work together — and with all countries that share these values — to strengthen their capacity to make decisions and act independently,” a spokesperson for Macron’s office said in an email.

The email said France and Canada “share the same values ​​of freedom, democracy, rule of law and respect for national sovereignty.”

Macron was scheduled to be on the islands from Sept. 19 to 21, ahead of his trip to New York City for the UN General Assembly next week. Carney, who will also travel to New York, will join Macron on Saint-Pierre for a few hours on Sunday.

Macron’s office said Carney will become the first Canadian prime minister to have an official visit to Saint-Pierre-et-Miquelon. Macron is the first French president to visit in more than a decade.

For Carney, it’s another chance to showcase Canada’s growing ties with Europe, just days after he visited the European Parliament.

On Wednesday, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said she wants Canada to become the first “associate member” of the European Union.

In her state of the union speech to the European Parliament, she said the two sides must “urgently reimagine” their partnership and move beyond a free-trade agreement to bring the relationship to the “highest level possible.”

Carney addressed the Parliament in Strasbourg, France, on Thursday, saying he welcomed von der Leyen’s ambitions for Canadian partnership.

Carney said while the name and nature of the new arrangement have yet to be determined, the partnership will go up for debate and a vote in Parliament. He said he’s interested in expanding a number of ties, including opportunities for young people, and an integrated market for financial services.

Canada and Europe already have a free trade deal — though it has not been ratified by all EU members — and last year Canada became the only non-European member of the EU’s new defence procurement program.

Carney signalled a desire to become closer to Europe immediately after becoming prime minister in March 2025, when he travelled to meet Macron in Paris, and King Charles in London, within days of being sworn in.

Diya Jiang, a researcher at McGill University at the University of Calgary, said Carney’s visit to Saint-Pierre-et-Miquelon reflects that vision.

“I also think the location of it in itself is symbolic. It is right off the coast of Newfoundland,” she said. “Canada geographically is far away from Europe but this shows … that actually we are closer than you think.”

The Prime Minister’s Office said in a news release that, during the visit, Carney and Macron will discuss “deepening the Canada-France partnership” in sectors such as aerospace, energy and critical minerals. They’re also expected to discuss advanced technologies in quantum science, satellites and supercomputing.

An official from Macron’s office who briefed reporters Thursday said the leaders’ meeting will be an opportunity to promote regional co-operation on fishing, transport, the transit of travellers, university exchanges and trade.

In addition to a working lunch, Carney and Macron will attend a wreath-laying ceremony at a memorial for Free France volunteers. In December 1941, Free French forces peacefully liberated the archipelago from the control of the Vichy regime, which aided Nazi Germany during the Second World War.

— With files from Nick Murray

stories.title: TSB investigating small aircraft accident near Kisbey, Sask.
stories.summary: The TSB says the plane was reported overdue around 10:30 a.m. Friday, and was later located by search and rescue.
stories.author: Rebecca Lau
stories.content:
Two people have been killed in a small aircraft accident near Kisbey, Sask., according to a Manitoba-based pilot training school.

Harv’s Air said a Cessna 172 was on a flight from Regina to Steinbach, Man. via Carlyle, Sask. on a night flight but did not arrive as scheduled.

The Transportation Safety Board of Canada (TSB) said the plane was reported overdue around 10:30 a.m. Friday. The aircraft was located later that evening by search and rescue crews.

A statement from Harv’s Air president, Adam Penner, confirmed both occupants of the aircraft were found deceased.

“The entire Harv’s Air family is shocked and saddened by this tragedy. Both pilots had close ties to their fellow students and instructors. We extend our deepest condolences to family and friends,” he wrote.

“Harv’s Air is working closely with the Transportation Safety Board, Transport Canada, and the RCMP to investigate the cause.”

A witness from the area said she watched searchers fly overhead looking for the crash site Friday evening.

“ I’m looking out the vehicle and I’m trying to drive safely. And then, I pull over, I pull out my binoculars and he’s got the tail. He’s got it open. And then I see two guys — two orange things — jump out. And they’re coming down like this. I’m like, ‘Those are parachutes,” said Chenoa McArthur.

“I see the orange smoke, like the orange smoke starts to build at the top of the hills. And I’m, like, ‘They located something.'”

The TSB deployed a team of investigators to the site on Saturday, which is located in southeast Saskatchewan.

stories.title: Tearful Danielle Smith addresses grievances with Ottawa, need for Alberta's referendum questions
stories.summary: Premier Danielle Smith was overcome with emotion as she launched into speech at an online forum Saturday.
stories.author: Cindy Tran
stories.content:
Premier Danielle Smith was overcome with emotion as she launched into speech at an online forum Saturday, tearfully relaying painful losses some Albertans have shared with her as she works to address grievances with Ottawa that have led to the Oct. 19 referendum question of separation from the country.

The weekend Alberta and the West Assembly, co-chaired by former Reform Party of Canada leader Preston Manning and former British Columbia Premier Gordon Campbell, ran for several hours Saturday morning with a few technical glitches and a presentation from Smith, who later took questions.

In her opening remarks, Smith recounted what she’s been hearing from Albertans, those frustrated and angry with an Ottawa seemingly deaf to their grievances over the past decade. As she spoke of growing affordability pressures faced by farmers and families being squeezed out of house and home, Smith paused to regain her composure several times, apologizing to listeners.

“When proud, hardworking people feel their contribution is taken for granted, and their livelihood is treated as something to be phased out, some begin to ask a painful question — does this country actually want us?” Smith said.

“So that question is what 700,000 signatures represent between the Forever Canada petition and the Stay Free Alberta petition. Some signed because they want to leave. More, many more signed because they want to stay.”

Smith reiterated her stance that she, along with her government and caucus, support Alberta remaining in Canada.

She said the fight to make Canada work for Alberta is working.

Putting the question about the future of Alberta’s independence on the ballot amplifies the message to Ottawa that some voters see it as a serious option.

“Sometimes when people just are hurt, feel mistreated and are angry, sometimes you’ve just got to create an avenue for them to express that,” Smith said.

One attendee asked Smith why she is not campaigning for the option to hold a binding referendum on succession, as he believes that would give Alberta further leverage against Ottawa.

Smith said that would detract from the other nine questions on the ballot around immigration and the constitution, issues she is looking to get a mandate on through the referendum.

“This really crystallized for me that my aspiration is to stay in my lane. I got elected because I want to focus on health care, education, social services and providing supports for seniors and addiction services and public safety,” Smith said.

“I want to really hunker down and focus on my nine, ON addressing the nine questions that I’ve put forward. That’s part of the reason I want such a strong mandate there, and I think it gives me leverage.”

The premier said receiving a mandate on the nine questions will help get the economy back on track. She said issues around immigration have been causing pressure “across the board.”

Taking aim at federal policies, Smith said that after the COVID-19 pandemic, federal immigration levels surged without proper consultation with provinces tasked with delivering more and more services. Alberta swiftly grew by approximately 600,000 people in five years, said Smith, noting spikes in housing costs and rent rose in tandem, while classrooms and emergency rooms became more crowded.

Those temporary residents cost Alberta’s provincial services more than one billion dollars per year, said Smith, emphasizing that permanent residents, or “lifetime taxpayers” will not be impacted by proposed changes to immigration policy.

“The harder question is whether taxpayers should carry the same costs for residents who are here only temporarily,” Smith said.

On the questions of constitutional reform, Smith is also seeking a mandate to work with other willing provinces and territories to attain the authority to choose judges, abolish the senate, give provincial law’s priority when dealing with shared areas, and opt out of federal programs without losing federal funding.

While willing to accept the results that come after the Oct. 19 vote, Smith said she remains hopeful Albertans will give her the mandate she is seeking.

“Every question on this ballot comes back to one thing, which is respect,” Smith said.

“Albertans want to be respected by their country and trusted to run their own affairs. I think every province represented here today wants the same. I believe that we can have that inside Canada.”

stories.title: Canada’s defence minister calls U.S. deal on Greenland ‘encouraging’
stories.summary: National Defence Minister David McGuinty says the United States' deal to boost its military presence in Greenland while keeping the island under Danish control is "encouraging."
stories.author: Catherine Morrison
stories.content:
By Catherine Morrison The Canadian Press

Posted September 19, 2026 4:42 pm

Updated September 22, 2026 2:17 pm

National Defence Minister David McGuinty says the United States’ deal to boost its military presence in Greenland while keeping the island under Danish control is “encouraging.”

U.S. President Donald Trump said Friday he has a deal with Denmark after months of threatening to take the island by force from the NATO ally.

3:32 Trump signs deal with Greenland, Denmark to strengthen Arctic security

The office of Denmark’s prime minister, Mette Frederiksen, says the agreement will be signed by three governments next week during the United Nations General Assembly, but parliamentary action is still needed by the Danish and Greenland governments before it can be enforced.

Speaking to reporters on Parliament Hill on Saturday, McGuinty says it’s encouraging that the U.S. and Greenland have found a way to move forward together.

He also says Arctic nations are coming together, adding that it’s encouraging NATO allies understand that the Arctic is part of their responsibilities.

With his return to the White House last year, Trump called on Denmark to sell Greenland to the United States, and wouldn’t rule out taking the island by military force, even though Denmark is a NATO ally of the U.S.

–With files from The Associated Press

Speaking to reporters on Parliament Hill on Saturday, McGuinty says it’s encouraging that the U.S. and Greenland have found a way to move forward together.
He also says Arctic nations are coming together, adding that it’s encouraging NATO allies understand that the Arctic is part of their responsibilities.

With his return to the White House last year, Trump called on Denmark to sell Greenland to the United States, and wouldn’t rule out taking the island by military force, even though Denmark is a NATO ally of the U.S.

stories.title: ‘Grief never goes away’: Dunn With Cancer Run raises $1.6M for brain cancer research
stories.summary: Hundreds of people gathered at Springbank Park on Saturday for the seventh annual Dunn With Cancer Run, raising money and awareness for glioblastoma research.
stories.author: Reta Ismail
stories.content:
Hundreds of people gathered at Springbank Park on Saturday for the seventh annual Dunn With Cancer Run, raising money and awareness for glioblastoma research.

The event was started by the Dunn family after Wayne Dunn’s daughter, Allison, died from glioblastoma at the age of 33.

Allison left behind three young children, who took part in Saturday’s fundraiser.

“The grief never goes away,” Dunn said. “And by doing something, we can’t bring her back. But what we can do is help other people and other families that are going through it.”

The annual event has raised more than $1.6 million over the past six years, according to Nicole Farrell, CEO of the Brain Tumour Foundation of Canada.

“It’s incredible,” Farrell said. “Over the last six years, the Dunn With Cancer event has raised over $1.6 million. One hundred per cent of those dollars go to fund research — critical research to support glioblastoma.”

Farrell said the funds are an important source of support for researchers working to better understand and treat the disease.

For Dunn, the fundraiser also provides an opportunity for families affected by glioblastoma to connect and raise awareness about the disease.

“Glioblastoma is nothing more than a death sentence,” Dunn said. “And my daughter had four months. The average is about 18.”

He said the money raised through the event is helping support research at hospitals and universities across Canada.

There is currently no cure for glioblastoma, but researchers are studying ways to improve outcomes and the quality and duration of life for people diagnosed with the disease.

Dunn said his family hopes the annual event can help other families facing the same devastating diagnosis.

More information about the fundraiser and how to support the ‘Dunn With Cancer’ campaign is available through the organization’s website .

stories.title: Toronto’s Absolutely Fabrics unveils its new flagship
stories.summary: Owner Kaelen Haworth says the store is meant to feel more akin to a home than a conventional retail environment
stories.author: Mira Miller
stories.content:
When shoppers walk into the new Absolutely Fabrics boutique in Toronto’s Summerhill neighbourhood, owner Kaelen Haworth wants them to feel right at home.

The 7,000 square foot clothing store , which opened Saturday, has been carefully designed to feel warm and inviting. For anyone familiar with the homegrown brand or former fashion designer Haworth, it’s also a given that the space is full of tasteful touches: A Lea Colombo Red Jasper coffee table and matching benches, sculptural lighting pieces by artist Dana Arbib, and artwork by designers carried at the store.

“I want people to come in and stay and have a lovely time whether they’re shopping or not,” said Haworth, who ran two clothing labels in New York before closing them and returning home to Toronto in 2020 to enter the retail space.

The new store is the brand’s flagship; the first location opened on Queen Street West in 2023. Since then, Absolutely Fabrics has become a go-to for premier luxury retail, selling a curated mix of up-and-coming designers, established labels and archival vintage. New for the brand, the Summerhill location will also feature a dedicated menswear floor.

Haworth hopes the new location will be “ the store you have to go to when you’re in Toronto,” in the same vein as Colette in Paris or Barneys and Jeffrey in New York.

Interior designer Clarisa Llaneza (who also happens to be one of the shop’s most loyal customers) created a space that blends into its residential surroundings. Haworth said Llaneza designed the store to feel more akin to a home than a conventional retail environment, with cozy details such as carpeting, dark wood and coffered ceilings.

Instead of window displays, Haworth said, “we have blinds that will close in the evening, and it will be like the house is going to sleep for the night.”

Haworth isn’t alone in her desire to build a memorable brick-and-mortar experience, nor in her choice to open up shop in Summerhill. Other Toronto brands have also been opting for quiet neighbourhoods over busy downtown streets, aiming to create a slower-paced retail environment while becoming part of a local community.

Despite the popularity of e-commerce, research shows that customers are hungry for elevated in-person retail. A survey by financial technology platform Adyen found that 58 per cent of Canadians enjoy visiting physical stores to browse or relax, even without purchase intent, while 52 per cent said they want to see, feel or try an item before buying it.

Brands are acting accordingly, said Santo Ligotti, the vice-president of marketing and member services at the Retail Council of Canada.

“Physical stores play a critical role, not just for the transaction, but for discovery, returns and brand experience,” he said. “What we have seen is ongoing optimization: Some retailers are reducing underperforming locations, others are investing in fewer, better stores and some are renovating existing stores to enhance them.”

Flagship locations in particular play an important role, said Ani Nersessian, the founder of VM ID Inc., a retail visual merchandising agency. A flagship is typically a brand’s largest and most important location, and highlights the best of what a company has to offer.

“While other locations May be more directly accountable for producing sales, flagship stores often have a broader responsibility to build awareness, strengthen brand perception and create experiences that influence purchasing,” she said.

Physical stores also provide opportunities for community events. Absolutely Fabrics’ Queen location hosts launch dinners, styling events and other functions that introduce customers to new brands. These kinds of events will be an even greater priority in the new space, Haworth said.

She enjoys introducing Canadian shoppers to brands she discovered in New York, such as Christopher John Rogers, Nomia and Proenza Schouler. She’s strategic about how she positions their products, placing them next to more well-known but similar designers so her customers can discover pieces that align with their taste.

“Conner Ives does not have Canadian representation,” she said as an example, “So, if we put Conner next to Marni and Fforme, people will then understand that they can buy this brand, too.”

Ultimately, Haworth hopes the new store will be a place where shoppers can enjoy a beautiful space, talk about clothing with knowledgeable staff, enjoy a beverage, try things on and feel good.

“ It started as – and it still remains – a place of discovery,” she said. “That’s what I want people to do when they come in: Discover new brands, discover something new about a brand they already know, and just have a really open and interesting experience.”

stories.title: Smith makes case for Alberta in united Canada ahead of referendum
stories.summary: Even with polls suggesting the remain in Canada vote will win, the number of those voting for separation is ‘too high for comfort,’ Smith says
stories.author: Bill Graveland
stories.content:
An emotional Premier Danielle Smith held back tears Saturday as she recounted a long list of historic indignities Albertans have suffered at the hands of the federal government.

Smith was the opening speaker at a virtual assembly discussing Alberta’s future in Canada, an event co-hosted by former Opposition leader and conservative elder statesman Preston Manning and former B.C. premier Gordon Campbell.

The Alberta premier has called a referendum for Oct. 19 that includes a question on whether Alberta should remain in Canada or whether it’s time to hold a second, binding referendum on starting the legal process to separate.

She was speaking on the reasons for a sovereign Alberta to stay within a united Canada in the future.

“A lot of Albertans are angry and some are more than angry. They’re hurt. I hear it at town halls, in coffee shops, at hockey rinks and in my email inbox,” Smith said before choking up and taking deep breaths before haltingly speaking about the impacts on Albertans.

“From the farmer that felt pressured ... sorry all,” she sighed. “By people who never made a living off the land. For the young family who did everything right and still can’t see how they can afford a home.”

Alberta separation could cost up to $170-billion over first five years, report estimates

Smith also spoke of parents watching an increasing grocery bill and opening a utility bill in January with “a knot in their stomach.”

Manning noted Smith’s emotional response to the issue.

“You should not feel embarrassed about showing your emotions at the front end. I’m reminded that Abraham Lincoln did not use the term public opinion. He said he was interested in public sentiment.”

Smith called the referendum earlier this year. She has said enough Albertans now view separation as a legitimate response to federal interference in provincial affairs, and that it’s time to put the issue to rest once and for all in a vote.

The Alberta premier told a virtual assembly discussing the province's future in Canada that a lot of Albertans are angry, but it would be a mistake to separate now that progress is being made with Mark Carney on Sept. 19.

The Canadian Press

Critics, including the Opposition NDP, say Smith is inflating and legitimizing the grievances of a small sliver of discontented Albertans in order to mollify hardline separatists in her United Conservative party.

Smith said Saturday that Western frustration with Ottawa is nothing new and for the past 10 years in particular, it felt like Ottawa was trying to shut down the province’s economy.

“When a proud, hardworking people feel their contribution is taken for granted and their livelihood is treated as something to be phased out, some begin to ask a painful question. Does this country actually want us?”

Opinion: Danielle Smith is no separatist – she’s something even more dangerous

Smith said even with polls suggesting the remain in Canada vote will win, the number of those voting for separation is “too high for comfort.”

But she said there is reason to be optimistic about Alberta’s future relationship with Ottawa, including battles over Bill C69, also known as the no new pipelines act, caps on oil-and-gas production, and on clean-energy electricity regulations.

“I support Alberta remaining in Canada ... I also believe Albertans deserve a say. The fight to make Canada work for Alberta is working. When Alberta stood up and refused to back down, the country started listening,” she said.

“It happened because Albertans got loud and stayed loud. Your anger was not wasted,” she said.

Smith said new Prime Minister Mark Carney has acted constructively with Alberta in coming up with an Alberta-Ottawa energy agreement and working toward a new West Coast pipeline.

“Not long ago the oilsands were treated as a national target. Today they’re increasingly seen as a national treasure,” Smith said.

“Why walk away from the table when we’re finally winning at it? And to those who have always wanted to stay -- staying should not mean settling. A future federal government could undo all this progress that we’ve made with a stroke of a pen.”

The Alberta premier has called a referendum for Oct. 19 that includes a question on whether Alberta should remain in Canada or whether it’s time to hold a second, binding referendum on starting the legal process to separate.
She was speaking on the reasons for a sovereign Alberta to stay within a united Canada in the future.

“A lot of Albertans are angry and some are more than angry. They’re hurt. I hear it at town halls, in coffee shops, at hockey rinks and in my email inbox,” Smith said before choking up and taking deep breaths before haltingly speaking about the impacts on Albertans.

“From the farmer that felt pressured ... sorry all,” she sighed. “By people who never made a living off the land. For the young family who did everything right and still can’t see how they can afford a home.”
Alberta separation could cost up to $170-billion over first five years, report estimates
Smith also spoke of parents watching an increasing grocery bill and opening a utility bill in January with “a knot in their stomach.”
Manning noted Smith’s emotional response to the issue.
“You should not feel embarrassed about showing your emotions at the front end. I’m reminded that Abraham Lincoln did not use the term public opinion. He said he was interested in public sentiment.”

Smith called the referendum earlier this year. She has said enough Albertans now view separation as a legitimate response to federal interference in provincial affairs, and that it’s time to put the issue to rest once and for all in a vote.

The Alberta premier told a virtual assembly discussing the province's future in Canada that a lot of Albertans are angry, but it would be a mistake to separate now that progress is being made with Mark Carney on Sept. 19.
The Canadian Press

Critics, including the Opposition NDP, say Smith is inflating and legitimizing the grievances of a small sliver of discontented Albertans in order to mollify hardline separatists in her United Conservative party.
Smith said Saturday that Western frustration with Ottawa is nothing new and for the past 10 years in particular, it felt like Ottawa was trying to shut down the province’s economy.

“When a proud, hardworking people feel their contribution is taken for granted and their livelihood is treated as something to be phased out, some begin to ask a painful question. Does this country actually want us?”
Opinion: Danielle Smith is no separatist – she’s something even more dangerous
Smith said even with polls suggesting the remain in Canada vote will win, the number of those voting for separation is “too high for comfort.”

But she said there is reason to be optimistic about Alberta’s future relationship with Ottawa, including battles over Bill C69, also known as the no new pipelines act, caps on oil-and-gas production, and on clean-energy electricity regulations.

“I support Alberta remaining in Canada ... I also believe Albertans deserve a say. The fight to make Canada work for Alberta is working. When Alberta stood up and refused to back down, the country started listening,” she said.
“It happened because Albertans got loud and stayed loud. Your anger was not wasted,” she said.
Smith said new Prime Minister Mark Carney has acted constructively with Alberta in coming up with an Alberta-Ottawa energy agreement and working toward a new West Coast pipeline.
“Not long ago the oilsands were treated as a national target. Today they’re increasingly seen as a national treasure,” Smith said.

“Why walk away from the table when we’re finally winning at it? And to those who have always wanted to stay -- staying should not mean settling. A future federal government could undo all this progress that we’ve made with a stroke of a pen.”

stories.title: Police investigating after Woodstock structure fire leaves estimated $1M damage
stories.summary: Woodstock Fire Department crews were dispatched to a reported structure fire on Upper Thames Drive at about 5:25 a.m. The blaze had extended to adjacent properties by the time firefighters arrived.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
A fire that spread to neighbouring properties in Woodstock early Saturday morning has caused an estimated $1 million in damage, authorities say.

Woodstock Fire Department crews were dispatched to a reported structure fire on Upper Thames Drive at about 5:25 a.m. The blaze had extended to adjacent properties by the time firefighters arrived.

Officials said a joint investigation involving the Woodstock Fire Department and Woodstock Police Service is underway to determine the cause of the fire.

Police and fire officials have not released further details as the investigation continues.

stories.title: Rescue Rendezvous returns to London’s Catty Shack
stories.summary: The family-friendly event features adoption discounts and an opportunity for residents to meet cats currently waiting for permanent homes.
stories.author: Reta Ismail
stories.content:
Cat lovers had a chance to meet their potential new furry family members Saturday as the City of London hosted its annual Rescue Rendezvous at The Catty Shack.

The family event at 756 Windermere Rd. brought together prospective pet owners and local animal rescue organizations, with cats and kittens available for adoption.

For some visitors, the event was an opportunity to add a new member to their household.

“My wife and I, we just moved into a condo together, and we both come from families that have cats,” said Aidan McLeod, who attended the event, all the way from Markham, Ontario, looking to adopt.

“So we’re looking to get some cats for our condo and complete our household.”

Kyle Quenneville was also hoping to find a new companion. “We’re looking to get a cat. The house is getting a little lonely, so we’re looking to get a little furry friend,” he said.

For those who found a cat they wanted to adopt, the process was relatively straightforward.

“The adoption process is fairly brief. It involves finding a cat you like, and then you will fill out an application,” said Ethan Wade, an animal care technician at The Catty Shack.

The event also gave local rescue organizations a chance to work alongside the city and showcase cats looking for homes.

Wade Jeffery, manager of Municipal Compliance and Animal Welfare Services for the City of London, said about half of the cats and kittens at the event were from the city’s facility, with rescue organizations bringing additional animals.

“We do have our rescue organizations that support the event. They bring in their cats and kittens to hopefully have them adopted out as well,” Jeffery said.

“So we kind of share the facility today and it’s a good opportunity to have that collaboration.”

The Catty Shack is a city facility that is operated by the City’s service provider, London Animal Care Centre (Lacc). It provides temporary housing for healthy, friendly and vaccinated cats while they wait to be adopted.

The centre is located at 756 Windermere Rd. and is open Wednesday to Friday from 1 p.m. to 7 p.m. and Saturday and Sunday from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m.

stories.title: Nato selects German general as next military committee chair over Canada’s defence chief
stories.summary: General Jennie Carignan had sought to become the first woman to hold the alliance post
stories.author: Kyle Duggan and Catherine Morrison
stories.content:
Nato chiefs of defence have elected German Gen. Carsten Breuer as the next chair of the alliance’s military committee, over Canada’s top military commander .

Chief of the Defence Staff Gen. Jennie Carignan ran against Breuer for the top Nato position.

Nato chiefs of defence met in Copenhagen, Denmark, Saturday to choose the next chair. It’s a prestige posting but it doesn’t carry the same level of clout as the alliance’s most senior role of supreme allied commander, a powerful command position that usually goes to an American.

Only three Canadians have ever served as chair of the military committee, and the last time was during the Afghanistan war in the mid-2000s.

In a social media post, Defence Minister David McGuinty congratulated Breuer on his election.

“Canada was proud to nominate Gen. Jennie Carignan, whose strong candidacy reflected her exceptional leadership, experience and deep commitment to Allied collaboration,” he said.

“We remain firmly committed to Nato and our collective defence, and look forward to continuing to work closely with Gen. Breuer and all of our Allies.”

Opinion: This week, Mark Carney laid out a vision of Canada’s future. Now comes the hard part

If she had won, Carignan would have become the first woman to be named to the position, and also would have to step down as leader of Canada’s military, a role she has held since 2024.

Carignan said in a statement posted to social media Saturday that it was an honour to stand as a candidate and to engage with fellow allied chiefs of defence throughout the process.

“I look forward to continuing that collaboration with all of my allied colleagues” she said. “There is important work ahead for our alliance, and I know General Breuer will bring strong leadership to his new role.”

Carignan said that, going forward, her focus remains on serving as chief of the defence staff and leading the transformation of the Canadian Armed Forces.

The current military chair, Italy’s Admiral Giuseppe Cavo Dragone, will leave his post next year.

Dragone said on social media that Breuer’s operational judgement, deep familiarity with the alliance and leadership of the German armed forces would “serve Nato well.”

“The Chiefs of Defence have placed their trust in you at a demanding moment for Euro-Atlantic security,” he said. “You will have the full support of the Committee and of the International Military Staff through the transition, and I look forward to working closely with you until the handover.”

stories.title: Opposition ‘politicking’ on Weedmark private flights unless evidence exists, says policy expert
stories.summary: Kevin Weedmark is defending his recent set of flights to attend government events, saying he paid for them out of pocket despite mounting questions from the Opposition.
stories.author: Vanessa Tiberio
stories.content:
As Saskatchewan’s Opposition presses a government backbencher to release receipts showing he paid out of his own pocket for private flights to attend government events, a policy expert says the criticism amounts to political posturing unless evidence emerges that public dollars were used.

Kevin Weedmark, Saskatchewan Party MLA representing Moosomin-Montmartre, says he paid out of pocket for flights across the province to attend government events on Aug. 27.

The assertion follows mounting questions from the NDP after a now-deleted “day in the life” video from a person travelling with Weedmark was posted to social media.

Weedmark says it would have been difficult to drive across the province to attend events in Lloydminster and Saskatoon.

The video also shows Weedmark stopping in Regina before returning to Moosomin.

“As a result, I decided to charter a plane from a local company at my own personal expense. There were no taxpayer dollars involved,” Weedmark said in a statement Sept. 8.

The NDP also pointed to a second video from August 2025, from the person travelling with Weedmark, showing a group of individuals touring Jim Pattison Hospital and the Ronald McDonald House in Saskatoon. The video has since been deleted.

“Does he expect us to believe he’s paid for all of these flights? Travelling for work out of his own pocket?” Meara Conway, the NDP’s deputy house leader and health critic, told reporters Monday.

The NDP is also questioning a flight taken on June 1, 2025, on a jet that has the same registration number as the planes in the social media videos, linking flight records to Weedmark’s location at an opening reception for the first ministers’ meeting in Saskatoon.

But Weedmark denies the NDP’s claim he flew last June to or from Saskatoon to attend that reception, saying he drove instead.

“The NDP’s latest attempted smear is a blatant lie,” Weedmark said in a statement shared with media Monday.

Global News reached out to Weedmark for an interview, but did not hear back.

There is no rule requiring a public official to prove to the Opposition that they paid out of pocket, said Ian Stedman, an associate professor who specializes in government ethics at York University.

“Unless the Opposition has some evidence to suggest that he is paying with taxpayer dollars, then all this is politicking and trying to get him to respond in a way that puts him in a bad light,” Stedman said.

When it comes to spending public dollars, Stedman says MLAs are typically expected to do so as economically as possible.

“Even if he is permitted to do it for his transportation, and he has a big budget, the next question is, is that the right thing to do with public dollars? And one is a rules question, and one is a perception and public trust question,” he said.

“A conflict of interest arises when you make a decision in your public capacity to benefit yourself or improperly benefit someone else and their private interests and their private capacity,” he said.

“This doesn’t appear to be that.”

The province’s conflict of interest commissioner investigates any potential breach at the request of another member, the premier or the legislative assembly after determining whether there are reasonable and probable grounds to proceed.

“This ensures that the threshold for proceeding to an investigation is based upon something more than innuendo, gossip, or hearsay,” Maurice Herauf, Saskatchewan’s conflict of interest commissioner, told Global News in an emailed statement.

Scott Andrew, owner Air Andrew, the company operating the three flights in question, told Global News that his company has not received money from the Saskatchewan Party.

Andrew is also pushing back on the NDP’s flight cost estimates, which it is sharing with the public, assigning a price tag of around $50,000 to each flight.

The video also shows Weedmark stopping in Regina before returning to Moosomin.

stories.title: Police arrest suspect after vehicle strikes pedestrians at Quebec music festival
stories.summary: Police say a man in his 20s was arrested about an hour later, but it remains unclear whether the incident was intentional
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
A driver who allegedly struck and injured six pedestrians at a Quebec country music festival had not planned an attack, provincial police say.

The incident happened at a western-themed festival in Saint-Tite, Que., around 4:30 a.m. Saturday.

Speaking at the festival site later in the day, police spokesperson Audrey-Anne Bilodeau said the person’s alleged actions did not appear to be premeditated.

“We are not dealing with an individual using a ram truck who planned the attack to intentionally injure people,” she told reporters.

She added that police are looking into the possibility that the driver knew the victims.

“Could there have been an altercation between some of the people involved that might explain the action this person took?” said Bilodeau.

The victims, aged between 17 and 21, were taken to hospital and were in stable condition, she said.

Police said the suspect, a man in his 20s, had fled. But his vehicle was spotted an hour later in the Quebec City area.

He was arrested and remained in custody later Saturday, charged with dangerous driving causing bodily injury and hit-and-run resulting in bodily injury. Bilodeau said he would be released after questioning and appear in court at a later date.

The suspect was not under the influence of alcohol or drugs at the time of the incident, Bilodeau said.

The festival organizers responded to the incident in a statement sent to The Canadian Press by e-mail, saying that their thoughts are with the victims and their families.

“The safety of our festivalgoers, volunteers, and staff remains our top priority,” they said. The festival is a celebratory event where everyone should feel safe.”

They added that Saturday’s activities would proceed as scheduled.

stories.title: 6 injured after vehicle strikes pedestrians at Quebec festival
stories.summary: Quebec provincial police say six people were struck by a vehicle and injured in the early hours of Saturday morning in St.-Tite, Que., where a 10-day festival is being held.
stories.author: Rebecca Lau
stories.content:
Six people were struck and injured by a vehicle early Saturday morning in St.-Tite, Que., where a 10-day Western festival is being held, according to Quebec provincial police.

A spokesperson with Sûreté du Québec said police were called around 4:30 a.m. to Boulevard St-Joseph, after pedestrians were hit.

Police said the vehicle fled the scene, but was found at around 5:30 a.m. in Quebec City.

A man in his 20s was arrested and will be interviewed by investigators.

According to police, the victims have varying injuries, including some that are serious.

Police said it’s unclear whether the incident was intentional, and that an investigation is underway.

Deputy Premier and Minister of Domestic Security Ian Lafrenière said Saturday there were “no reasons to believe it was planned, (or that) it was a terrorist attack.”

“We don’t have all of the details because now he’s getting questioned by the Sûreté du Québec but from what we learned, he’s been involved in a quarrel, a little fight. He left the scene, hit the pedestrians and he was apprehended about an hour later,” said Lafrenière.

The town is currently hosting its annual Festival Western de St-Tite, a country-western event. The festival continued Saturday.

“The fact is, this is an isolated incident — that’s what we need to keep in mind — and the site is extremely secure,” Danielle St-Amand, the festival’s board chair, told reporters on Saturday morning.

“This applies to everyone involved: the town of St-Tite, us (the festival organizers), and the Sûreté du Québec. So, I believe people can feel safe here, and we will do everything in our power to ensure their safety.”

In a statement, Premier Christine Fréchette said her thoughts are with the victims and that the ongoing investigation will determine what happened. She said she is in close contact with Lafrenière for updates on the investigation.

On social media, Parti Quebecois leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon said his thoughts are with the injured and those who witnessed the scene, and praised first responders.

stories.title: Bill will help reduce government interventions during strikes: Hajdu
stories.summary: Ottawa — Jobs Minister Patty Hajdu says upcoming legislation will help reduce the number of times the federal government has to intervene in strikes.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
OTTAWA — Jobs Minister Patty Hajdu says upcoming legislation will help reduce the number of times the federal government has to intervene in strikes.

Speaking to reporters on Parliament Hill Saturday, Hajdu did not provide many details about expected plans to amend the Canada Labour Code.

However, she said no government wants to intervene in a strike and that parties are better off if they can solve problems themselves at the negotiating table.

“The government already has the power to intervene,” she said. “The point is to reduce the times that the government is forced to solve the problem for employers and unions.”

Employers and unions have disagreed strongly on the use of Section 107 of the labour code, which has been used increasingly to curb work stoppages in key industries by referring disputes to the Canada Industrial Relations Board.

Employment and Social Development Canada said in a report earlier this month that employers and unions are divided over how much power Ottawa should have to intervene in labour disputes.

Transport Minister Steven MacKinnon told reporters Saturday that the legislation — which could be introduced in the House of Commons as early as next week — isn’t targeting the right to strike.

“What we want to do is make achieving collective agreements easier,” he said.

Bea Bruske, president of the Canadian Labour Congress, said in a statement that the right to strike is in the national interest.

“Canada’s economic security depends on workers having the power to bargain for better wages, working conditions and job security,” she said. “Any new power to prevent or shut down a legal strike, including before it begins, would weaken that power. Canada needs workers with our elbows up, not our hands tied.”

Derrick Hynes, CEO of Federally Regulated Employers—Transportation and Communications, said changes to the Canada Labour Code must include new tools to avoid “catastrophic” labour disruptions.

“The inclusion of a neutral, third-party special mediator who can provide a public report on bargaining and inform government actions would be a significant step forward,” he said.

Hynes added that in the rare circumstance where the impacts of a labour disruption on the Canadian economy are so extreme that they run counter to the national public interest, and an agreement is unlikely to be struck, cabinet must have the ability to impose binding arbitration “before the damage is done.”

Prime Minister Mark Carney met with his Liberal caucus in Ottawa on Friday and Saturday as MPs prepare to return to the House of Commons next week.

Looking ahead to the fall sitting of Parliament, several MPs said Saturday that they expect the pace to be fast.

Speaking to reporters Saturday, Liberal MP Robert Oliphant said, “It’s Prime Minister Carney, it’ll be fast.”

Carney said Friday his government is focused on bringing down costs for Canadians and defending the country’s sovereignty, though he acknowledged some of those efforts are in their early stages.

“This is a crucial session of the House of Commons,” he told the caucus. “We are going to introduce some of the most consequential legislation not just of this government, but in decades.”

Carney said the government will introduce legislation this fall to streamline project reviews, to be known as the Building Canada Strong Act.

“For projects and supply chains, our standard will be simple — one project, one review, one year,” he said.

“If we’re going to say no, say no quickly. If we are going to say yes, say yes on time. When Canada decides a project should go ahead, that project will go ahead.”

The Liberal government is also set to release a new budget in the fall sitting.

This all comes against a backdrop of continued threats from President Donald Trump’s White House against Canada’s sovereignty and economy.

Carney and his negotiating team walked away from talks with the White House in August, saying that what was on the table was a bad deal for Canada. The trade conflict then escalated, with Trump imposing another volley of tariffs and threatening even more, while Canada imposed its own counter-tariffs.

Industry Minister Melanie Joly said Saturday she is meeting with several Democratic politicians.

On Saturday, she discussed her recent trip to Chicago, where she met with Democratic Governor J.B. Pritzker. She said the goals of that trip were to work with him on how to eliminate tariffs and to speak with several companies.

Regardless of the outcome of the upcoming U.S. midterm elections, Joly believes — like Carney — that the trade relationship with the United States will never be the same as it was before.

“I think the prime minister is right when he says this represents a rupture,” she said in French. “I think we must always keep in mind that our Plan A is to build our country and ensure we attract investment here. And looking to Europe is important, but so is looking to Asia to reduce our dependence on the United States.”

Carney is set to attend the United Nations General Assembly next week. Canadian officials said earlier this week the General Assembly is large event and Carney and Trump could run into each other. They added that there are no meetings currently scheduled with members of the U.S. administration.

On Saturday, Carney did not give a clear answer when asked if he has any plans to meet with Trump in New York.

stories.title: Richmond Night Market prepares for its grand finale
stories.summary: After 26 years, one of Metro Vancouver’s most vibrant cultural gatherings will close its doors
stories.author: Justine Beaulieu-Poudrier
stories.content:
When the Richmond Night Market’s neon lights turn off for the last time on Sunday, the Metro Vancouver community will say goodbye to one of the region’s most vibrant cultural gatherings after 26 years.

The event, which ran on weekends from April to September, was founded by entrepreneur Raymond Cheung in 2000 to bring public night-time culture inspired by Asian night markets to the B.C. suburb.

Mr. Cheung announced the market’s permanent closing last month. He said the market’s lease near Bridgeport station was ending, and that the potential cost of taking on a new, pricier lease wouldn’t make sense for the business.

The market originally opened at Continental Shopping Centre in Richmond. Over the years, it moved to bigger sites, evolving into what organizers claim is North America’s largest night market. It drew more than one million visitors, tourists and locals alike, each year. The market hosted upwards of 200 vendors selling food, clothing and more in brightly lit stalls.

Since relocating in 2012 to its current location near Bridgeport station, the market became a major cultural and economic anchor in the region.

With its lease expiring and no affordable new site to welcome the large event, the only course of action seemed to be to close the market. “It’s a very mixed feeling,” owner Mr. Cheung said.

“The sad part, of course, is this is the end of the chapter. I didn’t expect this to last forever,” he said. “… But this market is about bonding, it’s about community – that’s what it is.”

For families like the Purbas, who drove from nearby Delta for their fourth visit this season, the closure cuts deep. “We’re sad that it is closing, but it is the last weekend we can attend, so that’s why we’re here,” Gagandeep Purba said.

The market’s reputation is known across borders. Jesica Vinson travelled from Seattle with her family to catch the final season. “Is there any way to save it?” she asked.

Behind the food stalls, however, many long-term vendors were feeling at peace. At Po Wah Dim Sum, Christopher Yee helped his mother, Lai Wah, wrap up a legacy of more than two decades running the family business. “My mom has been doing it for 26 years and she’s retiring this year,” Mr. Yee said.

Others, such as Francis Dela Chica of Bao Buns, have accepted the closing as bittersweet. He said that while it’s sad that the night market is ending, it was also the perfect incubator for small businesses like his own. “It was a good place to start, to test your products, to meet new customers.”
