stories.title: A blood test that detects brain injury could soon help intimate partner violence survivors
stories.summary: UBC scientists hope the results could be used to access treatment and as evidence in courts
stories.author: Qurrat Ul Ain
stories.content:
Kristen Sandborn was forgetting basic things: appointments, conversations, the sequence of some events. Her vision was changing drastically and she was avoiding social gatherings.

She knew this was most likely because of a head injury that followed another violent attack by her ex-husband. But she was never formally diagnosed: Going to the doctor or reporting the injury to police, she worried, came with the risk of her being found incapable of keeping her children should her partner contest custody.

“When you get punched in the head [by your partner], and you have kids, you don’t go to the doctor about that. You just don’t because you don’t want your kids taken away. It’s almost like the only option you have is to fight your body,” Ms. Sandborn, who is from Victoria, said in an interview with The Globe and Mail.

According to 2024 data released by Statistics Canada last October, Canadian police services reported 356 victims of intimate partner violence per 100,000 people aged 12 and older. In all, there were 128,175 victims of intimate partner violence in 2024. Those are the figures that are reported; such violence is widely believed to be under-reported by victims.

Yet, Canada has no standardized screening protocol for emergency rooms, primary care settings or transition houses – a safe, temporary home for women and their children leaving abusive or violent relationships – to ensure brain injury is documented when intimate partner violence is reported or suspected.

Scientists at the University of British Columbia, working as part of the Ascend-IPV (Advocates, Academics, Survivors and Clinicians to End Intimate Partner Violence) initiative, are getting closer to figuring out a simple blood test that would indicate the presence of a brain injury. The innovation could ensure vulnerable women get the health care they need and provide documented evidence of changes in the brain that could be used in court.

“Without a screening standard, there is no reliable diagnosis. And without a reliable diagnostic standard, there is no pathway to provincially fund brain-injury support or justice in family courts for identifying such injuries,” said Tori Dach, manager at the Cridge Centre for the Family , B.C.’s only established program that offers direct services to the victims of brain injury from intimate partner violence.

Cheryl Wellington, a professor of pathology and laboratory medicine at UBC, is among the researchers who published a paper in BMJ Journals last fall detailing Ascend-Ipv’s work.

The researchers studied blood samples of 177 survivors, looking for brain-related proteins.

“These proteins are released when the brain is hurt, like crumbs left behind after damage, which leak into the blood,” said Dr. Wellington in a recent interview with The Globe.

Finding them is difficult because brain proteins in blood “are very dilute; like needing to count a few grains of sugar in an Olympic-sized swimming pool,” she said.

But technologies to measure brain-related proteins in blood are advancing rapidly, and the UBC team has Canada’s largest and most comprehensive program for detecting blood-based biomarkers for brain disorders, Dr. Wellington said.

“We are creating a biological baseline of truth,” she said.

The research found about eight out of 10 of the women studied likely have some kind of brain injury from the abuse.

“What we’re trying to do is build a blood-testing system in emergency departments so that when someone comes in after intimate partner violence, clinicians can collect evidence that the brain is involved, something we don’t do right now,” Dr. Wellington said.

What is in Bill C-16, Ottawa’s legislation that seeks to toughen gender-based violence laws?

UBC neuroscientist Paul van Donkelaar studies concussions in hockey and football players by using tools designed to track how repeated hits changed the brain. He is working on the Ascend-IPV research with Dr. Wellington.

“We started applying the same tests to survivors of IPV,” he said. “We see the same sorts of changes in brain function as in young athletes and sometimes even worse because of everything else that comes with living through violence.”

In sport, he points out, the culture has shifted from “shake it off” to “if in doubt, sit them out.”

Coaches now pull players from the game and insist on a proper assessment after a hard hit.

“With IPV, we’re only at that beginning stage,” he said. “People are finally recognizing it’s happening, but now we need it written into policy and into health care and legal reforms so the brain injury is actually taken into account.”

The courts are starting to take notice of the impact of IPV.

In a landmark family law judgment in May, the Supreme Court of Canada created a new legal basis for people to seek damages for alleged intimate partner violence in relationships marred by coercive control.

The decision could make it easier for people who suffer wide-ranging abuse in an intimate partner relationship to win cash compensation in the civil courts.

Dr. Wellington believes the blood test could give the legal system something it has never had: objective proof that intimate partner violence can injure the brain.

“It is biological evidence that something has been done to this person to cause damage,” she said. “It’s kind of like the DNA of a brain injury, or an X-ray of a broken bone.”

In custody disputes, a diagnosis of brain injury has been used to argue cognitive unfitness to suggest a mother cannot reliably recall events, manage a household or protect her children.

“In our society, no one questions an athlete’s cognitive integrity or their fitness as a parent simply because they’ve sustained a concussion on the field,” Dr. Wellington said.

“Yet for a survivor of intimate partner violence, a brain injury is often weaponized against [women] in custody battles to suggest they are unstable or unfit.”

Nowhere to turn: Shelters can’t keep up with demand to help those fleeing domestic violence

Karen Mason is an advocate and co-founder, along with Dr. van Donkelaar, of the non-profit Supporting Survivors of Abuse and Brain Injury through Research, or Soar. She said, “While attitudes towards women who suffered brain injury from domestic violence are changing slowly, the efforts at a reliable diagnosis will be a game-changer for mothers embroiled in custody battles with their abusive partners.”

She added, “One of the challenges that we’re seeing coming up is that barrier with diagnosis; the court wants a hard line doctor’s diagnosis, which is difficult to get.”

For survivors, Dr. Wellington said, a diagnosis would change several things at once. It gives women a biological explanation for symptoms that are too often dismissed. “There is a reason they might be a bit forgetful,” she said. “It’s not just in their mind. There could be a biological basis that May be treatable or recoverable in some cases.”

It would also open eligibility for support and rehabilitation programs already used in concussion care, and for any new therapies developed down the road.

Dr. Wellington said her research team’s ambition is to enable every emergency room to perform blood tests for brain injury in suspected IPV cases, and to enable transition houses to refer clients to medical and support services.

But that’s going to take “a massive shift in both funding and public consciousness,” she said.

Evidence of a brain injury, while allowing access to treatment, could also be used against mothers in custody battles, as Ms. Sandborn was originally afraid of when she avoided her diagnosis. When Dr. van Donkelaar’s team asked family lawyers directly if a brain injury diagnosis could be turned against a mother in a custody fight, he said the answer was unanimously yes. When the researchers asked if the lawyers were acting for the alleged perpetrator, would they use a brain injury diagnosis, the answer was also yes.

“They even said they felt awful saying it, but it’s just the reality of the system,” Dr. van Donkelaar said.

Ms. Sandborn left the marriage, and she was able to keep her children, primarily because during a later assault, she was able to reach her sister before her ex-husband took the phone away; her sister called the police, who arrived on the scene.

Ms. Sandborn’s ex-husband received a conditional sentence after he was charged.

When his probation ended, his record disappeared, which is standard practice for conditional sentences treated as first offences by the court. He continued working in his white-collar profession.

“People don’t think that happens,” Ms. Sandborn said.

“They think it happens in poverty. But it happens at all different levels of the community, different statuses, ethnicities and religious groups. It’s just everywhere.”

stories.title: London mayoral candidate pledges two-year freeze on recreation fees
stories.summary: Josh Morgan is promising to freeze municipal recreation fees for at least two years if elected, saying the move would help keep city programs affordable for families.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
London mayoral candidate Josh Morgan is promising to freeze municipal recreation fees for at least two years if elected, saying the move would help keep city programs affordable for families.

Morgan announced the proposal Friday at the StarTech.com Community Centre. Under the plan, he said fees for city-operated recreation programs and facilities, including swimming lessons, public skating, fitness classes, drop-in programs and community centre activities, would remain at current rates for a minimum of two years.

Morgan said the fee freeze is intended to provide greater cost certainty for residents facing household budget pressures while encouraging participation in recreation programs.

The proposal would also expand the city’s Play Your Way Fund, which provides financial assistance to eligible low-income residents for recreation programs and activities. Morgan said the city would review eligibility requirements and the application process, with the goal of making the program easier to access and ensuring sufficient funding.

In addition, he said the plan calls for an increase in free community programming, including activities such as public skates and swims.

Morgan said the proposal builds on previous investments in parks, trails, playgrounds and other public spaces, and aims to keep recreation opportunities accessible to residents.

stories.title: Donating to the Terry Fox Foundation? Here’s what a cancer researcher is doing with the money
stories.summary: Dr. Tallulah Andrews remembers doing the Terry Fox Run every year when she was growing up. The Western University professor says it's a full-circle moment to be conducting a cancer research project using funds from the Terry Fox Foundation.
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: Dr. Tallulah Andrews remembers doing the Terry Fox Run every year when she was growing up. The Western University professor says it's a full-circle moment to be conducting a cancer research project using funds from the Terry Fox Foundation.
· Posted: Sep 19, 2026 9:11 AM EDT | Last Updated: 42 minutes ago

Dr. Tallulah Andrews says she remembers doing the Terry Fox Run every year when she was growing up. So it's a full-circle experience for the Western University professor to be conducting a cancer research project using funds from the Terry Fox Foundation.
"It's been really great seeing that it's all come back around," she said.
Andrews is in her second year of researching "metastasis," which is the process of how cancer cells spread beyond the original site of a tumour, she explained.
"It's to figure out where they go and why they go there so that we can hopefully develop some sort of therapy to prevent the spread of these tumour cells," Andrews said.
LISTEN | How a London, Ont., cancer researcher is scaling her work with support from the Terry Fox Foundation:
London Morning 6:05 Where does the money raised during Terry Fox Runs go?

Most people know that money raised during Terry Fox runs goes into cancer research, but what research benefits from the funds? Biochemistry professor Tallulah Andrews told London Morning about specific research that gets money from the runs.

Her project specifically looks at a rare type of cancer that starts in fat cells, called myxoid liposarcoma. That type of cancer is not typically deadly at first, but has a high chance of spreading and becoming more harmful, Andrews said.
For her research, Andrews recruited a group of Canadians with the disease. She started with 56 patients, but funding from the Terry Fox Foundation allowed her to expand the cohort to 86.
It's one of the largest groups of patients with myxoid liposarcoma to be analyzed in the country, she said.

"We really could not do most of this project without the Terry Fox funding," Andrews said. "It's been really fabulous to be able to expand the project and hopefully get a really good answer, and potentially now even start looking for a particular drug."

The Terry Fox Foundation has raised more than $1 billion for cancer research since Fox's Marathon of Hope in 1980. Over the past 40 years, the foundation says it has funded more than 1,300 cancer research projects.

"It's really rewarding to be able to know that there are people out there who will hopefully — maybe not this year or next year, but sometime in the future — be able to directly benefit from this research," Andrews said.
Don Clayton, who has been volunteering and fundraising with the Terry Fox Run in London for 26 years, also experienced a full circle moment when he was diagnosed with prostate cancer.
The Londoner was surprised to discover his radiation oncologist was a recipient of funding from the Terry Fox Research Institute.

The oncologist, Dr. Lucas Mendez, works at London Health Sciences Centre's Verspeeten Family Cancer Centre and has even been awarded the Terry Fox New Investigator Award to research radiotherapy for prostate cancer.
"That worked out, how lucky it was it to get him," Clayton said.
After six rounds of radiation, Clayton said he was cancer-free. "I'm glad that I beat it," he said.

Volunteering with the Terry Fox Run is fulfilling work, he said. At one point in 2008, he spent more than three months driving across Canada towing Terry Fox's refurbished iconic camper van with members of the Fox family, stopping at more than 4,000 spots along the way.
"Nobody else was like him." he said. "He's done so much for the country. It's heartwarming, and I'm just glad I'm part of it."
Clayton and other volunteers are gearing up for another event this Sunday at Springbank Gardens in London.
"It's my way of giving back," he said.

As for Andrews research, she said her research funds are paying off, with her team making some early discoveries. Most recently, the funding has also supported research into metabolism in cancer cells, which is how they process energy.
Cancer research remains important across the country, Andrews said.

"It's still one of the leading causes of mortality in Canada, and it's expected to grow as we have a more aging population," she said. "It's also a major burden on the healthcare system, so it's very important that we find ways to relieve this and hopefully prevent the worst outcomes."
The46th annual Terry Fox Run in Londonwill take place Sunday morning at Springbank Gardens.

Afternoon Drive 7:44 Cancer survivor still giving back to Terry Fox Run after 26 years

London's Bob Clayton has volunteered with the Terry Fox Run in London for 26 years. He talks with Josette Lafleur about his own cross-Canada journey in Fox's iconic camper van, and his cancer diagnosis.

stories.title: London edges Windsor in overtime after late equalizer forces extra period
stories.summary: The London Knights opened their season with an overtime victory after erasing a late push from the Windsor Spitfires and securing a 4-3 win in extra time.
stories.author: CTVNewsLondon.ca Staff
stories.content:
The London Knights opened their season with an overtime victory after erasing a late push from the Windsor Spitfires and securing a 4-3 win in extra time.

Windsor appeared poised to steal the game after London carried a lead into the final minute, but the Knights forced overtime when Bogdan Yakushevsky scored his first Ontario Hockey League (OHL) goal with just 14 seconds remaining in regulation.

Cooper McAslan netted the overtime winner off an assist from Kane Barch to give London the extra point.

Jonathan Kapageridis made an immediate impact in his Knights debut, recording a goal and an assist. Cohen Bidgood also found the back of the net, while Evan Van Gorp contributed a pair of assists.

In goal, rookie Charlie Weiss stopped 20 shots to earn a win in his first OHL appearance.

stories.author: Koylan Azofeifa Rueda
stories.content:
London is in for a mainly cloudy Saturday, with a chance of showers late in the afternoon, according to Environment Canada.

The forecast calls for a high of 19 C on Saturday, with a 40 per cent chance of showers late in the afternoon. The UV index is expected to reach 7, or high.

Cloudy conditions will continue Saturday night, with a 40 per cent chance of showers early in the evening before showers begin. The overnight low will be 12 C.

Sunday will remain cloudy, with a 70 per cent chance of showers and a high of 19 C, according to Environment Canada.

Sunday night will stay cloudy, with a 30 per cent chance of showers and a low of 10 C.

stories.title: 'Israel is safe': The Druze Israeli telling Canadians to come visit
stories.summary: Taimur Mansour, Israel tourism's new director for Canada, says he 'is a minority, a proud Israeli, lives in Israel, and is integrated.'
stories.author: Special to National Post
stories.content:
Israel’s new tourism representative in Canada has arrived in Toronto with a difficult assignment: persuading Canadians that Israel remains worth visiting at a time when war, security concerns and disrupted travel have reshaped tourism to the region.

Taimur Mansour, the Israel Ministry of Tourism’s director for Canada, is betting that Canada remains a promising market — not only because of the Greater Toronto Area’s large Jewish community, but also because of Christian pilgrimage travel, cultural tourism and interest in Israel’s history, archaeology, food and landscape.

Mansour brings an unconventional biography to the job. A Druze Israeli from Isfiyah, ON Mount Carmel near Haifa, he studied social work and Asian studies, spent a year studying Chinese in China, taught Chinese in Israeli high schools, and later qualified as a tour guide. Before coming to Toronto in August, he oversaw the ministry’s media and campaigns department in Jerusalem and coordinated a network of public-relations managers.

His background, he says, allows him to present Israel both as the Jewish homeland and as a country of intersecting religious, linguistic and cultural communities.

Dave Gordon interviewed Mansour for the National Post:

Many Canadians are concerned about security and flight disruptions. What do you say to someone considering a trip now?

People from all over the world are coming. Flights are resuming. People still have understandable fears. But I think one of our best ways of working with the community is to show people and talk to them, telling them that Israel is safe.

Why is Canada, and Toronto in particular, an important tourism market for Israel now?

One is because the Jewish community here is one of the largest in the world, and among the most loving of Israel, positive toward Israel, and has a good relationship with Israel.

The Christian community here is also strong — Evangelical and some Catholic communities. I know they want to visit Israel. They May be worried about the security situation … but I know they want to go. For me, it was very clear potential that had not been tapped for years, at least since COVID, to bring people from Canada to Israel.

What can the ministry actually do to reboot travel?

The job is to bring more people to Israel — more tourists. That takes time and effort. It is not about a single number; it is about sustainability in tourism, building it for years, so people come to Israel.

Practically, first of all, it means having partnerships in Canada with the tourism industry: agents, wholesalers, online travel agencies, airlines. We work together, because this is the infrastructure you work with. We have them meet Israeli private industry and develop joint projects. That is the bread and butter of the work: meeting the industry here and connecting it to the Israeli industry so they can actually send groups.

Second, there is work with communities and potential travellers. It does not matter if they are Jewish. We want to bring everyone, as much as possible, to Israel.

What about your background gives you a different outlook?

I understand what it is to be a non-Jewish Israeli. I understand how people look at Israel from other places. It allowed me to understand how you can connect to Israel without only being Jewish.

Israel, first of all, is the homeland of the Jewish people, a wonderful place. It is the cradle of all (Abrahamic) faiths. It is a place where you can connect to spirituality of any kind.

Through 70-something years, it has managed to achieve amazing things in medicine, high tech and other areas. Even if you are just a person who wants to support something great or come and see something great, you can come to Israel. You do not need to be Jewish for that. You can come and fall in love with Israel.

For those unfamiliar with the Druze, how would you describe its place in Israeli society?

Most people do not know anything about the Druze. It is a religion. It believes that you need to live in harmony in the place where you live. Usually, this translates into being loyal to, or having a good relationship with, the country where you live.

Druze serve in the army in Israel, but Syrian Druze serve in the army in Syria. Lebanese Druze are Lebanese 100 per cent, and have been very important in the Lebanese government, army, and other places.

I think Druze are a great bridge between different countries because of that. Different Druze communities have good relationships with each other, even when they live in enemy countries sometimes.

Prior to your path in Israeli tourism, there was much professional emphasis on China. How did that shape the way you think about attracting foreign visitors?

I love Chinese culture. I was always a fan, even as a child — like a child’s fantasy of kung fu, calligraphy and other Chinese things. I decided to go because I loved it, but also because I knew it was the future. It was not only something in the past, or cultural. China was growing to be very central on the world stage, even over the last 10 years.

Then I went to study to become a tour guide. For me, that was natural, because I was already guiding people, even not in an official capacity, to those who came to the Jewish villages and to Mount Carmel. I love working with people. I love Israel, history, archaeology, everything to do with Israeli culture, and walking in Israel.

There were almost 150,000 Chinese tourists a year in Israel before COVID. I started working with them. I learned that Israel was fascinating to them. It is the Near East and an ancient culture, and they saw similarities, because theirs is also an ancient culture thousands of years old. In the Chinese outlook, Jewish people are very smart and technological; a small country that managed to achieve great things, which is true.

It is one of the markets still waiting for recovery.

After COVID, I decided to go into work where I could represent Israel and tell our story, but also the story of a Druze person: someone who is a minority, a proud Israeli, lives in Israel, and is integrated. I wanted people to see the culture of Israel that is not Jewish, because for many people outside, they do not know the other cultures living in Israel. So, I decided to apply for the program in the Israeli Ministry of Tourism, to bring tourists to Israel and represent Israel. That is what led me here.

I love Israel, history, archaeology, everything to do with Israeli culture, and walking in Israel.

There were almost 150,000 Chinese tourists a year in Israel before COVID. I started working with them. I learned that Israel was fascinating to them. It is the Near East and an ancient culture, and they saw similarities, because theirs is also an ancient culture thousands of years old. In the Chinese outlook, Jewish people are very smart and technological; a small country that managed to achieve great things, which is true.
It is one of the markets still waiting for recovery.

After COVID, I decided to go into work where I could represent Israel and tell our story, but also the story of a Druze person: someone who is a minority, a proud Israeli, lives in Israel, and is integrated. I wanted people to see the culture of Israel that is not Jewish, because for many people outside, they do not know the other cultures living in Israel. So, I decided to apply for the program in the Israeli Ministry of Tourism, to bring tourists to Israel and represent Israel. That is what led me here.

stories.title: Half of Canadians say it's hard to stay friends with people who disagree on international conflicts: poll
stories.summary: Major international conflicts are making it harder for some Canadians to remain friends with people who have differing views, according to a poll.
stories.author: Kenn Oliver
stories.content:
There’s no denying that digital and social media have only amplified the identity politics, erosion of trust and geopolitical shifts that have polarized mankind this century. New polling by the Association for Canadian Studies shows that polarization is emerging at the interpersonal level.

More than twice as many Canadians (52 per cent) think it’s getting harder and harder for people with differing opinions “on major international conflicts to remain friends” than those who feel it’s not more difficult (21 per cent).

“These issues are increasingly divisive and polarizing,” Association for Canadian Studies president Jack Jedwab told National Post in an interview.

More than a quarter (27 per cent) are unsure, a feeling expressed by a third of women (33 per cent) and close to a third of the oldest demographics — 55-65 (32 per cent) and 65-plus (31 per cent).

Respondents were asked about the reconcilability of four conflicts — Russia and Ukraine; Russia and the U.S.; Iran and Western countries; and Israelis and Palestinians.

It didn’t surprise Jedwab then that the latter conflict emerged as the least reconcilable (14 per cent) among respondents.

“The polarity is probably confirmed by the fact that very few people think it’s reconcilable, which is interesting, because you do hear from many people that seem to, in their own sort of spaces, feel that these issues can be reconciled if both parties would do this or that,” Jedwab told National Post in an interview.

“So if you think that’s the case, one can only imagine how challenging it is for reconciliation with people who are living the experience on the ground where they happen to be, in this particular case, the Middle East.”

Only the mostly dormant Russia-U.S. conflict is seen as more reconcilable (35 per cent) than not (29 per cent), but the largest percentage (36) are unsure.

Polling found a consistent pattern regardless of respondents’ language, whether anglophone, francophone or allophone, “suggesting that the polarizing effects of international conflicts cross linguistic boundaries,” Jedwab wrote in the poll.

That consistency is “something that we can all build as a consensus around the extent to which this thing is divisive,” he added in conversation.

Reducing polarization, he said, begins with “thoughtful” conversations about complex subjects that involve the realities of the people on the ground for whom reconciliation is most difficult and for whom the situation is evolving.

“We need to sort of identify parameters for how these conversations can be done in the most thoughtful way possible, recognizing that… many of us, even though we May have disproportionate degrees of connections to what’s going on there, we still need to engage and find thoughtful ways of engaging in dialogue.”

The poll of 1,538 respondents, conducted by Leger on behalf of the Association for Canadian Studies, was conducted Sept. 4-6. A margin of error cannot be associated with a non-probability sample in a panel survey for comparison purposes. However, a probability sample of this size would have a margin of error of 2.5 per cent, 19 times out of 20.​

stories.title: ‘It’s so emotional’: Fear and unity on Alberta’s referendum campaign trail
stories.summary: Edmonton — Alberta’s summer of unrest over its role in Confederation is striding into a final phase of rallies, lawn sign rivalry and hyperbolic warnings of doom and demise.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
By Lisa Johnson, The Canadian Press

Posted September 19, 2026 8:00 am.

Last Updated September 19, 2026 8:10 am.

Edmonton — Alberta’s summer of unrest over its role in Confederation is striding into a final phase of rallies, lawn sign rivalry and hyperbolic warnings of doom and demise.

With one month to go before the Oct. 19 referendum, drivers going through many neighbourhoods can spot red and white lawn signs urging Albertans to vote to stand with Canada.

Blue signs are there too, supporting Alberta going its own way, but they look different. Keith Wilson, co-leader of the pro-separatist Let Alberta Decide campaign, says there’s a reason.

“We’ve had people who are supportive but don’t want to put a lawn sign on their home,” he said in an interview.

“(It’s) out of fear that their car will get keyed in the driveway.”

Wilson said his team is putting resources into their digital campaign and putting up giant signs, over a metre high, ON public land along roads to avoid singling out homeowners for abuse.

“This is such a divisive issue, and it’s so emotional,” he said.

There have been regular reports on social media of signs on both sides of the debate being stolen or vandalized.

Cory Morgan, a political online commentator and organizer with the Pathway to Independence separatist group, said he’s accustomed to angry emails but has never been on the receiving end of the kind of threats, obscenity and vitriol as he is now.

“It’s above and beyond.”

Morgan said a supporter called to donate $1,000 to his group, and Morgan asked if he could put up a lawn sign.

“Oh no, I can’t do that,” Morgan said the supporter told him.

Still, requests for his lawn signs have gone up, Morgan said, in part because more people are paying more attention to the vote.

“When they see a neighbour or two put one of those signs out, they feel more comfortable doing it as well,” said Morgan.

“As far as the sign war goes, I think it’ll ramp up.”

On the other side of the fence is Thomas Lukaszuk, a former deputy premier for Alberta’s defunct Progressive Conservatives.

For more than a year, he has been criss-crossing the province in a pink and red RV dubbed the Unity Bus.

Lukaszuk collected signatures to try to force a vote in the legislature on staying in Canada and, now that there’s a referendum, he’s travelling around making sure people show up to vote for Canada – and not to take it for granted that the vote will go their way.

Recently, someone shattered a window on the bus.

Lukaszuk said he has heard from people about their patriotism, sense of purpose and fear.

“I’ve never seen as much crying, both from women and men, because they’re worried about what’s happening.”

Lukaszuk said he believes almost everyone has made up their minds about the referendum.

“The vote is already baked in, and it’s all about voter turnout,” he said.

So how did Alberta get here?

Separatism has been in Alberta’s political bones for decades.

In the early 1980s, it reared its head when the national energy program under former prime minister Pierre Trudeau artificially depressed oil prices in the name of Canadian sovereignty. Oil-rich Alberta took a hit, and Albertans have not forgotten or forgiven.

Separatism was a fringe protest movement until recently.

In late 2022, Premier Danielle Smith took the reins of the United Conservative Party and railed against Ottawa policies. She said the concerns of those who wished to quit Canada were valid and needed to be addressed.

After Prime Minister Mark Carney’s Liberals won a minority government in April 2025, Smith’s government took action. It formed a travelling panel to let Albertans air their grievances. It changed the rules to make it easier for citizens to launch petitions. And Smith said if someone delivered enough signatures calling for a referendum to separate, she’d call it.

A separatist petition from Stay Free Alberta collected enough signatures earlier this year, but it was pushed into legal limbo after a judge ruled the government failed to consult First Nations.

The ruling angered Smith, who railed against judges going rogue. In May, she called the referendum question herself.

The question on the ballot asks if Alberta should stay in Canada or launch a second, binding referendum on whether it’s time to formally leave the country.

The issue has sparked pockets of anger and division.

In the town of Sundre this summer, a parade was cancelled after organizers were harassed for excluding a wagon featuring Alberta flags that risked becoming a flashpoint of separatist sentiment.

The Alberta flag has found itself subverted into a de facto symbol of disaffection, flown at separatist rallies.

A separatist billboard put up by Morgan in Taber also sparked a fight with town council, which issued a takedown order.

On the pro-Canada side, political luminaries from former conservative elder statesman Preston Manning to former premiers Jason Kenney and Rachel Notley have joined the fight.

Carney has also participated in the campaign, recently inviting Lukaszuk to pose at a cabinet retreat in Banff and signing the Unity Bus.

Smith’s motives have been questioned.

The premier has said that when you add up the pro and anti signature campaigns, Albertans sent a message that it’s time to settle the issue once and for all.

Critics accuse Smith of rolling the dice on Canada’s future, not to reflect Albertan’s wishes, but to placate hardline separatists in her party.

Election officials are busy assembling paper ballots for the separation question and nine others that ask if Alberta should fight for more elbow room on immigration and the Constitution.

Interest so far is off the charts. More than half a million Albertans have asked for ballots to mail in ahead of time.

In the weeks to come, more rallies and events are planned.

Monte Solberg, a former Conservative cabinet minister under former prime minister Stephen Harper, is part of the federalist Vote to Stay campaign.

His group has launched radio ads reminding listeners that one prominent Alberta separatist has bragged about meeting with the Trump administration in Washington.

Separatists are kidding themselves, Solberg said, if they think Alberta would remain independent “for more than five minutes.”

Solberg said he wants Albertans turn out and vote on Oct. 19.

“You see some Canadian flags, you see some Forever Canada lawn signs, that’s great, but you need people to speak up a lot more loudly.

“The real enemy, besides the separatist camp, is apathy.”

stories.title: After a summer of fire, B.C.'s Okanagan Valley mourns for a paradise lost
stories.summary: B.C.’s Okanagan Valley has long been Western Canada’s symbol of the sweet life. Now, locals are rethinking their way of life – or choosing to leave
stories.author: Nancy Macdonald
stories.content:
On an early August morning, Bree McKeage stood among the vines in paint-splotched work pants and Crocs, sunglasses on, a tattoo peeking from beneath her sleeve. She pointed to the hills beyond the vineyard.

Three fires were burning around the Okanagan Valley – one near Summerland, another in Manning Park, a third near Vernon.

Smoke had swallowed the sun-bleached vineyard. The mountains beyond had disappeared into a grey haze. The air tasted of ash.

For more than a century, the Okanagan has been Canada’s fruit bowl. The long, glacier-carved basin is threaded with vineyards and orchards of peaches, cherries and nectarines. It has also embodied a summer ideal: hot, dry days, aquamarine lakes, vines heavy with grapes and long evenings outdoors. Even the names – Peachland, Summerland, Lake Country – seem to promise leisure and abundance.

But ever since Ms. McKeage and her partner, Rajen Toor, bought their Keremeos, B.C., vineyard in 2022, they have been fighting to keep it alive. Three weeks after taking possession, a deep freeze killed every vine in the vineyard. They replanted, but the new vines would take years to mature. Two years later, another record-breaking polar vortex sent temperatures plunging to –30 C, killing most of those new vines.

The shorthand for the Western Canadian dream, for generations, has been: You were born in Regina, made your money in Alberta and retired in Kelowna. The Okanagan was the reward, where a lifetime of work in unforgiving weather could give way to something gentler. That dream helped make the region what it is today. People came to farm, to visit, to settle, to retire, to raise families. But the very climate that once made the Okanagan fruitful and drew generations of sunseekers is now beginning to undermine both its bounty and its appeal.

Deep freezes have wiped out entire peach, nectarine and cherry crops, and, in some cases, entire vineyards. Smoke is ruining vintages. Fires are keeping away summer visitors.

The forces driving those fires are becoming more extreme, too. On Aug. 7, when the Bald Range fire erupted near Summerland, the BC Wildfire Service reported that fuel conditions across the region were the driest ever recorded.

“We’ve been in triage for four years,” said Ms. McKeage, who was raised in Alberta, the daughter of a rancher and farmer, and worked in finance before turning to wine a decade ago.

But after four years of rebuilding, Ms. McKeage, who also owns Bella Wines, a local winery, was finally making her first vintage from her very own vineyard. It should have been a moment of arrival. The couple had put off having children, waiting for the vines to take hold. Instead, they were harvesting smoke-tainted grapes, still fighting to make and sell just enough wine to keep the bank at bay.

The strain was affecting their marriage and their health. Everything else was being delayed: the tasting room, the landscaping, the babies they’d hoped would by now be bouncing on their knees.

Ms. McKeage is willing to consider walking away. Mr. Toor, who was raised on a winery in nearby Oliver, would have to be dragged out. “Sometimes I’m like, how much further should we go?” she says.

“To the end,” he’ll reply.

Would she buy the vineyard again, knowing what she knows now? “No,” she said, her voice suddenly husky. “The old way is gone. We haven’t properly mourned it. We haven’t recognized it. We’re all still trying to make the past happen.”

“There’s no point in saying, we’re resilient, we’ll rebuild,” she said. “But into what?”

Ms. McKeage sees the vineyard as an early warning system for something much larger. Grapes May be among the Okanagan’s most fragile crops, but they are not the only ones suffering.

“Smokanagan,” some have begun calling it.

The valley’s defining season is becoming harder to count on, not simply because it is getting hotter, but because heat, smoke and fire are arriving all at once.

By early August, the fire near Summerland was moving faster than the models had predicted, forcing more than 20,000 people from their homes in a single night, and killing one. Farmers fled, fences thrown open in hopes their horses, cattle and goats might escape the flames. Evacuees streamed south through the dark, fire glowing on the mountains behind them.

Some 150 structures were damaged or destroyed in and around Summerland, with neighbouring Faulder nearly wiped off the map. Just a week earlier, fire had razed 230 homes near Vernon, at the Okanagan’s northern edge. In the space of days, roughly 400 valley homes were gone.

By early September, when the Bald Range wildfire was finally listed as under control, it had blazed through an area twice the size of the city of Vancouver.

A disaster on this scale once demanded a reckoning. In 2003, 238 Kelowna homes were destroyed by the Okanagan Mountain Park Fire, a catastrophe so extraordinary the province commissioned a sweeping review, led by former Manitoba premier Gary Filmon. The number of homes lost to fire this year is already substantially higher. What has changed is the baseline: Events once considered exceptional are now simply part of the region’s new reality. By area burned, 2026 is unlikely to even rank among B.C.’s worst wildfire seasons of the past decade.

Many of Summerland’s evacuees ended up in Penticton, a lakeside city built around summer. The crisis landed smack in the middle of Peachfest, the region’s signature summer celebration of sunshine, concerts, parades and peaches. The festival was celebrating a version of summer that was becoming harder to sustain.

A week later, Penticton’s waterfront was strangely deserted. The city should have been packed on an August Friday. Nearly a kilometre of sandy beach runs along the shore. Normally, it would be crowded with kids, towels, paddleboards and tourists moving between the lake and the bars and restaurants beyond it.

Instead, smoke had blotted out the lake and the mountains beyond. Ash lay on parked cars and outdoor tables. There were more ducks than kids. A purple trolley that shuttles tourists between beaches rang its bell, the chime echoing through empty streets.

The signs were still selling the Okanagan summer. “Sunshine and good vibes,” read one on Lakeshore Drive. Beneath it, a couple walked hand in hand, both wearing black masks. At the Okanagan Lakefront Resort, a billboard captured the contradiction: “Stronger Together B.C.” on one side. “Live the Life. Summer 2026,” on the other.

Tickleberry’s, an Okanagan Falls ice creamery that sells more than 3,000 cones a day in summer, told its 15 staff not to come in. “Feeling the feels today,” owner Kelsey Hoy later wrote on Facebook. “The smoke is thick and the valley is quiet.”

Even the licence plates told the story. In the Okanagan, Alberta plates are nearly as ubiquitous as vineyards. Their absence was another sign of a summer gone seriously wrong.

Climate models developed two decades ago were not wrong about where the Okanagan was headed. What they failed to capture was the violence of the transition: how warming, combined with less snow, extraordinary freezes, earlier runoff, deeper drought and more fire, could turn summer into a succession of fierce heat waves, destructive wildfires and weeks of suffocating smoke.

Geography magnifies the change. The Okanagan sits in the rain shadow of the Coast and Cascade mountains, making it one of the country’s driest agricultural regions. Its narrow valleys can act as smoke traps. As the climate warms, the snowpack is shrinking and emptying earlier, just as hotter temperatures increase the demand for water. The same conditions that dry the orchards and vineyards also prime the surrounding forests for fire.

So the valley is gaining heat but losing water; gaining growing days but losing certainty about what crops will actually make it through to harvest.

A few kilometres south of Penticton, Kevin Rossion is still trying to make a living from the landscape. He emerges from the vines, sweaty and out of breath, his black T-shirt darkened at the collar. He had been chasing a foal off the vineyard.

Mr. Rossion, a Belgian, moved to the Okanagan from Spain, where he had been working as a DJ when he met his wife, a native of the valley. Eventually, they bought a vineyard and farmhouse in Kaleden, high above Skaha Lake. Kaleden combines kalos , Greek for beautiful, with Eden, the biblical paradise. With vineyards climbing the slopes, a languid lake below, rugged peaks rising behind, the name could hardly be more fitting.

But today the smoke had drained the landscape of its colour. The blue of the lake had all but disappeared. The vineyards were shaded grey.

The shape of paradise was still there. It just hurt a little to look.

Mr. Rossion has spent the last decade managing vineyards for a large winery all while growing grapes of his own. “Whenever you have a nice day, you think – this is paradise. But we’re working so hard to maintain it.”

Grape prices have plunged. Many wineries turned to imported grapes after the 2024 freeze. The rebound in local production has since left some growers struggling to find buyers. Last year, Mr. Rossion left a third of his grapes on the vine: They weren’t worth harvesting.

“We don’t even enjoy it,” he said. “We’re just working all the time. We’re like, why are we working so hard?”

He’s not the only one questioning this way of life.

After two decades of drawing people from elsewhere in Canada, the region has begun to lose them. From 2013 to 2023, the Thompson-Okanagan had been gaining an average of 4,185 people a year through interprovincial migration. But in 2024, it lost 709 people to other provinces – the first such reversal in 21 years.

More than 20 per cent of the Okanagan’s 196 wineries are for sale or in foreclosure, according to Nicole Eastman, an associate broker with Sotheby’s International Realty Canada who specializes in wineries and vineyards. Thirty-five are publicly or privately listed for sale; another five are distressed sales.

The Rossions have started using their home to help make the operation work. One suite houses the vineyard staff; a second is rented through Airbnb to pay for their wages. Mr. Rossion, his wife and their three children share the third.

His wife, a lifelong Kaledenite, cannot imagine leaving. Mr. Rossion, gazing through the grey, is no longer so sure. “The point of being here is to be outside.”

For Ted Vollo, the question was less whether the Okanagan was still paradise than whether he could imagine living anywhere else.

When asked what he loved about Summerland, he started to cry.

He described the way a tractor, a chainsaw or an offer of help arrived just when you needed it most; how chance conversations could stretch to 20 minutes and leave you feeling a little more connected.

He had spent the previous week worrying about his apple crop and the place three generations of his family had farmed. But what seemed to undo him was talking about what it was all for.

He had left Summerland as a young man, studied geophysics and spent years working as a geologist in remote parts of the country. Eventually, he came back. He wanted to be close to people who knew his mom. And his mom’s mom.

It was home. But now it was becoming harder to recognize.

He was preparing to start picking his crop when the evacuation order landed. His wife was away working in Yukon, leaving Mr. Vollo to gather their 18-month-old son, and their cat and dog. At 2:30 a.m., with the electricity out, he carried his sleeping boy to the car. As they drove through the smoke, the baby stared quietly at the line of headlights snaking through the dark.

Gala picking was a week away. Honeycrisp and Ambrosia were close behind.

Mr. Vollo estimates he could lose about 30 per cent of his crop. Even saying that makes him uncomfortable. He knows farmers who have lost so much more. Ripe peaches were softening on the trees, ash settling over the fruit. Some cherry growers were just two or three days from finishing when the fire tore through. “There’s no point in complaining about 30 when your neighbours lost 80,” Mr. Vollo said.

So he just moves on.

“There’s always next year,” he said, channelling his father and grandfather. “Next year” is the farmer’s answer to almost everything.

Mr. Vollo, freckled and red-blond, has a boyish air, always ready with a joke.

He has been farming for only six years, but he has already seen enough to know that the rules have fundamentally changed. Betting on next year was starting to feel a little too ambitious.

Loving something doesn’t make the numbers disappear, though. Some years, the farm and cidery barely produce enough to cover the bills. His brothers didn’t want to take on the farm. Financially, Mr. Vollo understood why. But to him, legacy matters. He could not stomach being the one to let it go.

Grant Williams moved from Prince George to the Okanagan because he wanted what the north couldn’t give him: lakes he could swim in starting in May, a place where he never had to wear gloves or plug in his car. Eleven years later, he hasn’t even returned to visit.

But smoke that once seemed exceptional in the valley has become familiar.

Mr. Williams knows how quickly a summer economy can be thrown off balance. He and his wife once owned Medici’s, a coffee shop and gelateria in Oliver, which bills itself as the country’s wine capital. Summer was everything: eight weeks to earn enough to carry the business through the rest of the year.

Behind him, the restaurants and beach stores along Osoyoos’s main drag stood empty. The region has built a multibillion-dollar tourism economy around its summers. Now summer itself is becoming the region’s most unreliable economic asset.

For now, visitors keep coming. Short-term-rental demand has held relatively steady in the region for the past five years, according to AirDNA, which tracks vacation rental bookings. June demand was weaker than in the rest of B.C. in 2022 and 2023, but recovered thereafter.

Increasingly, however, Okanagan residents are escaping to the coast or Vancouver Island for part of the summer – taking their holidays and camping trips somewhere else.

The valley May have to find a new way to sell summer. May and June, September and even October could become its new sweet spots, as visitors shift away from the hottest, smokiest weeks.

But an orchard can’t shift its calendar to suit the climate. Apples ripen when they ripen; grapes won’t wait for the smoke to clear.

For some residents, the answer has been to leave.

Every spring, Tanis Houle packed an evacuation kit and moved her family’s most precious belongings into the crawlspace beneath their Oliver home, so they would be ready to grab if they needed to flee. Come winter, she brought them back out.

Her husband had been wanting to leave the valley for years, but those pleas went mostly unheeded. Then she sweltered through the 2021 heat dome while pregnant, and navigated extreme heat, smoke and an evacuation with a toddler.

For weeks, it was too hot to take her son to the beach. “We could only spend time outside if the activity involved being constantly submerged in water,” Ms. Houle recalled. She had to scoop ash out of his kiddie pool just so he could swim.

“Every other type of weather, you can dress for. You can’t safely dress a young child for extreme heat or off-the-charts air pollution.”

“We started noticing that sometimes the month of July, and almost always August, were write-offs.”

One summer after another, the signs kept pointing toward the exit. They chose Comox on Vancouver Island.

The move gave her a different perspective. After a couple smokeless summers, she began to worry about the health effects of the years her son had spent breathing it. She also realized how much they had bent their lives around conditions that, looking back, were extraordinary.

She had grown up spending almost every summer day outside, without thought of either heat or smoke.

But leaving sure didn’t make her love the Okanagan any less. She longs to swim in its turquoise lakes, to eat fresh cherries and peaches until her hands are sticky with juice. She misses the piney scent of ponderosa and the summers of her childhood – long, unbroken blue-sky days.

She was supposed to return this August, but cancelled because of the smoke.

“I know leaving the Okanagan was the best decision for our family. But I’m homesick for a place that doesn’t exist anymore.”

content_blocks.text: On an early August morning, Bree McKeage stood among the vines in paint-splotched work pants and Crocs, sunglasses on, a tattoo peeking from beneath her sleeve. She pointed to the hills beyond the vineyard.
Three fires were burning around the Okanagan Valley – one near Summerland, another in Manning Park, a third near Vernon.
Smoke had swallowed the sun-bleached vineyard. The mountains beyond had disappeared into a grey haze. The air tasted of ash.

For more than a century, the Okanagan has been Canada’s fruit bowl. The long, glacier-carved basin is threaded with vineyards and orchards of peaches, cherries and nectarines. It has also embodied a summer ideal: hot, dry days, aquamarine lakes, vines heavy with grapes and long evenings outdoors. Even the names – Peachland, Summerland, Lake Country – seem to promise leisure and abundance.

But ever since Ms. McKeage and her partner, Rajen Toor, bought their Keremeos, B.C., vineyard in 2022, they have been fighting to keep it alive. Three weeks after taking possession, a deep freeze killed every vine in the vineyard. They replanted, but the new vines would take years to mature. Two years later, another record-breaking polar vortex sent temperatures plunging to –30 C, killing most of those new vines.

content_blocks.caption: Bree McKeage and her partner own Bella Wines in Keremeos. On a recent visit, some grapes were ready to be destemmed and used, while others lay dry on the vine. Aaron Hemens/The Globe and Mail

content_blocks.text: The shorthand for the Western Canadian dream, for generations, has been: You were born in Regina, made your money in Alberta and retired in Kelowna. The Okanagan was the reward, where a lifetime of work in unforgiving weather could give way to something gentler. That dream helped make the region what it is today. People came to farm, to visit, to settle, to retire, to raise families. But the very climate that once made the Okanagan fruitful and drew generations of sunseekers is now beginning to undermine both its bounty and its appeal.
Deep freezes have wiped out entire peach, nectarine and cherry crops, and, in some cases, entire vineyards. Smoke is ruining vintages. Fires are keeping away summer visitors.

The forces driving those fires are becoming more extreme, too. On Aug. 7, when the Bald Range fire erupted near Summerland, the BC Wildfire Service reported that fuel conditions across the region were the driest ever recorded.
“We’ve been in triage for four years,” said Ms. McKeage, who was raised in Alberta, the daughter of a rancher and farmer, and worked in finance before turning to wine a decade ago.

But after four years of rebuilding, Ms. McKeage, who also owns Bella Wines, a local winery, was finally making her first vintage from her very own vineyard. It should have been a moment of arrival. The couple had put off having children, waiting for the vines to take hold. Instead, they were harvesting smoke-tainted grapes, still fighting to make and sell just enough wine to keep the bank at bay.

content_blocks.caption: Rajen Toor, Che the farm dog and the staff of Bella Wines have seen punishing seasons before: Not just fires, but deep freezes that devastated the vineyards. Aaron Hemens/The Globe and Mail

content_blocks.text: The strain was affecting their marriage and their health. Everything else was being delayed: the tasting room, the landscaping, the babies they’d hoped would by now be bouncing on their knees.
Ms. McKeage is willing to consider walking away. Mr. Toor, who was raised on a winery in nearby Oliver, would have to be dragged out. “Sometimes I’m like, how much further should we go?” she says.
“To the end,” he’ll reply.

Would she buy the vineyard again, knowing what she knows now? “No,” she said, her voice suddenly husky. “The old way is gone. We haven’t properly mourned it. We haven’t recognized it. We’re all still trying to make the past happen.”
“There’s no point in saying, we’re resilient, we’ll rebuild,” she said. “But into what?”
Ms. McKeage sees the vineyard as an early warning system for something much larger. Grapes May be among the Okanagan’s most fragile crops, but they are not the only ones suffering.

content_blocks.text: “Smokanagan,” some have begun calling it.
The valley’s defining season is becoming harder to count on, not simply because it is getting hotter, but because heat, smoke and fire are arriving all at once.

By early August, the fire near Summerland was moving faster than the models had predicted, forcing more than 20,000 people from their homes in a single night, and killing one. Some 150 structures were damaged or destroyed in and around Summerland, with neighbouring Faulder nearly wiped off the map. Just a week earlier, fire had razed 230 homes near Vernon, at the Okanagan’s northern edge. In the space of days, roughly 400 valley homes were gone.
By early September, when the Bald Range wildfire was finally listed as under control, it had blazed through an area twice the size of the city of Vancouver.

stories.title: Toronto man acquitted in cannabis-induced choking attack on young girl
stories.summary: The accused said he was suffering from a cannabis induced psychosis at the time of the attack, in which he punched and strangled the girl.
stories.author: Chris Lambie
stories.content:
A Toronto man who argued he was suffering from cannabis-induced psychosis when he choked a seven-year-old girl three years ago while naked has been acquitted of assault charges.

Ahmed Baig pleaded not guilty in the Ontario Court of Justice to assault causing bodily harm and assault by choking for the Aug. 2, 2023, attack in which he left his home wearing only a towel after vaping cannabis. His towel eventually fell off, and Baig started chasing a family he encountered in their driveway.

“He ran into the driveway and picked up a seven-year-old girl. He threw her to the ground, punched her and strangled her. He then abruptly left the driveway, and a short time later was arrested by police. At the time of arrest, he wore only a T-shirt,” Justice Mara Greene wrote in a recent decision.

The judge concluded that Baig’s attack was due to “nonmental disorder automatism.” She found him not guilty of both charges.

Baig didn’t “dispute that he attacked the seven-year-old girl,” said Greene. “He argued, however, that he should be acquitted of the charges because his actions were involuntary as he was suffering from a cannabis induced psychosis at the time of the attack.”

The Crown argued that “while Mr. Baig’s mental faculties May have been impacted by cannabis, his acts were still volitional,” said the decision.

In the alternative, the Crown recommended Baig should be found Not Criminally Responsible (NCR) due to a mental disorder.

The court heard Baig lived in a muti-generational home with extended family. On the day of the attack, he was left alone and got anxious.

“Home alone, Mr. Baig decided to consume cannabis to help with his feelings of anxiety,” said the Aug. 13 decision.

“He used a brand of cannabis recommended by the store, but one he had not used before. The cannabis was in vape form. Instead of relieving his anxiety, he felt more anxious.”

Baig called his wife, asking her to come home, then went to bed. “Mr. Baig testified that his next memory after lying down on his bed was being in a cell and then being fingerprinted.”

His victim’s identity is protected by a publication ban.

During the attack, which was captured on video surveillance, Baig “said both ‘I will kill you’ and ‘I won’t kill you,’” according to the victim’s mother.

“He also referred to Allah.”

He “sounded nonsensical at times and made comments about billionaires,” said the victim’s father.

When police asked Baig if he wanted a lawyer, he “stated that he wanted Neil Patrick Harris or a lawyer from a television show,” said the decision. “He also talked about bitcoin and lotteries.”

Baig answered some questions appropriately and obeyed a police command to drop to the ground, said the decision. “He also told the police that he was ‘mentally insane.’ Once at the police station he was able to answer questions posed to him and appeared more coherent.”

Baig, 38, testified about having a “history of sleepwalking,” and that he used cannabis in the past to help deal with anxiety.

A psychiatrist and sleep expert testified that Baig “was either suffering from cannabis induced psychosis, sleepwalking or a combination of the two.”

Sleep apnea led to Baig “being significantly sleep deprived,” said the psychiatrist, who opined sleep deprivation coupled with his history of sleepwalking and a new strain of cannabis caused the incident.

Another psychiatrist was brought in to determine whether Baig was NCR.

An acquittal based on an absence of criminal (responsibility) for a violent act is rarely a satisfying verdict

He testified that Baig “did not appreciate the nature and consequences of his actions at the time of the attack as he was suffering from a cannabis induced psychosis. He further testified that in his opinion, Mr. Baig’s actions were involuntary.”

The second psychiatrist determined that Baig “did not qualify for an NCR defence because he did not have disease of the mind. While Mr. Baig had a history of feeling anxious, he did not have an anxiety disorder, nor did he suffer form any other kind of mental illness.”

It was his opinion that, during the attack, Baig “was in a psychotic state that was different from mere intoxication.”

This psychotic episode “was so intense that his capacity for rational perception and his capacity to make a rational choice was grossly impaired,” the second psychiatrist testified. “Mr. Baig was rendered incapable of appreciating the nature, quality and wrongfulness of his actions.”

The Crown argued that the evidence, at its highest, established that Baig was intoxicated “but not to the point of being an automaton.”

Cases like this are difficult for trial judges, Greene said.

“An acquittal based on an absence of criminal (responsibility) for a violent act is rarely a satisfying verdict. Nonetheless, our law is clear, that accused persons who are not (criminally) responsible should not be convicted.”

The judge found that Baig “has proven on a balance of probabilities that he was acting as an automaton when he attacked the seven-year-old girl in her driveway. I am satisfied that Mr. Baig voluntarily consumed cannabis, had an unexpected reaction to the cannabis, that led to a state of psychosis where he acted in an involuntary state and attacked the young victim.”

He’s used cannabis before, but “never had a reaction like this,” Greene said.

The judge found that the risk of recurrence is relatively low. “This is because Mr. Baig has used cannabis intermittently since he was 15 years old without a similar incident, Mr. Baig does not have substance abuse issues, he has not used cannabis since his arrest and has found better methods of addressing his anxious feelings. In my view, this is not a case where oversight by the Ontario Review Board is required to protect the public.”

stories.title: With its new voting protocol, the Polaris Music Prize is a whole new horse race
stories.summary: Canadian music prize expands jury of 11 to voting pool of more than 200
stories.author: Brad Wheeler
stories.content:
This year’s Polaris Music Prize will be presented on Sept. 22 at a gala concert and ceremony at Toronto’s Massey Hall. Though the Quebec masked math-rock duo Angine de Poitrine is the favourite to win the $30,000 award, I predict Charlotte Cornfield , the Toronto singer-songwriter whose disarmingly honest Hurts Like Hell is hard not to adore, will prevail. But what do I know? What does anyone know?

More than we used to.

For two decades, it was a mug’s game trying to predict the winner of the annual prize, given to the best full-length Canadian album based on artistic merit. This year, however, the voting protocol has changed in a way that should make prognosticating easier. For the first time, everyone in the Polaris jury pool, not just a select few members, has a ballot for the final vote.

For Polaris’s first 20 years of existence, a jury composed of more than 200 journalists, broadcasters, bloggers, programmers, playlist creators, academics, podcasters and DJs participated in choosing the longlisted and shortlisted albums. But the ultimate winner was determined by just 11 jury members.

Those 11 voters were handpicked from the larger pool: one each specifically chosen to advocate for one of the 10 shortlisted albums, with one neutral member. Until the pandemic, the sequestered jury deliberated in person in Toronto on the night of the award gala, often in the Red Ritual Room used for fraternal ceremonies at what used to be the Masonic Temple (now the Concert Hall).

That music-nerd fandango could be overpowered by the most passionate voices, resulting in fringe preferences ruling the day. Mainstream artists, particularly in recent years, were overlooked in favour of sexier and edgier choices.

For example, Feist’s 2023 album Multitudes won a Juno Award for best adult alternative album, but lost the Polaris to Debby Friday for Good Luck . Other recent winners include Backxwash, Cadence Weapon, Pierre Kwenders, Jeremy Dutcher and last year’s prize-taker, Yves Jarvis.

With a bigger voting pool of 205, consensus now has a fighting chance in picking the year’s best album. Where in the past, an esoteric album might win on the strength of fierce championing, now a more mainstream record might very well prevail.

Amber Still, the prize’s executive director, told Billboard Canada that the change is a pilot initiative: “We will evaluate it at the end and then see if it will be permanent.”

For one year at least, then, it’s a horse race. Who do you have your money on from this year’s shortlist?

Angine de Poitrine, Vol. II : The polka-dotted drum-and-guitar pair are self-proclaimed aliens, but with their freaky, non-verbal schtick, they’re speaking Polaris’s language. The buzz is strong for the Canadian breakout act of the year.

Charlotte Cornfield, Hurts Like Hell : Long admired, the songwriter took a step up in class with her sixth album.

Beverly Glenn-Copeland, Laughter in Summer : Theatrical, choir-enhanced reworkings of previously released material. Honestly, it’s the weakest of the 10 shortlisted albums. But the late-career breakthrough that took place when the singer-songwriter was in his 70s was a feel-good story, and the public disclosure of a dementia diagnosis in 2024 only added to the compassion for a uniquely elegant and persevering artist.

Peaches, No Lube So Rude : The name actually undersells the raunchiness of the album from the legendary electro-punk provocateur. She’s the only nominee who won’t be performing at this year’s gala. Hopefully she’s taped a victory speech in case she wins − it’s probably a doozy.

Begonia, Fantasy Life : The effervescent Winnipegger and indie Adele has won the hearts of those in favour of soulful, tuneful pop with affirmative messaging.

Bibi Club, Amaro : This marks two consecutive years where the Montreal dream-pop duo made it to the shortlist. The record is flawless and in many other years – pre-Angine de Poitrine years − Bibi Club would be a top contender.

Tanya Tagaq, Saputjiji : I believe Polaris came of age in 2015 when the Inuk throat singer won the prize for her avant-garde masterpiece Animism . And while it’s possible Tagaq’s Saputjiji is just as worthy, only one artist – Jeremy Dutcher − has won the award more than once.

Aquakultre, 1783 : Historically inspired R&B from Lance Sampson , who musically marks the year that thousands of Black Loyalists arrived in Nova Scotia seeking a new life. If I were in the Polaris voting pool, I’d jump into Aquakultre with both feet. Not sure this concept album has the musical sophistication Polaris prefers, though.

Rochelle Jordan, Through the Wall : Sleek house music and professional R&B. Jordan gets compared to Janet Jackson and Diana Ross, but where’s the hit song?

Les Louanges, Alouette! : Montreal Francophone Vincent Roberge makes imaginative, often charismatic alt-pop. This isn’t his year.

For one year at least, then, it’s a horse race. Who do you have your money on from this year’s shortlist?
The frontrunners

Angine de Poitrine, Vol. II : The polka-dotted drum-and-guitar pair are self-proclaimed aliens, but with their freaky, non-verbal schtick, they’re speaking Polaris’s language. The buzz is strong for the Canadian breakout act of the year.
Charlotte Cornfield, Hurts Like Hell : Long admired, the songwriter took a step up in class with her sixth album.
The sentimental favourite

content_blocks.caption: Beverly Glenn-Copeland. Laura Proctor/The Globe and Mail

content_blocks.text: Beverly Glenn-Copeland, Laughter in Summer : Theatrical, choir-enhanced reworkings of previously released material. Honestly, it’s the weakest of the 10 shortlisted albums. But the late-career breakthrough that took place when the singer-songwriter was in his 70s was a feel-good story, and the public disclosure of a dementia diagnosis in 2024 only added to the compassion for a uniquely elegant and persevering artist.
The dark horses

Peaches, No Lube So Rude : The name actually undersells the raunchiness of the album from the legendary electro-punk provocateur. She’s the only nominee who won’t be performing at this year’s gala. Hopefully she’s taped a victory speech in case she wins − it’s probably a doozy.
Begonia, Fantasy Life : The effervescent Winnipegger and indie Adele has won the hearts of those in favour of soulful, tuneful pop with affirmative messaging.

Bibi Club, Amaro : This marks two consecutive years where the Montreal dream-pop duo made it to the shortlist. The record is flawless and in many other years – pre-Angine de Poitrine years − Bibi Club would be a top contender.
Poor post positions

Tanya Tagaq, Saputjiji : I believe Polaris came of age in 2015 when the Inuk throat singer won the prize for her avant-garde masterpiece Animism . And while it’s possible Tagaq’s Saputjiji is just as worthy, only one artist – Jeremy Dutcher − has won the award more than once.

Aquakultre, 1783 : Historically inspired R&B from Lance Sampson , who musically marks the year that thousands of Black Loyalists arrived in Nova Scotia seeking a new life. If I were in the Polaris voting pool, I’d jump into Aquakultre with both feet. Not sure this concept album has the musical sophistication Polaris prefers, though.
The long shots
Rochelle Jordan, Through the Wall : Sleek house music and professional R&B. Jordan gets compared to Janet Jackson and Diana Ross, but where’s the hit song?
Les Louanges, Alouette! : Montreal Francophone Vincent Roberge makes imaginative, often charismatic alt-pop. This isn’t his year.

Beverly Glenn-Copeland. Laura Proctor/The Globe and Mail
