stories.title: Holocaust educator Judy Weissenberg Cohen believed history could show the warning signs of hatred
stories.summary: She gave talks across Canada, helped fellow survivors tell their own stories and created a website offering Holocaust education through a gender lens
stories.author: Hannah Alper
stories.content:
In 1993, Judy Weissenberg Cohen was nearing her 65th birthday and mandatory retirement when, during a lunch-break stroll through downtown Toronto, she saw a group of young people clad in black leather marching in a circle and shouting, “White power! White power!”

A certain fear was automatic, she later wrote in her memoir, like the feeling of her stomach clenching when she witnessed people being selected for death at Auschwitz-Birkenau.

“For a terrifying few seconds, the lines were blurred between past and present. I wondered, was I looking back at history or ahead?”

As she approached the curious audience, she realized she had come face-to-face with members of the Heritage Front, a white supremacist, neo-Nazi organization.

Instead of turning away, Ms. Cohen marched toward the group’s leader, Wolfgang Droege. When he claimed there had been no Black slavery in the U.S., she assumed the Holocaust would be the next thing he denied.

Before he got the chance, Ms. Cohen stepped between him and the crowd and implored those watching not to listen. She later humbly joked she was not especially heroic, since four police officers were nearby.

“Lady, don’t aggravate yourself. They only have a permit for 20 minutes.”

“My luck!” Ms. Cohen later wrote. “I caught the 20 minutes that would soon spur me to action.”

For the next three decades, she dedicated herself to Holocaust education and public speaking, urging people — particularly students — to recognize the warning signs of hatred and become witnesses to history. She also became a leading advocate for raising awareness about women’s experiences during the Holocaust, eventually creating a website devoted to preserving those stories.

Ms. Cohen died on Sept. 6 at 97 years old.

“The memory of the death camps and being victims of the Nazi Holocaust never fades, but I no longer consider myself a victim,” she wrote. “Instead, through the decades, I became a politically and socially aware activist. I must work relentlessly to ensure that memories like mine will not become the memories of future generations.”

She was born Judy Weissenberg in Debrecen, Hungary, ON Sept. 17, 1928, just after Rosh Hashanah, the Jewish New Year. The youngest of seven children, she developed an early dislike of being ordered around — and a willingness to question people in power that never disappeared.

“Judy always had a lot to say,” said Liam Romalis, the producer who worked with her on video testimonies and the audiobook of her memoir. “She was so sharp-witted, and would disagree with you but was still so open to dialogue.”

Mr. Romalis would pick Ms. Cohen up for the 45-minute drive from her Toronto home to the recording studio. She barely stopped talking the entire way, whether about something she had seen or an article she had read.

In 1938, when Judy was 10, news of the war reached her family in Hungary. She wrote that the children absorbed the adults’ grave concerns by osmosis.

By 1944, Hungarian Jews were forced to wear yellow Stars of David in public. Judy attached one to her jacket but covered it with the books and notes she held as she travelled to and from local tutoring gigs. She called it her “little act of resistance.”

A few months later, Judy and her family were forced into the overcrowded Debrecen ghetto. It was only a month before they, along with hundreds of others, were packed into cattle cars. They were only given two pails: one filled with clean water, and one to be used as a toilet.

Three days later, they arrived at Auschwitz-Birkenau, where an estimated 1.1 million people were murdered. Men and women were immediately separated. It was the last time she saw her father, her mother and her sister-in-law, who was holding her infant son.

Then the processing began. The women’s body hair was shaved, they took a brief shower and were given clothing previously worn by other prisoners. Judy found herself looking at hundreds of now-identical prisoners. After shouting through the crowd to find her sisters, they could barely recognize one another.

“We started to painfully laugh, how drastically we changed within a few hours.”

One night, around 700 women crowded into a barracks to observe Yom Kippur. Jewish religious practices were forbidden in the camps, but the kapos – prisoners appointed to supervise other prisoners in exchange for special privileges – allowed 10 minutes while guarding the doors for SS officers.

Someone lit a candle and a hush fell over the barracks. One woman began to recite Kol Nidre, the prayer that opens Yom Kippur.

“In this place where we felt that instead of asking for forgiveness from God, God should be asking for forgiveness from us,” Ms. Cohen recalled.

The prayer turned into “the sound of this incredible cry of hundreds of women.” The moment eventually inspired the title of Ms. Cohen’s memoir, A Cry in Unison .

Her older sister Böske helped keep her alive, carving spoons from wood and sneaking her extra pieces of bread, until they were eventually separated. In her sisters’ absence, Judy found solace and strength in two young women who became her “camp sisters.”

As the war neared its end, Judy and the women she was with were forced on a death March, and what she called a never-ending road with no food and no water, wrapped in dirty rags and seeing corpses that looked like them dotting the path. One morning, after they slept in an abandoned barn, the mayor of the town woke them shouting, “Fräulein, sie sind frei!” This translates to: “Women, you are free.”

When Judy returned to Debrecen in August, 1945, she reunited with her brother Laci in her hometown and her sister Evi in the Bergen-Belsen Displaced Persons Camp in Germany.

Judy was later accepted to move to Montreal when a garment commission came to Bergen-Belsen looking for people to work in Canada’s clothing industry.

Entering a country filled with new people who spoke a completely new language, Judy learned to put her trauma on the back burner, as when she tried to talk about it, she was often met with apathy.

She met her future husband, Sidney Cohen, whom she would move to Toronto to be with and eventually raise their kids, Michelle and Jonathan. She took a business course and found jobs in bookkeeping and real estate.

“Mom set an example for us. She was active in the community. She was very proud to vote regularly, to do things to help other people. Not to show that she was any better than anybody else, but because it was the right thing to do,” Jonathan said.

While she tried to put the past behind her, she wanted to understand what had happened to her and the millions who perished. After her encounter with the neo-Nazis, she visited what is now the Toronto Holocaust Museum, asking how she could combat “this emerging assault on the Holocaust and the historical truth.” While this was no small feat, Ms. Cohen read intently about the events that lay beneath the decisions and actions of the Holocaust perpetrators as well as the experiences of its victims.

“She was always thinking, always theorizing, always researching. She and my father encouraged the value of education, books, learning, culture, art and definitely of treating other people well,” Jonathan said.

Over the final three decades of her life, Ms. Cohen emerged as a public speaker in high schools and universities across North America. As she found her voice, she became co-chair of the Holocaust Centre Speakers Bureau to help fellow survivors tell their own stories. She participated in four March of the Living trips, travelling to Poland and Israel with students as a survivor-faciliator. Her goal was not to make young people sad to hear her story, but “to be historically knowledgeable, and be able to recognize the signs if and when something similar re-emerges and combat it.”

As Ms. Cohen dove deeper, she noticed that most of what she was reading was written by male authors, seen through the eyes of men. Recognizing that the collective voices of survivors help bring attention to what happened, she felt like half of survivors’ experiences were excluded: those of women.

She learned about women’s roles in the ghettos and in the resistance, and “the immense suffering of women and their struggles to survive in the places I knew so intimately myself.” She made it clear that learning about gender differences doesn’t mean competing in a hierarchy of suffering. “The aim of researching gender-specific suffering in the Holocaust is to hear the voices of all the victims … so as to enhance our understanding of history.”

Armed with determination, a friend’s technical help and her husband’s patience, her website Women and the Holocaust — a Cyberspace of Their Own , was born. It offered essays, book reviews, poems, stories and educational material about women’s experiences to reach all audiences. She also contacted other survivors, transcribing and publishing their stories under the heading “Women of Valour.” Little by little, the research grew and the site became a home for Holocaust education, specifically through a gender lens.

Ms. Cohen’s voice will continue to be shared long into the future. Her testimony is available through the Toronto Holocaust Museum, and she was also one of the first survivors to record an audiobook version of her memoir with the Azrieli Foundation.

Last month, Ms. Cohen offered a reflection with the Temple Emanuel congregation.

“I turn 98 on Sept. 17. I never imagined I was going to live this long, honestly. I wish I were wise enough to have a message for the next generation, but I am a pessimist, that’s where I start.”

While she was a pessimist, she married it with real action. Audiences left every room she spoke in feeling inspired to act, and to be precise in how that action happens.

“For even a good ideology can go astray in the hands of people who are using it, not toward the original goal. That’s politics. People say politics is a dirty word but we have to understand that and handle it. This is my message for any generation,” Ms. Cohen said.

Armed with determination, a friend’s technical help and her husband’s patience, her website Women and the Holocaust — a Cyberspace of Their Own , was born. It offered essays, book reviews, poems, stories and educational material about women’s experiences to reach all audiences. She also contacted other survivors, transcribing and publishing their stories under the heading “Women of Valour.” Little by little, the research grew and the site became a home for Holocaust education, specifically through a gender lens.

Ms. Cohen’s voice will continue to be shared long into the future. Her testimony is available through the Toronto Holocaust Museum, and she was also one of the first survivors to record an audiobook version of her memoir with the Azrieli Foundation.
Last month, Ms. Cohen offered a reflection with the Temple Emanuel congregation.
“I turn 98 on Sept. 17. I never imagined I was going to live this long, honestly. I wish I were wise enough to have a message for the next generation, but I am a pessimist, that’s where I start.”
While she was a pessimist, she married it with real action. Audiences left every room she spoke in feeling inspired to act, and to be precise in how that action happens.

“For even a good ideology can go astray in the hands of people who are using it, not toward the original goal. That’s politics. People say politics is a dirty word but we have to understand that and handle it. This is my message for any generation,” Ms. Cohen said.

content_blocks.text: In 1993, Judy Weissenberg Cohen was nearing her 65th birthday and mandatory retirement when, during a lunch-break stroll through downtown Toronto, she saw a group of young people clad in black leather marching in a circle and shouting, “White power! White power!”
A certain fear was automatic, she later wrote in her memoir, like the feeling of her stomach clenching when she witnessed people being selected for death at Auschwitz-Birkenau.
“For a terrifying few seconds, the lines were blurred between past and present. I wondered, was I looking back at history or ahead?”
As she approached the curious audience, she realized she had come face-to-face with members of the Heritage Front, a white supremacist, neo-Nazi organization.

Instead of turning away, Ms. Cohen marched toward the group’s leader, Wolfgang Droege. When he claimed there had been no Black slavery in the U.S., she assumed the Holocaust would be the next thing he denied.

Before he got the chance, Ms. Cohen stepped between him and the crowd and implored those watching not to listen. She later humbly joked she was not especially heroic, since four police officers were nearby.
“Lady, don’t aggravate yourself. They only have a permit for 20 minutes.”
“My luck!” Ms. Cohen later wrote. “I caught the 20 minutes that would soon spur me to action.”

For the next three decades, she dedicated herself to Holocaust education and public speaking, urging people — particularly students — to recognize the warning signs of hatred and become witnesses to history. She also became a leading advocate for raising awareness about women’s experiences during the Holocaust, eventually creating a website devoted to preserving those stories.
Ms. Cohen died on Sept. 6 at 97 years old.

“The memory of the death camps and being victims of the Nazi Holocaust never fades, but I no longer consider myself a victim,” she wrote. “Instead, through the decades, I became a politically and socially aware activist. I must work relentlessly to ensure that memories like mine will not become the memories of future generations.”

content_blocks.text: She was born Judy Weissenberg in Debrecen, Hungary, ON Sept. 17, 1928, just after Rosh Hashanah, the Jewish New Year. The youngest of seven children, she developed an early dislike of being ordered around — and a willingness to question people in power that never disappeared.

“Judy always had a lot to say,” said Liam Romalis, the producer who worked with her on video testimonies and the audiobook of her memoir. “She was so sharp-witted, and would disagree with you but was still so open to dialogue.”

Mr. Romalis would pick Ms. Cohen up for the 45-minute drive from her Toronto home to the recording studio. She barely stopped talking the entire way, whether about something she had seen or an article she had read.
In 1938, when Judy was 10, news of the war reached her family in Hungary. She wrote that the children absorbed the adults’ grave concerns by osmosis.

By 1944, Hungarian Jews were forced to wear yellow Stars of David in public. Judy attached one to her jacket but covered it with the books and notes she held as she travelled to and from local tutoring gigs. She called it her “little act of resistance.”

A few months later, Judy and her family were forced into the overcrowded Debrecen ghetto. It was only a month before they, along with hundreds of others, were packed into cattle cars. They were only given two pails: one filled with clean water, and one to be used as a toilet.

content_blocks.caption: Ms. Cohen, sitting on the hood of the car on the right, and her sister Évi, sitting on the hood of the car on the left, with their friends, Montreal, 1948. Courtesy of Azrieli Foundation

content_blocks.text: Three days later, they arrived at Auschwitz-Birkenau, where an estimated 1.1 million people were murdered. Men and women were immediately separated. It was the last time she saw her father, her mother and her sister-in-law, who was holding her infant son.

Then the processing began. The women’s body hair was shaved, they took a brief shower and were given clothing previously worn by other prisoners. Judy found herself looking at hundreds of now-identical prisoners. After shouting through the crowd to find her sisters, they could barely recognize one another.
“We started to painfully laugh, how drastically we changed within a few hours.”

One night, around 700 women crowded into a barracks to observe Yom Kippur. Jewish religious practices were forbidden in the camps, but the kapos – prisoners appointed to supervise other prisoners in exchange for special privileges – allowed 10 minutes while guarding the doors for SS officers.
Someone lit a candle and a hush fell over the barracks. One woman began to recite Kol Nidre, the prayer that opens Yom Kippur.
“In this place where we felt that instead of asking for forgiveness from God, God should be asking for forgiveness from us,” Ms. Cohen recalled.
The prayer turned into “the sound of this incredible cry of hundreds of women.” The moment eventually inspired the title of Ms. Cohen’s memoir, A Cry in Unison .

Her older sister Böske helped keep her alive, carving spoons from wood and sneaking her extra pieces of bread, until they were eventually separated. In her sisters’ absence, Judy found solace and strength in two young women who became her “camp sisters.”

stories.title: Owner of one of London’s first Italian pizzerias dies
stories.summary: Vito’s Cave on Hamilton Road East was known to be a London hotspot in the 1950s, ’60s and ’70s.
stories.author: Nick Paparella
stories.content:
Vito’s Cave on Hamilton Road East was known to be a London hotspot in the 1950s, ’60s and ’70s.

Vito Moretti who immigrated to Canada from Bari, Italy started operating Vito’s Pizza in 1956.

When it first opened there was a large front window where people would gather to be entertained as they watched pizza dough getting thrown in the air.

A few years later Moretti transformed the shop into Vito’s Cave, serving up Italian cuisine.

The restaurant closed in 1985 after about 30 years of business.

Earlier this week, Moretti passed away following a brief illness.

His daughter Teresa Moran says he was in good spirits until the end, “He still had a wonderful sense of humour,” she added. “We had one last family gathering and he was the one who planned the whole meal.”

Moretti was 94. Funeral arrangements are set for Sept. 25 at St. Mary’s Catholic Church on Lyle Street.

stories.title: Manitobans brace for dark mornings, lighter evenings after time change nixed
stories.summary: Manitoban clocks will not fall back this November, Premier Wab Kinew announced Thursday. Mental health advocates say the end of the time change is 'a positive thing.'
stories.author: Tavi Dhillon
stories.content:
Manitobans are preparing for dark winter mornings and brighter evenings this winter following Premier Wab Kinew’s announcement that the province will stay in permanent Daylight Saving Time .

Kinew made the announcement while speaking to 680 Cjob Thursday. The move means Manitoban clocks will not fall back in November, as the province permanently remains in its spring and summer time zone.

This will result in later sunrises and sunsets this winter. The decision to stick with Daylight Saving Time, and not permanent Standard Time, was made based on the results of a survey that found respondents preferred the summer time option over Standard Time.

“I think it’s a positive thing,” Scott McFayden, executive director at the Anxiety Disorders Association of Manitoba (Adam), told Global News in an interview.

Committing to Daylight Standard Time will lead to fewer disruptions and more access to sunlight for people in the north, he said.

In Thompson, the sun will rise at 10:05 a.m. and set at 4:57 p.m. on the shortest day of the year, according to a Manitoba government report on the health implications of time policy.

“Access to sunlight, we know, has a positive benefit on mental health,” McFayden said.

“We live in a northern climate, there’s more instances of seasonal affective disorder with shorter (versus) longer days, and so, there is a connection between climate, access to sunlight and our mental health.”

Later sunsets May also help Manitobans get some sun in winter, he continued.

“If you walk out the door (after work) and there’s a little bit of sunlight, maybe you’ll actually go out and do something. It might be more difficult for people who start work really early in the morning. It will be dark an extra hour in the morning, but I think we’ll all adjust,” McFayden said.

Stopping the time change will also be beneficial for sleep, according to McFayden, who noted that regular, healthy sleep habits can help prevent anxiety from manifesting for some people.

The St. James-Assiniboia School Division (Sjasd) said it is in the early stages of determining how the switch to Daylight Saving Time will impact school day routines, Jaime Siska, assistant superintendent of educational planning and policy for Sjasd, told Global News in an email statement.

The sun is expected to rise at 9:24 a.m. in Winnipeg on the shortest day of the year in December, according to the Manitoba government.

Schools in the division start between 8:20 a.m. and 9 a.m., Siska said.

This means “most schools in the Sjasd will start prior to dawn on this date.”

Division staff is in the process of ensuring students will arrive at well-lit schools as mornings become darker this winter. Staff is also ensuring that community bus stops and areas surrounding schools have enough street lighting to ensure students are safe, the statement added.

“(We are) exploring best practices in safety measures to support students and caregivers as they prepare for this change,” Siska said.

“We expect supervising staff to be especially vigilant at drop-offs, bus loading areas, and street crossings during the first week of permanent DST (Daylight Saving Time), and anticipate using our communication channels to reinforce important safety messaging to caregivers and students in the lead-up to and following this change.”

Siska said the school division will work to ensure “students continue to arrive safely to school each day regardless of the natural lighting conditions.”

In ending the time change, Manitoba is joining the likes of British Columbia , Alberta , Saskatchewan , Yukon and the Northwest Territories.

stories.title: Carney to attend UN General Assembly next week in New York
stories.summary: As geopolitical instability, war and Trump’s efforts to dismantle the multilateral order hang over the event, Carney says ‘the world is looking at Canada differently’
stories.author: Kelly Geraldine Malone
stories.content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney is set to attend the United Nations General Assembly next week as geopolitical instability, war and U.S. President Donald Trump ’s efforts to dismantle the multilateral order hang over the event.

Carney will not give a speech in front of the 81st Session of the United Nations General Assembly while in New York City from Monday to Wednesday. Senior government officials said the prime minister will meet with world and business leaders and take part in UN events.

In a news release, Carney said “the world is looking at Canada differently.”

“At a moment when the international order is being remade, Canada intends to help shape it,” he added. “At the General Assembly, we will sit down with partners old and new, defend the rules that protect our sovereignty, and turn co-operation into real opportunity for Canadian workers and businesses.”

Government officials said Carney will co-host with France and the United Kingdom an event on the two-state solution, one year after the three countries recognized an independent Palestinian state at the General Assembly.

The officials said it will be an opportunity for the nations to continue to show support for the two-state solution, and to look at the implementation of key priorities and progress made.

Carney promises sweeping economic legislation, fast pace this fall during caucus meeting

Earlier this month, Ottawa joined European nations in a pledge to ban imports of goods produced in Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank. Canada and the other countries accused Israel of enabling settler violence and working to expand settlements that are widely understood to be illegal under international law.

While at the General Assembly, Carney will take part in an OceanEye International Alliance event – to secure sustained investment and open ocean data – along with European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen.

He also will participate in a round table discussion on strengthening multilateral collaboration with European Council President António Costa and Kenya’s President William Ruto.

The discussions come as the UN continues to tackle massive reformation efforts. Trump and his administration have demanded significant changes and have held back funding for the institution, putting it in turmoil.

The Trump administration has withdrawn from multiple UN organizations, including the World Health Organization and the cultural agency Unesco.

The UN is also in the process of selecting its next secretary-general.

The news release said Carney will work with partners to help build a more effective UN that is better equipped to deliver on its core priorities of peace and security, development and human rights.

As Trump pulls away from international institutions, Carney has worked on strengthening relationships with global partners, sometimes to the chagrin of the U.S. president.

Opinion: This week, Mark Carney laid out a vision of Canada’s future. Now comes the hard part

Earlier this week, von der Leyen used her State of the Union address to the European Parliament to open the door to Canada becoming what she called the first “associate member” of the EU.

Trump said he views the prospect of Canada becoming an associate member of the EU as a possible “hostile act” and threatened to impose more tariffs on Europe.

Trump has been escalating his trade war with Canada since trade talks broke down last month.

The president imposed 50-per-cent tariffs on an array of Canadian goods, moved to ban some Canadian imports outright later this month and signed an executive order to rename Lake Ontario as Lake America.

Trump on Wednesday signed a memorandum directing federal agencies overseeing government procurement in the United States to remove all products of Canadian origin.

Canadian officials said the General Assembly is large event and Carney and Trump could run into each other. They added that there are no meetings currently scheduled with members of the U.S. administration.

paragraphs: Prime Minister Mark Carney is set to attend the United Nations General Assembly next week as geopolitical instability, war and U.S. President Donald Trump ’s efforts to dismantle the multilateral order hang over the event.

Carney will not give a speech in front of the 81st Session of the United Nations General Assembly while in New York City from Monday to Wednesday. Senior government officials said the prime minister will meet with world and business leaders and take part in UN events.
In a news release, Carney said “the world is looking at Canada differently.”

“At a moment when the international order is being remade, Canada intends to help shape it,” he added. “At the General Assembly, we will sit down with partners old and new, defend the rules that protect our sovereignty, and turn co-operation into real opportunity for Canadian workers and businesses.”

Government officials said Carney will co-host with France and the United Kingdom an event on the two-state solution, one year after the three countries recognized an independent Palestinian state at the General Assembly.
The officials said it will be an opportunity for the nations to continue to show support for the two-state solution, and to look at the implementation of key priorities and progress made.
Carney promises sweeping economic legislation, fast pace this fall during caucus meeting

Earlier this month, Ottawa joined European nations in a pledge to ban imports of goods produced in Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank. Canada and the other countries accused Israel of enabling settler violence and working to expand settlements that are widely understood to be illegal under international law.

While at the General Assembly, Carney will take part in an OceanEye International Alliance event – to secure sustained investment and open ocean data – along with European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen.
He also will participate in a round table discussion on strengthening multilateral collaboration with European Council President António Costa and Kenya’s President William Ruto.

The discussions come as the UN continues to tackle massive reformation efforts. Trump and his administration have demanded significant changes and have held back funding for the institution, putting it in turmoil.
The Trump administration has withdrawn from multiple UN organizations, including the World Health Organization and the cultural agency Unesco.
The UN is also in the process of selecting its next secretary-general.
The news release said Carney will work with partners to help build a more effective UN that is better equipped to deliver on its core priorities of peace and security, development and human rights.
As Trump pulls away from international institutions, Carney has worked on strengthening relationships with global partners, sometimes to the chagrin of the U.S. president.
Opinion: This week, Mark Carney laid out a vision of Canada’s future. Now comes the hard part
Earlier this week, von der Leyen used her State of the Union address to the European Parliament to open the door to Canada becoming what she called the first “associate member” of the EU.
Trump said he views the prospect of Canada becoming an associate member of the EU as a possible “hostile act” and threatened to impose more tariffs on Europe.
Trump has been escalating his trade war with Canada since trade talks broke down last month.

The president imposed 50-per-cent tariffs on an array of Canadian goods, moved to ban some Canadian imports outright later this month and signed an executive order to rename Lake Ontario as Lake America.
Trump on Wednesday signed a memorandum directing federal agencies overseeing government procurement in the United States to remove all products of Canadian origin.

Canadian officials said the General Assembly is large event and Carney and Trump could run into each other. They added that there are no meetings currently scheduled with members of the U.S. administration.
Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand is set to deliver a speech during the General Assembly.

stories.title: 2 sudden deaths prompt public safety warning from Halifax police
stories.summary: Two sudden deaths and a person found in serious medical distress over the last 24 hours have prompted a public safety warning from Halifax Regional Police.
stories.author: Rebecca Lau
stories.content:
Two sudden deaths and a person found in serious medical distress over the last 24 hours have prompted a public safety warning from Halifax Regional Police.

Police say the Nova Scotia Medical Examiner’s Service is conducting autopsies to determine the cause of death in both incidents.

A release from police notes that while the investigations are in their early stages, “in the event” that the deaths are determined to be drug-related, police are warning people to be cautious.

Police point out illicit drugs May contain unknown substances, including highly potent opioids, which can increase the risk of overdose or death.

“If you see someone experiencing an overdose, call 911 immediately,” police add.

“If available, administer naloxone and follow emergency dispatcher instructions until help arrives.”

stories.title: Alberta limits voter information shared with political parties after major privacy breach
stories.summary: Copies of official voter list given to political parties will only include the number of voters in each voting area and municipality, province says
stories.author: Jack Farrell
stories.content:
Alberta’s government says it has made temporary changes to rules governing provincial voter lists after a major privacy breach.

The province published a new policy Thursday that says copies of Alberta’s official voter list given to political parties will only include the number of voters in each voting area and municipality.

The list previously included first and last names, home addresses, phone numbers and a unique identifier for each registered voter.

The list is managed by Elections Alberta and distributed to political parties, legislators, election candidates and constituency associations for things like campaigns and fundraising.

Alberta, Centurion Project sued over alleged data breach that affected millions of voters

The change comes after a separatist group published a database in the spring that elections officials said included private information of nearly three million Albertans.

Investigators traced the database to a copy of the list given to a fringe political party.

The new policy is in effect until the end of this year.

Justice Minister Mickey Amery’s office says the government plans to introduce legislation this fall and that Albertans should have confidence that their personal information is being protected.

stories.title: Mayoral candidates pitch affordability measures for Londoners
stories.summary: Incumbent Mayor Josh Morgan is promising to freeze recreation fees, while Susan Stevenson is pledging restraint on property-tax increases and an expanded tax deferral program.
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: Incumbent Mayor Josh Morgan is promising to freeze recreation fees, while Susan Stevenson is pledging restraint on property-tax increases and an expanded tax deferral program.
· Posted: Sep 18, 2026 4:58 PM EDT | Last Updated: 1 hour ago
Josh Morgan is promising to freeze recreation fees, while Susan Stevenson is pledging restraint on property-tax increases and an expanded tax deferral program.(CBC News)
Affordability is emerging as a theme in London’s mayoral race this week, with two candidates making new announcements focused on household costs.
Incumbent Mayor Josh Morgan announced Friday that he would freeze all City recreation fees paid by individuals and families at their current rates for at least two years.
The proposal would apply to programs and activities including swimming lessons, public skating, fitness classes and drop-in programs.
The role of school board trustees remains unclear. Here's why some Londoners want the job anyway

Morgan also said he would expand the Play Your Way Fund, which provides eligible low-income Londoners with up to $300 per person toward recreation programs and activities. He wants to make the application process easier and increase free community activities, such as swims and skates.
“Freezing these fees will provide much-needed certainty and relief for everyone in our city,” Morgan said in a news release.

On Wednesday, Ward 4 Coun. Susan Stevenson announced a plan to limit municipal property-tax increases to less than one per cent in 2027 and 2028, with a goal of zero. She said increases would then be limited to inflation or less in 2029 and 2030.

“Families need room in their budgets. City Hall has to make room in its own,” Stevenson in a news release. “Protecting families and seniors from rising costs will be a priority in every budget I bring forward.”
Got a minute? Tell us what changes you want to see in London, Ont., and area this election

Stevenson said she would require more detailed financial reporting to council, including line-by-line comparisons of actual spending against budgets and greater scrutiny of reserve and contingency spending.

Morgan and Stevenson are among 12 candidates running for mayor, including John Feher, Lawrence-Zachary Howe, Barry Douglas Jacklin, Tariq Khan, Kirsten Krose, Dan Lenart, Bronagh Joyce Morgan, Christine Rosehart, Jeff Yam and Mustafa Zeboon.
The municipal election is Oct. 26, with voting open from 10 a.m. to 8 p.m. Advance voting is available Oct. 1, Oct. 3 and from Oct. 5 to 10.

stories.title: FBI halted cooperation with RCMP after CBC 9/11 terrorism memo, N.Y. Times reports
stories.summary: Patel’s ire reportedly came from CBC a memo reminding reporters and editors not to refer to the deadly 9/11 attacks as “terrorist attacks.”
stories.author: National Post Staff
stories.content:
The New York Times is reporting that Kash Patel temporarily halted some FBI cooperation with the RCMP this month after the CBC “reminded its journalists of a longstanding policy not to refer to the Sept. 11 attacks as ‘terrorism’ without attribution to experts.”

The story is attributed to “multiple officials with knowledge of the event,” who spoke to The Times on the condition of anonymity “to describe the sensitive law enforcement dynamics.”

It dubs Patel’s temporary cooperation halt as an “extraordinary move to punish the Royal Canadian Mounted Police.”

The source of Patel’s ire, according to The Times, was a memo CBC circulated to reporters and editors across its news platforms ahead of the 9/11 anniversary reminding them not to refer to the attacks that claimed 3,000 lives and changed the modern world as “terrorist attacks.”

The CBC quickly reversed its policy after the memo was leaked to the media and criticized by Canadian and U.S. officials, including the U.S. ambassador to Canada and Patel.

In a pointed critique, the FBI director referred to the language policy as a “bastardization of history.”

“Any agency in Canada that doesn’t publicly reject this bastardization of history, and an insult to the souls lost during our largest terrorist attack in US history will no longer have friend in this FBI… Not to mention our heroes that responded in the aftermath,” he wrote on X late last month.

The cooperation disruption between the RCMP and the FBI “appears to have been short-lived,” according to The Times, which notes “it was specific to the F.B.I. Other parts of the U.S. government involved in intelligence-sharing continued with their operations. And not every element of cooperation between the F.B.I. and the mounted police was halted.”

The RCMP said it cannot speak to the intelligence-sharing practices of other law enforcement agencies and instead highlighted five criminal cases where the force did work jointly with the Americans. The most recent was in July when the Mounties and Los Angeles office of the FBI announced the arrests of the leadership of three organized crime networks, including the Bishnoi gang.

CBC reverses policy against calling 9/11 a terrorist attack without attribution

CBC tells staff not to call 9/11 a 'terrorist attack'

“We value our relationship with our U.S. counterparts, as we work closely to respond to threats to national security and maintain situational awareness of emerging risks. We maintain strong relationships with Canada’s security and intelligence community and work closely with domestic and international partners, including members of the Five Eyes community,” said RCMP Commissioner Mike Duheme in statement Friday.

A spokesman for Public Safety Minister Gary Anandasangaree also didn’t answer specific questions about the impasse with the FBI, saying the Government of Canada values its “close and longstanding law enforcement and security partnerships” with the United States.

“The collaboration is essential to keeping Canadians and Americans safe, and we will continue to engage with our American partners constructively and respectfully,” said spokesman Simon Lafortune.

Patel’s “abrupt move,” The Times report said, “risked disrupting F.B.I. operations with Canada and jeopardizing the organization’s relationship with Canada’s national law enforcement agency, which works closely with the bureau on a wide range of issues, including terrorism and cybersecurity cases.”

The Times reported that FBI officials cancelled meetings with their Canadian counterparts during the halt in cooperation, saying “they would be out of touch for some time, leading to a chilling between the two agencies.”

stories.title: MP calls on New Brunswick to reject proposed AI data centre in open letter to premier
stories.summary: Conservative MP John Williamson says the proposed AI centre in Saint John will trigger electricity rate hikes for nearby residents.
stories.author: Eli Ridder
stories.content:
A New Brunswick member of Parliament is calling on the provincial government to reject a proposed artificial intelligence data centre in Saint John, warning that it could overwhelm the power grid.

Conservative MP John Williamson says the proposed AI centre will trigger electricity rate hikes for nearby residents.

Williamson says the public utility NB Power lacks the necessary capacity to handle the facility’s demand for 200 megawatts from the grid.

He laid out his opposition to Beacon Data Centers’ project in a letter to Liberal Premier Susan Holt.

The New Brunswick Southwest MP also criticized Holt for highlighting the data centre project at a major Toronto investment summit earlier this week, even though it hasn’t received provincial government approval.

The New Brunswick government says any new data centre must pay for the costs it creates and cannot lead to higher electricity rates.

Beacon AI says its project requires 390 megawatts of energy and that it could produce up to 190 megawatts on site.

Williamson said the company wasn’t interested in generating all of its own power.

“I met with them and I raised this and they balked,” he told The Canadian Press in an interview Friday, referencing a meeting he had with the company a several months ago.

That’s why, he said, he wants the province “playing hardball” with companies that want to build data centres so that ratepayers are shielded from major price hikes.

stories.title: Clutch moments on an epic road trip from Vancouver to the Arctic and back
stories.summary: A group of friends drove six unlikely vehicles from Vancouver to Tuktoyaktuk, NWT, to swim in the Arctic Ocean, testing both their mechanical skills and the limits of their cars
stories.author: Ashley Joannou
stories.content:
When Jaden Konishi rolled his 1986 Porsche 944 into Vancouver after an 8,000-kilometre road trip to the Arctic Circle, he had a surplus of new memories but no clutch.

It had died about 3,000 kilometres earlier, somewhere in the Yukon’s Tombstone Territorial Park.

“It’s a part that you can’t replace on the car unless you remove the engine,” he explained.

Konishi and a group of friends have just returned from an epic three-week journey from Vancouver to Tuktoyaktuk, NWT, to swim in the Arctic Ocean and test both the limits of their mechanical prowess and the capabilities of six cars that might generously be described as novel choices.

In addition to Konishi’s Porsche, the cars chosen for the trip to the northernmost community on mainland Canada accessible by public road were a 1991 Isuzu Impulse RS, a 1993 Nissan 240SX, a 1989 Toyota MR2 Supercharged, a 1990 Mazda Miata and a 1994 Dodge B350.

Konishi said they planned for about a year and each driver had the skills to care for their own vehicle in an emergency. They shared tools, carrying everything from spare parts to a welder.

Fixes weren’t always an option. In the case of his Porsche’s clutch, Konishi relied on the starter motor to get the classic sports car moving and then used a method called “floating” the gears to shift without using the clutch.

“It’s not that he couldn’t come to a stop. His brakes and stuff work, of course. It’s just when he comes to the stop, his engine would shut off,” friend Adam Riddell recalled.

“So, there were many times where he would just be doing a circle in the parking lot, or he’d just keep turning right, if we didn’t know where we were going or trying to figure something out, because he couldn’t come to a stop on a hill or anything, or else the car would not be able to start again until he got to flat ground.”

Part of the challenge was returning the vehicles home under their own power, after traversing the Dempster Highway, the unpaved 740-kilometre route from Dawson City, Yukon, to the Arctic Ocean. All succeeded.

“We grew up watching shows like Top Gear, where they take sports cars or unconventional cars to do crazy road trips. And we’ve done a few in the past, but the Dempster is kind of this looming monster that we wanted to tackle,” Riddell said, describing his friends as “car guys” who wanted to see what they could accomplish.

Every year thousands of tourists make the drive to Tuktoyaktuk on a route that can challenge modern cars.

Konishi maintains that the group’s older vehicles – which had been retrofitted into makeshift campers, with a rooftop tent or the removal of seats – are simpler and easier to fix than modern vehicles with computers or complex parts.

“There were Jeeps and trucks and semis and all sorts of modern vehicles that do this drive and are meant for it that were on the side of the road that had to get towed out,” he said.

“It really just goes to show, no matter how much you prep and no matter what you buy, things are going to happen.”

The group documented their mechanical woes.

The Impulse leaked coolant. The 240SX lost a headlight and had its exhaust fall off multiple times. The MR2 wore through six tires and had blown front struts, while the Miata lost both its accessory belts. As for the Dodge B350, it suffered a laundry list of issues – batteries fell out, rotors warped, the transmission overheated and the dash rattled apart.

One of the larger bumps in the road came when the group had to cross the Peel River, which had flooded, making the ferry inoperable.

The group waited in line, sleeping one night in their cars, while workers rebuilt the banks.

Konishi and Riddell said arriving in Tuktoyaktuk was “surreal.”

“Adam and I didn’t think that all the vehicles would make it. We thought that maybe one or two of the cars would probably be left somewhere, and then we’ll go back for it and drag it out on the way home,” Konishi said.

“So, to see all of them there, all these old cars at the sign, it really was spectacular.”

“Actually, getting into the ocean kind of put that dreaminess away, as it was so cold,” Riddell said.

It was the people they met who provided the biggest lesson, Konishi said.

They took shelter in the ferry workers’ compound because of a bear in the area, ate smoked whitefish from a resident, and were lent a hydraulic press in Whitehorse for repairs.

“A lot of the people that we met around Whitehorse and in Yukon and on the Dempster, we would see them as we’re driving the highway, and everybody is going at their own pace,” he said.

“Some people have already made it; they’re on their way back. Some people are going up, and we pass their camp. But every time we’d be able to stop and chat and share stories, and it really felt like going on a backpacking trip, but with cars.”

The group documented the trip and plan to release a film on YouTube next month.

“This trip was not about efficiency or ease. It was about a group of friends banding together to work through the many issues we encountered along the way to achieve our shared goal. Surprisingly, no flats!” Konishi said in a social media post last week celebrating their successful return to Vancouver.

stories.title: Uncertainty hangs over Nackawic after pulp mill announces temporary shutdown
stories.summary: A pulp mill that's the backbone of a rural New Brunswick community's local economy is facing a closure that will impact hundreds of workers.
stories.author: Rebecca Lau, Johnny James
stories.content:
A pulp mill that’s the backbone of a rural New Brunswick community’s local economy is facing a closure that will impact hundreds of workers.

AV Group NB Inc., a subsidiary of the India-based Aditya Birla Group, announced Thursday it would temporarily idle its AV Nackawic facility west of Fredericton around the end of October.

AV Group says about 350 workers will be out of work, and attributed the decision to “prevailing market conditions” and other challenges.

“Nackawic has been challenging for a number of years. This was not a flippant decision by any means,” said Mike Legere, AV Group’s director of government relations and communications.

“There is presently a surplus of dissolving-grade pulp on the marketplace, which compounds the problem in terms of trying to get a higher price realization, and really the price for it is stable, but is not at all keeping up with production costs.”

Nackawic-Millville Mayor Tim Fox says the news isn’t surprising since there was already a slowdown in wood deliveries to the mill last month.

“(We) started having some concerns in August when they stopped purchasing roundwood, so it’s not a huge shock, although we are disappointed that they took the decision they did,” he said.

The mayor added it’s an uneasy time for their community, and the province’s forestry industry at large.

“It’s no secret the global forest industry is not great right now. There is a lot of uncertainty, and that plays heavily into the decisions that were made,” Fox said.

Unifor, the union representing 228 of the 350 impacted workers, says it believes action could have been taken much sooner on the issue.

“It’s a sector that ought to have been planning for the future and modernizing what that would look like. Unfortunately, in this mill, that didn’t happen,” said Jennifer Murray, Unifor’s Atlantic regional director.

“There is no space to shut this mill down and think it is going to restart again.”

Natural Resources Minister John Herron issued a statement saying he was “disappointed and saddened” by the news. He called it a “difficult day for New Brunswick.”

“AV Nackawic is an important cornerstone in New Brunswick’s forest industry, in the local community, and to our province’s economy,” he wrote.

Premier Susan Holt wrote in a social media post that she and her team have been in contact with community leaders and Unifor, and are putting a support plan in place.

“Teams across government are working together to make sure people have access to the support they need, and we will share more in the coming days. Your government has your back,” she wrote.

— with a file from The Canadian Press

stories.title: London Catholic trustees question province’s new family support offices
stories.summary: Trustees say direct access to elected representatives offers families more personal support than the new provincial model.
stories.author: Heather Rivers Davey
stories.content:
Two London Catholic trustees are criticizing the province’s new family support offices, saying families are better served by having direct access to elected trustees.

“Our communication model is based on direct access to elected trustees. When families need support, the expectation is that they contact a trustee,” said Gabe Pizzuti, chair of the London District Catholic school board. “Families can contact a trustee who lives in their community, knows their schools and understands their situation.

“More importantly, trustees can monitor progress, advocate on behalf of families and work to ensure concerns are addressed.”

Pizzuti said that on the first day of school, he received five phone calls and five emails from families, while board vice-chair Linda Steele received 12 phone calls and emails.

“Every one of those concerns was addressed within that same day,” he said.

Ministry of Education spokesperson Emma Testani said the London District Catholic school board’s support centre received about 20 inquiries in the first nine school days of the school year.

Earlier this year, support offices were implemented at school boards that had been taken over by the ministry, beginning with the Thames Valley District school board in January.

All other unsupervised school boards across the province were required to open their own family support offices in September.

The offices are intended to “help resolve matters that need to be escalated following initial engagement with a child’s teacher and principal,” the ministry said.

“Parents should have a clear and consistent way to raise concerns and get answers when it comes to their child’s education,” Education Minister Paul Calandra said in a Sept. 1 release.

“We are strengthening accountability across our school boards and making sure families can get the support they need when they need it. Everything we are doing is focused on improving student achievement and ensuring every student has the opportunity to succeed.”

But Pizzuti said the board support office offers a turnaround time of two days, while he had been told relatively few people had contacted the office.

Steele said trustees “are responsible for ensuring the system is working properly to meet their needs.”

“When it does not, we advocate for changes to the system,” she said. “All families are unique – so a one-size-fits-all approach is not effective or appropriate in all situations.”

Parents in difficult situations “often feel unheard, misunderstood, and are left frustrated,” she said.

“If they try to push harder, they worry about backlash against their child/children,” Steele said.

She also said the new system has only one phone number to call, with a message saying someone will get back to them.

“Trustees are accessible pretty much 24/7,” Steele said. “We field calls outside the scope of the call centre – from families outside our school system, other school boards, local politicians, special interest groups, local organizations, looking for assistance.”

stories.title: The Merriam-Webster online dictionary just added 1,400 new words to stay on top of slang
stories.summary: Want to know what ‘cuffing season’ or ‘looksmaxxing’ is? Now you can find some official definitions
stories.author: Sarah Wallace
stories.content:
Have you ever wondered what the “Sunday scaries” are or what “letterboxing” is? Well, Merriam-Webster has the answer.

The dictionary announced Tuesday that it has added 1,400 new words and definitions to its online dictionary. Some of the words will also be added to future print releases.

A number of the additions are directly related to social media, including “cuffing season” (a time of the year when people who are not married or in a relationship begin looking for a short-term romantic partner to spend the colder months of the year with), “glow-up” (a usually dramatic enhancement especially to someone’s or something’s physical appearance) and ” looksmaxxing " (the practice of taking one or more sometimes extreme or dangerous measures intended to increase one’s physical attractiveness).

Artificial intelligence-related words continue to be added, such as “vibe coding” (the act or practice of using an artificial intelligence system to generate computer code in a given programming language) and “AGI” (an abbreviation of artificial general intelligence – defined as the potential capability of computer systems or algorithms to match or exceed human cognitive abilities).

There’s also a distinctly Canadian addition to the American-based dictionary: “trash panda,” which is slang for a raccoon. ( Search for the term on Etsy , and you’ll see what we mean.)

Food items also make an appearance, such as “bao” and “cake pop.” And you’ll find the musical genre “yacht rock” and the clothing “shapewear.”

Merriam-Webster notes that its editors have three main criteria for adding a new word: frequent use, widespread use and meaningful use.

“The new entries reflect words and meanings that have demonstrated widespread use over time, offering a window into the world today,” its website says.

Last year, Merriam-Webster took the rare step of adding more than 5,000 words to its Collegiate print edition, including “adulting,” “doomscroll,” “cancel culture” and “dad bod.”

Merriam-Webster, one of several dictionaries that announces new words yearly, also puts out a word of the year, which it has not yet announced for 2026. “Slop” was 2025’s word, defined as “digital content of low quality that is produced usually in quantity by means of artificial intelligence.”

Some of the dictionary’s previous words of the year include “polarization” (2024), “vaccine” (2021) and “pandemic” (2020).

With a report from the Associated Press

stories.title: Ottawa mayoral candidate charged over alleged death threats against Mark Sutcliffe, Doug Ford
stories.summary: Police charged Geoffrey Nicholas Griplas with two counts each of criminal harassment and uttering death threats, along with several weapons-related offences
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa mayoral candidate Geoffrey Nicholas Griplas has been charged with harassment and threats to cause death related to online posts about Ontario Premier Doug Ford and Ottawa Mayor Mark Sutcliffe.

The Kingston Police say they were made aware of “concerning behaviour and comments” made on Sept. 13.

Griplas was arrested on Sept. 15 in Ottawa and has been charged with two counts each of criminal harassment and uttering death threats, along with several weapons-related offences.

The accused has been remanded into custody in Kingston, Ont., after a bail hearing and is due back in court on Sept. 21.

Griplas is listed as a certified candidate in Ottawa’s mayoral election under the name “Geoff Nicholas” and is one of 14 mayoral candidates.

Ottawa’s civic election is set to take place on Oct. 26.

stories.title: Carney set to attend the United Nations General Assembly in New York next week
stories.summary: Carney is set to attend the United Nations General Assembly next week as geopolitical instability, war and Trump's efforts to dismantle the multilateral order hang over the event.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
OTTAWA — Prime Minister Mark Carney is set to attend the United Nations General Assembly next week as geopolitical instability, war and U.S. President Donald Trump’s efforts to dismantle the multilateral order hang over the event.

Carney will not give a speech in front of the 81st Session of the United Nations General Assembly while in New York City from Monday to Wednesday. Senior government officials said the prime minister will meet with world and business leaders and take part in UN events.

In a news release, Carney said “the world is looking at Canada differently.”

“At a moment when the international order is being remade, Canada intends to help shape it,” he added. “At the General Assembly, we will sit down with partners old and new, defend the rules that protect our sovereignty, and turn co-operation into real opportunity for Canadian workers and businesses.”

Government officials said Carney will co-host with France and the United Kingdom an event on the two-state solution, one year after the three countries recognized an independent Palestinian state at the General Assembly.

The officials said it will be an opportunity for the nations to continue to show support for the two-state solution, and to look at the implementation of key priorities and progress made.

Earlier this month, Ottawa joined European nations in a pledge to ban imports of goods produced in Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank. Canada and the other countries accused Israel of enabling settler violence and working to expand settlements that are widely understood to be illegal under international law.

A major Jewish lobby group said Friday it shares the goal of securing a peaceful future for the region but called Ottawa’s approach a “dangerous double standard.”

The Centre for Israel and Jewish Affairs said the United Nations platforms “brutal regimes while systematically singling out the Jewish state.”

“As Prime Minister Carney heads to the United Nations, Canada should bring an approach that is consistent, constructive and grounded in Canadian interests,” the centre said in a statement. “That begins with fairness — and ending the double standard toward Israel.”

While at the General Assembly, Carney will take part in an OceanEye International Alliance event — to secure sustained investment and open ocean data — along with European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen.

He also will participate in a roundtable discussion on strengthening multilateral collaboration with European Council President António Costa and Kenya’s President William Ruto.

The discussions come as the UN continues to tackle massive reformation efforts. Trump and his administration have demanded significant changes and have held back funding for the institution, putting it in turmoil.

The Trump administration has withdrawn from multiple UN organizations, including the World Health Organization and the cultural agency UNESCO.

The UN is also in the process of selecting its next secretary-general.

The news release said Carney will work with partners to help build a more effective UN that is better equipped to deliver on its core priorities of peace and security, development and human rights.

As Trump pulls away from international institutions, Carney has worked on strengthening relationships with global partners, sometimes to the chagrin of the U.S. president.

Earlier this week, von der Leyen used her state of the union address to the European Parliament to open the door to Canada becoming what she called the first “associate member” of the EU.

Trump said he views the prospect of Canada becoming an associate member of the EU as a possible “hostile act” and threatened to impose more tariffs on Europe.

Trump has been escalating his trade war with Canada since trade talks broke down last month.

The president imposed 50 per cent tariffs on an array of Canadian goods, moved to ban some Canadian imports outright later this month and signed an executive order to rename Lake Ontario as Lake America.

Trump on Wednesday signed a memorandum directing federal agencies overseeing government procurement in the United States to remove all products of Canadian origin.

Canadian officials said the General Assembly is large event and Carney and Trump could run into each other. They added that there are no meetings currently scheduled with members of the U.S. administration.

Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand is set to deliver a speech during the General Assembly.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 18, 2026.

— By Kelly Geraldine Malone in Washington, with files from Dylan Robertson in Ottawa and The Associated Press

The Canadian Press

stories.title: This invasive species has just been found in Canada for the 1st time
stories.summary: The invasive spotted lanternfly has been confirmed in Canada, according to the Canada Food Inspection Agency, which is urging Canadians to take action if they spot it.
stories.author: Ariel Rabinovitch
stories.content:
An invasive species of insect known as the spotted lanternfly has been confirmed in Canada, according to the Canadian Food Inspection Agency (CFIA), which is urging Canadians to take action if they spot it or its egg masses.

Although all previous documented reports of the spotted lanternfly in Canada have either been an unconfirmed “sighting” or “interception” (live or dead specimen collected), this announcement marks the first time the insect has fallen under the “detection” label, meaning confirmed alive in the Canadian environment through official CFIA surveys.

In a press release from Thursday, the CFIA says it confirmed its first detection of spotted lanternfly in Canada on Sept. 15 in Windsor, Ontario.

Spotted lanternflies feed on more than 100 species of trees and plants, the CFIA says, but the only significant agricultural impact observed so far has been on grapes.

This means wineries in Canada could be impacted if the infestation spreads to vineyards.

The CFIA says it is conducting surveillance in the area surrounding where the spotted lanternflies were spotted to determine the full extent of the infestation and what the next steps will be.

Spotted lanternflies have been regulated in Canada since 2018, and to help prevent further spread of the invasive species, the CFIA says restrictions have been put in place to stop movement of regulated materials like plants that could be infested.

How did the spotted lanternfly get to Canada?

The CFIA says, like with some other invasive species, there are many “human-assisted” ways the spotted lanternfly could have been introduced into Canada.

Those include movement on cargo and containers, camping gear and outdoor equipment, patio furniture, cars and trucks, and the movement of plants and plant materials.

It’s for these reasons the CFIA is urging Canadians to check any objects stored outside while travelling to infested areas, including vehicles, patio furniture, tarps, yard and garden items and sports equipment as they may find the insects or their egg masses. The agency suggests checking around yards as well because spotted lanternflies could be on trees and plants.

The CFIA also suggests that anyone travelling back from infested areas of the United Stated should check their car, camper, trailer or RV before making the return trip, as well as any camping gear or equipment before returning to Canada.

What to look for and what to do if you spot it

In order to more easily identify a spotted lanternfly or its egg masses, the CFIA suggests learning about its various life stages.

The spotted lanternfly lays egg masses during the late summer, and those egg masses can survive winter temperatures and hatch in the spring, the CFIA says.

If you see a spotted lanternfly or its egg masses, the CFIA says, “Spot it? Snap it, catch it and report it.”

Anyone who thinks they may have seen a spotted lanternfly or its egg masses should take a photo or video, the CFIA says.

Collecting a specimen is also advised, if possible, including catching an insect or scraping the egg masses and placing them in a sealable container.

Once all available photos, videos and specimens are gathered, those persons should submit a report immediately to the CFIA .

stories.title: 20 years, 1,600 surgeries: London doctors’ mission restores mobility abroad
stories.summary: Operation Walk Canada is nearing its $1-million fundraising goal as it marks two decades of free hip and knee replacements in Guatemala and Ecuador.
stories.author: Brian Williams
stories.content:
Operation Walk Canada made its first mission to Guatemala two decades ago, providing free hip and knee replacement surgeries to patients who otherwise had no means of receiving them.

The volunteer-based medical organization was co-founded in 2006 by longtime London orthopedic surgeons Robert Bourne and Cecil Rorabeck. Its goal was to offer free hip and knee replacements – or, as Bourne puts it, “free restoration of mobility” – to patients with no other means of receiving the life-changing procedures.

Since that first trip, the organization added Ecuador as a second annual mission destination in 2009. In all, Operation Walk Canada has transformed the lives of roughly 1,600 people through 33 missions to the two countries, Bourne said.

“You see the gratitude in patients and people’s lives because we’ve done over 1,600 hip and knee replacements on our missions now, and we look upon it as we’ve affected 1,600 families,” Bourne said. “So, it’s really quite an amazing feat.”

Hip and knee replacement surgeries are among the most effective orthopedic procedures, reducing pain and helping patients return to active lives, according to the organization’s website.

But the surgeries are costly and complex, putting them out of reach for many patients in developing countries.

“If you don’t have money in Guatemala or Ecuador, you’re not getting healthcare, so the bottom line (is) the need for hip and knee (replacements) is huge,” said Operation Walk Canada board chair Steven MacDonald.

Operation Walk Canada sends teams of volunteer health professionals on its missions, including nurses, physiotherapists and surgeons from across Canada, Bourne said.

Having surgeons from other cities take part in the week-long missions helps avoid putting “such a burden” on patients needing care in London, he said, adding the work has been deeply rewarding for volunteers.

“People kept saying this is the most important thing they’ve done in their life, and they not only volunteered for next year, but many have come for 10 years or 15 years, even 20 years,” Bourne said.

“They all pay for it themselves. People take vacation time; they pay for their expenses going down. So, every dollar that we raise by the goodness of London donors goes to buy the supplies we need to do the surgery, and so it’s just been a remarkable experience for all of us.”

The Guatemala mission typically takes place in November, while the Ecuador mission is generally held in April. Between 100 and 150 patients receive operations each year, depending on the complexity of the cases, Bourne said.

Operation Walk Canada works with doctors in both countries who identify low-income patients in need of surgery. The organization then tries to select those with the greatest need.

MacDonald said all money raised by Operation Walk Canada goes toward the missions, paying for necessities such as surgical instruments and medications. The organization also receives donations from Canadian orthopedic medical supply companies.

“The most expensive thing that we would do would be the implant cost,” MacDonald said.

“The cost of hip and knee replacements. But the companies that we work with give us those in kind. So thankfully, we don’t have to buy the implants.”

To mark its 20th anniversary, Operation Walk Canada set a $1-million fundraising target earlier this year and has reached about 90 per cent of its goal, according to a news release. Through the Bourne family fund, Bourne and his wife, Donna, have committed up to $200,000 in matching support during the campaign.

MacDonald said the money raised will support future missions.

“What better way to celebrate the 20th anniversary (than) with a capital campaign?” he said.

For more information about Operation Walk Canada, visit operationwalk.ca .

Born and raised in London, Brian Williams joined The Free Press in 2023 and has reported extensively on London and the region. His primary focuses are health care and Elgin County.

stories.title: Eby vows to scrap plan to buy ferries from China in speech laden with promises
stories.summary: B.C. Premier addressed local government conference as speculation swirled that he would call a snap provincial election
stories.author: Jesse Winter
stories.content:
B.C. Premier David Eby made a series of election-style promises, including a plan to overturn a controversial move to buy replacement ferries for the province from China, during a speech to close a local government conference on Friday.

“I will be directing BC Ferries to ensure that the next generation of BC Ferries vessels will be built right here in British Columbia,” Mr. Eby said.

He also promised to delay expanding the provincial sales tax to professional services, and to create a task force of industry and ministry representatives to stabilize the forestry sector, with a “bridge to retirement” where necessary.

Mr. Eby delivered his speech amid swirling speculation that he’s about to call a snap provincial election. Earlier in the week, he confirmed he’d tapped interim chief of staff Cheryl Oates to be the party’s provincial campaign director and had alerted Elections BC and his own party to be “election ready.” Talk of a potential vote buzzed around the Union of BC Municipalities conference.

Elections BC confirmed that it is preparing for an early vote by inquiring about electoral office and voting place availability, restocking supplies and recruiting officials.

The Ubcm, which objects to an early vote, passed an emergency resolution calling on the province to safeguard the local election process.

If Mr. Eby calls an election in the next few days, the campaign period would overlap with the province’s municipal elections, which are scheduled for Oct. 17.

Meanwhile, the opposition BC Conservative Party appears to be in disarray. Party leader Kerry-Lynne Findlay has faced a raft of MLAs leaving the party caucus over several compounding controversies, including fresh allegations that party funds were used to hire a private investigator to spy on potential critics both inside and outside of her caucus.

B.C. Conservatives lose 10th MLA since August as Claire Rattée exits caucus

Addressing the Ubcm convention in Vancouver on Thursday, Ms. Findlay made clear she has no intention of stepping aside despite the growing discord in her party’s ranks.

“I’m not going anywhere,” Ms. Findlay told the gathering of local government and First Nations leaders.

Her address followed a remarkable month of upheaval for an opposition that came within three seats of forming government in 2024. Leaked recordings have fuelled allegations of misconduct, 10 MLAs have quit the Conservative caucus in the past month and police have interviewed some of them over assertions of illegal inducements .

Ms. Findlay herself is already in campaign mode, aiming to secure a seat in the legislature through a Sept. 26 by-election in the riding of Abbotsford-Mission that could be pre-empted by a surprise race to provincial polls.

The shifting political landscape could benefit Mr. Eby, whose approval rating had fallen in recent months, in part over concerns about the province’s finances.

An Angus Reid Institute poll released Wednesday put the Premier’s approval at 41 per cent, up from 31 per cent in June, with the organization pointing to his response to U.S. President Donald Trump as a possible factor in the rebound.

Ubcm president Cori Ramsay expressed concern about sending British Columbians to the polls twice so close together. Municipal elections often struggle with low voter turnout, and having to compete for attention with a provincial race could compromise municipal campaigns, Ms. Ramsay said.

“Local elections should provide space for discussions for local priorities without being overshadowed by a concurrent provincial campaign,” Ms. Ramsay said Thursday. “Ubcm’s concern is fundamentally about protecting the integrity and effectiveness of local democracy.”

With reports from Andrea Woo

stories.title: Q+A: Londoner Daniel Kilby finally gets his shot at Survivor
stories.summary: After years of applying, the 30-year-old game designer is among 21 castaways competing on season 51.
stories.author: Ryan Goodison
stories.content:
Londoner Daniel Kilby will be one of 21 castaways on season 51 of Survivor. The show, which has been on the air since 2000, only began allowing Canadian applicants in 2018. Kilby, originally from Mount Forest, Ont., will make his television debut on the show next Wednesday. The Free Press’s Ryan Goodison spoke with Kilby about who he is and why he thinks Survivor has endured for so long.

Q: For people in London who’ve never heard of you before, who is Daniel Kilby?

A: I would say I am a free-spirited, kind of wacky guy. My friends always call me the Energizer Bunny because I’m always doing all kinds of different events. Like, I think anybody who’s hanging around downtown a lot probably will recognize me, even if they don’t know me by name. I go to Molly’s karaoke all the time. I’m always hanging out around the movie theatre, everything like that.

But I really am sort of like an eccentric weirdo, sort of marching to the beat of my own drum, and I’m pretty much doing something every single day. You know, like the London Sports and Social Club, I’m there like three nights a week, playing volleyball, tennis, dodgeball, stuff like that. I love London because there’s so much stuff to do every single day that I’m never home. Like, that really is the kind of guy that I am.

Q: What’s your day-to-day like? You’re a video game designer, is that right?

A: I am a game designer, so me and my buddy actually met through the Survivor fan community, and we decided we’re gonna make a game studio, Noodle Goose Games. So we are the founders, and we do games of all types. We do video games, board games, as well as, like, experiential events and stuff like that.

A couple of weeks ago, we just did a whole game show on a boat in Toronto and brought a bunch of people onto the harbourfront on a big pirate ship down in Lake Ontario, and we did games and challenges and all those kinds of things on the boat. So we’re a weird company. We basically chase our own dreams. But right now we have two games in development, too. So, always hard at work.

Q: Survivor has been on television for 26 years. Why is this still something a 30-year-old from London wants to do?

A: Survivor is not only the best show on TV, it’s also, like, the ultimate social experiment, right? You’re really stripping people away from everything that ties them to status, power or influence in the world. It doesn’t matter if you have a degree; it doesn’t matter what your credentials are on Survivor. You are building a new world. You’re building a new concept of what it means to have power. It’s just who you are on that beach. Once your feet hit the sand, it doesn’t matter who you are back at home. And I think that’s what makes Survivor so magical.

Q: From the sounds of it, you’ve been a fan of Survivor for a really long time?

A: Genuinely, I think my first memory is Survivor. Like, my family, that’s what we bonded over. My mom is almost as big of a fan as me, and I remember being, like, four and running through my living room there and seeing Survivor on the TV.

Q: How does someone even go about getting on the show?

A: It takes a lot, you know. It really is learning how to tell your story. Why are you special? Why would anyone want to see you on TV? It’s doing a lot of soul-searching. People always say that higher education or whatever is a good way to kind of find yourself. I think the way to get on Survivor is you gotta find yourself.

So, you submit a video and tell your story and give a sense of your personality and stuff like that. I applied a bunch of times before, got my heart broken a few times, but I never lost sight of the dream. I knew one day I would be on that beach, and hey, if you’re delusional all the time, sometimes you’re delusional enough that reality just has to bend to that delusion, you know?

Q: Why do you think people are still watching Survivor, and why do you think people like you are still willing to play?

A: I think Survivor has a perfect format. I think it’s in the same way that if you were to ask why someone played football or why people still watch football. I think for a lot of people, Survivor is like a sport for them because, you know, it’s a game that you can play a million times and play it a million different ways.

I think that’s what makes it so timeless. How bad do you want it? Are you able to swindle your way to the end, and then get the people that you tricked to give you a million dollars? It’s a pretty timeless, unbreakable format, and it’s something they don’t really have to mess with that much.

It’s not like season 51 of Friends. It’s way closer to the World Cup or the Super Bowl. Like, I think that’s more what we’re dealing with, and I think people who don’t watch reality TV maybe miss that Survivor really is a lot closer to that sort of thing than your typical reality show.
