stories.title: Josh Morgan pledges two-year freeze on London recreation fees
stories.summary: The mayoral candidate also wants to expand the city’s Play Your Way subsidy for low-income residents.
stories.author: Jack Moulton
stories.content:
Josh Morgan is pledging to push for a two-year freeze on recreation fees and an expansion of London’s existing low-income recreation subsidy program.

Announcing the plan Friday morning across from the StarTech.com Community Centre in Bostwick, Morgan promised to freeze family and individual fees for activities such as swimming lessons, public skating and fitness classes for “at least two years.”

Morgan said the city already subsidizes recreation to a degree, with taxes covering roughly one-third of the cost of running recreation programs and user fees making up the other two-thirds. He argues the city can absorb the lost increases as families deal with affordability pressures.

“(It) benefits all segments of our community with a real focus on affordability, it’s something that the city can afford to do, it’s something that we can do as soon as possible,” he said. “This is a bylaw-driven initiative, so I have to take an actual motion to council to do this, but I’m 100 per cent committed to doing that, and I’m going to do that at the first available opportunity.”

User fees, one of the city’s main sources of revenue, typically increase by small amounts year over year, mainly because of inflation or changes such as minimum-wage increases. Many fees rose by between two and five per cent this year , with similar increases so far scheduled for next year .

Morgan also wants to expand the city’s existing Play Your Way Fund , which provides up to $300 per person annually toward city recreation programs for low-income individuals and families. He is pledging to review the program’s eligibility requirements and improve the application process.

He would also look to offer more free programming, citing events such as free public skates sponsored by his office and several other councillors’ offices.

“For the low-income Londoners, we know the Play Your Way program is always an oversubscribed program, there are always more people looking to access those subsidies than we have dollars for,” he said.

“When you think about affordability in the city and who needs relief the most, it’s those who are at the lowest levels of income in our city, and boosting the Play Your Way program is a way to get, you know, affordability into the hands who really need it.”

Morgan is seeking re-election as mayor and is running against 11 opponents: John Feher, Lawrence-Zachary Howe, Barry Douglas Jacklin, Tariq Khan, Kirsten Krose, Dan Lenart, Bronagh Joyce Morgan, Christine Rosehart, Susan Stevenson, Jeff Yam and Mustafa Zeboon.

Stevenson also made her first announcement this week after launching her campaign , promising property tax increases of less than one per cent in the next two years and at or below the rate of inflation in the final two years of the term if elected.

stories.title: Nova Scotia to mark 52 historic African Nova Scotian communities with new signs
stories.summary: Nova Scotia will soon put up signs marking the 52 historic African Nova Scotian communities across the province.
stories.author: Lyndsay Armstrong
stories.content:
Nova Scotia will soon put up signs marking the 52 historic African Nova Scotian communities across the province, in a move aimed at highlighting the province’s rich Black heritage.

NDP member Suzy Hansen brought forward the motion in the legislature Friday, which unanimously passed without debate. Hansen said the rare moment of unity in the chamber was emotional, and she’s “overjoyed” by the all-party support.

“I think this is a huge step forward in recognizing us as a distinct people in Nova Scotia,” she said in an interview after the motion passed.

“It was very emotional … just now realizing that across the province all of our 52 communities will have signage that expresses who we are as a community and the impact that we’ve made as African Nova Scotians,” Hansen added.

Shelburne, Africville, Cherry Brook, Sydney, and East and North Preston are among the historic Black communities that will be getting signs.

A spokesperson with African Nova Scotian Affairs, Ama Lorenz, said in an email that the department is “engaging communities on the design and wording so the signs reflect their history and identity.”

Between 1782 and 1785, about 3,500 Black Loyalists fled the United States at the end of the American Revolution and arrived in Nova Scotia as the first major group of Black settlers to the province. About 1,500 of them settled in Shelburne County.

The Black Loyalists were offered land, protection and freedom, but they were not given the rations, assistance or fertile land they were promised. Many were forced into work on public roads and in construction.

By 1792, more than 1,100 settlers left Halifax on 15 ships to Sierra Leone. About 65 died on the voyage.

Following the War of 1812, approximately 2,000 Black refugees, many from the southern United States, left America and landed in Nova Scotia. An estimated 400 of them travelled to New Brunswick. In Nova Scotia, many of these refugees settled in Preston, Hammonds Plains and Beechville.

The Canadian Museum of Immigration at Pier 21 says the government denied giving outright land ownership to these settlers. It also says the government settled them in areas that had rocky and infertile soil that would not support crops. This meant that many lived in extreme poverty.

“Despite their marginalization and impoverishment, the Black Refugees made valuable contributions to Nova Scotia’s cultural fabric as they established enduring communities throughout the province,” says a museum website.

Hansen said the signs highlighting individual communities’ histories will be “a huge pride,” and she’s eager for Nova Scotians and visitors to see these signs as they drive around the province.

“I think this will give us recognition … show our province and Canada how we appreciate African Nova Scotian communities and their impact on our province,” she said.

stories.title: Tessa Virtue, Sarah Nurse headline new YouTube shows
stories.summary: The Canadian Olympians are among the creators behind a new slate of shows launching on YouTube Canada
stories.author: Kaitlyn McGrath
stories.content:
Since retiring from competitive figure skating in 2019, Tessa Virtue has pursued academia, a career in the business world and mentored young athletes.

Now, the five-time Olympic medalist is venturing into another space: podcasting.

Virtuoso will appear exclusively on YouTube Canada and will see Virtue explore the pursuit of excellence, something the most decorated female figure skater in Olympic history knows a thing or two about.

The 37-year-old will interview a variety of guests, including athletes, artists, scientists and entrepreneurs about the experiences, habits and practical tools that shaped them. Virtue said she hopes listeners can apply some of the insights into their own career and lives.

“So much of my life as an athlete was spent actually honing kind of the mental skills and tools to perform under pressure on the world’s biggest stage. And that’s the thing that I think differentiates performers at a certain level,” she said on Thursday.

“I’m so interested in how people manage insecurities and doubt, how you put yourself out there (when) you’re vulnerable to scrutiny and criticism, how you pick yourself up after a failure and forge ahead and how you manage the expectations of success once you’ve achieved something.”

Virtue’s podcast, scheduled for release later this year, is a part of a new slate of creator-driven shows launching on YouTube Canada that includes reality and scripted series spanning topics such as entertainment, sports, food, comedy and lifestyle.

Seven years into retirement, Tessa Virtue and Scott Moir still share an Olympic bond

One of Virtue’s podcast guests is her former ice dancing partner Scott Moir, whom she skated with competitively for 22 years and won three Olympic gold medals with, including in 2010 and 2018. Virtue said interviewing her former partner was both easy and difficult because she knows so much about him.

“What I hope is that there’s some things that I can talk to Scott about that maybe no one else can. And so that’s one that’s close to my heart just because of how important a role that partnership plays in my life. And now as I’m venturing out into this new territory, it’s really nice to have the support of someone who’s lived those other big moments with me.”

Fellow Olympian and Professional Women’s Hockey League player Sarah Nurse is also introducing a reality series titled Sarah’s Side Quests . Slated for release next year, the show will see the Vancouver Goldeneyes forward learn new skills from experts in a variety of fields.

Nurse said she wants to be a lifelong learner and pursuing activities outside of hockey takes her out of her comfort zone, in a good way.

“It’s a way to showcase things that I’ve always been curious about, always had a love for, a passion for, but also a way to step outside my comfort zone and show people that not everything is perfect,” she said. “You don’t just pick things up super, super easily. A lot of times it takes a lot to master a craft or master something. But it also shouldn’t discourage you from just trying something new.”

Nicole Bell, head of YouTube Canada, said having projects from Virtue and Nurse is exciting given the growth of women’s sports in Canada.

“I just think audiences are going to love it. I feel it’s going be really powerful and (Sarah’s) just an incredible personality,” said Bell.

“Tessa is this person who we have all watched in these incredible moments of pure athleticism and being at the pinnacle of her sport. But she’s not someone whose voice we get to hear a lot,” Bell said. “She’s this person who I think is beloved by Canadians, and I think it’ll be really wonderful to hear her in this new perspective.”

stories.title: Woman killed in Summerside remembered as doting mom and friend
stories.summary: | CBC News | Posted: September 18, 2026 6:37 PM | Last Updated: September 18
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: | CBC News | Posted: September 18, 2026 6:37 PM | Last Updated: September 18
Mandeep Singh has been charged in the death of Raman Devi
Raman Devi was five months away from graduating from a registered massage therapy program, a course of studies she had thrown her whole heart into while raising her two young children.
“She was excited to be done [school] and to start her career,” said Devi's friend and neighbour, Sandra Sanchez.
“She was incredible. Kind, humble, caring, and always willing to help others if you have a problem. She was always there for you.”
Devi, who was in her 30s, died Tuesday evening after an incident at her home on Chelton Road in southeast London.
Her partner, Mandeep Singh, 41, has been charged with second-degree murder.
London police say the victim and accused were in an intimate relationship. Police have also said additional family members were at the home when the incident occurred, but none was injured.
Sanchez said Devi and Singh had two children, a four-year-old boy and a seven-year-old girl. Devi's mother was also staying with the family, having travelled from India to help care for the children.
“Raman was an amazing mother who gave everything for her children and her mom,” Sanchez said. “She loved her family deeply. Everything she did, it was for her family.”
Singh appeared in court Friday from the Elgin-Middlesex Detention Centre wearing an orange jumpsuit and requested the assistance of a Punjabi interpreter. His case was adjourned until Sept. 23.
Sanchez and Devi met about two years ago when they both began the massage therapy program at a private career college. They soon discovered they lived close to one another.
“It’s very heartbreaking and deeply unfair that something like this could happen to such a wonderful person,” Sanchez said.

Devi's son had started school for the first time the week before her death, Sanchez said. The two friends often spent time together in their neighbourhood, with Devi's children riding their bikes while Sanchez walked her dogs.
“We had a lot of laughs,” Sanchez said.
“She had a soft touch as a mom. Just last week, she talked to me about her youngest starting school, and she was emotional. I gave her a hug and told her it would be okay, and she gave me a smile.”
Sanchez has started a GoFundMe fundraiser to help support Devi's mother and children.
Police are investigating what they have described as a femicide and say they are examining the “historical context of the relationship.”

changed earlier this year to make certain killings of women first-degree murder , including an intimate-partner killing committed in the context of a pattern of coercive or controlling conduct. Most of those changes took effect July 18.
Singh has been charged with second-degree murder. The charge has not been upgraded to first-degree murder.
People who work with survivors of intimate-partner violence say violence can occur in any neighbourhood and that people may not always recognize what is happening behind closed doors.

“People don't want to believe that intimate partner violence can happen right next door to them, but it's unfortunately a reality that is absolutely very common,” said Jessie Rodger, executive director of Anova, an organization that supports survivors of gender-based violence in London.

“We know there are lots of people who need somewhere to go that aren't feeling safe enough to come forward. There's still a lot of shame and worry about coming forward, and a lot of risk in coming forward.”
Rodger said friends and neighbours can let people know they are safe to talk to by checking in with them or gently raising concerns about interactions that don't feel right.

stories.title: Expert insight: Planting trees in the wrong places is not a climate solution
stories.summary: Joy Kehinde Adebisi explains why planting trees in drylands can reduce water availability, harm biodiversity and undermine climate goals.
stories.author: Jacquelyn Mitchell
stories.content:
A recent United Nations report has stated the world will likely overshoot the 1.5 C target by 2030 set out in the 2015 Paris Climate Agreement.

Tree planting has become one of the most appealing symbols of climate action. It can be easily accounted for, visible and easy to communicate: more trees means more carbon being absorbed, a cooler planet. Everyone gets the point.

Global initiatives now promise restoration on a vast scale, including the Bonn Challenge goal of restoring 350 million hectares of degraded and deforested land by 2030.

But a tree is not automatically a climate solution, and land without dense tree cover is not necessarily degraded. When tree planting targets natural grasslands, shrublands and savannas, well-meaning efforts can replace one ecosystem with another, reduce water availability and threaten livelihoods.

In 2007, the African Union launched the Great Green Wall Initiative; a plan to stop southern expansion of the Sahara Desert by planting trees and restoring landscapes across 22 countries from Senegal to Djibouti. Yet, almost 20 years later, the initiative has had mixed results.

What truly works is simple: plant trees for restoration in the right ecosystems.

Drylands, including grasslands, shrublands and savannas, are often characterized by what they seem to lack: water, dense vegetation or agricultural potential. Yet they cover about 40 per cent of the Earth’s surface, support billions of people and play an important role in the year-to-year variability of the global carbon cycle – changes in the carbon absorbed and released from one year to the next.

Dryland ecosystems have evolved around low and highly variable rainfall, recurrent drought and disturbance. Native grasses, shrubs, scattered trees and biological soil crusts are not signs of an ecosystem needing restoration. They are parts of a functioning biome.

That distinction matters because global restoration targets can identify these naturally open ecosystems as candidates for tree cover. Ecologists have warned that planting trees to expand into old-growth grasslands and savannas can damage biodiversity and ecosystems rather than restore them. Planting trees May result in more woody cover, but the landscape itself May register ecological and diversity loss.

Firstly, trees use water. In some locations, appropriate native trees can provide shade, habitats, food and carbon storage. The problem is large-scale forestation that ignores the water balance.

Planting ill-suited trees in water-limited ecosystems can substantially reduce the volume of water flowing through rivers or streams and create a trade-off between carbon storage and water supply. The trade-off can affect groundwater levels, downstream ecosystems, farming and household water security.

Secondly, carbon is not the only component to bear in mind. Open vegetation and light-coloured soils often reflect more sunlight than a dark tree canopy. Converting them to forest lowers an area’s albedo – a measure of how much sunlight a surface reflects – and increases how much solar energy is absorbed.

Research shows that albedo change can offset a substantial share of the climate benefits expected from additional tree cover, with especially important consequences in some drylands. Counting tonnes of carbon while ignoring this biophysical effect can exaggerate the benefit of tree planting.

Farmer-managed natural regeneration can protect and manage native trees and shrubs that resprout from existing roots, stumps or seeds. In Niger, farmers’ regeneration of white acacia – a thorny tree native to parts of Africa and West Asia – and other useful species helped regreen approximately five million hectares without relying on mass seedling campaigns. Because farmers select and manage the regrowth, the approach can be adapted to crops, livestock and locally valued species.

In Burkina Faso, farmers have also revived and improved zaï, which entails planting pits that collect runoff and concentrate manure or compost around crops. Research on soil and water conservation shows how zaï and related practices can rehabilitate degraded land and improve production under difficult rainfall conditions. Here, restoration is not defined as making the landscape look like a forest. It is defined by recovering soil function, vegetation and livelihoods.

Other places May require protecting native grass cover, managing grazing pressure, restoring seasonal mobility, controlling invasive species, conserving biological soil crusts or assisting the recovery of locally appropriate shrubs and trees. No single technique works for all; you just need to do what works for your situation. That is precisely the point.

Tree planting can be valuable in deforested ecosystems and where locally appropriate species, water availability, land tenure and long-term ownership align. Growing trees alongside agricultural crops or livestock and allowing plants to naturally regenerate can also be effective in dryland farms. The mistake is turning those successes into a universal rule that equates more trees with a better climate.

Governments and donors should ask whether a project restores the natural ecosystem, protects water and retains native biodiversity before campaigning for tree planting.

Drylands are not failed landscapes. They are distinctive ecosystems that store carbon, sustain biodiversity and support people. We must not force forests where they do not belong and need to start valuing the life already adapted to thrive there.Image 1: The Conversation

Joy Kehinde Adebisi, PhD Student, Geography and Environment, Western University

That distinction matters because global restoration targets can identify these naturally open ecosystems as candidates for tree cover. Ecologists have warned that planting trees to expand into old-growth grasslands and savannas can damage biodiversity and ecosystems rather than restore them. Planting trees May result in more woody cover, but the landscape itself May register ecological and diversity loss.
Firstly, trees use water. In some locations, appropriate native trees can provide shade, habitats, food and carbon storage. The problem is large-scale forestation that ignores the water balance.

Planting ill-suited trees in water-limited ecosystems can substantially reduce the volume of water flowing through rivers or streams and create a trade-off between carbon storage and water supply. The trade-off can affect groundwater levels, downstream ecosystems, farming and household water security.

Secondly, carbon is not the only component to bear in mind. Open vegetation and light-coloured soils often reflect more sunlight than a dark tree canopy. Converting them to forest lowers an area’s albedo – a measure of how much sunlight a surface reflects – and increases how much solar energy is absorbed.

Research shows that albedo change can offset a substantial share of the climate benefits expected from additional tree cover, with especially important consequences in some drylands. Counting tonnes of carbon while ignoring this biophysical effect can exaggerate the benefit of tree planting.

Farmer-managed natural regeneration can protect and manage native trees and shrubs that resprout from existing roots, stumps or seeds. In Niger, farmers’ regeneration of white acacia – a thorny tree native to parts of Africa and West Asia – and other useful species helped regreen approximately five million hectares without relying on mass seedling campaigns. Because farmers select and manage the regrowth, the approach can be adapted to crops, livestock and locally valued species.

In Burkina Faso, farmers have also revived and improved zaï, which entails planting pits that collect runoff and concentrate manure or compost around crops. Research on soil and water conservation shows how zaï and related practices can rehabilitate degraded land and improve production under difficult rainfall conditions. Other places May require protecting native grass cover, managing grazing pressure, restoring seasonal mobility, controlling invasive species, conserving biological soil crusts or assisting the recovery of locally appropriate shrubs and trees. No single technique works for all; you just need to do what works for your situation. That is precisely the point.

Tree planting can be valuable in deforested ecosystems and where locally appropriate species, water availability, land tenure and long-term ownership align. Growing trees alongside agricultural crops or livestock and allowing plants to naturally regenerate can also be effective in dryland farms. The mistake is turning those successes into a universal rule that equates more trees with a better climate.
Governments and donors should ask whether a project restores the natural ecosystem, protects water and retains native biodiversity before campaigning for tree planting.

Drylands are not failed landscapes. They are distinctive ecosystems that store carbon, sustain biodiversity and support people. We must not force forests where they do not belong and need to start valuing the life already adapted to thrive there.Image 1: The Conversation

stories.title: B.C. Conservatives lose 10th MLA since August as Claire Rattée exits caucus
stories.summary: Rattée’s exit marks the latest blow to leader Kerry-Lynne Findlay’s party
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The British Columbia Conservative Party has lost another caucus member, with Claire Rattée becoming the 10th to leave since August.

Rattée says in a statement that party leader Kerry-Lynne Findlay is trying to “oust members of her own caucus” and must resign immediately.

The MLA for Skeena says it’s an example of poor judgment by Findlay that doesn’t befit someone who wants to become premier.

B.C. Conservative leader vows to stay as allegations emerge party funds were used to spy on critics

Rattée says at least 10 Conservatives have signed a letter calling on Findlay to quit.

The office of the clerk confirms Rattée is no longer a member of the official Opposition caucus, while the number of Independents in the legislature has gone up to 15.

Findlay said Thursday that she wasn’t leaving the helm amid speculation that Premier David Eby could call an early election at any time.

stories.title: World Cup brought uneven boost to Vancouver, Toronto neighbourhoods, data show
stories.summary: Handful of areas benefited, while many other were left worse off during tournament
stories.author: Andrea Woo
stories.content:
The 2026 World Cup drew huge crowds of Canadians to a handful of Vancouver and Toronto neighbourhoods, but left some districts with fewer visitors than usual.

New data from Toronto-based analytics company Environics Analytics, provided exclusively to The Globe and Mail, show how unevenly foot traffic was distributed in each city, bolstering reports from businesses that the tournament’s economic boost did not reach every commercial district even as governments touted broader long-term benefits.

“It was a bit of a non-event,” said Neil Wyles, executive director of Vancouver’s Mount Pleasant Business Improvement Association. Its members include the many retail shops, bars and restaurants in the trendy neighbourhood just a few kilometres from BC Place stadium, where matches were held.

“On game days, you might have seen a bit of a bump, but over the longer arc of the months no one was knocking it out of the park in Mount Pleasant.”

Canada, the United States and Mexico co-hosted the largest-ever edition of the World Cup between June 11 and July 19. Vancouver hosted seven matches and Toronto six.

In Vancouver, Yaletown saw the biggest boon, with average daily visits during the World Cup period up 18.2 per cent from the weeks before the tournament. On days that Vancouver hosted matches, visits surged 63.3 per cent.

Vancouver’s World Cup pitch finds new life beyond BC Place

Yet nearby neighbourhoods saw traffic move in the opposite direction. Compared with pretournament levels, average daily visits fell 12.7 per cent in Strathcona, 9.4 per cent in Mount Pleasant and 3.2 per cent in the West End during the World Cup. On match days, the declines were even steeper, at 15.3 per cent, 9.9 per cent and 11.4 per cent, respectively.

Environics Analytics’ MobileScapes database estimates foot traffic using cellular network signals with personal identifiers removed and calibrated to represent the Canadian population aged 15 and older

The estimates do not capture international visitors or other foot traffic originating from outside Canada’s resident population, an important limitation during a tournament that drew soccer fans from around the world. The exclusion May therefore understate the tournament’s impact in areas such as downtown Vancouver, an entertainment district where measured visits rose just 3.8 per cent overall and 8 per cent on game days, despite it being packed throughout the tournament.

Mr. Wyles said the findings for Mount Pleasant are not surprising, given that Vancouver’s World Cup festivities were concentrated in the downtown core. Warnings of traffic congestion and street closures also deterred some visitors, as they did when Vancouver hosted the 2010 Winter Olympics, he said.

As a BIA representing a neighbourhood with residential, commercial and light industrial properties – but no hotels – the association focused on appealing to locals, Mr. Wyles said. He also suspects that the high cost of hotels downtown during the games kept out-of-town visitors from taking more time to explore the broader city.

Meanwhile, Yaletown’s visitor surge was not left to chance. Sarah Vallely, executive director of that neighbourhood’s BIA, said the group actively sought to parlay its proximity to BC Place into longer visits by installing mini soccer pitches, murals and other programming. Local businesses also leaned into the effort with watch parties and transformed patio spaces.

“The biggest takeaway for us is probably that with these major events, you have to embrace them,” Ms. Vallely said.

“There will always be disruption, but if you give people a reason to spend time in the neighbourhood rather than just walk through it on their way to the stadium, there can be a really meaningful benefit for local businesses.”

World Cup delivered a tourism blip to Canada in June, early numbers show

Toronto saw a similar concentration of activity. Average daily visits to Liberty Village, adjacent to BMO Field at Exhibition Place, increased by 9.7 per cent during the tournament and 57.9 per cent on days the city hosted matches at the stadium. CityPlace and Fort York, which was home to the city’s official fan festival, recorded a 13.1 per cent increase across the tournament and a 37.6 per cent increase on game days.

Giovanny Restrepo, a spokesperson for the Little Portugal Toronto BIA, said benefits were uneven within the neighbourhood, with increased activity at the more than 18 bars, restaurants and venues that showed matches or hosted World Cup programming, but not at other businesses.

Similar to Mr. Wyles in Vancouver, Mr. Restrepo said messaging from the city and the media that emphasized road closures, overcrowding and difficulties getting downtown – while legitimate considerations – May have discouraged people from visiting the area. Recently implemented parking restrictions are also believed to have negatively impacted businesses, he said.

For future mega-events, Mr. Restrepo said better co-ordination and communication with the city and other stakeholders could create a broader economic benefit.

“Visitors should be given clear information about how to get around, where they can park, which neighbourhoods remain accessible and, importantly, reasons to actually explore the city’s many neighbourhoods and local businesses.”

Opinion: The World Cup shows that Toronto can think big. This can be its next bold bet

Beyond visitor numbers, Environics Analytics also profiled the types of communities that people came from by linking its mobility data to its Prizm segmentation system, which groups Canadian neighbourhoods based on shared demographic, socio-economic and lifestyle characteristics.

In both cities, the biggest increases came from multicultural communities outside the neighbourhoods where World Cup festivities were concentrated, according to the Prizm data.

In Vancouver, the groups that contributed most to Yaletown’s surge in visitors were associated with neighbourhoods with large Asian populations, including financially secure families on the urban fringe, younger and middle-aged South Asian families and younger, university-educated singles and couples of Asian descent.

In Toronto, much of the increased traffic into Liberty Village was associated with culturally diverse, middle-income neighbourhoods, including urban-fringe communities with younger and middle-aged families.

The Globe and Mail reported in July that, despite weeks of packed bars and restaurants and persistent fears of hotel-room shortages, data suggest the marquee soccer tournament did not amount to a major economic boost.

Figures from digital payment processing giant Moneris, which handles one in three transactions in Canada, show that from June 12 to 26 total spending at Toronto bars and restaurants was up just 3 per cent over the same period last year. Spending by international visitors, however – measured using foreign-issued credit and debit cards – was up 34 per cent at those same bars and restaurants. Total spending at Vancouver restaurants and bars, and total foreign spending, each increased by 6 per cent.

stories.title: Crtc approves Corus’s recapitalization plan
stories.summary: Commission says plan helps ensure company remains part of the Canadian broadcasting industry
stories.author: Daniel Johnson
stories.content:
Struggling media company Corus Entertainment Inc. CJR-B-T has received a lifeline.

The Canadian Radio-television and Telecommunications Commission on Thursday granted regulatory approval for a recapitalization plan that would see a change in ownership and shift effective control of all licensed programming services operated by the company and its subsidiaries.

Corus had indicated to the Crtc that the proposed deal is necessary to address its high debt load and improve its financial stability so it could continue to operate.

In a summary of the Crtc’s decision, the regulator said Corus is facing “significant financial challenges” from both broader industry pressures and its capital structure.

“The commission notes that the severity of those challenges threatens the continued viability of Corus’s operations and risks the loss of a key contributor to the Canadian broadcasting system,” the summary reads.

The Crtc said that in its view, the proposed transaction will help ensure the company remains part of the Canadian broadcasting industry.

“The commission notes that news services across Canada continue to face significant pressures, and considers that the continued availability of Corus’s news and information services – including those provided through its radio stations – serves the public interest,” the summary reads.

Corus lenders revisit a well-worn restructuring path

Corus owns 25 specialty television services and 15 conventional stations, 36 radio stations, as well as digital and streaming platforms.

In August, the company made cuts to its TV and radio operations, saying at the time the changes were difficult but necessary to ensure its teams are structured in a sustainable way, while minimizing disruption to local news and audio delivery. The company said the changes included jobs at Global BC, Global National, News 640 and talk radio.

Under the recapitalization proposal, first announced in November, some of Corus’s lenders would forgive approximately $500-million in debt in exchange for 99-per-cent ownership of a newly created parent corporation, called NewCo, that would wholly own Corus and its services.

Existing Corus shareholders would be expected to swap their holdings for shares that together would represent the remaining one per cent of the new company.

Corus said its business is expected to continue as normal with no anticipated effect on its obligations to clients, producers, suppliers or employees.

The reprieve comes amid significant financial struggles for Corus, which last month reported a net loss attributable to shareholders of $36.5 million in its third quarter, as its revenue for the period fell 16 per cent compared with last year.

The company announced in February it would seek court approval for the recapitalization deal that after a shareholder vote on the proposal failed to pass.

In March, Corus received an order from the Ontario Superior Court of Justice to proceed with its recapitalization plan.

The company said it expects the recapitalization transaction to close in the coming weeks, pending other conditions and customary approvals.
paragraphs: Struggling media company Corus Entertainment Inc. CJR-B-T has received a lifeline.

The Canadian Radio-television and Telecommunications Commission on Thursday granted regulatory approval for a recapitalization plan that would see a change in ownership and shift effective control of all licensed programming services operated by the company and its subsidiaries.
Corus had indicated to the Crtc that the proposed deal is necessary to address its high debt load and improve its financial stability so it could continue to operate.
In a summary of the Crtc’s decision, the regulator said Corus is facing “significant financial challenges” from both broader industry pressures and its capital structure.

“The commission notes that the severity of those challenges threatens the continued viability of Corus’s operations and risks the loss of a key contributor to the Canadian broadcasting system,” the summary reads.
The Crtc said that in its view, the proposed transaction will help ensure the company remains part of the Canadian broadcasting industry.

“The commission notes that news services across Canada continue to face significant pressures, and considers that the continued availability of Corus’s news and information services – including those provided through its radio stations – serves the public interest,” the summary reads.
Corus lenders revisit a well-worn restructuring path
Corus owns 25 specialty television services and 15 conventional stations, 36 radio stations, as well as digital and streaming platforms.

In August, the company made cuts to its TV and radio operations, saying at the time the changes were difficult but necessary to ensure its teams are structured in a sustainable way, while minimizing disruption to local news and audio delivery. The company said the changes included jobs at Global BC, Global National, News 640 and talk radio.

Under the recapitalization proposal, first announced in November, some of Corus’s lenders would forgive approximately $500-million in debt in exchange for 99-per-cent ownership of a newly created parent corporation, called NewCo, that would wholly own Corus and its services.
Existing Corus shareholders would be expected to swap their holdings for shares that together would represent the remaining one per cent of the new company.
Corus said its business is expected to continue as normal with no anticipated effect on its obligations to clients, producers, suppliers or employees.

The reprieve comes amid significant financial struggles for Corus, which last month reported a net loss attributable to shareholders of $36.5 million in its third quarter, as its revenue for the period fell 16 per cent compared with last year.
The company announced in February it would seek court approval for the recapitalization deal that after a shareholder vote on the proposal failed to pass.
In March, Corus received an order from the Ontario Superior Court of Justice to proceed with its recapitalization plan.
The company said it expects the recapitalization transaction to close in the coming weeks, pending other conditions and customary approvals.

stories.title: In polarized times, Ford and Chow have an unusual partnership
stories.summary: Doug Ford and Oliva Chow have found a way to work together despite their differences
stories.author: Marcus Gee
stories.content:
In background and politics, Ontario Premier Doug Ford and Toronto Mayor Olivia Chow are about as different as two people could be. And yet they have found a way to get along and to work together.

“The mayor and I have a phenomenal relationship, phenomenal,” Mr. Ford said when the two appeared at a news conference this week. He was responding to a reporter who asked him where he stood on the coming municipal vote in Toronto. Ms. Chow is running for re-election on Oct. 26 against two main competitors: Brad Bradford and Chris Alexander . “We’re going to continue supporting the mayor, so read between the lines,” the Premier replied.

Though (as the Premier’s office felt compelled to point out later) it fell short of an official endorsement, the remark was the latest evidence of the unusual partnership between the two, a rare example of cross-party co-operation in polarized times.

Ford’s praise of Chow was not an endorsement, his office says

Mr. Ford and Ms. Chow have intertwined histories. When Mr. Ford’s younger brother Rob was elected to Toronto city council in 2000, Ms. Chow and her husband Jack Layton were his fellow councillors. Mr. Layton had a seat next to him and took him under his wing.

Rob appreciated the kindness and spoke of it when Mr. Layton, then the popular head of the federal NDP, died of cancer in 2011 (a fate that Rob himself would suffer five years later). He said Mr. Layton told him to look for votes on both sides of the council divide. “He taught me never to take things personal,” he recalled.

Doug Ford jumped into the 2014 race for mayor after his brother fell ill. He found himself running against Ms. Chow. The two of them ended up coming second (Mr. Ford) and third (Ms. Chow) to John Tory. In 2023, Ms. Chow ran for mayor ran again in a special by-election triggered by the resignation of Mr. Tory over an affair with a much younger staffer.

Mr. Ford, by then Premier, said then that a Chow mayoralty would be an “unmitigated disaster,” nothing less. “God forbid Olivia Chow gets elected – your taxes are going up at an unprecedented rate,” he said. “Companies will leave.” He backed one of her rivals, former police chief Mark Saunders.

As soon as she was elected, though, he struck a different note. The two had a meeting the day after the vote and the Premier said all the trash talk was just something that happens during election campaigns. “We’re going to find common ground when we sit down because she’s actually quite a nice person,” he said.

It hasn’t been all sunshine and roses since then. The two have clashed over his plans to put a waterpark and spa at Ontario Place on the waterfront, his decision to rip out some downtown bike lanes and his desire to expand the Billy Bishop airport on Toronto Island to accommodate jet planes.

Editorial Board: Doug Ford should (also) stay in his lane

But Ms. Chow has had the sense to pick her battles, acknowledging the fact that Mr. Ford leads the senior government and that Toronto depends heavily on Queen’s Park for funding and approvals. There is a reason, she said, practically, that Ontario Place is called Ontario Place. The provincial government created and controls it.

Mr. Ford, ON his side, has done a lot to help Toronto pay its bills. Under a “new deal” between the city and the province, Mr. Ford agreed to take over the Gardiner Expressway and Don Valley Parkway and assume billions in city costs. As he put it, in classic Fordian terms, this week, “we’ve given the city of Toronto more money than they’ve ever seen in their lives.”

Of course, politicians often put on a show of bonhomie after fighting like alley cats behind closed doors. Mr. Ford and Ms. Chow May be cursing each other silently as they smile for the cameras.

It doesn’t matter in the end. They both care a lot about Toronto. Despite their different political views, they both want a lot of the same things: better roads, better transit, cleaner streets, more housing.

Their partnership is working – even if they sometimes vehemently disagree. When city council voted earlier this year to explore the idea of creating not-for-profit, city-run grocery stores, Mr. Ford went off.

“She wants city-run grocery stores? You’d be subsidizing it huge, because it’s just, it’s crazy. That’s socialism.”

“I love you, mayor,” he added.

stories.title: Conservative MP Larry Brock officially resigns from House of Commons
stories.summary: Conservative Larry Brock says he has resigned from the House of Commons, ending five years as the MP for Brantford-Brant South.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Conservative Larry Brock says he has resigned from the House of Commons, ending five years as the MP for Brantford-Brant South.

Brock announced his plans to step down last month , saying he planned to return to the office of the Crown prosecutor.

A byelection will be called in the Ontario riding, along with five others that are currently vacant, in the coming months.

Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre is planning to hold a rally in Brantford on the weekend.

Brock is the sixth MP to leave Poilievre’s caucus over the past year.

Four members defected to the Liberal government and Richard Martel joined the Senate this summer.

stories.title: Snowbird replacements ‘extremely manoeuvrable, powerful,’ Rcaf commander says
stories.summary: The Royal Canadian Air Force welcomed its new trainer aircraft, the CT-157 Siskin II, which will replace the old Tutor jets flown by the Snowbirds aerial demonstration team.
stories.author: Kyle Duggan
stories.content:
The Royal Canadian Air Force welcomed on Thursday the first two of its new trainer aircraft, the CT-157 Siskin II — the same planes that will replace the old Tutor jets flown by the Snowbirds aerial demonstration team.

The turboprop planes will soon be headed to 15 Wing Moose Jaw, where the air force eventually will station 19 of them to serve as its main training fleet.

Acquiring the Siskin II, also known as the Pilatus PC-21, is part of the Rcaf’s plan to modernize its fleets and overhaul its training.

Rcaf Commander Lt.-Gen. Jamie Speiser-Blanchet said the modern aircraft are well suited both to aerial acrobatics and to preparing pilots for the more advanced aircraft the air force is bringing online.

“It has an advanced cockpit and capabilities and the design is just a very contemporary one that is used by other allies as well. We’re very excited that we’re able to bring this on board,” she said.

The commander made the comments just after one of the new planes buzzed overhead in a ceremonial first flypast at the airport in Gatineau, Que.

The current Snowbirds will hold their last show in the National Capital Region in Gatineau, Que., this weekend. After their final flight at the Grey Cup in Calgary in November, the Snowbird team will start a hiatus that could last until 2030.

As the Rcaf brings in the new planes for pilot training, the federal government is still working on procuring extra Siskins for the Snowbirds team.

Speiser-Blanchet said these are “excellent” stunt planes that shouldn’t be underestimated — even though some have questioned whether a propeller aircraft is a suitable replacement for jets.

“It is extremely manoeuvrable and capable, and powerful, actually. More so than perhaps people’s understanding of other propeller aircraft from the past,” she said.

While the Siskin II has a slower top speed than the CT-114 Tutor and is not as loud as a jet, Speiser-Blanchet said “it’s not a quiet aircraft” and it will “really wow Canadians” once the shows are up and running.

The federal government announced this spring it would replace the roughly 60-year-old Tutor jets, which have encountered various problems with upgrades meant to extend their lifespans out to 2030. Costs, timelines and the growing scarcity of replacement parts threw a wrench into plans to keep them in the air longer.

The Swiss Air Force has been training its pilots on the Pilatus aircraft since about 2008, and Australia’s Roulettes aerial demonstration team also flies the same planes.

Speiser-Blanchet said that because so many Canadian pilots will be training on this aircraft, the air force will have a much larger pool of potential candidates for the Snowbirds. Having the multi-purpose aircraft based out of Moose Jaw will also make servicing and support easier to manage, she said.

The Rcaf has never before used a Pilatus aircraft. The new planes will replace the air force’s CT-156 Harvard II trainers, also known as the T-6 Beechcraft.

Ioannis Papachristofilou, deputy CEO of Pilatus in Switzerland, said the aircraft are advanced, high-performance machines that use Pratt and Whitney’s powerful PT6A-68B turboprop engine, which is made in Canada.

“This aircraft has an embedded mission-simulation suite, which allows you to simulate, for example, sensors like radar,” he said, adding the technology allows pilots to train faster on fighter jets in later phases of training.

The fleet of Siskins will work alongside other types of trainers under the new Future Aircrew Training program, which covers 71 training aircraft split up across five fleets.

SkyAlyne, a partnership between CAE and KF Aerospace, won a contract in 2024 for the 25-year, $11-billion training program, referred to within the air force as FAcT. It will replace the commercial pilot training aspects of the Rcaf program.

The fleet of Siskins will work alongside other types of trainers under the new Future Aircrew Training program, which covers 71 training aircraft split up across five fleets.

SkyAlyne, a partnership between CAE and KF Aerospace, won a contract in 2024 for the 25-year, $11-billion training program, referred to within the air force as FAcT. It will replace the commercial pilot training aspects of the Rcaf program.

The turboprop planes will soon be headed to 15 Wing Moose Jaw, where the air force eventually will station 19 of them to serve as its main training fleet.
Acquiring the Siskin II, also known as the Pilatus PC-21, is part of the Rcaf’s plan to modernize its fleets and overhaul its training.

Rcaf Commander Lt.-Gen. Jamie Speiser-Blanchet said the modern aircraft are well suited both to aerial acrobatics and to preparing pilots for the more advanced aircraft the air force is bringing online.
“It has an advanced cockpit and capabilities and the design is just a very contemporary one that is used by other allies as well. We’re very excited that we’re able to bring this on board,” she said.
The commander made the comments just after one of the new planes buzzed overhead in a ceremonial first flypast at the airport in Gatineau, Que.

As the Rcaf brings in the new planes for pilot training, the federal government is still working on procuring extra Siskins for the Snowbirds team.
Speiser-Blanchet said these are “excellent” stunt planes that shouldn’t be underestimated — even though some have questioned whether a propeller aircraft is a suitable replacement for jets.
“It is extremely manoeuvrable and capable, and powerful, actually. More so than perhaps people’s understanding of other propeller aircraft from the past,” she said.

stories.title: St. Thomas residents, councillors push for greenspace in railway lands development
stories.summary: Plans are slowly taking shape for what could be a new community within a community in downtown St. Thomas.
stories.author: Bryan Bicknell
stories.content:
Plans are slowly taking shape for what could be a new community within a community in downtown St. Thomas.

But many residents have ideas of their own as to what they’d like to see happen with the railway lands south of Talbot Street.

“I would love to see greenspace. The city is growing. It’s got like, 40,000 people, and we need as much greenspace as we can get,” said David Van Pelt.

“I’d like to see some parks come in here, some affordable housing. Nothing like the $2,000, $3,000 dollar apartments that they’re building in corners of the city. A dog park would be nice, and more centrally located. We also need a centrally located high school,” said resident Tasha Reid.

“I’m just looking for it to be developed into really nice parkland for families,” said resident Andrew Knowlton.

This week, St. Thomas council had a look at the Railway Lands Area Master Plan Preliminary Concepts.

The former rail lands downtown between Talbot and Wellington streets behind the Caso Station are being proposed for mixed use residential and commercial development.

Some councillors are pushing for an abundance of parkland at the site, including Coun. Joan Rymal.

“It’s a wonderful opportunity to have this downtown space central to downtown,” said Rymal at the Monday council meeting. “There’s so many things that could happen. I’m just thinking of, you know, Harris Park in London, where they have Rock the Park. You could have Rock the Rails, and have a wonderful concert venue there,” she suggested.

Concept 1 for the Railway Lands is Status Quo with Moderate Intensification, including up to 1,325 housing units.

Concept 2 is High Mixed Use and Connectivity Scenario with up to 3,550 units.

And Concept 3 is Hybrid Intensification Scenario with up to 1,325 units.

St. Thomas Mayor Joe Preston says while council can guide the project, ultimately it will be up to private landowners as to what they do with the property.

“So, are we going back to the owner of the land and buying it back to make our parks? You’re asking a developer just to develop a park. There’s no income there,” he told CTV News.

Developing the brownfield site is no easy or inexpensive task. According to the mayor, remediation will cost millions of dollars per hectare- which would be picked up by both property owners and taxpayers.

“I frown a little bit about how the railways left our community in a contaminated state that we now have to deal with,” said Mayor Preston.

“When it’s costing us millions of dollars to repair what they left us, then that will also contribute to how much we can do,” he added.

Preston expects council will approve necessary zoning changes in 2027. In the meantime, public meetings are being planned for November.

The mayor is also encouraging people to share their views on the project through the Speak Up St. Thomas web page .

stories.title: Ford says glowing comments about Chow were not an endorsement
stories.summary: Ford was asked about work on a new funding deal for Toronto and whether he'd be endorsing anyone in the Toronto election.
stories.author: Isaac Callan, Colin D'Mello
stories.content:
Ontario Premier Doug Ford is walking away from his near-endorsement of Olivia Chow in Toronto’s mayoral race, saying his glowing words earlier this week were misinterpreted.

Ford was asked about work on a new funding deal for Toronto and whether he’d be endorsing anyone in the Toronto election.

“The mayor and I have a phenomenal relationship, phenomenal,” he told reporters.

“We’ve given the City of Toronto more money than they’ve ever seen in their lives — over $9 billion. We’re going to continue supporting the mayor. She’s doing an incredible job, so read between the lines.”

The glowing words were interpreted by Brad Bradford, Chow’s closet rival in the race, as an endorsement.

“Of course the premier endorsed Olivia Chow,” his team wrote in a news release immediately afterwards. “She is the easiest negotiation he has ever had. Everything she told Torontonians she would fight and oppose, she handed over on a silver platter.”

The premier’s office was silent on the issue for more than a day, suddenly issuing a statement to clarify that Ford hadn’t endorsed Chow some 30 hours after he made the comments.

“We would like to clarify that Premier Ford did not endorse Olivia Chow and will not endorse any candidate in the Toronto mayoral race,” Ford’s office wrote in a 6:30 p.m. statement on Thursday.

“The premier has demonstrated that he will work with anyone no matter their political stripe to advance the interests of the people of Ontario.”

stories.title: Ontario Conservative MP Larry Brock formally resigns from House of Commons
stories.summary: MP for Brantford-Brant South announced his plans to step down last month, saying he planned to return to the office of the Crown prosecutor
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Conservative Larry Brock says he has resigned from the House of Commons, ending five years as the MP for Brantford-Brant South.

Brock announced his plans to step down last month , saying he planned to return to the office of the Crown prosecutor.

A by-election will be called in the Ontario riding, along with five others that are currently vacant, in the coming months.

Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre is planning to hold a rally in Brantford on the weekend.

Brock is the sixth MP to leave Poilievre’s caucus over the past year.

Four members defected to the Liberal government and Richard Martel joined the Senate this summer.

stories.title: Canadian dollar extends weekly decline, weighed by wider yield spreads
stories.summary: Currency is on course for its eighth straight ​daily decline
stories.author: Fergal Smith
stories.content:
The Canadian dollar added to its weekly ​decline against its U.S. counterpart ‌on Friday as recent widening of the gap between U.S. and Canadian bond yields weighed on the loonie.

The loonie was trading 0.1 per cent ⁠lower ​at 1.4010 per U.S. dollar, or 71.38 U.S. cents, after touching its weakest intraday level since August 7 at 1.40144. It left the currency on course for its eighth straight ​daily decline, which would be the longest ‌such streak since May.

For the week, the currency was down 1 per cent, as the Federal Reserve hiked interest rates and flagged further increases in borrowing costs in coming months.

“Wider front-end U.S.-Canada yield ‌spreads account ​for much of the ‌Cad’s slippage over the past few days, according to ​our correlation matrix,” Shaun Osborne and Eric Theoret, strategists ⁠at Scotiabank, said in a note.

The Canadian ⁠2-year yield was trading about 142 basis points below the U.S. equivalent, ​marking the widest gap since July 28.

The U.S. dollar rose on Friday against a basket of major currencies, including the yen, after two policy makers at the Bank of Japan dissented from a widely expected decision ⁠to raise interest rates.

U.S. crude oil futures were trading 0.5 per cent higher at US$102.43 a barrel as markets assessed Saudi supply alongside concerns about a widening Middle East conflict. Oil is one of Canada’s major exports.

Bank of Canada Governor ⁠Tiff Macklem is due to speak ​on Monday on economic developments.

“His comments May reaffirm the hawkish ⁠tone adopted following the Bank’s meeting earlier this month,” the Scotiabank strategists said.

Investors see ‌a roughly 60-per-cent chance the BoC would hike at its next policy ​announcement on October 28.

Canadian bond yields rose across the curve, tracking moves in U.S. Treasuries.

* The 10-year was up 5.5 basis points at 3.878 per cent but remained below ​the nearly 3-year high touched on Monday at 3.987 per cent.

The U.S. dollar rose on Friday against a basket of major currencies, including the yen, after two policy makers at the Bank of Japan dissented from a widely expected decision ⁠to raise interest rates.

U.S. crude oil futures were trading 0.5 per cent higher at US$102.43 a barrel as markets assessed Saudi supply alongside concerns about a widening Middle East conflict. Oil is one of Canada’s major exports.
Bank of Canada Governor ⁠Tiff Macklem is due to speak ​on Monday on economic developments.
“His comments May reaffirm the hawkish ⁠tone adopted following the Bank’s meeting earlier this month,” the Scotiabank strategists said.
Investors see ‌a roughly 60-per-cent chance the BoC would hike at its next policy ​announcement on October 28.
Canadian bond yields rose across the curve, tracking moves in U.S. Treasuries.

stories.title: Sarnia police seize more than $300,000 in drugs, charge local man
stories.summary: Police say more than $300,000 worth of illegal drugs have been seized in Sarnia this week, resulting in charges against a 42-year-old man.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
Police say more than $300,000 worth of illegal drugs have been seized in Sarnia this week, resulting in charges against a 42-year-old man.

Police said the operation led to the seizure of approximately four kilograms of crystal methamphetamine, one kilogram of cocaine, prescription hydromorphone pills in various strengths and 120 oxycodone tablets.

Investigators estimate the street value of the seized controlled substances at more than $300,000.

Officers also seized drug trafficking paraphernalia, including scales and packaging materials, along with $151,452 Canadian and $94 US in cash.

A 42-year-old Sarnia man was arrested and charged with possession of cocaine for the purpose of trafficking, possession of methamphetamine for the purpose of trafficking, possession of oxycodone for the purpose of trafficking, possession of hydromorphone and possession of proceeds of crime over $5,000.

The accused has appeared before the courts and the charges have not been proven in court. Police said the investigation remains ongoing.

stories.title: Pitching in: Friends retrace Toronto subway line on foot, raising money for unhoused people
stories.summary: Amanda Gracia and Samantha Ruth have walked along portions of the TTC, discovering the city while supporting Out of the Cold
stories.author: Paul Waldie
stories.content:
The organizers: Samantha Ruth and Amanda Gracia

The pitch: Raising $2,800 and climbing

The cause: Out of the Cold

A couple of years ago, Amanda Gracia came across a social-media post about someone who had walked from Union to Finch station along Toronto’s Yonge-University subway line.

She wanted to try the walk for herself and turned to her friend Samantha Ruth. “I asked Sam, ‘Hey, do you want to do this thing with me?’ Because we both like walking and we thought, well, there’s really nothing better to do anyway.”

So, last year they walked from Finch to Union station, a roughly 16-kilometre route that took them about seven hours. They enjoyed the walk so much they decided to make it an annual tradition. “We thought, ‘Okay, we did half of Line 1 last year. Maybe we’ll do Line 2 this year,’” recalled Ms. Gracia, a 23-year old dietician. “I don’t know, weird idea, but it was a lot of fun.”

This summer they set out from Kennedy station and walked to Kipling, a distance of 30 kilometres in total. Along with walking, the pair raised money for Out of the Cold, a Toronto-based charity that provides a range of services for unhoused people. Ms. Ruth, 26, has been volunteering with the organization for the past year.

“I’ve gotten to know that community really well. I’ve gotten to talk to people and see what they need in terms of food and housing,” she said. “And with the food costs rising and the amount of people who are using food banks increasing, I thought it would be a good idea to raise money for more hot meals for people in the city.”

The walk was a challenge, but it also gave the friends a different view of the city. They stopped in a variety of ethnic neighbourhoods and discovered new enclaves. “The walk just really reminded me of how diverse Toronto is and how beautiful it is,” Ms. Ruth said.

They’ve raised $2,800 so far and both have been humbled by the support and encouragement they’ve received. “We’re really proud that we’re able to do something for our neighbours and our community,” Ms. Gracia said.

They’ve already started thinking about next year’s walk and they’re considering Line 3, which has been closed, or the Ontario line. “We don’t really have a strict plan yet,” Ms. Gracia added. “We kind of just see where the summer takes us.”

stories.title: Canada and the EU want an energy alliance. What would it look like?
stories.summary: Prime Minister Mark Carney was in Strasbourg, France, this week where he and European Union leadership discussed strengthening ties on several fronts.
stories.author: Lauren Krugel
stories.content:
Canada has the potential to bolster Europe’s energy security through a new alliance, but experts say it doesn’t necessarily mean tankers crossing the Atlantic Ocean laden with oil or liquefied natural gas.

Prime Minister Mark Carney was in Strasbourg, France, this week where he and European Union leadership discussed strengthening ties on several fronts amid strained relations with the United States.

Werner Antweiler, an economist at the University of British Columbia, says Europe is in a “precarious situation” as it aims to pivot away from Russian energy imports following that country’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

Canada has pipelines and port infrastructure to export oil and gas from the West Coast to Asia, but no such option exists in the east, and any such project could take a decade or more to come to fruition.

In the meantime, Antweiler says European companies have the ability to secure a stable gas supply from Canada through what’s known as swap contracts, where a cargo headed for Asia, for instance, could be traded with another one bound for its shores.

Rachel Doran, executive director at Clean Energy Canada, sees a promising opportunity to supply critical minerals to Europe, helping it transition away from fossil fuels and grow its clean power supply.

stories.title: Man charged after alleged machete threats in Owen Sound
stories.summary: The Owen Sound Police Service says officers responded to a report of a man threatening individuals with a machete near 9th Street West and 1st Avenue West at about 11 p.m. on Sept. 17.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
A 63-year-old Wiarton man is facing several charges after police say he threatened people with a machete in Owen Sound late Thursday night.

The Owen Sound Police Service says officers responded to a report of a man threatening individuals with a machete near 9th Street West and 1st Avenue West at about 11 p.m. on Sept. 17.

Police said officers arrived within a minute of receiving the call, identified the suspect and arrested him without incident.

Investigators allege the man was in possession of a machete and a quantity of methamphetamine at the time of his arrest.

The accused has been charged with possession of a weapon for a dangerous purpose, uttering threats to cause death, assault with a weapon and possession of a Schedule I substance.

Police said no injuries were reported in connection with the incident.

The accused is scheduled to appear in court on Dec. 10.

stories.title: A paid skilled trade placement program is coming for Canadian youth
stories.summary: Ottawa plans to spend $880 million for the plan, which will begin in early 2027 and be available for young Canadians looking for on-the job experience in the trades.
stories.author: Uday Rana
stories.content:
The federal government is rolling out a plan to provide paid, four-month long placements for young people Canadians to build a career in the skilled trades , Jobs Minister Patty Hajdu said on Friday.

Ottawa plans to spend $880 million over the five years for the plan, which will begin in early 2027 and be available for young Canadians looking for on-the job experience in the trades.

This is part of a larger $8 billion financial commitment the Liberals made in the spring economic statement to promote skilled trades.

“By helping more young Canadians pursue careers in skilled trades, we are opening the door to meaningful work that will help build the homes, infrastructure and major projects Canada needs,” Hajdu said.

Additionally, those tradespeople who complete an apprenticeship and earn certification in an eligible Red Seal trade will be able to apply for a $5,000 completion bonus later this fall, she added.

The bonus will also be available to those who received their certification on or after April 1, 2025, Employment and Social Development Canada said.

A new program called Build Canada Apprenticeship Service will launch later this fall, connecting jobseekers to small and medium-sized businesses offering apprenticeships.

Businesses that offer apprenticeships under this program could receive up to $10,000 in grants to support hiring, the department added.

Hajdu also announced the Apprenticeship Training Grant, which will launch in spring 2027 and provide apprentices attending mandatory in-class technical training with a $400 weekly top-up in addition to Employment Insurance.

The federal government is also in “discussions” with provinces and territories on bilateral agreements that would provide them with $2 billion in federal funding to expand access to pre-apprenticeship and technical training, she said.

Canada will have more than 1.4 million job openings in the skilled trades between 2024 and 2033, according to the federal government’s estimates.

stories.title: Hudson Williams and Yaga premiere leave Tiff crowd buzzing
stories.summary: Heated Rivalry star talks about the show’s second season, Yaga’s ‘witchy feminist rage’ and working in Canada
stories.author: Aisling Murphy
stories.content:
Yaga , the upcoming Crave show starring Hudson Williams, Noah Reid and Carrie-Anne Moss, premiered at the Toronto International Film Festival on Thursday evening in a cloud of fandom for another project entirely: Heated Rivalry , which 10 months ago vaulted Williams to stratospheric levels of fame for his portrayal of closeted hockey player Shane Hollander.

While some premiere-goers sported Baba Yaga-inspired fashion – a chicken-feet handbag for Yaga creator and showrunner Kat Sandler, an ethereal black-and-gold robe for Heated Rivalry author Rachel Reid – a large percentage of fans showed up to the Tiff Lightbox in garb connected to a certain gay hockey romance, whose second season is expected to land on Crave in spring of 2027.

Heated Rivalry’s Hudson Williams sends fans into a flurry over this $2 Canadian Tire tote bag

But by the end of Yaga ’s screening, which featured the first two episodes of Sandler’s half-hour thriller, the audience was buzzing – and not only about Williams, who plays two people in Sandler’s folklore-inspired whodunit. As the audience slowly filtered out of the screening room, fans lamented having to wait until Oct. 23 for the series to land on Crave: “Yagaween” quickly became the vernacular of choice for the show’s release date.

First conceived as a play at Toronto’s Tarragon Theatre in 2019, Yaga follows a private detective (Reid) and a local cop (Clark Backo) as they investigate the disappearance of fishery heir Henry Park (Williams) in the fictional coastal town of Whittock.

Before long, the story morphs from a True Detective -style mystery to something more magical – and sinister.

Thursday’s premiere ended on a cliffhanger (no spoilers here), but during the first two episodes, the audience got a taste of Sandler’s quirky sense of humour and highly feminist approach to storytelling. (Moss, best known for her work as Trinity in The Matrix series, plays a middle-aged professor “with a taste for younger men,” per Crave’s marketing materials.)

It was a triumphant conclusion to a Williams-themed day that kicked off with an afternoon Q&A at the Royal Alexandra Theatre. In the leadup to the event, hosted by Tiff’s vice-president of public programming Keith Bennie, long queues snaked around the theatre, with some Heated Rivalry aficionados reporting standing in line since the early morning to try and score a rush ticket. (Some fans on King Street were rewarded for their patience when Williams showed up to the theatre early, offering autographs to a lucky few members of the enormous crowd.)

Bennie’s questions covered a wide range of topics, from Williams’s coming-of-age as a young actor in Kamloops, B.C., to his early career making indie films with friends at Langara College in Vancouver.

In the Q&A, Williams shared intimate details from the Heated Rivalry set, exploring at length scenes where Shane comes out to a girlfriend and sees Ilya Rozanov (Connor Storrie) win a championship game on TV. He also recalled being unsure what the show could lead to – while he remembered appreciating its writing during the audition process, he didn’t anticipate just how strongly Heated Rivalry would resonate with audiences.

“It’s weird that our memory of season one isn’t just our memory of showing up and doing the scenes,” he said. “It’s having watched them cut together. It’s fan reactions. Our memory isn’t ours, it’s everyone’s. It’s been abstracted and twisted, and it’s become this weird amalgamation of a memory.”

Heated Rivalry trounces competition with 13 Canadian Screen Awards

That feeling has made returning to Shane for Heated Rivalry ’s second season harder than expected, he said. (Filming is ongoing.) Both he and Storrie had a tough first day on set this year, but “it came back, thankfully,” he added. “Jacob [Tierney] does a really good job of making this set feel as tiny as it was in season one. It’s all the same crew, which is really great. But it was surreal to step into it. The only other character I’ve had to return to was Land Leopard,” he continued with a laugh, referring to his 2025 indie films Super Support and Super Support 2.

The Q&A soon pivoted to Apparatus, his upcoming film opposite Dylan O’Brien, and Yaga. Williams praised Yaga ’s “witchy feminist rage,” and recalled wondering “how the hell did they greenlight this?” Stylistically, the show is markedly different from Heated Rivalry : It’s “obviously a different world” in terms of genre, he said.

“Those were all exciting things,” he remembered. “I was constantly on the edge of my seat reading it, and I remember my team reading it, and we were like, ‘We’re almost near the end. Do you know what’s happening? No, neither do I.’ And a 30-minute episodic thriller is really interesting.”

Williams called Sandler “uncompromising” as a showrunner, and highlighted her trust in the Yaga cast to find their characters. Williams and Sandler traded voice memos and texts about his two characters, and overall, he said, the experience was highly collaborative. “That’s sort of your dream as an actor,” he said.

And the best part? Both Yaga and Apparatus , booked after the global success of Heated Rivalry , are Canadian. When posed the question of what being Canadian means to him, he quipped, “being American with manners?” before speaking more seriously.

“I was getting a lot of scripts, obviously, and when the show’s blow-up was happening, Yaga and Apparatus were just two of the coolest things that came in. It was sort of a no-brainer to simultaneously choose good projects and also get to be in Canada.”

stories.title: Third Marineland beluga dies after moves, this time in Spain
stories.summary: A third beluga that was a part of a massive move of whales from Marineland has died. Jelly Bean died “suddenly and unexpectedly” on Friday, said Oceanografic Valencia. The Spanish aquarium took in Jelly Bean and another beluga named Cleopatra in late August from the shuttered theme park in Niagara Falls, Ont. Two Marineland belugas […]
stories.author: Lucas Casaletto
stories.content:
A third beluga that was a part of a massive move of whales from Marineland has died.

Jelly Bean died “suddenly and unexpectedly” on Friday, said Oceanografic Valencia.

The Spanish aquarium took in Jelly Bean and another beluga named Cleopatra in late August from the shuttered theme park in Niagara Falls, Ont.

Two Marineland belugas and a resident beluga at Chicago’s Shedd Aquarium died within weeks of their move .

“In recent days, Jelly Bean had experienced feeding difficulties, prompting the veterinary team to intensify her monitoring,” Oceanografic said in a statement.

“During this period, she showed signs of improvement and remained responsive to her caregivers, while continuing to receive around-the-clock monitoring.”

Marineland had the largest collection of captive beluga whales in the world with 30. But the park had been put up for sale in 2024 before closing for good after that summer.

Nineteen belugas died at the park between 2019 and 2025.

Marineland said it was running out of money and needed the whales gone otherwise they would be euthanized.

Marineland and Oceanografic moved the two belugas along with four dolphins to Spain in a 20-hour odyssey on Aug. 27.

“At this time, it is not possible to determine the cause of death,” Oceanografic said.

“Oceanografic’s veterinarians will conduct a necropsy together with the pathology team at CEU Cardenal Herrera University to try to determine the factors that may have contributed to her death.”

Shedd is continuing its investigation into the three deaths there.

Marineland moved its whales and dolphins to five parks in the course of six weeks: SeaWorld locations in San Diego and San Antonio, the Georgia Aquarium in Atlanta, Shedd Aquarium in Chicago and Oceanografic in Valencia.

“We were deeply saddened to learn of the passing of Jelly Bean,” Marineland said in a statement.

“Our thoughts are with the people who cared for her – the staff and caretakers who knew her daily, and everyone who followed her story.”

In 2019, the federal government banned whale and dolphin captivity, but grandfathered in Marineland’s animals.

That was the beginning of the end for Marineland.

The last captive whale in Canada, Tofino, left Marineland’s waters on Aug. 31.

stories.title: Ottawa to fund paid placements in skilled trades at a cost of $880-million
stories.summary: Program funding to come from $8-billion pot set aside to support the sector
stories.author: Craig Lord
stories.content:
Jobs Minister Patty Hajdu says the federal government is putting $880-million behind a plan to get young workers paid, ON-the-job experience in the skilled trades.

Starting early next year, young Canadians will be able to access paid job placements for up to four months to get hands-on experience before beginning an apprenticeship.

The funding comes from a bigger pot of $8-billion in spending that the Liberals have set aside since the spring economic update to promote the skilled trades across Canada.

‘The trades are having a real moment’: As perceptions change, more young workers are choosing this path

The federal government has stressed the importance of recruiting and training a new generation of skilled tradespeople – such as carpenters, electricians and welders.

As part of that regime, later this fall, any tradesperson who has completed an apprenticeship and earned a certification in a Red Seal trade since April, 2025, will also receive a $5,000 bonus.

The federal government will roll out a program over the fall to help small- and medium-sized businesses offer more apprenticeships and Ottawa also plans to top up employment insurance payments for apprentices during training starting next spring.
