stories.title: Advocates promote an alternative to home demolition in Vancouver
stories.summary: About 90,000 detached homes will be torn down nationally over the next decade, and one third of those will be in Metro Vancouver
stories.author: Kerry Gold
stories.content:
Vancouver is the demolition capital of Canada. About 90,000 detached homes will be torn down nationally over the next decade, and one third of those houses will be located in Metro Vancouver, according to a new report partly funded by the federal government.

The Vancouver region averaged 3,210 house demolitions each year between 2013 and 2023, the highest demolition rate out of seven cities studied, according to Vancouver-based Light House, a 20-year-old non-profit organization that advocates for regenerative building practices. The group advocates for the relocation of unwanted houses where possible, and it studied demolitions and relocation potential in Vancouver, Victoria, Calgary, Edmonton, Toronto, Hamilton and Ottawa.

Lawyer Gil Yaron, managing director, circular innovation of Light House, said Vancouver tops the list for demolitions because of rampant redevelopment over the years, fuelled by investors and also by municipal zoning policies. For example, Vancouver’s Broadway Plan – at 500 city blocks, the largest upzoning in the city’s history – would see the demolition of around 1,000 detached homes if fully realized, said Mr. Yaron.

“We’re seeing over 3,000 homes getting demolished every year, and a lot of those homes are less than 10 years old,” he said. “It’s crazy. And it’s completely wasteful. Not only are we wasting material, but the sad irony is that we are destroying housing at the same time as we have a housing crisis.”

The group estimates about 20 per cent of the houses are salvageable and could be relocated and repurposed. They also estimate that about 6,420 units of housing are needed by First Nations within 100 kilometres of Vancouver, as just one example of pressing demand.

“And the events that just happened with the wildfires in Summerland and in the Okanagan made it evident that there’s an opportunity, as well, to provide housing to communities that have been ravaged by catastrophic climate events,” added Mr. Yaron.

House relocation is not new. Nickel Bros has been moving houses in B.C. since 1956 and before then in Manitoba. The company lists houses for sale on its website, often including delivery and placement on a new foundation, with price adjustments for accessibility to the new site. Prices are as low as $52,000, and the houses range in size and location, anywhere in B.C. and Washington state.

Glyn Lewis, founder and chief executive officer of Renewal Development, said there are about 300 house moving companies around the world, and it’s a service that could be scaled up with the right policies in place. The demand is there, and so is the supply, as cities such as Vancouver upzone their detached housing stock and the houses come down to make way for density. He has been moving houses for the last few years, including the historic 1912 schoolhouse from Henry Hudson Elementary School in Kitsilano, which was moved to the Capilano Reserve in North Vancouver and is now a Squamish Nation learning centre.

Renewal Development contributed research to the Light House report because the company has relocated 27 houses in Metro Vancouver, including 10 houses for developer Wesgroup, who had assembled 60 houses for redevelopment in Port Moody. Those houses were put on barges and shipped to the Sunshine Coast to be turned into 17 below-market-price housing units. The company is now working in Los Angeles as well, helping repurpose houses for residents who lost their homes in wildfires last year. That city also enacted legislation to upzone much of its single-family housing, so he saw an opportunity.

Mr. Lewis said he can save developers substantial money by taking the houses off their hands, eliminating the cost of abatement and demolition.

He said there are two critical factors in considering whether it makes financial sense to move a house: the condition of the building and the complexity of the required move. He said modernizing the homes before they are shipped to their new location makes them more useful to the end user, who May or May not have access to trades and materials.

“I think Vancouver is unique because we are one of the demo capitals of the world on a per capita basis, so there is a ton of supply of good homes being demolished every year,” he said. “And because we are on the coast, we have access to non-urban and remote communities where it’s really challenging to build housing. We can mine them from Metro Vancouver and put them on a barge and repurpose them all the way to occupancy.”

Although the real estate market has slowed, the demand for good housing has not, he adds. And even in a slower market, there are far more houses being demolished than saved.

“It feels like trying to drink water out of a fire hose,” he said. “There is so much supply we couldn’t possibly address all of it and save all these homes, even with the slowdown in the marketplace.”

None of this is to say that cities such as Vancouver do not need new development, which is a key part of the B.C. economy, added Mr. Yaron.

“Let’s be real, house relocation is never going to replace conventional construction entirely. We’re talking about a few thousand homes,” he said.

“There is a finite number of homes that are going to come down. Home relocation has its limits. But we’re so far away from hitting that limit. I think it can co-exist and it doesn’t have to undermine the economy.”

Vancouver economist Gary Lai wrote the book Poverty and the Unequal Society in Hong Kong and supports the idea of a 15-minute city in which residents can walk or ride to most of their daily basic necessities. It’s a concept that Vancouver should further embrace, he says. But he acknowledges that the cost would be demolitions.

“You’d have to take the long view on things,” he said. “Maybe urban demolition is acceptable as the cost for a variety of outcomes we want, like social and large green spaces, concentrations of small businesses that can thrive, and more schools and community centres.”

Mr. Lewis said he understands there is a housing crisis and there is a need for more housing and urban density to curb outward sprawl. He said the aim should be to either retain buildings where they are, relocate them, or deconstruct them, instead of sending them to the landfill.

“I understand why we are densifying urban areas, especially around transit corridors,” he said. “But the process to achieve this density shouldn’t be this wasteful. And municipalities and developers working with companies like us and others in the industry could be much more responsible about how we clear these sites.”

stories.title: Liberals will not compromise right to strike or bargain, jobs minister vows
stories.summary: Ottawa — Jobs Minister Patty Hajdu says the federal government will not interfere with workers' right to strike as Ottawa considers legal changes to improve labour relations.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
By Craig Lord, The Canadian Press

Posted September 18, 2026 8:28 am.

Last Updated September 18, 2026 11:28 am.

Ottawa — Jobs Minister Patty Hajdu says the federal government will not interfere with workers’ right to strike as Ottawa considers legal changes to improve labour relations.

Hajdu’s department held months of consultations with unions, employers and other stakeholders over the spring and summer about the state of the Canada Labour Code. Feedback from those sessions is meant to inform future legislation.

A report summarizing what the government heard during that review found that unions and employers were split over the degree of power Ottawa should have to intervene in disputes.

Most employers argued the government should have the ability to step in to quash a labour action when Canada’s national interests are at risk. Unions were staunchly opposed to any measure that could threaten their right to strike.

Hajdu was asked Friday in Ottawa whether she would respect unions’ concerns.

She said the government heard in the review that Canada needs a stronger labour regime to foster better relationships between workers and employers. The focus of the review was to find new supports for both parties, with an eye to leveraging the federal mediation service to maintain industrial peace.

“I can stand here and say that we will never interfere with a worker’s right to bargain or to strike, but we do all agree that there are circumstances where better tools are needed,” Hajdu said.

The minister would not say whether legislation to change the Canada Labour Code will come in the fall session of Parliament, which is set to begin Monday.

Canadian Labour Congress president Bea Bruske said in a media statement that the government’s labour review report did reflect what unions told Ottawa about its priorities.

“Canada needs stronger labour laws that protect the right to strike, support free collective bargaining and hold employers accountable when they break the rules,” Bruske said.

A Senate committee report published in June argued that labour disruptions in critical industries like transportation can harm Canada’s reputation as a reliable trading partner at a time when Ottawa is trying to diversify its trade beyond the United States.

Bruske said in her statement that worker protections, decent wages and collective bargaining are critical to making Canada’s economy more resilient in the face of U.S. trade aggression.

Hajdu was at Algonquin College on Friday to explain the federal government’s plan to get young workers paid, ON-the-job experience in the skilled trades.

Starting early next year, young Canadians will be able to access paid job placements for up to four months, giving them hands-on experience before beginning an apprenticeship.

The $880 million in funding for that program comes from a bigger pot of $8 billion the Liberals have set aside since the spring economic update to promote the skilled trades across Canada.

The federal government has stressed the importance of recruiting and training a new generation of skilled tradespeople, such as carpenters, electricians and welders.

Later this fall, any tradesperson who has completed an apprenticeship and earned a certification in a Red Seal trade since April 2025 will also receive a $5,000 bonus.

The federal government will roll out a program over the fall to help small- and medium-sized businesses offer more apprenticeships and Ottawa also plans to top up employment insurance payments for apprentices during training starting next spring.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 18, 2026.

stories.title: Barenaked Ladies bring ‘O Canada’ to Buffalo Bills home opener amid deepening cross‑border tensions
stories.summary: The Canadian anthem drew loud cheers inside the new Highmark Stadium, where the Bills have been emphasizing their southern Ontario fan base.
stories.author: Lucas Casaletto
stories.content:
By Lucas Casaletto

Posted September 18, 2026 8:26 am.

Last Updated September 18, 2026 8:31 am.

The Buffalo Bills turned their home opener into a rare moment of cross‑border unity Thursday night, inviting Toronto’s Barenaked Ladies to perform “O Canada” before kickoff against the Detroit Lions.

The Canadian anthem drew loud cheers inside the new Highmark Stadium, where the Bills have been emphasizing their sizable southern Ontario fan base — roughly 10,000 Canadian season‑ticket holders — even as political relations between Washington and Ottawa continue to sour.

O Canada! ???????? @barenakedladies | #DETvsBUF pic.twitter.com/eBxgaGjLmK — Buffalo Bills (@BuffaloBills) September 18, 2026

The performance came just days after the White House confirmed President Donald Trump had signed a memorandum targeting Canadian‑origin goods for removal from U.S. federal procurement , the latest in a series of tariff escalations and retaliatory moves that have strained bilateral ties.

Hawaiian‑born singer Auli’i Cravalho performing The Star‑Spangled Banner after Canada’s national anthem.

This isn’t the first time the Bills have played both anthems during games at Orchard Park. Under former owner Ralph Wilson, the Bills once hosted an annual Canadian fan appreciation game scheduled near Canadian Thanksgiving.

The Buffalo Sabres perform both national anthems before every home game, regardless of opponent, a tradition tied to Buffalo’s proximity to the border and its strong Canadian fan base. In April, fans helped finish “O Canada” after the singer’s microphone failed during a Stanley Cup playoff game against Boston.

Bills quarterback Josh Allen threw for three touchdowns and rushed for two more as Buffalo beat the Lions 41-31 on Thursday night to improve to 2-0 on the season.

With files from The Canadian Press

stories.title: Carney to address Liberal caucus after return from Europe
stories.summary: European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said Wednesday she wants Canada to become the first "associate member" of the European Union.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
A fresh round of tariffs and trade restrictions by U.S. President Donald Trump are a “miscalculation” in his trade war against Canada, Prime Minister Mark Carney said on Friday.

Canada made the “right decision” to walk away from trade negotiations with the United States last month, Carney told the Liberal caucus.

2:02 Carney rallies Liberal caucus in Ottawa after fruitful Europe trip

“It wasn’t tough to draw the red lines. We could not accept what they had offered, and we would not give what they had asked. When the U.S. is ready to return to the bargaining table, we will come there to strike a deal in good faith,” said Carney, who spoke to his caucus after he return from addressing the European Parliament in France earlier this week.

The United States has imposed “new unjustified tariffs” which would “hurt workers, companies and communities” in Canada, he added.

“They’re a miscalculation because Canadians will always take care of each other,” Carney said.

The latest U.S. tariffs on a small number of Canadian goods went into effect Tuesday as Washington presses on in its trade war with Canada.

The latest tariffs come amid an ever-evolving trade war between the two countries after Canada walked away from formal negotiations last month. Carney has said the Americans made last-minute demands that would undermine Canada’s sovereignty.

Canada wants to strike a deal that “not just protects, but promotes our official languages,” Carney told the Liberal caucus.

Carney was in Europe earlier this week, where European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen proposed making Canada its first “associate member.”

3:04 What Canadians think of closer ties with the European Union

In his address to caucus, Carney said Ottawa had “launched a process for a new alliance with Europe” but did not say whether this meant the “associate member” tag.

The Liberals will also introduce the Sade Social Media Act in the fall, he added.

“I know you are hearing the concerns of families and educators in your own communities. Children are falling victim to sexual abuse, cyberbullying, and extreme violence online. The current status quo is failing our kids, and we will not stand by it,” Carney told Liberal MPs.

stories.title: Third Marineland beluga dies after being moved
stories.summary: Two Marineland belugas and a resident beluga at Chicago’s Shedd Aquarium died within weeks of their move
stories.author: Liam Casey
stories.content:
A third beluga that was a part of a massive move of whales from Marineland has died.

Oceanografic Valencia says Jelly Bean died suddenly on Friday.

The Spanish aquarium took in Jelly Bean and another beluga named Cleopatra in late August.

Two Marineland belugas and a resident beluga at Chicago’s Shedd Aquarium died within weeks of their move.

Marineland said it was running out of money and needed the whales gone otherwise they would be euthanized.

The closed Niagara Falls, Ont., tourist attraction moved all 30 of its belugas and four dolphins to five aquariums in Chicago, San Antonio, San Diego, Atlanta and Valencia in Spain.

stories.title: Parole hearing for Hamed Shafia, convicted of murdering his sisters and woman
stories.summary: A man convicted of murdering his three sisters and another woman more than 17 years ago is set to have a parole hearing Friday.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
A man convicted of murdering his three sisters and another woman more than 17 years ago is set to have a parole hearing F.

It wasn’t immediately clear what type of release Hamed Shafia is seeking from the Parole Board of Canada.

Shafia and his parents were found guilty in January 2012 of four counts of first-degree murder in the deaths of his teenage sisters and his father’s first wife in a polygamous marriage.

The four bodies were found in a car at the bottom of the Rideau Canal in Kingston, Ont., in June 2009.

The trial judge had described the killings as being motivated by the Shafia family’s “twisted concept of honour.”

The family had immigrated to Canada from Afghanistan and settled in Montreal, where the father was a successful businessman.

After his conviction, the younger Shafia argued that he was too young to be tried as an adult in the case, but Ontario’s top court rejected his appeal.

The Supreme Court of Canada declined to hear the case in 2017.

stories.title: Toronto Biennial tackles watery themes around the Great Loop
stories.summary: Art exhibition’s spotlight on Great Lakes geography seems prescient
stories.author: Kate Taylor
stories.content:
When the fourth Toronto Biennial of Art launches next week, participants will be growing plants and harvesting vegetables along the Erie Canal in upstate New York, in the city of Detroit and on the Caribbean island of Martinique. The biennial aims for a North American reach this year, and the far-flung gardens and farms are the work of artists who are investigating the intersection of art and climate change.

“The projects are dealing with food insecurity, food sustainability, looking at the rupture of not having access to healthy food and proposing solutions,” said Allison Glenn, the American curator who picked Things Fall Apart as the title and theme for the 2026 exhibition.

The continental scope also fulfills the Toronto Biennial’s original ambition: to place Canadian art on the world stage. From its inception in the 2010s and its launch in 2019, the biennial has striven to bring global art to Toronto while showing the international art community what Canada can produce. By bringing in Glenn, after three iterations organized by Canadian teams, the exhibition is turning to the international model of hiring a prestigious outsider to curate a global gathering.

“We need a reoccurring international platform that can convene global and local voices, at scale,” said Patrizia Libralato, the biennial’s founding executive director. Back then, Canada was the only G7 country without an art biennial, to the clear disadvantage of Canadian artists, she said. “Successful biennials shape how a place sees itself and how it’s also seen globally.”

This year, one-third of the 34 participating artists are Canadian and, with a sense that the 12-week event must showcase the country’s senior talents, it features several well-known Indigenous artists – Kent Monkman, Bonnie Devine and Rebecca Belmore – who have not been included before.

After three iterations in borrowed spaces – 2019 featured an old car dealership on Lake Shore Boulevard and a former munitions factory in Mississauga, while the main venue for 2024 was a City of Toronto building in the Queen and Dovercourt neighbourhood – the biennial has entered into a partnership with the Art Museum at the University of Toronto, using its two galleries as the main venues.

Meanwhile, other institutions, including the Art Gallery of Ontario, the Royal Ontario Museum and Mercer Union, are once again contributing programming to the lineup.

“We don’t have a permanent home or a permanent space like some other biennials, so it’s nice to change up the model,” Libralato said.

The collaboration with U of T, and the collaboration among institutions in general, she added, has been driven by the financial constraints of an art scene where many public galleries are still trying to recover from the closings imposed by the pandemic.

She looks with envy to Australia, where the government of New South Wales invested $100-million to renovate an old power plant that now houses the Biennale of Sydney. The possibility of showing huge installations – like those displayed in the old naval warehouses used by the Venice Biennale – is tempting, Libralato acknowledged.

But instead the Toronto Biennial is looking for geographic scale, especially across water.

The Notebook of Return is a collaboration between two artists brought together by Glenn, the biennial’s curator: Jean-Marc Bullet is an innovative designer who runs a market garden in Martinique and Céline Semaan is a Lebanese-Canadian multidisciplinary artist based in Nyack, N.Y., and founder of the Slow Factory, a foundation dedicated to culture and climate education. She is also contributing a rewilding project entitled Slow Forest .

For their joint project, Bullet and Semaan have distributed seeds and notebooks to various groups, including the Toronto Black Farmers and Food Growers Collective and multidisciplinary Detroit artist and Wayne State professor Allana Clarke, who runs an organic garden. Elsewhere, New York artist Mary Mattingly has mounted a floating garden on a repurposed barge in the Erie Canal (in a collaboration with the 2026 Medina Triennial in Medina, N.Y.). The students of Sumner High School in St. Louis, Mo., who tend the garden of the Antioch Baptist Church in a historic Black neighbourhood, are also participating (in a collaboration with Counterpublic, a triennial in their city). All the participants are to plant the seeds, share the harvest and record the season.

The groups are all located along the Great Loop, a 9,700-kilometre navigable water route that covers the eastern United States and part of Ontario, and includes the Great Lakes and the Mississippi River. The watery theme is no coincidence: Glenn grew up in Detroit, near Lake St. Clair and the Detroit River, and now lives in New York in sight of the East River. Toronto, meanwhile, is busy re-establishing its connection to Lake Ontario with development in the Port Lands.

“I sometimes gaze out over the East River and wonder if it’s connected to Detroit,” Glenn said. “And that really started me on this journey of thinking about international waterways, trade routes and voyages.

“I was keenly aware that the inaugural biennial looked at the geographies of Toronto, and so I wanted to be sure that I was honouring that work,” she added, referring to the 2019 exhibition that included several waterfront venues and addressed the Indigenous history of the lakefront as a meeting place.

Glenn, who focuses on special art projects, has a Canadian great-grandparent and remembers travelling to Toronto and Montreal as a child while living in Detroit and also Rochester, just across the lake from Toronto.

paragraphs: When the fourth Toronto Biennial of Art launches next week, participants will be growing plants and harvesting vegetables along the Erie Canal in upstate New York, in the city of Detroit and on the Caribbean island of Martinique. The biennial aims for a North American reach this year, and the far-flung gardens and farms are the work of artists who are investigating the intersection of art and climate change.

“The projects are dealing with food insecurity, food sustainability, looking at the rupture of not having access to healthy food and proposing solutions,” said Allison Glenn, the American curator who picked Things Fall Apart as the title and theme for the 2026 exhibition.

The continental scope also fulfills the Toronto Biennial’s original ambition: to place Canadian art on the world stage. From its inception in the 2010s and its launch in 2019, the biennial has striven to bring global art to Toronto while showing the international art community what Canada can produce. By bringing in Glenn, after three iterations organized by Canadian teams, the exhibition is turning to the international model of hiring a prestigious outsider to curate a global gathering.

“We need a reoccurring international platform that can convene global and local voices, at scale,” said Patrizia Libralato, the biennial’s founding executive director. Back then, Canada was the only G7 country without an art biennial, to the clear disadvantage of Canadian artists, she said. “Successful biennials shape how a place sees itself and how it’s also seen globally.”

This year, one-third of the 34 participating artists are Canadian and, with a sense that the 12-week event must showcase the country’s senior talents, it features several well-known Indigenous artists – Kent Monkman, Bonnie Devine and Rebecca Belmore – who have not been included before.

After three iterations in borrowed spaces – 2019 featured an old car dealership on Lake Shore Boulevard and a former munitions factory in Mississauga, while the main venue for 2024 was a City of Toronto building in the Queen and Dovercourt neighbourhood – the biennial has entered into a partnership with the Art Museum at the University of Toronto, using its two galleries as the main venues.
Meanwhile, other institutions, including the Art Gallery of Ontario, the Royal Ontario Museum and Mercer Union, are once again contributing programming to the lineup.
“We don’t have a permanent home or a permanent space like some other biennials, so it’s nice to change up the model,” Libralato said.

The collaboration with U of T, and the collaboration among institutions in general, she added, has been driven by the financial constraints of an art scene where many public galleries are still trying to recover from the closings imposed by the pandemic.

She looks with envy to Australia, where the government of New South Wales invested $100-million to renovate an old power plant that now houses the Biennale of Sydney. The possibility of showing huge installations – like those displayed in the old naval warehouses used by the Venice Biennale – is tempting, Libralato acknowledged.
But instead the Toronto Biennial is looking for geographic scale, especially across water.

The Notebook of Return is a collaboration between two artists brought together by Glenn, the biennial’s curator: Jean-Marc Bullet is an innovative designer who runs a market garden in Martinique and Céline Semaan is a Lebanese-Canadian multidisciplinary artist based in Nyack, N.Y., and founder of the Slow Factory, a foundation dedicated to culture and climate education. She is also contributing a rewilding project entitled Slow Forest .

For their joint project, Bullet and Semaan have distributed seeds and notebooks to various groups, including the Toronto Black Farmers and Food Growers Collective and multidisciplinary Detroit artist and Wayne State professor Allana Clarke, who runs an organic garden. Elsewhere, New York artist Mary Mattingly has mounted a floating garden on a repurposed barge in the Erie Canal (in a collaboration with the 2026 Medina Triennial in Medina, N.Y.). The students of Sumner High School in St. Louis, Mo., who tend the garden of the Antioch Baptist Church in a historic Black neighbourhood, are also participating (in a collaboration with Counterpublic, a triennial in their city). All the participants are to plant the seeds, share the harvest and record the season.

The groups are all located along the Great Loop, a 9,700-kilometre navigable water route that covers the eastern United States and part of Ontario, and includes the Great Lakes and the Mississippi River. The watery theme is no coincidence: Glenn grew up in Detroit, near Lake St. Clair and the Detroit River, and now lives in New York in sight of the East River. stories.title: A CEO’s family home close to the ski hills
stories.summary: The the estate, called Winterbrook, sits on a two-acre site next to the Osler Brook Golf course
stories.author: Shane Dingman
stories.content:
2710 Nottawasaga 10 Concession N, Clearview, Ont.

Asking price: $3,975,000

Lot size: 290 by 300 feet

Property Taxes: $14,046 (2026)

Listing agents: Mark Veer, Mary Riopelle, Re/Max Four Seasons Realty Limited

In most families, what your home is like plays a big role in defining who you are and what you want as you get older. Sometimes, a second home (or a third) can play that same role.

For Canadian business veteran Joe Canavan, family is a foundational motivation. When he was building Fidelity Investment Canada in the 1990s and at other stops in his career, he says he has been driven by a commitment to helping Canadians build wealth since money is so often at the root of what breaks up families. When you build wealth, you reinvest in family.

Which is why it was an easy decision for him to build a ski chalet near Osler Bluff Ski Club in Collingwood, Ont. “That chalet was really built for our boys,” he said, referring to his three sons who have had almost unfettered access to skiing over the last 16 years. “Our family bonds are so much stronger, so much better because of our affiliation with the club.”

He was also driven by the role sports played in his own life and career.

“Playing hockey and football at a high level made me very competitive; that changed my character, my nature,” said Mr. Canavan. “I was never the most gifted athlete, but I was usually the captain of my team. My job was to be the guy who brought people together.” He’s been a CEO seven times over his career in finance and philanthropy, and still credits many of those lessons and experiences for his approach.

Home of the Week: Clapboard house is oldest documented wooden structure in Nova Scotia

It was friend and former National Hockey League Players’ Association boss Bob Goodenow who told him not to put the boys in hockey, which was his inclination.

“He essentially forbid me from putting my boys in hockey; he said our chances of having a boy in the NHL is 0.02 per cent. Goodenow said we should look at ski clubs. My wife Larissa, she was elated: she didn’t want to sit in hockey arenas all winter,” said Mr. Canavan.

So the boys began training for ski racing from a young age, and after a few years of renting chalet’s for the winter near Osler, Mr. Canavan found a two-acre site next to the Osler Brook Golf course and began construction in 2008 on the estate home now called Winterbrook. The design had a bit of everything the family wanted in a country getaway and at-home training facility: a full gym, boot and equipment room, hot tub, steam room and cold plunge tub (not to mention heated garage, which is a great perk when you’re running out to the lift on a cold morning) all of which reduces the friction to and from the slopes.

Mr. Canavan is proud of their accomplishments; his middle son was asked to join Canada’s national team (he declined, and has made a mark in Ironman competitions instead) and his youngest has coached in the sport. But they are grown up now, either in university or finished their degrees, and a full-season skiing hub isn’t as necessary for the family now.

Mr. Canavan said he and his wife were inspired by Belgian country homes featuring lots of stone and white oak for the motif of their chalet. Working with custom-builder Dalton Beachli, they came up with a series of spaces that emphasize natural materials and a connection with the landscape.

The front porch portico is made from big, chunky beams of Douglas fir from British Columbia, and those huge beams are used for structure and emphasis as you enter the main floor.

This central section of the house is a massive volume of space that’s open to the vaulted second-floor ceiling that is clad in Douglas fir. Directly across from the front foyer is a two-storey tall bank of windows that fill the great room with light and look out toward the golf course.

On the left from the foyer is a set of stairs (more chunky beams) that climb to a loft/bridge that connects the wings on the second level, and also descends to the partially above-grade basement. Passing under the bridge the great room opens up, with the wall on the right dominated by a chimney of mixed cut and raw stone, and to the left an entrance to the kitchen and dining area.

Home of the Week: A Brockville home steeped in history

The kitchen is built around a long stone-topped island prep space with induction cooktop built in, with an equally long dining space alongside it, all under more of the chunky wood beams and cladding. At the far end of the room is a set of double doors to a side patio with a built-in fire pit.

Back through the main room, the other wing of the house features a wood-panelled library/office, main-floor powder room, a large laundry room and the equipment rooms and garage access.

On the second level the primary suite is an airy space above the kitchen and its ensuite bathroom features double-sized walk-in shower, dual vanity and soaker tub. Three bedrooms for the boys and a shared bathroom fill the wing above the garage.

The basement rec room features another distinctive fireplace with huge stone slabs, and in addition to the gym on this lower level there are two guest suites (or nanny suites) and a full bath.

There are four fireplaces in the home, if you include the outdoor firepit, no accident since Mr. Canavan is a self-proclaimed fire fanatic.

“I wanted fire everywhere because my parents at home we didn’t have anything like that,” said Mr. Canavan, who shared that while his parents provided for the family, they were both new Canadians and often worked two jobs. When his career in finance began to take off, Mr. Canavan felt compelled as the oldest child to help support his parents.

“I bought my first cottage when I was 25, one of the reasons that place won out over other places, the beautiful stone fireplace, it was stunning and the centre of the home,” he said, and the effect this space had on his parents was profound. “I used to see my mother and father nattering at each other in the city but as soon as they went north of the 401 they were like lovebirds … it was crazy.”

He eventually gave that first cottage to his parents, and the gift he continues to give himself is spaces designed for his family to bond and connect. They host all the Thanksgivings and Christmases, the big anniversaries and birthdays. They never intended to sell this home, but the plan is to reconstruct a more modest version of it nearby.

When Mr. Canavan is at Winterbrook, he likes to start his day in that first-floor study, turn on the fireplace and get his morning reading done. If the kids are up for a ski run he’ll put together breakfast before they head out. When the day is done, winding down in the great room with the landscape shining through the windows and a fire roaring in the large fireplace is his idea of being at home.

When his career in finance began to take off, Mr. Canavan felt compelled as the oldest child to help support his parents.

“I bought my first cottage when I was 25, one of the reasons that place won out over other places, the beautiful stone fireplace, it was stunning and the centre of the home,” he said, and the effect this space had on his parents was profound. “I used to see my mother and father nattering at each other in the city but as soon as they went north of the 401 they were like lovebirds … it was crazy.”

He eventually gave that first cottage to his parents, and the gift he continues to give himself is spaces designed for his family to bond and connect. They host all the Thanksgivings and Christmases, the big anniversaries and birthdays. They never intended to sell this home, but the plan is to reconstruct a more modest version of it nearby.

When Mr. Canavan is at Winterbrook, he likes to start his day in that first-floor study, turn on the fireplace and get his morning reading done. If the kids are up for a ski run he’ll put together breakfast before they head out. When the day is done, winding down in the great room with the landscape shining through the windows and a fire roaring in the large fireplace is his idea of being at home.

stories.title: White Rock home sells $150,000 below 2021 purchase price
stories.summary: House sold for $1.5-million in 2021
stories.author: Kerry Gold
stories.content:
2168 165B St., White Rock, B.C.

Asking price: $1,397,000 (June 8)

Selling price: $1,350,000 (June 27)

Previous selling price: $1.5-million (2021)

Taxes: $6,923.25 (2025)

Days on market: 19

Buyer’s agent: Jeremy Sellmer, Oakwyn Realty

The sellers had purchased the property for $1.5-million in 2021, so the sale price shows the market adjustment under way, said the buyer’s agent Jeremy Sellmer.

“The clients loved the neighbourhood; they wanted something newer, they wanted a detached house, and they wanted to keep it under $1.36-million,” said the agent. “And this one fit the bill.”

His clients didn’t have any competition, he added.

“We put in an offer, and we went back and forth, and then sort of stalled out on this one for like a day or two. And then, probably an hour before our offer expired, they just sent it back signed. I guess they had a change of heart.”

This two-storey, 2,400-square-foot house is only nine years old, with five bedrooms, four bathrooms, air conditioning and a covered patio.

The design is open concept with a fireplace and large outdoor entertaining space. The floors are engineered hardwood, the countertops are quartz and the all-white kitchen includes a walk-in pantry.

The bedroom has vaulted ceilings with a walk-in closet and ensuite bathroom, and the basement includes a one-bedroom suite with a separate entrance. Shops, schools and parks are within walking distance.

“Buyers, they’re going to be very selective right now. And if you’re the same as three or four other places that are in your direct area, and you’re all priced relatively the same, the buyer is just going to get the best deal,” said the agent.

Mr. Sellmer said that, for sellers, it’s all about the number of private bookings that they get. Those are the best indicator that they’ve priced their house correctly.

The sale completed on Sept. 10.

stories.title: Lake Huron town turns to grazing goats for eco-friendly attack on invasive species
stories.summary: Since Tuesday, 52 goats and 20 sheep have been eating undesirable vines and bushes covering a key corridor for Goderich’s water and natural gas pipes.
stories.author: Scott Miller
stories.content:
Goderich has temporarily become ‘Goaterich’ as grazing goats take on a week of eating, in the name of infrastructure access.

“So back in 2008 or 2009, we had a piece of the underground water infrastructure fail. And when we came in to make the repair, the disturbance to the soil let the invasive species, the Japanese knotweed and the Himalayan blackberry get established,” said Director of Operations, Infrastructure, and Community Services, Sean Thomas.

“Over the last decade, we’ve tried different options or different methods to address the issue. This is the newest one, and so far it seems to be the most successful,” he added.

Since Tuesday, 52 goats and 20 sheep have been eating undesirable vines and bushes covering a key corridor for Goderich’s water and natural gas pipes.

Other options were considered to clear the utility corridor, but this unique approach won the day, says Goderich Deputy Mayor Leah Noel.

“Mechanical solutions aren’t great, right? The slope is steep and the area is wet, so it makes it really hard to get equipment in, and we don’t want to use herbicides so close to the lake obviously. So, this opportunity presented itself to bring in a herd of goats to graze,” said Noel.

The goat grazers have attracted a crowd each day as the chewing crew works its way from Sunset Park down to Cove Road near Goderich’s waterfront.

“Goats are built for this. They love steep hills, they love vegetation, they love everything leafy, so they’re going for it, they eat everything, said the owner of Big Crunch Grazing, Florentine Maathuis, from Caledon East.

“And because they’re relatively small and lightweight, their hooves are not a danger for erosion or anything. So they’re still respectful of the natural bluffs here,” said Maathuis.

According to Maathius, her goats and sheep have been booked all summer, travelling across southern Ontario, chewing up hard to reach areas of the province. She stays on site with her herding dogs, while her herd works away behind an electric fence.

They herd has until Sunday to complete Phase 1 of the job.

“It will likely take a couple of times of bringing the goats and sheep back in order to completely manage the site. But this is step one, and this is how we assess moving forward in an environmentally friendly way,” said Noel.

stories.title: London civic election: Ward 14 all-candidates debate
stories.summary: The race to represent Ward 14 on London city council is wide open, with incumbent Steve Hillier not seeking re-election.
stories.author: Jack Moulton
stories.content:
The race to represent Ward 14 on London city council is wide open, with incumbent Steve Hillier not seeking re-election. The ward is huge, taking in about a third of the city by land area. Two candidates gathered for a debate on Thursday night and LFP city hall reporter Jack Moulton was there.

Ward 14 under the new city ward boundaries will remain the largest ward by area in the city. It includes the Pond Mills, Westminster, Summerside, Brockley, and Wilton Grove neighbourhoods.

Ubaid Bhatti (absent)

Jason King: 52, intelligence analyst/investigator, part-time professor

Sarah Lehman: 35, executive assistant

Gurinder Pal Singh (absent)

Speaking to a crowd of about 60 at Chalmers Presbyterian Church, located at Commissioners Road East and Pond Mills Road, King spoke of his canvassing on his home turf to build his platform.

“It is important to me that no conversation is rushed, so that I can be a good listener. As time went on, my campaign platform evolved and developed from what I was learning from you,” he said. “From that, I formed an actionable and realistic vision for Ward 14. My ideas bear the fruit of our engagements at the door.”

Lehman unsuccessfully ran for the ward in 2022, finishing with 40 per cent of the vote to Hillier’s 45 per cent. She was recently endorsed by the London and District Labour Council and on Thursday night touted her public- and private-sector experience and also pledged to be a constituency-focused councillor if elected.

“London is growing, and the decisions we make now will shape the city for decades to come. I want to see real progress in affordable housing and homelessness, reliable public transit to Ward 14, safer, more connected neighbourhoods, inclusion and accessibility to those neighbourhoods, and enhancing our existing green spaces as London grows,” she said.

Several residents who put questions to King and Lehman were eager to hear how well they know their ward, asking if they lived in the ward or were familiar with areas like Brockley and Glanworth. King said he lives in Summerside and Lehman, a longtime Pond Mills resident, said she lives across the boundary at Commissioners.

One question dealt with how to make the largely rural Ward 14 more prominent in the city, with King suggesting it’s a matter of an available councillor to respond to residents, and Lehman saying it’s a matter of better communication through the office on what is happening in the ward and city.

“I think that Ward 14 is suffering from being neglected for so long because we’ve not had a strong voice and strong representation at city council,” King said. “It’s also a political job. The work is to be political at making agreements with people, like other councillors, and drawing them into finding solutions.”

The first question involved homelessness, with King expressing his opposition to harm reduction in drug addiction, and Lehman suggesting more preventive measures through housing protections and provincial support, explaining “property taxpayers cannot be expected to solve a housing crisis, a mental health crisis, an addiction crisis, and an income support crisis on their own.”

On property tax increases, King suggested aiming for a tax freeze by bringing in more revenue through commercial development, while Lehman suggested reviewing city budgets for waste and duplication.

King dismissed the city’s Indigenous reconciliation action plan as something he’s never heard as a priority from residents, while advocating for city-building to everyone’s benefit. Lehman suggested better accountability and reporting for the city’s strategy.

When it came to climate action, King said the city should prioritize flood protection and downplayed climate change, saying the city has experienced “ quite typical and normal weather behaviour in the past few years.” Lehman’s answer took a different direction, acknowledging climate change while advocating for better transit and active transportation options to reduce emissions, and a robust tree canopy.

“Climate change isn’t something that’s happening somewhere else or decades from now – Londoners are already experiencing extreme heat, flooding, poor air quality from the wildfire smoke, and increasingly severe weather,” she said. “I would prioritize investments that make our neighbourhoods and infrastructure more resilient.”

Voters will head to the polls to elect their next city council on Oct. 26, with several advance voting days on Oct. 1, 3, 8, and 10.

There are 81 candidates running for London mayor and the 14 ward councillor positions — read what most of them have to say, in their own words, right here .

stories.title: Is Canada’s future European?
stories.summary: The Big Story discusses why Canada and the EU are reaching for each other, and what its future might be in the age of President Trump.
stories.author: Patricia D'Cunha
stories.content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney has made history in Europe. On Sept. 16, he became the first foreign world leader to ever attend the State of the European Union (EU) address, delivered by President of the European Commission Ursula von der Leyen. During that address, von de Leyen invited Canada to become the first ever “associate member” of the EU. On Sept. 17, Carney himself addressed the European parliament, acknowledging the invitation and expressing Canada’s desire to become closer to Europe.

Host Caryn Ceolin is speaking with Dr. Kurt Hübner, professor in the European studies department at the University of British Columbia, about what it might mean to be an associate member, why Canada and the EU are reaching for each other, and what the future of Canada and Europe might be in the age of U.S. President Donald Trump.

stories.title: Lake Huron town turns to grazing goats for eco-friendly attack on invasive species
stories.summary: Since Tuesday, 52 goats and 20 sheep have been eating undesirable vines and bushes covering a key corridor for Goderich’s water and natural gas pipes.
stories.author: Scott Miller
stories.content:
Goderich has temporarily become ‘Goaterich’ as grazing goats take on a week of eating, in the name of infrastructure access.

“So back in 2008 or 2009, we had a piece of the underground water infrastructure fail. And when we came in to make the repair, the disturbance to the soil let the invasive species, the Japanese knotweed and the Himalayan blackberry get established,” said Director of Operations, Infrastructure, and Community Services, Sean Thomas.

“Over the last decade, we’ve tried different options or different methods to address the issue. This is the newest one, and so far it seems to be the most successful,” he added.

Since Tuesday, 52 goats and 20 sheep have been eating undesirable vines and bushes covering a key corridor for Goderich’s water and natural gas pipes.

Other options were considered to clear the utility corridor, but this unique approach won the day, says Goderich Deputy Mayor Leah Noel.

“Mechanical solutions aren’t great, right? The slope is steep and the area is wet, so it makes it really hard to get equipment in, and we don’t want to use herbicides so close to the lake obviously. So, this opportunity presented itself to bring in a herd of goats to graze,” said Noel.

The goat grazers have attracted a crowd each day as the chewing crew works its way from Sunset Park down to Cove Road near Goderich’s waterfront.

“Goats are built for this. They love steep hills, they love vegetation, they love everything leafy, so they’re going for it, they eat everything, said the owner of Big Crunch Grazing, Florentine Maathuis, from Caledon East.

“And because they’re relatively small and lightweight, their hooves are not a danger for erosion or anything. So they’re still respectful of the natural bluffs here,” said Maathuis.

According to Maathius, her goats and sheep have been booked all summer, travelling across southern Ontario, chewing up hard to reach areas of the province. She stays on site with her herding dogs, while her herd works away behind an electric fence.

They herd has until Sunday to complete Phase 1 of the job.

“It will likely take a couple of times of bringing the goats and sheep back in order to completely manage the site. But this is step one, and this is how we assess moving forward in an environmentally friendly way,” said Noel.

stories.title: Ontario trucker sent to prison in U.S. for hauling cocaine allegedly for Ryan Wedding's cartel
stories.summary: Iqbal Singh Virk admitted that he helped knit a drug transportation network in Canada to an immense cocaine cartel in Mexico and US.
stories.author: Adrian Humphreys
stories.content:
An Ontario truck driver who was caught at the border trying to smuggle cocaine from the United States into Canada — allegedly for Ryan Wedding, the Canadian Olympic snowboarder named as an international narco mastermind — was sentenced to nine years in a U.S. prison after court proceedings draped in secrecy.

Iqbal Singh Virk, 58, an owner-operator of a transport truck based in Brampton, Ont., admitted to a judge in Los Angeles that he helped knit a drug transportation network in Canada to an immense cocaine cartel in Mexico and the United States.

In keeping with the high stakes and high profile of the Ryan Wedding investigation — including the murder of a government witness who was cooperating with U.S. authorities in the case — Virk’s hearings featured more secretiveness than usual.

Several documents entered into the court record were ordered sealed by the judge and cannot be read or reported on.

Judge Sherilyn Peace Garnett issued protective orders over court filings that could reveal the identities of confidential informants, cooperating witnesses and cooperating defendants “who participated in the government’s investigation and provided information relevant to defendant’s sentencing,” the order says.

The orders were to protect sensitive information from unauthorized dissemination while allowing defence lawyers with enough information to adequately represent Virk. The order also refers to material marked “Attorney’s Eyes Only,” which the lawyers cannot even show their client.

Garnett also granted a secrecy motion requested by Virk to have his response to the government’s sentencing position filed under seal and not available for public viewing.

John Hanusz, Virk’s lawyer, declined to comment on the case or on how Virk was taking the sentencing decision issued against him on Wednesday.

Virk signed a plea agreement last August admitting he was part of a cocaine conspiracy comprised of members of a drug-trafficking organization who arranged with a drug transportation network to move more than 1,800 kilograms of cocaine from the Los Angeles area into Canada.

Virk was part of the transportation network and drove his long-haul truck from Ontario to California specifically to collect cocaine and hide it in a secret compartment in his truck.

He and his partner, Ranjit Singh Rowal, shared the driving, then tried to mask the purpose of their trip by loading legal goods into the truck for the return to Canada.

Virk and Rowal, however, were caught in an elaborate sting operation the FBI was running after infiltrating the ring. The man with whom Virk was arranging the cocaine pick up was really a confidential source secretly working with the FBI.

When the pair pulled their tractor-trailer up to the customs post on the U.S. side of the Blue Water Bridge, connecting Ontario and Michigan, ON Aug. 28, 2024, Virk was behind the wheel and Rowal in the passenger seat.

They didn’t stand a chance of getting across as authorities were waiting for them. Customs officers were soon pulling cocaine bricks wrapped together in cellophane from a hidden slot at the rear of their trailer just above their Ontario licence plate. Stacking them on the loading bay floor, they counted 115 bricks weighing slightly more than 124 kilos. An officer estimated it was worth close to US$4 million.

The arrests of Virk and Rowal were a sign of things to come.

It turned out that they were small fry in the scheme of things as U.S., Canadian and Mexican authorities targeted an international criminal enterprise — a violent and prolific cartel authorities said was headed by Wedding.

Wedding, who competed for Team Canada in the 2002 Winter Olympics, was named the mastermind behind a deluge of cocaine flowing from Colombia to Mexico and then to California where it was loaded in trucks for the drive to Canada.

Two months after the arrests of the two drivers, Wedding’s name was the first on a long list of accused in a U.S. indictment. The FBI called Wedding a modern-day Pablo Escobar or El Chapo Guzman, naming two of history’s most notorious drug lords.

The last two names on the indictment were Virk and Rowal.

Both men pleaded guilty, 10 days apart, to two charges: conspiracy to distribute cocaine and possession with intent to distribute cocaine. Rowal was sentenced in November to 37 months in prison.

In return for Virk’s guilty plea on two drug charges, prosecutors agreed to drop other charges and asked the judge to reduce his sentence. Since Virk faced a maximum penalty of life in prison and an $11-million fine, nine years and no fine might seem a good deal, despite it being significantly longer than his partner’s punishment.

Virk’s conviction makes it almost a certainty that he will be deported from the United States upon his release from prison. Both men are citizens of India and travelled on an Indian passport but had immigrated to Canada, where they had permanent resident status.

Wedding remains in U.S. custody, also in California, after his arrest in Mexico in January. He pleaded not guilty to multiple drug trafficking and murder charges and is awaiting trial.

stories.title: Sweden consistently outperforms Canada on universal health care despite similar spending: new study
stories.summary: Sweden maintains a higher physician-to-population ratio than Canada, with 4.4 physicians per 1,000 population, compared with 2.8 in Canada.
stories.author: Stewart Lewis
stories.content:
Sweden and Canada operate publicly financed universal health-care systems, but access to care in the Nordic country is “markedly better,” according to a new report from the Fraser Institute.

In 2024, wait times leading to unmet medical needs affected two per cent of Swedes, compared with 9.1 per cent of Canadians, says the report’s author, Yanick Labrie.

The study argues that the difference between the two national systems can be found in the way they are organized. Labrie states that almost half (46.9 per cent) of primary care centres in Sweden are privately operated, while still fully funded by public dollars.

Labrie notes that private providers in Sweden perform more than 40 per cent of publicly funded hip and knee replacements and over 70 per cent of cataract procedures.

Private providers have also expanded surgical capacity, rather than displacing it, he suggests. Between 2001 and 2019, the share of cataract patients treated within 90 days increased from 36.9 to 88.2 per cent while median waiting times fell from 6.2 to 1.8 months.

More particularly, 85 per cent of patients receive a medical assessment within three days when needed, the study states.

Labrie states that European health-care systems have attracted an increasing level attention among Canadian policymakers. For example, he states that in May 2026, Alberta Premier Danielle Smith led a delegation to Sweden to learn more about the country’s approach to organizing and delivering health care within a universal system.

Labrie notes that similar to Canada, Sweden’s health-care system is founded on the principle that access to medically necessary care should depend on need rather than ability to pay. But discussions of health-care reform in Canada often become highly polarized when it comes to expanding the role of private providers, says Labrie.

“As a result, health-care policy discussions in Canada often focus primarily on preserving existing financing arrangements rather than examining alternative models for organizing and delivering care to Canadians.”

The primary responsibility for organizing health care falls under Sweden’s 21 regions, governed by local political assemblies. Regional authorities are responsible for organizing hospitals, primary care, specialist services, and provider-reimbursement systems. Municipal governments are primarily responsible for long-term care, home care, rehabilitation support, and services for older adults and individuals with disabilities.

In contrast, says Labrie, beginning in the early 2000s several provinces (Quebec, Saskatchewan, Nova Scotia and Alberta) merged regional health authorities into larger provincial organizations, reducing the autonomy of intermediary bodies.

Meanwhile, in Sweden patients commonly pay modest co-payments for primary care visits, specialist consultations, emergency department visits and prescription drugs. Annual caps substantially limit total out-of-pocket exposure.

Sweden permits duplicate private health insurance for services already covered under the public system, whereas in most Canadian provinces, such insurance remains heavily restricted or prohibited. By the end of 2024 over 800,000 Swedes held duplicate health insurance coverage (15.8 per cent of the working-age population). Most insurance policies are financed by employers as part of workplace benefits.

“In Sweden, privately insured patients continue to contribute to the public system through income taxation. They do not opt out financially,” says Labrie.

One of the greatest health-care needs – physician access – seems to be better met in Sweden, which according to Oecd data cited by Labrie, maintains a higher physician-to-population ratio than Canada, with 4.4 physicians per 1,000 population, compared with 2.8 in Canada. Sweden also has a national waiting-time guarantee aimed at improving timely access to care throughout the country.

Sweden’s Primary Care Choice Act was implemented between 2007 and 2010. The new legislation introduced patient choice among accredited primary care providers, whether publicly or privately operated. Private providers were allowed to establish new clinics and compete for patient enrolment under the country’s regional reimbursement systems.

Overall, says Labrie, the study’s findings indicate that greater private-sector participation necessarily reduces publicly financed health-care system capacity. “In several areas of Sweden, private providers expanded the overall volume of publicly funded services rather than simply displacing activity from public providers.”

stories.title: ‘He’s a fighter’: Mayich family opens up about son, brother Matthew
stories.summary: Matthew Mayich came to Arizona State last month, joining the Sun Devils after four seasons with OHL Ottawa and another at Ncaa Clarkson.
stories.author: Lucas Casaletto
stories.content:
By Elliotte Friedman, Sportsnet

Posted September 18, 2026 6:47 am.

John and Christina Mayich have two requests.

First, they want the world to learn more about their son, Matthew.

“Matthew is a boy’s boy,” Christina said. “He’s a guy’s guy. He is a simple, simple guy who has an infectious smile. Anybody you talk to will tell you about his smile. He loves to fish. He fishes almost every day, every chance he can get. He loves his family. He likes to hang out at home. He doesn’t like to go out partying … he just likes to be with us. He loves his girlfriend, his siblings, funny guy, chirper.

“And he, as a teammate, he obviously loves hockey. That’s his world. He likes to stand up for his teammates. He has your back. I wish you got to meet him as the Matthew we all know and love.”

“He brings joy to a room, bottom line,” John added, before Christina continued.

“When he’s away for hockey, our house is different. When he is there, there is so much, so much life, so much energy. He brings a different vibe to our home, to our family, and to the neighbourhood.”

Their second request is this: no matter where you are from or what faith you follow, you pray for their 21-year-old son.

Matthew Mayich came to Arizona State last month, joining the Sun Devils after four seasons with OHL Ottawa and another at NCAA Clarkson. Days after his arrival, on Aug. 20, Mayich collapsed during an outdoor workout and has been hospitalized since. The university is reviewing the circumstances, and a spokesman emailed Wednesday that “we expect to be able to update everyone on our review process in the coming days.”

“We’ve been told there was a workout scheduled for early (that day), and I guess it was hot, and the conditions weren’t good for working out,” John said. “(Matthew) basically got heat stroke. (It) had nothing to do with his heart. He came in shape. He was 100 per cent ready to go this season. He worked all summer, and he was ready.

“And I guess just the heat … just snowballed from there. He ended up collapsing and is still in a coma. Considering the situation, I think we’re somewhat strong in just trying to push through. We’ve got no choice.”

What have doctors told the family about the prognosis?

“We’re taking it day by day,” Christina answered. “We’re here praying hard, praying to our Lord for a miracle.”

“He’s a fighter,” added John. “So we know that, and we’re giving him every chance to survive.”

John and Christina have a strong support group in Arizona, including daughter Stephanie and son Josh — two and three years younger than their brother, respectively — and Matthew’s girlfriend of four years, Alexa. But what’s really helped in immeasurable ways is support from the most unexpected places, including priests who reached out from Kenya.

“There’s so many countries that we were very shocked to hear,” Christina said. “Matthew is a simple boy from Stoney Creek, Ont., and we don’t know how he made it that far that people are praying for him. It’s just proof that there’s a lot of great people out there. We’ve seen a different side of humanity that we would have never seen if we didn’t go through this.”

The Mayich family is hugely thankful to the doctors, nurses and hospital staff; Anthony Houston, who oversees eight Arizona hospitals, making sure Matthew received proper care. They were embraced by the local Lebanese community after the family visited one of their churches to pray to St. Charbel, a Lebanese-born monk revered for his powers of healing.

Among many from the hockey community: Utah coach Andre Tourigny, who scouted Matthew back when he coached the Ottawa 67’s, Auston Matthews, Clayton Keller and the Xhekaj family. John and Jack Xhekaj — Arber and Florian’s father — have a long friendship.

“If we don’t speak one Sunday, we’ll speak the next,” John laughed. “We never go more than two Sundays without talking.”

And the Thompson family, led by Kim, Tage’s mother.

“Kim set up a lovely vigil for Matthew that included his (Arizona State) teammates, their family, and anybody who wanted to come out and pray for Matthew, which was very lovely and means so much to us,” Christina said.

“I think there was about 25, 26 current players and ex-players,” John said. “It was very nice to see.”

“For me, it was emotional seeing them,” Christina continued. “When you saw the team, it was like, ‘Matthew, you should be sitting there with them right now. You shouldn’t be up here.’ So it was tough, but it was also very warm, very … I can’t explain. It’s all in my heart, so I’m thankful to everybody.”

John Mayich has a message for Matthew’s Sun Devil teammates.

“I feel for them. I don’t want them to feel guilty at all that this happened. They had to see some ugly stuff, and I just hope they can push through. I wish them nothing but the best.”

If his parents are most proud of one thing, it’s that their son had an ability to make friends of all ages, from putting together a three-year-old neighbour’s bicycle to helping Alexa’s octogenarian grandfather with his garden tomatoes. John Mayich smiled reminiscing about Ring video of young kids from the neighbourhood asking Matthew to come out and play street hockey with them, a request rarely — if ever — refused.

“He was, just … he lived life,” John said. “That’s it. He really did live life and he didn’t judge anybody. Never.”

Thanks to old friends and newfound supporters worldwide, Matthew’s hospital room is personalized with unique items.

“Five of his friends flew down when they heard the news, and they bought him fishing paraphernalia,” Christina said. “Went to Bass Pro, just kind of decorated his room, which was very nice, surrounding him with the things that he loves.”

By his head there is a stone in a pouch. On his body, there’s a small medallion, called the Miraculous Medal. Christina describes the Mayiches as devout Catholics; the Miraculous Medal reminds you to keep the faith, never lose your trust in the power of prayer.

“A man from England found us, and he had sent the package, which was the rock and a Miraculous Medal. When he sent it, (with) a picture of a Sister, I didn’t quite know who the Sister was. She’s an Irish nun who had just passed, and she’s on her way to being Canonized.

“And he took a chance, and he said, even if you don’t believe, there’s nothing to lose if you put this by Matthew’s head. So I did, because I was just so touched. And the next day I reached out to him, and he explained to me that he felt in his heart when he heard Matthew’s story that he needed to deliver this to us, to somehow find us. And he explained that he is disabled and doesn’t leave home often, but this time he did. And he said this rock and this medal were blessed from a place that is near and dear to us in Medjugorje.”

(Medjugorje is a famous Catholic pilgrimage destination. Located in Bosnia-Herzegovina, it has strong historical ties to the Croatian people, which is the Mayich family’s heritage. For years, Matthew’s smartphone screensaver is him in a Luka Modric jersey, the Croatian soccer legend.)

“It was blessed by Our Lady, which to me meant the world,” Christina continued. “And I could not believe that was happening. And it was a sign that Mary, our mother, is with us. And she is leading us to her son and giving us that peace and calm. So, we thank you from the bottom of our heart that you found us all the way from England.

“There’s just so many, so many people we’ve met along the way that have touched our hearts and that are showing us the goodness of humanity, and they all give us hope and faith.”

“Seeing the support back home and all over the world, it’s like, unexplainable,” added Josh, the younger brother. “It’s something I never imagined and it’s honestly a blessing.”

Christina carries a spiritual necklace she also places on Matthew’s body during her visits.

“All the kids here with us all put their crosses on here,” she said. “His siblings’ crosses are here, his cousin Vicky, her husband, Owen. And we also have a special gift from Matthew’s new best friend, Sister Betty, who I forgot to mention. She has been a godsend. She comes every day to visit her best friend, Matthew, and she prays for him.

“She gave me one of her own personal relics. She was in a terrible car accident. And she said not one scratch came while she had this relic. And she wanted Matthew to have it. And she said Matthew is going to return it to her when he wakes up.

“We’ve had so many people from different religions reaching out to us, letting us know that their groups are all praying for him. And I cannot tell you. It just takes our breath away. How many people are fighting for him. And we’re just thankful.”

“It seems like it started on our street with the yellow ribbons and then just spread,” John added. “And that’s Matthew. That’s his personality. You meet him once. Someone wants to introduce him to someone else and it just spreads.”

“It actually started in Canada in there’s an Instagram group,” Christina added. “It’s called ‘Yellow Ribbons for Matthew.’ So people are tying yellow ribbons on their trees outside. And the kids are wearing yellow ribbons. And there was just a soccer tournament in Ottawa … they were honouring Matthew by wearing “M.M” (and the) number nine, his soccer number when he was little.

“So this yellow ribbon has grown.”

There are three yellow ribbons on his hospital room window.

The family realized Matthew’s hockey dreams had a chance to become reality when Tourigny, then head coach and vice-president of hockey operations for the OHL 67’s, started showing up to Matthew’s games and practices.

“People are driving six, seven hours to just watch him skate for an hour,” John said. “So to me, that’s pretty cool.”

Christina: “We were excited for Matthew because he was excited.”

The Coyotes hired Tourigny away from Ottawa before Matthew played a game. Enter Dave Cameron, who also developed a strong relationship with the player and family.

“I just remember dropping Matthew off the first time in Ottawa,” John smiled. “He’s 16 years old so we’re driving up and we get to the house. It was COVID so you couldn’t meet the billet family who are super people. I just remember this red door. I’m getting Matthew’s stuff out of the car and he goes to the front porch and the door’s closed. I started putting the stuff away, like what was left over back in the trunk. I look, he already shut the door. He was in the house, ready to go.”

“Yeah, we met the billet family and they’re like, ‘We’re new to this,’” Christina added while also smiling. “And I’m like, ‘So are we.’ And we’re like, ‘Okay, bye, Matthew.’”

John added: “But he wanted to be there.”

Was he ever homesick or anything like that? Both parents immediately jump in.

“No. No. No.”

“Yeah, he missed us,” Christina continued. “But he was, you know, this is his job. This is his dream. And he loved it. And he loved all his billet families. He was very close with all of them.”

Then came the lead-up to the 2023 NHL Draft. The calls were coming to Matthew’s phone.

“All sorts of teams were reaching out,” John said.

“Matthew would go in a room and I’d be at the door listening to him talk to the teams,” Christina laughed.

John grew up a Maple Leafs fan in the era of Wendel Clark and Doug Gilmour, his favourite players.

“I think when the Leafs called him, it kind of … kind of hit home a bit.”

Christina: “Yeah, they called a couple of times.”

John continued: “And, you know, when they call, you’re just like, ‘Wow. Like, how far (Matthew has) come with this sport. It’s unreal.”

The St. Louis Blues selected Matthew in the sixth round, 170th overall, in the 2023 NHL Draft. The family went to Nashville and saw it first-hand. John said they knew the Blues were a possibility, but “the reason why we went to the draft was because Tampa Bay told him to bring his skates, so you know there’s interest there.”

“So we’re like, ‘We better go,” Christina added.

“It’s surreal, right?” John continued. “You just think of all the work … You think of all the work that we did, all the work, his grandparents, his brother and sister, and his friends.

“One thing I’ll give Matthew: he surrounded himself with good people. He really has good people around. You can’t name them all, but that’s one thing he did right, is he surrounded himself with very good people.”

Good people attract good people.

John paused before answering: “Yeah.”

“Just seeing his dreams come true in that moment,” sister Stephanie remembered. “There was a point where I was … I don’t even know, but I was getting a little nervous. I was like, ‘What’s happening over here?’ When they finally called his name and you see that relief it’s kind of a blur. But, at the same time, it sticks with you. You see all his hard work. At that point, it was worth it.”

“Me and Matthew would always grow up watching the draft,” Josh added. “That was always our thing. We love the draft, and to be there and for him to be a part of it was surreal, and when I came to that moment where his name got called it’s something I’ll never forget, ever. For St. Louis picking him — and I grew up a Boston fan — the first thing I joked about was when St. Louis beat Boston. It was a dream come true seeing my older brother get drafted.”

“When we were leaving,” Christina continued, “we were out at the corner, and there was a group of guys also drafted as well. And I see a man walk by, and he went through the crowd … and I see him go over to tap Matthew.

“And I said, ‘Johnny, who is that guy? I know him. I’ve seen him before.’ And he’s like, ‘Oh, that’s Shane Doan.’ We asked Matthew, “What did he say to you?”

John, now: “(Doan) said, ‘Congratulations. We’ll be watching you.’”

“I don’t know if he just said that randomly, but to Matthew, that meant a lot,” Christina said.

Last spring, at a Buffalo Sabres playoff game to cheer on son Josh, Shane saw Matthew in the crowd. He walked over, tapped Matthew on the shoulder and said hello.

“It meant a lot to Matthew that he just found him in the crowd, tapped him and said that,” Christina added.

“He went out of his way to get a hold of him,” John emphasized. “It wasn’t just by fluke. He went out of his way to talk to this kid.”

Since Matthew has been in hospital, Doan has reached out several times to make sure the family is okay and offer whatever help is necessary.

John and Christina also wanted to recognize Matthew’s girlfriend, Alexa. There is a joke that the “official” relationship is four years, but they’ve known each other longer than that. She carries with her a scrapbook of great photos from their times together.

“So Alexa’s our special angel,” Christina said. “I met her at hockey. She came to support and watch Matthew. And ever since that date, she’s been part of the family. We had just met, but we were going on a road trip right away to Ottawa so she got a crash course into the family. Her family is Matthew’s family, too. Her dad’s one of his best friends. They’re so supportive and (Matthew) loves her so much.

“And I am so thankful, so thankful, so thankful for everyone and to share the story. If we can get prayers, more prayers for Matthew, it would mean so much to us.”

Last word to Matthew’s sister Stephanie.

“He brought light everywhere he went. He brought noise, but the best type of noise. He’s so humorous, and that’s something we hope and pray we can hear again. And I believe that we will.”
