stories.title: What would a Canada-EU energy alliance look like?
stories.summary: Calgary — Canada has the potential to bolster Europe's energy security through a new alliance, but experts say it doesn't necessarily mean tankers crossing the Atlantic Ocean laden with oil or liquefied natural gas.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
CALGARY — Canada has the potential to bolster Europe’s energy security through a new alliance, but experts say it doesn’t necessarily mean tankers crossing the Atlantic Ocean laden with oil or liquefied natural gas.

Prime Minister Mark Carney was in Strasbourg, France, this week where he and European Union leadership discussed strengthening ties on several fronts amid strained relations with the United States.

“Europe is in a precarious situation on multiple fronts,” said Werner Antweiler, an economist at the University of British Columbia.

The European Union has historically relied on Russian energy imports, but pivoted to other sources following that country’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Middle Eastern supplies filled some of that gap until the United States and Israel launched their war against Iran in February, crimping shipments out of the Persian Gulf. The United States itself is a major exporter of LNG to Europe, but U.S. President Donald Trump has thrown global trade into disarray.

Canada has pipelines and port infrastructure to export oil and gas from the West Coast to Asia. Not so in the East.

“There’s nothing imminent in the short-term that’s ready to physically take the oil and gas easily off the East Coast to Europe,” said R.J. Johnston, director of energy and natural resources policy at the University of Calgary’s School of Public Policy.

“No doubt that will take time, even with the new regulatory guidelines and additional public-sector support that seems to be available for those projects.”

There are options in the meantime, though.

European companies have the ability to secure a stable gas supply from Canada through what’s known as swap contracts, where a cargo headed from British Columbia to Asia, for instance, could be traded with another one half a world away. Earlier this year, two German companies signed agreements to buy liquefied natural gas from the Ksi Lisims LNG plant planned for the northern B.C. coast.

“The players that have been investing in LNG out there are really more trading oriented, so they can pursue things like swaps and moving cargoes between the Atlantic and the Pacific basins within their larger portfolio,” Johnston said.

Dynamics in the oil market are different, but Antweiler said there could be a more general “reshuffling” of supply: Canada adding to the broader market, freeing up barrels for Europe that meet its stringent environmental standards.

This summer, Alberta Premier Danielle Smith and Ontario Premier Doug Ford floated a plan called the Northern Shield Energy Corridor to ship Alberta crude to refineries Sarnia, Ont., with the potential of opening up new export paths via the Atlantic.

Antweiler does not see the European situation being much of a boost for that concept.

“European demand alone will not see such a project come to fruition,” he said, calling it “a value proposition to all of Eastern Canada that’s still relying on U.S. and other imports.”

Johnston said it’s unclear whether a European player would want to commit to a project that would take tens of billions of dollars to build and take years to complete.

He said Asia remains the more promising avenue for Canada to diversify its exports.

“We do have existing oil and gas infrastructure and exports to Asia. There’s more coming, and the demand signal in Asia is much more clear,” he said.

Both Europe and Asia want to find more reliable sources to meet their current needs, but Johnston said the growth projections for Europe are much softer.

There are other avenues for Canada to boost its energy trade with Europe beyond fossil fuels.

Antweiler said biofuels and hydrogen could be promising as Europe prioritizes low-carbon fuels. With the European Union’s ability to enrich uranium, Johnston cites Canada’s abundance of that raw resource as another opportunity to supplant Russian imports.

With the European Union’s ambition to become the world’s “electro-powered continent” — increasing its energy consumption to 46 per cent electric from 23 per cent by 2040 — critical minerals are also bound to play a major role.

A report last month from Clean Energy Canada laid out how Canada can seize that opportunity. Among other things, it recommended that Canada focus on trade in six minerals that are most crucial to electrification: cobalt, copper, graphite, lithium, nickel and rare earth elements.

“Critical minerals are really the new oil in this economy that’s emerging, which will be largely electrified,” said Rachel Doran, executive director of Clean Energy Canada.

Europe aims to produce just 10 per cent of the minerals it needs domestically, relying heavily on exports. Canada has made some headway in tapping that market, Doran said, but more needs to be done to sew up firm financing, offtake and investment agreements.

“The electrification economy is still something that we’re shifting towards. And maybe in North America, we see this as further off than in some other places globally where that transformation is a bit further advanced and people are seeing it in their day-to-day lives,” Doran said.

“I think it’s easy to maybe bet on what you know… We really need to keep an eye on the prize: where those countries are going and the kinds of materials they’re going to want from us.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 18, 2026.

Lauren Krugel, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Odds of an interest rate hike from Bank of Canada this year have jumped
stories.summary: Ottawa — Traders are increasingly betting that the Bank of Canada could end its string of interest rate holds and deliver a hike as early as next month.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
By Craig Lord, The Canadian Press

Posted September 18, 2026 4:00 am.

Last Updated September 18, 2026 5:30 am.

Ottawa — Traders are increasingly betting that the Bank of Canada could end its string of interest rate holds and deliver a hike as early as next month.

While many economists remain unconvinced that the central bank will raise the cost of borrowing this year, concerns that inflation could become a more persistent thorn than first thought have some pencilling in a tightening cycle to start in early 2027.

The U.S. Federal Reserve broke its own stand-pat stance and delivered the United States’ first rate hike in more than three years on Wednesday in an effort to rein in inflationary pressures bubbling up south of the border.

The Bank of Canada has sat comfortably on the sidelines for nearly a year now, content to leave its policy rate unchanged at 2.25 per cent as it waits to see how the economy and inflation will adjust to a series of shocks.

In the days leading up to each of the Bank of Canada’s six meetings so far in 2026, financial market odds have overwhelmingly been in favour of rate holds.

Before the central bank’s Sept. 2 decision to leave the policy rate unchanged, odds of a hold were pegged at 94 per cent, according to Lseg Data & Analytics.

With over a month to go until the Bank of Canada’s next decision on Oct. 28, markets now see that meeting as a coin flip. Odds have fluctuated sharply over the past few weeks, but stood narrowly in favour of a hike as of Thursday afternoon.

Claire Fan, senior economist at RBC, said bond market pricing can be viewed as something of a consensus expectation for central bank decisions and also as a barometer for how market participants are viewing fresh economic data.

Odds had already been titled in favour of a Fed hike but soared after the U.S. inflation data release a few days earlier, she noted.

In the Bank of Canada’s case, the shift in odds toward a possible October hike are likely a reflection of persistently high global energy prices tied to the war in Iran, Fan said.

The Bank of Canada’s governing council was worried late last month that oil prices were staying higher for longer, according to Wednesday’s release of the summary of deliberations that led to its Sept. 2 rate decision.

While there have so far been few signs outside of airfares that high fuel costs are spreading beyond the gas pumps, the central bank’s top decisionmakers agreed that the longer prices remain high, the greater the risk to inflation.

“If there’s one thing that’s really causing the pricing of the October meeting … it’s oil prices,” Fan said.

Market expectations for future Bank of Canada hikes are also reflected in longer-term bond yields.

Governing council also noted rising global bond yields in the summary of deliberations. Much of those recent increases have been tied to concerns over U.S. sovereign debt, though monetary policymakers noted some spillover into Government of Canada bonds, too.

When market expectations turn toward rate hikes, bond yields rise in turn. Fan said that reflects markets “pricing in” some of the expected tightening from the Bank of Canada.

Lenders use bond yields as benchmarks for mortgages and other long-term consumer loans.

Because rising bond yields make borrowing more expensive for Canadians, that can also take some of the pressure off the central bank to raise rates, said Randall Bartlett, deputy chief economist at Desjardins.

“In a sense, it does provide a bit of wiggle room for the bank in a more elevated inflation environment because some of the tightening of financial conditions is being done for it,” he said.

Both Bartlett and Fan said they expect the Bank of Canada will remain on the sidelines for the rest of the year before delivering a rate hike in the first quarter of 2027.

Bartlett said that while inflation risks are rising, so too are threats to growth from a re-escalating tariff dispute with the United States. Weaker growth prospects help take some of the steam out of inflation, giving the central bank the ability to be patient before adjusting the policy rate.

Stephen Brown, chief North America economist at Capital Economics, said in a note to clients Thursday that the Bank of Canada will “inevitably upgrade its inflation forecasts” to account for elevated oil price projections when it publishes its quarterly updated outlook at the end of next month.

Brown noted the central bank will also get a look at additional data for inflation, the labour market and gross domestic product before its next rate decision.

The bank will also release its own surveys of Canadian consumers and businesses, which Brown said he expects will show deteriorating confidence in the economy and rises in short-term inflation expectations.

“Our base case is that the bank will not hike in October, though it will likely be a close call,” he said.

Posted September 18, 2026 4:00 am.

Ottawa — Traders are increasingly betting that the Bank of Canada could end its string of interest rate holds and deliver a hike as early as next month.

While many economists remain unconvinced that the central bank will raise the cost of borrowing this year, concerns that inflation could become a more persistent thorn than first thought have some pencilling in a tightening cycle to start in early 2027.

The U.S. Federal Reserve broke its own stand-pat stance and delivered the United States’ first rate hike in more than three years on Wednesday in an effort to rein in inflationary pressures bubbling up south of the border.

The Bank of Canada has sat comfortably on the sidelines for nearly a year now, content to leave its policy rate unchanged at 2.25 per cent as it waits to see how the economy and inflation will adjust to a series of shocks.
In the days leading up to each of the Bank of Canada’s six meetings so far in 2026, financial market odds have overwhelmingly been in favour of rate holds.
Before the central bank’s Sept. 2 decision to leave the policy rate unchanged, odds of a hold were pegged at 94 per cent, according to Lseg Data & Analytics.

With over a month to go until the Bank of Canada’s next decision on Oct. 28, markets now see that meeting as a coin flip. Odds have fluctuated sharply over the past few weeks, but stood narrowly in favour of a hike as of Thursday afternoon.

Claire Fan, senior economist at RBC, said bond market pricing can be viewed as something of a consensus expectation for central bank decisions and also as a barometer for how market participants are viewing fresh economic data.
Odds had already been titled in favour of a Fed hike but soared after the U.S. inflation data release a few days earlier, she noted.
In the Bank of Canada’s case, the shift in odds toward a possible October hike are likely a reflection of persistently high global energy prices tied to the war in Iran, Fan said.

The Bank of Canada’s governing council was worried late last month that oil prices were staying higher for longer, according to Wednesday’s release of the summary of deliberations that led to its Sept. 2 rate decision.

While there have so far been few signs outside of airfares that high fuel costs are spreading beyond the gas pumps, the central bank’s top decisionmakers agreed that the longer prices remain high, the greater the risk to inflation.
“If there’s one thing that’s really causing the pricing of the October meeting … it’s oil prices,” Fan said.
Market expectations for future Bank of Canada hikes are also reflected in longer-term bond yields.

Governing council also noted rising global bond yields in the summary of deliberations. Much of those recent increases have been tied to concerns over U.S. sovereign debt, though monetary policymakers noted some spillover into Government of Canada bonds, too.
When market expectations turn toward rate hikes, bond yields rise in turn. Fan said that reflects markets “pricing in” some of the expected tightening from the Bank of Canada.
Lenders use bond yields as benchmarks for mortgages and other long-term consumer loans.

Because rising bond yields make borrowing more expensive for Canadians, that can also take some of the pressure off the central bank to raise rates, said Randall Bartlett, deputy chief economist at Desjardins.
“In a sense, it does provide a bit of wiggle room for the bank in a more elevated inflation environment because some of the tightening of financial conditions is being done for it,” he said.
Both Bartlett and Fan said they expect the Bank of Canada will remain on the sidelines for the rest of the year before delivering a rate hike in the first quarter of 2027.

Bartlett said that while inflation risks are rising, so too are threats to growth from a re-escalating tariff dispute with the United States. Weaker growth prospects help take some of the steam out of inflation, giving the central bank the ability to be patient before adjusting the policy rate.

Stephen Brown, chief North America economist at Capital Economics, said in a note to clients Thursday that the Bank of Canada will “inevitably upgrade its inflation forecasts” to account for elevated oil price projections when it publishes its quarterly updated outlook at the end of next month.
Brown noted the central bank will also get a look at additional data for inflation, the labour market and gross domestic product before its next rate decision.

The bank will also release its own surveys of Canadian consumers and businesses, which Brown said he expects will show deteriorating confidence in the economy and rises in short-term inflation expectations.
“Our base case is that the bank will not hike in October, though it will likely be a close call,” he said.

stories.title: Parole hearing today for Hamed Shafia, convicted of murdering his sisters and woman
stories.summary: A man convicted of murdering his three sisters and another woman more than 17 years ago is set to have a parole hearing today.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
In the time leading up to the murder of his sisters and stepmother, Hamed Shafia quashed his remorse by telling himself he had no choice and was simply going along with his father’s actions, he told a parole hearing Friday.

In reality, he was doing more than simply going along with it, said Shafia, who was 18 at the time of the killings. “I was aiding him in doing these things,” he said.

“So it was this back and forth in my mind, this game I was playing between moral obligation and then this whole notion that, ‘OK, I have to go through with it, this is honour,’ and all of that stuff.”

Shafia, now 34, was pressed about his beliefs and his relationships with his surviving family members as he sought two escorted temporary absences from the medium-security prison where he is serving a life sentence.

In the end, a Parole Board of Canada panel agreed Shafia should be allowed a brief visit to a minimum-security facility but rejected his request for another escorted absence to a mosque in Kingston, Ont.

“You’ve made a lot of progress. You’re moving in the right direction. You have gained insight ... but there is still work there to be done,” panel member Mike Bossio told him, stressing the need for a gradual approach.

The panel is expected to release a more detailed written decision at a later date.

Shafia and his parents were found guilty in January 2012 of four counts of first-degree murder in the deaths of his teenage sisters and his father’s first wife in a polygamous marriage. First-degree murder carries an automatic life sentence with no chance of parole for 25 years.

The bodies of Zainab, 19, Sahar, 17, and Geeti, 13, and 52-year-old Rona Amir Mohammad were found in a car at the bottom of the Rideau Canal in Kingston in June 2009.

The trial judge had described the killings as being motivated by the Shafia family’s “twisted concept of honour,” and their view that the girls had “shamed” the family by dating and acting out.

The family had immigrated to Canada from Afghanistan and settled in Montreal, where the father was a successful businessman.

After his conviction, the younger Shafia argued that he was too young to be tried as an adult in the case, but Ontario’s top court rejected his appeal. The Supreme Court of Canada declined to hear the case in 2017.

On Friday, Shafia agreed he “dragged his feet” in taking accountability, and pointed to his growing relationship with his surviving siblings, particularly his two sisters, as the catalyst that helped him accept responsibility and work toward change.

Growing up, Shafia spent most of his time with his parents, especially his father, and had only “surface-level” conversations with his now-deceased sisters, he said.

The family had been in Canada just under two years when he and his parents committed the murders, he said. For the first four to six months, Shafia didn’t go to school; after that, he spent his time in school or at his father’s work, he said.

“I was closer to my father than I was with my sisters. I spent most of my time with my father and only a fraction of that with my siblings and my stepmother. ... Simply put, he had more of an influence because I spent more time with him,” and there was no reason to question those beliefs, he said.

In the mid-2010s, however, Shafia began having deeper conversations with his remaining siblings, hearing about their feelings and their experiences “constantly being told that they’re in the bottom tier in the hierarchy,” he said.

“It put a face to this whole situation,” he said. “Before, it was just, ‘Hey, this is how things are and you being the eldest son should act this way.’ Whereas now it’s more that I understand who I’m acting against — it’s my sisters.”

Now, Shafia said he sees the beliefs he had in his youth as a way to control women, justified by misrepresenting religion.

His current view is that everyone is their own person, and no one should exert control over others, he said.

At one point in the hearing, Bossio asked Shafia what he would do if, while visiting the mosque on an escorted absence, someone recognized him and expressed disapproval. Shafia responded that he would simply walk away.

“It’s not hard for me to walk away from a person who quite frankly, has all right to not be fond of me. If I was a member of society, I wouldn’t be fond of someone who committed these crimes,” he said.

The board member replied that he had hoped Shafia would mention asking for support.

Shafia’s parole officer said he has completed several programs while in prison, including a moderate intensity violence prevention program.

He has also engaged in one-on-one meetings with the prison’s imam, focusing on extremist and misogynistic views of honour and women, “all with positive reports,” the officer said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 18, 2026.

stories.title: Shooter-for-hire attacks linked to Toronto police constable’s licence plate searches, Project South documents allege
stories.summary: Constable Timothy Barnhardt was allegedly paid by criminal figures to search addresses that were later relayed to hired gunmen
stories.author: Colin Freeze
stories.content:
Multiple shooter-for-hire attacks in the Greater Toronto Area last year allegedly trace back to Toronto Police Constable Timothy Barnhardt, who investigators say repeatedly used police databases to leak information to suspected organized crime figures, according to warrant applications that led to the Project South takedown.

The newly released materials allege that while he was being surveilled by authorities, Constable Barnhardt accepted money from criminal figures in exchange for making “numerous” licence plate queries. Those criminal figures went on to relay addresses linked to the plate searches to hired gunmen, who were paid to intimidate people and settle scores, the warrant applications allege.

“Barnhardt routinely abused his position as a police officer by selling confidential database information to criminal associates in exchange for cash,” wrote police Constable Antonio D’Onofrio, who signed an affidavit related to the 2025 search-warrant application materials.

“Barnhardt explicitly expressed indifference to the potential harm caused by the misuse of this information.”

Jail guard fears for his life after alleged botched hit that sparked Project South probe, court hears

The additional details of the allegations against Constable Barnhardt, who has been named as a central figure in Project South, were released in court documents this week following an application in Ontario Superior Court by a consortium of media partners, including The Globe and Mail. Those files included what are known as information to obtain documents, which investigators use to get judicial authorization to conduct searches and make arrests.

While some of the content of those documents was released in July , portions were placed under a publication ban as the Crown and media outlets argued over whether their release should be shielded to protect fair trial rights.

Project South was sparked by the alleged attempted murder of a corrections officer at his home in June, 2025.

The warrants, which authorized police search efforts, were issued after that attack and before raids in February that led to charges against seven serving Toronto Police officers including Constable Barnhardt, one retired officer and nearly 20 civilians.

Investigators have alleged that Constable Barnhardt was paid to use police databases to leak information about the corrections officer to alleged organized crime figure Brian Da Costa. Both Constable Barnhardt and Mr. Da Costa are in jail awaiting trial on an array of charges.

Key transcripts that led to Project South probe will remain under publication ban, Ontario Superior Court rules

Justice Laura Bird ruled Wednesday that some transcripts of key recordings that led to the Project South takedown will remain under a publication ban, concluding that inflammatory comments attributed to Constable Barnhardt would “deeply offend” the public and create an indelible impression on potential jurors.

However, Justice Bird lifted the ban on previously unreported evidence investigators gathered against Constable Barnhardt, including details of his alleged interactions with Mr. Da Costa, who police say is the key civilian figure in Project South. The ITO materials allege that Constable Barnhardt did many of his licence plate searches at the behest of Mr. Da Costa, an accused drug dealer.

The warrant materials allege the two were often spotted on surveillance together, at times exchanging documents, capturing images on their phones or even sitting inside a police cruiser that had a data terminal inside of it.

“While Barnhardt explained the meaning of the police query results, Da Costa ultimately handed Barnhardt multiple $100 Canadian bills which he placed in the front pocket of his police vest,” the newly released documents say.

Toronto lawyers Jason Dos Santos, who represents Constable Barnhardt, and Craig Bottomley, who represents Mr. Da Costa, declined to comment on the case.

Cases of police officers facing charges in Project South probe expected to go directly to trial in Superior Court

The information to obtain documents contain unproven allegations that have not been tested in court. ITOs don’t necessarily result in criminal charges and several of the people named in the documents do not face charges.

Constable Barnhardt’s alleged search of the corrections officer’s licence plate “was not his only improper query,” Constable D’Onofrio wrote. “The investigation revealed that he has conducted numerous such queries, for payment, at the request of various people in the criminal underworld. In many instances, the person who was queried was victimized in serious offence (e.g. shootings, extortions) shortly after the query.”

In the summer of 2025, authorities got authorizations to run wiretaps and surveillance on Constable Barnhardt; they also monitored his computer usage. On July 17, he allegedly did another plate search. Three days later, shots were fired at a home linked to the plate at 3 a.m., with a man awakened “by the sounds of gunshots,“ the released records say, adding that a bullet casing was on the floor.

Then, ON Aug. 6, at 3:07 am, there was a shooting involving 20 bullets fired into a gambler’s home two days after an alleged query of that address by Constable Barnhardt. The released materials describe the shocked resident as a man who owed money to “Italian Organized Crime, Hells Angels, and the Towing Industry.”

Former Toronto police officer charged in Project South probe gets 10-month conditional sentence

Constable Barnhardt allegedly searched more plates in September. The released materials say that on Sept. 6, shooters “fired at the vehicles, front door and windows” of a Vaughan home. On Sept. 10, another gunman, later arrested, fired 13 rounds through the front door of another house. And on Sept. 24, another gunman discharged six bullets into another residence.

More shootings and other crimes came to light. The released materials say police “completed a duty to warn” and conducted safety planning with some of the perceived targets, including people who newly moved into homes that gangsters were targeting based on outdated information.

In recent months, Toronto police have increasingly expressed concern about alleged shooters-for-hire networks. Toronto Police Chief Myron Demkiw is petitioning Parliament for new laws to enable police data searches of devices seized from suspected criminals.

Police say that an early-morning police raid in June that left a Toronto police officer dead, and that targeted suspects linked to a shooting at the U.S. consulate in the city, is connected to a wider probe into a network of shooters-for-hire.

A source with knowledge of the investigation previously told The Globe this network is also responsible for shooting at buildings that belong to Canadian waste giant GFL Environmental, as well as private residences and tow-truck companies. The Globe did not name the source because they were not authorized to discuss the case.

While some of the content of those documents was released in July , portions were placed under a publication ban as the Crown and media outlets argued over whether their release should be shielded to protect fair trial rights.
Project South was sparked by the alleged attempted murder of a corrections officer at his home in June, 2025.

The warrants, which authorized police search efforts, were issued after that attack and before raids in February that led to charges against seven serving Toronto Police officers including Constable Barnhardt, one retired officer and nearly 20 civilians.

Investigators have alleged that Constable Barnhardt was paid to use police databases to leak information about the corrections officer to alleged organized crime figure Brian Da Costa. Both Constable Barnhardt and Mr. Da Costa are in jail awaiting trial on an array of charges.
Key transcripts that led to Project South probe will remain under publication ban, Ontario Superior Court rules

Justice Laura Bird ruled Wednesday that some transcripts of key recordings that led to the Project South takedown will remain under a publication ban, concluding that inflammatory comments attributed to Constable Barnhardt would “deeply offend” the public and create an indelible impression on potential jurors.

However, Justice Bird lifted the ban on previously unreported evidence investigators gathered against Constable Barnhardt, including details of his alleged interactions with Mr. Da Costa, who police say is the key civilian figure in Project South. The ITO materials allege that Constable Barnhardt did many of his licence plate searches at the behest of Mr. Da Costa, an accused drug dealer.

The warrant materials allege the two were often spotted on surveillance together, at times exchanging documents, capturing images on their phones or even sitting inside a police cruiser that had a data terminal inside of it.

“While Barnhardt explained the meaning of the police query results, Da Costa ultimately handed Barnhardt multiple $100 Canadian bills which he placed in the front pocket of his police vest,” the newly released documents say.
Toronto lawyers Jason Dos Santos, who represents Constable Barnhardt, and Craig Bottomley, who represents Mr. Da Costa, declined to comment on the case.
Cases of police officers facing charges in Project South probe expected to go directly to trial in Superior Court

The information to obtain documents contain unproven allegations that have not been tested in court. ITOs don’t necessarily result in criminal charges and several of the people named in the documents do not face charges.

Constable Barnhardt’s alleged search of the corrections officer’s licence plate “was not his only improper query,” Constable D’Onofrio wrote. “The investigation revealed that he has conducted numerous such queries, for payment, at the request of various people in the criminal underworld. In many instances, the person who was queried was victimized in serious offence (e.g. shootings, extortions) shortly after the query.”

In the summer of 2025, authorities got authorizations to run wiretaps and surveillance on Constable Barnhardt; they also monitored his computer usage. On July 17, he allegedly did another plate search. Three days later, shots were fired at a home linked to the plate at 3 a.m., with a man awakened “by the sounds of gunshots,“ the released records say, adding that a bullet casing was on the floor.

Then, ON Aug. 6, at 3:07 am, there was a shooting involving 20 bullets fired into a gambler’s home two days after an alleged query of that address by Constable Barnhardt. The released materials describe the shocked resident as a man who owed money to “Italian Organized Crime, Hells Angels, and the Towing Industry.”
Former Toronto police officer charged in Project South probe gets 10-month conditional sentence

Constable Barnhardt allegedly searched more plates in September. The released materials say that on Sept. 6, shooters “fired at the vehicles, front door and windows” of a Vaughan home. On Sept. 10, another gunman, later arrested, fired 13 rounds through the front door of another house. And on Sept. 24, another gunman discharged six bullets into another residence.

More shootings and other crimes came to light. The released materials say police “completed a duty to warn” and conducted safety planning with some of the perceived targets, including people who newly moved into homes that gangsters were targeting based on outdated information.

In recent months, Toronto police have increasingly expressed concern about alleged shooters-for-hire networks. Toronto Police Chief Myron Demkiw is petitioning Parliament for new laws to enable police data searches of devices seized from suspected criminals.

Police say that an early-morning police raid in June that left a Toronto police officer dead, and that targeted suspects linked to a shooting at the U.S. consulate in the city, is connected to a wider probe into a network of shooters-for-hire.

A source with knowledge of the investigation previously told The Globe this network is also responsible for shooting at buildings that belong to Canadian waste giant GFL Environmental, as well as private residences and tow-truck companies. The Globe did not name the source because they were not authorized to discuss the case.

stories.title: Ford’s praise of Chow was not an endorsement, his office says
stories.summary: The Ontario Premier told reporters to ‘read between the lines’ when asked if he’s endorsing anyone for Toronto mayor
stories.author: Laura Stone
stories.content:
Ontario Premier Doug Ford’s office says he did not endorse Olivia Chow for Toronto mayor, a day after he publicly praised their relationship and offered his support.

Mr. Ford’s office issued a brief statement Thursday evening seeking to tone down his previous comments. More than 50 candidates signed up to run for the mayoral position in the municipal election on Oct. 26.

“We would like to clarify that Premier Ford did not endorse Olivia Chow and will not endorse any candidate in the Toronto mayoral race,” said Jennifer Cunliffe, a spokesperson for his office.

“The Premier has demonstrated that he will work with anyone no matter their political stripe to advance the interests of the people of Ontario.”

On Wednesday, Mr. Ford praised his working relationship with Ms. Chow, who was first elected in June, 2023. He has often spoken of his positive relationship with the mayor, despite, before she was elected, warning she would be an “unmitigated disaster” for the city.

Ford government says cities must not deviate from Buy Ontario rules

The two appeared together at a press conference Wednesday at the opening of a new biomanufacturing facility in Toronto.

Mr. Ford also spoke about giving the city billions as part of what was called a new deal for Toronto announced in November, 2023. It was intended to help the cash-strapped city.

The Ontario Premier was asked directly by a reporter about endorsements in the Toronto mayoral race.

“I just want to say the Mayor and I have a phenomenal relationship. Phenomenal. And we’ve given the City of Toronto more money than they’ve ever seen in their lives, over $9-billion,” he said.

“We’re going to continue supporting the Mayor. She’s doing an incredible job. So, read between the lines.”

Sanofi inaugurates Toronto facility that will produce seasonal flu vaccines for Canadians

Those comments raised the ire of Ms. Chow’s main rival in the race, Councillor Brad Bradford. Several of the Ford government’s ex-staffers are helping Mr. Bradford’s campaign, including the Premier’s former executive director of communications, Laryssa Waler. Kory Teneycke, Mr. Ford’s campaign manager for his three victories, also supports Mr. Bradford.

In a social media post on Wednesday, Mr. Bradford declared that Mr. Ford had endorsed Ms. Chow, alleging that she has “never stopped Doug Ford from doing exactly what he wanted to do.” He pointed to Ms. Chow muting her opposition to the province’s redevelopment of Ontario Place, and abandoning her previous campaign pledge of tearing down the eastern portion of the Gardiner Expressway. The province took over financial responsibility for the Gardiner and the Don Valley Parkway to ease the city’s financial burden as part of the new deal.

On Thursday, Mr. Bradford’s campaign struck a more conciliatory tone.

“As Mayor, Brad will have a productive relationship with Premier Ford. The Premier is not only Premier of Ontario, he is a resident of Toronto,” Mark Pelayo, a spokesperson for Mr. Bradford’s campaign, said in a statement.

“Brad has committed to doing a line-by-line review of the city’s finances to find out why Olivia Chow raised taxes nearly 20 per cent despite record funding from the province. The last mayor to do such a review was Mayor Rob Ford.”

On Thursday, Ms. Chow’s campaign didn’t directly address Mr. Ford’s statement, but said the two work well together.

“As Mayor, Olivia Chow has a good working relationship with the Premier, securing record investment in Toronto,” campaign spokesperson Shirven Rezvany said.

On Wednesday, Ms. Chow spoke about the importance of working together as a team, noting all three levels of government came together earlier this year to announce new subway cars will be built in Thunder Bay.

“At this very uncertain, stressful time, in the global turbulence, disruptive trade conversation that’s happening, the Team Canada approach, working together united, we are stronger and we’re proving it right now,” she said.

stories.title: London civic election: Ward 9 all-candidates debate
stories.summary: Six candidates are running to be London city councillor for west-end Ward 9, which includes Byron and Lambeth.
stories.author: Ryan Goodison
stories.content:
Six candidates are running to be London city councillor for west-end Ward 9, which includes Byron and Lambeth. LFP reporter Ryan Goodison was there as five of them debated at the London Public Library’s Byron branch on Thursday night:

Anna Hopkins (incumbent): 70, Ward 9 city councillor

Tammy Abi-Khalil: 39, works in a constituency office

Matt Millar: 41, farmer, IT specialist and software developer

Luke Thomas: 36, founder of Healthy Eats

Veronica Warner: 57, salon owner

Dino Jose (absent)

A crowd of more than 60 people came out to the Byron library branch on Thursday night, with five of the six candidates attending the Urban League-organized debate.

In her opening statement, Hopkins said that from her debut as a councillor in 2014, she has been committed to being transparent and accountable to her constituents.

“There is much more to do, and I’m ready to keep serving residents and moving our community forward. Supporting economic growth, creating jobs and re-inventing our downtown will be the next council’s priorities,” Hopkins said.

If re-elected, Hopkins would be serving her fourth consecutive term as councillor for Ward 9. In the most recent election, in 2022, she won with roughly 62 per cent of the vote, a total of 4,281 votes overall.

Warner spoke about her experience as a business owner in Ward 9, as well as her experience providing apprenticeships to students throughout the year. When Warner ran for Ward 9 councillor in 2022, she received 323 votes, finishing with 4.7 per cent of the total.

Millar told the crowd he was running because he was “tired of the city trying to make us fit their plans instead of making plans that fit us.” He previously ran for Ward 9 councillor in 2018, finishing second to Hopkins with 2,355 first-round votes when the city used ranked-choice voting.

Thomas said he was running to offer more accountability for the ward. Abi-Khalil spoke in her opening statement about her experience working in a constituency office and helping people navigate the different levels of government.

Development was a common theme Thursday night, with candidates facing multiple questions on different projects, such as supportive housing, recent developments in Ward 9 and if the city should continue to prioritize downtown.

Ward 9 is a relatively huge ward, in terms of land, and includes Lambeth and Byron.

In a question about whether a new supportive housing project was proposed in a neighbourhood where many opposed it, Hopkins said she would need to know the specifics of the plan when looking at this scenario. But she mentioned she’s heard from other councillors about the need to spread these units out across the city.

Thomas said the most important thing was to listen to residents in the area and get all the information on a project before approval.

Millar said he doesn’t believe a developer or a “bureaucrat” from downtown should get to decide what the neighbourhood should have to live with. He said if a project came to a neighbourhood that didn’t want it, it would be his job to voice concerns for the people living there.

In response to a question about whether they believe downtown London should continue to be a citywide investment, Abi-Khalil said that where public funding or incentives are requested, there should be a clear public benefit in a realistic plan.

Hopkins said the city has already made investments in downtown and should continue to build on those same investments. She said that in order for the 10-year downtown plan to work, which was approved by the current council, city hall has to spend money there.

Warner said the city needs to invest in core areas, which are not only the places where people gather, but they’re also one of the first things newcomers look for when deciding to move.

There was a question from the audience about why there have been so many recent developments in Byron and how candidates would approach new building in the area. Hopkins said she assesses every development proposal on its merits, looking closely at infrastructure, capacity and traffic.

Millar said the problem is plans are approved before proper infrastructure is in place, when he says it should be the other way around. Abi-Khalil expressed a similar thought, saying city council needs to prioritize infrastructure first.

“Obviously, London’s growing. We can’t stop that. But there needs to be proper planning done and we need a city council that works together,” Abi-Khalil said.

Voters will head to the polls to elect their next city council on Oct. 26, with several advance voting days on Oct. 1, 3, 8, and 10.

There are 81 candidates running for London mayor and the 14 ward councillor positions – read what most of them have to say, in their own words, right here .

stories.title: Ontario helps family doctors learn and stay in the province
stories.summary: The province of Ontario is helping more future family doctors learn and practice locally.
stories.author: Lauren Stallone
stories.content:
The province of Ontario is helping more future family doctors learn and practice locally.

“I am pleased to announce that our government is investing $220 million to create a new stream of the Ontario Learn and Stay grant for medical education and applications open today,” announced Nolan Quinn, Minister of Colleges, and Universities.

Launched in spring of 2023, the ‘Ontario Learn and Stay Grant’ provides funding for students in priority post-secondary programs in high need areas.

“Expanding the number of medical seats is only part of the equation,” said Quinn. “We also need to ensure talented students can access the education and training they need to become the family doctors of tomorrow.”

The province said the expanded program could help up to 2 million people become or remain attached to primary care.

“Recipients will practice comprehensive family medicine for at least five years anywhere in Ontario,” said Quinn. “That means more doctors who are trained in Ontario will stay in Ontario.”

The increased investment will support four cohorts of future family doctors, totalling more than 2000 medical students.

“We’ve invested over $182 million to train more than 13,300 future health care workers and today we are building on that success,” said Quinn.

Alan Shepard, president of Western University said students across southwestern Ontario will feel the impact of this announcement firsthand.

stories.title: Ontario students return to school amid new rules, expired teacher contracts
stories.summary: Ontario students are back inside classrooms with new requirements around exams, financial literacy and classroom supplies, but a local teachers’ union says the province’s back-to-school messaging is distracting from financial and labour concerns facing public education.
stories.author: Reta Ismail
stories.content:
Ontario students are back inside classrooms with new requirements around exams, financial literacy and classroom supplies, but a local teachers’ union says the province’s back-to-school messaging is distracting from financial and labour concerns facing public education.

Education Minister Paul Calandra outlined several changes for the 2026-27 school year in a letter to Ontario families, including mandatory written exams for students in Grades 9 to 12, a new financial literacy graduation requirement and changes to classroom supply funding.

John Bernans, president of District 11 of the Ontario Secondary School Teachers’ Federation, said the changes are relatively minor compared with the financial pressures facing school boards.

“Really, it’s a distraction,” Bernans said. “I think the minister is trying to distract from the chronic underfunding of education that’s happened since 2018.”

Bernans pointed to what he described as a $22-million deficit at the Thames Valley District School Board, which has been under provincial supervision for about a year and a half.

“The supervisor was supposed to fix everything in terms of the finances, and even with the supervisor, he still can’t make the numbers work,” he said.

The Thames Valley board did not make a representative available for an interview.

The board’s secondary teachers are also working without a new collective agreement after their previous contract expired at the end of August.

Bernans said teachers asked the province to begin bargaining in March, but talks did not begin until June.

“We’re now waiting for a ruling from the Ontario Labour Relations Board about what we can bargain locally and what can be bargained centrally,” Bernans said.

While labour negotiations continue, the London District Catholic School Board says staff are adapting to the changes being introduced by the province.

Mark Santandrea, the London Catholic District School Board’s (Lcdsb) executive superintendent of education, said implementing changes across a large school system can come with challenges, but staff have generally welcomed them.

“So there’s been a few growing pains, I think there always are, but staff are welcoming it,” Santandrea said. “The consistency really helps in communicating with parents and communicating with students.”

Santandrea said the Catholic board’s biggest pressures are not related to the new curriculum, but to rapid enrolment growth and the need for additional space.

“The pressures for us ... are really growth and the number of students and how fast they’re coming to us, and space becomes a big issue for us as we look to accommodate the request for all the students that are coming in,” he said.

Among the province’s other changes this school year, students in Grades 10 will have a financial literacy requirement as part of the Grade 10 Career Studies course to earn their high school diploma.

The province is also introducing a new Kindergarten curriculum focused on foundational skills in literacy, math, science and technology.

History curriculum changes include expanded learning about Black history in Canada in Grades 7, 8 and 10, as well as new learning about the Holocaust in Grade 10.

Elementary teachers will also have direct access to $750 for classroom supplies, while paper report cards will return for students from Kindergarten to Grade 8.

As students settle into the new school year, both local teachers’ unions are working under expired collective agreements, with negotiations continuing at the bargaining table.

Requests for an interview with Education Minister, Paul Calandra were not answered.

stories.title: West Kelowna’s next mayor vows to restore public confidence after cost overruns
stories.summary: Two-term councillor Stephen Johnston has been acclaimed as the city's next mayor after no other candidates came forward for the position.
stories.author: Klaudia Van Emmerik
stories.content:
Municipal elections are still a month away, but residents in West Kelowna already know who will lead their community.

Two-term councillor Stephen Johnston has been acclaimed as the city’s next mayor after no other candidates came forward for the position.

“I’m just so honoured to have this opportunity to serve as the next mayor of West Kelowna,” Johnston told Global News.

Johnston says he will remain focused on key issues such as homelessness, addiction and wildfire resilience.

However, he says restoring public confidence in the city’s government will also be a top priority.

The incoming mayor is currently a member of the council that faced criticism over what some residents described as a lack of transparency and accountability, particularly around major capital projects and cost overruns.

“It’s no secret that we did have a couple projects that went over budget. It was a difficult and challenging time,” Johnston said.

The new city hall and library project came in more than $6 million over budget while the Rose Valley Water Treatment Plant also faced significant public scrutiny, including questions about how a large portion of the project would be financed and repaid by property owners.

West Kelowna resident Jackie Haynes said the city’s recent record raises questions about whether public confidence can be rebuilt.

“Not very, based on the recent past,” Haynes said, when asked how optimistic she is about Johnston restoring the public’s confidence.

“The water treatment plant was a big disappointment for everybody.”

Another resident, Cindy Charters, said she’s more optimistic.

“I think he can restore public confidence,” Charters added.

Following the cost overruns and capital project challenges, the city commissioned an independent review that identified improvements that could be made to its capital project delivery model.

While some changes have been made, Johnston says more are needed, including the budgeting process.

“One of the things I advocated for this year, which we’ve already changed, is historically West Kelowna has never shown budgeted versus actual expenses, and so we’ve got actuals in there,” Johnston said.

Johnston said the changes will provide greater accountability and will be important as council oversees major projects.

“Accountability is very important and for council to be able to follow the budget from conception through to completion of projects is really important,” he said. “We’ve been missing that piece for a long time and so big changes are coming.”

Johnston has spent the week at the Union of BC Municipalities (Ubcm) convention.

He says knowing he will be West Kelowna’s next mayor has already helped him build relationships with provincial politicians and cabinet ministers.

“It’s opened so many doors for me,” Johnston said. “You know, I’ve been bumping into cabinet ministers, MLAs. We’ve been going for coffee, exchanging phone numbers and it’s just been a huge leg up on building those relationships that we’re going to need to compound and grow over the years.”

stories.title: Two Ontario Sikh Temples face lawsuit over $13-million in loans linked to former Liberal MP
stories.summary: Rajvinder Grewal’s law firm allegedly failed to properly execute paperwork associated with the loans
stories.author: Shane Dingman
stories.content:
have been pulled into the widening array of legal and business controversies related to lawyer and former Liberal MP Rajvinder Grewal.

A pair of companies are suing the temples for the return of more than $13-million in loans obtained using the religious groups’ property as collateral. Mr. Grewal’s law firm allegedly failed to properly execute paperwork associated with the loans, a claim that has been repeated in other litigation faced by the former politician. In addition, $250,000 from an alleged cheque fraud connected to his firm was routed to a temple’s bank accounts.

Mr. Grewal and the law firm he founded and named after himself – RSG Law Professional Corporation – are at the centre of a series of civil claims related to lending and real estate development. The collective claims top more than $200-million and some cases involve allegations of fraud. None of the allegations have been tested in court.

Mr. Grewal is also facing disciplinary action from the Law Society of Ontario that could result in the revocation of his licence to practice law; currently he has agreed to an undertaking not to practice while awaiting a procedural hearing over the Lso’s probe against him scheduled for January, 2027.

The civil lawsuit against the temples, or gurdwaras, Sikh Spiritual Centre Toronto (Ssct) and Nanaksar Thath Ishar Darbar, seeks the return of funds lent to them. The suit was filed in September in the Ontario Superior Court of Justice

Both temples are federally registered charities and share some members of their boards of directors, according to public records that are current up to 2024. It is unclear whether the loans were intended to support charitable activities.

The plaintiffs in the case are Ssmt Management Inc. and Oculus Mortgage GP Inc. (which occupy the same office suite in Hamilton), run by Jason A. Waxman. He is also president of Addison Wealth Management Inc., a company that lent money to borrowers connected to other civil cases related to Mr. Grewal. Mr. Waxman didn’t respond to a request for comment.

According to the court filing, the president of both Nanaksar and Sikh Spiritual Centre Toronto is Amarjit Singh Deol, who is also listed as a personal guarantor of the loans. Another guarantor, Gurmail Singh Nirman, is identified as a treasurer and member of the board of directors of Ssct. Joining them as a personal guarantor of the loans is Mr. Grewal, but according to federal charity records he is not a member of either board of directors.

Ssmt claims that on April 25, 2025, it extended a $10-million loan secured against the Sikh Spiritual Centre Toronto. Then on May 20, the original loan was expanded to a $15-million commitment and was also to be registered against the Nanaksar gurdwara property located in Brampton.

Cibc asks court to appoint a receiver to oversee businesses run by lawyer and former MP Raj Grewal

The interest rates were as much as 15 per cent (about $187,500 a month) for the first six months, rising to 24 per cent after that (or about $300,000 a month).

According to the September filing, RSG Law’s owner and operator, Davinder Khattra, was supposed to register the second charge against the Brampton property. However, Ssmt argues that Mr. Khattra never fulfilled that part of the deal, leaving Ssmt vulnerable to arguments that the loan never really existed.

The alleged manipulation of records for loans on land title shows up as a pattern in cases related to RSG Law. The Ontario Land Registry Office has frozen more than 100 properties “in connection with allegations of fraudulent discharges registered,” according to court documents filed by the LSO regarding Mr. Khattra.

Mr. Khattra’s licence to practice law has been suspended by the LSO Tribunal, and his continuing disciplinary case could result in losing his licence.

A preliminary ruling by Justice Frederick L. Myers on Sept. 11 ordered that the Brampton property not be sold or encumbered pending the outcome of a hearing scheduled for mid-January.

“My understanding is that this matter has been resolved,” Mr. Grewal’s lawyer, Simon Bieber of Adair Goldblatt Bieber LLP, said in a Tuesday e-mailed statement.

Maria Naimark of Tyr LLP is representing Ssmt in the claim and while she declined to comment in detail on the case, she said in an e-mailed statement Wednesday that “It has not been resolved,”

However, there are more financial ties between the gurdwaras and RSG Law, according to records spread across multiple court filings.

In the Lso’s application against Mr. Khattra, it included records of payments from RSG Law Professional Corporation’s trust account that showed several large sums of money transferred to the Ssct gurdwara – $250,000 on April 7 and April 10 – and another $250,000 payment to Guru Nanak Darbar, the more common name for the Brampton gurdwara.

In a related matter, another $250,000 that was the proceeds of an alleged cheque fraud against the Bank of Nova Scotia – involving Rajkiran Sidhu, another lawyer connected to Mr. Grewal – was also traced to have been paid to Ssct through RSG Law. Mr. Sidhu is facing disciplinary action at the LSO Tribunal.

Mr. Sidhu alleges in an August affidavit to the LSO that he was the victim of a fraud scheme by someone identifying himself as Parminder Singh, who on April 13 and 14 gave him three cheques totalling $6,095,000. Two of the cheques were from numbered companies that the bank said it could not confirm existed, However, ON April 14, Mr. Sidhu transferred $5,314,000 from his trust account to five parties at his client’s direction.

The bank has traced the funds sent by Mr. Sidhu and has indicated in court records that one of those parties was a company called 16410031 Canada Inc., which received a $1,414,000 wire payment. On the same day, 16410031 wired $1,410,000 to RSG Law’s trust account with instructions to pay that money out to 11 other payees.

One of those payees was Ssct, which received $250,000 of the allegedly fraudulently obtained money.

Lawyers for The Bank of Nova Scotia did not respond to requests for comment, but filings indicate that this money has not been recovered.

stories.title: Construction underway on new northwest Calgary library amid gap in amenities on city outskirts
stories.summary: The new library at the Symons Valley Centre in Calgary's northwest community of Sage Hill is expected to be complete in mid-2028.
stories.author: Adam MacVicar
stories.content:
Shovels, and not just the ceremonial ones, are in the ground on the Symons Valley Centre Library in the northwest community of Sage Hill, as Calgary works to address a gap in amenities in new communities.

Officials from the City of Calgary and Calgary Public Library were on hand Wednesday to break ground on the $43-million project, which includes a 15,000-square-foot library, a multi-modal street, and parking facilities.

The facility will replace the current library in Sage Hill which, at 1,700-square-feet, is one of the library’s smallest branches; it opened in 2017 as a temporary space.

“It was a small library that was just meant to fill the gaps until the new Symons Valley library opened,” said Calgary Public Library CEO Sarah Meilleur. “It is packed. This library and the users of this library circulated over 180,000 books last year; this is a community of readers.”

The $43-million project is set to be complete in mid-2028 and comes after years of advocacy from the community.

According to Ward 2 Coun. Jennifer Wyness, the project was deprioritized when she was first elected in 2021 and required significant work to demonstrate the value it would have to the communities of Sage Hill, Kincora, Sherwood, Nolan Hill and Evanston.

Wyness said building amenities for new neighbourhoods in her ward remains a challenge.

“We just don’t have the services. I do not have the transit, I do not have the libraries, to meet the growth of people choosing to live in the suburbs,” Wyness said. “Building a library like this allows us to show that we have not forgotten about where people are choosing to live.”

According to city officials, Sage Hill is one of Calgary’s fastest-growing areas and is one of more than 40 new communities in various stages of development on the city’s outskirts.

Despite recent announcements about Calgary Transit in the area, some who live in the area said the services and amenities still haven’t caught up to the thousands of new residents.

“It would be nice to see infrastructure while they do their planning,” Inge Kelly told Global News. “At least plan for it, not 10 or 12 years down the road.”

David Cooper, principal at Leading Mobility, said the challenge of increasing the level of services and amenities isn’t a new issue for neighbourhoods on the city’s outskirts, and it isn’t unique to Calgary.

Cooper said developers build the core infrastructure like water pipes and roads but city services take longer to catch up due to constraints for operating funds in the city budget.

“We’re good at putting in the infrastructure so that the area can function but there’s always been a lag in getting the city services that Calgarians expect in these new communities because it’s costly,” he said.

According to the city, there are a number of a new projects underway to address the gap including the Rocky Ridge Athletic Park, as well as the Belmont Fieldhouse and Library, as well as a library and fire station in Walden.

Catching up with the backlog is part of the city’s $50-billion infrastructure gap, Calgary mayor Jeromy Farkas said Wednesday, in which which he has vowed council will begin addressing during the next four-year budget.

Farkas said there will be “hard decisions” during budget talks in November to ensure service levels meet the needs.

“There’s a term that I think Calgarians are going to get used to from this council in the next four-year budget: capital velocity,” he told Global News. “How do we get these plans, these strategies, these hopes off the shelf and shovels in the ground as soon as possible? That’s job number one.”

The mayor noted city council will also need to find ways to grow the city in “a more even way” to address some of the root causes of the infrastructure gap.

He said Calgary’s growth has historically been through “starts, stops and spurts.”

“In the seventies, there were a lot of rec centres and libraries built and then nothing was built for a good 15 to 20 years. What that meant is the bill came due for maintenance on all of these facilities simultaneously,” Farkas said. “It’s about smoothing out these major facilities so it’s not feast and famine, but we’re gradually chipping away at the deficit.”

stories.title: Two people charged after woman assaulted, bystanders intervene: Police
stories.summary: Woodstock police say their investigation determined she had been sexually assaulted and assaulted by a person known to her.
stories.author: Free Press staff
stories.content:
A London man is charged with sexual assault and aggravated assault after an incident in Woodstock that left a woman seriously injured, police say.

Officers were called at about 4 p.m. on Wednesday to the area of King Street and Wellington Street South following a report of an incident, Woodstock police said.

Police said officers found a woman with injuries, adding that their investigation determined she had been sexually assaulted and assaulted by a person known to her. Bystanders intervened and helped the woman, police said. During that intervention, a man was assaulted by “members of the public,” police said.

A 35-year-old London man is charged with aggravated assault and sexual assault, Woodstock police said.

A second man, 29, from Woodstock is charged with assault with a weapon and possession of a weapon for a dangerous purpose, Woodstock police said.

The woman was taken to hospital for treatment of serious injuries, police said.

Police are asking anyone with information to contact Woodstock police at 519-537-2323 or Crime Stoppers at 1-800-222-Tips (8477) .

Windsor police are searching for a man accused of throwing a lit cigarette at a 15-year-old girl, sexually assaulting her and following her in a minivan as she tried to get away.

Police received a report about the assault Monday. The incident happened the previous day in the 1100 block of Parent Avenue.

Police said the girl was sitting on a public bench near Parent Avenue and Riverside Drive East when a man she didn’t know approached her.

Investigators said the man spat toward the girl and threw a lit cigarette that struck her ankle. He then “touched the youth in a sexual manner as she repeatedly pushed his hands away.”

The girl took a photo of the man before getting into a relative’s vehicle and leaving.

Police said the man followed them in an older-model blue minivan until the girl’s relative was able to lose him.

Police described the man as white, 30 to 40 years old and tall. He was wearing a black hoodie with red and grey colouring. He is wanted for assault with a weapon, sexual assault and sexual interference.

Anyone with information is asked to contact the Windsor police Child Abuse and Sexual Assault Unit or Crime Stoppers.

– With files from The Windsor Star

stories.title: ‘Father of Nunavut’ challenges territory’s refusal to pay for his housing, home care in Iqaluit
stories.summary: The Nunavut government was previously funding John Amagoalik’s higher living costs in an Ottawa long-term care home
stories.author: Kristy Kirkup
stories.content:
John Amagoalik, often called the Father of Nunavut, has filed an application for judicial review in the Nunavut Court of Justice over the territorial government’s refusal to pay for his at-home care and housing.

Mr. Amagoalik, a former politician in his late 70s, is credited for his involvement in the creation of the territory in April, 1999.

He and his legal team are challenging the government’s refusal to provide Mr. Amagoalik with home care and housing in Iqaluit, even though it was willing to pay double the cost for long-term care access more than 2,000 kilometres away in Ottawa.

In February, 2025, Mr. Amagoalik had surgery at the Qikiqtani General Hospital in Iqaluit, where his right leg was partially amputated.

He was transferred from the hospital to Embassy West Senior Living, a long-term care home in Ottawa that offers care to patients under a contract with the Government of Nunavut’s health department.

In his affidavit filed on Monday, Mr. Amagoalik said he did not “knowingly consent to being moved to Embassy West on a permanent basis.”

Mr. Amagoalik returned home to Iqaluit in June, after writing a letter to Nunavut’s health minister describing his deep desire “to live out my final days with my family in the territory I fought to create.”

But it was a trio of advocates that included Anne Crawford of Iqaluit, Steve Kelliher of Victoria and Mark Stiles of Ottawa, who teamed up to support the Amagoalik family. They reached out to friends and former colleagues to help establish a care plan for Mr. Amagoalik.

They also used donations to help pay for medical assessments, equipment, supplies and daily home care from personal support workers in Iqaluit.

Mr. Amagoalik and his supporters were hopeful his return to Nunavut’s capital could pave the way for other elders from the territory to return home from Embassy West.

More than 60 Inuit live at the long-term care residence because the territory does not have enough long-term care beds and specialized supports.

Ms. Crawford, Mr. Kelliher and Mr. Stiles said they met with Heather Hair, Nunavut’s assistant deputy minister of health, ON July 14 and expressed to her that the territory’s health department needed to assume responsibility for Mr. Amagoalik’s continued care.

Although they said that Ms. Hair expressed a desire to look into all possible means to support Mr. Amagoalik’s long-term care needs, they received a letter in August that said the government would provide a maximum of two hours of personal support care a week.

They also learned the territory would not assume Mr. Amagoalik’s housing costs of about $2,000 a month.

stories.title: CBC gauges awareness, important issues for city elections at Fanshawe College
stories.summary: https://youtu.be/eg6rSM7JDMk The normal buzz of the Forwell Hall was there as usual: Students bustling about, ...
stories.author: Curtis Stokman
stories.content:
The normal buzz of the Forwell Hall was there as usual: Students bustling about, hurrying from place to place, perhaps stopping to sit at a nearby table for lunch or peruse a small kiosk selling assorted toys and keychains. People stopped, talked, looked around, and then went back about their business.

That was until another kiosk, one with a phone mounted on a tripod in front of a banner emblazoned with the CBC logo, caught their eye.

CBC News London was at Forwell Hall on Thursday, Sept. 17 from 11 a.m. until 2 p.m., interacting with students and finding answers to key questions regarding the awareness of students about the municipal elections in London and the issues that matter to them. Hala Ghonaim, the Community Engagement Producer with CBC News across Ontario, explained that they were on a fact-finding mission.

“We’re doing this for a lot of CBC newsrooms across Ontario,” she said.

CBC reporter Kendra Seguin speaking with a student at the ‘Speaker’s Corner’ in Forwell Hall. The CBC hoped to learn what issues in the municipal elections matter most to students. Photo by: Curtis Stokman

Beside the kiosk itself was a ‘Speaker’s Corner’, where students could be filmed answering questions about issues in the city election. If they declined that option, students could instead fill out a survey, and no matter what they chose they could grab a CBC-themed tote bag, pens, and other items as souvenirs.

“We decided to also go the extra mile,” Ghonaim said.

Lya Skinner and Eve Brandael-McKay, both students in the Fine Art Foundations program at Fanshawe, said that the giveaway items were what attracted them to the kiosk.

“I saw a spork on the [kiosk],” said Skinner. “It really catches your eye.”

The free items were simply the first step, though. Before long, both Skinner and Brandael-McKay were speaking with CBC reporter Kendra Seguin on the issues that mattered the most to them in the city. Both cited the affordability crisis and London’s unemployment rate, which currently sits at 8.7 per cent according to Statistics Canada , as being important.

Ghonaim said that affordability and cost of living were the major issue for most students.

“Another issue that’s been raised is also transit… getting from Point A to Point B is taking a really long time, so they’d like their elected officials to do something about that.”

Ghonaim also said that while students seemed to know what issues were important to them, awareness of the city elections was mixed.

“This could look like… they know there’s a municipal election coming up,” she said. “but they’re unsure when voting day is or where to go to vote.”

For Skinner and Brandael-McKay, this was their first time hearing about the elections, which speaks to the trend in London of a lack of youth voter engagement.

Even so, after stepping in front of the camera for the CBC and receiving their free pens and disposable cutlery, Skinner and Brandael-McKay

Tote bags at the CBC kiosk. Items such as these were offered to Fanshawe students who spoke to the reporters. Photo by: Curtis Stokman both believed the kiosk was raising awareness of the elections.

“There’s still so much local stuff you could actually get into,” said Brandael-McKay. “Just spread the word.”

Ghonaim added that while spreading awareness wasn’t their specific goal, students at Fanshawe were receptive to them.

“They really have a lot to say,” she explained. “We’re happy to be talking to students.”

stories.title: Former director of B.C. Conservatives hired private investigator, lawyer alleges
stories.summary: Legislators critical of Leader Kerry-Lynne Findlay claim they were targeted
stories.author: Wolfgang Depner
stories.content:
British Columbia Conservative leader Kerry-Lynne Findlay said Thursday she was “not going anywhere” on another day of tumult for the Opposition, roiled by revelations that a private eye had been hired to look into her critics and calls for her to resign at an overnight caucus meeting.

Lawyer Bruce Hallsor, a King’s counsel, said the party’s former executive director Elaine Allan had hired the investigator, although Hallsor would not name him or those he investigated.

Allan, who served briefly as executive director of the party until being relieved of her duties last month, did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

But legislators critical of Findlay, including current caucus member Claire Rattée and Brennan Day, who recently quit the party, said they were targeted by the private eye.

“I am deeply troubled by these allegations,” said Rattée, who issued a 1,000-word critique of Findlay’s leadership this week. She said on social media that the private investigator May have violated her privacy.

B.C. Conservative Leader Kerry-Lynne Findlay vows to stay as party faces turmoil

Day said in a text message that being among the MLAs targeted for investigation “only reinforces why I chose to part company with the Kerry-Lynne Findlay Conservatives.”

“It is impossible to point your guns outward at the government when you’re too busy pointing them inward at your own caucus,” he said.

Findlay had earlier acknowledged a lawyer’s investigation into the claims about the private eye, while denying knowledge of the activities and vowing not to stand aside amid speculation that an early election call by Premier David Eby is imminent.

Nine legislators have quit the official Opposition caucus since Findlay took over in May, with defectors complaining about her leadership, the party’s direction, and an ideological push that one of them said was a “hard right.”

The Canadian Press confirmed from sources that two Conservative legislators asked Findlay to resign during a caucus meeting on Wednesday night.

The next morning, Findlay told the audience at the Union of British Columbia Municipalities convention in Vancouver that those who have quit the caucus are welcome to have a conversation about coming back, but “it has to happen now,” because Eby could call an election “as early as tomorrow.”

“Twenty-seven thousand party members voted for me as a leader who will collaborate with anyone, from any background or political alliances … who share our common-sense vision for change,” she said.

Findlay’s speech before about 100 political leaders drew sparse applause, except from some of her caucus members sitting in the front row.

She called the prospect of a snap election being called by Eby a “cynical move.”

“So, the premier will impose on British Columbians a costly election two years early, trample on the by-election he just called, and he knows I was about to win,” she said.

Findlay is campaigning in the Abbotsford-Mission by-election, scheduled for Sept. 26, in a bid to gain a seat in the B.C. legislature.

She addressed reporters after the speech, saying the Conservatives were a “young party” that was still feeling “growing pains.”

She said her team was excited about “probably heading into a provincial election very soon.”

Findlay, who was flanked by legislators from her 28-member caucus, said after her speech that she was open to talking to anyone who wants to rejoin the party, and she had been speaking to a number of former caucus members.

She said she didn’t think it was her leadership style that forced the members of her caucus to quit, but she took responsibility for the defections.

“There have been adjustments, there have been changes, and what is really more important is, do we have a working, fighting team that’s cohesive? And here we are. I’m proud of them all, and we are moving forward together.”

Eby, who is due to address the convention on Friday, said Wednesday that he told NDP legislators they need to be “election ready,” amid disruption posed by the trade war with the United States.

He did not offer any details about its timing.

The Conservatives responded Thursday by launching an “emergency” fundraising drive.

The party sent out an e-mail launching the effort, saying it wanted funds in the next 48 hours to roll out digital and print advertisements, to distribute voter messaging and to mobilize volunteers.

A provincial vote could overlap with next month’s municipal elections, sparking a rebuke from the association representing municipalities.

Cori Ramsay, president of the Union of British Columbia Municipalities, said in a statement that it was incumbent on provincial leaders to uphold the principle of separate periods for local and provincial elections to avoid distractions for voters.

“At a time when B.C. is facing considerable economic and social uncertainty, overlapping elections would be a disservice to our citizens,” she said. “One hopes that provincial parties would temper election rhetoric as local campaigns are set to begin, but the spiral of speculation continues.”

The formal campaign period for municipal elections starts Sept. 19 with a general vote on Oct. 17.

He did not offer any details about its timing.
The Conservatives responded Thursday by launching an “emergency” fundraising drive.
The party sent out an e-mail launching the effort, saying it wanted funds in the next 48 hours to roll out digital and print advertisements, to distribute voter messaging and to mobilize volunteers.
A provincial vote could overlap with next month’s municipal elections, sparking a rebuke from the association representing municipalities.

Cori Ramsay, president of the Union of British Columbia Municipalities, said in a statement that it was incumbent on provincial leaders to uphold the principle of separate periods for local and provincial elections to avoid distractions for voters.

“At a time when B.C. is facing considerable economic and social uncertainty, overlapping elections would be a disservice to our citizens,” she said. “One hopes that provincial parties would temper election rhetoric as local campaigns are set to begin, but the spiral of speculation continues.”
The formal campaign period for municipal elections starts Sept. 19 with a general vote on Oct. 17.
